these are minro things that are being adressed.

In all, a really-excellent game.  Definitely recommended.  I'd buy it again in a heartbeat.
The graphics are really enjoyable, and ran at a comfortable 60+ fps on my i5-3570k + 970gtx.  I had been worried reading all of the other reviews that my system was going to be incapable of handling this game at a high-graphics setting; but all the worrying was for naught.
My first playthrough, at a comfortble, immersive pace took about 12 hours.  I bought the game on the Steam sale, so it's a reasonable cost for the length.
The first-person perspective was fantastic.  I didn't miss the classic 3rd-person perspective of other resident evil games.  The first-person perspective made it more suspenseful, I believe.
The storyline is surprisingly good (as some of the resident evil storylines can be a bit incoherent).  I certainly wasn't expecting the plot twists it provides, though they do make for a more believable, enjoyable experience...tying-together much of what you learned beforehand.
Some people argued that it's relatively small, intimate setting and first-person perspective made it not "Resident Evil" enough.  After playing it all the way through, I'm comfortable saying that this argument comes from people who probably haven't played it at all.  It's definitely "Resident Evil."
This was the best Resident Evil I have ever played. The last Resident Evil I enjoyed was RE4. Worth the full price. I hope the next  RE will be as good as this one.

Among the Sleep is horror type adventure game where you are a 2 year old boy who has got a brand new talking bear for his birthday. You work your way through progressively harder and longer puzzles to find your mother who has gone missing.
I really enjoyed the atmosphere set by the lighting and sound in Among the Sleep. It is on par with Amnesia in that sense. Although it's not as scary as Amnesia, there are still times where it had me pausing the game for me to catch my breath because I was wetting myself.
For some reason I couldn't get my controller to work with this game, which is a shame since it is the perfect game to use with a controller, but there isn't anything wrong with mouse and keyboard controls, ever.
I'd say wait for this game to go on sale before you pick it up, it's quite short and the £14,99 is a bit much for a game which is only about three hours long.
Rating: 8/10

AirMech is a mix of both simple 2d pvp and RTS style unit manipulation.   You choose the assortment of units you will be using for a particular battle with various advantages / disadvantages / costs / tradeoffs / etc...  There are multiple strategies that are viable, so it doesn't seem like there is merely one right path (though there are a few better ones).  Your command unit can similarly by selected for various tradeoffs, and then buffed up and modified with its item configuration.  This is where you may start to bump into the 'Free to Play' nuisance, as paid players will have more and better options to work with.  The premium currency is completely blocked from your usage until you buy some directly, so although it shows that you are earning some over time, you can't actually use any of it until you pay (so it is simply a carrot that grows).  AirMech mostly suffers from a limited player base, probably caused by its vaguely annoying F2P experience.  Its worth trying out, particularly with a friend, but it is unlikely to affix itself to your frequently play roster.

You can go from kicking♥♥♥♥♥on a "boss" to immediately being taken out without ever landing a punch by a random npc right around the corner. Or the next time you come to the same area the reverse could happen. In addition to this it is pretty much impossible to determine how hard any given NPC will be. The closest you can come to is maybe recognizing the same NPC model and remembering that that guy was hard last time (but then this time the randomizer could have calculated differently and it could be completely different). I don't mind hard games. I don't mind losing. The issue here is that the level of feedback you get before, and more importantly after, you lose if pretty much none. The only way to get better, to learn more, is to fight, but if you lose you get nothing. So unless you get a nice randomizer roll you're screwed.
In the end, perhaps I just really really suck at fighting games (they haven't been my go to games in the past), but even if I suck it should at least be somewhat possible to figure out what I need to do to get better. In in case of Absolver the amount of random is just too much to work into your improvement plan.
TLDR: If you are really, really good at fighting games you may get along well with this - but if you are hoping for an entertaining jaunt into the world of fighting that helps you develop and improve you best move on.

Absolver is an amazingly innovative and immersive brawler with an astonishing amount of customization. The world is small, but well crafted, visuals are breathtakingling beautiful  and combat is seamless while sporting some of the best animations I have ever seen. I have been waiting for a very long time for something like this and on almost all fronts Slowclap delivers.
The campaign is short which is not much of an issue. I wouldn't say its as short as many other reviewers seem to claim, though if you run through it at a neck breaking pace, the game's campaign can be finished within 5-6 hours. This is not an issue and I very much enjoyed my time slowly exploring and getting in every brawl I possibly could. But after beating the campaign the player is left with little more to do than learn new moves, level up and pvp. Normally this would be absolutly acceptable as the combat is so well implemented and enjoyable that beating up badies and players alike never really gets old. The problem lies with the servers.
The servers are bad, yes, I'm sure you've even read that on here. But I cannot stress enough just how unforgivably bad they are. Living in the US I drop constantly. A friend of mine who has been playing along side me spends more time offline than connected and has never been able to connect to me for a co-op session. The games formal competitive mode which offers 1v1 combat is a blast, except I have never once been able to finish a match. In a good match, both players will drop before the 3 rounds are over. In a bad match I will be met with a load screen that seemingly lasts an eternity and is impressivly resistant to Alt+F4. This wouldn't be so bad as even the PVE content is quite challenging and engaging, but unfortunatly some content is locked behind successful competitive matches leaving players unable to progress to new boss fights or start a martial arts school of their own.
If the above information does not bother you than I highly suggest picking this game up as it is one of the most innovative experiences provided in a world where we seem to be locked into medicore sequals and redundant gameplay. As for me, I feel quite burned by a brilliant game which leans heavily on a PVP focus marred by servers that would be considered unnaceptable even in early access.
I will continue to press on and hope for the better. As for now I'm going to leave this with a thumbs down until the issue is resolved.

Fun, intricate, and engaging combat in a beautiful semi-open world. The nature of the combat deck system allows for an absurd number of combinations and subsequent playstyles, allowing the combat to always feel fresh. Many fighting games are about having prior knowledge of "the matchup" between your character and your opponent's character. Absolver chooses to move away from this trend, only giving you knowledge of your opponent's options once they have used them. This creates a PvP system where you must learn on the fly, actively looking for weaknesses in your opponent's strategy. Properly observing your opponent to find patterns and responding accordingly is extremely satisfying and gives an incredible depth and skill-cap to the combat. If you're a fan of PvP, this game is a must.
PvE, however, is lacking in the game's current state. The story can be completed in mere hours, and combat vs the AI is much more predictable and same-y than combat vs a human player. It is similar to Dark Souls or Breath of the Wild in that it does very little handholding, and gives you a general objective while leaving the player to make their own progression order. It is quite clear that the story serves mostly as a very flexible tutorial and a starting boost to level up a few times and learn a few moves.
Lastly, it's worth noting that the game is half the price of a AAA games, and the devs have promised consistent updates to freshen up the experience. While the game's servers were a little rough on launch, it seems much of the trouble has cleared up now. I have had a ton of fun with this game even with the few hours I have put into it at the time of writing the review, and sincerely hope the future of this game turns out as bright as it looks.

Call of Juarez®: Bound in Blood is the second game in the series and story-wise it's a prequel to the first game. It is a story of a younger Ray McCall and his brothers Thomas and William.
Like its predecessor, the game is a first-person shooter with the Western setting. And like the first Call of Juarez it has a captivating story, a little "dark" atmosphere, two playable characters with two different playstyles (and this time - the ability to freely choose your character for a given episode, except for the first two "tutorial" episodes and the one near the endgame) and lots of gun-blazing action.
What I am going to say is that this game is in my opinion the best Call of Juarez game and one of the best western and FPS games I've ever played. Almost all the flaws from the first game are gone here, Bound in blood runs smoothly, has beautiful graphics, great atmosphere and soundtrack, cool plot that will keep you in tension for the whole game, epic finale that will probably make you shed a small manly tear, and two badass characters to play.
About the characters: Ray McCall plays almost the same as he did in the first game being able to dual-wield pistols and throw dynamites, although personality-wise here he is not a preacher and acts like a total badass. His brother Thomas is a little similar to Billy Candle - he is the agile guy of this game, he can do some lasso swinging, he can use throwing knives for stealthy kills (although you won't need to be stealthy in this game as much as it was needed in the first) and he can use a bow with arrows. There are still not that many weapons in the game, but there is definitely more, than it was in the first CoJ, and you can buy upgraded versions of the same weapon.
In the end, there is really nothing serious I can point out as bad things, I was completely satisfied with the game. If you liked the first CoJ, this is a must. If you like Western theme this is a must. If you want a cool story and a decent FPS game this is a must.

This game was really a big let down for me. Back in the day in school I've heard of the great new shooter Far Cry. Everybody was so hyped about this.
I finally played it since I got it in a game collection. I immediately noticed some things that really bugged me. But the real bad things came later throughout the game.
First of all this game clearly sets the difficulty level high. So even on Normal difficulty I experienced quite skilled enemies with XRay vision and a not really clear priority list. You got to parties fighting each other and you, the Tridgen and the Mercenaries. They are in an all out war together, but once you just peek around the corner everything doesn't matter until you are dead, the teamed up on me every time, which made it really really hard to get past some choke points.
The next thing is the far sight, which was highly praised by the developers, seemed to be only for the landscape (which really is beatiful, good job there). The enemies were faded out over long distances, which didn't seem to bother them at all to snipe me down with an M4, while I HAD to zoom in with the sniper to just be able to see them. This thing alone cost me about 2 hours in whole.
Then came the glitches. Having two armies standing in a room, fighting each other, while staying back in order to thin them out worked like a charm. But once I entered some specific rooms the dead where still standing making it almost impossible to figure out the real survivors before getting shot. But this just adds to all the other things I encountered, like, invincible enemies to a certain trigger, recurring sounds once you step over the tirgger again, stuck sounds which sounds like someone just keeps shooting even so you got him already, strange rackdoll effects which block you view etc etc. the list goes on and on.
That wouldn't be much of a problem, since many game encounter those bugs, even so not many have almost all of them , but once you are dead you have to start from the last autosave which can be about 30 minutes in the past. I had to play for 2 hours to get past a certain point in the river chapter, since you have to take out about 40 guys with choppers, patrol boats and rocket launcher, without having the game savin even once.
The story itself is quite what you expect from a shooter this scale, but the cutscenes always cut out a second to early so you sometimes miss the last word.
Well after all this game is quite old, so maybe I judge to hard, but I definetily can not recommend this game to anyone who is no masochist.
Finished in 11 hours on normal, which could have been done in about 6 hours without the problems above...

NEW REVIEW:  Many of the camera problems, I am happy to say, have been eliminated in the current updates.  The campaign is here and it looks like it will be a lot of fun.  The game garners a resounding "YES" from me now as I actually feel like the game is playable in its current state.  The only comment I would like to pass on to the developers is that the lack of a complete tutorial places the new player in front of an overwhelming amount of choices and options.  I believe a comprehensive tutorial that isn't just a text box would benefit this game greatly.  Warhammer and Mordheim fans, you won't be disappointed.
PAST REVIEW: I will say that for Mordheim: City of the Damned captures the feel of its namesake very well, providing a gritty skirmish experience set in the Warhammer world.  However no amount of "feel" or "essence" can cover up the fact that this game is obviously still very, very, VERY much still in Early Access.  The constant shifting of camera views, the clipping of the camera into random objects during combat "cut scenes" and inability to simply have an overhead view where I can control my warband kept me from completely enjoying the game.  Die hard Warhammer fans will enjoy the scenery and the little comments about Chaos in the loading screens, but the average gamer will not find much to thrill.  I appreciate that this is Early Access, but I believe that there is such a thing as too early of an Early Access.  The game overall garners a "No" vote from me, and I feel like I'd have to wait for a Mordheim: Chaos Edition to truly knock out all of the bugs.  Personally: a dissappointing purchase.

I must say that I was impressed that the developers have stuck to it, addressed the problems I've previously called out and made compelling content for which I CAN recommend this game.
The warband management was cleaned up and it mostly makes sense.  There are some small UI things that I'm sure will be optimized.  The charcter development is a grind, but others have mentioned going (essentially) bankrupt, I've not had that problem.
The maiming system is fun, but frustrating.  I had a character I got quite attached to get rekt by a daemon boss and ended up with missing an eye, a cracked skull and lost her leg.  So now she passes a 'stupidity' check maybe 1-2 turns for the who game and moves maaaaaaaaaaybe 5m but I just can't bring myself to fire her... so the character development is definitely a hook. (I've been bringing this dead weight to increase her intelligence, but it doesn't seem to make much of a difference).
You do need to utilze the tactical map to plan out your moves to ensure you're getting the most resource/loot possible.  The deployment definitely needs work, it is confusing to understand WHERE you are deploying (something I'm sure will be addressed).
Additionally, I had problems with game crashing but fixed it by running it in windowed mode.  Load times are still long, but something the devs have called out as a area of improvement.  Previously I had issues with getting characters stuck,  I've put another 10-12 more hours since the latest content patch and have not had and gameplay issues.
I look forward to see what other directions they take, but I'm pretty into the game thus far.  The campaign really adds a lot.  Great job, keep it up.  (and maybe at some point add some DLC for new factions?)

A spooky playground by a vivid imagination. We may not recall what it was like when we were two years old but at times, during the game, I could "almost" feel the uneasyness and unsettling moments we had when we were just a little child.
So basically, it is a game that comprises of a playground mostly by night and that is usually a good location, but all that happens in it is a prolonged fetch quest to solve a physics puzzle. This is what irritated me the most.
The foes in this game were mostly proper for the game progression.
PROS:
+Interesting perspective as a little child (everything is big in the game world!).
+Visuals are mostly well done.
+Excellent sound designs, music ambiance and voice acting are decent.
+Never felt so safe hugging a teddy bear!
+Free Prologue DLC.
CONS:
-Lenght of the game is VERY short. 3 hours at best including the prologue DLC (No replay value).
-Big fetch quest.
-Underwhelming ending.
OVERALL:
Interesting title that you can play in one night setting. I'd advise to get this on a sale 'cause 21.99$ is steep for a 3h long game, with basic interactions.
RECOMMENDATION:
Game itself ain't scary, at least to me, and may gives you a few scares at certain areas but overall, it's a pretty straightforward game to fetch items so you can move on to the next level. The strong appeal of the game is the point of view from a young child. I don't think it was exploited to the fullest so I do hope if a sequel get's made, it adds more diversity on the scenario and missions!
I recommend for those who are intrigued in the premise of the game; "young child" exploring house and venturing the areas while seeing things!
Just don't expect "OUTLAST" scare factor!

Sooooo.... I, personally, hate kids.
They're just pooping, crying sacks of meat for the first few years of their lives, and then after that they grow into spoiled brats, obnoxious teens, and potentially crazy adults...
HOWEVER, that's all beside the point as Among The Sleep, complete with "goo goo ga ga" baby sounds as ambiance, is a very good game. I picked it up while it was on sale and I certainly don't regret it. Sometimes there are glitches in lighting and movement is stiff, but the tale it tells is enthralling and dark. Without spoiling it for you, I highly suggest you look up no plot/storyline before playing the game -- I didn't and it opened up about 50 unforeseen storylines all made up in my head. Any time I was wandering around unsure of where to go, my mind was stewing up this beautiful schmorgesborg of storylines, making literally every second entertaining.
I've tried Slenderman games and a few other "atmospheric horror" games, but Among The Sleep is the only one I've been able to get through 100%. Complete with frequent "AH OH **** OH MY GOD GET AWAY FROM ME OH ****," there are plenty of instances of jump scares while not  being overwhelming -- the anxiety inducing wait is far worse than the scare, of course, but isn't that why you're looking at this game anyway?
The really scary part, however, is, even though you're PLAYING a two year old, you tend to feel more like you're PROTECTING a two year old -- this is a clever tactic that I've yet to see in any other game (mostly because I've never played a game from the perspective of an infant). Though the game runs extremely short, comparatively speaking, I really support the length the developers took it to -- it's certainly not too long, and they keep their story "short and sweet," so to speak. They get across everything they need to in just a few hours of gaming.
So if a short but very good atmospheric horror game is something you're interested in playing, pick this title up. You won't regret it.
Oh yeah. Also, you get to brag about being a two year old... Do people brag about that?..

Beneath all the features and complex game mechanics, Empire remains a mix of turn-based empire building and real-time strategy, these two elements kept separate but affecting each other throughout the game. In the one half, you're developing your cities, raising and moving armies and sending out agents to spy, sabotage or steal technology on your behalf. You also have to maintain diplomatic relations with allies and rivals, steer scientific progress to develop new military, social and technological assets, and ensure that your economy remains headed in the right direction. When conflict rears its ugly head - and inevitably it will - it's time for the other half of the game to take over. This is the 3D real-time strategy that you'll remember from previous Total War games or the BBC programme Time Commanders; a fast-paced, realistic simulation of warfare featuring dozens of units and thousands of men on the field at any one time.
It's a mix designed to satisfy would-be Bismarcks and would-be Napoleons, and the game cleverly allows you to play the way you like best. Handling both portions gives you the full, rich Total War experience, but if you want to let the AI handle the management of the economy and the society, you can. If you want to let battles resolve themselves and concentrate on the political drama, then that's fine too. If you want, you don't even have to spend a second in the central 'Grand Campaign'; you can just set up your own battles or play the pre-defined scenarios, and just enjoy the sounds of booming cannon, musket-fire and clashing steel.
It is totally worth the money!

Holy moly. I don't play story-focused games on hard mode because I want to feel like a master at it, but Mafia II is clearly an older third-person cover-and-shoot-em game that has made me rage quit from its ruthless difficulty on Hard. The beginning chapters are easy, but once you reach the last couple, you're practically stabbing yourself over why you're continuing at this point.
I came into this game with the expectation that I would be able to become a Mafia Boss, kinda like how Saints' Row has it.  Do a couple missions here and there, gain influence, and the Mafia Boss gets food poisoning, riding down to your hands kinda style. Even the story pointed at the thought of it, but no, you get saddled down to the linearity of shallow Italian stereotypes followed by side characters even your main character jeers towards.
**
It definitely feels true to its style, and has a lovely charm to it, but if you choose hard mode, be prepared for unskippable cutscenes followed by enemy AI that take more shots and fire more powerful shots. Even your friendly AI get shot within the next five seconds leaving you with the revolver to headshot them. Some things that I liked while in cover was that the cover is destructable. You can't stay in one place forever, but you also can't sprint during that state, which gets really annoying when you don't have much place to breathe.
There are quite a few things that it does differently from our Saints Row / GTA counter-part, and while it's nice to have, I don't think it necessarily compels others to be the reason why one would get this game. Again, the game is more of a linear feel. Unless you can somehow wedge yourself outside of what you're usually doing in a mission, Not doing the mission may actually feel less satisfying. At least, that's what I thought when I tried going on a killing rampage.

This game left an important legacy, I'll give it that. It was one of the better-in-class during its day, but ultimately it hasn't stood the test of time. It's not a bad game, but it's not great either. I understand the "cult" following - it was and still is a beautiful game in its own right, the levels are quite large and sprawling, it's got tons of content, and it has a 90s pulp craziness about it.
Honestly though, it's just not a well designed game. The movement is too sluggish for the level sizes, vehicles handle fairly bad, the ai are really stupid but equipped with incredible vision and aim, and it's unjustifiably difficult at times. I started to wonder why it was such a mess until I realized it was Crytek's first game. Ubisoft Montreal has improved the series dramatically, lack of innovation in the present titles aside. If you're coming from Far Cry 3-4 or even Far Cry 2, this game is completely different aside from some general level design motifs.
Don't get me wrong, It's absolutely worth the current 10 dollar asking price and it can be quite a lot of fun, but do yourself a favor (if you haven't already played this) and dont treat it as a game to be played through to completion. It's not worth your time and energy. Just treat it as a fun FPS sandbox to play around in. Once the mutants show up it all goes down hill pretty fast (actually somewhat slowly since god damn, this game seems long). There are some mods to check out too, so if the free form open-ish world gameplay wasn't enough, theres that.

Far Cry 1 is definitely on my list of top 5 favorite shooters of all time. Graphics still look amazing even up to today's standards. This was the first PC game I ever played. It started my entire PC gaming career, and for that reason I have to give this game extra credit. Far Cry brings back a lot of memories and nostalgia whenever I hear the sound effects and environment of the jungle. What I've always loved most about this game is the sound and "feel" of the guns. I've played a lot of FPS, but Far Cry has a way of making each and every weapon equally satisfying and fun to use. The physics are really well done. The hit detection makes your kills feel very satisfying. This is my main game that I can always fall back on even to this day no matter how old it is.
This game will challenge you. The AI are tough. If you're new to this game then it is no walk in the park. The "Medium" difficulty alone was rough my first time around. I still have my retail copy of this game. With enough experience and improvement I've managed to move up to the higher difficulties in campaign. It's not one of those games where you can jump right into the highest difficulty and expect to do well. To this day I haven't even dared to try "Realism".
This game blends in the role of stealth and action. Most scenarios require you to think of different tactics in order to take out each and every enemy one by one instead of the typical "run and gun" shooter.
Adding new singleplayer Mods and Maps will greatly enhance the fun of this game.
is where you need to go to download new levels and content for this game. You just have to know where to put these files in the FarCry directory because this game doesn't support Steam Workshop unfortunately. There are also map editing tools you can download to create your own single player levels.
The sequels to Far Cry are completely different compared to this one; story wise and gameplay wise. I'll always prefer the original Far Cry over the newer ones any day. This is the real Far Cry experience. I always thought it was disappointing how the sequels do not continue the story of the main character, Jack Carver. He is without question the true protagonist to Far Cry above any of the newer playable characters in the sequels.
Every FPS veteran should know of this game and played it before at least once. If you haven't, I highly recommend buying it. Crytek has developed some of the best games of all time, such as the Crysis series, and Ryse: Son of Rome. Aside from that, it's too bad Crytek abandoned Far Cry and didn't develop the sequels.
I wouldn't feel too skeptical about some of the negative reviews. Do not hesitate to buy this classic. Highly recommend. 10/10.

#No spoilers, relatively unbiased
Abstract; Short campaign with little replay value, but a good concept - Think Amnesia with a baby protagonist.
Full; Among the Sleep begins strong with an immersive environment and mysterious backstory, however it struggles to maintain this as the story progresses and the dreamworld becomes surprisingly dull. You take the role as a 2 year old struggling with family issues which manifest inside the dreamworld you spend the majority of the games inside. To complete the game you will have to solve basic puzzles and overcome distressful memories and this can become moderately scary in both atmosphere and shock. The biggest let-down of the game is the very short length (including the dlc) and missed opportunity to explore more issues that may haunt children (aggressive pets, strangers, being lost, etc) leading to the conclusion that the developers ran out of time or ideas. There is a good reveal at the end and playing through the eyes of a confused toddler is a neat concept (and original in games media), however I would not recommend   buying a game with less than 2-3 hours of gameplay.

The appeal of Faster Than Light is the robust gameplay: managing resources, ship to ship combat, and micromanaging crew members in a bid to outrun the Rebel fleet and defeat their Mothership. The graphics are simplistic, but the clean interface conveys a situation clearly at a glance and makes the simple icons mesh into a solid presentation.
A core aspect to the game is its replayability, falling into the 'roguelike' genre. Different encounters and upgrades available encourage different styles of play, in addition to unlocking different ships by completing challenges. And it is this variability that makes journeying to the final battle engaging. Even if you fall short, playing again gives you a fresh take to travel the stars and defeat your foes.

DMC4 is worthy follow up to its excellent predecessor. It may not be as revolutionary but it is an improvement in almost every aspect. The biggest complaint about it is the backtracking that takes place during most of the second half of the game. This is a little overblown though, as the playable character for that part has a different fighting style and the environments have also changed quite a bit. Then again, and while there is a variety of bosses, you will have to fight them again and again which ends up being little bit too much. The PC version of DMC4 is better than the console versions, unlike the troubled port of DMC3. The performance is great and the graphics are nice but not outstanding. The soundtrack takes after DMC3, so it may not be entirely to your liking but even then it shouldn't bother. The plot is passable, it has a few surprises, some funny moments and many well choreographed cut-scenes. Just make sure you have a gamepad - the game can be played with a keyboard but only if you prefer fighting the controls instead of the enemies.

L.A. Cops can probably best be described as an inferior Hotline Miami played in an isometric view.  The game oozes doughnut eating, retro-style cop shows from the eighties through its minimalistic graphics, audio and voice-overs.
Gameplay has been designed to be very simple, choose two cops and arm them with two weapons.  Take control of one character at a time across several crime hotspots at different L.A. themed locations.  There are only two game styles in mind: go stealthly and make arrests; arm up and go rambo!  Completing missions awards experience which can be used to upgrade your squad.
+ Minimalisitc art style suits the concept but will not be to everyones tastes.  Personally I preferred it to HM's retro pixels.
+ Minor RPG elements.  Though you can upgrade particular stats to specialize characters you will only really ever use two.
+ Mission briefing cutscenes add enormously to the overall 80s cop show ambience.  Voice-overs are bang on!
- Not enough missions.  Even if only five or so were added, or the mission length were increased it would be enough.
- Locations are generic with no real differences between location other than were cover is to be found.
- Controls are sometimes flaky in key parts.  The worst is when you press F expecting the focus to switch automatically to the nearest goon but it doesnt and you die.  Die again!  Again, and again!
- Not enough enemy types.  Would have been good to have alot more themed enemies, like gangs, armed robbers etc.
- Last mission and some optional missions are bugged.  They are not saving correctly.  Therefore cannot gain 100% in achievements.
- Shoddy developer support.  Problems not fixed for several months.  Maybe they have gone out of business.  Game looks completed abandoned.
* Missions are almost all linear apart from a few optional ones. Their only purpose is to increase experience.
* Could have done with a few more weapon models or types.
* Soundtrack & game audio is well-made, fits the ambience but its the minimum I'd expect.
* Basic A.I. that relies on speed to defeat players.  Functional at best.
* The alert mechanic works mostly but if you mess-up placement of one character and switch more of the time they will be dead before you can re-act.
* The three difficulty types provide some decent replay value.
LA Cops is a game of two halves.  Gameplay is very limited and simplistic, yet fast-paced and at times it can be fun.  Though its campaign and levels are short, it looks designed for repetitive play.  The speed of the AI on fast PCs is as annoying as it was in Hotline Miami, and loses hands down in terms of style and panache in its use of dialogue and tropes.
If you dont have quick reflexes, this isnt a game for you.  Though in LA Cops the isometric view helped my senses process the situation more easily.  Focusing on the next target is supposed to help but unfortunately its very fiddly to do this on your preferred target, often causing the cops to die.  On the later missions mistakes are fatal.
Suffice to say if you didnt enjoy Hotline Miami, you probably wont enjoy this game.  The developers did add local multi-player after release (maybe more for the console crowd) but even that must have failed to bring enough interest to make the game successful.  Maybe adding a PvP mode and Steam online support would have made this a little more palatable to PC gamers.
L.A. Cops should have been worth a play or two but there just isnt enough and the final missions are broken.  I did enjoy playing some of it but if you want to complete it - its a total waste of money.  Its a shame because if you enjoy fast & frantic, punishing but rewarding gameplay then this may could have been for you.
If you are still not put off, then I would urge caution on how much you spend.  The game's length suggests a much cheaper price than its retailing for.  Its been likely buffed so when it comes sale-time the price will no doubt be reduced to a more reasonable one.  Thats just my opinion of course.

Absolver has a very Dark Souls type gameplay. You have no idea where you're going during your first time playing the game, but you figure it out with more experience you put into it.
Marked Ones and bosses can be very difficult to defeat, depending on your combat style, if you're cooperating with someone, and what level you are.
Your first few hours playing this game is gonna be filled with joy and anger. Joy from the innovation and how cool the combat feels. Anger from constantly getting pummeled by other players and bosses (Dark Souls).
It feels like one of those games where you feel obligated to train yourself, earn more experience before taking on more difficult Marked Ones and bosses.
Absolver is a game that's certainly not for everyone, but for people who are fans of martial arts, people who are drawn to difficult challenges, and people who are willing to put in a lot of time to learn the game.

Holy moly. I don't play story-focused games on hard mode because I want to feel like a master at it, but Mafia II is clearly an older third-person cover-and-shoot-em game that has made me rage quit from its ruthless difficulty on Hard. The beginning chapters are easy, but once you reach the last couple, you're practically stabbing yourself over why you're continuing at this point.
I came into this game with the expectation that I would be able to become a Mafia Boss, kinda like how Saints' Row has it.  Do a couple missions here and there, gain influence, and the Mafia Boss gets food poisoning, riding down to your hands kinda style. Even the story pointed at the thought of it, but no, you get saddled down to the linearity of shallow Italian stereotypes followed by side characters even your main character jeers towards.
**
It definitely feels true to its style, and has a lovely charm to it, but if you choose hard mode, be prepared for unskippable cutscenes followed by enemy AI that take more shots and fire more powerful shots. Even your friendly AI get shot within the next five seconds leaving you with the revolver to headshot them. Some things that I liked while in cover was that the cover is destructable. You can't stay in one place forever, but you also can't sprint during that state, which gets really annoying when you don't have much place to breathe.
There are quite a few things that it does differently from our Saints Row / GTA counter-part, and while it's nice to have, I don't think it necessarily compels others to be the reason why one would get this game. Again, the game is more of a linear feel. Unless you can somehow wedge yourself outside of what you're usually doing in a mission, Not doing the mission may actually feel less satisfying. At least, that's what I thought when I tried going on a killing rampage.

Targeting items to pick up is still incredibly annoying and hard to do, with you needing to be at specific spots, at ground level, and facing specific angles, with the pointer targeting a specific pixels.  Ingame background assets like trashcans and boxes can still be knocked around and get stuck in weird angles, and/or between textures, and can somtimes block your access to things - in one game I was in I actually got trapped and stuck by a bunch of trashcans and had to restart the game.
Actual gameplay has potential, with an interesting setting and overall graphics and gameplay designs.  However all the complaints I had for this game during launch still persist, and I'm guessing won't be fixed at all at this late stage.

Phantasmal is a survival horror roguelike title with Lovecraftian influences, and it's the first game that we've seen on Steam from New Zealand based publisher/developer Eyemobi Ltd. The combination of essentially three gaming genres is a brave, yet unique, step for an up and coming company, especially given the roguelike elements that are thrown into play. Boasting procedurally generated rooms, permadeath, stealth mechanics, along with health and sanity meters, one question begs to be asked; does this amalgamation work well together?
There's a small storyline within Phantasmal, and basically you're a guy looking for his missing aunt. For one reason or another, you've been led to unfathomable depths that continue to grow deeper and deeper as each elevator and staircase plunges you deeper into the heart of madness. Along the way you'll encounter various, and numerous, enemies through randomly generated levels; the further you progress, the more plentiful and deadly your foes will become. Along the way you can pick up weapons such as a spiked bat, wooden plank, and a pistol to fend off the monsters. Your sanity meter will go down if you stare at them for too long with your flashlight on, but if you stand in the dark for a period of time you will also start to go insane. There are sanity pills and health kits scattered sparsely about to help aid you on your journey, along with coins that you can use to buy upgrades from the vendor at the starting area.
From my experience the stealth mechanic doesn't work well at all. Supposedly if you crouch you're silent, and as long as you stay in the dark you're safe. I've had enemies charge at me despite using both of these techniques together. Their AI is also fairly terrible, given that they become stuck on stairs frequently and will run head-long into walls. I'm also pretty certain that I encountered areas with unlimited respawning monsters, and also an invincible foe. I'll also add here that the first trailer for the game (the second that appears on the store page) is very misleading, and is entirely cinematic; it is not at all how the game plays.
Now, let me say that I have an i7 6700k and GTX 1080 combo, along with 16GB of DDR4 3000 RAM; additionally my monitor supports 1080p, 144Hz resolution. For those who aren't tech savvy, basically my rig is on the very high part of high-end; my graphics card in particular is second only to a newer NVIDIA card that released a mere 3 months after my card. I'm not saying this to brag by any means, but how would you feel about buying a game that can't even hit 30 FPS in some areas on a powerful rig? Would you spend $16.99 CAD on a title that struggles to hit even 60 FPS during its core areas? Let's say the graphics are also on low, and special effects are turned off. Comparatively speaking assess your rig against mine, how well do you think yours may fare given that mine cannot sustain a suitable framerate on Phantasmal? And before you ask, yes my drivers are all up to date.
Needless to say I was beyond shocked, since every game I've thrown at my rig has hit 60+ FPS; The Witcher 3 with all settings maxed? Check. Grand Theft Auto V with everything but distance scaling maxed? Yep. How about the new Doom? Blows it out of the water. Metro Last Light Redux? Far Cry Primal? All run beautifully. Since many of the assets and designs are very similar to UNLOVED (a far superior game, I might add for those who're interested), I'm going to assume that Phantasmal runs on the Unreal engine. Though it doesn't matter what engine it runs on since it shouldn't perform this badly, it's especially unacceptable for such a high quality, acclaimed engine in particular; it's downright unforgivable. If I'm wrong and it's the Unity engine, well I'm no longer as surprised but still incredibly disappointed.
Heed the warnings of this review and all others. Aside from some of the most abhorrent optimization I've personally witnessed (and I thought Obscuritas was bad), Phantasmal has a large amount of bugs, it's even a chore to set your resolution as you cannot even see all of the options and you must select blindly, restart the game, and try again. There's also a problem with keybindings staying put. Developer, instead of giving us new rooms, how about making your game functional to at least some degree? This is an appalling mess, and one that I've refunded. I had been looking forward to playing this game for quite some time, needless to say it's a huge letdown.

LA Cops Review
Publisher: Team17 Digital Ltd
Developer: Modern Dream
Release Date: March 13, 2015
Graphics
The graphics in this game are quite good overall, with clean 3D looks, and retro 70’s feel this game nails it. One of the biggest flaws that I noticed was in certain rooms the floor had lines that confused me and looked like walls, causing me to get shot. The destruction is nice with particles when objects and NPC’s get shot, and colors are bright and vibrant. With a steady 60FPS occasionally dropping to mid 50’s during cut scenes, the overall look and feel of this game is very good.
Gameplay
This is a very well playing top down game, it is a quick game to pick up and learn, and the tutorial is very fast and easy. The game is fairly well balanced but occasionally an enemy who is faced the opposite way will turn around and kill you immediately. The lock on system is easy to use and works well, but I find it unnecessary as it is smoother to just point and aim.The mini-map is pointless, made small and shoved into the corner, I find myself forgetting it’s even there. The weapons are well balanced and designed. The NPC is either half brain dead or Einstein, when it comes to finding where you are. The missions and cut scenes are funny and entertaining enough to keep me enjoying the game. Overall the game is quite enjoyable and is very funny, but is not very entertaining the second time around.
Controls
The controls are decent, with the aiming and lock-on system being this games forte. The viewing controls are great with easy to use zooming and rotation of the camera, it is easy to see big parts of the map so that you can plan out your next move. The only thing I didn’t care for was the movement system, the WASD movement system is setup in a way that W is always up and accordingly for the other keys. Normally in a top-down this is no problem at all, but this game’s maps are oriented very diagonally making it challenging to move in the way you want to, leaving you vulnerable and open to enemy fire.
Story
The story is funny and entertaining, with the cut scenes being my favorite parts, this will keep you intrigued though the whole story. With a theme of 70’s cops in LA doing crazy jobs from hold ups to drug deals, and music to match, the story is very well laid out. My only complaint being that it is a very short 8 levels.
Achievements
With only 13 quick and easy achievements, the game seemed somewhat short. Though a few were a challenge to get.
Overall
Overall, I think this was a very fun and entertaining game, with good graphics and a well thought out story, I found this to be quite a good game. With an original purchase price of $14.99 on Steam, I would wait to get a sale on the game as I don’t feel it is wholly worth that price.

Top-down-view shooter about "good" cops whacking and occasionally arresting some bad mobsters, intriguing by its 70' fuzzy visual style and cover-your-flank-partner mechanics. I'd like to praise that game, I'm really more into upholding law, rather than go frenzy like in the Hotline Miami or Hatred. But at current stage of game development, I really can't vouch for LA Cops. So far it is a broken experience, therefore I suggest you to simply stay aside.
Details:
Visuals are 70' style, everybody male have mustache or beard, and looks really groovy at first sight. Until you see some "cutscenes", especially with Katsuo. Ever heard some noise about facial animations? There are none. Totally faceless characters. That's the point where fuzzy getting into foul.
The main problem of the game - is the lack of content. 8 levels of campaign mode can be finished in about hour or two (depends from difficulty level and your luck).
Game mechanics are quite simple: you have a level with rooms infested by gangsters, which you need to storm either by yourself, or with help of your partner on crime scene. So you storm the place, kill or incapacitate mobs, complete some secondary goals like freeing the hostage, or destroying the pile of "drugs". Simple not mean good, though, for its pretty luck-based. The first levels can be opted by planning-before-moving, but, after 3rd level, you'll see a pure roulette: to kill or to be killed... And since the mobs tends to swarm in packs, and shoot through impenetrable walls once they discover your location, with drastic damage and accuracy... You'll be dying alot out of no reason and thanks to bad camera view angles and not working properly control buttons.
The most anticipated - bugs! First, the controls: for some unobvious reasons you can't switch your cops, until you die on mission. After that buttons seems to work... for some time. But the main irritant right now is the fact that you can't finish the game properly - after you deal with the last main mission, and see the credits, your progress with the Casino mission will be forgotten. That means you can't get achievements for completion of the game.
Also I've noticed several questionable game design solutions. On the start screen there are only two options, single player or multiplayer. So to quit the game I use Alt+F4. Next dubious thing is that you need to complete every level triple times, since completion on the highest difficulty don't mean you're good with easy and medium difficulties.
Conclusion:
So far it is not worth any money asked. The amount of content is just slightly more than we had in the demo versions of games not so long ago. Yeah, before they started to sell betas as full-scale games, that is. The whole "Copper" thing is not relevant, you're doing almost the same things as in Hotline Miami, just not so messy. And that is thanks to simplified mechanics, compared with That Another Game. So, to answer the question "Is it a poor man's Hotline Miami?" - I must say that it is a fair assessment.
My mark now will be 4.7/10. I can revise it some time later, if they fix at least problems with achievements... But now, it is broken piece of unfinished code that could be a decent game, were it made properly Before release and sales.

Absolver is a deck-building action RPG that follows a vague yet mysterious and awesome aesthetic, choosing to put the player in a "feel" your own adventure setting. Personally, I wasn't bothered by the lack of a step-by-step guide on what was happening in-game, nor was I concerned about the absence of a minimap. There is a justifiable balance of instruction and discovery left for the player to both find and create the experience.
While online mode has been touted by other players as the real substance of Absolver, I have found myself thoroughly enveloped in traveling the--albeit small--territories, battling the ever-increaingly difficult npc's, and experimenting with perfecting my deck. Taking what you've learned offline into the online world provides a real buzz of adrenaline, and both victory and defeat gives one a subtle euphoria, while either relishing in your skills or anticipating the coming revamp of your deck. I find both online and offline modes to be co-experiential and co-beneficial.
While I do think certain minute details of combat could be fixed, such as parry causing a slightly longer stun to prevent fast attack interrupts, the fighting-system is close to flawless. Even when your opponent has built an ultimate spam deck, there is some pleasure in thinking up on-the-fly strategies to foil it. And when the plan works, it is grand. That being said, it takes time and conscious effort to learn how to execute combat seamlessly and build an efficient base deck. One's own reativity and imagination are ignited, and I love that about about this game
Despite initial release server hiccups, Absolver offers a most elaborate and engaging martial arts experience in a game.

A Great Game Plagued With Weird Design Choices
First off let me say that this game is genuinely entertaining for any FPS fan but is much more enjoyable if you have even a slight affinity for the Wild West, which I have.  The primary reason I enjoy this game is because of its combat, which should be very good since it is more then 90% of the game, the remaining 10% being weird sandbox sections and the, in my opinion, oddly unsatisfying duels.  If not from these duels I would, without a doubt, give this game much higher praise but left me just bring up for a second how weird these duels are.  Through all of the other fights you have regenerating health, so you can take several thousand bullets over the course of the game but during these duels, well, to quote Ben 'Yahtzee' Crowshaw "...it's whoever can fire an insta-kill, regenerating cancelling bullet."  Another reason I find this choice, if not bad, just very weird is that it comes out of no where.
[SPOILER WARNING!] In an early mission, very early, you catch up to a man you are trying to kill and he simply tells his body guard to save him and the guard simply goes "I know who you are..." and then the duel starts! Who is this guard? Why is he risking his life for this other guy? [END SPOILER!]
As my last word harping on these duels I'll just say their guns are nothing specials.  You might think "They can one shot you, so their pistol must be something of legends!"  No, sadly.  I lost a late game duel, reloaded, killed the man, walked over to his pistol lying in his corpse's hand.  "Rusty Quickshooter" read the weapon's name.  This is easily the weakest weapon in the entire game, and I had died to it in one shot despite the fact that I had been shot by guns similar to this, and stronger, from the millions of goons that the man had sent after me.  Anyway, overall the game is incredibly competent in almost every aspect, although it has the odd desire to be a sandbox but only half commits to it.
TL;DR: If you want a linear western shooter with a decent story and a really weird "boss-fight" mechanic, then this is a must-buy, for everyone else, it's a good FPS.

So, bought this game after eyeing it for its absurdity and strange nature. Came into a bit of expendable money, so I grabbed it. I laughed the whole way through and enjoyed it more than I thought I would, lost track of time and had a great time with all the humor, which can be very dark at times (I will describe one of the times that sprung to mind in the spoilerific review below). I was taken by the charm it had, even if it wasn't perfect in execution which I was willing to overlook when they came up. The problem I had was the same as many of the other reviews; the ending. It took me out of the experience and just killed the steam I had, at least at the time of writing this... I may likely pick it back up to see what other options it has to offer.
This part of the review will involve the spoilers. Proceed at your own risk.
When I started the game, I had never played a dating sim because they never really interested me, but as anyone that looks at my library will see, I love the little oddballs when I can find or get them. The first half hour, I was mostly trying to figure out the details of what everything was about. The rest of the time, I was rather pleased to fall into the jokes and the charm I spoke of earlier - You're sent to check on the German tanks by the VP to make sure they're not summoning the elder gods again. Which is precicely what they were up to, and the entire scene made me grin like an idiot. You suggest they take up a bake sale, which you regret near instantly.. WW2 era tanks and ovens apparently don't mix well. That entire scene was one of my favorite of all the humor because of how it unfolded; they needed money for a class trip and their first thought was to dive head first into the occult, summon the elder gods for money or weapons which led into holocaust jokes. A bit of the charm I spoke of earlier that just endeared itself to me. All is great even after the hot springs (Where I somehow ended up spending the night with a super tank).
Now, again, I loved the gameplay and was able to forgive the oversights for what the game was. As I've said before, the end completely took the steam out of my sails with the abrupt and honestly... Compeltely lazy way it was handled. I get that it's supposed to lampoon the dating genre and maybe I'm missing some vital element here since i've never played any other dating sim but... What the hell happened? All of the charm, all of the humor... All of it was tossed in the trash bin the moment you get your tank girl. Suddenly, you're drug to a kangaroo court where, for some reason Heartmann is your lawyer and its his first case. The judge decides you're guilty from the moment you step into the room, but the girl you romanced comes to your defense (Or not at all, in IS-2's case). The whole thing of going AWOL is... Slightly hinted at in the very beginning but it's dropped when Heartmann cuts you off from talking to the school's admin. Even if you manage to beat the AWOL charges, you still get slammed with fornicating with a military vehicle which Heartmann publicly denounces and pretty much signs your guilty verdict there. The entire game, he's been the biggest pervert regarding the tanks and he was the butt of many a joke regarding this, even giving you tank porn at one point (Showing it's sold, publically... Wouldn't it be punishable to even own these things if it was something you can get court marshalled over...?)
I mean I'm probably overthinking a game like this, but again, I really enjoyed the humor and charm it supplied til the sudden end... And it disappointed hard there. I mean if it built up to it, had some more flavor than "Oh♥♥♥♥♥♥ we need to end this game somehow...", I would be much happier about it. Again, I'm probably missing some vital part of this puzzle here in the parody of the dating sim type game, but I don't even care if it was a happy ending. You spend the entirety of the game laughing and getting to like these characters to have it all... Dustbinned to end the game in an almost copy-and-paste ending where all you have done amounts to virtually nothing.
?/10 Would likely lay a tank to waste in bed again and stop Panzer from summoning Cthulu again.

I want to like this game. From the sharp aesthetic with bright colors to the intricate implementation of real-time strategy elements. It has planes, it has mechs, it has customization and RPG mechanics, it mixes rabid twin-stick shooting with clever strategies; what more could you ask for?
I've come back to this game several times over the past few years because of these elements. And again, I want to like this game. Each time, I stop playing after a few rounds and wait a few more months, hoping for one thing to change.
Let me paint a picture of what can be a great game: you start by signing in and choosing a loadout before going into battle. You can choose from 9 different mechs (after unlocking them), each with different strengths and weaknesses. There are items that strengthen your mech in different ways, pilots, style points, but those mechanics are icing on top of the core gameplay.
Now, jump into a 3v3 match with all bots. As someone who doesn't like to start their day with an embarrasing loss against a competent player, AI are an excellent alternative to failure. Each bot comes with a different mech and a different assortment of troops.
So in addition to picking your big angry mech, you also get to pick 8 types of troops to bring into battle. Want super defenses? Bring all turrets. Do you like tanks? Really, who doesn't? Bring heavy armor. You can mix and match to make the perfect army.
The battle starts off well; you move forward, pick off some neutral mobs, take over a fort or two. There are several forts scattered between each team's base, and these resupply your mech and can produce troops closer to the frontlines. Infantry have to capture them, so blitzing with tanks only does so much good; you need to strategically take the point with weaker units after the big ones knock out the defenses. Tactics 101, and they even have a tutorial mission for it. Again, so far so good.
If an enemy mech strays too close to you, between your mech's firepower, special abilities (missiles, gatling guns, death rays), and the help of allied troops, you can blast them out of the sky.
And this is where the problem starts.
When the enemy dies, they have to wait a set amount of time before respawning. This is pretty standard for most MOBAs. Players can choose to spend money that would go towards troops to get back into the fray just a little faster. At the longest, it seems like it can take roughly 30 seconds for a player to respawn and be back at the front lines. This is great for keeping the player in the game.
This is not so great for any semblence of strategy. In order to take an enemy fort, you have to knock out the defenses, destroy the infantry occupying the fort itself, and capture with infantry of your own. Even if the enemy is completely incompetent, chances are they have set up turrets, and there are turret emplacements that will regenerate the health of a few turrets around most forts. Great for defense. Lousy for offense.
If the enemy has turrets, light vehicles and infantry aren't going to cut it. Tanks will knock out defenses, but they aren't notorious for their agility. By the time a tank lumbers to an enemy base and starts shooting it, the turrets have damaged (if not destroyed) them, probably with the help of an enemy mech that has the brains to acknowledge the minimap in the corner.
So reinforce the tanks with repair troops! Cool idea, mobile healers keep your troops rolling. They even salvage money from destroyed enemy vehicles! Or, more accurately, they will stop whatever they are doing to salvage enemy vehicles. I can't count the number of times my tanks were being destroyed next to an enemy fort while my repair units were gleefully dissecting the ruins of an enemy unit half the map away. Even if they aren't distracted and grazing in a field somewhere, chances are the autohealing turrets and mech defenses are more than enough.
If you destroy an enemy mech and attack, chances are high that they will be back to thwart you long before your meandering vehicles reach the enemy fort. Fun fact: watching your two superheavy tanks attempt to mate due to poor pathfinding on the road is not as entertaining when you're 45 minutes into a game that has gone nowhere for half an hour.
If you just attack and try to fend off enemy mechs, they can just retreat (in most cases far faster than you or any troops) and heal
at any fort. So while you're attempting to attack a fort, an enemy can harass your troops and almost die, retreat and be immediately healed, then return to obliterate the rest of your troops.
You do have the option to pick up and move your troops manually, which increases the speed they can get somewhere. However, since you have limited carrying capacity, most times this just means you bring troops piecemeal to set up a neat shooting gallery for the enemies that are entrenched. Even if this was a viable strategy, why on earth would anyone want to play and awesome twin-stick shooting strategy game shuttling idiot troops from point A to point B for a match?
Regardless of strategy, at key points just when the action is ramping up the conflict dissolves into the banal grind of trench warfare, with players sitting on forts praying that something will break through and keep the game moving.
Maybe it's just been bad luck, maybe it's been the brilliant AI on my team that I caught more than once sitting idle over a patch of nothing in the middle of the map, or maybe there is something key that I am missing, but it seems the game could really benefit from some stronger punishment for for players that aren't on their toes. Forts don't need to heal, produce units, and have regenerating turret slots.
I can appreciate the delicate balancing act; if players have to retreat to base every time they need to heal, it's a slog and instead of shooting they spend more time ferrying their broken mech back home. If the forts don't construct units, players have to babysit them everywhere on the map to ensure they don't get destroyed and lose the freedom of roaming the map. If bases don't have regenerating spots, players need to sink more resources in upkeep for defenses.
This doesn't mean it can't be tweaked; give a sharper experience penalty so enemy mechs that get shot down can't easily recoved. Lower the regeneration rates at forts so players can heal and be close to the front lines, but they can still get destroyed by overwhelming firepower and can't just sit on forts. Make production slower at forts.
Even though I sign off and come back every few months, the great thing is that there are changes each time I come back. If you like robots, explosions, strategy, twin-stick shooters, or just need to kill some time, the leat you could do is try AirMech. It has a lot of promise, and it is definitely worth watching as the game develops.

This Game was excellent.
I had been looking for a good western game far a while, and I found it. Bound in Blood was exceptionally fun.
The story was decent, though a bit lacking with motivation and it had a few plot holes. It did make me feel for the characters though, more than many games that focus on the story. This game did not. First and foremost, it was a game. I really apreciate that fact. And boy does the gameplay shine.
(I should note here that I use a gamepad whenever possible. I find keyboard/mouse to be awkward, and did not use it, so I cannot remark on that.)
The controls were good, a bit awkward at first because they aren't very standard.
Most levels, you can play as one of two characters: Thomas, a marksman, and Ray, a gunslinger. Thomas has the bonus of zooming in after aiming for a while for better accuracy. He tends to play more slowly and requires you to take advantage of cover. Ray is a close quarters expert. He can dual-wield his pistols and, at close range, has an auto aim. Combine this with his ability to break down doors, and you can enter and clear a small room full of bad guys within a couple of seconds. It's stinking awesome!
Each level ends with a showdown, which requires players to keep their hand ready at their pistol and their ememy in sight while waiting for the strike of high noon. Normally I hate games that have the bosses as little more than interactive cutscenes. Bound in Blood pulls it off the best I have ever seen. It keeps the control in your hands while maintaining the drama. It also maintains the level of fun thoughout.
One final plus is the fact that it's old and even a laptop could run it smoothly.
I thouroughly enjoyed this game and would recommend it to anyone who enjoys shooters, westerns, or fun.

LA Cops is basically Hotline Miami, with a partner - which is a great premise! Unfortunately I didn't find the game fun at all for several reasons.
Let's do the good stuff first. The game looks and sounds great, the presentation is spot on and the writing is fun. The game is a Hotline Miami clone with an isometric view, with the addition of a second character you can give limited orders to and swap over when you're shot down, which adds a lot to the run and gun formula when it works.
As for the bad...
The AI is atrocious and worse still, completely inconsistent. Enemies tend to walk in slow circles, grinding stoically against walls until they complete their trajectory. They walk by obliviously by downed and arrested comrades, and sometimes they miss a gunfight going on in the same room. But sometimes they don't, and come running from a couple of rooms over.
Similarly, you can issue your partner an order to stand by, and she'll fire at anything that comes into her line of sight - the problem is you can position her, but you can't tell her were to aim, so it often takes a lot of fiddling to set up an ambush (which is one of the things that would make the game awesome if it worked properly).
The isometric presentation is also a huge problem. There's a reason why Hotline Miami is top-down, and this game illustrates that beautifully. Lining up shots is a huge pain; I think you're meant to rely on the lock-on option, but that also causes problems, since its implementation basically sucks. Instead of sticking to the enemy closest to your reticle, it... well, it seems to do whatever the hell it wants to. Which usually means that while a maniac is running at you with a shotgun, you're stuck aiming at an oblivious target through two walls.
The stylized presentation also often makes lines of sight unclear - is this grey gap rubble or a hole in the floor? can enemies see me through this?
Finally, technical issues galore! From the off I had a ton of problems - the game doesn't run fullscreen at my 16:10 monitor resolution, The key to swap partners just doesn't work, "kill x number of enemy" achievements got stuck for me and my DS4 controller just won't work properly with it (the first game I've had problems with.) All of these may be due to a problem on my end, and the sort of thing I'd forgive an indie game for. Still, doesn't help.
If it feels I'm bringing up Hotline Miami too much, well, this game makes no bones about being indebted to it. But in trying to imitate (what I consider) a masterpiece, LA Cops shows just how much goddamn talent and thought went into creating its inspiration. In HM... well, I won't say all deaths always feel fair, but they are always fun; not so here. I stuck with the game, trying to enjoy it, until timed missions and "monster closets" made their appearance, and enemies became a bit more bullet-spongey. At which point I gave up; And it's a shame, because I really wanted to like it.
Well, crap. I hate giving an indie game a bad review. As always with this sort of thing, this is just my opinion, I might just be crap at the game, etc. etc. However, if you're still tempted do have in mind that unless the last couple of missions are way larger than the first six or so, the game is pretty light on content.
(I wasn't able to play the game with a controller. Who knows, maybe the game works a lot better with one? Also, the game has co-op, which may again make it worthwhile.)

Make no mistake, Phantasmal has quite a few bugs and a lack of polish, but the core premise is compelling enough, and the scares real enough, that I keep coming back for more.
Phantasmal is an FPS Roguelite taking place in the infamous city of anarchy Kowloon. You play as the nephew of a christian missionary who went missing while running a heroin addiction clinic, who descends into the city to find her before the whole thing is leveled by the Hong Kong government. Obviously, things aren't that simple, and he finds that the despair of Kowloon has opened a doorway into something horrid beyond mankinds imagination.
Pros:
> Great setting, good atmosphere, interesting premise,
> decent enough stealth mechanics
> The money you earn in each run can be used to permanently upgrade John Hope's abilities, meaning the frustration of dyng is tempered a bit knowing that you at least progressed towards making John stronger.
> Genuinely scary enemies. We're talkin stuff like armless women made of scar tissue who gyrate towards you in an offensive pantomime of seduction before they vomit acidic lumps of flesh at your face. Severed heads which cling to ceilings and ambush you, chuckling hearily as you swing after them and miss. Spiders the size of a large dog who can cling and descend from ceiling. Ghostly children who are content to stare at you from the shadows with glowing eyes, until you're dumb enough to shine your flashlight on them....
The Bad:
> Glitches are common. At least none of them are game breaking.
> Physics can get a bit wonky, such as a table tipping over when I landed on it and launching me all the way accross a room.
> The RNG, while rarely, can occasionally make levels that are impossibly sadistic or laughably easy. One time world 1-3 (the sewer) was a gauntlet of pipe tunnels with no lights and had two mini boss level enemies at the exit door surrounded by a pack of about 12 normal level enemies. The other time it was literally one room, with the exit right infront of me.
> The graphical quality varies wildly at times, with some textures and models looking great and others looking PS2 era.
Overall, Phantasmal has a lot of serious problems but I am enjoying it far more than several AAA horror games I've played in the last year. A good analogy would be an uncut diamond.

By the current costs for any permanent item -muzzle, scope or otherwise, not to mention weapons themselves- insanely excessive grinding or pay-to-win features are practically required to make the game playable beyond a basic two-hit-kill rifle that is borderline useless and a simple assault rifle.
In other words, unless you pay, you'll wander the game as 'the noob' model, gear and all, for at least a few weeks before you can even THINK of purchasing a weapon customization item.
This aside, there is also the issue of the player base.
"The Stomping Grounds", a low-level player matching system? Broken. You will almost never, if ever, see another in this matchmaking list. Whether this persists is unknown, as from my first few hours I felt nigh-certain I was playing the same three cash-cow fellas game after game in Team Deathmatch.

If you want to advertise options in appearance and weapon types, make them accessable, not grind-heavy to a mind-numbing degree. This just isn't feasible and is blatantly 'encouraging' others to spend for their choice of weapons.
Hey. Why not GIVE the player whatever weapon set they chose from the Tutorial, huh? That would give them a head-start on their 'class' of choice, at least...

Looking for a grueling horror experience with well-designed setpieces and well-timed jumpscares? Well, look elsewhere cuz that isn't what this game is about.
I came into this game with little to no understanding of what it was or how to play it (or any roguelike game for that matter). For the first couple hours, I heartfully denied any stealth element of the game, running about willy-nilly, smashing junkies with boards and popping Amnesia monsters with my faithful sidearm. And I died. A. Lot. Doesn't help that I believe that games should be enjoyed with a cold beer (or 5), and I played and I died and I played and I died. And I hated it.
I went through to double-check this, almost every negative review has less than 2 hours of gameplay and had I written this review in the same amount of time, I would have added my voice to theirs, decrying the buggy gameplay and the long meandering levels. When you get further than you ever have and a tidal wave of spiders have you swinging futilely like a child at a piñata party until you collapse, defeated, there is an instant of rage where you want to cast the game down the darkest hole... Then you reload and try again.
Even while this game drove me crazy, I came to realize that the real problem I was having was a lack of understanding. Fellow Youtubers will find that this is not an easy game to film, as the random generation means you do not know when the action is coming and if you play this without patience, you will only get so far. So I improved. I evolved. On Day One, I was a stumbling fool, with all the stealth of a water buffalo wearing tap shoes. By Day 8, I was a ninja, creeping through every room and quietly collecting goods, distracting monsters with a well-timed flare, smacking flaming, floating heads out of the air with ease, and those spiders? I went John Goodman on them ("Arachnophobia" reference, for those under 30).
I dodged monsters and grabbed coins, buying (very expensive) upgrades, and as I slowed my own pace, I allowed the atmosphere to finally get to me. Though you see the same rooms often, this also helps you learn them and know just where to go to get collectibles in a hurry, and the dark setting and ambient sounds through my headphones began to unnerve me, until I would hear the distant beep-beep-beep that signified the end of the level was just a little further. Though I have many, many games to play, I was finding myself coming back to Phantasmal to push myself harder, to get a little further, and I was rewarded for it. Everything is random, so after playing the game for a week, when a new scare occurred, it took me completely by surprise because I thought I had already seen everything, and I soon realized how wrong I was.
When I finally completed the first chapter, I was elated, then confused, as I thought I was going to have to start back at the beginning and again, I had an urge to say "That's it, no more, I've paid my dues, dammit!" And then I began again. With all the practice during my early days of hardcore failing, the second chapter turned out to have its own differences, and I have a feeling there are some new enemies I have yet to face, new strategies to formulate, and more detail to a story that I at first scoffed at, but over time, realized might be more intriguing than I first thought. I wasn’t even filming as I breezed through the second chapter, and when things took a new turn, I was scrambling to set up equipment and I learned again not to underestimate this game.
As a closing thought, this game is a challenge. While some bugs drive me crazy, there is an active community discussion board that includes personable developers LISTENING to their players, giving guidance and seeking to improve where they can. This is a game that charms over time; don't be one of those gamers that tries to play just enough to get in a flippant review. The game's unforgiving perma-death adds tension and makes survival meaningful, and reminded me of the old times in videogames where there was no Quick Save, no easy mode; you didn't buy games for a quick experience, they were meant to challenge you for weeks, as this one did. If you're willing to put some time into a game, take failures as learning experiences, and tolerate some (occasionally exceedingly comical) bugs, all surrounded by a dark, brooding atmosphere, give Phantasmal a try.
You can watch my own personal journey from "game hater" to "gaming harder," monster-bait oaf to flare-slingin', sneakity-sneak ninja yourself at Beard+Beer Gaming. Laugh at my idiocy in the first few episodes, and witness my learning curve get its swerve by Ep 4 or 5, then test yourself.
