'Our Darker Purpose' is a game that stereotypically gets compared to 'Binding of Isaac'--a top-down rougelike shooter that offers a challenging risk/reward gameplay system with heavy randomization on loot dropped from enemies you kill.  Chances are, if you love BoI, you will love ODP, but the two games have major differences regardless.
ODP is incredibly difficult at times, and heavily based on your luck with RNJesus, but successful gameplay rewards you with better items and weapon modifications, level ups to give to your character, and "tuition credits" that you can use to purchase "lessons", which are perks to permanently give to your character's account through multiple playthroughs.  ALL Steam achievements are inherently locked, and each achievement unlocked/earned grants a specific reward to be used.
What drew me in completely was the creepiness of the lore and storyline, along with the environment itself, and the beautiful soundtrack that is both haunting and enjoyable in rhythm (I'm not kidding, the soundtrack is AWESOME), and the feel of you actually having some control over the build of your character, albeit it is heavily based upon luck as well.
My major complaints with the game are the limits to its controller support, as well as I am truly convinced it is impossible to get 100% achievements in this game, unless hacking or glitching was used.  However, the keyboard controls are optimized to be an efficient and comfortable system (which is a good thing, because you cannot change them), and getting the achievements rewards truly rewards you well.
If you want 'Binding of Isaac' in a creepier, more haunting format, with a bit slower <and difficult> gameplay, and a level up system that allows you to have some control over building your character, then this game is a necessity.  Plus, the music is #&@%'ing awesome (did I say that already?).

Our Darker Purpose is definitely very similar to The Binding of Issac, but with a very different artistic approach. Personally, I very much enjoyed the art, music, and story the game had to offer. The gameplay I would say was not quite as fluid and well developed as TBoI, but I was willing to sacrifice that portion of the experience for a greater focus on narrative and storytelling. TBoI, for all its successes, was hardly known for a well developed story.
My biggest complaint with Our Darker Purpose was the ending. Now, I have not completed the game on hard mode yet, and so there may be a different ending there. I will update this review when I discover if that is the case. That said, it may seem odd that I praised the greater focus on storytelling but then criticized the ending. This is because all throughout the game, the subtle hints as to what was really going on from every aspect of the game, from items to quest descriptions to literal sacks of potatos, was building up to what should have been a fantastic reveal that left the user stunned. What was actually at the end seemed barely related to anything that had been hinted at previously.
It's fine if a game doesn't answer every question with its ending, in fact, I don't think it should. It's fine if a game opens up more questions with the ending, in fact, I think it should. However, ODP's ending didn't answer any questions and opened up way too many. It felt as though it did not deserve its place as an ending, and should instead have been just another chapter before the true ending is revealed. I think what ODP needs is some extra content, whether in a paid DLC or just a free update, that actually gives some sense of closure to the story. Again, it doesn't need to answer every question, but I feel that at least some question should be answered.
With all of this in mind, I would still recommend the game. It won't change your life forever, but I think it is still pretty good. If the devs give it a little more time, make a couple small additions, I think it has the potential to be fantastic.

I see a lot of people upset about this game simply because it's not Resident Evil 1, 2 or 3, whatever game they prefer. If this game was titled anything else, I'm sure it would receive even better reviews from those people (goes to show how subjective some people are).
I'm one of the fans who's played Resident Evil since it originally came out. RE 2 and REmake 1 are my favorites in the series. I absolutely love 4, I think 5 was fantastic (though I was worried with the decline into more shootery gameplay) especially when played cooperatively. 6 was 'good' at best (still haven't had a chance to play it coop, anyone interested?). This may help you align yourself to my opinions and ideas.
What I love and what I think this game does great is it gives you a sense of powerlessness and then gives you some power to fight back, and then takes that away. I started the game unarmed and afraid. Having played the demo's previously, I knew a bit of the guest house area somewhat intimately so I was expecting things to jump out at me at certain spots. Time to change diapers. When I obtained my first weapon I received a very strong burst of confidence and I had a level of comfort thinking I could fight back!
Boy was I wrong.  Even when you get gun, most weapons are only good at slowing down the family members who are hunting you, so save your ammo for the other things lurking in the house. I pulled myself to the end of the game where I had a lot of ammo stored up, armed to the teeth, only to fight quite possibly the easiest enemy in the game. Queue the muted trombone. Wop wop wopppp.

The duration of the game was great, it took me maybe 19.5 hours with my first playthrough on normal, though I was very thorough and spent quite a lot of time hiding and trying to find ways around enemies. My second playthrough on Madhouse took me around 11 hours (Madhouse changes the placement of items around and could be considered as a different game mode, I suppose.).
The guns feel great and powerful, if you line up a headshot you'll do exceptional damage and stagger enemies more often than not. Close range shotgun blasts are as beautiful as ever. The few issues I have with them is that I felt there weren't enough weapons, the sounds are a bit weak and there's no customization or upgrading which has been a standard in the series for a while now. Part of the new direction, I suppose!
All in all, I thought this game was fantastic. I was afraid it was going to be a last ditch effort to copy more modern horror games such as Outlast, but it copied that style so the player could immerse themselves more into the game. Get ready to feel empathetic pain! I'm eagerly awaiting the free content scheduled to come out this Spring so we can see what's going on with our mystery character!
Feel free to comment, critique, crochet and cackle!

FTL is a game that you still feel good about beating on "Easy." The ship-to-ship combat can become a complex dance of percentages and risk-aversion. You may find yourself with a ship nearly devoid of oxygen, a desperate attempt to stop the fires generated from an encounter too close to a sun, with your life-support offline, doomed to watch your crew suffocate slowly. Then you'll remember you could have bought emergency respirators, or put an extra point into your O2 system and you'll kick yourself. The next run you'll do just that, and it won't be a problem... but then you'll be missing valuable scrap you could have bought a Mk 3 Burst Laser with, so you decide the best course of action is to save your scrap, dooming your next run to a shortage of systems in a tough fight. It's a balancing game, really. You have to balance your desire to become powerful with your desire to survive while keeping enough fuel to make survival purposeful. It's a challenge, and it's a blast.
It's written well, you'll come across stories of alien spiders, inquisitive glow-in-the-dark creatures, ships in peril, arms dealers, and you'll have to decide how to handle the situation. Any number of things could happen, and having specific stuff can give you extra options... which may or may not come with extra negatives. It's a game full of seemingly random encounters. Take every edge you can, take as few risks, and you'll finally get to the end of your story, an unbelievably difficult fight against the Rebel Flagship. What a beast of an encounter that is at first. I won't spoil the mechanics, but it's a very rewarding fight and a satisfying climax to a good run.
This game is extraordinarily replayable, with awesome unlockable content and difficult challenges. It's unique, nothing plays quite like it. If you're a fan of challenging strategy games, you've probably already played this game. If you haven't... what the heck are you waiting for? Buy this game.

I've been using ShareX for about two years now and it's an absolute must-have for me. The default settings are already good, which makes it simple to use, but there are lot of settings – some quite advanced – that let you make ShareX exactly what you want out of a screenshot/-capture program.
It's easy to take screenshots of specific monitor(s), the active window or even a custom shape. You can choose what to do with it after capture. Edit it in an image editor of your choice? Copy it to your clipboard? Upload it to Imgur, some other image upload service or even on your own server.
Video/GIF capture is just as easy, though sometimes seems to take two attempts before getting a proper FPS out of it.
And to top it all off, there are a bunch of simple, but useful tools built-in ranging from color pickers to FTP clients to macros.
One feature ShareX does not have is an easy way to synchronize all your settings between computers. Some parts of the settings can be exported and imported, but it's not as easy as say Steam Cloud syncing it all would be.

Experience Terror that is Never the Same Twice with Phantasmal: City of Darkness, a survival horror game where every playthrough is completely different. You will need to face off against otherworldly horrors as well as a totally unpredictable procedurally generated environment.
Right from the title screen, I started to get chills...
Phantasmal is a game that runs smoothly with above-average graphics and lighting. It suffers from multiple bugs and glitches, but still is a great experience for those willing to overlook that fact. Currently in early access as of writing this review, so the glitches are almost expected to occur. I hope that they can be fixed, because if they are, this game has potential to be a great horror game.

Please note before reading that while I think this game has the potential to be enjoyable, it is currently flawed and I would not reccomend it in this state. This is supposed to be a horror game, and it is just not scary, at all. I'm not even a horror buff, but I can safely say that the Penumbra series is infinitely scarier than this.
I absolutely love randomly generated exploration games, Reciever is one of my favourite games on steam, and I would love for this game to reach its full potential, but it's just not nearly there yet. I understand that it is an early access title, and that it is therefore unfinished, these are just my opinions on what needs to be improved.
- While the environments and lighting look very nice on higher graphical settings, the animation, specifically that of the zombies, is VERY janky right now. Hopefully that can be improved upon
- Spiders are (if you will forgive the pun) very buggy, on multiple occasions I saw spiders walk around a wall, that is to say, rotate on the spot through a wall, as if it were climbing to the other side, before dissapearing completely. Spiders also often span erratically and took a while to right themselves after spawning
- Enemies just run straight at you the second they spot you, which often occurs through walls and doors. Their AI is just programmed to chase and attack, so every encounter ends up being a slugfest of you bashing them with a wooden plank until it breaks, running to find another wooden plank, and kiting them to the best of your ability (which is largely impossible because when you have to stop to hit enemies, they can easily outrun you). This means damage is inevitable and while they don't do very much of it, a group of them can kill you easily with no way of getting out of it besides still having pistol ammo to hand.
- Health pills pickups refill very little health, getting them from a crate has absolutely no impact on your survivability because if too many enemies spawn at once you just die no matter how much health you have. Implementing something like the health pill system from left 4 dead whereby they give you a significant amount of health that ticks back down to where you were over time would be more useful than this.
-There is a door near the very start of the game through which there is nothing, you can walk into it and fall into a bottomless abyss and die.
- Enemies often spawned, appearing out of nowhere, while I was looking at them. They also had a tendency to crawl through doors, environmental objects, the walls, and eachother.
- There's no feedback to tell you that you've hit something - it's just a case of swing away until the enemy (usually) falls through the floor and disappears.
While this game is by no means terrible, the good amount of atmosphere created by the spooky sounds and the (actually quite nice!) environments is ruined by the zombies, whose animations and models look just plain silly, and the overly agressive AI turning every encounter into a 5v1 cage match.

This is a horror game as seen through the eyes of a two year old, and it brilliantly handles this through creepy sights and sounds and some ambiguous monster that starts to hunt for you as the story progresses.
There are a couple times where you will jump a little, but it isnt really a scary game per se. It is however creepy, and the subject matter is quite dark and depressing. The end is both sad and hopeful all at once.
I will say without giving anythign away that this topic will be relevant and quite poignant for a lot of people, and it may even be the sort of game that brings real tears to you depending on your own set of circumstances growing up. While I didnt experience the things that happen in this game, I can appreciate how much this might affect some people.
Outside of that, the adventure is filled with mystery and awe.
I think this was a very well made game that also handled a sensitive topic quite well and did an amazing job of bringing the world as seen through two year old eyes to life perfectly.
This one is a 10/10 for sure.

I was pretty nervous during the introductory phase, then I NOPEd out pretty quick once the Groots actually started killing me. There's a reason I don't play a lot of horror games. But I watched the rest of it on youtube and I gotta say, this game is absolutely genius. So many things to love about it, in terms of both narrative and gameplay. If you've ever been reading and come across something profound and your reaction is "yes! someone else said it!", you'll have a lot of moments like that during this game if you think through the implications of what you're being shown.
The horror comes in two flavors: gentle suggestion of a threat that causes you to scare yourself via the power of imagination, and actual Slender-esque sequences that will result in a game over. We get the former exclusively for about the first 2/3rds of the game, and it works extremely well although it might wear out it's welcome if the player decides that the game is all bark and no bite. However, after a seemingly arbitrary point you will start dying, and it will seem random and arbitary, which is of course jarring as hell once you're good and tired of the game being harmless. My only issue with this is that you aren't given any indication that this change has happened, and the advice on how to deal with it came 20 or 30 minutes ago. Basically just try not to make noise since that's what usually causes the Groots to spawn, and if they spawn anyway just run.
All-around it's a genius game and I hope it gets some quality imitators. 10/10 would reccomend.

Among the Sleep is an excellent game that expresses mental horror in a child's point of view. Many people give negative feedback to this game since it doesn't have a scary approach, but this game differs from your normal horror game. It has a powerful and unique inner meaning and the noises you hear throughout the game are horrifying. I felt anxious and slightly afraid during certain parts of the game and the graphics are actually quite impressive. The game is short but I honestly loved it, not only is it anxious and frightning at times but puzzling, causing you to use every part of your brain. Great mixture. 7.8/10

As others have stated, Among the Sleep is a short game, but a rather enjoyable one. For those thrill seekers looking for nightmares and psychological scarring, this isn't the game for you, but if you can put yourself in the mindframe of a toddler, it has some good 'jump scare' moments. Overall I would give this an 8.5 out of 10 rating.
I'd like to see a sequel made, perhaps even when the child is another year or two older and the challenges are a bit more difficult. There is potential for a series of games that one can grow with, if the creators can stay true to the original style of game play, but advance with each storyline.

First of all, this game series is damned fun. I just want to get that out of the way.
Now that I have, here's something wrong with this game in particular.
While the gameplay is fun, the mechanics are the same (with the exception of one or two moves) across the series, and the setting is believably grim, the story is a little funky in this particular game.
I know this is supposed to be an alternate reality of WWII, but the direction that the game heads in its second, I want to say "half", felt to me like it was out of left field. When it made that change (not giving out spoilers), it was cool, novel, and interesting, but only maybe for the first area or so. Then it became disjointed with the rest of the game. That's all I'll say on that besides this:
This game feels like an unfinished game slapped together with a lengthy DLC, which have which have been tied together using a common goal. It just felt a little sloppy.
However, this doesn't take away from the fun you'll have playing this game. And that ending.. it sure was nice to see Fergus again~ :)
This game is polished, with the exception of the odd bug I've found, fun, and allows you to take each area (dependent on story) in the way you wish - either stealthy or loud.
=========
Do I recommend?
Hell yeah~!
This series is great fun~ :)
Just don't feel too weird when the jarring second "half" comes into play. It's still fun too, just out of left field IMO ;)

Although the game looks like a relatively generic, low quality The Binding of Isaac clone; honestly it's a better game.
As said the game visually looks quite bad compared to most games. The graphics do not look like a world but instead just like assets, the animations are primitive and there's little atmospheric design visually. However the game does manage to retain a unique art style despite its rough appearance. And it feels very unifying as a whole once the player has gotten used to it. Which is built on even more by the music which is very atmospheric and consistent to the theme.
The two biggest similarities to this and The Binding of Isaac are the top-down-ish room design and the basic combat. The combat however at first feels very awkward and poorly designed, but once the player has adjusted it is very satisfying to control because of how much agility the player can utilize and how forgiving the protagonists own damage recieve hitbox is. Weaving and rolling between projectiles, moving around and through hazards with precision and dexterity.
The greatest strength of the gameplay itself is in the diversity the player has. Players have a pool of over a hundred items which they can acquire from chests, drops from powerful enemies or purchase from the shop. However, most items are actually effective even if its in a humble way, and the useable items are actually useful as well. It is exciting to get the items, because the game is challenging and each new item is potentially a new asset to survive. The player can become powerful but not ridiculously so, it's not a contest to get the most absurd run it's getting the most interesting and unique run. But beyond the items there are two more levels of depth to the gameplay. Players level up with experience during their playthrough each time and with each level up they get to choose from a random two perks which boost their statistics, apply unique beneficial effects and open new possibilities for builds and survivability for that specific playthrough until they die. Beyond this, players gain a special currency from completing floors which they can use to purchase upgrades which apply to all future playthroughs; and purchase customizable passive perks which are equipped in the main menu. Three totally different layers of gameplay diversity which are all tethered to progression as players not only gain currency from playing to buy new passive perks which they can equip, but they also gain new abilities and strength as they level up each playthrough and with each new item pickup.
Players also need to perform special challenges and tasks while playing to unlock new perks they can purchase or new items for the pool. Often these challenges involve fighting bosses in certain ways, which makes the boss fights more interesting and gives players a reason to look forward to finding certain ones so they can attempt the challenge. Making it a hunt to find certain bosses, to do certain things or get certain items to complete challenges and unlock even more new things.
There is a good amount of randomization and visual diversity to the different floor layers, as well as a moderate amount of unique factions of enemies which show up on specific floors. The bosses being the high point of this all as there is a wide selection of bosses for every floor type and each of them is completely unique. Every floor also potentially has its own modifier which changes things on that floor and can give it certain advantages or disadvantages. Adding even more to the diversity of each playthrough as some floors players may choose to go to for a specific benefit while others they may avoid because of a specific disadvantage.
The writing is the highest point of the quality of the game, even though it is not the focal point of the game itself. The lore is creative and unorthodox, confusing and obscure. It gives the player enough to work with overtime but not enough to give them any hard conclusion and for a long time players will barely know what is happening. It is thrilling to read every unique backstory to every boss and faction, and every piece of lore found in the Memory rooms which all builds onto one final absurd truth that is only hinted to subtly throughout all of the writing. It is the highest tier of creative writing and serves as one of the fundamental pillars to the games deceptively deep and well crafted design.
Only real significant problem with the game is that Hardmode is completely imbalanced and unfair. It is really great that the developers actually gave enemies new abilities and changed things for their Hardmode, but the changes in the end completely imbalance the game and make it perpetually overbearing; with some bosses being straight up mandatory damage spam races. It is so bad, I can complete the actual game ten times in a row without losing once; but sometimes I cannot even get a quarter of the way through Hardmode. Fortunately, it is not an integral part of the game. But it's still in the game and players can thus still end up suffering it, and it's a low blow to any player who likes the game enough to want to get every achievement.
The Binding of Isaac and its pseudo metal story, over the top desperacy to be offensive and sporadic, vast pool of useless items and completely unbalanced character build system. It does not compare. The Binding of Isaac only served to set the foundation for this game.

Really tries to be Binding of Isaac but the movement is clunky, the character models and hit boxes are just bad, and the controls are terrible.
EDIT: Since so many people are downvoting my review and coming to the comments to complain that I didn't spend enough time on this game (Go spend 20 hours on Rogue Legacy and tell me how much different it really is from the first 30 minutes you spent, it's the same thing just with more unlocks, same controls, same game), I'll elaborate.
I feel like most of the arguments here aren't defending anything I said, they're just attacking me because I didn't spend that much time playing. The game's controls did not feel polished. The enemy animations and hit boxes felt off. I felt there were more times than not that I should have dealt damage or walked clearly around a trap on the floor only to find the opposite.
The game "Dead Cells" controls AMAZINGLY. The hitboxes and animation are fluid and look great. "Hollow Knight", "Shantae: Half Genie Hero", "Battleblock Theater". When you fail, you realize it's a shortcoming in your skill, not because the game design is bad. Not because enemies are animated to take up room that they don't actually take damage in. Not because there's traps on the floor that take up more or less hit box room than they look like they actually do.
There are literally dozens of other games I could browse through my Steam Library and rattle off, where when I start the game, from the START, you can tell it controls well. It's not a level of skill where "Oh I died, this game is dumb." It's a matter of game design. I didn't say Our Darker Purpose was just hard. I spent 5 plays defeating a total of 4 bosses, dying, and unlocking things. It just wasn't fun. Unlocking new things wasn't fun. The dark levels reminded me of the curse floors in Binding of Isaac and I hate those. The crap littering the floor I would get stuck on or take damage from randomly was frustrating too.

The game is really enjoyable and challenging. The difficulty cap is ultimately set quite high, thus making it replayable as much as it is rewarding for reaching ever further, while, quite admittedly, it may be off-putting at times. It also has great atmosphere with its grotesque style (reminescent of Tim Burton) alongside with gorgeous and fitting art design and plot setting as well as lovely soundtrack. Gameplay is not much different from Isaac and yet feels a bit slower paced, just enough to make it less frustrating. Another good thing is the pre-run upgrade system which gives a little more control of the setting while reducing the RNG factor.
Overall score of 8/10

This is a review on the base game, not any of the DLC.
A fantastic return to a more creepy and scary Resident Evil game!
I'll give some brief pros and cons first and follow up with a more detailed write up so some people can read it quickly and those looking for a more thorough opinion have a reason to read too!
Pros:
Turn your brightness down, use headphones and play in the dark. Wear adult diapers.
: My first run was 19 hours. A bit of time was spent hiding.
: The game looks and runs great on my older system.
: The game has superb audio, some gun sounds are weak though.
: The graphics + audio combined make a fantastic atmosphere. It's intense.
: The story is not perfect, but it's interesting and made me wanting to know more!
: Controls surprisingly well using keyboard and mouse.
: This game has put the failing series on a new path in a new direction with scares and fright as the focus. I can't wait for what comes next!+++
: There are simply not that many different enemies in the game.
: Could consider this a positive since it provides a better story and experience, but the game gives you little choice.
: I felt there were too few weapons throughout the game and no customization of weapons.
: No Mercenaries or any modes. Where are they, Capcom?! Madhouse is a difficulty, not mode!
: A joke of a fight, even on Madhouse the fight plays out the same no matter the difficulty.

I see a lot of people upset about this game simply because it's not Resident Evil 1, 2 or 3, whatever game they prefer. If this game was titled anything else, I'm sure it would receive even better reviews from those people (goes to show how subjective some people are).
I'm one of the fans who's played Resident Evil since it originally came out. RE 2 and REmake 1 are my favorites in the series. I absolutely love 4, I think 5 was fantastic (though I was worried with the decline into more shootery gameplay) especially when played cooperatively. 6 was 'good' at best (still haven't had a chance to play it coop, anyone interested?). This may help you align yourself to my opinions and ideas.
What I love and what I think this game does great is it gives you a sense of powerlessness and then gives you some power to fight back, and then takes that away. I started the game unarmed and afraid. Having played the demo's previously, I knew a bit of the guest house area somewhat intimately so I was expecting things to jump out at me at certain spots. Time to change diapers. When I obtained my first weapon I received a very strong burst of confidence and I had a level of comfort thinking I could fight back!
Boy was I wrong.  Even when you get gun, most weapons are only good at slowing down the family members who are hunting you, so save your ammo for the other things lurking in the house. I pulled myself to the end of the game where I had a lot of ammo stored up, armed to the teeth, only to fight quite possibly the easiest enemy in the game. Queue the muted trombone. Wop wop wopppp.

The duration of the game was great, it took me maybe 19.5 hours with my first playthrough on normal, though I was very thorough and spent quite a lot of time hiding and trying to find ways around enemies. My second playthrough on Madhouse took me around 11 hours (Madhouse changes the placement of items around and could be considered as a different game mode, I suppose.).
The guns feel great and powerful, if you line up a headshot you'll do exceptional damage and stagger enemies more often than not. Close range shotgun blasts are as beautiful as ever. The few issues I have with them is that I felt there weren't enough weapons, the sounds are a bit weak and there's no customization or upgrading which has been a standard in the series for a while now. Part of the new direction, I suppose!
All in all, I thought this game was fantastic. I was afraid it was going to be a last ditch effort to copy more modern horror games such as Outlast, but it copied that style so the player could immerse themselves more into the game. Get ready to feel empathetic pain! I'm eagerly awaiting the free content scheduled to come out this Spring so we can see what's going on with our mystery character!

Now Absolver is a difficult game to describe. Absolver is a mix between an open world game and a closed arena game. You can do tasks in the world with your friends and people you meet or just fight them in a 1v1 arena. Items, such as armour, weapons as well as abilities, can be found in the world by defeating enemies, minibosses, bosse,  random spawns and secret locations. Now i will try to describe each aspect individually.
The PVE in Absolver can be tackled offline or online and lasts about 6 hours (depending on how good you are and how much you roam). There is a light story that drives ahead the experience and gives you an idea of what to do. There are no GUI features to help you locate tasks or where to go, this adds to the atmosphere of the game. It is also fairly simple to find all the minibosses and bosses throught the map. PVE is a great way to practice your abilities before going into duels however the story is also something not to ignore.
The PVP is Absolver's winning point for most people and it is easy to see why: the combat is really clean and heavy on martial arts. There are no flashy energy blasts or spams of punches, every move in Absolver has to be carefully planned and executed at the right moment in order to secure the win. This game, furthermore, gives the player the bility to create their own combos of heavy and light attacks, unlike most games which give you a set and you have to memorise them. The community is not toxic and actually very helpful which can be a plus to some people looking to have fun.

This is a superb sequel to an already super Western-themed FPS. Bound in Blood is the prequel to the critically acclaimed Call of Juarez. We play as the younger Ray McCall and also his brother, Thomas. Unlike the first episode, BiB is not strict when it comes to player selection: you can complete the larger part of the story just playing one of the protagonists. I preferred Ray as with him I believe the Western experience is better - he shoots first and asks questions later. Thomas can use a lasso and handles the rifle better but he is the weaker brother.
Ray and Thomas fight in the war between the states when they become deserters as they find it important to save their farm. This is an interesting turn of events as not only do you fight bandits in this episode but also the soldiers of the confederacy along with the Navajo and Apache native tribes.
Gameplay-wise CoJ did not change one bit: you pretty much shoot everybody who's moving. Occasionally you use dynamite to blow things up and this time you can complete sidequests sometimes before progressing the story further. Also, your pistols do not overheat, thus, you can just play the game with what you have without having to stop for one sec.
The game looks beautiful. The explosions of your dynamite, the forests in the mountains, the riverbed and ghost town all are examples how well Techland's Chrome engine performs. The game is also optimised very well, so no glitches are found throughout the game.
For those of you who liked the original game Bound in Blood is a must. For those who never played it can pick this one up right away as this is a prequel, thus, not directly linked to its predecessor.

Before I start off this review, I just want to say that I've always been a fan of anything RTS, and I have been interested in this video game genre for as long as I can remember. Another thing, Empire: Total War was my first Total War game I ever played. Initially, after playing the game for a few hours, I was somewhat confused because I usually played real-time strategy games such as Stronghold, Age of Empires, and similar titles. Although confused at first, since Empire: Total War was turn-based and focused more in-depth on economic & government management, I was not disappointed whatsoever. In fact, I honestly enjoyed playing this game very much and I still do. I recall purchasing this game when it was on sale along with the full DLC bundle. I honestly can say that the various DLC that is available for this game is definitely worth your money. Before I continue, I am going list the pros and cons of this game.
Pros:
-Fairly large campaign map. The campaign map (excluding the American Revolution campaign), includes the regions of Europe, North Africa, India, North America, Northern South America & the Caribbean. However, there are minor trade areas such as the Ivory Coast, far eastern Asia, Madagascar, etc...
-There are many playable factions that are featured in this game. These factions include Great Britain, France, Austria. Spain, the Ottoman Empire, and much more. There are also many 'emergent' factions that are basically nations that are created whenever certain provinces revolt, such as Hungary or Ireland.
-Implements historical references through the use of short articles  (This might be more of a personal preference of mine, but as somebody who looves history, I've always found the historical implemented articles interesting.) Another thing, these historical articles pop up throughout the vanilla campaign as in-game years advance.
-There are many unique and fun mods that you can download. These mods include Darthmod (my personal favorite), the civil war mod, and much more. I definitely recommend you to check out these mods.
-The in-game real-time battles can be very engaging. These battles can either be naval or land, however, they are very interesting to see and participate in, especially when you play multiplayer matches.
-The soundtrack accurately fits the game. I've always found the soundtrack during the campaign soothing and calm, and warlike during battles respectively.
-The multiplayer aspect of this game is good at best. Although not very crowded with players, whenever you do join a multiplayer match, you and your opponent generally feel competitive and focused.
-Although the governmental and economic managing may be confusing at first, especially if you aren't familiar with this type of RTS, you will eventually get the hang of it. The managing aspect isn't a very difficult concept to understand.
Cons:
-During battles and sometimes during campaigns, you might run into a few bugs here and there.
-The AI during battles might be an annoyance from time to time. These annoyances include not reacting to your orders, not responding to enemy fire, and basically being bullet sponges. These annoyances are often an occurrence during large fortress battles.
-The campaign AI, such as other factions, may do random actions, such as invading an isolated province far away from their own nation without any real reason. This is especially evident with the Maratha Confederacy, as they tend to become pretty powerful during the vanilla campaign if they are isolated long enough, and this faction tends to invade provinces far away. Although I do not expect this game to be totally historically accurate throughout the campaign, I've always found it funny and somewhat annoying whenever the Maratha Confederacy, an Indian faction, invade Rupert's Land in North America.
So there it is, my pros and cons of this game. Please take note that many of these pros and cons apply to the vanilla game (without mods). I highly recommend buying this game if you are into turn-based strategy and real time battles. This game is definitely worth the current price it is being sold for.

As far as campaigns, so far I've taken on England, Prussia, Austria, Maratha, and the United Provinces.  The biggest challenge to date was playing the Dutch.  They are badly spread out and there is too much to defend.  However, on the 4th try I finally figured out that the road to success was to simply abandon trying to defend Ceylon.  Milk it for the money while you can, but when Maratha invades it's time to pack up and leave.  There will be a time to come back to get it later.
If you concentrate on the Dutch army at home, and play aggressively with small armies in the Americas it's possible to make headway in the Americas while you knock out France quickly and early.  This breaks up their American colonies and you can pick them off one by one.  The European army needs to work quickly.  Once France is out it's time to take out Spain.  Those galleons are big and tough and with Spain out, its colonies also break up.
With America firmly in hand (say 10 or so provinces) and with another 10 or so in Europe it's time to raise that army and go back and take Ceylon.  Maratha is a lot easier target than Prussia and Sweden, and those elephants aren't nearly as tough as they look at first.
I've been playing the current game for a LONG time now.  It's 1783, and the United Provinces control all of India, all of Europe except for Greece and 12 Ottoman provinces, and all of the Americas except for the northern Indian provinces, Quebec, and 8 US provinces.  Austria just fell (Hungary, Austria, and Bavaria all fell on the last turn).  I'm repositioning troops, and will invade Greece with 2 armies.  These will be positioned for a quick attack on Rumelia, while individual armies go after the other two provinces the Ottomans have in Europe proper.  Other armies will fall on the Middle Eastern provinces, and 2 armies will be ferried to Africa to take out their two African provinces.
I'm currently fighting in America with 3 armies, but will transfer armies from Europe as soon as possible to conquer 100% of the world before 1799.  I'm also 4 turns away from researching all technologies, also a first for me.  Great game, I'm thinking of trying either Russia or Poland next.  Not sure I'll ever play the frogs.  It's too much fun watching France get eliminated.
Another fun thing to do is to defend a fort against forces that badly outnumber you.  Occasionally the computer sends my guys out the gates or over the walls at the enemy, but if you pay attention you can order them back inside so that they don't get wiped out.  Nice to hold the fort at the end of a long battle with all of the enemy units broken and fleeing the field!
Definitely recommend the game.  I save frequently so can always back up to a prior save if a glitch comes up.  I've found that the glitches don't tend to repeat themselves.

It is painstakingly faithful to Mordheim's aesthetics, as a result - it looks excellent. The game's mechanics have certainly captured the 'feel' of playing Mordheim perfectly. (I spent many hours playing it growing up.) It is however, as has been made clear, incomplete.
Only two warbands are currently playable and only two more are confirmed. There is currently maybe 10-15 hours gameplay and that's pushing it. I'm really, really excited as to where this game could go; and I really believe it has the makings of a huge success. I say this guardedly though. They've been very tight-lipped as to exactly what features are to be expected in the future and I can't help but feel we'll be waiting an incredibly long time for a game that will really hold our attention.
Currently the only really playable feature is playing one of two warbands (Skaven or Human Mercenaries) in a pretty easy match whilst you fight against a warband with half your numbers.
The maps are interesting, the gameplay rewarding. But as of now - there's no reason to pick this up over say, X-Com; unless you're purely playing for the Games Workshop IP.
It's expensive for what it is, but I consider it an investment into a really solid game so far. I'm very excited as to where this goes in the future. Don't disappoint us Mordheim!

Early Access Review:
This game was a huge surprise. Even though it has a lot of bugs, it is now my one of 10 favorite horror games of all time. Coming from me as a huge horror junkie, that is a HUGE praise.
The mixture of ultra creepy atmosphere, stealthy roguelike, unpredictable procedurally generated environment, and extremely scary creatures delivered a true and awesome survival horror experience.
After each time I die, the floors are not same as the last one at all. Well, the rooms are similar but the pathways are always different which give a lot of repayability and unpredictable results. Amazing.
The creatures are extremely creepy, smart, and not to be messed with. At first, I was thinking, "I can plow through the game killing all the monsters and running. Yeah no problem." He he... Well no. Never happened. Each time I do that, I die immediately after 20 seconds. The monsters are very mean. The game requires a lot of stealth, careful planning with the guns (with very low ammo, use it wisely!), flares, keys, and a very small amount of health packs, and confidence. You will NOT want to see the huge monster right before you die ever again.
My most favorite part about the game is the atmosphere. It is really well done. It is so creepy and gives a lot of goosebumps. I can't spoil it any more. Buy it and find out!
The only problem I have with this game is the bugs. That's it. I highly expect the devs to iron out those bugs right before releasing this game officially. If they do that, this game is going to be one of the best survival horror games within the same tier as Outlast, Amnesia, Silent Hill, and System Shock 2.

For lovers of Hotline Miami there's a lot of potential to be found in LA Cops, even if this early access release is pretty barebones. Yes, all of the agents are already available and the level that's been implemented feels complete. But at the moment it's pretty short and can easily be finished within 30-60 minutes. That number includes repeatedly dying and therefore replaying some of the sections over again. Let's keep in mind that it's an early access title, but I have to be honest, I've seen games with more content than this. Anyway, let's forget about that for a moment and continue with this little review.
LA Cops lets you control 2 cops, in realtime, but you can switch between them on the fly with the press of a button. Your partner won't move along with you; he or she will stand still and cover you as long as enemies move in their FOV. Unlike Hotline Miami this game doesn't entirely rely on fast movement, but you actually have to carefully plan what to do. It requires a bit of strategy and tactics. It's recommended that you let your partner cover the corners so you can let the criminals come to you, if you don't get killed in the process, that is.
The graphics are cel shaded and look absolutely gorgeous and stylish and have that 70's look that the developers are aiming for. Just excellent. The game really looks 2D but actually is 3D and you can freely move/rotate the camera around.
I haven't really paid attention to any music, just to some sounds, so I'll have to update my review later with better impressions. Still, the gunshots sounded good and the voice acting was also pretty solid, but limited.
And of course, there's plenty of room for improvements: the AI, for example, needs some work. I also frequently got stuck in the doorway/between the doors and got shot that way.
The camera is too low/has a funny angle so it's sometimes hard to see. I understand this adds to a tense atmosphere, but it doesn't always work as far as gameplay is concerned. Obviously, real cops also never know what can happen so, again, I understand the choice, but when I stand in a large room with 4 or 5 enemies that I could've easily killed if only the camera gave me more room then, for me, it's a bad choice. Hopefully they'll improve it in the future.
Also, the UI is clumsy. If I select an agent I want to instantly see their stats. I don't want to click on another button to just see that. For upgrading them it makes complete sense, but their stats can easily be shown on the character selection screen.
And I also confused the ammo bar with the health bar while playing, but that could also be me not paying enough attention and wanting to just jump in.
And yes, we all know this is work in progress and I'm sure lots of things will change in the next couple of months, and lots of stuff will also be added so I can't tell you yet if it will be worth the money, but for now I will absolutely recommend it.
I'll try and update this review to reflect future changes and additions and that way keep it as accurate as possible.

They always say you shouldn't judge a book by it's cover, but that doesn't mean the cover is never accurate. One look at ♥♥♥♥♥daria 2 tells you everything you need to know about it. This is the lowest of the low-rent Symphony of the Night imitations, hacked together with little or no attention to detail. Game balance is going to be all over the place, levels aren't going to make much sense, and the art is going to be a slideshow of MSPaint doodles. The nicest thing I will say about it, and I mean this, is that there's a not completely terrible game hiding in here somewhere, and if everything I just said didn't put you off, you might actually find it.
The game opens with a rousing intro featuring a butchered rendition of the DIE MONSTER opening of Symphony, establishing your goal of wresting a bag of infinite potato chips from a wizard. You can be a ninja or a swordsman on this quest through a sprawling, sparsely-decorated castle of zombies and spikes. As you delve deeper and defeat basic bosses like recolored enemies, you'll pick up magic spells and items that allow you to move about the castle more freely and grab those pesky powerups that were always just out of reach.
Parody is the name of the game here, pretty obvious between the potato chip wizard and the useless crayon castle map you get at the start. The first boss you fight is a recolor of a regular enemy and says as much when you face him, and all the other bosses accuse you of killing their sibling at some point. None of the parody is actually worked into the game itself, mind you, it's all just layered uselessly on top of a flimsy framework. This needs to be rule #1 for anyone trying to make a parody game, you need the humor woven through everything, the enemies and items and game flow included, not just tacked on in scenes that try way too hard. Actually rule #1 is "Don't make parody games, what the hell is wrong with you" but that other thing I said makes a good rule #2.
Once you get past the forced humor, you're left with an extremely sparse metroidvania that's going to take you an hour to beat, if you have the fortitude. There's something like six areas of the castle, each with health, magic, and mobility upgrades to find. The ninja ones include a double-jump and a super jump that both make him invincible for a second, not exactly groundbreaking but at least a little interesting. Magic is just tossing fires or boulders, and is used to open certain paths. The freezer area is unique in that it does constant damage to you unless you have a scarf item, but is also entirely beatable without it. Most of the bosses are brain-dead easy but a few of them have way, way too much health, including the final boss which is an unpleasant hike in difficulty.
I can see little hints of decent gameplay here and there, and honestly outside of the awful forced humor, it's not an awful game. There's a castle to explore and items to get and monsters to fight and it all works, if not terribly pretty or polished or balanced. ♥♥♥♥♥daria 2 would make a great student project or practice game before pulling together a team for a real release, but as a retail project I can't possibly recommend it. If the developer is reading this then I implore you, focus less on humor (as in not at all) and more on game mechanics. Do that and hire an artist, and I bet you could come up with something I could recommend.

Authentic, believable, and abseloutely faithful to the ways of the old west, Bound in Blood is the most realistic and complete FPS experience of the old world to date. All the guns, buildings, attires, accents and entities are expertly recreated. The graphics are the breakthrough variety that helped inspire games like Crysis 2 and Far Cry 3. The gameplay is top notch. Concentration mode is improved upon from the previous Call of Juarez and lets the game perform the shooting once you've picked out the targets with Ray, or use  the mouse properly with Thomas.
In terms of story, Bound in Blood delivers a compelling adventure, a riveting quest for glory and restoration mixed with greed and betrayal. A little short and the end could have been extended, but a game worth the both the money and the effort needed to play it.
However, history buffs, beware, the Colt single action army  used in the game hadn't been invented yet, nor had the Winchester model you see in the game. Bound in Blood is somewhat inaccurate in terms of time period weapons, but they're well designed, nonetheless.

At the moment I heavily recomend this game, though I haven't fully cleared it (when I do I will update this review). If you're a lontime fan of the rougelike/rougelite genera you should have no qualms with picking this game up for full price, if you're new and your skeptical then I would still recomend picking up full price but if you have a tight budget then consider putting it on your wishlist and picking it up when you find the funds or when it goes on sale.
As a cavieat to that I will say that if you haven't played rougelike/rougelite games that you should understand what those labels mean. This type of game will challenge you and it will frustrate you, but if your patient and dedicated then you will find that the feeling you get when you push past whatever was holding you back before is one of the most rewarding things you'll experience in gaming.
General Gameplay:
The gameplay of this game is increadibly fun and while it's difficulty can be frustrating at times, like many games in the rougelike/rougelite it's increadibly rewarding when you do finally manage to beat whatever you might have gotten stuck on before. The controls are very smooth and responsive and everything works as described. I haven't encountered any bugs or glitches so far.
Design Of Levels & Enemies:
The design of the enemies/levels/rooms/hazards/bosses is such that there is a very smooth difficulty curve. You really never find yourself in a position where the game is impossible to beat and you will never find yourself in a position where your victory is assured. Yes, because of the RNG involved in the game you will find that some runs are easier and some runs are harder, but every run win is a victory earned and every defeat will be something in the end you can only really blame on yourself and mistakes you've made.
My only gripe about the level design is that the procedural engine requires that the levels broken into linear branches. I.E. if a room has two diffrent doors that lead to two diffrent branches then those branches won't meet up again even if two rooms in those branches end up touching later on. Though it doesn't really distract from gameplay so it's a really minor thing.
Story/Atmosphere/Theme:
The atmosphere of this game is increadibly compelling with an artstyle and soundtrack that while simple are quite compelling. The theme is very dark and sinister and after more and more of the backstory is revealed about diffrent enemies and bosses and about the games world in general you'll find yourself wondering what exactly happened in the halls of Edgewood before Cordy woke up after the encounter again and what is really going on in the school.
I have noticed many people commenting about the game's story feeling unfinished, but I can't really comment on that due to the fact that I haven't actually finished the game yet.
My only advice in that regard is that if you do get this game that you should keep playing, the end might not exactly be where you thought it was and it might take a few more runs through before you can get to it. That's something I learned that plesantly surprised me.
Replayability:
The game like many of the more recent additions of this genera is predicated on being replayable. You will try and fail multiple times before you're finally able to succeed, and when you do succeed you'll unlock new content that will give you a reason to play through a few more times.
The game also has a system where you can customize your character to a degree between runs. This is not only something that is nessary for you to do to be able to get through to the endgame content, but it's also something that allows you to experiment with competley diffrent playstyles and turn the game into something diffrent. An example of this would be that after you complete the prerequisite challenge and then unlock the option with the games credit system you can change Cordy's dodge roll into a blink. Another example of this is the option to drastically increase Cordy's health pool at the start for the downside of not being able to replenish your health normally. There are a number of big changes you can make like those as well as a very large number of minor tweeks you can make as well.
As I mentioned in the above paragraph there are a multitude of challenges in the game and they all reward something, be that additonal credits, lore, item unlocks, character options, or even staight character upgrades. Some of them are rather simple, while others are diaboliclly difficult. If you are a completionist you will not be wanting for something to do with this game. Though if I remember correctly there is one specific challenge regarding the champion cat enemy that can appear that is either bugged or is just virtually impossible because the chance of finding that particular variant is effectivley zero.
Oh, and did I mention that this game also has a hard mode for those of among us who might find the base games content too easy? I haven't tried it myself, so I can't speak about it, but whenever finish the game's base content then I'll be sure to let you know if it's balanced as well as the rest of the game.
tl;dr
This game is better than Binding of Issac, and this is coming from someone who has completed the original Binding of Issac and has 100% cleared Binding of Issac Rebirth and it's Afterbirth DLC (currently working on Afterbirth+ so I can leave a proper review on that game)

Comparisons to The Binding of Isaac are unavoidable, but Our Darker Purpose is no clone. While the rogue-like elements, dark tone, and general playstyle are certainly similar, ODP adds plenty of new elements to the formula. Any resemblances to the 2011 indie hit should be considered characteristics of this new genre. The first thing veteran BOI players will notice is that the individual rooms are different sizes, the majority of them significantly larger than before. Visibility then becomes more of an issue and - combined with a reduced movement speed - positioning Cordy around obstacles becomes more critical. This is reenforced by a roll mechanic that increases movement speed for a short time after dodging.
The leveling system and the more persistent credit system makes for an experience that leans on its RPG elements rather than the arcade-like variability BOI relies on. Each level up is rewarded with a choice between two power-ups, keeping things random while providing an opportunity for strategy. Credits allow for even more control with consistent upgrades, but in turn encourage grinding to get a better chance of overcoming the challenge at hand. And those advantages are needed as the developer has specifically stated that parts of this game were meant to give even Platinum God BOI players a run for their money.
While the feeling of a desperate and narrow survival invoked by all the challenge, randomization, and even the permadeath suits the game's narrative perfectly, the richness of Edgewood's story struggles to be told through the long string of failed runs required to learn a new set of patterns and terrain. Repetition allows for a greater ability to strategize; however, ODP does not avoid tedium like BOI does. Don't get me wrong, the enemies themselves are a joy to learn and become familiar with. Each is distinct and varied, most even possessing a rare champion version which adds yet another layer of complexity. Each new room is chosen from a list of predesigned rooms meaning strategies can be formulated not just around particular enemies, but also particular combinations of enemies in specific surroundings. Overall the game is a slow build that pays off wonderfully, the only frustration is a result of impatiently hunting for the next tidbit of such an enticing story.

It should be noted that this game is a work-in-progress to a game which the developers deem ideal, and that progress in making the game is slow. Hopefully this will become true and the developers make the game they could be proud to present as a complete game.

Is it fun? Yes. So why do I not recomend it? Because I could be playing a handful of other Rogue-Lites that do this better. BoI has more items, more characters, more bad guys, more variance and that adds up to more replayability.

This game has style, a lot of it. It's fun throughout and hit the right part of the imagination so many games miss these days. It has a dingy street vibe accompanied by the neo-cyberpunk fit. Inspirations like Johnny The Homicidal Maniac and The Maxx come to mind. It's right down my alley and I give it a 9/10.
Technical Impressions: First playthrough I had a lot of tearing I couldn't figure out even with vsync on, so I was quite distracted by it and this game deserves to be played without any hindrances to quality. After digging around on the internet I found a fix for the tearing (Aero desktop settings have to be on in Windows7, weird but it got rid of all the tearing). There's not a lot of advanced settings for the graphics, but if you have a newer rig you shouldn't run into any slowing due to hardware.
Gameplay is fluid and easy to follow, level layouts are randomly generated to give it a good amount of replay value. Graphics and sound aren't the best, but this game unloads with a resounding style and the retro-fit of the quaility gives it a certain charm many developers don't understand. I don't know what to say, I'm going to cut it short but this game is an instant classic tickling many sub-genres in my mind and deserves to be on par with some of the most style-defining classics like Clive Barker's Undying.

Very scary and atmospheric, with some impressive graphics and  design. The levels are randomly generated each time you start over (which will be a LOT at first ... it's hard!), but it's executed with such care that each new layout feels like it's been lovingly hand crafted by a team of artists just to scare the pants off of you.
The game still has some rough corners that you'd expect from a pre-release. Once or twice I saw a monster walking into a wall. And sometimes it can be a bit difficult to gauge when you are hitting a monster in melee.
As mentioned earlier, the game is punishing, so I wasn't able to see much of the story, though that looks promising (I like the Lovecraftian theme in a Kowloon City setting).
This certainly doesn't play like your typical FPS, and not your typical Survival Horror either. The pacing and tension in the game feel different from anything else I've played. Because of permadeath you have to be ALWAYS alert. But because of the randomly generated levels, you don't mind starting over when you do inevitably fail.
So, if being scared silly is your thing ... then this game is definitely worth checking out.

Nostalgia is a funny thing, I first played Far Cry back in 2006 or something on my first PC I'd ever owned. It was a Dell Laptop and could only run the game at minimum setting but I could bump the resolution up so at the time I remember thinking it looked amazing. Far Cry does not hold up to the test of time in terms of Graphics as we've become accustomed to much better looking games but it is 10 years old at this point so thats acceptable. I remember the game being more serious but with all the action movies I've seen and the modern shooters I've played since then it felt very corny which is not a bad thing just goes to show how your mind changes over time and under different circumstances.
I discovered a few different things playing it this time around. There are Bugs and they are noticeable such as emeries shooting through tents. Secondly the game is harder then I remember, like... MUCH HARDER.... on NORMAL, I died a lot and in a few cases I had to go back a checkpoint to make sure I had more health and armor but I got through it in 8.8 hours so I guess it wasn’t too bad. What I put this down to is I'm more impatient then I was back when I was a kid which I can put down to the conditioning process of modern gameplay.
On the positives it’s a nice change of pace to go back to a game that uses Health and Armor that you have to find and collect. Every modern shooter uses the whole health regen which from a gameplay perspective I understand but the good thing about having to find health kits is you need to be aware of your health at all times and maintain it through-out the level.
Ammo was never really an issue, Sniper and Rockets can be difficult to find as they only spawn sometimes in armories and from dead enemies who have that weapon. In the other side of things Rocket Enemies were by far the most annoying enemies to face the moment they spot you... from all the way across the map they fire rockets at you which do a TON of damage and if you’re in a vehicle and don’t realize you just blow up.
It's pretty normal that I would spot all the issues with the game this time around and not back when I first played it. I only had a few games back then such as Warcraft 3, Call of Duty 1 and Star Wars Battlefront 1 so I couldn't really pick and choose and just had to enjoy what I had, I was also like 10 so I didn't even know what a "bug" was xD
Multiplayer is non-existent, I remember playing it a few times over LAN with my friends and it was fun.

I LOVE IT! It's a realtime squad based tactical shooter where you can switch between two different cops with the press of a button and the AI takes over the other to shoot but not move. This means you meove your cop into position and face him/her in a direction to cover a doorway or corner and then move the other cop into position, leapfrogging and so on. It makes for fun, tense situations and surprises. Occasionally panicked shootouts occur but most of the time you feel like a badass methodically moving through the building taking out bad guys with one shot. You can pick up their weapons, like shotguns, micro-uzi(semi auto), M79 thumper grenade launcher, M16 assault rifle, and more in the full game I believe. It plays like a combination between a top down/Iso version of Hitman meets Hotline Miami. In fact, It's a LOT like Hotline Miami with two switchable characters. It would be a ton of fun if it was co-op, which I am hoping they find a way to add.
The art and music are great. The weapons are satisfying to shoot. The AI is pretty decent already with a few rare idiot moments like getting caught on a doorway, but good overall. The polish of design and mission structure is very good.
Now for the bad.......there's not enough of it. Once again an early access game launches with not much more than a proof of concept. I love the game and look forward to it, but I'm not super comfortable with them charging $12 for 1 level of a game that may not get finished if sales aren't decent. I think developers(I am one) need to start being realistic about what they are asking of consumers. Don't ask us to pay full or even half price for a game with less content than a demo that may never be finished. This game once complete would be worth $14 to most of us at most. It will most likely live at $9.99 after it's first month on the market and I feel it should really be priced around that now.
The one mission included, Level 5 of 9, has four stages and takes about 20 minutes to play through. I can see myself playing through maybe another 3 times if I get bored. That's an hour of gameplay. I spoke to the developer on the forums and they are awesome, open and friendly. They are not hiding anything and have been wonderful in everyway. It is for that reason that I don't regret my purchase and I can recommend the game to you all. The price is subjective.......great game, little content now.....your choice. They did say they hope to have monthly updates.  I can't wait for the full release.

I believe this game deserves a positive review, but instead of just saying some stupid comment or offering my worthless opinion, here is the quick and dirty (Though slightly biases) of everything you need to know about BL:R from my experience.
Positives:
+Fun Arena shooter gameplay
+quick rounds, resonable damage model
+FULL weapon customization, a wide array of weapons and attachments so you can make your weapons perform exactly how you want it to
+diverse arsenal, something for everybody
+depot system where you can do things like refilling your health and ammo and spawning various heavy weapons to imposing EXO Suits with points you earn by killing enemies and completing objective in the match
+Lots of different Gear to select, so you can make your own custom classes (Ever wanted to be an armor laden medic with a heavy machine gun?)
+Fun with friends, can lead to some fun tactical gameplay
+no obviously "broken" weapons, equipments, or armor.
+re-worked UI is much easier to navigate than before
+Good Graphics
Neutral, but necessary information:
=Decent maps, but nothing to write home about
=PvE content is severely lacking, though PvP is still very fun once you get the hang of it
=Small, but very active community

Beautiful, tense, and moving.
Yes, the game is short, and it should be short--nothing would have been gained by dragging out any element of this wonderfully crystalized story. It could easily have been ruined by a misguided attempt to extend gameplay, but thankfully, it doesn't overstay its welcome. It is possible to get very slightly lost in a couple areas, but none of the them are really big enough for this to reach frustrating levels. It is pretty much always clear what you need to do--the tricky part is typically steeling yourself to leave the safety of your hiding spot and do it. Saying this game has "puzzles" is a bit of stretch. There is nothing in this game that would strain the ingenuity of --ahem-- a two-year old. At times it feels a little like a walking simulator, scary hiding sections nonwithstanding. None of the above is meant as a bad thing; this is a story-oriented game, and its gameplay mechanics serve the story admirably.
Many have commented on its similarity to works by Frictional Games, such as Amnesia. And yes, it is true that this game emphasizes your vulnerability and requires you to hide a lot, but really, what do want when the protagonist is a 2-year old? A baby bazooka? The world in this game is strange, magical, and often frightening, just as two-year old would see it. The mundane is new and interesting, rules are arbitrary, and frightening things really can hurt you. Any little kid knows this, which is why most of them will start crying over things which seem inconsequential or at least managable to adults. The sense of tension and the mechanics are very similar to the style pioneered by the folks at Frictional, but this game makes those mechanics its own, and the feeling of the game is quite different.
I'd estimate it will take you between 1.5-3 hours to finish this game, depending on how personally vulnerable you are to this particular brand of horror--if you just go straight through, it is possible to finish very quickly, but you could very well spend half your playtime exploring the nooks and crannies of the gameworld, or cowering under tables and chairs. Possibly my biggest quibble with the game is that there isn't more opportunity to do more of the first. It does make for a more focused game experience, but I enjoyed the little details they built in, and would have liked to have seen more of them. (The playroom in the beginning had a nice variety of toys, but why weren't there more things in the house to make a mess with?) The interacting controls are Amnesia-style, and sometimes a bit clunky, especially when trying to do fine manipulation. I could write this off as an accurate reproduction of a child's manipulation skills, but I think the controls just needed more work from the development team.
Graphically, the game is not ultra-realistic, but nonetheless very pretty. There is a slight issue with clipping, but it's not terrible, and it certainly doesn't affect the gameplay. Teddy, in my opinion, looks unnecessarily creepy, but it could just be that talking teddy bears are instrincally creepy.
Don't let any of my minor criticisms turn you off. It won't be everyone's cup of tea (nothing is), but this is an excellent game, and it may perhaps leave you with slightly more empathy for any young children you may know. I found it deeper than most video games, and very scary. I highly recommend it.

As a huge Total War fan, I have to say that Empire is my favorite.
What's Good
-Theaters of War
I thought that the different theaters (India, Americas, Europe as well as all the trading nodes) were very well done and really help immerse you in the feeling that you're creating a powerful global empire. I loved being able to monopolize trade resources both through trade nodes and colonies overseas. I hope to see a return to this in future total wars, as its been abandoned since (due largely to subsequent games taking place in earlier time periods, except Napoleon)
-Giant campaign map.
Its not the biggest and it doesnt have the most settlements as compared to other total wars, but the variety of locations and ability to send your navies and bring armies anywhere makes this game a lot of fun.
-Gunpowder era armies.
Total war has had gunpowder units in the past, but Empire, set in the 18th century was the first time they were a necessity and the backbone of an army. I thought this was a really cool addition to the total war series because of this as well. AI wise, Napoleon cleaned up a lot of Empire's mess when it comes to battles, both siege and land, as Empire had some glitchy AI and unit response problems.
-NAVAL BATTLES.
The naval battles in Empire were very well done. Of all total wars with playable naval battles I find Empire to be the most interesting and rewarding. Destroying an enemy ship's sails and masts with chain shot and coming back to finish them off with round or grapeshot is thoroughly satisfying and realistic as well. If you are skilled enough you can easily take out a much larger and more powerful fleet with only one or two ships, and I like that.
-Technology
I think all Total War fans appreciate the introduction of technology into the series by Empire! Technology and research gives a whole new aspect to the game, as you now have a new way to get ahead of your enemies militarily and economically. Its not about just making money and building bigger buildings to recruit better units, research requirements help balance a nations ambitions and ascent to dominance well and give other bonuses as well
What's Bad
-AI Battle Glitches (Specifically the Siege Glitch)
During fortified siege battles in which the AI is defending, you WILL experience ridiculous FRUSTRATING FPS drops after you break down a section of wall. This is due to the genius and decisive AI issuing 50000000000 commands at once to certain units, as it is confused about what happened to its lovely walls. If you can see the enemies units, you should notice one or a few fidgeting around in place, as the AI is telling them to run and then halt at the same time, resulting in unit wide seizures. The only way to stop this that I've found is to move your units into the fort or close enough to the point that they decide to come and fight you. Once the unit is activated the problem immediately resolves itself. Many other glitches persist too during battles. Unresponsive units, artillery units being unable to reman their guns, etc. AI wise, Napoleon cleaned up a lot of Empire's mess when it comes to battles, both siege and land.
-Maratha the Conqueror (The Orange Horde)
In response to complaints from players that the Maratha Confederacy was too passive, CA decided to address this in a patch, and in their infinite wisdom, turned the Marathas into a ROFLstomp machine. By the time they have defeated the Mughals and united India, they'll blitzkrieg Persia and the Ottoman Empire, and pursue Europe that way while sending multiple stacks to the Americas. In my Spain playthrough I had a trade agreement and alliance with them and we were "Very Friendly"....yes "Very Friendly" and they show up to Mexico with 2 full stacks, land another in the Bahamas and have a huge navy just chilling in the Caribbean. All in one turn. Fun, fun
-Overpowered AI on Legendary
Legendary mode gives the AI nations a slew of ridiculous economic and morale benefits and curses you at the same time. I owned most of the world in a campaign as the Marathas except for mainland europe from france-lithuania. In said area, the Poles had created a mega impenetrable empire-fortress, literally with at least 30 stacks ( some 3/4, most full) and that was just from what I could see around the borders and with my spies. These were no militia, they were winged Hussars, elite infantry and cannons most of which had around 4xp. There was no way except for the fact that they're just given money every turn and don't have to pay upkeep that they would ever be able to afford these armies. I sued for peace to rethink my strategy because they were absolutely unbeatable, and 5 turns later they came to India with 3 full stacks and navies, while pushing back against my borders in romania and all along easter europe, super blitzing me. The AI is also hyper sensitive and aggressive, usually many far away nations you barely have contact with will declare war on you in the first few turns for no reason, and any nation you get close to, even if you were destroying their enemy who borders them, will declare war on you shortly after.
-Random save file corruption, crashes.
Several times in different campaigns, the game would crash upon end turn, other times certain events would trigger crashes. One time I was playing as Spain on legendary and had control of India, most of western europe, north africa and the americas conquered. I was working on taking out Persia, and everytime I took control of their capital the game would immediately crash. I ended up giving them a peace treaty just so I would'nt have to give up on the campaign, but that only bought me a few turns before it crashed on end turn..
End conclusion
Empire Total war has its pillars and its flaws. For me, it has been my favorite total war all the way through Attila because of the time period and sheer size of the world, your ability to colonize far away lands, monopolize trade resources, variety of factions and naval battles. Empire feels like its own separate Total War unlike any of the others, and I'm glad CA took it in that direction of world exploitation and conquerage as opposed to a single theater, and I hope one day there will be a sequel!

I definitely recommend this game when you can get it on sale for at least 50% off, and the graphics and especially the sound design are pretty good and work well with the game’s theme, but it mostly just feels like a ‘good start’ for the developers and there needs to be more of a game next time around.
