I'm not a big FPS fan but I really enjoyed this game. Got it cheap and had many hours of fun. I would the describe the levels as sandbox-corridors. The levels overall were fairly linear, but most levels had breathing room and were wide open for experimentation with the ways you could approach combat. There are plenty of opportunities for vehicle/boat-based combat, but I found navigating the vehicles too cumbersome to really enjoy driving and shooting at the same time (especially the land vehicles).
Played on Medium difficulty and it was definitively challenging. The game sometimes seems to steer you towards a stealth-based approach, but I didn't see any real mechanics to actually support stealth. Enemies could spot you really easily in thick brush or when you're far away, hear you even when you're approaching in crouch. and were ridiculously accurate when firing. Plus, you only carry a machete if you sacrifice a weapon spot. There really should've been a dedicated knife button or slot. So usually I would tag as many combatants as I could from afar with the binoculars, pick off the closest enemies or the most dangerous ones with available sniper ammo, rockets and grenades, and then charge in to mop up with the shotgun or machine guns. The game does a great job of slyly adding better weapons as the levels progress, so you never get too bored if you're paying attention and trying new guns. Used the TILDE key constantly to save the game via console. The auto-save spots were too infrequent.
I enjoyed the enemy variety. You start off fighting vanilla mercenaries, and the game introduces different enemies and varieties throughout. Fun addition to game was that one group of enemies was constantly fighting another, and they'd only pause battle so both could attack you. Levels that included three-way combat were great.
The story and characters are goofy fun. The way the game's plot reveals itself slowly over the 20-ish levels was well done, and maybe I'm dense but there was a twist near the end I didn't see coming. I was pleasantly surprised. The voice acting was hit and miss, but I thought the voice actor for Doyle the scientist did a great job, which is vital since he essentially narrates the game.
Played 30+ hours, experienced zero crashes or noticeable bugs. Very stable game. Graphics were great for a game this old, and I really enjoyed the overall look of the island/sea setting. Crytek's specialty is advanced graphics and its reputation is well earned here.
Give this game a chance if you haven't already, it's great fun. It's also a lengthy game so it's a great value proposition.

This game was one of my early childhood favourites, if only for the fact that my father couldn't play the game without god mode, and whenever I stepped in I would easily get around his problem.
Farcry is different from all of its offspring in the sense that Farcry focuses on a semi-linear path. While you are still out in the jungle trying to survive, you always have a sense of where you need to go. However, this game is brutal on new players, and still is brutal on me today.
Pros:
- Semi-linear path, with only one objective. You always know what you are doing.
- The first game in its series, and if I must say, my personal favourite.
- Despite an out-of-date engine, it still easily supports modern hardware and operating systems
- Several hours of gameplay guaranteed. Several days of gameplay highly probable.
Cons:
- Outdated engine: This is evident in vehicles and aiming instantly. While it doesn't prevent you from winning, it will be very off-putting if you just came out of a more modern game.
- Outdated Graphics: Grass is a lot more annoying than it would be in modern games, and the lack of detail speaks for itself as you walk through bases and foliage.
- Difficulty is a bit intense: Players may find themselves dying over and over simply because they made a poor decision earlier on, or messed something up, even on easy. Thankfully each checkpoint creates its own save, meaning you can roll back until you think you stand a chance.

Ok, before people asking why I make a review to a game in which I have 0 hours...
I played this already hundreds of hours I guess. Not on Steam and with mods. FCAM mostly.
Back when I played it, it wasnt even on Steam and I played one of the first proper 64Bit games, with patch.
You are Jack Carver and you are on a trip to a island.
Unexptected your companion disappears and you get attacked by mercs. You have to escape onto the island.
You are swimming and a grenade explosion underwater throws you into a tunnel and you get unconscious.
You wake up in a old sewer and need to escape. You fast meet a guy called Doyle which seems to want to help you.
He gives you cordinates and tips how to survive and what to do. So your trip over the big island starts.
The gameplay is a classical FPS shooter. Located in a openworld tropical island most of the time. You have several wespons like a knife, pistol, machine gun or sniper to fight against the enemies. You will meet many on your way over the island and the interesting is that they are quite inteligent, especially for old 2004 enemies. There also some sort of mutant enemies next to the typical mercs but those come later into the game. You also have some sort of spy glasses to mark enemies on your map marker or just check the situation. On your way you sometimes also can use cars. Thats pretty much it. Simple but extremely well made, especially for 2004.
The engine is the CryEngine. Back in 2004 this was one of the best looking games out then and it really changed the way of FPS shooters. Well, notably together with HL2 which came out around the same time.
Also this was the first game of a German developer named Crytek. Which is also known for the Crysis series.
This game has nothing to do with the Ubisoft Far Cry games like 2,3,4.
The only thing they have in common is that they are FPS. Dont make this mistake please!
The graphics are extremely good for the time and even today it somewhat still looks good or decent at least.
All graphic options you can imagine are ingame. There are even Render options ingame with that you can let the game for example look like a cartoon game! Rarely I seen such options in games! Far Cry turns into Borderlands. Also sound settings are extremely advanced! Extremely good and well made PC game. There is also a 64Bit patch available. You need to install it extra though. I personally recommend using the mod FCAM instead. Delivers pretty much the same graphical enhancements. On the top there are even more graphical improvements. This mod really pushes the engine to its real limit. Even my HD 5870 some years ago couldnt handle it on 60FPS on maxed settings, 1080p and 4xAA. For the fact that the game was like 6 years or more old this was astonishing. FCAM also adds proper ironisghts which work really good! Also it fixes many of the annoying bugs like enemies which can shoot through objects and hit you...
FCAM is a must have! Even for first time players! Grab the latest 1.999 version on moddb guys!
Positive:

- Really good FPS experience
- Challenging difficulty, good enemy AI
- No regenerating health!
- Great graphics with many options
- Mod FCAM makes the game even better and makes it "perfect"
- Crytek! Because yes!
Negative:
- Difficulty is high
- Multiplayer is dead as of 2014. Gamespy is down but it was never played that much in MP anyway
Replayability: High
Rating: 9.5/10

Phantasmal
Randomly-generated Survival Horror
Eyemobi Ltd.
Eyemobi Ltd.
is a first-person randomly-generated survival horror game in Early Access developed and published by Eyemobi Ltd. The game will have AI improvements, procedural generated story, NPC interaction and more notes, endings and polish, so keep this in mind while reading/watching this review.
The game is heavily influenced by the Cthulhu Mythos by H.P. Lovecraft (which I love), and the monster design and notes scattered throughout remind you of them. However, there isn't much story to judge in the current state of the game: the developers said that they will tie the game more to Cthulhu and all that good stuff. So far, all we know is that you are in Kowloon Walled City before its destruction in the early 90s.
As Unity games go, this looks good. The Motion Blur is quite aggressive, so I highly recommend turning it off after you start the game. The monster design is interesting, and the deeper you explore, the more varied they get. The environment has been crafted by Brian Bell, lightning director of movies like
and
, and they look dark and eerie. There is currently little variety to some rooms, but it can be easily improved.
The goal of the game is to go from one point of the map to an elevator, to further descend into madness (see what I did there?). The game map is randomly-generated, and the best approach against the monsters is to stealth your way through by crouching and staying out of lit areas. As far as weapons go, so far I only found a handgun (M1911 to be precise), a shotgun, a wooden board and a metal pipe. The guns can be found in locked cases scattered around the map, and they can be opened by finding keys that are usually hidden inside a box or a cabinet.
If you cause a lot of noise, you will startle a Cthulhu-like monster: more noise you make, more angry he'll be, until he starts chasing you, and there is no way to kill him and hide from him because he is using a noclip cheat code.
While the game is not scary, it does get really intense when you are carefully strafing near a monster, hoping that he doesn't feel you. You will also die really easily, making stealth and sprinting skills that you will develop really fast.
Unlike most modern horror games, the game brings back the survival horror that I like: you should avoid the monsters, but if you get seen you have at least some resources to fend them off for a while. You are also not overpowered: melee weapons break after ten hits, ammos are scarce and monsters are aplenty.
Unfortunately, it got a little frustrating a couple of times: sometimes enemies would just spawn right in my face, or some times there were just too many of them in the way. Also, every time you die you will spawn back at the first level. These are just some annoyances that might turn off some gamers, but if you can look past them you will have a good time.
Nothing to write home about: the sound of the monsters are generic, and the music is pretty weak. However, hearing your footsteps and the monsters' immerse you further into the game's dark corridors.
Lots of good stuff here: there are currently five levels (more will be added) and 10 achievements, as well as the constantly different environments. You also have to take into account that it will be updated in the next few months.
Overall,
has a great start as far as Early Access games go, and the developers always answer even the most little of problems or questions. The atmosphere is good, the gameplay is solid. If you like this type of games, you should buy it.

Phantasmal is a unique and unexpectedly addictive new indie horror game. Set in the backdrop of Kowloon Walled City, the game provides a compelling take on one of the 20th century’s most interesting communities. The best strategy in this game is usually stealth rather than killing everything that moves. Of course, in many situations fighting is unavoidable, and smacking a walker in the face with a two-by-four is immensely satisfying:)
They got the visuals, music, and sound effects just right to build up a truly creepy atmosphere. The procedurally generated maps makes each play-through unique so you can’t anticipate what’s around any corner, adding to the fear factor in this game.

Playing this at early access steam launch, so keep that in mind!
If I had to describe my experience with this game in one word, I'd use the term "Potential". Solid foundation to build on, set on becoming great by the end of the journey.
The setting is the star of the show. Kowloon City is an excellent location to base a horror game around. If you watch documentaries on it, you'll know how crazy the construction was in the Walled City. A fact which surprisingly fits the procedurally generated maps element quite well. Justice is done to the setting, fits the atmosphere quite right in my opinion. With more variety potentially added down the development road, it can be one of the most interesting places to visit in a video game.
The presentation itself takes a little getting used to. The sound design is excellent but visually, the motion blur and flare effects can prove to be irksome initially. However, once past the barrier, you do start to appreciate it. It ties quite well with the gameplay elements and provides for a more immersive experience.
The gameplay is good, with a decent amount of variety already in the game. Primarily, the focus is on stealth; the objective of each level being to find the exit of the map. Though, you do have some leeway and can kill some of the monsters if you chose to. Be warned though, make too much noise and you'll awaken the Sleeper. You cannot hide or fight him once he's awakened. Your only chance is finding the exit, fast! A prospect which from my experience, was seldom met with success xD.
A neat feature which I'm a huge fan of is the possibility of you losing your sanity. Light can be your best ally or your worst enemy. You have to use vision smartly. Flash your torch at the wrong creature and you will go crazy, leaving you disorientated, fast. Doom is almost certain in these moments. There are light switches to turn on and flares to throw (Can distract certain monsters), so you have a lot to think about each time you turn a corner!
Exploration is encouraged as you may find written notes that help build the picture of the tale that explains what caused the Walled City's doom. Plus, you'll have a chance of finding items or weapons that'll aid you in your ways. Though, with you being constanly being on edge due to fear, I rarely found myself taking the adventrous route xD. With the generated maps, each area of each run you play will hold something different! Things may turn out in your favour one time but completely screw you over in the next moment xD. Keeps the experience fresh every time.
I will reiterate that I am playing this at early access launch. I did encounter a game bug or two, but generally nothing major which is worth mentioning. I'm confident the little nitpicks will be fixed as development goes on. Though, I would like to see a better options menu in the near future.
To sum it up, I can safely recommend this game to people interested by the premise. As of right now, it has good value attached to it. With more tweaks and additions coming in future updates, it has the potential to become a great product in the horror genre.

An evil version of the wayside school looms in a vast depressing void where you the player will guide a seemingly innocent fire ball girl named Cordy, who recently had all her friends murdered when all the adults vanished, through a school filled with psychopathic orphanage/boarding school students up an irrational amount of floors to seek answers from the entity known as the administrators. Cordy is destined to die many times, but still mysteriously can restart her journey a bit differently every death afterwards. In the afterlife you can take classes which if equipped give different abilities to help you on your journey.
Pros:
•	The boss fights are epic and each requires a different strategy for beating them.
•	The story is one of the best I’ve seen in videogames with a lot of world building, secrets, and interesting characters, but not many people will find that out because of the lore/memory room system.  This game’s story is mysterious and is slowly fed to the player over time through boss battles and memory rooms (more on that later).
•	The gothic pencil drawn art style is unique and really makes ODP stand out.

•	There’s tons of content and gameplay mechanics to master.
•	Understanding and strategizing juice box health management and exactly how to approach a screen are key here. Much more about item management and survival than running and gunning, so this is much more slowly paced than many top down shooters.
•	There are tons of different challenges that give you access to new items, classes to you if you beat them and also encourage experimentation in what items to buy and how you approach bosses.

•	The game definitely has a good sense of humor which is mainly shown through the Administrators who make sarcastic comments in a very GLaDOS like way.
•	The class system allows a variety of different lessons to equip which significantly alter the way you play. You can run a crit build, a juice box build, a chalk build, there’s a lot to choose from, but you have to unlock the classes first.
Cons:
•	The various pieces props like the potatoes, furniture, rocks, and pipes have strange clipping detection and more than once I’ve got stuck on one of their sides when trying to roll away from an enemy.
•	Certain important aspects of the game like the class/period system and memory rooms are not explained and huge parts of the game can be missed out on.
•	There is a high skill ceiling on this game, more so than with the Binding of Isaac. Many people will get stuck on the Woundwort Dormitory which is the first difficulty spike and will feel like they can’t progress causing them to stop playing. Most of the fun items, abilities, and the majority of the story are beyond this first spike of difficulty so a lot of players are going to stop playing before they even crack the surface and actually know what the game is all about. I played this game off and on for more than a year before actually beating it, so you either have to be good or have enough patience.
•	The majority of the power ups in this game are very boring and scarce, whereas with Binding of Isaac almost every power up alters the game and your appearance in a major way ODP’s power ups are more conservative like with damage, speed, and drop boosts that don’t alter appearances at all. The power ups in ODP that aren’t stat boosts like the classes and items are still pretty boring besides a select few.
•	Some may think that after a while all the environments look the same and become boring.
•	The Shakespeare references to King Lear and Romeo and Juliet don’t have any strong parallels to the plot and as a result are pointless.
•	Hard mode for me at least isn’t even really fun, with my skill level there are only a couple builds and items that let me get anywhere, so it always feels constrictive and dependent on RNG.
Things I wish I knew: Our Darker Purpose doesn’t explain things well sometimes, and those omitted instructions kept me from progressing and understanding the story for a long time. Hopefully now you can understand the game immediately with these slick reminders.
Memory Rooms: There are these ghost librarians called Archivists which occasionally walk from room to room on certain floors. You’re supposed to follow them and when they walk into a wall you can go inside that wall also. Through that wall is a memory room where there are either props scattered through the room which you can investigate with the E button to find coins and important lore pages or an Archivist to fight which drops lore or items. The game never tells the player they can walk through the wall after the Archivists and go to a secret room to find all the non-boss specific lore that is ESSENTIAL for understanding the real story and that is a big screw up. I hope I just skipped over the instructions that tell the player about this.
Challenges/Lore: Lore pages are really important not just because it’s the only way to find out the full story, which is awesome, in game, but it also gives the players challenges at the bottom of their pages that if completed can get new classes and items that the player will probably need to finish the game. So definitely complete the lore challenges.
Class System: I’m probably really stupid but I did not figure out how the class-equip system worked until my 40th hour. Basically throughout the game you get new lessons you can learn in the afterlife by completing challenges, you take these classes with periods which are basically reusable aptitude points that you allocate between your desired classes. I didn’t understand that the periods were reusable so I just stuck with the first classes I spent them on for 40 hours when in fact I could have tried tons of new classes with those same periods during that time. But, now you know that if you don’t want to spend periods on a class anymore you can just click on that class and get your periods back to spend on whatever you want.
Final Verdict: I’ve tried to give this game a fair review, but I definitely am biased because after 90+ hours I really do love this game a lot faults and all. I ignore all the problems this game has or have adapted to them at this point, but I can understand why they might put some people off especially the steep difficulty. This game isn’t for everyone. But, for patient gamers Our Darker Purpose has amazing boss fights, an intriguing dark story that unfolds organically through found lore, a striking and beautiful art style, and deep gameplay which allows players to play how they like.
I will probably update this review in the future to fix mistakes and improve it.

Binding of Isaac gameplay meets Risk of Rain character development, with Don't Starve style art.
This game may not be extremely novel, but it stands by itself nonetheless. Despite its playability, it has a strong whiff of 'devs first game' about it. Look to a newer release from Avidly Wild Games if you like high polish (as far as I know, no newer release is actually forthcoming, but playing this game convinces me that it should).
If you can get past the poor polish, you'll see that the game has its own strengths and weaknesses.
Strengths:
-Strong storybased gameplay. This is often difficult for roguelikes to achieve, but Our Darker Purpose does an admirable job with its lore and achievement system.
-Strong sense of progression. Again, the achievement system, along with a credit system and a chapter progression, combine to make you seem like you're moving forward even if you're dying over and over.
Weaknesses:
-Non-procedural generation. There are only so many rooms that spawn. Fighting the same enemies in the same room gets old after the tenth time, even with multiple play styles.
-There are bugs. Aside from the somewhat klutzy feel of the hitboxes in the game, some interactions don't work as explained or intended (I'm looking at you, the 6 people you meet in Edgewood).

Our Darker Purpose was a game where you can simplified to "Binding of Issac Clone". The game does took a fair share amount of inspiration from the said game and somehow able to convert all into their own style. Instead of go Pro/Con like Usual, This time I'll be more detailed than usual. This game deserve it anyway.
The Story
You play as once muted little girl name Cordy, whom somehow survive from class massacare which occured when Mr.L (The teacher) absent from class to see "the administrator" and never came back. Cordy will fight her classmate with her "power" and anything she could found in school floor only to climbing up higher and higher to the top of her school building to discover the mastermind behind all of this madness.
Gameplay
Its simple really, especially if you were ever beat Binding of Issac. You got either seperate movement/attack direction or movement+attack control scheme. You will also equpied with "passive" item which will usually boost your stats and also a "manually" use item which will take time to cool dow before able to used again. All are almost as identical as Binding of Issac but the most standing out mechanic in this game was these three things:
-Rolling: You can roll all the time you like, which will temporarily boost your speed and evade yourself from oncoming danger.
-Darkness: As you progress your "Range of view" will slowly taken away bit by bit to the point where you can't see a whole room without moving your character here and there.
-Level Up: This game has a leveling up mechanic which will popped out "two books" for you each time you get into the point of leveling up. Each book has its own advantage and disadvantage but mostly govern around Speed/Damage output/Token etc.
The Graphic/Art
Got to admit but this game done the 'art' quite pretty well. The style look dark and gothic like. I believe the most highlight on this game was when you finish each chapter and saw the background art, It was quite intersting to look at. But the movement of character are a bit "flat".
Ps. This game was quite very interesting in term of reading an art style. But I  would suggest anyone who aint "roughlike" fan to stay away from this game.

My experience with this game can be summed as thus: every update I found myself testing the changes, nodding in satisfaction, then quitting the game to await the next update.
Arkane knows how to make a good game. No question. But if you film an Oscar-worthy movie and the lens is smudged while filming, you can't judge what's underneath without acknowledging what's been marring your experience the entire time.
=============================
PERFORMANCE
Everyone is aware of the performance issues, and these still persist to this day. It runs much better than at launch, where it was literally unplayable, but that's because the game looks worse than before - the most noticeable change being the extremely aggressive LOD scaling. Out of the corner of your eye you notice the shapes of window frames and posters on distant buildings morphing in shape, or the furniture at the opposite end of a long hallway suddenly blinking into existence. FPS dropped to 15 when stabbing a gravehound, so they simply removed the inky visual effect that was causing the problem instead of optimizing it.
Also, Denuvo authentication is one of the longest "loading screens" of the game. Around half a minute to a full minute or more every startup.
=============================
GAMEPLAY
For the most part, gameplay is excellent and is Dishonored's strongest suit.
Dark Vision was changed to a blurry short range sonar so unlike Dishonored 1 you aren't constantly seeing blue and yellow because you had no reason not to
AI is much smarter
Nonlethal combat options are a blast
Bonecharm crafting system allows for player flexibility and "builds"
Each level feels lived-in while maintaining the duality of directive flow and open options that made the first game so good.
Emily and Corvo have distinct animations and final weapon upgrades. The animations are supremely cool.
Each level is fairly distinct, some with extremely interesting central "gimmicks." I do, however, wish the game relied less on them and had more "regular" areas.
However, under the hood lie other problems. Most of them are quality-of-life issues:
Gone are the hotkeys for journal, inventory, bonecharms, powers. Only one "journal" exists now, despite still having separate subsections.
It took months for the power wheel to be fixed. It took almost a full second after activating to pop up and be usable, breaking flow so badly I almost never used it in the first place. It's finally fixed now, but this issue was glaring and it took so long to be addressed most of us played through without it fixed.
Thrown objects don't always go exactly where your crosshair is. While this adds a layer of difficulty, it feels noticeably more clunky than in the first game.
Mana regen is pitifully slow. From using a power to fully regenerating, Dishonored 1's time is 4.7 seconds -> 3.1 seconds with Spiritual Pool. Dishonored 2's time with 4x Spiritual Pool is 6.3s -> 5.5s. The devs said they fixed this effect, but it was only made worse.
Bugs. Street speakers not playing. Dying after possessing gravehounds. An arc pylon never shutting down after pulling out its power, leaving it to either be dangerous to you to dangerous to your nonlethal playthrough. Some of these still aren't fixed.
=============================
STORY AND ATMOSPHERE
Reactivity
Great. My favorite part of Dishonored. You need to hide from a gang member to access a certain black market shop, and there are different scenarios and dialogue for if you hide, if you run into him outside, kill him outside, or kill him inside.
Emily and Corvo
Emily and Corvo are voiced. And... they don't talk enough. It's good that they're silent for most of the game, but there are times when you come across a portrait or photograph with an "Inspect" prompt. I'd love to hear Emily's thoughts on the High Overseer as see how that compares to Corvo's, or if it changes based on whether or not you accept the Outsider's Mark. Instead, all I get is the protagonist muttering the name of the person pictured. What's the point? Might as well keep them silent.
It made sense to me to play Emily first, but her story felt lackluster, like people at every turn were saying "check your royal privilege" despite my efforts to resolve everyone's problems without drawing blood. Corvo's is MUCH more interesting as a veteran of Dishonored 1.
The Outsider and The Void
I hate the new Outsider and his new voice. He felt threatening and malicious in the first game due to how calm and composed he was, and the Void felt like a strange and otherworldly place. The vignettes of Dunwall made it feel both unnatural and unnerving yet fundamentally woven into the universe. In Dishonored 2, it's just smoky blackness and sharp rocks. The Outsider is much jollier and moves around erratically, making grandiose hand gestures. They actually had a plot plot that could explain this change, but it was never addressed, so it just seems like a pointless retcon to me.
Main Plot
Dishonored's worldbuilding was always one of its appeals, and that remains true in Dishonored 2. However, the villains felt lackluster. Only the main villain has a real presence throughout the game, whereas everyone else feels introduced abruptly only to fall by your hand, all within the same mission. In Dishonored 1 everything felt personal and real. Perhaps it was because of the long intro where you interacted with most of them, or the Hound Pits's cast of characters all having different connections to your targets.
=============================
As you can see, I've played this game a LOT and have put a lot of thought into it. It was definitely worth all those hours and all that money, but the condition it was at launch and the sluggish drip-feed of support we barely get now is unacceptable. To set a precedent for future games, I can't recommend buying this unless they manage to fix all the performance issues and bugs, which doesn't seem to be happening anytime soon.

The detail and love that has been invested in this game should be readily apparent from the 10 minute gameplay trailer above. However its so much more than that.
The system is easy to learn, and yet has the kind of strategic depth that will keep Turn based Tactical players coming back for more and looking further and further into the little numbers that control the world.
Flanking/Charging/Parrying/Dodging, reloading ranged weapons, jumping over gaps and off ledges. All make the genius of how they have you use your Strategy points (movement) within a series of rings marking where you will use a point up via movement. Go down some stairs and the lines readjust as you move making it always clear where and WHEN you will use one.
Overwatch/Ambushes Keep moving players on their toes and make scouting important.
And yet the game/battles/skirmishes themselves play out fast enough that no individual game will take longer than an hour and most will be over LONG before that. Especially in the early days of your Warbands when there arent maximum members.
Theres a lot to love here from a gamers perspective. Turn Based Tactical games are easy to turn into "Turn Based Repeat every other battle you have ever had here" This one has enough fresh content with random maps that you can run even the 2 preset warbands in the first early access release at each other again and again and it will not play out the same way.
If the final product (due for release Q1 next year) continues in this vein and from all the information i have found i see no reason why it shouldnt. It will be 10/10 from me.
For now, 10/10 for the content provided. (its Alpha so i expected more bugs than i saw, theres literally only one that ive encountered in 7 games. and it wasnt game ending)

Very immersive game, that had me wanting to find out the ending.    I really am drawn more to the story based, adventure style games that engage your mind to work through puzzles and reword you with more clues/pieces of the story (i.e. not so much into the quick twitch nonstop shooting games), so understand the style of games you like and take that into account when reading this review.
This Indie game was really enjoyable,   I hesitate to call it a horror game, even though I feel it fits in that category, as it does not follow the normal tactics of most horror games.    I love the use of sounds to provide the tension without the need for gore.   Another new concept (at least for me) was playing as a very small child, which added to the tension of the game as it taps into our normal protective nature for children, and made me more concerned for the characters well being.    The idea to play as a small child was genius, as it opened up new obstacles and adventures (as well allows for the concept of the story) that I had not really experienced before (things like reaching a door knob became an adventure).
The game mechanics were good and provided interesting twists...such as being able to crawl faster than you can walk (as is fitting for a small child), and being able to run for short bursts, but falling down if you run too long (again...this felt very realistic).
Graphics were ok, with a few glitches here and there, but overall decent enough (especially considering the Indie nature of this game).     I truly enjoyed the game and the story that it told.   I talked about it to my wife and friends, and while I don't think I conveyed the full affect of the game to them (they did not seem as impressed as I was), just the fact that it had me talking about it is something not a lot of games do.
I highly recommend you give this game a whirl if you are into this genre of game.

It's hard to judge the Old Blood, because obviously, being a Wolfenstein, it will ultimately be compared with The New Order, and nowadays, with The New Colossus.
There is a greatness in the Old Blood, in the fact that it DOES bring you back to, and, let me be clear, stop reading right now if you don't want ANY spoilers before starting your game. You probably know that already, but even though this review is mostly spoiler free, there is a very tiny one coming....
So, as I was saying, it DOES bring you back to MOTHER F****ING Castle Wolfenstein, and it takes place right before the new order. To be fair, it does bring you right the day The New Order starts, so it does piece itself together with the New Order beautifully.
In terms of content, you're getting a rather short game as far as The New Order is concerned, about 8 hours to 10 ish hours, and you're basically getting The New Order menu with no sauce and no extra salt. There is a story, so this is a bit unfair, but the story is miles away from the New Order. It's a somewhat standard and soulless war story. It's not bad, and compared to most FPS, it would be rather good, but remember we're judging the old blood with TNO or TNC (New Order or New Colossus if you're wondering) in mind. So The Old Blood is a little bit crazy story, but it's alright. And when it comes to the gameplay, it's Wolfenstein TNO. Different Perks, different weapons but the same old, same old, and it's great. Wolfenstein TNO had this great action FPS DNA, and the Old blood simply uses it to build a great distraction.
Should you buy it ? If you like TNO, yes. If you like TNO and TNC, yes. If you "just" liked TNO enough to feel you didn't waste your money but not enough to feel like you want to play it again, shy away. The Old Blood is for fan. It's a great starter to the main menu that is the TNO and TNC, but it's just this, a starter. And without the main meal, it will feel a bit short.

As a huge Total War fan, I have to say that Empire is my favorite.
What's Good
-Theaters of War
I thought that the different theaters (India, Americas, Europe as well as all the trading nodes) were very well done and really help immerse you in the feeling that you're creating a powerful global empire. I loved being able to monopolize trade resources both through trade nodes and colonies overseas. I hope to see a return to this in future total wars, as its been abandoned since (due largely to subsequent games taking place in earlier time periods, except Napoleon)
-Giant campaign map.
Its not the biggest and it doesnt have the most settlements as compared to other total wars, but the variety of locations and ability to send your navies and bring armies anywhere makes this game a lot of fun.
-Gunpowder era armies.
Total war has had gunpowder units in the past, but Empire, set in the 18th century was the first time they were a necessity and the backbone of an army. I thought this was a really cool addition to the total war series because of this as well. AI wise, Napoleon cleaned up a lot of Empire's mess when it comes to battles, both siege and land, as Empire had some glitchy AI and unit response problems.
-NAVAL BATTLES.
The naval battles in Empire were very well done. Of all total wars with playable naval battles I find Empire to be the most interesting and rewarding. Destroying an enemy ship's sails and masts with chain shot and coming back to finish them off with round or grapeshot is thoroughly satisfying and realistic as well. If you are skilled enough you can easily take out a much larger and more powerful fleet with only one or two ships, and I like that.
-Technology
I think all Total War fans appreciate the introduction of technology into the series by Empire! Technology and research gives a whole new aspect to the game, as you now have a new way to get ahead of your enemies militarily and economically. Its not about just making money and building bigger buildings to recruit better units, research requirements help balance a nations ambitions and ascent to dominance well and give other bonuses as well
What's Bad
-AI Battle Glitches (Specifically the Siege Glitch)
During fortified siege battles in which the AI is defending, you WILL experience ridiculous FRUSTRATING FPS drops after you break down a section of wall. This is due to the genius and decisive AI issuing 50000000000 commands at once to certain units, as it is confused about what happened to its lovely walls. If you can see the enemies units, you should notice one or a few fidgeting around in place, as the AI is telling them to run and then halt at the same time, resulting in unit wide seizures. The only way to stop this that I've found is to move your units into the fort or close enough to the point that they decide to come and fight you. Once the unit is activated the problem immediately resolves itself. Many other glitches persist too during battles. Unresponsive units, artillery units being unable to reman their guns, etc. AI wise, Napoleon cleaned up a lot of Empire's mess when it comes to battles, both siege and land.
-Maratha the Conqueror (The Orange Horde)
In response to complaints from players that the Maratha Confederacy was too passive, CA decided to address this in a patch, and in their infinite wisdom, turned the Marathas into a ROFLstomp machine. By the time they have defeated the Mughals and united India, they'll blitzkrieg Persia and the Ottoman Empire, and pursue Europe that way while sending multiple stacks to the Americas. In my Spain playthrough I had a trade agreement and alliance with them and we were "Very Friendly"....yes "Very Friendly" and they show up to Mexico with 2 full stacks, land another in the Bahamas and have a huge navy just chilling in the Caribbean. All in one turn. Fun, fun
-Overpowered AI on Legendary
Legendary mode gives the AI nations a slew of ridiculous economic and morale benefits and curses you at the same time. I owned most of the world in a campaign as the Marathas except for mainland europe from france-lithuania. In said area, the Poles had created a mega impenetrable empire-fortress, literally with at least 30 stacks ( some 3/4, most full) and that was just from what I could see around the borders and with my spies. These were no militia, they were winged Hussars, elite infantry and cannons most of which had around 4xp. There was no way except for the fact that they're just given money every turn and don't have to pay upkeep that they would ever be able to afford these armies. I sued for peace to rethink my strategy because they were absolutely unbeatable, and 5 turns later they came to India with 3 full stacks and navies, while pushing back against my borders in romania and all along easter europe, super blitzing me. The AI is also hyper sensitive and aggressive, usually many far away nations you barely have contact with will declare war on you in the first few turns for no reason, and any nation you get close to, even if you were destroying their enemy who borders them, will declare war on you shortly after.
-Random save file corruption, crashes.
Several times in different campaigns, the game would crash upon end turn, other times certain events would trigger crashes. One time I was playing as Spain on legendary and had control of India, most of western europe, north africa and the americas conquered. I was working on taking out Persia, and everytime I took control of their capital the game would immediately crash. I ended up giving them a peace treaty just so I would'nt have to give up on the campaign, but that only bought me a few turns before it crashed on end turn..
End conclusion
Empire Total war has its pillars and its flaws. For me, it has been my favorite total war all the way through Attila because of the time period and sheer size of the world, your ability to colonize far away lands, monopolize trade resources, variety of factions and naval battles. Empire feels like its own separate Total War unlike any of the others, and I'm glad CA took it in that direction of world exploitation and conquerage as opposed to a single theater, and I hope one day there will be a sequel!

"No kingdom last forever, no man can stand the test of time."
Kingdom: New Lands is an update of the original Kingdom game. Base gameplay is the same - you light a campfire, hire followers and equip them with various tools, then build up your kingdom 1 wall at a time.
In the day your kingdom is bustling hive of activity to generate the Coin that is the lifeblood of your growing realm. At night the monsters come out and your citizens cower behind the safety of your walls as the archers valiantly try to stop the encroaching darkness. And if you can last the night, dawn will come on a new day...
What New Lands adds on to that base gameplay are additional building types, additional shrines that provides different bonuses and an additional objective - to build the ship that will carry you and your followers to the promised land (or at least, another land).
The last thing that is added is the seasons system, which gaurantees that your kingdom will die - eventually. Because winter will come and it will never leave...
Simple, engaging, fun. 2d gaming at its best.

This is of course an early access review.
Full disclosure: I was given a key by one of the developers, and (unbeknownst to them) wrote game reviews semi-professionally.
Fantastic concept, randomly generated roguelike survival horror FPS! Phantasmal has a real Call of Cthulhu / Penumbra / Amnesia vibe to it, it's dark and mysterious, and generally better to opt for stealth over bravado. As the game is a brand-new early access release, there are still a few bugs to iron out. Sometimes the AI is either a bit too dumb or a bit too smart, doors randomly open and close, and the level of environmental interaction can leave a bit to be desired, however the atmosphere is spooky, the sound vs danger mechanic is nice, and the levels change on every playthrough, so you're never gaming a predefined path.
Probably my only real disappointment so far is the lack of an options menu. I've been gaming for a very long time, and as such still use inverse-Y mouse. It's a throwback from 80's flight sims. Trying to play through with my vertical axis backwards is ... challenging ... but these are early access issues, and should by no means diminish the achievement of this small Kickstarter driven indie team. Inverse mouse players may wish to consider a controller.
Speaking of achievements, there are a bunch of them already available, with more to come.
I believe that as Phantasmal approaches its official release, any concerns will melt away, along with your ability to maintain bowel control. It's a diamond in the rough, worth checking out, and if you're not into the whole early access thing, there are already a bunch of (highly entertaining) videos up on Youtube.
So, sneak away ye frightened gamers, and slay thee many roamers! (Or fail miserably, screaming like a scared little kitten!)

If you like the look of this game you should buy it. Just do it. It took me 2 hrs (which is a good length, didn't overstay it's welcome) and now I can't stop thinking about it so now I'm writing this review for why this might be one of my favorite games in recent memory.
You're some person with a sword and shield who, by some coincidence, arrives just in time to a haunted mansion that a plane is going to crash into, occupied by a family, completely oblivious to the danger they're in, that refuses to leave for own safety until you cook dinner for them. That's your  mission and basically the entire story of Tarotica Voo Doo. It's completely nonsensical and perfectly complements the experience of playing the game itself, bizarre but engaging.
It's a point and click basically? Except it's more like an arrow and spacebar, since space and the arrow keys are all you need to play. Clicking on hotspots of the map, based on the room you're in, usually brings you to a minigame where you press up and down to go through frames of animation, for doing things like opening doors or lighting a torch. Some people will think opening door after door this way is annoying, I think it necessary to make the world feel more tactile, more like I'm walking through rooms than just clicking on the map.
Combat is similar to these minigames, controlled with up to go for a stab and down to return to your shield, all based on the rhythm of the enemy's attack animation. Dying is no big deal, it just means restarting the fight, and you'll likely die alot while you try to figure out the timing of the battle. Its not that deep, like the rest of the game's systems, but it's cool to feel out when you can go for that greedy third hit, maybe even a fourth, and oh no you ate♥♥♥♥♥♥before you could return to your block. Also there is one fight in the game that's actually impossible to tell you to try something else, youll know when.
The worst thing I'll say about TVD is that it, true to old school adventure games, likely has at least one moment where youll get stuck, especially if you're not used to how these games work. The worst offender is when you activate something only to have something change in a completely different room. That being said, the game remedies this a little by having a limited number of things to click on, keeping it from being a pixel hunt. And most of the time there IS a strange logic to the puzzles; the one time I got really stumped, near the end, had a solution that made sense in a way that I couldn't get mad.  I went into it expecting way worse from a game that started development in the 90s.
But anyways the real reason I love Tarotica Voo Doo is for its immersive quality that I don't know if I can describe properly. I felt more like an adventurer in a mysterious dungeon in this than in games that actually have you as an adventurer in a dungeon. Navigating the mansion feels so technical and imperfect, like piloting a rover on Mars, yet moments of it are seen it up close through simple but incredibly charming animations, some of which you push and pull like a flip book. It feels both like it's perfect for the MSX system but also too nuanced to be anything like the games the system is known for. This is kinda gushy but that's how I felt just playing the game. It's old school but in a way actual old school video games never were. Far from perfect, but if it tried to be perfect I'd like it less. Tarotica, with all its simplicity and messiness and jagged edges, has value just as it is.

Cute, but short.
Disclaimer, this is a point-and-click adventure game built on MSX-era gameplay and the graphics are completely hand drawn. If neither of these are appealing, this may not be the game for you. The fun is in figuring out what needs to be done and the results of your actions.
The initial premise is pretty goofy and points you at the overall tone of the game, an airplane is about to crash into a mansion and your job is to convince its occupants to evacuate before impact. Although you'll fight dogs and monsters along the way, the focus of the game is solving puzzles while interacting with the household.
The interface is very simple, just the keyboard arrow keys to move a cursor and spacebar to select. Interacting with most objects involves pressing up and down to toggle between ON and OFF states. There is a map in the center and a cinematic window on the top right, but there is no traditional menu outside of this. While this can be criticized as being lacking in gameplay features, it is the result of highly focusing on an experience that harkens back to older games. There is a primary map for navigation in the center and a few windows on the side for animations, only the necessities. As a result of this, the game doesn't have a built-in save function and it is necessary to use the emulator's save states. However, the game is only a little over 1 hour in length, so you may not even need to save.
I really enjoyed the animations and how they portrayed the lives of the mansion's inhabitants in contrast to you breaking into their home. Since I didn't grow up playing any MSX games, it is interesting to play something that is clearly from a different generation. I haven't looked at it, but the game also includes a document that details development of the game and technical specifications. Development that focuses on electric circuits rather than dedicated video game engines brings us back to the dawn of programing.
All in all, I recommend this title due to how unique it is compared to whats currently available and my preference in aesthetics, but know that one playthrough will only take about 1 hour. You'll only get a bit of enjoyment from this title if you do not have any interest video game development from a generation where games only had 4 colors, 1 sound effect and maybe 2 soundtracks.

Among the Sleep is a psychological adventure game where you are put in the shoes (so to speak) of a toddler while he tries to find her missing mother during nighttime with the help of his fellow, rather talkative teddy bear companion.
You navigate the various environments of the game from the very eyes of the toddler: you are mainly tasked to overcome various obstacles along your path (by either crowling, climbing or rarely use some items you collected and put in an inventory) and advance further through the chapters. You can also hug Teddy to illuminate your surrondings (even if, sadly, this feature isn't brought up as much as one would expect).
While many believe this is a full-fledged horror game, Among the Sleep is more interested into make you see how disturbing reality can be when saw from a toddler's point of view and how it twists everything it touches. Therefore, don't expect any jump scare or chases: the game is very tense and will sometime try to screw with you, but that's pretty much about it.
The graphics are stylized enough, with their strongest suit being the peculiar and warped level design. The same cannot be said for other models in the game, but they don't tend to stand out that much.
If you love that kind of games that can offer you an unique and "artistic" experience without being that keen on a superb gameplay, Among the Sleep could be yet another game to add to your Steam library

I bought this game shortly after spotting a post by someone who stated that they were extremely moved by this game and could personally relate to it as they were currently going through similar circumstances. Not realizing that this game 'could' be based on a true story I decided to give it a gander.
Let me first start off with saying that if you are able to relate to the things this kid goes through, then I feel extremely sorry for you, knowing that your just a couple of steps away from blending in with the Addams family. I would also like to state that I will try my hardest not to ruin any surprises in this game as the game has very 'little' to 'no' replay-ability value.
After playing most games I ask myself, 'Am i a better person now for having played it?', more often than not the answer is 'no!' In fact some times its even 'I am worse for having played it'. Not so with this game. In fact I left the game having a better appreciation for certain things than when I entered into it. Here's the beauty of the game and where the game shines. Basically your paying for the experience you get from having played this game and it's concept of making you view life from another perspective, that being said ... a 2 yr old.
Here's where I began to appreciate things more. I began to appreciate how dangerous life is for a 2 yr old, a small puddle is something I can potentially drown in and a drawer in the kitchen is a ladder I can use to get to that toaster which could easily burn my face off.
That being said, the main enemy in the game is a handful of monsters and the main one being a cross breed between a clump of seaweed, a Triffid and a stick of Broccoli drawn by Timothy Burton. The game has nothing to do with the supernatural, however you do know that with the need of avoiding monsters and finding memories, something must be wrong somewhere.
The biggest downfall to the game is the controls, they were hardly precise and often felt awkward. For instance the hand icon to show you could interact with an object often appeared even if you were not close enough to 'really' interact with it and the designated controls on a controller for walk or crawl are the same ones needed to rotate handles. Hence instead of rotating you often would spend five minutes not being able to make up your mind if you wanted to walk or crawl on a handle. Granted you can customize controls, but i'm lazy and my idea of going outside is to turn on supermario 64 and get my character to look up into the nice blue sky. Also with the monsters always snapping at your baby feet, every millisecond reaction counts and if an icon appears to say you can interact with something, but you really can't because your not close enough, well it just heightens a players frustration level as they're spine begins to tickle the tonsils of the 'satanic evil brocolli'.
There are a couple of ways to avoid the monsters. 1) Hide under beds or in confined cupboards 2) Hug teddy so hard you snap it's neck 3) Soil your pants and hopefully the smell will send the monster away. Unfortunately options like lay a couple proximity mines down are not in the game.
The developers have really gone into quite extensive detail with the game which often gets missed by the players. For instance the mother has a pale skin impression on one of her fingers where a wedding ring would have been. All the books and covers in the game seem to have Japanese writing on them, this is because to a 2 yr old everything would look Japanese would it not?
I would also like to point out that the developers have a 'credit fetish'. Seriously! The longest credits I have ever seen in a game. After the game finished I felt sorry and took my mum out to lunch, when we got back the credits were still rolling. The best part is, I later discovered that those credits were just a prequel to the real credits. After finishing the game you get to play some DLC and then treated to even more credits. Seriously the credits are so long that even the seasons change and winter steps in.
The game will take you 5 hrs at the max. Most of that will be spent watching credits. There are very few games in the market which force you to think in the shoes of someone else and maybe we need more games like this so that we become more conscientious, tolerant and sympathetic . I really do recommend the game, it's worth the experience, but that experience is not worth $20.00 which is the normal price. Wait for it to go on sale. By the way my mum tried to make me eat broccoli soup once and it did feel a lot like what was going on in the swamp in this game. So yes you could say it's based on a true story...Addams family here I come!

HOLD ON A MINUTE. Is this a positive review? Yes and no.
Do I think this game is worth your time? Sure.
Do I think it's worth your money? Ehhhhhhhhh
Among the Sleep is good for what it is, an Amnesia lite of sorts that makes an honest- albeit fumbling- effort at poignancy. I won't bother you with how the game works or what it's about since I imagine you've already taken a look at the descriptions/screenshots/videos on the store page. What I'll tell you is that the game is good.
Mechanically it's fairly sound as my playthrough had no particularly frustrating moments.
Visually it's pretty impressive on high settings- particularly the lighting- but the human models disappoint (lucklily there's hardly any).
The audio is pretty great save for a few awkward moments where it can feel a little thin.
Most importantly it's got a thick, engaging atmosphere, which for me is the driving force of any good game in the horror genre.
Among the Sleep also suffers from a few unfortunate flaws that make it a hard sell though.
Most damning is the price point, especially considering the length of this game. I can assure you my playtime listed above could have been shaved, and there's virtually no replay value here, so if that's a major concern I'd say turn away now.
It's also not a spotless experience either despite the short run time, as you'll likely feel like the game resorts to a couple of cheap moments near the end in order to get at least 1 "Continue?" sceen on you.
The story also gets too heavy handed at the end which sullies the pleasant subtle nature it manages for the majority.
All in all, if you're a fan of the genre that wants a different, more creative skin atop your game then Among the Sleep is probably for you. BUT NOT FOR $20. Unless you're Warren Buffett, no one should spend that much on this game. Wait for a sale and I'm talking a minimum 75% off sale.

I don't think it's hard to say that Resident Evil 7 is one of the best games in the series. The first few hours of the game were an absolute blast for me. The atmosphere and presentation are excellent, and the gameplay and area/puzzle design are pretty solid too. It also manages to be pretty scary without really abusing jump scares or just being gross.
By the end my starry-eyed wonder faded a bit, but I think the slightly disappointing ending bits are mostly only very negative in comparison to the perfect beginning bits. Some irritating enemy types are introduced, the later areas are smaller and more linear than the main house, there's a bigger focus on boss fights and shooting and the Bakers start to lose their scary intrigue and become less of the focus. Also I guess for some reason the beginning led me to believe the story would resolve with some unepected revelation or explanation for everything, but it's really pretty standard Resident Evil stuff in the end.
That said, this game's worst parts are a lesser game's best parts, and I didn't reach the end feeling unsatisfied. I think this game came out a bit like a cross between the best "classic" Resident Evill and the best "modern" one, and that is a good direction to take the series in my opinion. Not just a callback, but not simply carrying on the status quo either.

This prequel to the splendid The New Order excels in creating a mood similar to that of the legendary Return to Castle Wolfenstein. It blends WWII action with paranormal mystery. The game takes place at Castle Wolfenstein and its environs: a quaint village, a cave system, a historic town and finally the dig site where some spooky actions are going on.
I must say, this was a pleasant experience for me because it really did capture the unique, mysterious atmosphere I remember from so many years ago. The Nazis, poking the supernatural carelessly, blinded by the prospect of infinite power. It will, of course, get out of their hands pretty quickly, which means more work for you. The exciting globe-trotting plot of the previous game was exchanged for a more isolated, personal experience. There are not that many characters or allies and the cutscenes play mostly from your point of view. The world war is far away from this place, which allows for a less Hollywood-style of unfolding of events and helps in creating a great old-school one-man army setting. You are put against a ruthless Aryan dog trainer in one half of the game and an ardent lady archaeologist in the other one.
Like The New Order, the gunplay is great and the guns feel fantastic with the new addition of a bolt-action rifle and a double-barreled shotgun. Enemies are reasonably resilient and threatening on the highest difficulty and again you can traverse the levels stealthily, at least to some degree, effectively using your new melee weapon: the pipe.
The game documents every goal, enemy and location with a short description or a note, so you can read a lot about everything, just not that much as in the previous game. Graphically the game is a notch higher mainly because of its wonderful vistas that are not blurry. Michael John Gordon softened his style a bit to capture the more isolated and mysterious feeling of the game starting with a great remix of the main menu theme and ending with a wonderful credits song.
One of the few things I could criticize about this game is its short length and that its supernatural element is not that threating gameplay-wise like it was in Return to Castle Wolfenstein. But it's very effective nonetheless.
8/10
+ Castle Wolfenstein, nostalgic reminiscence of Return to Castle Wolfenstein, action, atmosphere
- length, weakness of zombies

Firstly I'd just like to say that this is a "Recommended with hesitation"
I have a mixed bag of feelings for this game.  It's a game that I feel would have felt right at home in my DOS collection in the years of the early Duke Nukem games and games of the like, by today's standards it just feels a tad lacking, but in an odd sense that's not entirely negative.
Picture if someone from the mid to late 80's travelled in a time machine to modern day and saw games like Castlevania: Sympthony of the Night or other Metroidvanias, and decided to take that knowledge back with them and used the technology they had to work with in the late 80's.  I'd almost put this game in between a cozy place of Metroid and Legacy of the Wizard for NES; but a heavy C:SotN vibe.  Is it beautiful?  no.  Is the music stellar?  hardly.  But it still has a slight retro charm to it, whether it be intentional or not.
The game gives two characters to play, I've only played as the ninja, and it's pretty straight forward.  You get a ranged attack, melee attack, backdash and jump.  You find powerups and spells later on which help you progress further in the game.  The combat is really straight forward, later bosses you will have to learn their attack patterns at times to avoid certain death, but aside from that the combat is simplistic.
I can't rightly not recommend this game since it's not broken or dreadful albeit a little bland at times, yet giving it a thumbs up I do so with hesitation.  Another game where a thumbs in the middle would be appropriate, since I think there are far more games in this genre I'd sing the praises of first.  I got this game in a bundle so the price isn't hugely a deciding factor for me, but for anyone purchasing at the full retail price I may suggest waiting for a sale or it to appear in a bundle, that aside though I think there is still some enjoyment to be had from this game regardless, I just feel $5-$7 would be a more appealing price to the consumer for having them feel like they got their money's worth, due to just how saturated the market is with this genre of games that are competitively priced.

Tough, at times unforgiving, especially on harder settings but a great FPS for those who are tired of millitary based games. The graphics are not great and the dialog a bit campy but when taken in context of it's release date a very high quality game.

Graphics are lovely with a real tropical feel to the game and a small amount of awe as you realise you can go anywhere on the maps, which are sometimes HUGE, Objectives are well paced and not confusing. There's no wandering around wondering what to do next.
The enemy AI is very good, especially considering the open nature of the game, often they will try to out-flank your position or simply get behind cover so you must then flush them out leading to some pretty tense moments. However, it's not perfect, sometimes you will see the bad guys rooted to the spot for an easy kill or they simply charge your well hidden position and it's a turkey shoot. If anything, the flaws in AI make the game easier which is preferable to the opposite situation!
The weapons are beautiful: a mix of real and futuristic improvements. Ammo is never really a problem (well, with the exception of the Sniper rifle bullets and the RPG loads when they would really tip the balance in your favour) and, most importantly, the damage they inflict is balanced: both enemies and player go down with about the same amount of damage. Where the game falls down is near the end when a couple of pointless nonsensical plot-twists ruin the story. The game 'ends' three times, with some ill-thought through extra levels tagged on each time.

This game is a prime example of the unnecessary need of complicated mechanics. While the game could use more content to keep it entertaining for a longer time, the initial relaxing experience I got from the game was fantastic and blew me away. The use of pixel art (that water man) was done brilliantly and is an example of pixel art done right. And the overall difficulty of the game was pretty hard given that the sole mechanic of this game is dropping/using coins to build structures and hire troops to defend your base in the center of a 2D map.
The big question I think a lot of people have when they play this game though is the "potential" it has to be so much more than it already is. And I don't think that's a wrong way to look at this game, I just think that the developers were aiming to make the experience like it is now. This is a game I can take and ask anyone to play, and even with 0 game knowledge they could easily pick it up and have fun building their little kingdom against the creepy yet adorable endless waves of enemies. And that doesn't diminish the strategic value the game has. It gets very hard to defend your kingdom over time, and when winter rolls in, you're in sudden death mode with your only source of income being whatever you saved up in the bank. The overall good strategic elements combined with a super relaxing aesthetic really makes this a quality game for a great price (sales make this game a steal!).
There are many games out there this year that would have taken game of the year for me (dark souls 3...) but this game actually takes it for me because it proves that the true love of building video games is what matters the most, and Kingdom: New Lands makes me say "this is why I love video games".

This version adds a lot of replayability to the core game, the art style is enhanced, there are new units and a lovely custom banner creation tool.
The differences from the base game make the experience a lot less tedious than it used to be in the first episode, while 15 euros might seem a bit pricey i'd suggest this game to anyone willing to spend some hours on a well balanced and crafted 2d scrolling game.

Phantasmal is a procedurally generated first-person horror game which has made its way from Kickstarter, to Greenlight, and finally onto Early Access. It borrows liberally from other successful horror franchises (Outlast, Amnesia, and Silent Hill 2 come to mind) with the added twist of random level design. On one hand the game is, in theory, infinitely replayable. On the other hand, it lacks some of the tension and methodical pacing of more traditional horror games. It's tough to really call Phantasmal "horror" at all. Its more of a dark stealth experience with some unpredictable jump scares. Overall, there's a lot to like here--optional combat while stressing stealth, a cool risk/reward mechanic with light sources, and of course the unkillable tentacle monster. Unfortuantley, like many Early Access games, it's impossible for me to recommend Phantasmal in its current unfinished state. The lighting effects and motion blur are nauseating and the enemey AI and frequent glitches turn what should be a horror experience into something unintentionally comical at times.
Phantasmal has a ton of potential and it's worth keeping an eye on to see how the game continues to evolve.

I love horror and especially the H.P Lovecraft mythos, so I had to try this game. The game is set in the dark and foreboding Walled City of Kowloon, which was a twisted maze of buildings that was built without any planning, and came to have one of the densest populations on earth. It was eventually demolished by the government, no doubt to stop the dark cults of Cthulhu from corrupting the rest of Hong Kong :)
The game generates as you play, so no two maps are alike. This means you have to trust your senses to make your way around a map, and locate the enemy. Once you find them you can either run or try to kill them. The problem is that if you engage,  your sanity quickly slip away, and you're left a gibbering mess, who can't see straight, let alone aim your weapon.
This game is hard! I've made it past a few creatures so far, but no further. I'm not even sure what the goal of the game is yet. You get two clips of ammo to start and can scavenge for planks to use as weapons. You can take a few hits before you die, but if you're getting hit you're pretty much going to die badly. It's much better to be quite, turn your torch off, and hope they can't hear your heart hammering out of your chest.
The sound is atmospheric and the graphics are great. The game needs polish, but it's early days yet and I expect the developers are working hard to do just that. BTW, this game is made by Kiwi developers so if you can support them!

*Spoilers Ahead*
Among the Sleep turned out to be a wonderful surprise. You play as a wee two year old toddler navigating a world which appears nightmarish to your infant eyes. Many people will be reminded immediately of the Penumbra series when it comes to world interaction (chests, drawers, opening doors, object manipulation).
Artistically, this game is lovely to look at. Coats, boots and everyday objects are made out to be creatures in the dark or stylized into the creatures themselves. The baby's room is well done and being able to look down and see your tiny self fidgeting like a child might actually do in reality is a neat little thing to include. The mother looks fantastic and the lighting sets the mood for the rather dark and sad story they are telling.
This is where we get into spoilers. The gist of the story is that the creatures from your nightmares are actually your mother and, from what I am guessing, either your father or some form of social services worker. As you might have guessed from that last sentence, your mother is losing you. The symbolism that is put forth in the child's drawings scattered around the level was an interesting inclusion to go along with the theme of child abuse, alcoholism and misunderstanding that children have when these things happen really sealed this up into a gem.
Seeing your mother in the floor of the kitchen, your bear in one hand and wine glass in the other weeping left me cold inside at the end. Realising that the witch in the well from your children's story is your mother and her alcoholism struck a chord and is relatable I'm sure to many people growing up from all walks of life.
This is easily a gem and worth it at any price.
Not really a horror title as I thought it might be more-so, but actually something much deeper and more meaningful.

The monster only appears a handful of times, and it usually disappears immediately after if the player finds a hiding spot in time. The interaction with the monster is very limited, and so it's not that significant an element in the game. It doesn't stalk the player, and there's no real cat-and-mouse interplay. As long as you keep aware of the nearest thing you can crawl under, then you won't have to fear much for your safety.
If the developers had come up with an actual need for hugging the teddy bear, and if they had expanded upon the evasion of the monster, then there could have been a lot more gratification and strategy in the gameplay. If the monster was a bit smarter and more persistent and methodical in its search for the child, then the teddy could have been used to calm the child to prevent it from crying and giving away his position. Or something like that.
The $20 asking price for this game might be a bit steep for the limited playtime and lack of any real scares. But if you can pick it up on a Steam sale (as I did), then the novelty makes it worth a few hours of your time. It's story is shaky in the middle act, but the conclusion is very human, very blunt, and terrifyingly real, in a way that goes far beyond the childish terror that any imaginary closet monster can create.

The Old Blood pays homage to the truly old-school, pre-3D Wolfensteins in its early prison escape portions, and I can see why they wanted to have that, to try and make you feel like a badass who gets out on only your wits and makeshift tools. But...
It's not very good.
There aren't any interesting tricks to it, to be frank, you just watch enemy patterns and timing, then go through the trial and error of hoping you got it right. And there's error. A lot of it. And that's too bad, because the longer The Old Blood goes on, the better it gets. By the end, I was having a ball with cutting my way through enemies and dual-wielding to cut down NAME OF ENEMY REMOVED FOR SPOILERS. But that was after a long progression where the enemy throws hordes of enemies at you, each one capable of crippling you in an instant, and reloading and returning to the fray over and over. So it's a long slog to get to that point. And the plot is- well, it's standard Nazi occultism nonsense. Though well-presented, acted, and thought out, the actual setting of superNazi Germany just isn't as interesting as The New Order.
The Old Blood relies on stealth much more than its forebear, which is too bad, because that was easily the weakest part. And it's not like you get a toybox. But by the end, you're down to fun run and gun, and it all feels like it was worth it... but getting to that point is a tough slog. The arsenal and enemies are only really slightly adjusted from The New Order as well, so the running and gunning still relies on you using cover and luring AI enemies into hallways of death, and then walking over the dully gunned down mountain of corpses.
It's a tough call - do I recommend this game despite the first third being weak and frustrating, given that the final third is a delight? Well, there are a lot of good shooters out there, and I don't have to compromise as a result. If you really liked The New Order, go back and play this. If you really like shooters in general and have exhausted all the better ones, go back and play this. But it wouldn't be high on my recommendations. I wouldn't say it's a waste of one's time to play by far, but it's a lot of really rough gameplay in an appealing but unchallenging wrapper. So I just can't recommend it. I wouldn't necessarily tell people not to play it, but there's just a lot of better gun games out there.

All in all a fun game by itself, but I'd recommend downloading Darthmod to improve the visuals and add even more units.

An excellent turn-based RPG/Strategy adaptation of the table-top Warhammer model Mordeheim. This game feels very atmospheric and true to the franchise, the art direction is suitably gritty yet gorgeous. That being said, the game does need some refinement - but thats what Alphas are for right?
The general flow of the battle can feel clunky at times, due to some small issues with pathing and combat initiation. Some turns feel a little awkward and slow as you control units with WASD and not with the mouse. Combat animations look good but lack variety. Spellcasters add an extra layer of strategy to your turns but lack battle presence and majesty. Granted i am not so familiar with the spellcasters of Mordeheim but i am very familiar with Warhammer Fantasy and the likes of the Bright Wizard.
Multi Player is where its at - if you can get a game going. Being Alpha, there are currently issues with connectivity, load times and the odd desync. I have played a few games and they were pretty awesome. The battles can take a while to get going as both sides map out their strategies and asess their opponents but once your Warbands collide the action picks up.
After some refinement, general optimization and tweaks to the flow and meta of Mordeheim i can see this becoming a *great* game. We have still yet to see the best parts too - looting, warband customisation, match making and unit progression. And im hoping the game files are moddable as this game will go down well within the modding community and Warhammer fans alike.
8/10.
