They thought The Binding Of Isaac was dark.
This is DARKER.
Set in a supernatural boarding house surrounded by an endless wasteland, you play as a cute little girl who is fated to die hundreds of times in the Worst School Ever. Children are heartlessly sacrificed to the various horrors of this ever-changing labyrinth of death, while the administrators crack jokes, admire the obituaries, and encourage increasingly-fatal proposals to make their deaths even more humiliating and horrifying. The few children who have survived this far have grouped into factions that fight each other to the death using anything they can find, and punish unaffiliated students with suicidal fervor. The stew is jumping. The potatoes are rambling. The desks and beds are discussing the intricate madness of the world they live in, unaware that they are not as invinicble as they think. Everything else has a lock on you and will grow in damage and dakka until you are dead, dead, dead.
Your character has a few advantages. Her main attack involves throwing high-damage fireballs and she can acquire up to a hundred different upgrades and a dozen special attacks. Unlike Isaac, she can dodge roll away from danger, which increases her speed and can be upgraded with a few extra items. She also has access to a limited number of perks from both the start of the game and whenever she levels up.
But none of this power compares to the sheer atomosphere of this cursed hellscape. Hands will claw their way into the room and swipe at you. Rooms will lose power to the lights. Ghosts will explode various objects at will. And sometimes, everything is on fire. You are the prey, you are SO out of your element, and you need to get to the end with enough health to destroy the insanely difficult bosses.
Good luck. Morsel.

Woldenstein: The Old Blood is a really fun game, the gun play is just as fun as last time and its just fun to be back in the saddle again

It's just a series of linear, boring, overly straightforward core-genre FPS levels. The stealth is the same skeletal, quasi-functional peddlery from the first game. The shooting is still the same grindy, mostly-competent-yet-mediocre-feeling gunplay from New Order, but without that game's awesome story to keep it afloat (this game features a story that sleepily reinterprets Return to Castle Wolfenstein). The game wants you to Doom Space Marine it up against hordes of Nazis, but, just like both New Order and New Colossus, your health depletes far too quickly to allow for any kind of prolonged Rambo tactics, so shooting feels more desperate and perilous than badass and fist-pumping.
I kept playing until the zombies appeared, since that's the main gimmick/highlight of this standalone DLC. They look cool but are boring to fight against. The last boss is Kromog from Blackrock Foundry (a World of Warcraft raid boss), which doesn't fit the aesthetic of New Wolfenstein at all.
If you must play this, get it when it goes on sale for $5. Not worth full price unless you're a meat head.

Remember that episode of The Simpsons where Homer goes to space and saves himself and the other astronauts by lodging the Inanimate carbon rod in the shuttle door. Once back on earth the Inanimate carbon rod is seen as the hero rather than Homer. Yeah, that is how Wolfenstein: The Old Blood feels.
Near the beginning of the game you get a Pipe that you use through out the game for every purpose.
Climb a wall ✔️
Kill guards ✔️
Kill super soldiers ✔️
Open doors/vents ✔️
Break Chains ✔️
The list goes on.
B.J Blazkowicz is not the hero of this game, the hero is the Pipe.
Saying that the game is enjoyable, however feels more like a a DLC Campaign for Wolfenstein: The New Order, rather than a standalone prequel game. There is also the Nazi Zombies that seemingly come from nowhere, although it is a fun twist, it feels out of place for a Wolfenstein game, despite going to the moon and all the Super Soldiers and other advanced Nazi technologies in The New Order.
In the end I would recommend this game for a quick playthough and to fill that Wolfenstein craving. PIck it up when its in a sale.

Blacklight Retribution is the sequel to Blacklight Tango Down. While I have not played the previous game, I can only assume it's very similar to this one. But I'm ere to talk about Retribution. Where to start? Let's start with the good stuff. The graphics are very impressive same goes for the maps. The customization is practically endless considering how many guns there are and the mods you can attach to them. Character customization is not as expansive like the weapons, but there is quite a lot of armor, camos, and emotes. Now this wouldn't be a free game without microtransactions and this game is full of that. Though you don't have to use them, it makes getting stuff a whole lot easier. Before I go onto the next good, you can either permanetely purchase an item or rent it to see how you like it which is a god send to me considering how many mods there are to choose from. Now if you want to go into battle, you have several game modes, similar to COD or Halo. Team Deathmatch, Capture The Flag, Deathmatch, etc. There is also a zombie mode called Onslaught but you need a good team for that. The maps that you'll be playing on are absolutely beautiful and remind me ALOT of Ghost in The Shell. Now this is a multiplayer only game so if that's not you're thing then this isn't the game for you. Now there is ALOT of bad in this game. Firstly, you can die insanely fast even if you have the best armor, it's incredibly slow to level up when you're a high level, most of the items you can buy you actually have to buy with real money, several bugs and glitches when playing onslaught and I don't know if this is a good or bad thing but you can use HRV (basically Batman's detective mode) to see where everyone is at but the enemy can also use this on you. But despite all of the bad (I haven't listed it all but there's ALOT) this game has found a special place in my heart. If you want a game that is addictive, very simple, adrenaline pumping, badassery, then I'd reccommend Blacklight: Retribution for you! I'll see you in the game, agent. (BTW the achievements are broken)

I just finished the PvE compaign and feel compelled to further support this game and to help people decide whether this game is for them by providing a proper review. Do note that this is a primarily PvP oriented game with some minor PvE elements as of this review.
- Movement: Perfect. There's no (noticeable) wind-up time or stop time that many modern games have nowadays to make it seem "realistic". To me however that kind of movement just ruins the game. This game however has very smooth and responsive movement that I appreciate greatly.
- Combat: Very responsive, difficult, punishing and customizable. You will most likely die a lot at the start of the game. Combat in this game punishes button mashing greatly. The best part of the combat system is the ability to put together a move set that matches your playstyle. One con I personally have however with the combat is how long time-to-kill generally is.
- Environment: Looks really great. I love the "cartoony" simplistic art style this game has. The world is kind of maze-like however which can be a pro or a con depending on the person. I personally didn't have too much difficulty getting around the world but if you don't properly search all the nooks and crannies you might have to back track a lot at some points in the game, which can be a real downer.
- PvE campaign: Short. Pay no attention to my steam playtime as I deleted a character on which I spent the majority of my time customizing my controls. It took me 2 hours and 18 minutes to complete the PvE campaign as someone new to the game. There are still things to be done after the PvE campain besides PvP such as collecting new moves and finding prettier armor for that fashionsolver end game.
- Controls: Both controller and KB+M work really well. Both can be customized in the settings as well apart from stance changing and class abilities (dodging/parrying/absorbing/staggering). Some people will say you have to play with controller but honestly, KB+M actually feels REALLY good and might actually be the superior option due to easier reach of buttons such as class abilities and stance changing compared to the controller where they share the same button (right joystick) with a modifier (right trigger) while on KB+M they're bound seperately. If playing with a controller I highly recommend changing the keybinds as the default layout is kind of ♥♥♥♥♥♥ IMO.
- Performance: I had near perfect stable 60++ FPS (didn't actually check, but it felt really smooth) with everything on ultra on a gtx 970. There were however some very noticeable frame drops at certain points in the game while walking around. I can't comment on online play performance since I have not yet experienced it.
So far I feel like this game is 30 bucks spent well if only for putting together movesets to try out and learn.

I've just competed Resident Evil 7 on easy mode. It took me 18.8 hours, a length of time that I'm sure many gamers may consider extensive. First, before I begin my review, let me say that I have been a fan of Resident Evil since the first iteration. Also, I should state that, while I enjoy being challenged enough to become emotionally involved, I am not the most talented gamer in the world, and that is fine with me. I tend to play games with a narrative. I prefer to play a game wherein I feel I am a protagonist in a story, and I am usually at least as interested in the story as I am in the gameplay aspects of the experience.
Having said this, Resident Evil VII was the most immersive game I have ever played. Every aspect of this game is brilliant, from the story to the music, to the artistry of the environment and the characters. I love the intemate, almost clostrophobic, cabin-fever inducing combination of the first-person perspective with such enclosed, dilapodated environments. I actually felt afraid! It takes a lot to get an emotional reaction of fear out of me... hesitation about what is around the next corner... tension in response to the unknown... The well-crafted sounds of the environment and of my movements over the floors and his/her breathing, etc., added greatly to this, just as did the visually stunning, artfully crafted environments and immersive story.
In addition to the visual, auditory, and narrative aspects of this game, the pacing was closer to perfect than I have ever experienced in a horror game. I love the shorter length of the game, too, as I feel that it adds to the horror focus of the experience. One problem with many horror games is that they go on for so long that I feel I am losing track of my immersion in the story... This usually arises from there being too many conflicts, objectives, and fights that seem to be simply for the sake of challenging gaming prowess at the expense of the narrative and the immersion therein. For this reason, the relatively shorter format of Resident Evil VII is a move in the right direction. Quality vs. empty quantity.
Finally, in re the Resident Evil series and RE VII's place amongst them, RE VII brings the Resident Evil series back to the intions and ambience of the first few games. When Resident Evil began, the overarching intent was to immerse players in a horror environment... elliciting fear was the main goal, not challenging battles with monsters, as the 4th, 5th, and 6th iterations drifted to in focus. Resident Evil VII is a return to Resident Evil's roots, using current game design technology to achieve that goal, and yes, first-person perspective is a part of this goal as well.
I applaud everyone who worked so artfully, mindfully, and creatively, to bring such a wonderfully unnerving, utterly immersive experience to us in the gamming community. Thank you, Resident Evil VII team, for this wonderful return to the essence of what Resident Evil is meant to be.
If there were one dischordant thing I could say, as a recommendation for the next game by this wonderful team, I would suggest doing away with the over-the-top monster bosses encountered as the 2nd and final "boss" encounters, and replacing them with character-centered bosses more similar to Jack in the garage scene... These were the two moments in the game wherein I fell out of immersion in the story and felt I was, again, back in the usual "fight some bosses for the sake of gaming-prowess-testing tradition"... remove moements like these, and you could be approaching the perfect, horror survival game.
...as a side note, I LOVE the introductory sequence that plays whenever the game starts. This is the first game, wherein I enjoyed the introductory sequence (animation and music) so much that I never once skipped through it in restless haste to begin playing the game...

This is a golden gem of a game.
I've played far more than the meager 76 minutes it says on Steam. Possibly due to offline mode, possibly due to unknown issues.
Regardless, as you might guess by the fact I went out of my way to earn the "10 games wining streak" achievement, I absolutely love this game.
Let's list it's few cons first:
-It's extremely luck based. The traits and items you get can and will make or break a run. While skill has a ton to do with it as well, it's simply impossible to win if you didn't get any options for bonus damage items or traits; enemies have far too much health and deal way too much damage in projectiles that are all across the screen.
Even if it was possible to kite and slowly whittle away at the enemies until you won, you would've had to have spent hours doing so.
-It's heart breaking to lose because of an unlucky boss fight; perhaps you picked a few things that were bad against that one specific boss, or you just made a mistake (some bosses can hit HARD, so one mistake is enough), and lost a run that had potential.
-The game is very difficult, with no choice for easy mode. There is hardmode once you've finished the game, but if you aren't sure of your skills you should probably NOT play this game. Seriously.
-Some of the items (especially a few of the actives) are worthless without synergy. For example, if you override your dodge roll with a haste effect then dodge roll modifiers will have no effect. If you have no non-standard damage types then a non-standard damage amplifier will do nothing for you. Etc.
-For you completionists out there, hardmode doesn't always feel fair, and might be a real stopper from getting 100% achievements in this game.
And now, the pros:
-The sound design is SUPERB. From the music to the sound of things breaking, sounds of bosses as you fight them - everything is perfect.
-Items are plentiful and varied, and are not all boring in their effects. Yes, there is some "+range" or "+damage" items, but most of them are "+25% attack speed but your shots now have an angle variance" or "you get double-damage, but if you miss you lose health" etc. This makes the items not only powerful but also fundamentally alter your play-style.
-The traits you can choose can also drastically change your play-style; they offer health, sustain, damage, attack speed, movement speed, increased item drops, increased mini-boss spawns etc.
-When a run goes well, the game is amazingly fun, and when the run is close it's a true nail-biter. Especially if you're on the "10 games wining streak" challenge.
-Environments are detailed enough to be interesting, but not enough to distract you.
-The story is told through bits and pieces; each time you beat a room's challenges the furniture might spout some dialog. Each item has a description or comment from the administrators, and each perk you choose also contains a similar thing. Beating challenges (or discovering them) also usually yields some lore, in addition to unlocking new items or skills.
-The game is fair in it's hit-boxes. You'll rarely think "That shouldn't have hit' or "I was sure that'd have hit!"
-All of the controls are extremely simple and very intuitive.
-The somewhat dark, depressing theme is excellently contrasted with the game's humor. This is about as well done as Darkest Dungeon's depressing and hopeless theme.
-And finally, it's fun.
If you have your doubts, pick this up on a sale. You probably won't regret it, if you're up to the challenge and spending some time in RNG-land. 8/10.

Among the Sleep was a very interesting and unique horror game. The gameplay style is similar to Amnesia. However, this is not a violent/gore-infused game since it clearly involves a toddler (and ripping a toddler apart would be kind of weird). It is a very short game, one that took me about 3 hours to complete (and I take my time sweet with these types of games).
However, this game is definitely worth your time. Even though there is no gore and violence, Among the Sleep definitely captures the essence and perspective of what it is like to be a defenseless toddler and have a wild imagination. The storyline is something that many people can directly relate to and it is a sad reality that many individuals go through/have gone through (I chose not to say anything further in order not to spoil anything). This game's spookiness will surprise you!
P.S.: Although I thoroughly recommend this game, I suggest you wait until it goes on sale. I feel that $20 may be too steep for the amount of game time that one gets.

I just finished this game, and to be honestly, I really cant recommend it. I did enjoy it, its much more of a classic sort of 'Return to Castle Wolfenstein' than the New Order is but there are some things about this game I just couldnt look past.
#1- Performance is down right abysmal. I have a 1070 ti and an i-5 7600k running at 5.0 ghz and this game game runs like crap. Its so poorly optomized I see as low as 20% GPU usage and 5%, yes, for real, 5% CPU usage in game causing terrible frame rates and constant stuttering. The graphics settings have little to no effect on performance, certainly not in any meaningful way. This is a common issue, you can look it.
#2- There are some parts of this game that are truly just unfair to the player at higher difficulties. No I'm not that bad, I played most of it on Uber difficulty and there were 2 seperate points I tried over and over before I gave up and just turned down the difficulty.
#3-Boss fights are just ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t. All I'm gonna say, they're just lame, they're not creative or intuitive. They're just bad.
Overall, if you're a die hard Wolfenstein fan and its cheap (like $5 cheap) and you can put up with some seriously pathetic optomization, go for it. Anyone else, Just stay away. You wont be missing out on anything from the New Order/Colossus story line, you're better off just skipping this one.

One of very few Western FPS games out there, Bound in Blood is still worthy of the fame its older brother, the original Call of Juarez, received. The graphics are highly improved, and they look pretty awesome. Gunplay is hectic, no matter which of the two brothers you choose, and it's so satisfying to both drop people dead with just one Heavy Rifle shot as Thomas, or send a hail of lead from the mouth of a dismounted Gatling Gun as Ray. The story is only there to keep the game together, but that doesn't mean it's badly written. Civil War, mexicans and indians. What more could you ask for from a Western? On the other hand, the player character's animations are just as awfully unattractive, and the game engine is riddled with bugs, but that's come to be expected of Techland. The multiplayer is also deader than dirt, but that doesn't stop the singleplayer from being a pleasant and somewhat replayable experience. You should buy both this and Call of Juarez together, in order to complete the story and find out what happened to the McCalls after all.

Call of Juarez Bound in Blood is a game that tries to recreate that atmosphere of a western movie within an FPS game and while it succeeds in more places than any game I have ever seen attempt this is still falls short in the end.
While the game does limit the speed and number of enemies somewhat in an attempt to accomplish this it still devolves into a massive shootout far too often and the speed of the game prevents you from truly getting immersed within the western feel.
The multi-player works quite well although it is all but dead these days. Open maps which often boils down to one vs. one's and quick draws.
The game does deserve credit for attempting a scenario that works contrary to how the FPS genre is structured and coming away quite well from it. It is unfortunately not quite enough and that condemns this game to be merely a footnote in the history of gaming.

A short enjoyable game (SP or Co-op) OR a complex and refined PvP combat experience that is definitely worth the time. You choose. ABSOLVER isn't an MMO or RPG, even though it contains some elements, Attributes and loot/ armor stats but I still found myself completely immersed in the world and gameplay. The art style is akin to Prince of Persia games with a 'Naruto/Ninja' feel to the characters with KungFu'ee moves out of your favorite martial arts movies. And, it has tons of room to grow/evolve with new maps, fighting styles, weapons, etc.
The fighting (Main feature) is the real meat of the game. You unlock moves, add them to your combat deck(s) to create your very own style and go out into the world to try it out. The main story, the little you learn, is just a simple yet entertaining enough 8 hours or so tutorial to get you ready for the games main dish, ' PvP Fighting'. This is where you bring what you've learned and refined into the player arenas and test your skills. And SKILLS is the key here. This is NOT a button smasher but a 'Smart, tactical and very flexible' fighting game that requires you to adapt to each opponents style and find that little kink in their armor. I very highly recomment this game as a good 'Fighter' and 'Co-op' experience.

Empire: Total War is an amazing strategy game set in the 18th century.  The grand campaign gives you 3 maps: America, Europe, and India, as your sandbox of a dozen playable nations with the objective to conquer a scripted objective list of provinces, or to do whatever the heck you want for virtually as long as you want.  For the most part, all factions have their unique advantages and disadvantages, along with their sovereign image and other factors to guide your choice of play.
On the campaign map, each turn allows you to build up your provinces, raise funds, and create armies.  There is a degree of micro-management, but it is user friendly and not overly and unreasonably complicated as most dominant turn-based-only strategy games (and more recent TW games).
Battles are where the game shines brightest for me with beautiful renderings of the battlefield and hundreds (or thousands) of individual soldiers among your units.  The battles are won simply by making the other side route first through casualties and moral shocks.  However, you will take advantage of the terrain, and shape your lines correctly to make your enemie's strategy submit to yours.  This seemed vague and overwhelming to me at first, but after only playing defensively for a time, I found how to get a feel of correctly placing units to support eachother and find my own creative ways of bringing doom to my enemy!
The only problems I've had with the game are pathfinding bugs.  This is prevalent during some seiges involving a large amount of defending units.  As the seige goes on the units in the fort will start making repetitive and strange movements/commands, and after a while the game will start moving in slow motion, which is frustrating and time consuming.  The only way to fix this is to distract/kill the unit you see causing this glitch or just blow down the walls and storm the place ASAP or seige the enemy on the campaign map until he comes to you
You'll easily find yourself lost in Empire and give each faction a try.  I recommend starting with the Road to Independence campaign and then one of the easier campaigns such as Great Britain and Sweden, but you'll probably start with something more interesting (Spain is the hardest in my experience).  Buy this game, it's cheap now, if you find it on sale with dlc it's a total steal for so much content and hours of gameplay in just the base game alone!

Some people are not happy at all with this game. I can understand why you'd say that. The community only has a few hundred people. There is very little recoil on the game. There's probably tons of other things you can talk about, all of which are more than likely legitimate complaints, which I agree with, but I still absolutely enjoy this game. I will therefore tell you what I like and dislike about it.
Let me tell you why I enjoy this game:
1) You can design your own gun (after buying the gun/gun parts with in-game currency that is free or currency that you must buy), and depending on your playstyle, you can get this gun to work anyway you want. Possibilities are endless.
2) You can design your own character (after buying the armor components with the currency I have mentioned above, including gear such as grenades or tomahawks). This doesn't mean just mean making your character as fancy as possible, because designing your character also means designing one that can fit your gameplay style. Do you want your character to be a slow, heavy tank that can take tons of damage? Do you want your character to be a light, extremely fast speed demon that can take unsuspecting players by surprise? Do you want a medium character that allows you to easily adapt to any map? The possibilities are endless.
Concerning the two points mentioned above: This is what I absolutely love the most about this game. You can literally do anything with your playstyle here. No weapon is OP or overused. No build is OP or overused. You can do absolutely anything. The only thing you need to worry about in regards to your character is that you need to consider your preferred playstyle before buying items, and once you decide to buy, you should always buy items relative to your playing style.
3) There are loadouts. In each loadout, you can design a special weapon and character build for it, meaning that you can change characters that can fight well on the game's map.
4) Just about any weapon, piece of armor, or gear item (grenades and tomahawks) is free on this game. Everything practical is free, so you can obtain these items with game currency that is earned from playing matches.
Here is what I dislike about this game:
1) Your guns have almost no recoil at all, meaning that everyone can spray and easily kill you. This makes the game unusually fast paced. You'll need fast reflexes to do well at this game.
2) Even though everything practical on this game is free and can be bought with freely-earned game cash, some items are just so crazy expensive that it literally will make you want to consider buying in-game cash. While I believe that people who make a game do deserve funds and support, I believe a line needs to be drawn between making a game pay-to-win and pay-to-support-so-we-can-make-this-game-better-for-the-community.
In my personal opinion, since just about everything practical on this game is free and can be bought with the free currency you earn on here, why not just get rid of the extra time that has to be wasted in order to obtain these free items? Why not let everyone basically have every single one of the players have these weapon components, armor pieces, and extra gear such as med kits and grenades so everyone has the unlimited freedom to create their own perfect character and gun builds that suit their playstyles? And really awesome looking cosmetic items require real cash?
3) There aren't many new players, meaning that the community won't grow. It's not that much fun when you realize there are only a few servers online. The few people who continue to play this game are hardened veterans. Keep in mind that if you're new, just remember not to give up. It only takes a matter of time for you to understand the mechanics of this game, and if there's one thing that pays off the most on Blacklight in terms of getting better, it is identifying your own playstyle. Once you've learned your playstyle and know the necessary equipment for your character to suit that playstyle, the game suddenly doesn't become so difficult anymore, even if you're up against vets. This does not ensure you'll become a master of the game, but your skill will definitely improve.
The bottom line is if you would still enjoy a game with a small community, one that gives you tons of options regarding character and gun builds, then you'll probably enjoy it.

This game is amazing. The atmosphere, the cars, the music, the shooting, the audio. I have never felt more at home in a game than Mafia II. It is a very awesome recreation of 1940's and 1950's America. The shooting mechanics are smooth, you can holster a weapon so cops don't arrest you, and each gun feels unique. When you finally get your hands on the M1928 Thompson you will be delighted at how awesome it feels to mow down enemy gangsters. It feels like a movie and has a few references top films, one reference is to Goodfellas when you sell cigarettes in the back of a truck. The game has some cool collectibles, as well as some Playboy magazines a time traveler left in the 40's and early 50's. If you didn't understand what I meant in the last sentence it is simple, the game had to be rewritten, so instead of going to 1957, it goes to 1951. This of course leads to some inaccuracies, like songs from later in the 50's, later 50's car designs. That being said, even knowing of these things it doesn't take away from the atmosphere of the game. The story is very well written, it is entertaining the whole way through, the charachters are interesting, and most are important to the story line. The missions have a fewe moment that can be a breeze, or very tense, depending on how you do them. One of my favorite missions is a mission where you get gas stamps, you are told that getting the stamps without killing the guards will get you as bigger cut, so you either stealth your way through with your heart pumping at triple speed, or you take the guards out stealthily, oh and did I mention you also can disable the alarm on the safe so the cops don't show up? The mission can be played about multiple different ways and each can be fun in a different way. Oh and once you get back with the stamp collection, you find out that it is almost twelve on the day the expire, so you have to drive around town and sell the stamps before time runs out. Missions with tension make the story that much more compelling. Worth every cent of the 30 dollars and the DLC cars prices to me, but you may want to get it on sale if you are hesitant to pull the trigger on purchasing this game. Oh and one last thing, you may want to pass on the story DLCs unless you just want a more openworld arcade type of gameplay.

Very promising and reminds a lot of the old cult classic tabletop game. So far only 2 warbands, Skaven and human mercenaries, but they will add a lot more over time. Mechanics are fun, graphics and sounds are good. Overall a fun turnbased experience with a very interesting new take on action points, and how they work.
Update: With the full release here and 4 warbands instead of two. They added Sisters of Sigmar, a hard-hitting band of religious nutcases Warhammer style as well as adding Cult of the Possessed, which is a Chaos warband, with all that that brings. Mutations, weird way of thinking and just plain barbarism.
With over 100 hours logged, I have this to say: The game is very unforgiving, and at times extremely frustrating. Very long load times, which seems to be something the company can't fix because of how the game is built. it has a built in anti-rage quitter system, meaning if you quit during any mission or skirmish, it treats it as if the warband got routed and EVERY SINGLE WARRIOR in the fight will have to roll on the injury table to see if they suffer any injury or lose any equipment. This is very harsh, especially for single player where you don't really hurt anyone by abandoning a mission that goes really, really bad (considering the loss of one skilled warrior can set you back around 10 hours of game time). it doesn't help the AI is dumb as bricks, and pathfinding for large units really is an issue. More than once, I see them stuck by a door and just can't move.
Still, even with its flaws this game is very addictive and I stand by my early access opinion, the game is great.
2nd and last update: Loading times has been fixed, it now loads very fast. Gone from over a minute of loading time to around 15-20 seconds. (I use a SSD).
They've added 2 new Warbands: The Witch Hunters, a warband of Witch Hunters (think the psychos from the witch hunts in Europes history) and their cohors: religious nutcases (Flagellants and Zealots). Their impressive unit is a very large human with the suiting profession of executioner. He likes to set his enemies on fire. While they're alive.
The second new is Undead, set to be released tomorrow as I write this (the 25th of october 2016). I can't wait. Vampires. Zombies. Dregs. Necromancers. Crypt horros. Oh my.

I own over 100 games on steam and this is my first review.  I feel like I just have to leave a comment here - partially for the potential buyers, but also for the developers.
Rogue - you have created what could be a true epic strategy game.  So far, i am loving your design choices.  Continue to pour love into this game.  Warband development / progression / equipment is probably going to be what makes or breaks this game.  If you do this well and reward players for good play and gently punish those that choose poor strategies - you will do well.  It should be fair and over time the better players should build stronger warbands.  I also feel that the possibility of having assymetric multiplayer could help this feel awesome.  Allow the community to build "clans" and allow clans to challenge each other for even greater rewards and risks.  This "style" or genre of game could become a HUGE thing.
Warcraft 3 initially was going to go with this style of game (small persistent warbands that developed over time), but they abandoned it.  I always wanted that game to be made and this could be it.  The possibilities are endless.  You could overlay a "mordheim strategy map" that clans could vie for control over.  Limit a server to a certain number of players and let different clans and factions fight for dominance.
Anyways - i'm excited.  This game so far shows an INCREDIBLE amount of potential.  Please continue to listen to the community, but also know when to NOT listen to the community.  So far, your vision looks like it's paying off.
Good luck, Rogue.

Among the Sleep is really something. It's such a unique game and a fresh and new take into horror - something original that hasn't been done before. The story and game are really short, but the story-telling is incredible and beautiful and so well done.
You play the protagonist role of a 2 year old toddler, you're movement is slow and sluggish, you can't travel anywhere too fast or you'll fall over, but crawling around is great because you're used to that! You can interact with the world around you by pushing buttons, picking things up, turning them around and looking at them and doing other things as you explore the world around you and develop. However, this is where the story telling begins. You experience the story in such a parculiar yet fascinating perspective of the young and still developing mind of this 2 year old. So things aren't as they seem, things are confusing and odd, but a key piece of detail I love the developers for is simple yet so effective.
The world around you is new and scary.
There's not a great deal I can tell you without spoiling the game and I don't intend to as it is an experience that is satisfying to indulge into.
Is this game worth buying? Yes, but be sure to pick it up on a sale as it is REALLY short. You can get through the game and its DLC in a matter of a couple of hours, but don't let that put you off, it is a truly interesting and amazing game that almost brought a tear to my eye when I understood the story behind it.
I rate this game a strong 8.9/10
I recommend this game to horror go-getters, people who want an interesting short story to experience and anyone who can appreciate a new take on this genre.

A prequel to the first Wolfenstein game.

PROS:
Great Storyline- The storyline for "Wolfenstein: The Old Blood" was one that I enjoyed following throughout the game. Each character had something that immersed you in the plotline even further.
Runs Great- I have a low-end computer, and I'm still able to play at decent FPS and enjoy the game. There were only a few times I was lagging. Overall great optimisation.
Lots of Weapons- I feel like some games in the stealth/action genre can leave you lacking with weapons choices, but The Old Blood makes sure you have what it takes for each play style. You wanna go in guns ablaze? Have at it. You wanna sneak around and take out each person one by one silently? Have at it. This game doesn't really hold your hand in that aspect or tell you how to play. It's up to YOU.
Lots of Different Difficulty Levels- While I feel like playing the game over and over again can feel repetitive (with no DLC to add more content to the game), the difficulty levels that are added into the game make it feel a little more fresh. These modes span from "I just picked up this game, and I can complete it", to "I've played this game through twenty times, but it's still a challenge".
It's not a long game- I finished my first run of this game in under 10 hours, which for somebody who had no idea what they were doing, that seems reasonable. This game won't drag you along for forever like other stealth first person shooters do that have many parts.
Arcadey Feel- As somebody who experienced Wolfenstein 3D before playing this, The Old Blood still has a very "arcadey" feel to it, as the levels are set out so that encounters are necessary, but you are given a choice on how to deal with them. If you're looking for the Wolfenstein nostalgia, you will definitely find it in this title.
CONS:
Levels can get repetitive- As somebody who loves this franchise, I still felt like the levels repeated too much. As is with stealthy/action hybrid games, they have the same layout. While they don't hold your hand through the game, it can be frustrating progressing through levels with nothing but killing people just to do it again in another level with different scenery.
No DLC- I know there's The New Order (which serves as a sequel in the storyline), I wish there were DLC like in Dishonored that added more depth to the game. Most of The Old Blood is quite repetitive, and I just wish there was something to spice up the gameplay so I could keep coming back to it instead of just doing the same levels over and over again.
Stealth route is tedious- When I try to sneak around and play a more passive and challenging level run, I feel like the AI can discover where you're hiding randomly. When you're discovered by the AI, EVERY SINGLE PERSON IN A 10 MILE RADIUS LOCKS ONTO YOUR LOCATION. You just get swarmed, which means you have to start over. The AI won't leave you alone either if you leave the scene like in a game like Dishonored, they just always know where you are at all times.
Tries to be too many things at once- The Old Blood seems like it's trying to be too many things at the same time. It encourages you to "play how you like", but stealth is tedious, and the agressive route just repeats every gunfight over and over again. I feel like I'd have liked it more if it chose to be centred around stealth like Dishonored, or if it had been shamelessly centred around an agressive playstyle like Wolfenstein 3D or Call of Duty.
Overall, I love this franchise, and it never ceases to be amazing. I wouldn't pay the full $20 for this game, but if you could get it on sale, I'd definitely pick it up. Nice rainy-day entertainment. 7/10

I've beaten the game within 7 hours, I made two characters and I've reached level 25 on one of them. I'd say I'm as experienced in this game as I'm going to get until the serves are brought online.
Things I like about this game:
- You can unlock multiple/different types of kicks and punches while progressing through the game.
- You can create combo attacks using various unlockable attacks. Imagine like High-kick, Low Punch, Right Hook ect..
- You have special abilities with each fighting style you choose, as well as additional "power abilities" that you can unlock while progressing the game.
- The graphics and sounds are superb on Ultra Settings.
- There's a difficulty in learning, every enemy can kill if you're not careful/time your attacks properly.
- It's very similar to Dark Souls in that the structure of the game's map-system is inter-connected. ( minus a few areas ).
- Enemies can drop items that can be equipped and are visable during change.
- Allocation of stats when leveling up to focus-build your character.
- Weapons that you can pick up/or spawn to change up your fighting style during fights.
- Learn NEW attacks while fighting enemies who have them.
Things I don't like about this game:
- The servers have been down for the last 24 hours and I haven't experienced the Online at all.
- There are loading screens when starting the game, exiting the game, and in some areas during story progression.
- There are instanced fights that you can't escape.
- Single Player mode can't be paused.
- When allocating stats, there's a loading phase.
- Falling Damage is INTENSE.
- There aren't any throwable items.
- There is no teleportation, everything requires running.
- THERE IS NO IN-GAME MAP (.....????)
- The Single Player is very short, only 6-7 Mini-bosses and 1 major boss.
- The MAP IS SMALL. ( About the size of any ONE area within Dark Souls series ).
- The paths are very singular. It feels open, but it isn't. There are blocked paths everywhere and everything leads to one place.
- There is tons of pottery, destroying them yields nothing.
- The AI is proximity based, if you run away they will retreat/heal themselves.
At the end of the day, it's not worth buying in it's current state. They need to get everything functional and increase the single-player progression and map-size. Right now it's unacceptable for $30. It's closer to $15 in it's current state. That's about it for now though, will update once Servers are Online.

Its been a long time since I played an FPS game, so I thought why not give FarCry a try. I've never played a FarCry before , nor seen any playthroughs of it. So I went at this one blind and simply said it exceeded  my expectations.

This is not a game that you raise your gun and run through without taking your share of fire. On the contrary you take fire and suffer multiple deaths througout the game. FarCry forces you to use tactics to survive.The AI can be brutal at times utilizing actual tactics to hunt you down and kill you. It is a common ocurocurrence to get cut down by a sniper , walk into an ambush , or get caught up in crossfire. Often times the mercs will distract you with a 3 man squad while the fourth member is creeping silently to flank and destroy you.
You must use stealth , cover, and keep your *** down in the bush or you will certainly wind up dead. Throughout the game I would crawl  through the jungle to avoid contact as long as I could. Recon is a must in FarCry , if you go into an enemy camp unprepared you are dead. Even the best trained soldier dies if he is unprepared , so remember to recon and  take the best weapon synergies possible into the fight. You must learn to adapt as the batlle will shift from jungle to corridor frequently.

FarCry forced me into a very slow methodical pace , and as such may not be for everyone. I really enjoyed playing FarCry and it renewed my interest in FPS games again. If you are the kind of gamer who enjoys a real challenge then I would highly recomend that you give FarCry a play. FarCry is filled with many interesting twists and as a result I never really knew when it was going to end. As I've said before "If you are not very careful you will die alot." Try not to get frustrated FarCry was intended to be difficult. If you should survive until the endgame hopefully you will have found FarCry a rewarding experience. I highly recommend FarCry to people who appreciate a challenge in an FPS.

Mafia 2
Some of you might compare this to the GTA-series but Mafia 2 is a lot more fun and realistic. In this 'short' review, you're going to read why you should buy this instead of GTA.
I'm going to structure this review like that:
First of all, I'm going to talk about the plot.
2nd of all, I'm going to be talking about the technical information, especially graphics.
My 3rd point is going to be about the atmosphere this game makes you feel like, including music, details, characters and collectibles/extras.
My last point's going to be my conclusion and my final statement.
I hope I can help some of you guys to make your decision wether buying this game or not.
Plot:
You play as Vito Scaletta, son of Sicilian immigrants. Because of a jewelry store robbery at the age of 18, you get arrested. Instead of going to prison, Vito decides to serve as a paratrooper in the U.S. Army, Operation Husky. About one and a half years later, a battlefield injury causes your homecoming. Joe, a friend of yours, manages to get you counterfeit discharge papers so you don't have to go to the Army again. At this point, the thing gets rollin'. Joe helps you getting in touch to various mafia members. Soon after, there are plenty of jobs waiting for you...
Technical information:
Mafia 2's graphics are a feast for the eyes and very "eye-candy-like" in many ways. The game was released in 2011, there's no other game out there this old running that good with that kinda graphics. All in all it's a beautiful game with many graphical details which make this game look even more beautiful.
Atmosphere/Feeling:
Mafia 2's charming and all good vibes. It's bedecked with gorgeous 1930's-60's music, from Mr. Sandman to Lucille, there's something to suit all tastes.
Details are a big deal in the world of Mafia 2. Besides the 50 collectible Playboy magazines, which are pretty, pretty awesome too.., there are plenty of things to collect but also things that make the game a lot more realistic. For example, if there's a police cab next to you while you're driving like a freakin' maniac, the cops are not gonna let you go. Wether you try to escape or gently pay your speeding ticket, is your own decision. The cops are a lot more smart than the ones in GTA anyway. They do not forget your looks or your license plate number, unless you get dressed in something else or take a visit at the body shop. Another awesome feature is the radio, wanna know why? Everytime you make a little mess, like a gunfight or something, it's broadcasted on the radio. In my opinion, that's pretty cool and realistic.
Conclusion/Statement:
The feeling Mafia 2 spreads is unique. Everytime I play it, I feel like I really was in the 1950's. It's a truly masterpiece and my favorite game of all time and I think it can't ever be beaten. If you're into 3rd person shooters, buy it. If you're into adventure games based on a great story, buy it. If you're into any kind of atmospheric games, buy it. If you're annoyed by online games and just want to relax while playing an awesome game, buy it. It doesn't matter, anybody who thinks he has already played a perfect game, try Mafia 2.
If you actually read this completely, I'd like to thank you, it took a damn amount of time to write this but it was fun, though. Just because I could re-experience this game with all of its nice parts and features.
Also thanks to 2KCzech for making this game, I hope there will be another Mafia game developed by them in the future.

Binding of Isaac with more story to uncover. Has lots of things to unlock, lots of different options and way to approach each playthrough, and a lot of nifty stories and text to uncover.

Think of it as a less random Binding of Isaac, with more persistent unlocks that affect how you play.
It doesn't look pretty all the time, but Our Darker Purpose has it where it counts. It's got a bit of awkward style, but where it really shines is in how it plays. Enemies interact in interesting ways with the environment. It has two separate tracks of progression, items and levels, as opposed to Isaac's items, which means fewer runs where you end up daunted by the random item generator. The persistent unlocks, meanwhile, let you emphasize specific builds, making a lot of choices pretty tactical.
And you can roll! Rolling makes this game. Isaac tends to overwhelm you with bullets as it ups the difficulty; Our Darker Purpose throws very angry, charging enemies at you, and expects you to be able to dance around them. Which, with the roll, you definitely can.
The writing's pretty cute, too. The level up books are a nice touch, as are the series of in-universe middle grade excerpts that come as lore.
It's not a classic of videogaming, but it's charming and challenging and strangely compulsive.

Binding of Isaac meets Tim Burton? Add some magic to the already surrealistic world and you get Our Darker Purpose: the story of Cordy who has to survive in this magical, yet treacherous school as all students turned on one another.
The similarity to Binding of Isaac is out of question. Procedurally generated world? Check. Going from one room to the next till we reach a randomly picked boss in every chapter? Check. Very (and I mean VERY) difficult, challenging gameplay that is unforgiving from the very beginning? Check. When the going gets tough, the tough get going: just because you have only one life you will still return to see if you can defeat the boss during the umpteenth time.
I liked the game's graphics as well as its excellent soundtrack. Both create a unique atmosphere: the further progress you make (you basically go upstairs in the school) the more diverse the rooms and enemies get. Levelling up and collecting items (that either give you passive or active abilities) make you stronger which is a must especially when it comes to boss battles.
One particular thing I liked about the game is how it rewards you with "lessons" for achievement completion. These are all aids that help you during your next run: you can activate them from the main menu by spending the credits you earn during each floor. And if you haven't gotten any achis unlocked during an unsuccessful run, don't worry: the counselor is always waiting you in the main menu and by donating credits he gives you various bonuses. Make sure you look for the archivist as by exploring his study you can get info on what achievements you need to unlock for rewards (you need information on the game's lore as all achievements are hidden).
The game is tough. Boss fights require you to get to know your enemy very well. And if you mastered the fight with them you can still add an extra challenge by defeating them with a criterion; this must always be met if you want the corresponding achievement. I still find it hard to believe the Disciplined can be eliminated just under 75 seconds. Also, there's still a hard mode for those that find normal not challenging enough. I do not think there's such a person, though.
It's always nice to see the active support from the community. ODP started as a Kickstarter project and people pledged their support by donating around 50,000 dollars. Half a year later the game was greenlit on Steam and in just a couple of more months it was fully released.
If you liked Binding of Isaac and are happy to try something a bit more gothic in style then you are in for a treat. Just don't forget: trial and error will be the ultimate problem solving method here.

Among the Sleep is a game of perspective and confusion, seen through the eyes of a toddler in a world vastly larger and more terrifying.
Its appeal is largely wrapped in this unusual viewpoint, but it's so novel and well executed that it's a strong enough hook to pivot a game around that if shown any other way would likely fall entirely flat. Seeing the dark and often surreal world around you from barely a few feet off the ground, your awkward steps making a quick escape unlikely as you stumble and fall in an attempt to run from the nightmares that haunt you, is frightening and enthralling. The vulnerability felt through playing as such a small character is immense, and had me scurrying under chairs and attempting to pry open cabinets as my only defense was to hide where the monsters pursuing me wouldn't think to look.
It's hard to deny that beyond making your way from each twisted environment to the next there's very little interactivity to be found in Among the Sleep, but in most cases this works in the games favor and makes sense given a toddler's limited motor skills. There aren't involved puzzles or elaborate mechanics to deal with, it's simply you and your teddy bear trying to find your mother before the horrors around you find you first, and this simplicity allowed me to fully embody my role in this world that was intentionally beyond my comprehension. Much of the narrative is told nonverbally through the environment, with themes of alcoholism, domestic abuse, and child abandonment dripping out of bits and pieces of the world as they painted an exceptionally bleak picture in an already oppressively eerie game.
Among the Sleep isn't without its flaws; there are moments when its gameplay becomes too shallow even for how deliberately designed it is to be that way, the voice acting ranges from acceptable to weird, and many of the textures can be shockingly muddy. But what it's trying to be, and in most ways entirely succeeds, is something that will stick with me long after the credits finish and I sit in the dark hoping the child I'd been playing as finds better days to come.

Did you play Space Invaders on Atari? Are you a fan of games that get exponentially more difficult as time goes on? Do you want to have to adapt and vary your playing style? A yes to any of the questions and Darwin's Demons is right for you.

Essentially Space Invaders, but with a true natural selection system which facilitates evolution of enemy behaviors, resulting in progressively greater challenge (and virtually inevitable defeat for the player, given enough time.) Heaping helpings of player ship, weapon, and ability unlocks. Somewhat of a rogue-lite sensibility is present here as well, in that the object is to adapt and survive as long as possible against an equally (or more) adaptive opponent. But unlocks are persistent, so your tools expand over time.
How many different takes on the basic formula Space Invaders and its kin created 40 years ago have we seen down through the deaces? Probably too many. I find most to be boringly derivative, and very few that are at least fun, let alone compelling. Fewer still, though, can be called truly remarkable. Darwin's Demons firmly positions itself within that handful of Space Invaders re-interpretations to distinguish itself in a truly novel way.
"Adaptive difficulty" was briefly a buzzword in game design a few years back, along with procedural generation, verticality, and the like. But as with those, few games truly leverage the concept to do anything particularly noteworthy. And rarely has it ever been truly adaptive, so much as simple difficulty scaling.
It's surprising then that no one has thought to marry the basic premise of natural selection to a wave-based SHMUP before. Because the result - at least this implementation of it - is astonishing both in its "Why didn't anyone do this before now!?" DUH-ness, and the sheer fun it provides.
Other games do incorporate something along these lines, albeit in a less direct form (Boss Constructor comes to mind, wherein you can pit designs against one another to determine fitness, and then either use those designs yourself or deploy them as enemies.) But the simplicity of the Space Invaders inspired gameplay here makes the product of natural selection so much more immediately apparent, transparent, and, for me, entertaining.
As in the classic shooter, you move your ship left and right while firing at advancing waves of enemy spawns, possibly utilizing the cover of various optional, player-selectable defense barriers (more of which can be unlocked.)
At the end of each battle (called "generations" here,) the game chooses enemy types based on fitness - measured by speed, movement types, aggression, dominance, and projectile speeds, among other under the hood calculations. The most successful designs, coupled with the potential for mutation and genetic anomalies, then get "inherited" into the next generation. Thus the game becomes progressively more difficult over time.
The player can likewise earn a form of currency by playing skillfully and dispatching waves quickly, with which to unlock their own ship, weapon, health, and defense upgrades. You are therefore essentially in a race against time, trying to establish an equilibrium that allows survival for another generation in the face of an increasingly deadly AI.
The brilliant thing about this design, is that the way you choose to play can influence how the AI evolves over time. Some examples I noticed while playing:
These are just a few examples. I doubt whether they would be so clearly communicated, so fun, or so immediately apparent if this were a more sophisticated game. Somehow the simplicity of a Space Invaders-like design is a perfect fit not only for demonstration purposes, but also for the most important thing in any game: FUN.
In addition to the main Arcade mode, which has multiple difficulty settings, there is also the Experiment Mode. Here you can adjust all sorts of modifiers to make the game harder or easier for yourself, change how the AI evolves, its biases, how it measures fitness, player rewards, and more. This allows you to do exactly what it says: experiment.
You can use it effectively like a cheat mode if you want to, or you can genuinely make the game more challenging than it could ever be in Arcade mode even on Insane difficulty. The choice is yours.
This is a surprisingly clear & direct demonstration of user-interactive natural selection at work in a software environment. More importantly, unlike more advanced evolution sims, it's a functional, intuitive, fun gaming experience. If you like Space Invaders style SHMUPs, you'll likely enjoy this one. Even more so if you like rogue-lite style progression, and have any fascination with truly adaptive difficulty.
It's Space Invaders, evolved... literally, and pun intended.

It is important to note that when Herzog was released, the genres of RTS and MOBA did not properly exist. Nobody had yet got this idea ossified in their skulls that such games should be one or the other. The game helped
both genres, and as a result, the play style it displays falls somewhere between the two. Players can choose focus on directly engaging the enemy. Alternately, they can focus on manufacturing, deploying and commanding troops. This means the game can alternately feel like an RTS or a MOBA to the modern player, who is used to the labels.

Upon my initial reading of the reviews here, what I took away was that Our Darker Purpose was a harder, gothier Binding of Isaac clone. And I figured that I would be okay with that; I picked the game up on sale, and I've honestly spent two dollars on worse things.
If you've played Binding of Isaac, the gameplay is done in the same style. The floor layout and enemies are randomly generated. When you die, you go back to the beginning. Yeah, that all sounds familiar.
But Our Darker Purpose is so much more than Binding of Isaac in a different skin. I've played a handful of hours (at the time of writing), and have barely cracked the third floor. I mean, I'm not a hardcore roguelike player (or usually a fan of the genre at all), so my thrill comes from getting just that little bit further each time. Right now I think of Hard Mode and shudder, seeing as how I regularly get mowed down by run-of-the-mill enemies.
But that's part of what makes the game accessible. Well, to me at least. People in the same boat as myself can enjoy the game. We can hunt down the bits of lore, delight in our achievements (because, to us, they really ARE achievements), giggle/sigh at the conversations between inanimate objects, wonder at the art and the music, raise a very pointed eyebrow at some of the character design, and then get back to business because we ARE going to beat Chapter 1 tonight, d@mmit!
And then the people who are great at these games, who want a challenge, can chew their way through Hard Mode. I honestly don't know if story matters as much to that type of player as the gameplay itself; I can image that is where disappointment lurks.
Our Darker Purpose pulled me in in a way that Binding of Isaac never did. It's that drive to find more nuggets of dialogue that brings me back to empty rooms. It's getting to the next floor with 9 HP and, for a lark, seeing how far you can get anyway. It's not having enough juice boxes to heal through the boss's damage, but he's almost dead, and oh god I hope I can kill him before he kills me.
If you're a player who enjoys sinking into a fresh new world, where the details come in bits and fragments, where wit and charm can overcome a few oversights in artistic direction, then this game might be for you.

However, the combination of sloppy design and unrewarding gameplay quickly dissolved what enjoyment I was deriving from the otherwise gorgeous art style.
Problems arise the moment you press a directional key to shoot your fireball projectles. Hit detection is unreliable, your range is rubbish and the sound for smacking an enemy in the face is almost exactly the same as your projectile puttering out fight in front of them: I found myself firing at a boss thinking "boy, this guy is really soaking up the hits" only to realize that half of my shots are either landing harmlessly in front of him or striking/passing through a section that apparently doesn't take damage (And no, we're not talking about bosses who can only be hurt in one vulnerable section). And don't get me started on the fast, unpredictable bosses who are hard enough to hit WITHOUT the crazy amounts of shots they fire out.
Enemy/room balancing leaves a lot to be desired. The game uses a "lighting" mechanic which makes it hard to see very far: a nice gimmick, but incredibly annoying when faced with enemies with extremely fast projectiles that come with no warning in huge rooms, or traps that spring when you come vaguely close. The props dealt about rooms lends some aethetic charm, but at times are difficult to predict whether they'll block movement or projectles. My main bugbear are certain enemies that fire slow moving clouds in your general direction. Doesn't sound too bad? Wait until there's four of them in a tight room, and they're all huddled away in hidey holes that can only be shot at from one direction (which you can't reach because the clouds chase you away while your aforementioned rubbish range can't hit them), AND there's an extra enemy who's raining down chairs so you can't even stand in the sweet spots for two seconds.
I like hard games. I don't like games that get their difficulty from tedious play and horrible controls. I want to fail for reasons that are my fault, not because I didn't want to spend two minutes in ONE room taking potshot at those goddamn entrenched smog ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s, or because I couldn't tell all my shots were missing because there's no goddamn audio/visual difference between hitting and missing something, or because the game wants to be a bullet hell without polished, reliable mechanics.
And to think some people accuse this game of being a Binding of Isaac ripoff. If only that were true...

"Our Darker Purpose" is a "me too" roguelike that no doubt means to sail in the wake of runaway successes like The Binding of Isaac. Unlike the others, though, ODP offers significantly more in the way of RPG elements.
In terms of gameplay, ODP is very much in the real-time roguelike tradition, with a series of rooms in which the player faces challenges of combat or dexterity. You are locked in a room until you complete it, and then may enter an adjoining one.
Compared to other roguelikes, ODP has level progression per session, with choices of perks at each level-up. Your choices are effectively a build for the session, and reduce the randomness normally associated with roguelikes.
The gothic art style is a good choice, and was no doubt influenced by Edward Gorey, a personal favorite of mine, as well as more recent expressions of the genre, such as "Don't Starve."
ODP has a story that unfolds in fragments, and while it's hardly a masterpiece, it's far more than one would expect for the genre.
The lack of controller support is a big mark against the game, and an oversight that is more egregious considering the genre.
I like the sketchy, gothic art style, but ODP's art style feels amateur and inconsistent. Some objects feature sharp, fine lines and hard edges, while others are soft and look like they've been heavily resampled. Also, there is insufficient variation in room props. I've seen many pixel-perfect-identical desks or chairs spawn in neat grids in the room.
The pacing is poorly managed, and the rooms quickly become boring and repetitive. Many rooms require far more patience than actual skill, at times making the game a tedious slog.
Pickups are mostly uninteresting and give small bonuses to stats like health, critical chance, and damage. Roguelikes usually feature a variety of highly powerful objects or abilities, or at a minimum, very interesting ones with multiplicative synergy. ODP's pickups lack synergy and (generally ) only linearly affect stats.
The game's difficulty is disappointing. The game is very easy when compared to hardcore roguelikes, and will probably disappoint players who expect a serious challenge.

Well I will start with the bad and get it out of the way. This is a great game however it is full of bugs. It has a notably horrible camera that you will learn to master like it is it's own fighting style trapping human enemies in the corner is a legit strat knowing how badly it performs you will see an uptick in victory from doing this alone.... There were several crashes as well that may or may not have been fixed...I had at least 3 while playing. I got an unreal engine 4 crash with a text window  that I sent off to the developer, a black screen of death while I was loading and a random bug where I got caught on terrain and couldn't press any buttons or move.
These were rare in the 15 or more hours I played but they are known issues. To the developers credit there has already been a patch put out apparantly there were some save file issues where some players files were being corrupted in addition to the afformentioned crashes.
I have not had any issues since the patch bar some enemies getting stuck on terrain... lag "because the internet/ server architecture...." and odd enemy behaviors.....It is worth noting that the majority of my internet pvp games were lag free...not all...but most however there are people saying that the servers in coutries other then the US may have some issues I would do a thorough reddit read before purchasing outside the US to make sure that the servers are not borked in your country of origin...I wanted to front load all the bad so if these are deal breakers for you you know up front and can make an informed decision if this is a game you want at 30 dollars...
If you are still here you are in luck because this is the best Indie game so far in 2017 and possibly in the last decade...I have yet to playthrough Hollow Knight, Brigador,Cryptarch, Dead Cells, Sundered, Deadwood and several others that had proper early access releases this year but from what I have seen of the gameplay loop in those titles I think this comment is a fair assessment. Many indie games have been stuck in the rut of offering a familiar experience. Very few have dared to redefine what the gaming norms are or frankly outperform the AAA studio's at their own game. Some of the games I listed earlier are genre defining however they did not invent the genre they mearly made it better for existing Absolver one up's the convention of fighting games so hard it goes beyond the definition of familiarity and has become it's own thing.
Name that fighting game you played that lets you create your own style of fighter from scratch slot in each and every move of a combo string and still retain the depth of a AAA fighter while also marying RPG elements like stats and armor so you can have unique builds on top of the insane depth not to mention magic abilities you earn from PVE in the open world while taking out bosses that will own you so hard you will be ready to whip a 50 dollar controller through a 1000 dollar monitor while screaming a random curse word at the ceiling.
You know the one that has a minimalist style, hints at deep and rich lore throught it's story campaign and creates a world you wish was the length of a full on RPG so you could live in it the next 6 months you know umm what was it called...oh yeah.. Absolver...
There is no comparison...if anyone says For Honor...in the same sentence they have no idea what they are talking about. I love for honor it is a great game as well....it does some things better (like the camera and graphic's) and alot worse...however these games are not anywhere near each other in terms of overall gameplay loop.  For honor is a weapon based class based fighter. It is the best of that breed.
Absolver lets you create your own fighter ...weapons, and hand to hand combat are all at your diposal you can even mix weapon and fighting moves in the same deck ... you slot each punch, kick, sword swipe or fist weapon punch  into a deck and decide the combo structure for better or worse...you asign stats as you level and each punch and kick must be learned and has a progress bar till it is unlocked. You go into the wilds of the PVE and PVP and fight enemies and literally steal their moves from them by beating them...if you deftly parry, absorb, dodge or , spin your way out of a move you will learn it faster but blocking it as it comes at your face or feet also works. Oh and you have to not die and actually defeat the enemy to get the XP everything in this game is earned ....as 2-5 super ninja's try to assasinate you on every pull and come at you from every angle like an IRL kung fu movie...with various weapons and combat styles...you will soon learn that this game pulls no punches and is down right soul crushing.
The pve portion can be beaten in a few long days of grinding but that will not make a master out of you...Even when you defeat all the bosses you will have a metric ton of moves and styles yet unlocked to learn and master if you want to be the best...You will literally be living out a kung fu rpg training at a school or starting your own to learn or teach fighting styles in a quest for world domination....each enemy you defeat literally makes you stronger as you will unlock progress for the moves you blocked and deflected after each battle...every enemy will be worth fighting so you can get that much stronger... You will learn quickly that every move has a direct counter and you have to decide how to build a deck to be powerful and diverse so you can counter whomever you meet in battle.
Here in lies another flaw however as when you begin you will have fewer slots to load moves in and much to learn so you will find PVP to be an uphill battle to say the least...if you are just starting out and come across someone using the drunken fighting style before you know how to do sweeps or have a poking kick or jumping spin kick to knock them back or shut down their circle straffing bullcrap you will be hating life...all I can do is encourage you to stick with it because the reward of learning that next move that will shut them down is quite gratifying when you get there.
It is hard to quantify this as a balance issues as everyone is capable of learning everything the game has to offer or trying out any crazy build they want however because you can do anything...if you start out making bad decisions...or if you go for a style that has effective counters that take a long time to come online then you will have a harder time progressing then someone else. I would suggest looking at streams and reddit to find guides on effective builds if you want to make your life easier. For myself I went parry out of the gate and fought the bosses in the wrong order ...I took out the 6th marked target 1st...solo no less..."a few of you know my pain"...lets just say this is not a mission for the faint of heart....
however the fact that you can literally face the bosses in any order is great design....well, aside from the final one that is locked behind a gated tower and that mystery apprentice that you must defeat to get to through the door where you learn the drunken style   (he is in the tower of Adal either in the hallway at the top of the stairs next to  where the shrine is located or on  a grass path betwen Adal and the Aviary where the crows are circling the wooden tower and you fight the man and woman duo boss, then you need to go to the collesium and unlock the door to join the school...thank me later)
The PVP is the bulk of end game however there are PVE challenge fights that you can unlock, 3 bosses you fought earlier that were activated by a glowy aura (you will know it when you see it) can be redone once you raise your pvp rank...I hear this also alows some of the boss masks to drop but I have not progressed far enough to confirm this... I also hear the developers have plans for more PVE content in future patches....This is my Indie game of the year hands down  9.5/10 a new genre is born the fun outweighs the issues.

In short: The core gameplay and the minimalist visuals are okay. The rest is not.
The basic mechanic is simple and time-tested: Click on the start tile, drag the mouse to create a line, fill all tiles to complete the level. After a while new mechanics are introduced: locked tiles that require you pick up a key first, arrow tiles enforcing a direction, color changers, etc. Most of them are fine additions. I didn't really like the tiles removing or adding other tiles as they changed the level layout on the fly and it took me too long to work out how to predict which tiles would be affected.
The game starts in fullscreen. The undocumented windowed mode (Alt+Enter) doesn't allow you to resize or change the resolution and isn't remembered the next time you start the game. There are no keyboard controls, even though gameplay would lend itself to it. This being a mobile port does not excuse the lack of desktop support, as other developers manage just fine.
There is exactly one music loop which starts to grind on you around the 30 minute mark. But the really frustrating kicker is the sound it plays when you don't interact with the game. I liked staring at a new level, figuring out my path in advance. But apparently the developer thinks their players are so stupid, they need to be reminded to play the game they're looking at. So every two seconds the starting tile pulses and this really terrible *DING* sound pierces your ears. Perhaps as mockery, perhaps out of cruelty, the dev chose to include a message recommending to use headphones as the game starts. Don't. You'll have to click the tile and hold down the mouse button while you figure out the level if you want to keep your anger levels low.
And then after less than an hour the game just loops back to the first level. No end, no congratulation, nothing.
This is not a horrible trainwreck, but it just doesn't offer enough to warrant a recommendation. The price is probably fair though. If you want a much smarter game with a similar theme, a lot more content and brilliant audio design for the same price tag (on sale) check out LYNE instead.

It isn't the most memorable puzzle game I've played, but I did enjoy it.

I've pretty much only started with this, but so far it lives up to what I hoped it would be.
Basically, it's Space Invaders, but with a lot more player options, and more importantly, aliens that adapt to your ship and strategy. I unlocked a ship whose strategy relies on blocking enemy fire with its own fire... and before 10 waves were out, wound up going up against a population of lightning-eyes aliens whose projectiles all favored moving in a right curve. Thus neatly avoiding the projectiles that were supposed to block them.
Other rounds I've done so far have ended with other really interesting setups that clearly show adaptation to the ship used, and incidentally to a strange playing quirk of mine... my hearing is bad in one ear, so I tend to "ignore" one half of the screen in playing a game - if I'm not paying attention, it's the one on the same side of the bad ear, if I am paying attention, I usually overcompensate and so don't pay enough attention to the other side. Pretty much every game I've played so far, the aliens will "huddle" on the side that I'm failing to watch properly. This actually hasn't done a lot to help them so far, because I don't actually fail to watch that side, I just will show imbalanced favoring - but I bet it would make a difference in later rounds, when I get better.
These are just a couple examples of the interesting behaviors I've seen develop. This is a fascinating use of adaptive AI, and I look forward to playing with it in the experiment mode more, which I've only just started with.
Also, the lore is a nice bonus - the game didn't NEED any lore, strictly speaking (I mean, it's a Space Invaders thing), but having it there adds some extra interest, I think.
I'd say that this is a good game to get if you:
A: Are interested in adaptive AI techniques
B: Like Space Invaders type games, and would like one that gets pretty darn difficult
C: Enjoy the ability to play with a game's systems for yourself
