This fun, sharp, fast-paced, story-rich, mob-noir game does more than just stroke nostalgia for yesteryear. It also takes me back to the days of my own youth.
Back in the dark ages of my middle-school during the wild-west days of the internet, before Limewire downloads would riddle your computer with malware, I used it to pirate the first Mafia game.
The cracked version promptly riddled my computer with malware, eventually forcing my friend to help me reinstall the operating system, teaching me once and for all that CRIME DOESN'T PAY... and that Limewire downloads always gave you malware.
HOWEVER, before the end, I got to play the first and best GTA clone of all time: Mafia.
Seriously, even if you're not a huge mob-movie fan like I am, Mafia and Mafia II are excellent games, without comparison. (There's also Mafia III, which does not exist, has never existed, and anyone who tells you that the travesty released last fall was Mafia III is a liar.) I cannot name a single other game series that fills this niche so well, and very few that fill it at all.
As the "sequel" to the first Mafia game, 2K Czech brings their A-game yet again to give us the fictional city of Empire Bay and the rival gangs that run its underworld.
The Pros:
- The graphics: Are still good, nearly six years after it's release. Everything in this game is beautfiul, from the cars to the scenery. More importantly, large chunks of the scenery will take damage from weapon fire. You want to chip off the edge of a column someone is hiding behind, or blast them through a crystal-glass wall? Good.
- The AI isn't ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥: Mafia I and II have to be some of the only open-world crime RPG's where the police aren't blithering idiots. They aren't as much of a threat as they were in Mafia one, but they still doggedly pursue you for breaking the law; even minor ones. More importantly, the gimmick where they continue to pursue both you AND your vehicle while either of you still match their description is pretty neat.
- The cars: If you've ever been to a car museum or a classic car show and thought "I would absolutely love to smash this up in a surprisingly clumsy street chase with the police," then welcome home. The cars are fun, varied, and like everything else, look amazing. Plus you can steal and sell them for cash. Which is neat.
- You're not a terminator: While you still replenish health after staying out of combat for a while, your character is pretty squishy, and there's no "upgrade" process to make yourself a bullet-sponge. If you don't use cover or avoid open firefights altogether, you'll die. Which is good. You're a mobster. Not superman.
- The Plot: It's full of cliche moments and entirely expected plot twists, but that's indicative of the genre. Otherwise, the voice-acting is phenomenal and the story moves along quickly, barely ever letting up. There's even a brief overlap with the story of the first game that's pretty wild. This is pretty much the only confirmation that the two are related, but it's still a nice touch.
The Cons:
- The environment: While the aforementioned destructable scenery does exist, it's only during the mission set-pieces. The majority of the open-world is still frustratingly bullet-proof. More importantly, the dynamic damage system for vehicles in the first Mafia game, which would generate dents and damage wherever it was hit, is conspicuously absent. You can still smash up your car, but only in predetermined ways. No matter which side of the car you clipped an innocent tree with, your fender will still stubbornly break on the passenger side. Every. Single. Time. Also, gone are the days when you can destroy a car with your fists. Bullets and traffic accidents only, son.
- The "Open World:" Because the story is so fast-paced and linear, you don't get much chance to enjoy the open world they created. The few instances when you're left to your own devices, running around the city, are incredibly fun, but incredibly rare. However, EVEN WORSE, is the fact that the "Free Ride" feature the first one offered upon completion of the game, is ANOTHER feature conspicuously absent. It wouldn't have been hard to put in, or even offer as a DLC, but it's not there, and so the "Open World" doesn't get explored much.
- The Ending: No spoilers, but the ending is depressing. Not the bitter-sweet ending of Mafia I. Just bitter. It's crappy.
Overall though, if you enjoyed the first Mafia game, you'll love this one too.

This game deserves so much more attention! I can't think of many reasons why anyone would dislike it, except maybe its difficulty. One thing that might be putting people off is the game's seeming similarity to Binding of Isaac, which is understandable, but very superficial. I played the hell out of Binding of Isaac. I finished both the original and the remake with all their DLCs on 100%. It's got a very special place in my heart. But I would never say Our Darker Purpose is a cheap copy of it. It's very much a game of its own. Besides belonging in the same game category as Isaac, it's not affected or derived from it in any way. There are indie games out there that downright copy Isaac and use the word 'homage' as an excuse for their lack of creativity.
And creativity is something any sane person can't deny this game has. The gothic/Burtonesque art style is so neat and polished, it almost tops the phenomenal orchestral soundtrack, which is probably the thing I loved most about this game. It's unheard of amongst indie games. Yes, Binding of Isaac had addictive tunes, but it's like comparing the Looney Tunes theme to Star Wars. Both are addictive, but only one is epic and blows your mind. Too bad you can't truly enjoy it, until you reach higher floors. From the little background I could find, the music is made by an experienced composer who writes scores for famous TV shows. Big thumbs up to the devs for getting him on board! One thing I shouldn't forget when mentioning creativity is the story. While I love the art style of Binding of Isaac, I've always felt it lacks a deeper concept, yet alone a story. It's gore-ish and grotesque, but somehow bland. This game has such a dark, depressive and deep story, it actually feels like playing a game based on a novel. Have you ever read through the Harry Potter books and thought the last book was dark and depressing compared to the first ones? Well imagine the same leap, but use the last book as a starting point.
The gameplay itself is much less fast paced, bullet-hellish and much more about strategy. Where Isaac relies on reflexes and synerging good items, ODP is much more about the learning curve, which is very distinguishable and steep. Every time you play, you get at least one step further. Also there's almost no grinding involved, which in my opinion is a good thing. Sure, there are better items unlocked by finishing challenges, but they aren't essential for a succesful playthrough. Each time you finish a floor, you get to choose between 2-4 ways to continue. There are different sets/clans of enemies on each floor type and random floor traits you get to choose from. Usually floors with the more rewarding traits (e.g. higher loot rate) have more difficult enemy sets. You also level up during every run and gain perks in the process. Another thing I really appreciate is that ODP, unlike Isaac, isn't locked to 60 FPS (let alone 30), so I can fully enjoy it on my 120hz screen.
I never really loved bossfights in Binding of Isaac. Most of them feel the same and instead of finding a strategy and/or weak spots, you just have to keep dealing massive damage and dodge projectiles. Bosses in Our Darker Purpose remind me more of Dark Souls / Titan Souls. There's a total of 24 bossfights and each one of them is smart, unique and requires a different approach.
All in all this game is very though-through and if it had half the support and fanbase Binding of Isaac has, it could be legendary. I can't wait for another game by the same developer and I'll do my best to spread the word about it, so it doesn't die off.

Darwin's Demons brings something new to space invaders. The whole premise is to apply the evolutionary theory of "survival of the fittest" to the aforementioned invaders. The invaders that have the best survival stats influence the next generation of invaders.
This manifests itself in the most annoying way possible.
and soon you are facing entire waves of enemies that know the best way to defeat you.
My first run lasted 2 waves. In the first wave, I let too many reach the bottom of the screen and in my panic to stop them, I let them land a few hits on me. In the second wave, I died to lots of enemies trying to rush to the bottom.
I spent my time targetting enemies that were the closest to the bottom. This served me quite well. Around wave 5 I took a stray hit form an invader that could shoot diagonally with a high degree of accuracy, and more of those popped up. Around wave 7, I accidentally let a few reach the bottom, and the dreaded zerg rushing invaders came back for more.
Darwin's Demons is incredibly simple in it's presentation, yet this simplicity belies an interesting game with complex mechanics at the core.
The UI is simple and minimalistic, and serves it's purpose. At the end of each wave, you can take a look at the invaders' evolution statistics - you can see which patterns are emerging and preemptively change your strategy to counter the least desired traits. You can also spend some time upgrading your ship and defenses using currency you earn from completing waves. Give yourself more lives, upgrade your ship, secondary weapon, and planetary defenses.
Speaking of which, the game offers a variety of different ships, secondary weapons, planetary defenses, and other perks. Each ship handles differently and has a unique weapon, secondary weapons offer a variety of unique effects, and planetary defenses help you... not lose. You can unlock ships, secondary weapons, and planetary defenses using currency you earn after completing matches.
Another thing, which I will try as soon as I find some friends, is the local multiplayer. The game supports 4 players on the same screen. You only ever use 4 buttons, so you could conceivably play with 4 people using a single keyboard.
Darwin's Demons is something special. It's not going to redefine gaming, but it is well polished and great for what it is. For only $5, it's hard to go wrong with it. Highly recommended.

This student project from the University of Idaho brings a new bent to the classic and beloved Space Invaders.
Gameplay, is of course, basic, but the real beauty of this game is the algorithm behind the scenes. Every ten generations or so, the aliens would evolve enough to really start giving you a challenge. The further you go, the more of a bullet hell it becomes.
No matter how much you try and manipulate the aliens gene pool, they will eventually match you, and then better you. You will lose, but how long will it take?
Crisp graphics, great art style, addictive, simple and complicated all at once, has better procedural content generation than No Man's Sky.
And this is a student project. Eat that, Hello Games.

Far Cry was one of this games which I remember playing as a child. So I bought it on Steam and don´t regret it.
Short:
+Good gunplay, weapons feel strong.
+Tactic matters in taking out enemys.
+Good mix between linear and open world sections.
+Thinking outside the box will reward you.
+It´s looking pretty good for a 2004 game.
+/- ITS HARD AS♥♥♥♥♥♥
+/- Story is not really deep, but still cheesy enough to entertain me.
-AI sometimes goes full Cyborg-mode and see you through vegetation and geometry.
-Render distance is pretty low, AI will often attack you outside your watchable space. Using scopes is the only solution.
-At some points, enemy placement is simply unfair.
-I got stuck in geometries a couple of times, seems like just bad collider.
Long:
Far Cry is one of the last true "old-school" games which means it is designed to be hard. If you want an easy shooter to kill some time, this is the wrong game for sure. To say it lightly you WILL die, a lot. For starters I recommend to play your first run on "easy", even for hardcore shooter-fans. Because every difficulty setting has an invisible +1 on it, what I mean is: easy is normal, normal is hard, hard is super hard etc. You get the point.
That said the game feels very good, the gunplay is strong, the AI is somewhat intelligent and tries to actively get you with a variety of tactics. Also the graphics are okay (especially for a 2004 game) and exploring feels rewarding. Hidden armorys, shortcuts and pathways are waiting in nearly every level for attentive players to be found.
On the other hand Far Cry suffers from two major flaws: The first is the fact that the render distance is very low, so what happens is that enemys WILL attack you outside your see-able area. You have to get closer or use scoped weapons to even see them. That said the enemys are unbelievable strong, especially when they somewhat go full ARMA 2 cyborg-mode and see you through obstacles and hit you with every shot at insanely distances.
The second flaw are bad colliders. I got stuck several times in different levels and sections, which got me killed and that’s frustrating.
Well every other aspect is not worth mentioning, the music is okay, story is not great but cheesy which makes it okay.
So I would say:
Gameplay:        5*
Graphic:            4*
Music&Sound:  3*
Story:                3*
Overall 8/10 Points, I had fun and that is a good sign.

When you first play Our Darker Purpose, everything about that game seems frustratingly hard. I remember playing this for the first time and thinking that everything was unfair. Your character, Cordy, is painfully slow and she does barely any damage. The enemies on the other hand seems to have too much health, too much speed, and whittle away your health very quickly. You can dodge using the roll to move faster, but you can't attack while rolling and you always seem to roll into the enemy attack and harmful environment instead of away from it. Why the hell can't I attack diagonally? How does anyone get enough tokens to pay for the exorbitant prices of items in vending machine? How am I supposed to get stronger if the items are too expensive to buy? How can anyone maintain decent health with the lack of juice boxes around to heal you? The bosses were incredibly difficult too. Their sole purpose seem to be to lower your health to less than half percent so that even if you do somehow beat the boss, you'll probably die to the more difficult enemies on the next floor. These bosses aren't even the main boss, there's a chapter boss after three "mini" bosses. After my first playthrough, I remember thinking that there was no ♥♥♥♥ing way I'd ever get good enough to beat even the first chapter. I didn't feel like playing anymore. But I got this game as a gift and I sure as hell wasn't wasting that person's money by playing less than an hour. So I kept playing, and I'm glad I did.
One thing you have to realize is that this game is hard. The learner's curve is freaking huge and you will die a lot. A lot a lot. You will die every time you encounter new enemies, you will die when you see new bosses, you will die when you play in different floor types. However you will eventually get used to the game. You will learn the way certain enemies move. Eventually you'll be breezing through entire floors while only taking a few hits the entire time. You start rolling and dodging like a champ. The slow movement and low damage no longer becomes an issue. The credits you earn after completing a floor can be used to gradually improve your character by unlocking "lessons" and permanent upgrades that last throughout your subsequent playthroughs. Every time you encounter a new boss or enemy, it seems like the difficulty suddenly spikes. Yet the game always gets easier after the first time you defeat a boss. You
learn how to play this game, but only if you keep playing it.
People like to compare this to Binding of Isaac. They say it's BOI except worse. Same twin-stick gameplay with a dodge mechanic and gothic artstyle, but less variety in items and clunkier mechanics. I myself have never played BOI, but I'm telling you now that the more you compare this game to BOI the less likely you'll enjoy this game. There are some criticisms I'd agree with, like having less variety in items. But Our Darker Purpose is NOT BOI. If you try to play this game like how you'd play BOI, then you're going to have a bad time. The game seems sadistic and cruel and UNFAIR when you first play, but once you learn how to play the game gets much easier. Personally, I don't view the smaller hitboxes, weaker character, and slow movement as "gameplay flaws" but rather as things you better get used to and use to adjust your playstyle accordingly. I understand if you don't enjoy this game because of that, but I disagree when people call them bad mechanics.

I have mix feelings about this game. The game is very unique in concept. First off, you play as a toddler, so your abilities and interactions are extemely limited, as you would expect. This works very well with this horror genre, as it truely does make you feel vulnerable. Also, because you are a toddler, you have a big imagination, and this is how the levels are designed. Sounds good, right? A childs imagination = endless possibilities for level design. However, it feels like the developers are no so experienced in level design, and are better versed in art. The levels are linear and the puzzles are too basic and simple. However, a counter-argument can be made that the puzzles are suppose to be easy because a toddler is suppose to be capable of solving them. Fair enough. The game also feels to be design to appease a broad audience, including the "casual gamer", so its understandable that the levels are easy and the game short. The graphics are not amazing by any means, and doesn't feel optimized. Maxed out, the game often times dipped below 30 FPS on my GTX 780 rig. Thats completely unexceptable performance for a game of this graphical intergrity.  All in all, I felt pretty disappointed in this game...Until the ending.
Without giving out any spoilers, the ending to this game, makes the game. It serves as a reminder that video games are an amazing medium for story telling. The ending had be stunned and a bit choked up, and makes you realize all the tiny details you missed out while playing the game, much like how the movie "The Sixth Sense" did. The imaginative game is very symbolic and heartfelt.
I highly reccomend this game. For everyone, anyone. Even for those that don't play games often. The simple mechanics and controls makes this very possible.

Kingdom: New Lands is a tower defense game done right.
The level of involvement for the player is perfect for relaxing, while still requiring careful attention to defenses and economy. I appreciated the limited arsenal of defenses (archers, walls, catapults, and a few others), which allowed the focus to be on strategy and management rather than customization. (Too many tower defense games have so many defense options that they feel like customizable card games...) The intuitive interface easily allows a new player to learn the simple mechanics of building, upgrading, and repair. Worker automation is effective enough.
The visuals are phenomenal, exemplifying the artistic potential of pixel graphics. I found myself taking far more screenshots than other games simply to capture the ambiance. The music completes the setting nicely, and I even regret a little bit that I didn't purchase the royal edition with extra tracks.
Kingdom: New Lands expands upon the original by providing a five-level progression with increasing difficulty, in addition to new defenses.  This took me about 20 hours to complete, although I still have a few features to unlock.
The serene and engaging setting makes Kingdom: New Lands one of my new favorites. Even after having mastered the basic strategy, this one is still worth a replay.

Like before, the Kingdom: New Lands has as its main goal to survive and build a kingdom in a way that your crown is safe without losing the charm of the classic kingdom, but now everything has changed, you have to constriuir boats to conquer new lands, and more land, and more other lands actually are not that many.
Despite having an unusual mechanics, and a little more frustrating compared to its predecessor, New Lands is a great sought for those who really like an adventure, something much further than before.

Do I recommend this game?
If you are a fan of Binding of Isaac and roguelike genre, and if you already played Binding of Isaac: Rebirth enough (more than 100-200 hrs) then YES, I will definately recomend this game (specially on 85% off).
This game adds some new elements to the BoI's genre, like leveling up and selecting paths between school's floors. Plus this game has a beautiful art style and atmosphere, but unfortunately there are three problems that prevent this game to shine like a true gem. And what are those 3 flaws of the game?
1. Lack of enough polish 2. Lack of enough polish 3. Lack of enough polish.
In fact this game still look like an early access game, even 1 year after release. Here are some examples:
- There are problems with colliders, for example door's collider is placed so poorly that going to next room is always frustrating.
- Particle effects and FX of the game isn't in proper shape for release.
- Sound design of the game is ridiculous: lots of charracters doesn't have any sound for their actions! and the in-game music doesn't match the gameplay, it's more proper for a walking simulator genre. devs should definately look into BoI's musics
- Animations of characters don't have enough frames, so they aren't catchy enough.
- Some here and there bugs.
- Chalks aren't as useful as BoI's bombs. one reason for this is very low item/coin drop rate in the game. so you will never have enough chalks on the path to make them game changing.
- After all leveling up and picking different items, you will never feel that your character is powerful enough. usually effects of items aren't very tangible. for example at start of the game, fire rate of our hero is 1.6 and at the end of the game it's something like 2.4 and that's something like 2 shots per second (not so fast). shot's range and damage are the same as fire rate. the result is that items and leveling up aren't rewarding enough.
This game could be a wonderful game with a score of 8.5 or 9. But in the current state, it still is a good game but it's more like a wasted potential.

It's a challenging roguelike with mechanics somewhat similar to Binding of Isaac (in that you uncover rooms and pick up activated and passive items), but the gameplay feels very different.  There are OP builds and bad builds for sure, but it doesn't go too far in either direction.  Your skill plays a big roll in whether you'll succeed, which is a nice thing.  I also like the theme.  The artwork, music, and lore are really nice.  I really like the writing in this game even though it's not super common.
My favorite thing about this game is probably the floor generation.  Each floor can have a different modifier that adds a special trait to that floor.  The traits can be good or bad, but a lot of them are both good and bad at the same time.  For example, "wealthy" makes more money spawn on the floor, but you can't spend money on that floor because there are no shops.  After you finish a floor, you're allowed to choose the next floor from a pool of 2 to 3 floors, and you can consider these special traits in your decision.
My least favorite thing about this game is the bad controller support.  Walking/attacking/using items are all fine, but the default keymappings for the menus are really dumb and you can't change them.  It makes no sense to hit the start button for "confirm" and the back button for "cancel", rather than the A and B buttons.  I get that the A and B button are also used to shoot, but you're not shooting while you're in a menu.
But the biggest offender is how you have to press down the right stick to pick up an item.  This is already a weird button, but what makes it really dumb is that
the right stick brings up the menu.  So if you're trying to pick up an item, you might end up bringing up the menu instead.  Even better, there's a glitch where if you bring up the menu while you pick up an item, the item's description pop-up goes blank so now you don't know what the item does.  You can see the item's description in the menu, luckily, but if it's an activated item, you're out of luck since those don't seem to show up in the menu.
So yeah, keyboard users will have no trouble, this game is great.  Controller users... well, the game is still playable and enjoyable, and you can try joy-to-key.  But I hope they fix these issues someday, since it's really the only thing that annoys me about the game.
So far, so good---really enjoying this one.  If you like The Binding of Isaac, I'm sure you'll like this game.

I really liked Among the Sleep. They did a good job with putting the player in the role of a 2 year old and seeing the world through his eyes. The game isn't really scary. It does have tense moments, though. It's dark, disorienting and sometimes confusing...like how the world can seem to little kids at night. This is a fantasy game set in the world of the kids projections of his surroundings as he tries to find his mom. There was one part in the beginning that really creeped me out. The kid is seemingly all alone in his room, but a man's voice is clearly heard giggling from somewhere nearby, unseen, like a psycho murderous clown waiting to leap out and murder the kid. I'll say no more about that! The puzzles of the game were really easy to figure out, but this was a really fun and interesting world to explore. The art direction is fantastic. The atmosphere of the game is really well done. The game is only a few hours long. I'm a busy guy and I appreciate that I was able to start and finish it in one night. The only part that actually seemed like padding is the added DLC that is essentially a side story that was only slightly related to the main game. Still, it was nice to have that extra little bit to play when the game was done. I suggest playing this one in the dark with head phones, and turning the brightness down. Among the Sleep is solid and an easy recommendation.

The storymode is rather short, but this is to be expected from a fighting game. It's definitely interesting, and I had fun participating in it. Introduction:
Huniecam Studio was released on April 4, 2016, as a spinoff to Huniepop. Huniecam Studio while in the same universe as Huniepop is not canon to the storyline. Huniecam Studio like its predecessor is a parody game, however, unlike its predecessor, it is targeting the tycoon or management game genre instead of the VN or the dating simulation genre.
Rating (1-5 stars)
(2 stars) Gameplay: Gameplay is straightforward with the tutorial guiding you through everything. Unfortunately, the gameplay is redundant and there is not much more to explore in term of gameplay after the tutorial you spend most of the time repeating the same procedure to obtain your end goal. The game is, however, a bit challenging if you are trying to obtain all the achievements.
(2 stars) Characters: There is some new character introduced in this game with some voice lines, biography, and an unlockable wardrobe. In addition, the old cast is also in this game with the same feature as the newer characters. Aside from that, there is nothing worthwhile to mention about the characters.
(1 star) Storyline: The storyline is straightforward with nothing to really explore, you are there to raise money for x reason.
(3 stars) Replay Value: Surprisingly there is a lot of replay value if you are trying to obtain the achievements otherwise there is not. Each run will take 2 hours and it will take a minimum of 3 runs to get all the achievement if you are lucky and have experience in this type of genre.
(5 Stars) Steam achievement: It is possible to obtain all the achievement although you might pop a few blood vessels in the process, it is possible!
(2 stars) Pricing: For what you get out of this game the price tag of 7 USD is not worth it, there is not much gameplay, storyline, and the rewards are not really all that great.
(2.5 stars) Overall: I cannot recommend this game as it is not worth the 7 USD price tag when there are much better games out there. Objectively as a critic, this game looks like it is piggybacking off the success of its original brand game Huniepop. If anything, the amount of content and what is offered in this game is worth 3 USD game at best. If there is a sale and this goes for 3 USD and under it might be worth a grab. Otherwise, this is a so-so game at best with no redeeming feature, repetitive gameplay, and lack of creative direction.
TL:DR: Why are you paying for this when you can go and actually watch the real thing for free?

The graphics are ♥♥♥♥ing amazing, CAPCOM using a graphic style of photogrammetric was perfect, it really brings the fear to life, it makes you feel more uneasy as everything looks more real around you, you pick into the littlest details making sure everything is right later game, and listen out for audio and shadows for the new enemy type "molded", this enemy type feels scary but a bit lacking compared to actual zombies, but the story to them makes sense.
And the audio in the game is near perfect, and it had to be, this game needed superb audio, and CAPCOM damn right made the audio near perfect, the atmosphere from the audio is superb and realistic and adds to the tension.
The story in the game sounds simple, after 3 years you recieve an email from your missing wife called "Mia Winters", she tells you to go save her, the protagonist - Ethan Winters - goes to the house, and then the game starts, that sounds innocent well, the game is by far not normal, you meet the Bakers family and well it just goes downhill from there for Ethan. Sadly outside of the story there's nothing, seriously it's just the game's story, no horde mode just like RESIDENT EVIL 5/6/Revelations 1and2, and though it does make sense due to it's nature, it would've been nice to have a extra mode. + Really ♥♥♥♥ing tense, thanks to the atmosphere and well placed jumpscares
+ The Bakers' Family
+ Smooth Gameplay
+ Great Audio
+ Brilliant Graphics
= Short story, but replayable.
- Nothing outside of the story
Overall a 9/10.

As a person who has barely played Resident Evil before and who is completely immune to horror, this is my basic view of the game.

Positives:
- Great graphics

Negetives:

Overall, I would describe this game as the first Resident Evil and Alien: Isolation trying to emulate PT (at least for the mansion bit). If you are interested in survival horror games and like Resident Evil, then I recommend this game. If you're looking for just a survival horror game, then get Alien: Isolation, then this if you want more (for the sheer fact that A:I is cheaper and longer).

Our Darker Purpose is a very addictive, fast paced, challenging game.  It keeps you on your toes, becoming reckless in just a few rooms can ruin a great run. As I discovered
in the Steam Store I was really happy. I was always interested in the "Binding of Isaac"-like gameplay but I just couldn't get over its special art direction. While
has an equally special art direction I like it personally a lot more. The goth design of the whole game works very well with its Lore and is interesting to watch.
As for the gameplay: The game begins with Cordy awakening after surviving the attack of her co-students. Your goal is to reach the highest floor (there are twelve in total) of the  Edgewood Home for Lost Children. Every floor consists of multiple rooms (taken from a pool of predefined rooms) which will be arranged in a random order. Everytime you enter a new room you have to kill all enemies inside to unlock the doors to the connected rooms. In order to ascend to the next floor you have to beat one of the many floor bosses. At floor 4, 7 and 11 you will always meet the same boss since they are story-based encounters. While playing you will die a lot and everytime you die you have to start anew from floor 1. The same happens the FIRST time you beat any of the story bosses. To help you in your quest to reach the top of the building there are several ways to get stronger:
- On every floor you can find items either in chests, dropped by a champion (a stronger version of a normal enemy) or buyable in a vending machine with collected coins. They range from giving you an additional attack like bubbles or to slowing down enemies or reducing damage when hit. What items you get is random so there is a certain amount of luck involved in the game. Atleast at the vending machines you have some choice.
- For killing enemies you get experience and so you can level up. Every level up you have to choose between two randomly chosen perks so have the possibility to adjust them to your playstyle or your found items.
- In the process of the games you will earn (for example by unlocking the in-game achievements) different lessons and a number of periods needed to "equip" those lessons. This is the part you have to choose between two game sessions and where you have the largest influence on your own playstyle.
So as you see there is a lot of luck and random elements to assure replay value but also the possibilty for some own choices to adjust the game to your liking.
For the story: Genre typical it appears rather easy, has an interesting lore and another story hidden behind the surface. Take your time and find it yourself.
For the graphical and musical aspects: As stated before I really like the goth-like art style. The whole game fits nicely together and doesn't make a difference between high and low end pcs. The music fits the game nicely, most time more eerie and for the boss fights  more action orientated. If you find yourself liking the game I can only recommand to buy the available OST.
All in all "Our Darker Purpose" is a very recommandable game with a lot of replay value, an interesting art style, good music and a challenge for every skilled and/or patient gamer. As a special side note: The developers still update the game irregularly and try to give their customers the best experience possible. You can check this out in the update section yourself (Edit: It seems that there are no longer updates but the game is working and has a lot of content).

I love The Binding of Isaac. I love roguelikes, I love twin-stick shooters, and I love that bizarre crossing of dark and cute. I mention this because it's impossible to review Our Darker Purpose without bringing up BoI at almost every turn. The gameplay, the progression, the enemies, the items, even the aesthetic are all heavily informed by Isaac, and while there are some interesting tweaks to the formula, they come at a cost.
ODP poses you as a wayward resident at the Edgewood Home for Lost Children, a mix of orphanage, asylum, and Hogwarts. Within its randomly-generated halls you will meet all manner of disturbed students, monstrous school supplies, and debris. While the first two are interesting and varied in their Tim Burntony designs, the debris and traps are the only features of the rooms, lending them much less variety than the maps in Binding. Levels themselves can have random attributes, though, like lower light (+light radius is a thing again!), extra healing items, or more damage.
Items can be found in rare chests, from defeating rare minibosses, or buying them from vending machines. They come far less frequently than BoI items and have far smaller effects on gameplay, usually providing a random chance for an effect or a very corner case bonus. Your main method of progression is earning EXP from kills, leveling up, and picking one perk from a randomized pair. The game definitely has a stronger RPG vibe than you-know-what, with full stats for your character, critical hits, dodge chance, and so on. It adds a bit of complexity but also dilutes some of the raw appeal of combat and simple progression.
Hopefully by now you're recognizing the trend that Our Darker Purpose follows. Everything it does in deference to Binding of Isaac is done in half-measures, never quite meeting the quality of the originator. The look is interesting and more detailed, but lacks weight and impact. The progression is more complex, but never gets as creative. The sound design is also rather off, reusing many effects and missing some key feedback cues. Worst of all, though, is the uneven difficulty. Some rooms and bosses will just absolutely wreck you in ways the progression may not account for, ending otherwise promising runs in pretty sour ways. There's an overarching progression system with more perks to unlock, but it looks to take ages to get anything particularly interesting, if it even exists.
It's not a bad game by any stretch, just one that never lives up to the example set for it. If you've burned out on Binding of Isaac it's worth a try, and fans of the look or the RPG progression may even find it more engrossing.

Honestly I feel that this game is criminally underrated, as a big fan of Binding of Isaac (which is a very easy game to compare this to) I felt that this game, while similar in mechanics and gameplay, was successful to make it's own identity, because while I see Binding of Isaac as a moderately difficult game when you figure things out (aside from the Lost but let's not go there) I felt that no matter how much better I got at Our Darker Purpose I would always end up getting bested by this game's difficulty. This game is a real challenge compared to Isaac and I enjoy it profusely, I haven't felt as much of a rush as I did when I got to the game's second "final" boss and to know that there's so much more is just outstanding. And the progression system the game has to offer that keeps gaining progress even if you lose your run is just great, giving you an extra currency that stays with you throughout your entire game career that allows you start off better than your last run really helps, I probably would never be able to progress as much as I have without getting the extra 4 juice boxes (basically health kits) to start off the run with that I earned through my many past mistakes I had made through the corridors of Edgewood.
Speaking of, the story of Edgewood and the character you come to play as is quite interesting, with the strange happenings of this orphanage linked towards a dark and paranormal conspiracy surrounding "The Administrators", a mysterious group of adults who seem to run the place and have apparently never been seen by any child living there. A lot of the lore you find throughout the game is unlocked by defeating new bosses, finding a "memory room", or even sometimes from random desks and potato sacks lying around who somehow have the ability to speak (and break the 4th wall too I might add). It very much reminds me of the Dark Souls way of storytelling with giving you very little at the start and then giving you the option of looking into it and seeing what's really going on or just ignoring it and continue slaying your makeshift cardboard dragons and living elevator controls.
The artstyle of this game has a very Tim Burton-esque feel to it that compliments the mood of the game rather well and is sort of charming in it's own, creepy way. Another point I enjoyed a lot with this game was the music, which seemed to compliment the environments and the bosses they usually accompanied, which is what is to be expected of video game music
My few complaints of this game though is the annoying hitboxes that some bosses or enemies have, where the attack clearly connects with them but it yields no damage. Another complaint is the attack you use itself, which to me, is a bit hard to keep track of due to it's tiny size, I'm not saying they should make it bigger but at least make it more noticeable, especially in some of the more bullet hell-type areas later on.
Overall I'd say Our Darker Purpose is a great game that deserves a lot more credit then it's given, and while it doesn't contribute a huge amount to the genre, it makes up for it in an interesting story and a higher difficulty curve that for me, felt a lot harder then Isaac had. However I wouldn't necessarily call Our Darker Purpose a replacement to Binding of Isaac, but I would definitely say it deserves to be played by so much more people then it has currently attracted.

I'm pretty impressed with this horror game. While the short length might be off-putting for some, I think the game is exactly as long as it should be; lengthening this sort of game would produce fluff, and I dislike fluff more than a short game.  Among the Sleep is well executed in terms of mechanics, tone, and narrative.  The story is better than I gave it credit for when I started playing, and it is told well through the environment and character design.
**minor spoilers**
While the mechanics are simple, there are design choices worth noting.  For one, the option to crawl or walk is done in an interesting way; the player can't grab things or clutch the teddy bear for light while he crawls, but he moves faster, has a lower profile, and is not prone to falling.  I felt much more comfortable and "safer" while crawling.  Walking is clearly made the riskier choice, but  the player has to do it regularly in order to progress.  The player is faced with a similar delima with holding the teddy bear.  It sheds some light, but the toddler can't interact with objects while he holds the bear.  I thought  the developers made some very good choices with even the limitted mechanics options.  The player had to consistantly perform actions outside of a toddler's comfort zone (and mine; I would have liked to crawl  the whole game) in order to continue processing what was happening to him.
The environmental design (visual and sound) is wonderful, sets a consistant tone, and is meaningful.  Look at the screen shots and trailer.  Enough said.  I won't say much about the character design except that when I first saw it, I hid under the bed for like two minutes (in game, of course...).
I won't spoil much about the story either, but it is great to see more video games using things like themes, motifs, mechanics, symbolism, and subtlty to tell a story rather than strictly dialogue/text.  I thought all of the "words" in the game being random squiggles was a very cute yet alienating detail.
Overall, this is one of the most well-executed games I've played recently.  There are a few parts that drag a bit toward the beginning, but the game as a whole is worth the slow parts.  Movement, opening drawers, and throwing objects is cumbersome at times, but, well, you're playing as a baby.  It kind of comes with the territory.
Fans of horror and story-centric games would probably enjoy this.

A creative, if short, experience for those looking for a new horror fix.
GAMEPLAY: Mostly consists of exploring environments and solving fairly simple physics-based puzzles (think Penumbra/Amnesia), with the odd stealth/hiding section to avoid enemies. It's not groundbreaking, but this game does some cool things, adapting the gameplay mechanics to fit its subject matter. Given that you play as a toddler, you crawl faster than you can run, and you can fall down if you run for too long. However, crawling can limit your perception of the environment somewhat, and just "feels" strange. It adds an interesting dimension to the gameplay. Furthermore, rather than just giving you a flashlight, your source of light comes from cuddling your teddy bear. Sure, the effect is mostly the same (albeit with a more limited radius) but it's creative and serves to immerse the player.
GRAPHICS: Looks pretty good. There's a nice contrast between bright coloured objects in dark environments, and the lighting adds to the environments by bathing them in an eerie glow.
ENVIRONMENTS: Surreal, they seem like dark fairytales and nightmares, but with a lighthearted twist at once. They're not overbearingly scary, but rather, serve to make the player feel lost in a dream. Perhaps their most interesting attribute is that everything is "big" (sometimes disproportionately so), reflecting the youth of the protagonist. On the downside, they're sparsely decorated at times and there isn't a whole lot to explore along the fairly linear paths.
AUDIO: Good sound effects all around, and the music is ambient and serves it pretty well. The highlight is definitely Roger L. Jackson as Teddy (of American McGee's Alice fame) whose distinctive voice lends its warmth and sense of curiosity to the story. Some creepy sound effects punctuate the generally quiet of the game, with one enemy noise in particular being pretty jarring.
ENEMIES: There aren't many (only two from what I recall) but they're pretty eerie and are the impetus for the stealth sections. They continue the theme of childlike wonder, being large and overbearing. One seems like a creature from a fairy tale, with another looking like something a child would see in the shadows at night from everyday objects.
HORROR: This is the department that the game falls a bit short in. I don't think this game was going for Amnesia-style horror here, but it still isn't particularly scary. For me, it was quite tense at the beginning, but I found that it wore off unless I knew there were monsters present.
STORY: Without giving away anything, it pulls a few punches and is very good. The ending is quite impactful, and I was quite surprised at the direction it took.
VALUE: It's a pretty short game, so I'd recommend getting it on sale.

12 Hour Review
I'm not too good at making reviews, so I'll just try to get my thoughts out there the best I can. Absolver is definitely a good game, with some great combat mechanics and smooth gameplay to say the least. The only issue I really see (as of now) is a lack of content. The game's single-player story can last between 3-6ish hours (it's more of a neat tutorial kinda thing anyways), but after you finish the game and become an Absolver, the only real thing you can do is run the Combat Trials (PvP) or help out new players.
On to the actual gameplay side of things. The combat is very fluid and every attack chains together nicely. What makes this better is the Combat Deck system, which allows you to customize your own moveset to use in battle. There's also swords and "wargloves" as weapons in the game, which help spice up the game a little as well.
Customization is pretty cool too, with tons of items to choose from. That's pretty much all I'll say about that. Lots of cool stuff for your dude/dudette/apache helicopter.
Playing with friends as of right now is ok. If you and a friend just got the game together, then you can play through the story together. Problem is, after that, all you can really do is fight each other. There is a School system though, where you can be lent a Combat Deck of a Mentor, meaning you can use all their moves even if you haven't unlocked them.
All in all, Absolver is a really cool game that just needs a wee bit more content to make it the best it can be. In its current state, I'd give it an 8/10.

I've tried to justify this game in my head so many times, but I've reached my limit; Empire: Total War is complete garbage. There's a fantastic game hidden deep beneath the countless bugs, but these bugs are so game-ruining that even after six years Empire feels like it's unfinished and still in development. The A.I is ridiculously poor, during sieges the infantry refuse to shoot, or cannons knock down their own walls, and if the computer is the attacking faction the game seems to know that the A.I won't be able to attack on its own, so it cheats. I've started sieges with sections of my walls already knocked down, and sometimes the enemy need only come into close proximity of my gates for the computer to unlock them for the A.I. More often than not the infantry units simply walk around the map, allowing themselves to be killed or routed. I've installed one or two mods to help with the A.I, which has improved it slightly, but sieges still remain horrible affairs, with soldiers trying to shoot through walls, or even killing men on their own team. The combat aspect of this game is utterly broken, and considering that this is the crux of Empire's gameplay it leaves me to wonder why it has such glowing reviews.

The microtransactions in this game are especially obnoxious and expensive for a "Free-to-Play" game, in fact, I would wager the worst I have ever seen.  The game is specifically designed to require more and more real-world cash through microtransactions in order to maintain a reasonably enjoyable experience.  For those who came here looking for a remake of the classic PocketPC game "Artificier", this game isn't it.
While Shop Heroes is initially a fun game, the player quickly runs into supply problems and will find themselves sitting idle waiting for resources to replenish in order to continue crafting.  The player will continually feel like they're short of resources, short of employees, and short of shop space.  Don't be fooled into thinking these are obstacles or challenges for the player to overcome... they're not.  They're simply deliberately-designed game mechanics intended to force the player into resorting to microtransactions to get started.  The problem is, it only gets worse... so this game can barely be called "Free-To-Play".  If you're reasonably patient, it's easy enough to play without microtransactions during the first 10 or so levels... beyond that it becomes increasingly difficult to continue to "play for free".  By the way, it will probably average you an hour a level for the first 10 levels.
It seems Cloudcade went to great lengths to develop a game that not only will require you to spend money to play... but they've set it up so that you will have to spend more and more real world cash just to maintain the same level of play. How?  Well, as you level up, the game frequently hamstrings the player by placing various demands on them that cannot be overcome without waiting several levels and spending obnoxious amounts of in-game-free currency, or spending considerable real-world money in the form of blue gems just to return gameplay to a sense of reasonableness.
For example, you start out with 2 employees.  They can make weapons and some wood items.  Eventually you'll need to decide between a leatherworker and an armorer for your third employee... even though you'll have customers coming in looking for both items.  Then you'll need a fourth... and a fifth... but, you're stuck waiting until level 14 when you can spend a whopping 200k gold to buy another slot (at which point that fifth slot will already be inadequate).  Say you opted for a leatherworker and suddenly decide you need to craft some armor... if you don't have enough slots, you can fire one of your workers, make armor, then hire the leatherworker back... at an increased cost.  That re-hire cost skyrockets quickly so the fire-and-rehire strategy is only a reasonable action a few times.  Obviously you can side-step both the gold and level requirements through microtransactions, but the blue gems the game uses for it's currency medium, are ridiculously expensive at around $.01 to $.02 each.  You can get this down to ~$.003 each by buying the larger gem packs but the gems really don't go that far.  The game sucks them up at every turn.  The scenario I just mentioned would cost about $1.00 in real-world money to buy your way around.  Next time though it'll be $2-$5, then $10-15, and so on.  I'm no stranger to microtransactions and I don't have a problem with them in most "free-to-play" games, but Shop Heroes seems to be rife with sneaky ways to waste the player's blue gems and force them to buy more and more and more.
The devs have cleverly created numerous ways for the game to suck up your gem supply.  For instance, your heroes equipment has a chance of breaking in combat, if it breaks, you either have to remake the item or... spend gems to repair it.  As I mentioned earlier your crafting supplies run out rapidly, but you can of course replenish them by SPENDING GEMS... that's to be expected.
But instead of spending a few gems to fill your entire resource bin... Shop Heroes has a ridiculous exchange rate of 1:1.  That's right, if you're 5 leather short when you're trying to build something you can either wait a few minutes or you can spend $.05 in gems to get those 5 leather.
Need special crafting materials like "Elven Dew"?  This is rich, these can only be obtained by sending your heroes on quests.  They flow in quickly enough at first, but as you grind the quests, it takes longer and longer and longer and longer for them to complete the quests.  So even to craft a low level item it could conceivably take hours to get the required materials once you reach higher player levels.  Oh, but wait, you can exchange gems for these materials, again at the ridiculous exchange rate of 1:1.
The progression of in-game currency costs is also heinously steep.  Take the worker slot expansions I mentioned before as an example.  I don't remember what the third worker slot costs, call it 1000 gold.  The fourth slot cost jumps to 10,000 gold and the cost for the fifth slot rockets up to 200,000 gold!  Expanding your town buildings is similarly expensive.
Finally, with most free-to-play games, if you leave the game alone for a few to several hours, various mechanics will "recharge", allowing you to play for a while without hinderance.  While this happens to some degree in Shop Heroes, it's effect is severely muted.  There's no real benefit to walking away for a few hours and coming back.  Again, yet another mechanic that rudely shoves the player towards having to resort to microtransactions to keep the game going.
I'm not against free-to-play but pay-to-boost games or microtransactions, but it's easy to see that the real-world costs of this game can rapidly get out of control.  It seems this is exactly what Cloudcade intended when they developed the mechanics for this game.  As such, they've ruined a good concept with poor, really dishonest, execution.  Had Cloudcade simply made this a $20 purchase and not hamstrung the player at every turn (unless they spend thousands of gems) it would have been a far better game.  But as it is, I'm 10 hours in and I'm done because I can see the game is designed to require more and more real-world cash to keep playing instead of allowing a managable play level at a reasonable cost.
Oh, almost forgot to mention... the multiplayer "arena" is ridiculously stupid.  As others have said, the matchmaking is severely broken... to the point that it matches you with opponents 5x your heroes power.  This too seems to be yet another mechanic designed to trick the player into resorting to microtransactions in order to get anywhere.
Multiple players can occupy a player town, but there's generally very little benefit to this because if you have a player who has made any advances at all, the costs to upgrade buildings will be far beyond what newer players entering their town can afford... so the primary player still ends up being the one paying for virtually all of the town improvements.
And the tutorial... I've never seen a tutorial for a game like this that requires the player spend their in-game currency in extraordinarily ineffective ways.  Instead of prompting the player to improve their resource generation, the tutorial demands they sink money into their town center in order to unlock another building they won't be able to use for a looooooong time.  The tutorial obviously wasn't designed to help new players learn the game, it's designed to prompt them into poor decisions which will slow down their game experience or otherwise try to make their experience frustrating enough to resort to microtransactions.
To sum everything up, if you're independently wealthy and can pour hundreds to thousands of dollars a month into this game... you'll probably have an enjoyable experience with it.  Those are exactly the sort of players Couldcade wants playing this game.  Everyone else will find their experience rapidly becomes frustrating without dumping ever increasing amounts of real-world money into the game's microtransactions.

This game was fun at first, but it falls apart after a few hours.
There is a system in-game where you have adventurers who will quest for items needed to craft gear.  You can equip your adventurers with the gear you make, increasing their power.  However, each item has a chance to break while questing.  If an item breaks, then you have to use gems to repair them.  Gems are the in-game currency you have to pay real money for.  If you can't repair them due to a lack of gems, then they are destroyed and you have to either craft a new one, or hope you gain the rare item you earned from a reward again.  You can see how this becomes a problem quickly.
The first 10 hours, none of my gear was breaking and I was questing the first 3 adventure areas.  Then, as soon as I hit level 11, every time one of my adventurers returned from a quest, an item broke needing repair -- the cost being around 3 gems on average.  Needless to say, there are not a lot of ways to get gems without paying real money for them.  Eventually I ran out of all my gems and it was getting to the point that all of my adventurer's gear was breaking left and right, despite the chance for it to break being no more than 5% per item.
The arena is a waste of time.  There is no form of fair matchmaking system in the game, so you'll be put up against a ridiculously high level adventuring group each time.  I played 9 matches and even used gold to reroll a different group to go against on more than one occasion, and they were so out of my league I didn't stand a snowball's chance.
If more than one adventurer goes on a quest, then it comes back with a sort of roulette wheel in the additional gear they found.  Usually it's just gold, but sometimes it's items.  The game will toggle between the two adventurer's loot and you click the screen when it highlights what you want.  Every time I have tried to get the bigger cash reward, or the nice item, the toggle immediately snapped to the opposite item and selected it.  It's not lag, but really comes across as if the game is "cheating".
To progress in this game without spending money on gems is very, and I mean VERY difficult.  If you want a 4th crafter in order to get anything done (each crafter has 2 specializations, so it's impossible to create everything with only 3 crafters) , you have to either wait till you're 14 level and spend 200,000 gold.  Or spend 500 gems ($5) to unlock that slot -- and that is just one small part of the game.  Want to unlock other stuff?  Well, that's going to cost you even more dosh.
Overall, I know this is an app-game that follows the same formula a lot of other app-games do with how it handles money.  But this game was a lot more cash-grabbing than most.  Honestly, I'd rather just pay for a base game, and not have to worry about gems at all.  It might actually be a game I really enjoyed noodling with while I wait for other things if it wasn't for all of the soft pay-walls.

This is an old game.  It's one of those games that pioneered what we take for granted in a modern shooter.  Like those pioneers, it shares a similar plot; guy with military background gets sent to a secret facility to beat up grunts and fight a bad guy, who is going to release an evil plot device that will ultimately destroy the world if not stopped.
Those kinds of stories were the heyday back in the days, and Far Cry is no exception.  It's sad that what modern shooters have chosen to take from their roots to apply to their current games is just the cut-and-paste plot and the state-of-the-art graphics.  I had to stop playing this game and give it a break multiple times throughout the playthrough because I kept running into parts where the game was incredibly difficult.  This ranged from a lack of waypoints (which you find in almost every shooter game) which meant that it was nigh close to impossible to figure out where to go, to a lack of the right weapons (you'd think that having a pistol might actually be helpful in one of the early games where the great focus was the hitbox health system where headshots could one-hit-KO something), to having to deal with a horde of enemies all at once with almost no health and an escort mission to boot.  It's a game that makes you have to stop what you are doing and leave the computer for a while to think and recharge your brain cells before going back in again.
I miss that in a lot of today's games.  Shooters could do with the increased difficulty that doesn't require cheat codes or a paywall to bypass.  It's nice to take a step back from the LCD induced graphics and hardware and just play an old game in order to appreciate how far we've come.
Really linear, but still good, old fashioned fun. Also, if you can beat this game on any difficulty higher than easy....you're really good at video games and should probably find another hobby.

Your goal is to create a kingdom in each land, defend that kingdom, and make a boat so you can move onto the next level. There are four levels and it gets harder with each map. I'm going to start with the Pros:
*Beautiful Artwork
*Color customization of both character and your Blazon (flag).  Note:  During the "load screen" when you watch your character run, push the "down arrow key" and it will randomize your character, including gender...  When you set your Blazon (flag) later, this will also customize your character's outfit color.
*Lots of mounts to choose from.
*You can have a dog follow you around.
*Build a city to your heart's content (and the limits of the game).
*Refreshingly simple gameplay (only three buttons to worry about).
*Enjoyable strategy game.
*Fun to just run around and "explore".
*Nobody dies...  Sounds silly, but it's just good-hearted fun.
*Though it's "easy to beat", If you stay on a single map long enough, it gets harder... to the point of insanity.  If you want to avoid this, take the boat to a new map... otherwise, stay on that one and see how long you can survive.
*Ride a Bear and eat bunnies.
*Ride a Stag (which is awesome).
*Ride a Unicorn.
Now for the cons:
*While you do build your own kingdom, the "customization" of this is somewhat limited.  For example, you can only build towers on "these rocks"...  Which helps with the strategy part of the game;  you have to pay attention to your surroundings...  But leaves a little to be desired as far as "build my kingdom my way".
*AI is decent, but sometimes frusterating...  Though "stupid archerers" happen very rarely, when it does it really hurts your survivability.
*You'll play this game many times (which is a good thing, obviously)... however, when you unlock everything (about 30 hours of gameplay in) - you end up "running out of stuff to do"... that is to say;  the game feels repetative after about 30 hours or so.
Over All?
Totally worth buying and giving a try.  Sink in some good hours, build up your kingdom, and unlock everything you can.  Have respect for the hermit and bread-maker (unlockables), and enjoy whichever mount you choose.
I'm highly looking foreward to more DLC or updates;  but certainly worth buying and playing as-is.

Having never played the original Kingdom, I don't have anything to compare this to. But by itself, its an interestingly addicting little game, especially if you happen to like resource management games in any capacity. Kingdom: New Lands has you acting as King/Queen in a brand new, unbroken land. You get two peasants(?) to start off with, a sack full of gold, and a ghost. The ghost points to things like walls or fires, and you build them. (The ghost doesn't stick around past the tutorial, so if you're worried about spending the entire game being haunted by a dead relative, you don't need to be.)
The first island is easy enough to get through, but beyond that things can take a turn for the difficult. I think in this regard, it can actually be EASIER to have some experience with the first Kingdom game, since you know what to expect. I played the second  island and didn't realize that enemies can come at you from more than one portal in more than one direction until the second night happened. I lost my gold, my crown, and had to restart.
It makes things easier supposedly if you manage to destroy the portal with your knights, but that's something I've never managed to do. Either way, in 20 days winter sets in - and yes, the game does go through an active season change, its very pretty - and then your rabbits vanish, your deer retreat into the forest, your farmers can't bring in any new crops, and the only money you've got is from the little man with the donkey and your banker. It's possible to get a boat up and running and your kingdom fully armored by the time 20 days rolls around, but it gets harder on each subsequent island, as monsters can come on you from both sides, meaning if you want farmers that will be safe (since they stay in their own little hut at night, OUTSIDE the walls) then you have to extend the walls to keep them safe, which will mean extra coins for walls and catapults. It can be  nerve-wracking, especially when it gets down to the wire.
But overall, its a good game. Mindless enough to enjoy running back and forth, but intense enough on the resource management that six or eight hours could easily pass without you noticing.

Our Darker Purpose is what the spawn of Dark Souls and Binding of Issac would be if it raided Tim Burton's wardrobe and splashed just a dash of Lovcraftian horror onto its plotline.
With tight controls and well programmed enemy A.I. your heart will be pounding as you attempt to traverse the halls of Edgewood's Home for Lost Children and repeatedly die with each new or old enemy you encounter. This doesn't mean the game is unfair, no despite the steap learning curve it is possible to even traverse (at least) the first floor without getting hurt using the knowledge from all your previous failings which is to be expected. There's also small upgrades that you can choose from in and before the game that while don't make the game easier will help you survive an extra minute if you learn to utilize them.
The plot is simple: you are Cordy, a little girl trying to untangle the mystery behind the orphanage when all the teachers dissapear and the students scream Mad Max-esqe rules and start killing each other while establishing a new heirarchy with the most nasty creatures at the top floors of the svhool.
My favourite part however has to be the bosses, all amazingly unique in design with the only similarites being in how some of them attack or defend. But this is only one overlap between a miniscule amount of monsters who accidentally showed up wearing identical pairs of socks while the rest giggle in their ballgowns made of the player's carcass.
However there is a point in the game where it (not completely) delflates a bit where as you progress you only come across maybe two levels (at most) of the really hard enemies. You could say I was being greedy at this point and the game was only trying to reflect a traditional social triangle, but when I'm being beaten by enemies and they finally bring out a paddle to add to the fun I'd like it to last more than two wacks!

At the end of the day, this is a cute (from a goth/emo perspective) twin-stick shooter in the same vein as Binding of Issac or even Geometry Wars. There are power-ups to be had, boss and mini-boss battles, and a fun sorta "Classic Addams Family Comic" vibe to the art style. The controls are not terrible, but not great - you're stuck with either awkward keyboard or slightly less responsive gamepad, but gamepad works well enough to not get in the way of the fun, so I say use that.
I'm not gonna lie - my favorite part of this game is the art. It seriously looks like the old Addams Family comics (the ones that inspired the TV series and, later, the movies). It's dark and gothic, but not opressive. Combine that with consistant atmosphere that matches the art style, and you've got a real visual winner.
I've reviewed this one twice before, making this my third review for this game and, if the devs keep improving it, not my last. It's an almost great game on the way to greatness, and I'm loving it. It can kill five minutes or a couple hours, and that's pretty awesome, too.
So, yeah - get this one. I mean, if twin-stick shooting is your vibe, and you have a decent game pad to use (I advocate for the Xbox 360 or PS3 controllers, but what the hell do I know?) - no matter what, though, the art is great and the game itself is fun. Thanks to a recommendation from a close friend, I started this game with mild expectations. I did not think that by the end of the game, it would become my favorite game of all-time. These are a few reasons why.
1. The shooting and aiming in this game is amazing. The gunfights are super fun to play (Although some get tiring when you've replayed it 5 or six times).
2. The characters' dynamics, interactions, and developments are spot on. Never have I seen a game where the characters work so well with each other. No character is dull, and no character is too pointless to be forgotten.
3. The story itself is the best story I have ever seen in a video game. No chapter gets annoying, and no chapter is dull. Each one adds something new and exciting, making this game fun to play even after the tenth time.
4. The final mission is one of the best final missions I have ever played. It adds to the ambience of the whole story, and you feel like a badass the entire time. It was so much fun to play, and I will play it many times afterwards.
5. The ending. I will not spoil the ending, but everything in the game leading up to this ending is all worth it. I have never shaken at a game's ending before, and this one was the first. I had to take a 5 minute breather just to accept and intake the ending. It was one of the best endings, if not THE best, ending of a video game.
These are a few of the reasons why I love this game.

I heard about this game on the podqisition podcast thanks to the lovely Laura K.  I must say that I do enjoy the overall theme of the game and the tank innuendo is a nice touch.  The only real issues I have with the game are all in the user interface.
Pros:
-nice humor
-tanks all have flaws based on the tank models they were designed after
-reasonably priced for the content you get
cons:
-to scroll through the text you need to click the mouse button.  To the best of my knowledge this cant be rebound.  My personal preferance is to either use the mouse wheel or the down button and the constant need to click is annoying to me (though I know that is just personal taste)
-I haven't found a way to go back in a conversation.  In most games like this you can press either the up button or spin the mouse wheel up to read past parts of a conversation.  I personally like this feature encase i missed part of a joke.
-As far as I can tell there is no full screen mode.  (again personal preference)
_lastly there is no option to change text speed.  The current speed is ok but I find that I tend to read faster than the scrolling allows.  This can be remedied with a double click of the mouse but it simply feels like an extra step.
All in all it is a nice game that I feel just needs so minor tweaks that can be remedied with a better options screen.  This is a purchase that was worth my money and will be looking for future games from DEVGRU-P

Absolver is a really hardcore combat game with really good fighting mechanics but note that this game does not have a full PvE experience, its fairly short with like 4-6 hours of gameplay depending on how much you explore,this game is about learning and knowing your combat deck better than your opponent.

I still plan to play the game more to give it a better review, however heres my current thoughts:
So far, my major issue is random lag spiking. Ive played fine for a while, then randomly hit spikes where id be in one location, getting pummeled in a combo by an enemy that appears to be "no where near me"... Frustrating, but Im sure itll balance out once the game ages a little.
My next is the way combat vs multiple enemies go. The controls dont make for swapping targets to be the most fluid... While it its just one extra button to hold and swap triggers - It hasn't always locked from what Ive seen. You already have plenty to juggle in this type of a game, it would be easier to just make it a quick trigger squeeze to target swap.
Not to metion, until you start getting yourself a few levels above the area you are in... Fighting multiple enemies in pairs of 3-4, is not so much difficult as it is a consistent♥♥♥♥♥♥fest. Now, Im an avid dark souls player, so Im ok with♥♥♥♥♥rape into oblivion because I haven't learned the fight... However, mix in the lag spikes + 3-4 enemies comboing on you while dodge or block isn't able to trigger you out of it... You're dead. I would have preferred less 2+ vs 1's, since their AI is actually quite difficult as is. (Compared to most games, lets be real lol). Especially the mini bosses - Coming in a pack of 1-2, plus a few cronies... It feels more like "Good ♥♥♥♥ing luck ya prick" instead of "Damn, this is gonna be rough."
As for the actual combat, graphics and deck building/skill learning - Mind you I am just hitting the first actual boss you have to fight solo - I think this is AWESOME! The move sets really do move fluently. If you pay attention to how to build your moves, you can make endless good chains and swaps, dodges, counters. It does take a lot of memorization to know your abilities and when to use them so give yourself time. This isnt simply Learn when to press X or press Y.
As you fight, you will learn new moves from dodging/blocking the enemies. When you kill the enemy, you gain the progress on the abilities you started learning. Once unlocked, you can go into practice mode and start making your personal build with a plethora of skills (so it seems, id say at least 8ish per section and this is just my first style learned.)
It does have a steep learning curve, which is where peoples frustrations could come in. Youre not walking through this game spamming X and Block... just not the way itll go. Mix and match your armor to keep your mobility/defense/damage in check, plaay with the move sets, grind mobs or players to learn more moves. Rinse, repeat. Hey, least you dont need to go running and recovering your souls every death! :D
Graphically it is very pleasant. I feel they matched the theme nicely with the art style and music. Even on an older system like mine, it runs pretty damn flawlessly (with exception of these random lag spikes hmm...)
My recommendation? Watch some gameplay and combat footage, ingame play. If you like mentally challenging fighting games, where you cannot button mash to win, you'll be pleased. If you want a more DMC style action-rpg - this isn't it. You will struggle. You will die, a lot. You will learn and grow. If challenging combat, character customization, and some RP elements are your thing - I'd say this game could help quench your thirst.
For those that enjoy a COOP experience, you CAN coop with 2 additional players, except for major boss fights it seems. So be sure to level up plenty and prepare your character!
Overall I'd say 8.5/10 - few tweaks such as targetting, making multiple enemies a tiny bit easier to deal with (not by a lot, maybe even simply making their stamina deplete a little faster for weaker opponents a little easier could help).

Premium Pool Arena:
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

Hey mate, how are you going? Should we have a bet on the pool table or just play for fun! Well, whatever tickles your fancy! In Premium Pool Arena you can get it all . . . so, this is the question; are you ready for a game of pool?
Premium Pool Arena is a casual / sport game which you can play against your friends, online opponents or the computer.
As you reach the main menu, you will be able to click into nine different menus. Four of them will be for online gaming (Quick play, Casual, Friends and Play online), challenges, play offline, shop and the other are options and your profile. In the offline mode, you can play against the computer or a local opponent. There is another gameplay called speed, where you have to clear the table as fast as you can.
The game play is simple and easy but very fun. With each new game you play, the side of the table will change colour, giving you a fresh approach. In terms of the game play, you can use your mouse and keyboard or your gamepad.  In a nutshell, place your cue on the selected ball. Figure out the angle, the spin and the power and you will hopefully sink the ball into the appropriate hole. Occasionally, you might sink the ball in an unintended hole, but it doesn’t matter due to the fact that you sunk it.
If you play against a friend, online or quick play, you can choose to bet on each game. If each fo you bet 100 coins and you are the winner, you’ll pick up 200 coins. If you have amalgamated enough coins, you will be able to buy better queues at the shop and new coloured balls.
