Kingdom New Lands Review
I played the original Kingdom when it came out and found it pretty frustrating, yet relaxing and stimulating in its own way, Kindom New lands is a free expansion (if you already owned Kingdom) that expands on it by featuring new mounts and npcs that will aid you on your quest to get the heck out of a bunch of cursed islands. This became my go to game for when I wanted to listen to a podcast or watch a video on the side with the game scaled down slightly... and that is where my problem began.
Before this game I would usually play Risk of Rain as my go to “podcast listening game”, which would last roughly an hour (usually shorter), which was fine, Kingdoms on the other hand... aside from the first 2 islands, you will spend longer and longer if you want to have a session where you get off an island each time, the last island can take over 2-3+ hours, 3 REPETTIVE, NOT FUN hours and that's the crucial bit, I realised after playing this game for hours over and over that I wasn't really enjoying the game, but why?
My main reason for why I am not recommending this game is for this purely subjective reason; This game is a productivity killer. Because for the most part, this is “Running while waiting for stuff to be done the game” (well, not really, due to the fact that each of the mounts are the only hypoglycaemic animals in the world and cant run for more than a few seconds without needing to eat).
The game asks for an ABSURD amount of waiting, want to cut some trees? You have to wait for the carpenter to run and cut it, you want to charge an enemy portal to destroy it? You have to wait until your castle reaches a certain level, have enough peasants to equip the armour and to also have enough archers (for which you also need peasants), so how do you get peasants to work for you? You pay them a single coin, oh but you also need to find their spawn points (unless you have a cook) but guess what? Only 2 peasants spawn per spawn point per day, one in the morning and one at night, which you will have to wait for. That's not all, if you want any hope of having enough cash to recruit the peasants, you will need to make farmers, but before that you need to wait until you have a carpenter and enough cash to build some farm land, but oops! Turns out you REALLY NEED a 2nd level farm built because the farmers will walk back to the main camp otherwise, which forces you to WAIT EVEN LONGER! Oh and the farming? You have to wait for that as well. The games forces you to wait and forces you to REPEAT waiting for your tasks to be finished.
I spent hours on games like Risk of Rain, Far cry, Assassins creed etc But while some of those games require patience, I rarely spent over two hours (or even an hour) per session, nor did ANY of those games ever ask me to wait for things to happen like this game does. The payoff for beating the game or getting off any of the islands is not worth it, you will just get a stamp of the day you left and credits roll.
Truth be told, at times I found the game alright (obviously, you don't play a game for hours and hate it completely), but just know this, if you decide to really to get into it, it will just become a complete time waster, do something productive, go outside or play a better game, there are so many awesome indie games that you can afford to skip this one, you will thank yourself for it.

This all comes from someone who rarely enjoys strategy games, as I find them too steep to dive into. Sure, I've played my StarCrafts and WarCrafts, and Red Alerts, mostly for lore and fun custom games, but I've never actually felt good while playing them. A constant hope for survival gripped at my throat, knowing I had the odds against me, because there were far too many things to keep track of and I felt overwhelmed.
Kingdom is the first strategy game that makes me feel knowledgable. It's learning curve is intriguing, in the sense that I constantly felt interested when I was figuring out how things worked. It took me around 5-6 hours to find out most things, but I never felt frustrated during that period. I found joy.
The game is also rich in beautiful, serene moments of clarity, giving you the peace to figure out your next move. But you best use that time wisely, as often one mistake can cost you lots of progress. Sometimes, even everything. But that's the beauty of it - it's your fault, you know why and what you did. You learn from that mistake, and next time - you conquer further and further, until there is peace. For a time (that's where this wonderfull expansion comes in).
All during this - wonderful pixel graphics and superb music are your company, and on this new quest - a journey is ahead of you. And it tests all you've learned in the game; how far are you capable of going? How much stress are you able to manage? Too much? Never fear, you can always start anew and enjoy yourself, because now you are stronger. And next time - you will go to new lands and meet new challanges.
And all this is superbly executed, with minor problems here and there. For instance, one of the few things that always bugged me is how the catapults are prioritized by workers, still moving slowly as ever, which can cost you the game at certain points, or how some things aren't that clearly hinted at, or how there is a very real chance of a map location generating, which simply offers no possible solution to beat the game in. Then there are still some technicalities worth cleaning, like torches on towers lighting up as reflections before they actually light up on the tower. But none of these ever stopped me from enjoying everything else, because it's more than enough.
Thank you to the team who made this amazing game. Certainly one of the best games this year - Kingdom is a must play. Might not be for everyone, but it's guaranteed that you will appreciate your time with it.
Overall: A superb addition to a great and fresh strategy game.

Thanks to a recommendation from a close friend, I started this game with mild expectations. I did not think that by the end of the game, it would become my favorite game of all-time. These are a few reasons why.
1. The shooting and aiming in this game is amazing. The gunfights are super fun to play (Although some get tiring when you've replayed it 5 or six times).
2. The characters' dynamics, interactions, and developments are spot on. Never have I seen a game where the characters work so well with each other. No character is dull, and no character is too pointless to be forgotten.
3. The story itself is the best story I have ever seen in a video game. No chapter gets annoying, and no chapter is dull. Each one adds something new and exciting, making this game fun to play even after the tenth time.
4. The final mission is one of the best final missions I have ever played. It adds to the ambience of the whole story, and you feel like a badass the entire time. It was so much fun to play, and I will play it many times afterwards.
5. The ending. I will not spoil the ending, but everything in the game leading up to this ending is all worth it. I have never shaken at a game's ending before, and this one was the first. I had to take a 5 minute breather just to accept and intake the ending. It was one of the best endings, if not THE best, ending of a video game.
These are a few of the reasons why I love this game.

Oh Absolver, how I swooned over you my sweet. Too bad you stole my DLC gear.
Now for the real review. As a huge fan of this game I was kinda let down. Most fights are unenjoyable and sometimes downright BS. I do think it's like Dark Souls, A LOT. The only difference is ones got ♥♥♥♥♥♥ enemys in large quantities and one has good enemys in large quantities.
Kahlt: The unfair one. Get ready to find a ton of scrubs using this one, all you have to do is use your right stick or whatever it is with keyboard, and you will win your fights. It's easy to use, and unfair.
Windfall: The hardest of the three despite what the game says. You have to dodge at very exact times, and fighting other fast pace characters is extremely hard as a Windfall. I don't reccomend this to newer players, so if you are reading this, probably don't try this one.
Foresaken: The best one for newer players. You have to parry left or right to gain a few seconds of time to go ham on the enemy, it's not that hard, it's not that easy. You want to see how the other person plays for a second then go in for the kill. Foresaken is the most reccomended one from me.
Offline mode and servers: Offline mode is broken. I hate to say that, but please don't make my mistake and play Offline mode. You risk losing DLC or Deluxe Edition gear. I lost my entire priest set because my game crashed in Offline mode. This is why I'm probably not gonna reccomend this to many people. The servers are unstable on PC, and if you can, get it on PS4. Sloclap doesn't manage PC version because the player base was gonna be smaller. Even though it's ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t, the servers are broken and awful.
Customization: While I don't like the hair styles, you have a wide range of things to customize, such as clothing, fighting style, and weapon type. First the clothing. Clothings is set in a few catagories, Mask, Undershirt(?), This robe thing you wear or a poncho if you are me, Pants, Gloves/Hand Item, and shoes. In the beginning it will be very mild, and you will have literally nothing. As you progress it get's better but don't try to look fly in the beginning cuz you gonna look like a mexican I promise you. Now onto fighting COMBO*****'s. You can customize combo's to match your fighting style. Windfall should have a dexterity based attacks as a Kahlt should have strength attacks, and Foresaken can have whatever they want honestly. Now onto weapons. You have 3 weapons if you count fists. The other two are a Sword, and Bear Knuckles or whatever you call 'em. Bear Knuckles do blunt damage and won't change your fighting style. But swords are far more diverse. Swords have an entire seperate combo list to find and unlock as well as it changes your moveset. Swords do more sharp damage so overall if you are good swords win out, but Bear Knuckles are alright I think.
Conclusion: I don't think this game is finished. And it should be labeled early access, but it is the first week. Once this game ages then you should buy it. It's fun, it's diverse, and it's not like every other fighting game. I believe that Absolver is a fun game, but not a finished one, and Sloclap needs to improve it.
tl;dr - let it age and drop about 10 bucks

Absolver is a game that seems to have got the core of its premise surprisingly spot on however everything supporting it doesn’t quite manage the same level of quality.
I tend not to be pulled in by fighting games simply due to the fact I’m honestly not very good at them and they frustrate me. Absolver seemed different and the idea of being able to build your own combo deck ala God Hand appealed to me greatly. I wasn’t sure if the combat itself would click with me but thankfully it does. Unfortunately everything else I hadn’t considered is so odd and managed to seep into every aspect of the game that it’s soured the experience as a whole.
The short single player is a mess and you can tell the developers have been inspired by the Dark Souls franchise. You’ve got your vague story-telling, you’ve got what are essentially bonfires, you’ve got a small intertwining world you can run around in, people are able to join your world to fight or help you. While this is unexpected it wouldn’t be bad if it didn’t seemingly take most of its inspiration from Dark Souls 2, the worst in the series. Despite the game only really working in a one versus one situation you’ll have to fight off groups of enemies at a time constantly including the small number of boss fights. This is a design decision that really baffles me quite honestly and immensely frustrating. You can team up with people in your world but then you’ll find yourself breezing through it with no issue. While the world it’s set in is beautiful it’s very lackluster in content and there’s nothing interesting about it to make it worth while for a single player purchase alone. This alone wouldn’t be a problem if it didn’t bleed into the multiplayer.
Before delving into the multiplayer I want to quickly talk about how the combat works. You’ve got 4 possible stances that you can switch into at any time that position you for your next attack and these attacks naturally flow to each other in between each stance. You’ll unlock sets of moves that you put into a combo deck which basically means you set up your own style of playing, how your moves and stances flow from one to the next is all up to you. Maybe you’ve set up a combo deck that just flows naturally across all stances but when you go try it out and you get beaten to a pulp, so you head back into the combo deck and come up with an entirely new strategy and flow. It makes for an extremely compelling experience with it being less about memorising preset attacks and more about just finding something that works for you. You can also pick one of four styles which give you bonuses to blocking, dodging, allow you to parry, or allow you to take on a drunken style. Once you’ve really nailed a combo you’ll find yourself being able to chain moves effortlessly along with minor attack buffs for flowing into the next attack at the right time instead of just mashing buttons. Unfortunately it’s not all wombos and combos, you’ll need to unlock moves and that’s where a big issue comes in. Absolver has you unlock moves by going against them and defending or dodging that specific move until the EXP bar for the move has maxed out. This might not be so bad but you have to then beat your enemy to keep that EXP. If you die during the fight without killing the enemy all the EXP is gone. This means you have to either tediously grind out enemy NPCs, assuming you don’t get ganked to the high heavens and luck out with their spawns, grind it out with friends who have joined your world, or go online where victory isn’t assured so any EXP you could have gained might not even be secured. While I can appreciate them trying something from a tradition unlock system this certainly wasn’t the way to go. One simple fix for this would be for players to keep their EXP regardless of the win or not, otherwise newcomers down the line are going to be put on some serious tilt.
The online PvP element is where the real meat of the game is. Given how the core of this combat is so much fun it naturally creates some extremely entertaining rounds. Getting put against someone where you’re both using the emoticons to bow and gesture to each other followed by intense fights that are neck and neck with you side-stepping, jumping, ducking, blocking, and parrying moves constantly is just a whole lot of fun. Unfortunately, once again, there are certain design choices here I just don’t understand. Matches are set up to be the first to three victories but whoever wins the round only receives a partial health boost instead of a completely one which isn’t something I’m in favour of at all. When I beat someone I want it to be because I’ve taken them all the way down, not because they’re still being punished from the last round. It takes away some of the satisfaction. Cheap abilities you can gain from the single player make an appearence here too. As you defeat minibosses in the single player you’ll be given moves and unlocks with things such as health regen, stamina drain on nearby enemies, or stuns. While these can naturally be avoided and countered they feel entirely unnecessary to the core of the game and somewhat gimmicky. There’s one in particular, shockwaves, which pushes nearby enemies away from you. Seeing as there a good few maps that have instant death edges on them you can see where this is going. People just focus on getting you as close to the edge as possible and using the ability to force you over. This would be less infuriating if there was a mode which at least disable these abilities but there’s not. Currently the only online mode outside running around in the hub area together is 1v1. The developers are apparently adding a spectator mode, a mode that allows you to host private 1v1s, and a 3v3 capture the point mode which I can only picture being a mess but we’ll see.
In conclusion Absolver is a frustrating game. It’s managed to deliver on the hardest part of its concept but stumbled on everything around it so much that it’s hard to just straight up recommend. It’s certainly not a bad game and if the main issues I’ve mentioned sound like something that won’t bother you too much then you might find yourself having a decent time especially if you have some friends you want to play against.

By no means has this game been perfected, lots of issues are present in this game that need to be addressed as well as changes that will increase the quality of life for players. so in order to get all that out of the way im just gonna list the things that im hating about this game before singing it's praises.
1. bugs
Ok by no means is it the most bug ridden game out here but my god there are too many and all of them get in the way, one bug which has me become rich off of all the salt i produce littarally prevents me from 'dodging', attacking at all and using my abilities. there are others as well that include and are not bloody limited to terrain fazing out of existance (and falling through it in some cases), the path sometimes becoming unusable due to invisable walls that should not be there (as part of the bug) and sometimes (only happened three times) the mini bosses spawning twice so that there are two of a marked one.
2. the servers.
Grabbing the low hanging fruit i know but its certainly valid, as if the bugs weren't enough i have sometimes lost fights (that by all rights i should of won) because of sudden lag spikes mid combo and my opponent (sometimes plural) wins because im unable to defend myself on account of the lag.
3. The AI
Ok, this one is less serious then the last two but it is fricking annoying. As a solo player i do not want to be in a fight with 3 enemy AI that will all fixate on me, not only is this incredibly frustrating but it makes the game incredibly boring because i then have to take on a incredibly boring playstyle where i have to sit back and let the AI beat up on themselves when they're trying to kick my teeth in. this can be fixed easily by letting us just pull one at a time. their pathfinding could also do with work.
4. 'story' length and issues within the bosses and minibosses
You can beat all six marked ones, the two bosses and the final boss in aproximately 4 hours if you know where they're at and what to do, for the pve crowd (which im a part of) this will not do. now i get it, its a pvp game by design and beating up on the roaming NPC prospects to learn their moves is in of itself a massive task but its still something. its also really stupid, i have had more trouble with Ana saba (birdwatch marked one) then the final boss of the game, but more trouble with the enemies in the final area then the final boss and marked ones (though thats probably because theres usually groups of three enemies).
5. game difficulty
Ok, now for some hypocracy, what has determined game difficulty is how cooperative the servers are (which they are ♥♥♥♥ing not), the amount of enemies that your fighting and stat variances between the regular enemies. if the server issues and shared agro ranges were fixed the game would only have the stat variances of enemies that would make it more difficult, and if those issues were fixed the game would be♥♥♥♥♥♥easy, thus even bloody shorter. so pick your poison on this one.
With all that said, I love this game when it these issues aren't in my face, i have a bit of a interest in fighters but gonna be blunt i am♥♥♥♥♥♥at them, its the imputs. this game has two imputs, normal attack, alternate attack, for someone who is♥♥♥♥♥♥at those ♥♥♥♥ing super fast precise imputs the fact that i only have to think about X and Y is like a dream come true for me since now i just have to think about timing, stance and knowledge, the sound track and art direction are also quite good. the moves themselves are nothing too special but this is actually to the benefit of the players since if they were super flashing it might be unnessessarily hard to react to an attack properly, though i'd think it would be an improvement to make it so that when you've locked onto someone your character becomes a bit see through, this would allow us to menuver much safer since we know exactly whats infront of us (like in punch out for the wii). it would also be interesting to not only get pve content as well. one idea is pve instances that make use of multi stage bosses, rare enemies and rare items. combat is in my opinion one of the few things that sloclap got right from the start, i'm not one for comparasons but its a more indepth version of dark souls, instead of having a single weapon with a moveset you have four weapons each with four attacks each with their own stats and special properties...and thats not counting the fact you can then get an actual weapon (so far there are just swords and gauntlets which is kinda disapointing) and then you have another four weapons with another four attacks with their own stats and properties, its just great.
I'd give it a 5/10 or a 3/5, its good and you can have fun with it but there is certainly problems that are holding this game back.

EDIT #1 : Ok so i played it again for the first time in awhile and i must say im disapointed, i did three rounds of pvp and found that NONE of the problems regarding servers were fixed and discovered and even worse ♥♥♥♥ing issue.

as for my second verdict i simply cannot recommend this game, there are simply better fighting games out there.

The different cues remind me of RPG elements which is pretty interesting in a pool game. It revolves around leveling up, getting coins and tokens and just having a good time. It runs really well on pretty much any modern system. Even old potatos can probably run this game flawlessly. I didn't experience any bugs or glitches so far either. You can change the volume (or mute entirely) for the ingame music which I'm glad they added. The ranking system gives you something to work towards as you can "prestige" like in COD.
Negatives:
It seems way too focused on using a Xbox controller. I prefer mouse and keyboard for 2d-birds-eye-view pool games like this and there isn't much explanation as to what all of the controls are. The lack of different game modes also hurts the game. It needs more depth in that department. Currently the playerbase is small so it may be difficult to find a match online with other random players. Playing with friends on your Steam list doesn't even count as an actual online game which I think sucks. No stats count, no earnings, no random drops... nothing. There is also no way to chat with random players globally or even with your friends. You have to go into a steam group chat with a friend to talk and/or type while playing. That's very unfortunate. I feel like the community would be better, more active and an increased playerbase if people were at least able to communicate to each other while playing.
Overall:
For only 2 bucks you easily get what you pay for if this is your cup of tea. I still need more time playing to edit/update/revise my review but after about an hour and a half of playing this is what I gathered. Will update my review after playing it more.

Solid gameplay, a haunting atmosphere, and a great soundtrack. There are plenty of items to find/collect providing some replay value and the game looks good even on medium and lower graphics settings. Now if only they could have tied it all together with a decent story....
You have some ability to roam and make decisions, but for the most part the story is linear and kind of let down. Especially since every one of the reviews I read prior to buying said it was great. The game excels at creating atmospheric suspense, but also relies heavily on jump scares which come off as rather gimmicky after a while.
I spent a good 14 hours the first time through and still didn't find everything I was trying to, but the storyline itself amounted to maybe 9 or 10 hours. A more serious player can probably get through normal mode in less than 8 hours.
It's a good game, but it could have been great if the writers had tried just a wee bit harder. You'll know what I mean after you play through it. I think $60 is a little much for this one, but that's the norm now so I guess you just have to deal with it or a wait a while for it go on sale.

Soundtrack - A
Story - C+
Replay Ability - B+

Early Impressions:
I've always enjoyed the gameplay of Binding of Isaac, but honestly, the heavy scatological themes in the visual design never really did it for me, along with some of the story themes being too squicky for me personally. Plenty of people won't have the same experience with BoI, and that's fine, but it just made me not as interested in playing in the long run. In that regard, Our Darker Purpose is the precise game I've been waiting for.
Make no mistake, the themes of this game are still dark, but in more a way that I'm personally comfortable with. While it lacks some of the polish in terms of gameplay of BoI, especially compared to the later Rebirth addition, I enjoy the Burton-by-way-of-Don't-Starve aesthetic a lot more. I also always enjoy a dash of persistent progress in my Roguelites a la Rogue Legacy, and Our Darker Purpose has that in the form of unlockable/equippable bonuses that tweak and improve your overall power as you continue to play. It gives a little feeling of accomplishment, even on play sessions where you seem to be mostly bashing your head against a wall or two.
The roll/dash is a nice addition to the gameplay, although my Dark Souls experience makes me expect invincibility frames (hint hint, Avildly Wild), so I had to get my brain past that mental block. The chalk is...weird, at least at first. It only has a single charge, recharges are rare, and it's not *so* powerful that it seems a good balance with that. The power-ups tend to lean more on the positive side so far, and less on the "really messes you up unless in very specific builds" side of things like you'd see in BoI. The coin curve overall seems better in early levels, and while I never have enough for *everything*, I can usually get at least one item in a vending machine per time I encounter one unless I'm just starving for juice boxes, the game's health-recover item.
These are nit-picky points though. It's a bit more of a slow and deliberate pace than BoI, but by no means would I call it very easy, especially as you progress. I think that this would be very welcome to anyone who either liked the idea of Binding of Isaac but didn't dig the aesthetic and/or themes, or even anyone who loves Binding of Isaac but would like a change of pace and a way to enjoy this little sub-genre of roguelites in a different way.
Recommended.

It's obvious -- an overhead, oldschool Zelda-inspired, 4-directional dual-stick shooter in which you play as a hapless, ambiguously 'innocent' child in a dark, gothic setting, moving from floor to floor collecting powerups and fighting huge, challenging bosses in a rogulike gameplay shell.  Yep, it's Binding of Isaac.  But not
.
First of all, the little aesthetic differences on the surface; to start off with, you play as a girl (though one could argue you can technically play as a "girl" in BoI, and this game's Cordy looks kinda like Eve, but that's besides the point).  And instead of tears, you shoot fireballs.  And instead of going down an increasingly surreal basement, you go up an increasingly surreal schoolhouse / orphanage.  And instead of vicious, freakish abominations of nature, you fight vicious, freakish orphaned children (and eventually abominations of nature).  Yeah, really similar stuff... though overall ODP has a slightly less cartoonish, more Tim Burton-esque gothic style to it, which depending on your tastes may look a lot better than BoI's, and it's at least marginally "classier", with a LOT less bodily fluids and toilet humor, though its share of less-than-prudish bits here and there; it's more on the "somewhat unsettling/disturbing, but kind of cool" level than the "gross-out until you get used to it and just laugh the rest of the way" level BoI sits on.
But what about the gameplay?  Well, it is indeed EXTREMELY similar to Isaac, but with a few fundamental differences.  The biggest ones are:
A) an experience/levelling system, which guarantees at least semi-regular increases in power comparable to a useful passive item upgrade, especially if you're one of those players like me who insists on clearing every single room in every floor.  This kind of replaces BoI's item rooms on each floor, though this is somewhat of a blessing since level-up bonuses are nearly ALWAYS good if not great.
B) a persistant upgrade system to make yourself or the world around you more geared for your success as you build up tokens earned by completing floors and getting achievements, which you can spend on either 'lessons' (passive effects you earn through achievements as well) or your 'guidance counselor' (which is basically a way to bank extra currency for gradual bonuses, similar to the coin bank in BoI in a way)
C) the ability to DODGE ROLL.  You have no idea how good this is and how it changes the experience compared to BoI!  Not only is it just a universally useful thing to have but it allows you to, say, take a slow movement-speed build and not be forced to tank countless hits from enemies/projectiles that are literally unavoidable without speed past a certain threshold like in BoI.
There are other smaller differences, like the fact you get to manually choose your next floor out of 2-4 choices and see the variables they have (kind of like curses in BoI but often with both positive and negative, or even outright positive, effects)... or the fact that instead of bombs which I say are of dubious quality anyway in BoI, you get chalk which is basically a very rare but very powerful utility that can be used both offensively and defensely.  Also, as opposed to your regular bombable secret rooms, in this game they're rather obvious and easy to find and only occur once every few floors on average, anyway.
Aside from those points, it's more or less an identical game.  But that's not a bad thing.  Like so many great games of PC gaming past copied the original Rogue and created the genre we now know as roguelike, ODP copies Binding of Isaac which is this generation's most well-known and quite possibly well-made roguelike.  And it is a great game.  There's really no reason I can think of NOT to buy it if you like Isaac at all, or just action rpg/overhead shooter/roguelikes in a general sense.  The graphics are unique and lovely, the music is atmospheric, the gameplay is tight and spot-on, and it never seems unfair, far less than Isaac.
I suppose if I had one criticism, it'd be that it's more 'subdued' than BoI... besides in an aethetic sense as mentioned earlier, there are definitely far less ways to make your character / shots nearly as 'wild' or unique as you can in Isaac, and it's basically a matter of doing what you can to make them stronger, faster, have longer range, and add as many supplementary alternate 'bullets' as you can through various means.  But since the game's designed and balanced around this less over-the-top style it's really not that big of a deal.

This game is really fun. Tough as nails, but fun. The enemies and bosses are lovingly designed. It has a charming art style. What little music there is is haunting and well put together. It still sees periodic updates that are carefully balanced and improve the overall experience.
The most glaring problem with this game is that Cordy has no firing animation aside from some swirly fire that moves independent of her. That will never stop bugging me even though I'm not looking at Cordy most of the time when playing this game. The hitboxes are also strange and not entirely obvious upon looking at the sprites.
That said, the items and upgrades you get can change your gameplay in important ways, but it seems as if there are a specific few upgrades or items that you absolutely need in order to beat the game. At least a few of the items from that group, anyway. But overall the pacing and balance of the game is pretty good, especially after unlocking better lessons (permanent upgrades in-game).
Is it worth 15 bucks? It's getting there, yeah. Every update refines the experience. If I were writing this review for past-me, I would tell myself to get it for 15 dollars. But this game certainly isn't for everyone.

Good storytelling but predictable and ruined by the bear.
I wouldn't recommend this game except for the way it handled the storytelling.  Even though I figured out everything by the second painting, I felt it did a good job getting the whole feel across from a young child's perspective.
The game isn't really scary, although it conveys the same sort of childhood 'spookiness' that a dark house and strange sounds bring.  That is it's greatest strength, conveying a nightmare from a child's perspective -- full of strange places and monsters.  This emersion is then quickly ruined by the addition of the damn teddy bear pulled out of some children's show who you HAVE to take with you and who ruins everything.
It controlls well, looks good, and conveys a feeling of helplessness that a two-year old child would have along with the potential havoc and trouble a two-year old can get into.  At least, until the bear opens his stupid mouth again.
I can't state this enough, but the bear ruins the whole experience by talking.  Listening to him suffer in the washing machine or trying to hang on to you is one thing; I hated him from the get-go but even I felt bad for him at those points.  If they cut out his dialogue and just left him emotion he would have been an excellent companion, but as implemented he screams "HELLO YOU ARE IN A GAME WITH TALKING BEAR WHO POINTS OUT THE OBVIOUS".
The game is short, and it would have been a nice bit of art if everyone would learn to shut up.  As is, I think some people will enjoy it a lot and ultimately what it does well it does well enough that I can forgive the rest.
This game is NOT for you if:
1. You are immune to childhood fears
2. You want a long game (I've logged 3 hrs and that includes taking the time to write swears in blocks)
3. You want a scary game (unless you are very vulnerable to childhood fears, in which case this is for you)
4. You hate physics puzzles
This game IS for you if:
1. You are vulnerable to childhood fears and like being haunted by them.
2. You enjoyed the demo (despite how badly the bear ruins the experirence)
3. You like 'artistic' game experiences and an interactive way of telling a story.
I'm personally in the middle, and would have recommended this stronger if the bear was mostly mute as well.

This is a criminally underrated game. Surprisingly deep with all the different combinations and play styles available.
It's a squad-based management game, in the same vein as XCOM or Darkest Dungeon. The management aspect is quite good and forces you to make some choices, do you low ball a lot of high potential guys and risk losing them but having an amazing squad, or do you play it safe and pay a few great guys well and fill out your team with cheapos? I always felt that the fact that new recruits just kind of showed up in XCOM and Darkest Dungeon was problematic, and this game has a fun way of dealing with that by making it more like a sports game like EA's NHL series.
The difficulty is pretty intense, not quite Darkest Dungeon, but enough to give a serious challenge, which is probably why a lot of people don't like it. It really takes many play throughs to figure everything out, and the fact that it keeps your high scores gives it an almost rogue-like FTL vibe.
Overall a really well thought out and well designed game. I hope ManaVoid makes more games soon!

I love this game as much as Alien Isolation and I love it more than outlast. I had never played a Resident Evil before this one and I was VERY pleasantly suprised by this masterpiece of a game. It takes the Gore and insanity from Outlast and puts you in a world where you have weaponry, but ammo is always in short supply, like in Alien Isolation. For me, I like being able to have a weapon, while also feeling scared for my life. This game perfects that. Plus, guns in this game are used more like a flash bang or stun in other games, at least for really powerful enemies like papa Jack in the first section of the game when you first enter the center of the mansion. Shooting him will only delay him,  and knocking him out will only do so for a couple of minutes, until he comes back to life.
The shooting feels suprizingly good for a game like this. Each weapon has a distinct purpose and feel to it. At first, I hated the feel of having such limited space in my inventory, but over time I learded to plan ahead and put items in my "chest" which is in almost every save room in the game. It didn't help that in my first playthrough I missed one of the few bag upgrades to increase the space in my inventory. The story was good. Not amazing, but passable. Even though I haven't played any other RE game I still know the basics of the story like the T-virus and Umbrella Corp, and this story fits in with that plot line, but only barely (so far). The Atmosphere is amazing in this game. At every turn I felt freaked out and grossed out at the same time. (Minor Spoiler) In the beginning of the game your wife cuts your hand off, and this moment took me totally by suprize.
The bosses were super memorible for me. My personal favorite is Jack, or Papa Jack as I like to call him. He is super scary for me, but sometimes I can't help but laugh at his quotes and personality (I mean this in the best way possible. His funniness didn't hinder the game at all for me). Margurette is Jack's wife. she is by far the most discusting (if you don't like bugs, beware). She is my least favorite but I have a feeling she was made to seem that way. Lucas is their crazy son who sets up saw-like traps for you to solve. Zoe is the daughter of Jack and Margurette, but she isn't nearly as crazy as either of them. She is your "quest giver" but she ultimately isn't a very important part of the story. I don't want to spoil the plot, so I won't waste time telling you about why you're in such a hellhole of a mansion. It's better if you unravel the story on your own.
I haven't played or purchased any dlc for this game yet, so I can't tell you anything about that. Though I have heard that it's overpriced and other complaints. I highly recommend this game to just about anyone who has the money and time to play through it. For me, this game is a 9.5 outta 10.

Cordelia somehow managed to survive her peers violently taking over the Edgewood Home for Lost Children. Starting from the "Waking Floor", she must travel to the highest library to find out exactly what is happening in a school with only the most casual relationships with reality. Along the way, she'll fight her feral peers, former best friends, and horrible monsters that dwell within the shadows.
A fantastically fun and brutal game reminiscent of Binding of Isaac only with a heavier emphasis on movement and slightly more player choice. The inclusion of the ability to roll changes the pace of combat entirely, allowing for quick escapes from bum-rushing foes or projectiles. Outside of the items that buff your character to various degrees, you also get level ups which allow you to choose between two potential boosts in a variety of stas--speed, attack power, health, etc. Further, completing floors gets you credits, which can be used to buy "classes" which serve to alter the base abilities that Cordy starts with, either by giving her more items, more selection at vending machines, exchanging the roll for a teleport, or other minor-to-game-changing options.
The art style is Edward Gorey-esque (basically the guy who Tim Burton wants to be), the soundtrack effectively atmospheric, and the story is peppered with subtle "ah ha!" moments for those who take the time to dive into the lore. It's also a charmingly (though darkly) funny game, with witty descriptions and dialogue detailing the slow unravelling of Edgewood's secrets. The bosses are the game's biggest strength, in my opinion--creative and fun to fight, each big bad needs to be approached in a way that is different from everything else. Nothing seems to be a simple reskin of an earlier foe with extra health, which is greatly appreciated.
There are some downsides, the biggest of which is the fact that hard mode is a bit too geared against the player in that if you don't have 2-3 damage boosting levels/items by the first chapter boss, later bosses are going to be nightmarish slogs of whittling down massive health bars protected by obscene defense stats. While I appreciate difficult games, patience isn't really the thing to be testing. It also makes me dread fights I was looking forward to--to reiterate, the boss battles really are some of the game's strongest moments.
But, really, my misgivings are just on the optional hard mode. And it could be that I'm just awful, so what do I know? If you like this kind of game, check it out.

There is a box I did not check referring to if I received this game for free; I am a ruthless discount shopper, and often wishlist dozens of games in hope of making the move to acquire a license if one is ever appallingly cheap.  As a result, I usually have a handful of classic games on deck that I'm not ready to *play* yet,
I don't remember which game it was or what became of it, but I once regretted missing that greenlight game in which the protagonist is a retired adventurer who now buys or otherwise acquires cool items, then offers them as rewards to heroes he dispatches on quests.  The premise quite captured me, but I was a Mac gamer when it came and went. I've searched hard for good attempts at that concept.  Recettear gets a little too grindy too quickly.  Empire TV Tycoon is similarly addictive, and similarly impressive while still lacking replay value that it is growing into gradually as the Devs add content.  Any good team eventually gets bored and decides  to build a whole new game - usually a better one, not unlike in the games they make.
When I finally beat Epic Manager - including what is considered the last quest - it only took a few hours.  That said, I had been playing the game on a furious bender for two days straight.  There were also plenty of times when I was stressing about finding enough time for real life work, but still found a couple hours to really MAKE A GO of a run built around some strategy.
The main downside for me was the occasional game over, although in any good roguelike that frustration ends up becoming a part of the game's satisfaction.   The technical event of victory takes place - or doesn't - a couple hundred turns into the game.  Survival is the most easily commodifiable reward.  If you overperform and show up the rival teams, the game "punishes" you mildly by directing more of their aggro at you for taking their business.  Over time, you'll find yourself fastidiously monitoring your relationship with the camps you intend to defeat.  And if your only team gets lost too far from a portal without money to get back quickly, and when you were running the whole team on unbreakable contracts to save money - not yet fully understanding the game's mechanics - it can be frustrating to put so much hard work into a successful build, only to spin out because you haven't mastered gamecraft like allocating your portals intelligently in a randomized map.
The game has a reason and a rhyme, and really won my heart.  Occasionally, glitches would cause one character to have around 4k HP or some other anomalous behavior - in a game where 600-700 HP is enough to carry oneself at endgame and anything above 1k is overpowering in competent hands.  There are classes that are overpowered in their fundamental usefulness, and with experience you'll grab quickly for them - but only if they came with the move you like.
The level cap is 5 per class; epicness is rated 1/5 per perishable character, and can be increased only with a prohibitively expensive item.  Rather, the game sponsors you for about half a year's contract with a single 5/5 unit, and a license to run one lineup of up to 4, and some startup cash/items to easily overpower your first quest.  You will only able to hire 1/5 (avoid if at all possible) and 2/5 (should be the staple of your first lineup, but eventually your standard for mediocrity during midgame).  Epicness, level and cumulative career paths influence salary demands, so while it might be tempting to pack your stables with 5/5 early on, they can bankrupt you if you don't first establish your ability to reliably destroy any 150 Fame quest.  Fundamentals like these are not explained in-game; it really doesn't hold your hand to a point that will get you through the gold leagues.
On that: The game advances one week per turn.  12 weeks to a competitive period - 12 teams to a "league." Your level 1 license comes free, while I've rarely survived the late game without a level 5 license, which requires hoarding an amount of money with 1 team that can be tricky unless you are creative, aggressive, experienced and/or lucky.  There are licenses vastly beyond what I have yet found the money for - but the better you play the game, the fewer items you use and the more you sell, and the more and better items you tend to find.  The game has few "elements," but each one has class, stat, buff/debuff and build implications, and there are items out there that are truly game-changing in the right hands.
The game has more content than you can afford to unlock easily in one winning play-through; I had no staff whatsoever when I finally became the Epic Manager.  I hoped for an open sandbox postgame so I could unlock the whole map, max out my license, etc.  My first hire was only level 19, and on the verge of unlocking a powerful prestige class I was looking forward to trying out.
The game is delightfully tasteful, and I found Normal mode, on Ironman, quite challenging.  Turning off Ironman and SAVING YOUR GAME is probably a better approach for learning than playing on Easy.  Any idiot can make it through the Bronze league rounds on Normal, but during Gold League you'll drown if you can't produce three-figure Fame per round off of the starting whistle.  So the game starts easy, gets engaging, then becomes outright ruthless as you approach endgame.  I was annoyed that I couldn't prospect the final boss, whose party involved complex and frustrating resistances.
I hacked through with a single party member who specialized in "wild" magic, against both individuals and groups. Anybody who knows the game well will tell you that was agonizing and took forever - but I had come too far to give up.
4/5 ; I hope the Devs will continue to patch based on feedback from players.  A larger map, and some form of sandbox mode, or continued expansion of the game's delightful political plot, would be nice - and there are those of us who would be willing to pay a few bucks more for more of a good thing.  I look forward, also, to any other games they might come up with in the future.

I'm a horror game enthusiast that grew up playing classic Resident Evil more than any other games and they remain my favourites to this day.  After being told Resident Evil would be going back to its roots as part of the marketing for RE6, Revelations, and Revelations 2, I had literally no expectations for this game on that front.  But my dear friends bought it for me as a gift, and I played it.  From that perspective, let's review it.
My overall impression was that I thought it was excellent but that it didn't feel like Resident Evil.  I hadn't expected a first-person game to feel like Resident Evil, so I wasn't disappointed.  I was just glad it was good.
Gameplay:
The gameplay mechanics are intentionally sluggish.  I'm personally biased against first-person games because I never feel as in tune with my character ironically (I feel third-person compensates visually for the other senses and perceptions that physically being somewhere would yield for you).  Other people may not have this problem but sometimes the sluggishness felt off and I didn't know exactly where I was in relation to some other nearby object, or my timing was off as a result of a sluggish animation.  Again, could just be me and my first-person problem (FPP).
None the less, the sluggishness is usually a really good thing and feels just right.  And the enemies seem designed well to move in ways that complement the sluggishness of the player character.
The game is primarily designed with atmosphere in mind and it's fantastic atmosphere.  The enemies are in my opinion not always great, but for once they're not exactly the focus.  The atmosphere is.  And the enemies frequently synergise well with that atmosphere.
The main antagonists of the game were interesting.  They were extremely well acted and there was a lot of diversity from one to the next.  They were often derivative of modern horror films and that sort of annoyed me at times, but at least I can say I don't really think I've seen it done in games before, not like this at least.
A great thing about this game is that your actions are often capable of driving the situation in an utterly different direction, depending on how quickly you work sometihing out or if you choose something totally different to what would be the obvious choice.  There are glaring exceptions to this here and there, but overall it's impressive how well developed the various scenarios sometimes are, and their quantity.
I enjoyed the save rooms.  I didn't enjoy having infinite saves but I did like that I had to be in a specific location and save my game manually (with some exceptions for surprise boss fights and the like).  On Madhouse difficulty, it appears this is rectified.  Brilliant.  In my opinion, limited saves are crucial for good horror.  Perma-death is usually a bit too much I think, but if saves are limited in a well balanced way you can hit the sweet spot between the torture of perma-death and the hedonism of auto-saves every time you enter a new room.
All the boss fights were well done I think.  Rarely frustrating but rarely very challenging, and each one was highly individual and unique.
On the one hand, I'm impressed that there's not only loads of DLC but that one of them is free, and on the other hand, I'm essentially against DLC in general.  I miss the good old days when everything was unlockable and on the disc you'd purchased, and it was there as soon as it was released.  But no-one forced them to make one of them free, whether or not we need to wait a while, so that's nice.
Story:
The story is compelling.  It's not high art but it does make you want to go on.  The acting is great and the writing is great.  A lot of stuff is left unexplained but there's reason to expect most of it will be handled by the DLC.
My biggest complaint is a minor spoiler, so I won't reveal it here.  Fortunately, by the end of the game things change and my fears are unfounded, but I feel that overall the design came first and the story used a sort of afterthought to make an excuse for the design, and I feel that the baggage of being a Resident Evil title conflicted with their ideal design in this respect, which was the cause of the awkward situating of a few of the relevant plot points.
My other biggest complaint is that the game's story punishes you to some degree if you're a critical thinker or if youdon't agree with their simplistic view of the situation they've presented.  I'm avoiding spoilers so that's essentially what you're getting here.
Actually, following from that, I can complain that the characterisation in general was pretty poor.  The villains were done well enough but anyone that isn't trying to kill you is just such a barely explored character.
Audio:
I was thoroughly impressed with everything in this regard.  Great voices, great music, great spatialisation, and great detail afforded to the sound effects.  The music was refreshingly traditional overall.  The footsteps were just slightly overdone in my opinion, as there were too many instances when I heard my own footsteps but was barely moving and I thought it must be another entity.  Even so, the footstep sounds were still well done, despite being unrealistically loud at times.
Graphics:
The graphics are middling.  I've heard great praise but I just don't see it.  I think the lighting was rather nice, but the textures just don't appear to be as well done as my PC's workload would imply.  A lot of jagged edges and swimming texture artefacts.  The trouble is diminished on high-end GPUs for sure, but I've seen these problems remain on YouTube videos made specifically to showcase specific higher-end GPUs' optimal settings for this game.
After a good deal of tinkering I did get the game running extremely fluidly without looking poor on my GTX 750 Ti.
Length:
If this is important to you, the main game was about sixteen hours for me, and I like to look around a lot.  Madhouse difficulty is from what I hear worth playing.  It's said to change the game considerably.
As a Resident Evil game:
I like the game very much but I don't see this one.  A lot of great homages are present but you could say that about Last of Us or Evil Within.  This game reminds me far more of Outlast but I personally found Outlast scarier.  By miles.  In fact, I didn't find this game scary at-all.  I've read that Madhouse difficulty is more frightening, so I'm willing to have a go with that.
I do see that there's a bit of resource management, that there are some great keys and doors, and that the franchise is horror for the first time in ages.  But I find the gameplay mechanics entirely antithetical to the classic games, the inventory space not limited enough, saves not limited enough, the characters and story not similar enough to the calssics, the enemies not similar enough to the classics, and the atmosphere quite different to that of the classics.
The atmosphere in this game is more about showing you things you wouldn't want to see, whereas the classic games were about juxtaposing abandoned opulence with a sense of threat and the occasional evidence of death.  It was more about mystery than making your skin crawl.
Another point is that the story is finally successful as an American story, and the game no longer seems as Japanese as its predecessors.  They finally got everything right.  I personally miss that Japanese signature but I imagine a lot of people prefer this.  It's certainly easier to take it seriously (besides a couple of really ridiculous points I won't spoil).  The acting and dialogue are very well done.
Overall:
To evaluate this game without expecting any Resident Evil qualities, I'd say it's really a great game.  But I'm not sure it's worth its asking price.  I'd probably give it a 7 out of 10.

Alright, no beating around the bush. This game is not quite as perfect as most of the reviews would have you believe. It
hasn't aged well.
The first half(?) of the game before the monsters are revealed is entertaining and keeps your interest going. The wide, open levels are certainly well appreciated, as well as the graphics, which are still very appealing to this day. However, a lot of the alleged freedom is superficial with lots of wide, open areas having nothing whatsoever to justify exploring them, untraversable cliffs, and areas which misleadingly appear to lead somewhere (I know, poor sentence construction right there), but they end up being dead ends and the player ends up having to go
back. This is definitely not helped by
slow movement speed (think you can swim around the island to get to the objective? Think you can spare about 3 hours?) It boils down to the maps being inconsistently populated with the objective areas being heavilly populated with enemies and the rest of the space being "filler" with no weapon stashes, secrets or easter eggs to justify exploring them (another issue that Crysis inherited, though to a much lesser extent).
The gunplay is pretty standard for the time. Most of the enemies are very bullet spongey and the only feasable option is to land a headshot (an issue, which CryTech did not amend in the spiritual sequel to Far Cry, Crysis), which ended up making most of the weapons feel pretty weak, the notable exception being the shotgun, which was just heavenly to use. Watching the enemies ragdoll around after finally taking them down is immensely satisfying. The enemies' bullet spongey nature would be fine if it weren't for the
.
The difficulty is artificial, it is not fair, it is bullsh*t. The game heavilly encourages stealthy and/or slow paced approach to combat. The problem with that is that the ai isn't at all good enough nor are the stealth mechanics fleshed out enough to make stealth a feasable option. The AI will see you through brush, rock, and solid f*cking walls. Silenced weapons aren't worth sh*t. Silent takedowns? Ha! Just try, try to get close up to an enemy and not alert him. It's doable, I guess. With a lot of blood, sweat, and elbow grease you can get through certain areas without the f*cking Red Army on your tail. But is it fun? Not in the least. I don't get a smidge of enjoyment from sluggishly crawling past a group of mercs through bland, unpopulated brush. And no, it's not tense, it's not atmospheric, my heart isn't in my mouth when I'm trying to avoid getting spotted. It doesn't have
going for it.
The best moments of the game where  dodging the amusingly slow-moving rockets of the big, lumbering mutants as three of them approached me, one charging me, while pumping shotguns into them and running loops around them. But don't expect to do a lot of that, because you are made of wet tissue paper. Besides the lumbering giants, all other enemies have rapid firing firearms and prestine aim. Good luck dodging or weaving your way through that sh*t (have I mentioned the movement speed is god awful slow?). The forced slow pacing is reinforced by
sparse ammo and health locations and an ever depleting stamina bar. Maybe, maybe the slow pacing would work if youthe player had regenerating health (yeah, I know: "CoD fanboy, go back to your Medal of Modern Battlefield 4!" Bite me), but instead you find yourself grinding through encounter after encounter, while incurring unavoidable damage, and finally having to face a roomful of enemies with some 2% health or whatnot.
Well... that's a lot of negativity. Never the less, there is fun to be had in this game. Despite the often time empty and pointless areas, the levels' large scale and detail is very appealing, esp. the first level they packed
into that level. Any B-movie enthusiast will adore the voice acting and plot, despite their bullet-spongey nature a lot of the enemy design is cool (shout out to invis-guy and proto-Berserkers (disclaimer: not a big fan of GoW)), and the basal gunplay is appealing. The game's biggest problems stem from the open ended level design and forced slow pace. I can only recommend it to the most patient of gamers. To the curious casual I recommend entering a couple cheats (if this game has cheats, I know the Xbox version has cheats) and playing through it on the lowest difficulty. One should approach this as one would approach a B-movie, not a timeless classic. I would certainly recommend (the first half of) Crysis or the X-Box spin off series over this one, seeing as the stealth, gunplay, and movement are much more solid in those games.
More disclaimer: (Have not touched the multiplayer, and this is my first review on Steam, which I just sort of winged right now w/o really thinking it through.)

Ok... let's be perfectly honest about this.  Our Darker Purpose is a very close rip-off of binding of Isaac (which itself is a rip-off of Smash TV, which is a rip-off of that robot shooter arcade game I used to play when I was a kid (forgot the name)).  It's important not to get overly self-righteous about this.  But Binding of Isaac was comlpetely  original in it's weird, demented atmosphere.  The imagery of the setting, the enemies, and even the protagonist himself reflects this obtuse reality.  Our Darker Purpose tries to imitate that, but with less success.  It draws the line at being creepy.  And creepy is good.  But it falls short of it's predecessor.
Now, that being said, it does pass the most important test of all... it's fun!  My favorite gameplay element is that you can build your character between playthroughs, which means that your progression isn't entirely skills-based -- good for those of use who lack the natural fast-twitch abilities of the modern teen.  I like the creepy as well, though not as much as I relish the deranged from Isaac.  But the designers did an excellent job of crafting a dark, unpleasant locale.  Also, a big positive over Isaac is that rooms are larger and can extend beyond the screen.   This makes for much more frenetic combat.
If you liked Binding of Isaac, you will have fun with this... no question.

Our Darker Purpose is fantastic, and despite its superficial similarities to The Binding of Isaac, it's a very different beast; for one thing, this game is not afraid to punish the player for failing to use her dodge button, or for attempting to tank his way through damage. This game is very much focused on making the player think strategically and defensively. Moreover, I dig the game's institutional-Gothic aesthetic quite a bit, and the lore he game revels to you bit by bit I find enthralling. Go buy this--it's worth it.

The idea behind 'Kindgom' seems to be to control, expand and protect your land and its people. It's basically a tower defence game crossed with some resource management, set in a beautiful, almost oneiric pixel world. At first, the feeling one gets while playing is rather peaceful, despite the somewhat harsh difficulty, which comes in the form of nightly enemies who try to rob you of your kingdom and your crown, but also from having to figuring out how the game works.
The game has an addicting part to it as well, with a very "one more turn"- like symptom; always getting the player to think, "oh, I will just quickly recruit those peasants", only to find oneself playing on and on without even realizing it.
There are multiple problems however.
First off, there is the repetitiveness of it all, which can still fit into the whole peaceful mind-set of the game, but there is no denying that the player is always doing the same thing over and over again. The fact that the setup of each kingdom is randomized changes little in that regard. Once you have found a winning strategy, there is little to no reason to deviate from it and the soothing and calming slow pace of the game tends to become tedious with the added repetitions, especially since you can't rush the different phases of the game; everything needs to happen in a certain order, if you want to survive that is.
However, it is true that, contrary to the base version of the game, "Kingdom – New Lands" offers more options, more buildings, more mounts, and even unlockable structures; all of which are a most welcome addition as well as a must-have for the challenges of the later levels.
Yet, this raises another issue of 'Kingdom': the mechanics of the game, especially in regards to these new additions, as remain poorly explained. Figuring out what happens for what reason can be fun sometimes, but all too often this leads to encountering counterintuitive design decisions or glitches.
For example, hermits are characters that can upgrade some of your buildings. Winning the last level without them is almost impossible. Yet, these characters wander of, constantly putting themselves in danger, screwing you over indirectly by denying you access to their upgrades: once they are gone, you can't find them again for the duration of that level.
And then there are the drawn-out nights which are an infuriating death sentence over which the player has little to no control over. Those are nights that never actually 'end' for the scripts of your population because the enemies that spawned at night took such a long time to reach your kingdom. Thus, your economy grinds to halt even during the day. It gets even worse during blood moons, -which are basically 'boss nights'-, or badly timed artificial blood moons linked with the destruction of lesser portals spawning enemies. Even the workers refuse to repair your walls during those bugged times, and that might just as well be treason for all the good it does to you. But sometimes, reloading the game will fix that issue… but for that day only…
But it doesn't stop there! Prairies, and their bunnies, are a great way to make a decent amount of money at the early stages, but how, when or why these prairies expand themselves is a mystery. Buildings seem to stop their growth… except when they don't… Cutting down trees should also increase the size of the prairies, except… not always! And you are stuck with vast stretches of muddy ground. It is unrealiable at best, and sadly this seems to be the permeated feeling of 'Kingdom'.
The lack of control, -and I'm not just talking about unrebindable keys here-, is really what drove me away from the game. The fact that you can't order people around directly is cute at first, but all too often it ends up being infuriating since the players is at the whims of the IA. When you see your knights abandoning a wall, leaving unassigned archers and workers to their doom, how can one not sight in desperation? Archer towers actually become a death trap in that regard since the scripts of the game seem to order them to man the towers even amidst intense battles, even if this means facing a horde of enemies to reach them. The best part? These archers in towers are as good as dead as soon as flying enemies start to spawn. What is the point of a defensive building that is more a liability to the player than anything else? Also, when the defensive walls are built too close to enemy portals, the archers tend to walk right into them, and die. It's quite exasperating to have to deal with an IA too stupid not walk straight into death.
Tackling a challenging game can be fun, but only if it is fair and honest in its mechanics, which 'Kingdom – New Lands' isn't good at. And sure, one can push through the minor setbacks and annoyances, yet the reward for doing so is just more the same, with only the certainty of getting screwed over, sooner or later, not necessarily by your own hand, but by the obscure glitches or weird game decisions. Fun at first, annoying in the long run.

Among the Sleep instantly grabbed my attention when it was first announced due to its interesting premise and an unlikely protagonist: an infant. The survival horror genre excels at making players feel uncomfortable due to an increased sense of vulnerability the fact that you play as a toddler is Among the Sleep's most unusual characteristic, and also one of its best. This isn't just a first-person game in which the camera is lower to the ground than it would be if you were playing as an adult. When you walk, your steps feel unsteady; you can get around more quickly by crawling, but walking has its advantages. On foot, you can drag objects around, and you can open drawers, which you often need to clamber up onto in order to reach doorknobs or get to higher areas. By making you interact with the world in this teetering way from this perspective, Among the Sleep makes the fact that you play as a toddler not just a narrative conceit, but an integral part of your experience.
Surreal atmosphere and easy but interesting gameplay.

There are people who are praising this game for it's difficulty and saying you need to "get good" at it, but there's a difference between a good difficulty and a bad difficulty. 90% of this game is random chance, so it isn't skill that gets you through this game; it's whether or not the game decides to spare you from interacting with an overpowered enemy. The little planning aspect is only when you want to buy something or choose a route to follow, but even those have random chance in them. Basically, what makes a difficult game good is if you have control over the consequences, like you forgot to dodge and a boss kills you, that's on you. If a series of random encounters  doesn't favor you in a 1 to 10 chance for every move you make in this game, you're screwed and you weren't in control of that, making a game like this incredibly frustrating and unsatisfying.

TLDR: The complexity really opens up as you learn the various mechanics making it a fun and challenging strategy game.
When I first started playing Epic Manager I thought it a bit simplistic, but as I played I started to realize that there was a lot of skill and knowledge required to be a particularly effective manager. Party compositions matter as much as knowing the individual heroes' strengths and weaknesses. You start to learn that certain enemies have specific weaknesses, making that particular element really useful for that fight. I'm half way through the game because it has a set amount of weeks you have in order to rise to the top. The really wonderful thing is that I'm already starting to realize how I could have better chosen my heroes to be more prepared for higher level fights. The fights are fun and challenging, and there is enough other content so that you can make a serious difference with your management.
I really recommend it for anyone looking for a slightly more relaxing (than Darkest Dungeon or XCOM) strategy game that isn't overly simplisitic.

This game neatly meshes fantasy RPG's with sports management sims - level up your adventurers while making sure that enough money comes in via questing so you actually pay the fellows!
While some rough edges remain to the game, and some of them are down to personal taste (I for one find the map too bright), the novel concept has been adorably executed. Although I would have loved more variety in the quests and in a perfect world an engine that procedurally produces quests for endless replayability, this would have been a bit too much asked from a debutee studio.
Even with the limited (but sizeable!) pool of quests available, the 16 different basic classes of adventurers at hand allow to approach the game from multiple different angles and a variety of playstyles beyond a basic setup of thumper-mage-healer-control guy are possible.
Nine of ten raccoons would merrily quest with this game again!

If this game had the D&D license (and the game wears its D&D influence on its sleeve), it would probably be titled as Lords of Waterdeep.
You control a Manager who commands various heroic parties, deciding who to hire (and at what price), where to dispatch them, and which factions to appease. Depth happens on both the strategic and tactical level, and with various class combinations, there's a lot of replayability.
There are a few constraints to the game though. For one, despite having 16 Classes to choose from (and some hidden Prestige Classes), there's no option to play a female character. There's also a few bugs, although at the time of this review, the game-breaking ones have been solved.

Instead of going on adventures, have you ever wonder what it'd be like being the guy who sends the heroes out and then keeps all of the money? If so Epic Manager is the game for you!
Borrowing from sports management games, the purpose of Epic Manager is to have your Agency become the number one ranked Agency in the business - measured through how famous it becomes. Each year your goal is to amass as much fame from quest completions as you can to beat everyone else in the league.
You achieve this by recruiting and sending adventurers out into the wild to perform quests to help line your pockets with gold, and level themselves up with experience. Adventurers are skilled 1 to 5 stars (called epicness) which allows them to gain 5 levels in a single class for each star in their rating (a 3 star adventurer can get 3 different classes in the end). Crafting the perfect adventurer is tricky, with positive and negative traits but ultimately the better you do at hiring and firing, the easier you'll find it to acrue fame.
Every 13 weeks the lowest 2 teams in the league are eliminated, making it a cutthroat business in the world of mercenaries; do you have what it takes to raise your guild from a wooden shack up to an international global army? Play Epic Manager to find out!

Enjoyable game but very misleading description. It is 99% fantasy mangement and very similar to many other games especially to the many hero squad type games on mobile platforms. The only thing Sports like about it is that you get to draft your first character. Even then it is not at all like a sports management game. You only get to draft your first player, you always pick 3rd, there are no player rankings or deep stats to help you determine who is worthy of your first pick, there are no player rankings at all, no individual stats, no win/loss records. It really just depends on what kind of classes you like. After your one and only draft pick you can "sign" more heroes to complete your team but it really is nothing much different than a fantasy game letting you recruit other heroes or having heroes ask to join you. From the description I was expecting a full draft experience. Also you never get to play against the other teams. There are rankings based on accomplishments but you never go head to head against them (I have made it to the highest league and have yet seen an opportunity to go head to head against another team). It's a fantasy strategy game where you manage resources and gold income but there really is nothing extra unique about it and it is a stretch to call it a sports/fantasy mash-up. Blood Bowl for example would fit that description but not this. This is just another casual enjoyable fantasy strategy game where you go on quests and manage your squad's abilities, classes, eqiuipment, etc. Not a terrible game, a little overpriced, but not at all close to what I would have expected from the description.

Epic Manager is an innovative marriage of the Tycoon and RPG genres.  Deceptively simple on the surface one must learn its intracacies to be successful.
The tycoon aspect is relatively simple in nature.  You must hire adventurers to go forth and complete quests to earn money.  You negotiate salaries for adventurers and pick upgrades for your "Company".  Sadly, there isn't much more meat to this aspect than that.  Its only complexity in this aspect is planning which adventurers you want to keep and which are replaceable.  Make no mistake though, you do need a long term plan to win.
The RPG aspect is a bit more complicated.  Adventurers have different classes, in each class they have one skill that they upgrade four times.  Then they can multi-class or pick a prestige class.  The classes and skills interact in complementary ways when well planned though.
For instance, if you want a healer you can start as a Priest and pick boosts to healing, then multi-class into Paladin and gain more boosts to healing making the Priest skill stronger.
Combat is as simple or complex as you wish it to be.  You can just fire off skills and be successful,  but if you plan your moves and skill uses you can stack up significantly greater power and win difficult fights above your level.
Loot is implemented and random in nature, but unfortunately does generate some wonky results.  Like a class specific piece of loot such as a Warrior kit that generates with Arcane modifiers, the Warrior doesn't use Arcane skills.  Under certain multi-class configurations it works, but more often than not it is useless.
The game's only drawback is that it doesn't explain much of its functionality to you.  For instance, I completely accidently discovered that if I "Search for quests" twice I get double quests.  It's unintunitive because if you search from the main screen twice it looks like you can't search twice and only get results for the first search, but if you search again on the quest pane you get double.  Similiarly the game doesn't explain "Epicness" which is a limit to how many times you can multi-class a character represented by stars under the character's portrait.
The game does share a bit in common with Rogue Legacy and Darkest Dungeon, two amazing games.  Characters have traits exactly like Rogue Legacy and most are disposable like Darkest Dungeon.
Overall I recommend this game for most fans of RPGs, especially fans of Darkest Dungeon.  It is extremely fun and addictive and well worth its relatively low price!

Having played Resident Evil 4 and enjoyed that game, I decided to buy the newest installment in the Resident Evil series even though I'm not a hardcore fan of the series.
The game takes place in Louisiana, USA, and the atmosphere is creepy and bleak. If you've seen some American horror movies, you can notice the references to them throughout, particularly The Texas Chainsaw Massacre (1974). The American references are mixed with Japanese elements, as the game's developed by Capcom. I loved the return of one of the monsters from RE 4. RE 7 often relies on jump-scares throughout, but also creates tension through the use of foreboding music and disturbing surroundings. There were several sections in the game when I was stressed and entertained, but the scariness wanes a bit halfway through.
Personally it took a couple of hours for me to get used to the feel of the game, particularly how to use the environment in the boss battles, and how to stay alive without much firepower at hand. The game's also hard, even on normal difficulty, and I felt that having to repeat some sections and boss-battles repeatedly was tedious. However, many boss fights later in the game are enjoyable and challenging.
RE 7 is the first Resident Evil game in first-person. Even though the gun-handling and inventory system is great, the player movement is frustratingly slow. Yes, it's meant to be that way, creating more tension, but it doesn't feel realistic. No-one in real life standing face to face with a monster would run as slow as the protagonist. I can usually handle logical inconsistencies in games and movies, but it's not hard to notice several of them in RE 7.
I would've appreciated a more black-humoured feel to the game (like the SAW-like puzzle sequence), as it gets pretty depressing and brutal at times, but overall Resident Evil 7 is a great horror game with a memorable story. Finished it in 10 hours.

This game was great, I was not expecting it to be so good. The thrill factor in this game is so fun and each part is really intense. You have to play smart and utilize your resources effiectivley.
