The map, which is beuatifully crafted, becomes your home as you traverse your way to different sections and rooms looking for pieces of puzzles, all while trying to survive.

A departure from the style this series has gotten you used to with the last few titles, RE7 is a legitimately spooky haunted house FPS ride that keep you on your toes. Going in blind and hoping for something better than RE6, I was very impressed and enjoyed the time I've spent with the game.
Graphics are stellar, no bugs or crashes occurred during my time with the game. I used M+KB. The difficulty level stays pretty even throughout the experience. There is not a lot of scenery or enemy variety, and overall the game is somewhat short. It can certainly be completed by a first timer within a few play sessions. The combat feels fluid, and introduces a blocking mechanic even when using ranged weapons. Learn to use it well, often it will be the only thing giving you a shot at making it through a fight. Other reviews state that ammo is very limited but playing on normal I didn't really run into any problems with that.
Cool game

This game has little to no real content. It's difficulty lies in the fact that you are always outnumbered and always being beaten down from all sides.
Before I get shouted down by Dark Souls fans. At least in Dark Souls you had the dodging roll. In this the dodge will move you about a foot and usually into one of the three or four enemies attacking you.
As far as PvP goes. You will find that the matchmaking is happy to put you as a new player (maybe level 5 max) against anyone (I played 6 matches as a new player and didn't come across anyone below level 27). That includes people who have unlocked weapons (which you don't start with).
If you don't want to fight in 1 vs 1 matches then why not try the story mode. Which includes running about getting killed repeatedly because as I mentioned before you will never find an enemy by himself. No one to try to block so I can get some more moves. It's hard to block 3 punches and a kick all at once. Even if I do manage to obtain a new move through extensive blocking then I still have to kill all four of my opponents or my efforts are in vain. If you die you get nothing.
Then there are the players who run through every crevice of the game with their leveled weapons and armour. All with a far greater move set than you and able to execute these moves in half the time you can. These players will chase you down and not relent until you are dead or you run to another zone. Which you can't do if you are in a fight, which is what it counts it as when a level 37 is chasing a level 5 around a map. That's what the game considers a fight.
Then there's the bosses. None of the ones I faced were overly difficult. Or at least they wouldn't have been difficult if it wasn't for the 6 guys he had with him. I killed 3 of them and he called in another 3 to replace them. This continued until eventually I killed him. I wasn't however able to aquire any new moves as during the fight I was far too busy trying to avoid punches and kicks and deal some damage of my own to really give any focus to learning new moves.
Then there's the server issues. You will be lucky if you can find a server than will support your game for any longer than 25-30 minutes. I spent more time backing out and restarting my game than I got actually playing the game. (P.s. I would have been fine playing offline if it wasn't that case that one of the bosses requires you to be rank 10 in the Combat Trials. The Combat Trials are the 1v1 Pvp arenas; but if I can't get online then how can I play against other players?
Overall I'd say this game was a good idea in concept but I really just want my money back and if possible the time I wasted playing this game.
As a final thought, these guys are on Reddit asking people to leave positive reviews for their game. If you wanted positive reviews maybe you should have thought about producing a decent piece of work. This is shoddy.

I really Really want to give this game a Thumbs up and recommend it.. but I can't.. I see allot reviews praising it simply for being diffrent.. But also reviews hammering it down as the worst game ever simply cause of some flaws or some desynch.
What Is absolver? Well it's kinda like Dark souls, But It's kinda not.. It's kinda like For Honor.. But It's kinda not.. In idea It's an open world MMO fighting game. But It's kinda still not.. Easiest way of explaining it to explain how i went through it.
You get some slight story aspect and sent in to this world as a Prospect, a guy with a mask that knows fighting. pretty much it. Then you get to a what could be called the Firelink shrine or whatever where you see a giant stone tablet or statue with a bunch of glowing lights on it. Each light represent a marked one which is a boss or well a special named AI fighter that you need to find and kill. Each one of them gives you a new abillity, Finding them can be confusing as there's hardly anything explaining well anything to you. There's also boss scenarios that you are forced to do solo that look like Glowing mist in specific locations that you interact with. Get a cutscene then fight a boss scenario.  Add that there are schools which actually are either player made or a specific stagger fighting style school that you can find and join. Thos schools can be leveld up by doing pvp in 1v1.. So far I not unlocked anything but 1v1..  And you learn new fighting moves by parrying them, avoiding them or blocking them. So spamming attacks may win a few fights but you won't learn anything new by doing it.
That's all you do in this game... The overall story can be completed in around maybe 3-5 hours or faster if you sprint past all no named bad guys and use a group to gangbang the bosses..  As the Solo bosses are pretty easy to just hit, step back. Hit. Step back and keep doing so until you win.  The only thing that feels like it require any skills if you try to take on big groups of enemies alone or if you do pvp.. The game really has a lack of content. Sure It's not that expensive but It's a problem for me.
What do I like? The fighting is amasing, The combat is fluid it feels very skillbased and there's allot of moves and combos you can set up and learn to really perfect yourself. Pvp is fun but allot of the arenas are instakill ring out and you learn a shockwave move that pushes people off very early. And It makes it feel very cheap when that happens.
I finished the game in a few hours, but i spent allot of time just grinding pvp to get better moves. So if your coming for PVE and story.. Hold your money it won't last you long. Kingdom: New Lands is easily one of my favourite ever games.
The premise is incredibly simple; you are a king or queen and you pay money for things to make a kingdom happen, all the while the 'greed' attempt to destroy your kingdom and steal your crown. You hire vagrants and vagabonds and buy them either a hammer, bow, scythe or shield and set them to work in the respective roles of builder, archer, farmer, and knight. Your men then earn money for you and you put that back into building walls, towers, catapults, etc.
+ Its very easy to pick up but difficult to master.
+ It can be highly unforgiving, but 'death' (losing the crown) doesnt carry too much penalty.
+ The game is SERIOUSLY beautiful too, the pixel graphics are simply stunning.
+ THE ART STYLE THOUGH.
+ Don't forget that gloriously minimalistic but emotionally evocative soundtrack.
+ There's a decent 40ish hours of gameplay to be had just until you unlock everything, then comes the task of trying to survive indefinitely.
+ a reasonably novel concept, certainly a different take on a survival game
+ all round very fun and challenging
- sometimes the unit AI is pretty terrible, and men will run to their deaths in order to try and fill an empty archer nest, for example. That said, the men dont ever die, they just become 'un-hired'.
Solid 9/10 really excellent and worth playing.

Among the Sleep takes players on a journey through a nightmarish dreamworld concieved by a toddler's imagination, and molded by the disturbing issues he faces in real life. The concept is certainly fresh, but does the game itself hold up under scrutiny?
It's abundantly clear from the start that the developers of Among the Sleep have spent a lot of time carefully constructing the environments in this game. Many of the objects and locations are made up of very authentic-looking artifacts that you might see scattered around a toddler's room in real life. Some of them are used to frightening effect, such as removing the eyes from an otherwise adorable stuffed animal, or making the seemingly innocent drawings of a child take on a far more sinister meaning. All of these conscientious design choices come together quite effectively, and the atmosphere benefits greatly from it.
One of the biggest concerns I had for this game was if it could deliver true horror. The kind of horror that slowly and carefully builds into a suffocating climax of fear. Thankfully, I was not dissapointed. The game doesn't pull any punches, and although it takes some time at the beginning to establish the story, the rest of the game is a non-stop, exhilariting tour into darkness.
Well...for the most part.
The puzzles in the game are never demanding, and they don't really increase in difficulty much. Most of them involve collecting specific items or keys, and taking them to the correct location, which is all too easy considering how linear the game is. It's almost a nitpick, considering how frequently the game excels at building tension and fear through its various assets, but I would have appreciated a bit more complexity and origniality when it came to the actual gameplay.
At the end of the day, the biggest problem I had with this game was its length. Sure, its well-paced. It has great visuals, great voice-acting, great sound design...but if the game can be beaten in 2 hours or less, you're not getting much value for your money. I expect a little more content from a game thats list price is $20. Some might argue that all of that money is well-spent considering how much obvious love and effort was put into this game, and how amazing it turned out to be considering that it was created by a very small indie development team, but in my personal opinion, $20 is still too much to ask for such a short game, with so little replay value.
If you can get it on sale though, Among the Sleep is a very solid horror experience. If you've enjoyed games like Amnesia or Outlast, Among the Sleep will deliver more of the same great storytelling, audio design, and horror you've come to expect from those games, albeit on a much smaller scale.

I have just got the game, but it was love at first sight for me!
TLDR;
I can recommend this game for anybody who is into hard games and does not get discouraged after losing a few of his main characters to some crazy monster ;)
If you like rougelikes, with complex rpg elements and fantasy comedy style (really some of these quests and random encounters are hilarious) this game is for you! Despite the fact that the game does not try to take itself seriously, it is hard to play and takes a lot of time to discover the hidden depths of all types of skills and stats, how they work.
What I really like about this game:
- Very complex strategy, you can play a lot of ways with a huge number of character styles
- Random equipment stats, character traits and overall a lot of randomness which gives a lot of replayability.
- Funny characters, quests, dialogues
- Gets very hard after the first few quests, especially when you advance to silver league it takes a lot of management to keep your balance positive and important decision which quests you can take distances
- Ability to purchase gear, and a HUGE number of consumables (single character effects, group effects on both your team or enemy team, damage or debuff)
- Love the contract negotiation also
What I don't like about the game:
- There are still a few bugs, mostly visual, but the team actively releases patches so these will soon be resolved (nothing major though).
- Music gets very repetative after a while and bit annoying.
- High retail price (totally worth it for me, but friends don't want to try it because of this, hopefully there will be some sales ;) )
Overall its a great experience and totally worth trying, if you don't want an easy game and like challenges!

For a game with Manager in the title, you do very little management.  Management is centered around your heroes, herefor referred to in my own experiences as the Badasses of the Happy Snack Cake Adventurer Agency.  Recruit your badasses, send them on quests for gold and fame.  All good, the combat isn't silly or hard, smack him, heal him.
Some classes and skills are just useless though, why have a priest heal one person when a shaman heals everyone.  A rogue's special attack, Arrow Volley, costs 6ap, regular attack 3AP, and does, wait for it, twice the damage.  Why would I wait to build up 6AP?  But my mage's ice dagger was doing 5x the damage of a regular attack for the same AP costs as Arrow Volley, why would I use a regular attack?
If you end up in the bottom rankings for guilds the game ends.
Here's my biggest issue with that.  The quests are randomly placed around a map, sometimes taking as much as six turns to reach one.  Each turn I lose gold to pay my badasses.  So I spent 600 gold to get to a quest, made 800 gold from the quest, and then spent 400 gold to get to the next quest... I just lost gold doing the only thing available to do.  Do harder quests and get more gold, seems reasonable, and then my badasses meet bigger badasses and they die because I can't run from a fight like a coward so those badasses I spent gold and time developing into steroided killing machines are dead, I have to spent more gold to recruit new ones and they have to do the poorer quests because they're weak because I SPENT ALL MY DAMN GOLD MARCHING IDIOTS TO THEIR DEATH...
Quests need to be worth more gold, I want to swim in that crap early on like Scrooge McDuck.  Let me finance two parties easily, let me get the low level upgrades for guilds without paying 13000 gold when a quest pays 1000, but my heroes cost 150 a turn.  Let me blackmail heroes into working for free because I'm a capitalist willing to do anything to make Happy Snack Cake Adventure Agency the best damn Agency around!
It's not terrible, but it does need some balancing.  I liked my characters, I didn't want them to die, but after the first six went down, I saw their replacements are disposable meat bags just there to finish the job and get me paid, and if they died, hey at least I didn't have to give them part of that gold.

This is a Science Fiction Rogue-Light. That means things will be different every time you play. It is a mix between Choose-Your-Own-Adventure and ship combat. You upgrade your ship and do some simple micro-management once your crew is in danger. You have to live with your own choices as you try to outrun the threat on your tail, adding a time limit which does not feel too restrictive while adding an ever-present feeling of danger. Do you stop at the distress beacon? Is it a trap or an opportunity? Or should you just keep going and hope that you will be ready once you face the ultimate enemy? It doesn't offer a deep story but the events you trigger will definitely make you feel like you are on a journey...or on the run.
Even more content is available via modding.
This is what a well made indie game is all about.

Then, after a little bit it started to grow on me, until finally I was taken over by the gory brilliance and the exhiliration of experiencing something new. I seriously not sure I can recommend this game to anyone. It isn't particulary bad, but...
You have to navigate in a cave with "sound" or actually waves of light... or, actually, waves of visibility of stuff around you (it's like highlighted borders of crossections). The problem is these waves supposed to simulate sound waves and it's rather improbable to "see" through a wall with just footsteps. Yet, you can "see" like that very far and through walls. And that is rather distracting. It's especially annoying when you can see a clear way in front of you, but then you realize there is actually a solid wall right in front of your nose. From one side you are "blind" in the game and not being able to see a wall is normal, but at the same time you see pillars, rocks and leafs behind it (and on a large distance)!
There is a way to see everything in solid (including these "transparent" walls), but it's just illogical. Instead of just shouting or throwing rocks and sticks (which layin all around) our heroine throws local oversized hamster-like creatures. They are soft and covered in a thick fur, and in fact produce even less sound, than the girl while walking, yet their sound somehow makes everything much clearer. Logic! BTW, to pass through some gates you have to throw these hamsters into hamster wheels. So, they clearly are local analogue of hamsters. DISCLAIMER: I was a Kickstarter backer. Also, this is my personal opinion on the game, based on my personal taste. TL;DR at the bottom.
The idea and concept of the game were amazing, but, for me, it failed to deliver.
First of all, the game is VERY short: I got the achievement to finish it in less than 30min on my first playthrough.
Second, the blind mechanic is quite frustrating: when you walk, there are waves of "sight" that come to the player, symbolising something like a sound echo, but it doesn't linger for very long. Therefore, when you walk, you have something like wave-space-wave-space-wave, and, at least for me, it was horrible to try and assert size and distance of things.
Third: if you're going to take out your player's sight, give them hearing. The sound should have played a major part here, with noises that would guide you, and give you a feel of the world around you. Instead, the game relies oddly on visual cues, which feels completely against the idea of it.
Fourth, the overly vague story. It gives too many questions, too little answers. Instead of feeling like an interesting mystery, it felt rather pretentious, wanna-be-smart-and-cool-and-mysterious.
And fifth, the mokos. Don't get me wrong, they're ABSURDLY cute and loveable, and you just want to hug them and take them home... and then you realise they're actually your tools. You can throw them to the monsters to distract them, or to use their bouncing to find your way around, but you don't
to do that because it feels like using puppies as throwing stones.
At the end, $15 is way too expensive for such a short, flawed experience.
TL;DR: Short game, mechanics don't feel cohesive, story is too vague, throwing mokos feels bad.

Back in 2013, when the developers run a Kickstarter campaign, Pulse was a beautiful tiny experiment, a promise of a great surreal experience. Now, in 2015, when the game is finally out, it is an ever more beautiful tiny experiment, a glimpse into a great surreal experience that was never delivered.
The core mechanic makes the game gorgeous, it changes the way you perceive the game's world and move around it. This would have worked great as a stealth action, espcially if the enemies were as confined to their vision as Eva is to her hearing. Sadly, the game has just one stealth sequence, and I have no idea how it is supposed to be beaten: I just crawled around randomly until I got to the exit. It would have worked as a puzzle game, but the most difficult puzzle the game has is putting a hamsterlike furry creature into a wheel. If developers had no resources for a game with a gameplay, it would have worked beautifully as a walking simulator, a place to explore and marvel.
Instead, the second core mechanic is first-person platforming.
Yes, you play as a blind girl who has to make presice jumps over the platforms she can't see. With glitchy collision detection.
Why.
For all the game's flaws, it's unique and is still worth experiencing. I can only hope that one day the team behind it would be able to make a next version, the one that fulfills all the promises of the current one.

Love this game,  despite it's faults.
It's aesthetic, visual and soundtrack,  are great.   Some sound effects could use some work,  namely for the basic attack.
The only real problem with this game is how slow the progression is.  It feels like it takes way too long to make a difference.  Dozens of play throughs before you earn things to use throughout the playthroughs.
There's a lot of polish that could be done, including new features that would help it out.  Such as the ability to spend credits to directly increase starting stats as perma-buffs persistent throughout play.   Perhaps the ability to choose starting abilities that replace chalk, juice, the basic attack, and even the roll with similar but different effects.
If I were to change anything about Our Darker Purpose,  and believe me I'd love to see the change,  is a drastically increased pacing.  The hit box issue people often complain about isn't much of a problem once you get use to it and can even benefit you on occasion.
The pacing however is a serious problem and limits the enjoyability.
I'd say to -DOUBLE- the amount of XP gained,  start with the option of a level up perk from the get-go,  and have bosses award either an immediate level up perk or an item,   then up credit gain significantly.   From there I really do believe that having the ability to spend credits to directly augment stats persistently would be a fantastic addition.   With these,  I think Our Darker Purpose would be one of my favorite games to play.
It could be really fantastic then.    I still prefer it over Binding of Isaac personally,  I think the biggest reason is the aesthetic and lore but also the timed cooldowns on items and numerical HP rather than room-based cooldowns.
I would recommend it.  It seems to be a love/hate thing for most Binding of Isaac players,  who either prefer the differences or tote it as being "inferior in every way".

The premise to this game is to create your own agency (guild) of adventurers and become the best in the realm. You start off small with enough resources to recruit a couple of heroes, forming your first party, and sending them off to do quests. As you complete quests, you gain more resources and your fame increases, which allows you to expand your agency. Soon you'll have more options for recruiting more experienced adventurers and creating more parties to send out on quests. Your adventurers will grow in strength, have the ability to unlock multiple classes, and take on even more difficult challenges resulting in more fame, more gold, and bragging rights to the best agency ever!
The challenge is that you're competing against other agencies. Every 12 weeks the lowest ranked agencies within the league will be eliminated. You have to make sure you're not one of those agencies in order to continue. This adds some urgency to the game in that you need to keep pushing ahead and completing quests to keep building fame.
So what is this game? After having played it for a few hours, I feel that the store description is pretty much spot on. Everything it states is what the game is. The one exception is that it doesn't really mention the fact that you're competing against other guild within the league and that you need to accumulate enough fame to keep from being cut. If you're cut, it's game over.
Don't let the graphics fool you, there's a lot going on in this game. I will be honest, there are things that aren't intuitive at first and I did struggle with a few things and made mistakes. It wasn't until my second game where it really started to click and the depth of the game became evident. Initially with the single party, it starts off a little slow. However once the second party is unlocked, it becomes fun and challenging. Choices as to how to use scout points, research points, what skills to unlock, whether to renew a contract or hire a different adventurer, which quests to take, etc.
Last thing I'd like to say is that the development team has been very active in the forums and have shown that they are accepting to feedback. It's wonderful to see that the really care about their game.

At the end of the day you get a 2 hour, semi-pretentious, game that's overpriced at $20 dollars. 6/10 worth a buy if you buy it on sale.

I've always been a fan of indie games, particularly indie horror games. I went into Among the Sleep with minimal information, I just saw that you played as a infant, and I knew I had to have it. The adventure that followed starting from 12 to around 3 in the morning some might say was shortlived, however I loved every bit of it. The atmosphere, symbolism, and thought that this game provokes stemming from the question of what is real and what is imagination from the point of a two year old was comparable in complexity to the ending of Bioshock Infinite. I also find it comparable to movies such as American Psycho and Donnie Darko in the same way. Not everyone will have the same interpretation, although I have heard very good ones in the forums. If you expect from this game cheap jumps scares or award winning graphics or action, look somewhere else. This game is more of an allegory within a haunting art form, and I will fondly remember those nearly three hours I spent on this game, as  I will also remember what I took away.

You may reark that I have very little time in this, yet review it.The reason is that Absolver takes the "Crackdown" approach to game design. There are six or seven minibosses called "The Marked" and four or so major bossfights. Once you beat that, PvP must be done in order to unlock the advanced versions of the above bossfights. Thus Absolver is not so much a game you beat, but you master.
The entire game revolves around a rather tight combat system involving developing your own personal fighting style out of the moves you both start with and eventually learn through blocking them frequently. There are four major branches of martial arts built around a general theme (Kohlt Method is a heavy boxer style, etc). While defeating the bosses unlocks new abilities and weaponry, all of your fighting knowledge is going to be coming from well... fighting.
This means that while a player can use co-op to quickly beat the story in about four hours and thus become Absolvers (Worth it, the armored cloak they give you is top-tier) the real point of the game is to actually focu on learning the fighting styles through close observation of how your enemy reacts. Because Dodging and Blocking are the primary way to both avoid getting killed and learn new abilities; you rarly forget that blocking exists. Even if you do forget, you will notice the learning shards appear and go "That's right, I can learn stuff by blocking!"
Usually, fighting games suffer from a boring grind of beating typical opponents. While you can identify the broad style of an enemy by how they move and attack, you don't have a way of knowing what they actually know how to do until they actually do it. Even fighting rank and file goons can be a blast! Fighting particularly tough players is damned excited, because you start getting into a trance of blocking, weaving, and counterattacking. I have never played a fighting game where I really feel like I am out-martial-arting somebody.
Lastly: The map design is whimsically terrible. It's way too easy to get lost, run on redundant pathes, or find dead ends. Plus it's way too easy to fall off ledges. 80% of my deaths are because I fell off a ledge due to either kicking or being kicked. I found myself having to guess and just keep running around until I finally found out where bosses were hidden.
So yeah: If you are expecting a deep RPG with 50+ hours of deep hardcore story mode this is not your game. If you like the idea of living in Kung-Fu world, then this IS the game for you. As yeah, that's what everybody does all freaking day. They meditate, train, and beat the ever loving crap out of eachother.
Thus I dub thee "CrackSouls: The Fightening!"

I've played this game a lot - primarily via kongregate and my mobile phone so don't let the low number of hours on here fool you. It's a great idea with a lot of potential but ultimately is let down by a lack of thought about "endgame" (or even late mid-game) and by a lack of development.
The idea of crafting to make money, crafting to equip heroes, heroes bringing back items to make better equipment for you to sell for more money or equip for better questing is a fantastic feedback loop. The cities you join, invest in to upgrade and work together on raids are great. The PvP while far from perfect is also relatively engaging for a while.
The big issue is that once you hit the mid-game there is no point anymore. Recipes become harder and harder to craft, requiring more time, more resources and rare resources. This is if you can even get the recipes at all, because you get them as a rare drop from chests and there is no good way to get the keys for the final three chests. You can't trade them with other players until you've opened X amount of chests, creating an annoying chicken and egg scenario. Even the chests you can get keys for from raids will take forever given it's one key per week.
That said, even getting the gear is pointless, as all the quests and raids in the game can be completed with mid-level gear provided you sensibly equip your heroes. So spending days and weeks grinding out a single addition which will make little to no difference is very uninspiring.
And thus we get to the final issue - there hasn't really been any updates in the past year or so. The updates there have been have been minimal, adding a few extra super-late game items which are vastly inferior to lower level P2W items. The only other updates have been general nerfs such as the aforementioned limit on buying keys from other players. The only thing that is reliably updated is the P2W shop, which is updated pretty much monthly with new, pointless, goodies for cash players to spend money on. Not planning to dump cash? I wouldn't hold out for anything new for you anytime soon.
This game has been dying a death for a year or more and I can't advise anyone to jump on ship now.

Shop Heroes is about running your own fantasy shop, selling items such as weapons, armour, rings, potions and the like. At your disposal are workers, each with their own skills, that fashion these items for you to sell. As you produce more and more of the same items they become more valuable, cost less resources to craft, allow you to craft new products to sell, andsoforth.
Wandering adventurers visit your shop in search of specific items. You can sell them if you have them in stock, suggest other items or  flat out refuse to sell, to name a few options.
Crafting items levels up your workers; selling items allows you to use that money to either upgrade your shop - for instance, increase the shops size, decorate it or upgrade the working stations - or upgrade buildings in the city. By upgrading buildings in the city, you get better resource gathering, access to different adventurers and those you already have get a higher level cap.
The other building apart from your shop you can access is the Inn, where you can send adventurers out on quests for special resources, needed for crafting. Here cou can also send your adventurers to battle other players in the arena or trade with those players; you can also exchange gathered blueprint fragments so as to be able to produce new products for your shop.
I do very much like this game, however, there are three criticisms I want to aim at it.
The first is that you are very encouraged to actively team up with other players. Multiple players can set up shop in the same city, and as such can upgrade the buildings in that city much faster, if they choose to work together. If you, however, rather forego on the social component of this game you can still make progress with the game, but it will cost you more gold and will take a lot longer. Simply put: 8 > 1 in terms of money to spend. This social component may or may not be a positive for you, but that's for everybody to decide.
Second, this game is a port. Although I have not encountered any problems so far, the images used sometimes do show they were originally drawn for handhelds, with some characters looking pixelated.
Third, this game is free to play. As most of those games, you get a free currency (gold) and a premium currency to speed up crafting, gathering and the like (gems). Gems can be bought with real money, because ofcourse they can. However, the store also features Packages. These contain a combination of new workers, clothes for your shopkeeper to wear, abilities to use in the arena, items to craft, et cetera. Everything in these packages is exclusive and can only be bought with real money. Currently, the cheapest package goes for 15 USD and the most expensive for 50 USD. This is an amazing amount of money for what you get in terms of new content, specially given that the base game lets you craft and upgrade hundreds of items for free. Currently the shops has about 250 dollars worth of DLC packs and personally, I feel those prices are egregious.
Despite my misgivings about the DLC pricing I do have a blast playing this game. I like the genre, find the artstyle appealing and like discovering new items to craft. So, all in all, I very much recommend this game.

My main issues with it are the enemies in the bits in between the main encounters, they are very generic and don't really do anything smart, they just walk towards you and their limbs explode if you shoot them.
Another issue (and this is a big one) is the DLC, it's basically an assortment of mini-games which really shouldn't have been DLC worthy. The only real story experience in them is Daughters, which was the most disappointing of all! I was expecting a slow deterioration of the Bakers' sanity but it was so instantaneous and the mode itself was only 10-20 minutes long, granted there are 2 endings, but that's it.
I love this game regardless of those problems though, I even bought the soundtrack (unfortunately it didn't include the DLC songs, which would be nice as Jack's 55th Birthday's music is amazing)

Skip to the summary at the end if you dont want to indulge in the details:
Play this game with the right brightness setting, the atmosphere is really important; and with the right brightness settings it will scare the life out of you. The horror aspect of this game is incredible; 9/10. The story line is solid, and although I have not played previous resident evil titles, I did feel like the game tried to make a connection to them at the end. At least there was a hint to the first Resident Evil movie.
The gameplay mechanics are well thought out except for the heal animation (I wish there were more animations then just pouring down antiseptic liquid with cellular regenration promotion properties on your hand). Ammo conservation is required to some extent. The inventory managment system is good and easy to get a grip on even during fights. I see that a lot of people are complaining about Ethans running speed. The fact of the matter is that its quite close to realistic. We as gamers have gotten accustomed to fast walk and run speeds which makes us feel like this one is slow. But given the distance covered per unit time in terms of visuals (a hallway, a yard, a room) the run speed can only said to be as slightly slower than real life. Which I approve of anyways since the game intends to give you a feeling of helplessness.
Finally the graphics. The good thing going on here is that the textures are really good. The lighting is exceptional and so are the shadows. However, the game does suffer from some optimization issues as far as shadows are concerned. I personally have a GTX 980 Matrix from Asus and I can max out everything at 1080p except shadows. Shadows at only high give me +60 fps. Very high shadows start to give me frequent and random fps drops. Hopefully this will be fixed in any patches they release.
Finally the worst aspect of the game that I encountered is (some, not all mind you) AI characteristics. AI seems to be fairly smart during combat and does present a challenge. However, there are times when they are supposed to be looking for you and your job is to complete your objective and (optimally) not run into them while doing so to avoid greivances. Their field of vision is unrealistically narrow and they seem to be deaf to the sounds you make completely. Although fixing this issue to the realistic point would make the game massivley difficult, some improvment could be used here (i.e. slightly improved periphal vision plus some radius in which they investigate sound disturbances).
Summary:
Unlike a lot of games released this year and late last year, the developers have taken their time to produce an excellent game albeit some fixing required which is not something that should degrade the game. Hopefully the issues I mentioned above will be fixed soon. There is some replayability factor. Once you end the game and start it again, some item locations seem to be changed which is good because it discourages walk through consultation.
Graphics: 9/10 (10/10 if optimized fully)
Gameplay (including AI mechanics): 8/10
Controls: 8/10
Environment setting (including sounds, lighting and dialogue): 10/10
Story: Solid 9/10
Replayability: 6/10
DLC: 4/10 (from what it looks like from the description.
Hope this helps you make your decision.

I would recommend Pulse but with a few caveats.
What first interested me about Pulse was the whole sight by sound mechanic. I like when games try new things and that is definitely true of Pulse. The sight by sound mechanic is quite interesting and is a unique experience.  The designers did a really good job creating this mechanic since it feels like the sound you and the world make actually reveal different parts of the world. The visuals work really well with the mechanic as well.
The problem is that while the game has some interesting mechanics, it fails to live up to its' potential. Outside of the sight by sound mechanic, the game is a pretty average platformer. I wish the game would have created more puzzles that actually utilized the sight by sound mechanic.
The biggest problem with the game is the fact that it is short. The game is only around two hours long.
While it could have been better, Pulse is still a good game and an interesting experience. If the concept interests you I think you will enjoy the game. Due to the length and the cost of the game though I would probably recommend waiting for a sale.
Note: I received a free review copy of the game from the developer.

Empire Total War (E:TW) is a RTS set in the 1700's. It has a single player campaign mode on a strategic map which add to the game greatly (and therefore is a shame that is not multiplayer). A worthy successor to the Total War series and an excellent historical battle simulator.
Graphics are much improved over Mediaeval and Rome TW but the movement controls are worse as the system struggles to path and place units according to their formation and position units around cover: you can often find a unit moving accross the map to nowhere. Indeed AI is generally extremely problematic: units have more of a tendency to not follow movement orders once engaged; units can be blithely matching through enemy ranks as a pitched battle occurs around them; troops will march in front of their own cannons and get killed; horse carriages will go over obstacles (like cannon emplacements and get killed).
Also the campaign game forces storyline battles on you. I had just finished capturing Canada from the French and was ready to re-enter real life when I was thrown into Bunker Hill without warning or explanation and had to fight another battle: a battle I subsequently lost because I had to stop the game and was not allowed to save the game. I had to beat the French in Canada four times before I got the game to a save point where I had won Bunker Hill. This is done for the sake of storyline momentum but but there would have been no harm putting in a save point.
This lack of attention to player experience in interface and storyline is seen also in the exposition in the in-game help. Nowhere does it say that unit will fire into their own troops or how this operates (sometimes they do, sometimes they hit their own troops, sometimes only the enemy), nor how to cancel a building destruction/construction order, how cover works and how units wrap around them, how to cancel a broadside, why are only the first line of troops firing etc. Forums help here but a few more tool tips wouldn't go astray as the experience of using gunpowder weapons is different to the previous more melee centric TW series; archers can arc over troops but muskets travel a flatter trajectory after all.
On broadsides, ship battles are very well done. I haven't player other ship simulators since Port Royal, but it was very satisfying demasting a ship. Again, not a lot of exposition, like that the compass actually refers to wind direction.
Individual unit animations are very good and troops will even jump over obstacles.
Loading times are very slow and the system does not quite know how to handle two monitors.
In all, a very good game that is puntuated by poor AI, poor exposition, forced stroyline battles you cannot save, and no restart button as in other TW games.

Detailed Review:
In this VN, you play as a guy dating iconic WWII tanks personified as Japanese schoolgirl. It doesn't get much weirder than that. And this weirdness is the game's selling pont, as well as its biggest strength. And the game delivered this strength very very well and in the most memorable way possible.
The game is not without its flaw, however. The main premise doesn't make a whole lot of sense and would probably irritate serious readers (that somehow pick up a story about dating personified tanks and try to make some senses out of it). There are technical issues like s bug in a conversation. There are also no option for full screen (not a problem for me) or mute (which I find a little problematic, as I normally play VN with the sounds off) and there are only 5 save slots, which aren't nearly enough. And the ending is very abrupt and confusing and doesn't reflect enough the player's choice. The first time I reached it, I thought that I had hit some wrong conversation options somewhere and locked myself int a bad end. No, that's just the ending...
But still, despite all the flaws I have mentioned, the good far outshines the bad. The writing of this game is pure, comedic gold and the jokes are top notched, especially if you have some knowledge on WWII and history in general. The tank girls are adorable and manage to reflect the quirks of the tanks they represent very, very well (though I'm a little disappointed that they focus more on Tiger I's mechanical problems than legendary prowess, but, well, they aren't wrong). There are a lot of choices in the conversation which, why doesn't affect the story much, give the player the satisfying illusion of control, as well as open up to many different jokes and make the flow of conversations seem natural. It's one of the most bizarre and hilarious VNs I've ever read and I've a lot of fun with it. And since the devs are still working to fix bugs and add in stuffs, I'm sure it will only get better with time.

Now, I've played through and gotten the endings for Tiger I, IS-2, Panzer IV, and Sherman.... and have decided to give up on t-34, my guess is that it will be exactly the same as the rest.
now the strength of this VN is the jokes, and references to WWII (being a history major myself I found them extra humurous) while the writing overall isn't great, it get's the job done, when needed too.
the writing in this game, is honestly pretty shallow and vapid most of the time, only being raised to acceptable with the clever references that the tanks would know.
however the game falls ultimately flat with its endings *obvious* spoilers are obvious.
the endings consist of the character being suddenly called to court marshal after courting the particular tank of your choice. there is some ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t that would never happen in a legitamite trial, but whatever, and this all ends with essentially you are either executed or sent to a penal batallion, or you simply die.
tl;dr you die.
that's it, no payoff for your efforts, none of this is affected by your choices, etc. this is simply a copout lazy and shallow type of ending.
and for me, the ending is one of the most essential pieces to any form of media, you could have a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ game with a fantastic ending and you can get me to love it, however, with this game it seems the focus was on writing jokes instead of creating a satisfying ending.

It's a turn-based strategy game where you run an organization of fantasy characters who take on quests.  They're on a team in a league, the more jobs you do the better you do in your league (and possibly rank up to the next of I think 5 leagues).  Or get demoted if you don't do enough.
There's a bunch of different classes but not much customization.  The customization really only comes from multiclassing, which allows for I think 5 classes on any one character.  So that kind of makes up for the lack of individual class customization.  It's not quite as in-depth as I'd have preferred; I would've given up a lot of other parts of the game for more ways to customize your heroes and bigger skill trees.
The biggest problem I have with it are some of the random events, which often seem either too obvious or too random.
And the fact that certain classes and builds seem strictly better than others.  Why would anyone ever not have a Witchdoctor on their team?  I don't think it's subjective that the one class with a solid early game AoE heal is going to be one of the best, if not the best.
The talent choices seem obvious, there's AP reduction passives but there's also some massive buffs to active skills which are well worth paying the extra AP for.  I think this should be tweaked in the future, but I think the numbers are a bit too small to make balance work without changing a lot of what's in place.  2 AP reduction is great, eventually you'd get to do skills for free.  But 1 AP reduction isn't really that much.
It's also got a campy as hell sense of humor, but it's kinda cute in the way that Shakespeare used to like watching ♥♥♥♥♥♥ plays.  That's not an insult btw, I really did like it in that way.  There's also a managerial aspect where you trade heroes with the AI, sign new players, scout for new job opportunities, etc.  I haven't delved too much into the trading because that comes later than where I got to so far.  But it's pretty good so far.

Though this game has some good and bad aspects, overall it feels to be an average game.  I do recommend that you pick this up but just know what you're going to get before hand.
One of the biggest things that sets this RPG game apart from others is that you're supposed to recruit and then negotiate your adventurer's contract before they will join your party.  Which sounds fun until you actually go and do it.  Adventurers are a dime and dozen and there's not much that separates them apart from one another besides level and traits and class.  Once you do settle on one, negotiating their contract is nothing more than a slider which yields a % of success, rejection and failure.
For me I thought the adventurers would be more exclusive and that you would need to bump into them or search for them so you can hire them.   Even if there was a "flyer" that was LFM.. then people wouldn't just show up like a shopping list.
There isn't any personality given to the negotiating process either.   It either succeeds or rejected and you have to try again or fails.   However even if it does fails - who cares?? because adventurers are a dime a dozen and you can get another person the next turn at the worst.
Easy to learn game that isn't complicated.  The tutorial does a pretty good job walking you through the key points.
The UI is fairly clunky when you're trying to equip items and look for party members.  Don't forget that you can't do any of this without being at a spot in which you have a home teleport to (which aren't too many).
The nicest thing about this game is the multi-classing leveling up feature.  Every 5 levels you can choose a new class for the adventurer and still retain your old skills/spells with their old augmentations.  Building up your adventurer is fun and trying to unlock a secret legendary class is even more so.
Though the world and quests are randomly generated, It doesn't necessarily have a huge impact on how you play the game.  Since this game is essentially a race for how much fame you can achieve - it is best to repeatedly look for quests every single turn and make it to where the quests are as close to your current position as possible.
Turn based combat with action points works really well.  Finally a system that has more to do than just "fight, special skill, item and flee".  Certainly you still do those actions but now you can strategically wait and focus more action points for your next action and possibly gain 3 attacks in 2 turns.
Though overall an average "alright" game - this is still a fun enough game to pickup at this price point and comfortably play.

Heres my video review version.
Among The Sleep is a first person horror adventure Indie game developed and published by Krillbite Studios for PC, MAC, Linux and PS4.
Krillbite Studios is a Norwegian games Developer who has received over $300,000 Euro or ($500,000 USD) in total donations from The Norwegian Film Institute and from crowd funding..
Was their money well spent..
In this adventure you play as a 2 year old child on his birthday, when a stranger knocks on the door… to give you a present. the identity of this person is hidden from the player.
Shortly after this event your mum decides its time for you to play with your new gift, the teddy bear, so she takes you upstairs.
While going upstairs, the game is quick to kick in the creepy factor by making a wall of darkness follow you as the developer overlays there intro into this section.
I won’t tell you anything else beyond this point as it will ruin it for you.
Although I wouldn’t call Among the Sleep a horror game but it is still incredibly creepy and presents horror in a new light, more on that shortly.
This is essentially the prologue and basic knowledge about Among The Sleep, but it doesn’t really give you to much because I don’t want to give the story away. Any more story elements I lay out for you will completely destroy the story for you.
The gameplay consists of basic aspects such as crawling, running, object throwing and simple puzzles.
The walking animation is by far the best thing in this game :)
All jokes aside, the gameplay is simple yet fun and this is probably one of the first horror games with a defenceless protagonist that actually makes sense….
The visuals in Among the Sleep were impressive for an indie game running on the Unity engine, unlike most Unity based games there wasn’t any motion blur that was over powering me while I played, this feature can get quite annoying so Im glad they opted out of that idea.
There was one instance in the game were an object I needed to collect for progression didn’t actually fall down after hitting it sooo in order to continue I had to use a no clip console command to get it…
Later the game crashed and luckily they had a checkpoint before as when the game reloaded I was able to collect the object correctly.
Other than a few bugs here and there the game looked amazing and it really did feel like I was actually in this house, which for me made the experience that much more enjoyable.
The sound design in this game played an extremely important part, with ambient sound alone adding yet another layer of creepy to the environment which helped pull off a horror type experience.
Some sounds that would appear to be scare sounds, weren’t scary at all but seemed placed there to keep you on your toes which I thought was a neat inclusion.
Rather than trying to scare you constantly throughout the game, Krillbite decided to ease you into scares which if you havnt seen part 5 of my playthrough I would strongly recommend you go watch that, to get a real understanding as to what I am referring to.
P.S. I nearly flew out of my chair
Although there was a decent amount objects clipping through walls here and there… the core game didn’t get effected by this and the creepiness of this game grasped me in and made me want to understand what was going on in this world.
Which for a horror game is a great step up from the rest… and well you’re a 2 year old with a talking teddy what more can you ask for.
Bugs and issues aside, Among the Sleep was a solid indie game developed by Krillbite Studios and seeing as this is their first game… they didn’t do a whole lot wrong.
That is why Among the Sleep gets an 8/10.

I really enjoyed this game. At first I didn't know what to make of it, considering its from the perspective of a toddler and was leery about getting it on that merit alone however I am extremely glad I got over it. The unique perspective of the toddler really lends to the whole story portrayed throughout the game. (sorry no spoilers :) ) DLC really does expand upon the story and though it does leave a couple more questions in the mind for possible more DLC later on down the road, what it does add does make you pause and blink. I know I did.
Pros:
*Unique perspective of the toddler + eye level items ( makes you have to *THINK* to get around some obstacles you'd normally just walk up to and click, in other games)
*Dispite being a first person camera perspective, the shaking/movement animations do *not* incite the usual motion sickness nausea that usually accompany's such "realistic" perspective in a game. I contribute this to this game being VR compatible and that it must have gotten play tested very well to look for such problems for VR users. (don't know how many games utilize this first person camera perspective and because the camera is going EVERYWHERE, its a game I cannot play in one sit thru. Among the Sheep, does *NOT* have this problem. Was able to play through it in one sitting with much enjoyment had.)
*Ambience + level music lends more to the suspense/horror as you play. ( If I'm not mistaken some of the undertones are suppose to supposedly resonate with the player to highten this suspense. Probably mistaken but if your ears are keen or have heard those tones before that may influence mood, might make the same mistake in thinking the undertones are the same. *shrug*)
*The drawings, pictures and monsters = story line goodness (try and see them all!). Especially if playing pretty much uninterrupted by RL things, the monsters (there's technically two if take into consideration the DLC) really lend to the feeling of dread and will probably have you either shock/startle when they appear, or hiding in a closet from a meer noise that might possibly somehow in a far flung galaxy be indication that the monster's coming to possibly eat you, or whatever it does when the screen turns black! ( dun dun Dun!)
* Teddy Bear Companion. This little guy, how they put him throughout the game, there's always this nagging feeling, just by how he talks, what he asks of your character, if you should trust him. I think because of the way the companion was made and what it adds to the game, you do have that added layer that some games lack in creating attachment to sidekicks.
*Graphics=Awesome. There's not much more to be said on that point, provided you have your settings at the optimum for your system and calibrated the gamma correctly to give that spooky look, you're gonna have a great time. Even the pieces of wood have breakpoints and lines, the detail on the items the toddler has to crawl over you can tell someone put a lot of work into those little points that really bring out the mental mind trip Alice in wonderland vibe. ( Makes you almost wonder what exactly was in that happy birthday baby bottle at the begining before the cake!  Ha.)
Cons
Unfortunately, with how much I *loved* playing this game. I did find two picky little Cons.
* End Credits. Awesome to pay respect to all the backers from ever and always but it does make the credits uber long to sit through. Took me a good few times of pressing escape before being able to get out of the long list of credits. Sitting though the whole thing on the DLC, took enough time to get up, get a drink, go use the washroom and come back in enough time for it to still be going through the R names. LOL. Certainly there has to be an easier way on the main interface to give all the backers and such recognition than a long scroll screen where its hard to catch all their names, but again, like I said. "that's me being picky."
* DLC is a little hard to find. At first I didn't realize it had downloaded DLC when I first booted up the game. If it wasn't for beating the game and deciding to go back and replay some chapters, I wouldn't know that the DLC is listed in the Chapter Selection, portion of the main menu and I may have missed out on playing some EPIC DLC. The extra story the DLC adds on, especially if you play it AFTER the main game, makes one sit back and go Dayuum.
Overall this is a great game and I recommend it, especially if you have time to dedicate going through an entire playthru uninterrupted. Another time I tried playing it, and I constantly had to set it down and pick it back up again, really had not as many of the features pop out or strike me as the first time, when well, you've been playing it for hours and all that ambience has gotten to you. HA! :)  I really recommend playing the DLC after the Main game, for a different perspective on the game story. I played it both with DLC first, then main game, and also Main game with DLC after. Found doing it one way over the other, tends to lend itself to one verson of understanding the story while doing the other, makes one almost ponder a complete nother.  As to what I'm talking about! Play the game! can you note the difference I"m speakin' of?

Resident Evil goes back to it's roots.
As a longtime Resident Evil fan, I was dissapointed by where the franchise started to go when Resident Evil 4 was released. Although a good game in its own right, the only thing that it shared with the original RE was it's name. The franchise switched from survival horror to full on shoot-em-up.
Resident Evil 7 brings the series back to its survival horror roots. You can no longer buy ammunition but instead have to pick and choose your battles. The decision to make this a first person game is excellent and the fact that you are and were so vulnerable increases the fear factor. This is the most disturbing game I've ever played. I've never played a game where the characters make such brutally vulgar threats towards you while you run away in panic: it scares the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of you.
The graphics are extremely well done. I often took time just to look at the small details in the scenery. The shower curtain with drops of water on it, how the light shines off of concrete bricks in a basement - it's extremely well done and runs well.  The real winner here is the sound. Every ambient creak and crack made my hair stand up as it made me expect another monster ambush.
The only downside is it is *relatively* short. Capcom plans to release a free DLC as Chris Redfield so hopefully that will add to the replay value. I look forward to the next installment of this game and hope the series stays with this format.

Gameplay, Story, Port, DLC
-----------------------
The first thing I have to say is this game was not what I expected but I had to high of expectations for it anyway. I have played the original RE to RE Revelations 2, and I can say this is a great return to the RE series with a new engine and a new view on the world! The gameplay is good, nothing special your average shooter. Brings back the classic weapons such as the shotgun, grenade launcher, a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ knife, and a classic weapon that you all will love. There are not a lot of enemies to fight against, only because you're in a farmhouse, but the interactions with the Baker family are nothing less than scary. The story starts out strong and works its way up to a disappointing ending with a choice that makes no difference at all, the voice acting is great (No Troy Baker, and Nolan North). The story does not tie in with the canon until the end and there will be a free DLC coming in spring to really tie in the RE universe. The Port of this game is very well done, really good FPS with a GTX 970 and a AMD FX-8320 above 100+ fps most of the time. No widescreen support or FPS slider to have a noticeable difference, something with the engine I guess. The DLC I can say is not worth $30.00, the most time you will get out of both VOL 1 and 2 is about 1 1/2-2 hours of gameplay they are very short, well done, but short and is not worth the full $30.00 price tag it holds.
-----------------------
Score Counting
+ RE will be taken in a better direction with the first person perspective, the custom engine is very well done.
-/+ Story starts out strong but fails to entertain near the end, voice acting is very good and fits the tone of the game.
+ Good port. A very refreshing start for ports in 2017.
- DLC is not worth any amount of money hopefully the Not A Hero DLC will be longer than 2 hours.
Final Score
-----------------------

Fantastic game, well worth the price and easily one of the (if not the) best horror/survival games I've played.
Gamplay: 9/10.
Well paced, with great boss fights that are a challenge wihtout being cheap. I died a handful of times, but was able to learn from my mistakes and make steady progress each time. Health/ammo/item placement is spaced out enough to make the first 2/3 of the game tense and require careful use without being impossible, although this changes quite a lot in the last 1-2 hours, where ammo and medical supplies start raining from the sky. Most of the game had me sneaking around at a crouch jumping at shadows and unexpected noises. Think Alien: Isolation but replace the alien with a deep south hillbilly axe murderer. The level of atmosphere and that genuine feeling of survival is just superbly done. The only two complaints that I could level at this game is that a handful of times walking past a certain point obviously triggered the game to spawn a Molded directly behind me, which came over as a bit of a tacky 'monster closet' moment, even if it only happened 2-3 times in the entire game, and that the hit detection for the giant fat guy things vomit attack had a bad habit of hitting me through solid objects and stunlocking me. Overall though these are *very* minor complaints and I felt like the game was a masterpiece from start to finish.
Graphics and performance: 10/10.
None of the issues that so many releases have these days with consolitis making it's way into PC versions. Full graphical options, full mouse/keyboard and controller support, and it ran flawlessly at 2560*1440 on my GTX970 with most settings on high. Not a single crash or bug in my entire playthrough. Graphically this is also one of the best looking games I've seen, rivalling the likes of Doom for level of detail and effects. The attention to detail in small things like foliage and the surrounding environment give parts of the game a borderline photo realistic look.
Take the best parts of the franchise over the years, ie good and engaging horror/survival with a belieavable setting and remove the worst parts, ie ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ tank controls and horrible over the shoulder camera angles, stupid corny 3rd action gameplay, and you have this. Exceptional all round. Buy it.

-Graphics: In my opinion Capcom kept with with graphics this time, and combined with the great gameplay this truly is a survival horror game.
Cons:
The only thing that I hate about this game is that Capcom added a season pass to a ~10hours-long single player game that has no multiplayer at all...
I know that, unfortunately for us gamers, we live in the season pass era, but if you look back to other RE games, along the main storywe had multiplayer, other side-stories to play or same story from another perspective and other game mods that would provide many more hours of gameplay, I really think this game should have provided the full experience for 50euros, not 80.

People will compare this to The Binding of Isaac, and they aren't wrong in doing so. They are both very similar, and yet play very differently.
The similarities follow:
That is where most of the similarities stop however, and the games become very different.
In conclusion, The Binding of Isaac and Our Darker Purpose are both great rougue-like twinsticks, however, they are pitched very differently. The Binding of Isaac is made to make you feel powerful, yet fragile, while Our Darker Purpose makes you feel weak and alone, trying to survive, while also being relatively sturdy.

At first glance it is easy to make comparrisons to The Binding of Issac, and in this case it is to the games benefit. The very stylish art combines with a moody atmosphere in a dark and creative story that makes it a hit in my book. Where as the Binding of Issac is the shining light of Rogue-Likes and good gaming all around, Our Darker Purpose is a sleeper hit, often overlooked BUT completely worth your time as its endearing concept has the potential to become it's own heavy weight like the Binding of Issac.
Given some tender loving care, and time this could potentially become some truly awesome.
However it would be remiss of me not to point out that its down side is that it is only partially controller supported. I would like to see it fully supported in time.

Our Darker Purpose is a great tribute to classic (older) and modern  rogue-like games. True, it does share similarities to many familiar ones (Binding of Isaac is a frequently over used comparison by example), however, it is quite a bit different in quite a few ways.
This game has a harsh learning curve, you will die, you will be punished for mistakes, you will in general get stomped in some runs when you wished you hadn't. In return though, your experience in learning the patterns of the enemies, unlocking challenges, items, courses, and more will help with your progression through this amazing, yet harsh game.
The soundtrack is a mixed bag, many of the themes are quite memorable in my opinion, including but not limited too:  Welcome to Edgewood (level 1 theme) to Madness theme a later stage boss's theme. Catchy, dark (sinister), and very suting for your romp through Edgewood's dark halls.
The level up system you gain from killing enemies by obtaining EXP, are actually quite useful most of the time which some powers can easily make or break a run, depending on the RNG of which traits you manage to obtain in a run. For example one level up trait allows you to gain +1 damage for each Edgewood coin you pick up. Which doesn't sound that good until you start picking up large quantities of coins and watch your default 60-80 damage hitting for upwards of 150-300 damage in later stages if you manage to find a fortune of coins.
The course system which are perma-traits you can unlock and choose which to use can also be quite helpful, whether it be giving you a few additional starting Juice Boxes (which help restore HP when you are damaged by enemies or the misc. traps within Edgewood) to giving your critical hit a boost, to even expanding each individual room by 3 rooms.  Sure, you are forced to pick and choose which one you will start with, but most of them feel quite useful.
The enemies and bosses within the game are well varied,  and as you progress main enemies get improved in their damage dealing capabilities, and how much they themselves can endure which is also true for the bosses.  Sure, for a few floors you may face similar generic enemies, but they do switch up as you progress. Like I made mention of the learning curve, of how you approach each floor, the traits of each floor (which also givs variety to each independent floor) makes this a very harsh but rewarding game.
In comparison to similar games (Binding of Isaac): Yes, they are both rogue-like games, that have you progressing through levels, killing bosses, and obtaining a random assortment of items with varying effects, that's about where the comparison ends however:
Where Binding of Isaac is only moderately (at best) difficult, Our Darker Purpose is quite a learning experience in both success and failure.  Where Binding of Isaac most runs are easily feasible as long as you don't get certain items, Our Darker Purpose requires you to be wise to your own playstyle, and make wise decisions if you wish to progress far.
Where Binding of Isaac main mechanics revolve around the items, in Our Darker Purpose, the items, level up traits, Course abilities, and even level traits will majorly effect how the game plays out.
But in the long run, if you can handle facing a challenge or don't mind a learning curve, this game is certainly a worthy purchase, and now and then it still gets updated with tweaks (new level traits/items/etc.)...
To finish, this game is great, and I easily recommend it.

So obviously this game is a top-down shooter and will be indefinitely compared to The Binding of Issac. So here's my two cents.
First of all, I love The Binding of Issac. But between the two I much prefer Our Darker Purpose. And with all mechanics aside, I love this game's story, art style, and atmosphere. It's as if Lemony Snicket decided to create a video game centered around the nonchalant killing of children. Its concepts are gruesome, but presented in a humorous, light hearted manner. Even reading the flavor text for items gives me the chuckles. The enemies are neat, the bosses well thought out, and the setting of a boarding school has never been more depressing.
What makes this game more appealing to me than The Binding of Issac is the fact that not everything is randomized. Unlike Issac where your ability to do well often depended on what items you recieved as rewards from chests and bosses, this game allows you the option of planning. Do you want to be centered around survivability or damage? Dodge or firing speed? The periods and item selection from vending machines allows this type of focus.
So don't knock this game just because it's a top down shooter and you're unable to look past similiarities. It's clear that the developers spent a lot of time and work on this game. And to top it off, it's pretty damn fun.

Empire Total War (E:TW) is a RTS set in the 1700's. It has a single player campaign mode on a strategic map which add to the game greatly (and therefore is a shame that is not multiplayer). A worthy successor to the Total War series and an excellent historical battle simulator.
Graphics are much improved over Mediaeval and Rome TW but the movement controls are worse as the system struggles to path and place units according to their formation and position units around cover: you can often find a unit moving accross the map to nowhere. Indeed AI is generally extremely problematic: units have more of a tendency to not follow movement orders once engaged; units can be blithely matching through enemy ranks as a pitched battle occurs around them; troops will march in front of their own cannons and get killed; horse carriages will go over obstacles (like cannon emplacements and get killed).
Also the campaign game forces storyline battles on you. I had just finished capturing Canada from the French and was ready to re-enter real life when I was thrown into Bunker Hill without warning or explanation and had to fight another battle: a battle I subsequently lost because I had to stop the game and was not allowed to save the game. I had to beat the French in Canada four times before I got the game to a save point where I had won Bunker Hill. This is done for the sake of storyline momentum but but there would have been no harm putting in a save point.
This lack of attention to player experience in interface and storyline is seen also in the exposition in the in-game help. Nowhere does it say that unit will fire into their own troops or how this operates (sometimes they do, sometimes they hit their own troops, sometimes only the enemy), nor how to cancel a building destruction/construction order, how cover works and how units wrap around them, how to cancel a broadside, why are only the first line of troops firing etc. Forums help here but a few more tool tips wouldn't go astray as the experience of using gunpowder weapons is different to the previous more melee centric TW series; archers can arc over troops but muskets travel a flatter trajectory after all.
On broadsides, ship battles are very well done. I haven't player other ship simulators since Port Royal, but it was very satisfying demasting a ship. Again, not a lot of exposition, like that the compass actually refers to wind direction.
Individual unit animations are very good and troops will even jump over obstacles.
Loading times are very slow and the system does not quite know how to handle two monitors.
In all, a very good game that is puntuated by poor AI, poor exposition, forced stroyline battles you cannot save, and no restart button as in other TW games.

When i first got this game, I didnt have a graphics card, and it goes without saying that having a Intergrated chip made the game run like♥♥♥♥♥♥  Fastforward a year later, I got a cheap but effecitve card (650 gtx) and can thus run this on max quality.  This game has been sitting on my shelf of games to play and I finally picked it up and I realize that I should have played this game a long time ago.  First reactions, were wow, this is cliche, but then it just kept getting better.  Not a perfect game mind you, but a really damn good one with a great story.
Story:   You play as a young named Vito who comes back home from war.  Being a vetren, its hard to find work so you find a sort, different lifestyle, kinda of work.  The title of the game spoils what line of work our friend Vito does.   Along the way, you meet various people.  Some are neutral, others, have their own motives.  From there, I cant say much more due to spoilers, but you got through the ups and downs of being a part of the mafia, and while there are plenty of good times, there are equally as many, low times.   The story to me, was what really brought the game together.  There are plenty of twists and some are predictable, while others were big surpises.   Even the end caught me off guard because I just didnt see it coming, or rather, I really didnt want it to end this way, but hey, thats what happens when you become a part of a mafia.
Gameplay:   This is where things can be a bit tricky.  There is a mixture of driving, fighting, gun shooting and odd ball stuff.  The shooting is good, but not great.  The fighting is good at first, but then you can exploit the AI to always win.   Driving is stiff but you get the hang of it.   Police chases would happen here and there.  Heck, if you drive too fast or bump into someone, you get a cop who tells you to pull over.  Doing so has them give you a ticket or you can bribe them.   Sure it can be annoying, but its kinda nice to have these features to keep you in check.   Ampther feature they have is a ID and car tag thingy where if you get caught doing something bad, the police will look for you.  If you did wrong with just a car, then they will look for your car but not you.   Likewise, if you did wrong with your character but not with your car, then they will ignore your car and look for you when you are on foot.
Visuals:   The game is a bit dated when compared to modern standards, but thats understandable.   Even if they are dated, they look pretty good.  The attention to detail, is great.  The more you wreck your car, the more it looks like its falling apart.  Damage it enough, and you  will have to fix it on the road.  One small detail I liked was one where snow would pile up on your car and then as you drive, it blows off.   Its amazing how much they focused on details.    The game is a decent size openworld but many parts are just visually pleasing to look at and have not much value in driving around.

This game gives you the choice of riding a variety of tanks. You have to choose your tank wisely, as each one has their strengths and weaknesses depending on the terrain and situation.

For example, the M4 is a very versatile medium tank with a 75mm gun, and although it's armour isn't particularly strong, a skilled commander can utilize it's sloped surfaces and rounded turret for maximum effect. Meanwhile, the T34 has great sloped armour and wide tracks for effective traverse in rough terrain, but lacks the more sophisticated equipment and reliability of the Pz.IV. Of course, choosing the legendary Tiger I might be tempting with it's great 88mm and thick front armour, but you have to be mindful of it's unreliable engine.
I have to admit though, that the selection of tanks could, and should have been greater. There are several other NPC tanks that you will meet through the game, like the Maus and the B1, but unfortunately you don't get to drive them. The areas in the game are also not as varied as they could have been, but includes a beach, a mountain and several urban areas.
However, despite it's shortcomings, this is a very charming tank simulator.

Pulse is an interesting idea, and fun to experience.
You play as a blind girl who visualizes the world through the sounds she hears. The visual effects used to show this off are really cool. Wherever a sound is emanating, a wave of colour will light up the world.
Luckily the devs keep the world from being too frustrating to navigate. There are usually a few loud objects in the world which keep small areas visible. Additionally, as you walk around, you leave footprints, which help keep your orientation on where you came from. Although, you might find yourself lost ever now and again, it isn't too hard to navigate the beautiful looking world.
Speaking of the beautiful world you don't get to see it much, but the glimpses here and there reveal a simplistic, yet interesting environment. The place is filled with ruins, vegetation, and some cute little critters. These guys are called Mokos. As you pass by them they'll follow you. You can pick them up and toss them around. When they hit surfaces, they make noise, allowing you to see ahead.
The game's atmosphere does a really good job and making you feel helpless at times. Loud noises will frighten you, but also light the way.
As for the story, it's kind of a mystery at the beginning. You start to get a better feeling of it as you progress through the game, and are talked to by some strange spirit-looking thing.
Overall, it's a unique mechanic for a game, which I personally didn't get tired of due to the stuff the devs put in place to prevent you from being totally lost. The game is also not incredibly long. There's even an achievement for beating it in under 30 minutes. Granted, that's probably by speedrunning and not really enjoying the game properly, but it's still something to keep in mind. Still, I think it's a fun little experience!
