Do you like creepy atmospheric environments? Do you like jump scares? Do you like piecing together subtle hints and disturbing clues to a horrifying scenario that the protagonist cannot fully comprehend? Do you like playing the role of a toddler? If you answered yes to any of these questions, give Among The Sleep a try. You will be even more affected by this if you try to get into the mindset of the main character--though if you are prone to getting very far into the headspace of first-person-view characters, or are easily startled, I would recommend wearing a diaper.

This is another survival/exploration horror game, but one in which you play as a two year old child. Somehow, this makes the whole thing that much more terrifying, even if the game itself isn't a pants-filler like Outlast. It's not just that you're defenseless and don't want to get eaten by some monstrosity, but you also don't want the little kid you're playing to get hurt either. It definitely adds to the fear.
As others have said, the game is a bit short, although they recently added some free DLC, which helps round it out a bit. The design is interesting in that it actually feels like what a toddler might imagine based on the pieces he can put together from the world and events around him. It even reminded me of snippets that I can remember from when I was a little kid, from imaginary worlds to fragments of dreams.
The mechanics are relatively simple and involve a fair amount of finding Tab A and getting it into Slot B before progressing. It's a common element in many games, and at least it isn't obstructive or overt here.
The story is what got to me, though. I don't want to spoil anything, but pay attention to those crayon drawings you see littering the place and various recurring themes and objects. Some parts were fairly obvious, some were a bit of a surprise, but regardless, it was heartbreaking at points. Making the player a little kid brings out the sadness of many things.
I definitely recommend picking this one up. If you're wary, grab the demo or wait for a sale. Parents playing this game might just find themselves giving their kids a big hug after playing.

One of the most fun and original puzzle games I have played in a long time. As a mafia hitman it's your job to eliminate all human targets on the screen using a limited supply of bullets. One has to try and kill said targets by ricocheting bullets off various surfaces in order to directly kill as many targets as possible or by setting off objects such as explosive barrels, mines, bowlingballs, crates etc. that will then go about doing their nasty business.
The game comes with 100 puzzles that start of really simple but get increasinlgy more difficult if you're a completionist like me and want to try and get a full 3-star rating on every assignment (as long as you kill every target you will automatically move on to the next puzzle regardless of how many stars you earn).
The sound effects are fine, the music is a bit repetitive but soothing and graphically it's simple but fits the theme perfectly. Yet it's the gameplay where it's truly at: For the price this game is extremely good value for money.

This game is well crafted with some nice music and decent graphics for an indie game.  The controls are solid and don't leave you frustrated.  The key game mechanic is aiming and calculating angle deflections.  Exploding barrels come into the picture later, but the same principles apply.  I think the author should be proud of their work here.
That said, I still do not recommend the game unless you're a hardcore fan of puzzle games like this that require many repetitions with rote memorization in order to succeed.  Hard gameplay is one thing, but unless you're prepared to sit in front of your computer screen with ruler and protractor, you're going to simply be guessing at each move at first, an then learning which shots to take.  The right mouse button let's you place little markers to keep track of these, but even with that, it's simply not fun.
On top of that, once you get stuck on a level, your only option for gameplay at that point is to either persist or to repeat a previous level to try to better your score.  That limitation, coupled with the singular gameplay mechanism of aiming/calculating, means most will lose interest very quickly.
That's not to say this game, or any successor which may in the works is without hope though.  I'm only bothering to write this because I think there is potential here and because I still liked it well enough to comment on it.  Some ideas that come to mind for improvement include:
- gameplay branching into different areas with an accompanying storyline; possibly with comic book style vignettes complete with heroes and villains to back the story
- more weapon choices with various firing characteristics
- weapon path firing prediction via firing lines that show reflection paths; which would allow for level design in which shots could be easily placed, but must be placed in a certain order to allow completing the level - in other words, more strategy over pure angles calculation
- and of course a variety of more background, music, and sound effect assets
Games are worth different amounts to everyone of course, but my interest in this wanned after 2 hours, so I'm glad I paid around $.50 for it as part of a bundle.  I would be feeling a lot less good will towards it if I had paid the current $5 price tag.

The grand campaign is the meat of Empire: Total War, and it's there where you're likely to spend the most amount of time. The game stretches across the 18th century and lets you choose from a number of world powers, from Great Britain and Russia to fallen domains such as the Maratha Confederacy and the Ottoman Empire. Once you choose an empire, you can select from a few different campaign types that determine victory conditions and campaign length. Whichever you decide, be prepared: Even a short, 50-year campaign can take a good amount of time to complete, given that each turn requires strategic thinking on multiple fronts. Battles usually determine how regions are won and lost, but diplomatic relations, economic strangleholds, assassinations, and many other subtleties must be tweaked and considered at each turn, and they have noticeable impact as the years progress. If this sounds overwhelming, or if you're an American history buff, you'll want to check out the Road to Independence campaign before jumping into the grand one. This is essentially a long American tutorial that slowly introduces you to the basics and culminates in a grand campaign of its own.
The factors you must consider run the gamut, starting with an important new feature: the technology tree. Three areas of research and multiple subtrees let you improve your military, industry, and philosophy; in turn, your choices may benefit your economy or your success in battle. The benefits may seem minor at first, but as the campaign wears on, their effects are more noticeable, and your choices within these trees must be informed by the strengths and weaknesses of your particular empire. Do you concentrate on industry and use sheer numbers of troops to overwhelm your enemies, or do you focus on naval improvements and reap the ensuing benefits of successful trade-route blockades? As your campaign wears on, your needs may shift, whether because enemy blockades require a stronger navy, because you are spreading quickly across land, or because your economy is unable to sustain your growing army. Technology is also a limited diplomatic option, given that it's a commodity that you can not only trade during negotiations but also steal from foes. Additionally, it's not easy to convince a friendly nation to offer technology. Even when offered multiple technologies or monetary compensation, your closest allies rarely accept a request to share even a single technology, which makes it a limited political tool. In Empire: Total War, knowledge is more easily stolen than shared.
In fact, your more successful political dealings are the underhanded ones. Your agents may differ between nations (for example, gentlemen and rakes for the British, scholars and hashishin for the Ottomans), but the tasks are similar: covertly disrupt the affairs of your enemies and potential enemies. Religious agents such as missionaries will slowly but surely convert the populace, staving off potential rebellion in newly captured regions. On the other hand, the impact of religion is not as deep or impactful as in the Europa Universalis series, in which social and diplomatic events are more fully explored. Regardless, it's great fun to cripple whole economies, especially when your strategies work in tandem with each other. Sending in a naval fleet to seize enemy trade supplies, sending another directly into an enemy's port (and therefore obstructing incoming goods), and dispatching an agent to sabotage commercial ports can have profound effects. In cases like these, an angry, resource-deprived public and cash-strapped armies then ease the way for a quick triumph.
Overall i think this is one of my favorite games of my childhood, which i totally suggest anyone who hasn't been able to play this game to get it and try it.

Brace yourselves, I have definitely a lot to say on this one. I got the game at a reduced price of 16€ with all DLCs in this years Christmas Sale and I really enjoyed playing it. However there are some points of criticism which I want to clarify and which might be of interest to anyone who wants to buy the game:
1. The Main Story (Spoiler Alert, Scroll down):
The main story of Mafia II is great and I dare say the characters are way better developed than in many other gangster games (eg. earlier GTAs and the Driver Franchise). You really get to know the two main protagonists from the beginning and you learn why they made the decisions that they did and why they ended up in organized crime. This is clearly not a humorous game, like GTA, it's more of a Drama and I think that that is really something that sets it apart and makes it very enjoyable.  But I have to say that I really think that the ending is bad, not to say atrocious, because it does not really close the story arc, but leaves it wide open, not really satisfactory, especially if the rest of the main story is so well written.
2. Gameplay:
Perhaps the biggest flaw that the game has lies here. I expected a totally different kind of gameplay with the product being advertised as an OpenWorld game, but the truth is it doesn't give you a whole lot of freedom. The game keeps sending you from one point to the next, you always have something to do and if you feel like taking your new freshly tuned sportscar for a spin there's always the next target nagging at you from your minimap. That's something I found plainly annoying and  which also didn't integrate itself well in the game. It feels like they intended to make it an open world game and started to integrate some features along these lines (e.g. set your own waypoints), but then suddenly changed their minds and turned it into a linear action game. Also the point in the game at which you have the most possibilities is the MIDDLE of the story. It all goes downhill after that (You quickly are stripped of all of your money and your property) and the open world aspect gets pushed even more in the backgrounnd. That really made me feel kind of left out as a player, because with every step that I was progressing in the game it made me long more and more for the middle part with all it's freedoms because there were many things that I would like to have done and it turns out there is no way to ever do them except for playing all the way to the middle again. There's no end game like in GTA, where the town is yours and you can do everything, the game just ends and you have to start anew. Especially I don't understand why they didn't at least implement a freeroam mode that lets you do what you want.
2. Mission Design:
The second biggest thing that keeps Mafia II from being a stellar game is the mission design: The game starts out with really diverse missions. Some stealthy, some more centered towards fast driving and some shooting missions, that are all in all very easy, but of very high quality. As the game progresses the tasks become mondane and uninteresting as well as increasingly difficult: If you raid one place and shoot it to bits that's fun, but to do it 7 times in a row? Not so much. The game starts to repeat itself and makes you do the same things over and over again and since your character is constantly losing money and his weapons players are denied a real sense of reward.
Closing Statement:
I was surprised myself on how bad it all sounds when I read the lines above all the way through, there is no denying I had fun with Mafia II, but I felt and I still feel, that the creators left out every chance to make a good game a great one. I still recommend the game, because as I stated before I enjoyed playing it for its sense of realism, the great story and the great character design, which is also why I recommend it to you.

This game is a great mix between Turn Based and Managing Simulators. That said it does have it problems that I don't like. I like the game and would recommend it to anyone who likes "Sim" or management games.
There are some indicators that it's still in Alpha (Payed not paid on the contract page for example) but I haven't noticed any random crashing. I have noticed that it doesn't seem to be remembering my previous games, so when it wants to compare how well you did with previous attempts, it doesn't find anything.
This is one of those games which is really easy to pick up and really difficult to be good at.
There are so many elements, that you won't get a full overview of it from the tutorial or even a couple of play throughs.
Pick a starting character who will be able to be levelled to five stars. That's not level five. Each character can progress through a class tree and once they reach the end of it, they can start on another class. So it's possible that your starting character will in effect know five classes.
Subsequent recruits will only be able to master one or two trees (at the start of the game). As you progress, your recruitment attracts a better quality of recruit.
Once you put your party together, you can deploy them and start doing quests. (I suspect you might be able to have more than one party, but I haven't got that far yet.) It's certainly possible to have the four people in your party and 'extras' in the wings to take over from people in the main party.
You can pick quests - and scout them so you don't bite off more than you can chew. Quests give experience, gold and fame. Fame is important to progress in the League.
Now the League is good and bad. It's good because you get to compete against other in-game Agencies. You can spy on them, knobble them or make friends with them. It's a good portion of the game. However, I would LOVE to see an League-less option. So you could play without worrying about being dumped out of the game because you have finished too far down the League. (I'm getting dumped regularly at the second Trimester of the second League.)
While you can pick different recruit strengths and build a party to suit, a League-less option would enable more flexibility and role play in that area. Want to try an "all buffer" group? How about "all Hellfire"? This is very difficult if you're constantly worrying about the League and I think it would give an extra dimension to the game.
Speaking of dimensions, you can open portals, so you can shortcut between cities. There are different factions with whom you can work to gain their favour.
Quests get progressively harder and you need that to get the gold to keep your party happy and the fame to keep up in the League.
Your Agency has it's own levelling system where it can open up additional staff, extra portals, reduce wage demands and alter contract negotiations. This is also important because if you don't level up your Agency, then your wages will be capped and you won't be able to pay the demanded salaries of your parties.
The graphics are cartoony but they work well in the game. This isn't a FPS or Diablo, after all. The information layout is pretty good on screen. My only criticism is that if you equip an item on your party, it still shows up in your inventory. This means you can accidentally sell something you're using. I'd like to see some indication that an item is in use. This also applies when you're equipping your party and one member is wearing something; it shows as free to use for another member.
The quests are two-fold. A story progression and random encounters. There's a reasonable variety but I suspect most people won't read them after a while. They'll look at the location and the quest level. The game will sometimes throw you a curve to keep you on your toes. I got a quest that turned out to have my level 2 or 3's fighting a level 10 monster. Yeah, that got left for later and he got smacked when they were older!
Every four weeks, you get to see how far you are in the League and if you haven't progressed enough, your Agency is closed. As I said, this is the most frustrating bit to me.
Overall an excellent game, well worth the money and I hope the development continues.

Kickstarter backed the game as a big fan of the idea.  I'm aware the game is still in early access and will certainly revisit the game at a later date as I still hope to see the concept really work out.
The current release has some great management elements with salaries, contracts, and management options that could be part of a very unique and interesting game.  The initial draft, team creation and starting out is exciting and feels like team management.  Recruiting staff, leveling up your guild abilities and competing for the top spot are good as well.  However it feels like they aren't central enough to the game play and the game just slows down the more you get into it.  The tutorial is very long and wordy making it difficult to get through while absorbing the needed information.  The majority of your time in the game will be spent moving teams around to new quests and controlling battles.  It plays much more like a mediocre turn based RPG than anything else.
Battles are boring and drag the entire game flow down.  The battle system plays like a flash or mobile game at best and the vast majority of the time feels like an annoying task to grind through, not something exciting to play.  Being able to "skip" easy battles wouldn't even really help much without more options of other things to do being added as well.  This really saps the fun out of the game and makes it get boring quickly when it's just repetitive turn after turn of doing the same thing for similar quests and the only combat variations feeling like if the enemy is high enough to wipe you out.
The class system feels like it could just be dumped almost entirely and just replaced with one large tree you spend points in to pick skills with branches to level up those skills.  Multi classing in the current form feels tacked on and out of place and many of the classes feel very similar.
The flow of movement around the map feels slow as well, travel time ends up being one of the biggest concerns of the game.  If the travel time is too long you can end up losing a lot of gold with the salary cost you're paying while you travel to a quest.  Early on when you only have one team you will select where to go, click end turn multiple times maybe having a few scout actions or grindy battles to get to one quest.  I felt like later in the game waiting for movement and grinding battles was almost the entire game.  I often wouldn't have any useful scout actions to use, I had multiple full teams and couldn't grow more due to salary cap, so all I had to do was hope quests I found were near a team and had good rewards a reasonable difficulty and then wait enough turns to move to them.
The game also suffers from some balance and RNG issues that can result in a quick game loss, heroes being ruined by a random bad encounter giving them -AP per turn, traits that reduce AP cost or increase AP regen being wildly more powerful than anything else, difficulty spikes, etc.  However balance isn't terrible and I'm pretty confident the team will continue to work on that so it's not a major concern.
I think my TLDR would be - Still has potential with overhauls of some game aspects, but not worth picking up in its current state.

This is almost a broken game...
It is barely playable and feels like a early access game. After an hour, it stops being fun and all the bugs seem to appear twice as annoying. There is something wrong with about every aspect of the game, which is a shame because the game would have be really fun, and is if it's not buggy.
A few problems it has:
- The controls are clunky. Movement is not very responsive and sometimes buttons don't do anything or are significantly delayed. This is very fustrating and one thing that has lead to the game being bad.
-The AI is terrible. Every now and then there is a match where it doesn't totally mess up but on average the AI is bad. For instance, one of the opposing players missed a goal, feet from my goal line, with the special move. In fact, the ball shot off at a 90 degree angle...
This then lead to a goal kick?! Which makes no sense and leads on to another annoying bug. Sometimes you can score a goal and it be a corner, other times the opponent could kick it out (miss the goal) and it be a corner to them. The opponents are also the only people that seem to be able to cross it...
-The interface is full of english mistakes. I'm assuming this was done by someone whose first language is not english, and there is nothing wrong with that, however if you are going to release a game in english at least make sure it's actually english. A lot of the terms are wrong, such as throw ins are called 'touch'?, goal kicks are 'penalty kicks', shots are 'shoots', dribbling is a button for special abilities and has nothing to do with dribbling and the list goes on. It makes the game feel very amatuer and like a really lazy translation.
-The story mode is stupid. The story itself I have no problem with and the variation between opponents and teams is good, one of the only good things about the game however the way you have to progress is stupid. You have to collect a few stars (which are linked to the achievements) throughout the story mode, challenges that you can complete during the match i.e. score a total of 10 goals. Again that's great and another reason why this would be fun HOWEVER if you do not get all the stars you can not simply replay the match. You have to complete the entire story mode and then restart it from the beginning and play the entire story mode up until that point... The majority of the stars you can get in one go however one match requires you to win a match without any fouls as well as winning a match with 5 or more fouls, which means to complete that level you'd have to complete the whole story twice (assuming you can get them in one go, which is really hard due to the whole tackling mechanics being just as bad as the rest of the controls).
There is barely anything that makes me want to continue playing and if I wasn't such an achievement hunter I'd have given up but I have to play through the story a few more times for the stars... Even at £4 this isn't a great game, I'd go as far as saying you shouldn't even really pick it up in a sale unless it's really cheap and you don't get fustrated easily. If this is in a bundle, I'd say get it but only if this isn't the best game in the  bundle...

--------------------
Let's be clear here:
I Love This Beautiful Game, and my hours played on Steam don't reflect how much I have actually played because I own a copy of Absolvers on
as well.
But I can't recommend it to the general public because, being honest...
1. The UI is 101 terrible; it's annoying to navigate through it on the first time through, and one of my friend vomited while making his combat deck because the white colours were nauseating.
2. For a single player experience, Absolver is pretty bad; I only took almost 4 hours to finish the main story (and I was fooling around for most of the time), and I still don't know what the heck the story is about despite reading every NPC text and exploring everywhere (i.e. do not expect Dark Soul-esque lore). This is important for those not playing Absolver for PvP but - instead - for a brawler or an artsy game.
3. The map is very vague and you will most likely get lost on your first time getting around, a lot, unless you have a friend to guide you through.
4. The learning curve varies from player to player, but it's pretty steep. The tutorial does not explain all the mechanics; in fact, some of the mechanics can only be learnt via talking with the NPCs. Some combat deck combinations will be clunky and your first will most likely be pretty clunky unless you 'know' these kinds of games. As you can tell, if you're not the experimentative type, you're going to hate this.
5. The music is... What music? My music kept stopping by itself while I was playing despite having the volume at full. Whenever there was music, the music is forgettable.
6. There are moments where you have to grind, especially to unlock certain moves or to get clothing/fashion drops, and - while the grind takes reasonable time - it's mind numbing if you proactively do it.
7. The lock-on system does not work properly with more than one target; in fact, your character may even hit the closest target most of the time and not your locked-on target. At times where you're fighting 3 or more NPCs, the lock-on system can be downright broken and can even mess up your camera.
8. The camera is sometimes frustrating; it loves rubbing itself on the floor or walls and, because of that, you can't see sometimes.
9. The sound effects are unimpressive, except for when you hit hard - which then it's pretty satisfying.
10. Despite having good connection, myself and a lot of other people are having inconsistent connection issues - ranging from 'smooth' to 'broken'. As you can tell, this is very frustrating for a fighting game.
11. The game's main seller is PvP; if you don't like PvP... Well... Absolver is not for you. Period.
12. Even with the PvP, there's not much content in this game; even now, some players and a few Twitch streamers have already quitted the game because they're done. I don't know how they maxed out their level so fast though; I'm only level 46 as of typing this review.
13. There's always friendly fire for both the NPCs and for you and your friends. This can lead to some hilarious results, but I can see this being annoying. Also, I know a few of the player base who proactively kill/hunt newbies so... I'm not really sure what to say about this?
14. I got hit by a save corrupting glitch during launch. The developers said that they will fix this soon though.
15. You can't skip cutscenes nor dialogue.
16. I have gotten stuck on a loading screen at least 4 times throughout my experience playing. I had to Alt Tab and turn off the game and then turn it on again to continue playing. I have crashed once, and I do still experience glitches. Hopefully, these will be fixed via patch because - otherwise - the game is running at 60 frames VSync for me.
17. You can't manually save; the game auto-saves but doesn't even explain how or when so you have to guess when the auto-save happens.
18. There is region lock despite having limited servers so... Hahahahaha...\
19. ... And there's still more but I'm tired of listing new stuff because I want to go back in and fight.
--- VERDICT OF RECOMMENDATION CHANGED DUE TO CURRENT CIRCUMSTANCES ---
With all this aside,
If you're here for the PvP, combat and multiplayer, and if you don't mind the learning curve while having a good internet connection, I would definitely recommend this game; otherwise, no because it feels unfinished and - sometimes - plays like it too.

However, there's one huge problem: PC difficulty is artificially increased due to bad controls. Now, I don't have experience with all of the styles in game, but the way you use the special ability, which is a kind of defensive ability is by flicking the mouse. Now this on the other hand means that camera is locked when you are locked to an enemy, to whatever angle the game sees fit...
AND IT REALLY RUINS the entire experience! Controls are frustrating, because the MOUSE is not designed to be flicked, it's designed for constant fine motor control, which is perfect for camera, and 3rd person fighting games like this are dependent on a good camera angle - since if you cant see whats happening you get your♥♥♥♥♥kicked. The first twelve hours or so of the game were quite fun. New things to do, special orders to fulfil, new heroes to hire, quests for your heroes, weekend raids, and levelling up city buildings. After a while, progress slowed WAY down (and real money wouldn't really speed it up). I kept expecting to keep having fun, because I started out having fun, but I guess it faded while I wasn't watching. (Note: I left the game running 24/7, but only a small portion of that time was spent "playing", so my "hours played" is skewed).
To "build" the city, you spend gold or gems on a building (no resources). You can craft (which takes resources and time) and sell items to your shop's customers to get gold (small amounts), or you can buy/sell on the auction house for either gold or gems. Most of my time in this game was spent buying/selling things on the auction house, which I often enjoy, but many people do not.
Real money purchases cost a lot, but deliver little. (At the time of writing this review, $25 buys 3750 gems).
* Shop cosmetics, cutesy decorations, cost thousands of gems to unlock them all.
* The first fuse upgrade slot costs 1000 gems. Second is 3000.
* Even low-to-mid level items can be listed on the auction house for hundreds to thousands of gems each.
* The first trade slot upgrade is 1000 gems. Second ???. I have 5 non-upgraded trade slots.
* Healing your heroes after a quest can cost hundreds to thousands of gems.
* Items break during quests at an unexpectedly high rate. Repair costs are in gems, and expensive. Do not repair.
* After all my hours of play, I've acquired less than 2000 gems from in-game sources (including auction house).

If you haven't played TNO, then this game is a fun 8 hr adventure that shows you what's in store for TNO.

It only gets a pass, because it's cheap on sales if you want the full MachineGames Wolfenstein experience. Be warned however that it's really not very good.
The Old Blood is a direct prequel to The New Order, taking place shortly before the core game begins. It's also a soft-remake of Return to Castle Wolfenstein, minus the Deathshead subplot from that game; B.J. and another agent are captured and have to escape Castle Wolfenstein; from there, B.J. has to stop Helga Frau♥♥♥♥♥, who digs underneath a church and raises a demon creature thing, according to the writings of some King Otto from a thousand years ago.
It doesn't work on any level. For one thing, it's inconsistent with The New Order, which is more science-fiction and grounded. For another, the story just isn't well-written. The characters are cardboard cutouts, the fun antagonist gets slaughtered half-way through and the tone is the same as that of The New Order, which is out of place for a game involving ancient religious cult secrets. Old Wolfenstein worked, because it was balls-to-the-walls insane and it knew to make fun of itself. This one is even more straight-faced than the 2009 Wolfenstein. On occasion, you'll see chunks of The New Order's brilliant writing popping up, particularly from Bazkowitch's own Nazi-killing banter, but it's rare.
From a gameplay perspective, The Old Blood is sloppy through and through. The game starts off with a forced stealth section, which leads to a massive difficulty spike. Stealth is all over the place, in general; I get the idea of having to take down officers so they can't call for backup, but the level design is so lazy and unimaginative that every time I saw the signal indicators on-screen, I groaned. The core mechanics are the same as those of the original game, so it's still fun to run'n'gun, but there isn't nearly enough of that or the level design to support it properly.  Especially the second half of the game is a drag. There is also a distinct lack of super-weapons; if you're going to remake RTCW, have the decency to at least add a Tesla weapon.
My 'favourite' moment is probably the Chapter in which you get to ride a robot... and use it as a car, getting of the damned thing every two seconds to kill zombies and restock and pull levers. Then you fight the final boss, a hulking behemoth that doesn't even have the decency to focus on you long enough to kill it. Boring and incompetent design that is so unlike MachineGames' own standards it actually hurts.
As I said, buy it on a sale for the complete package, but ultimately what I got from the experience was merely a waste of my time.

While Wolfenstein: The New Order appears to be about one man's desperate struggle to singlehandedly murder every single nazi in the universe, The Old Blood appears to be about one man's desperate struggle to hold onto his trusty pipe shiv.
I played through the game on hard and was more or less pleasantly surprised with how smooth it was considering the concept of The Old Blood seemed like an afterthought or an excuse to use the same engine configuration twice. There is some frustration in the game, though. Some of the sections feel less like hand-crafted challenges and more like bashing your brains against a wall until you get lucky. (Especially some of the stealth sections. There's maybe two to three out of the couple dozen that either offer you one choice, or give you a single enemy-saturated hallway to sneak through.) However, other than that, the whole game manages to keep a rather nice rhythm and the combat is exciting and visceral, moreso because B.J. is nowhere near invincible and the game punishes you for being coy and hiding behind cover for more than a few seconds at a time, just like TNO.
Because there's like, five difficulties ranging from Very Easy to Very Hard under different names, the game's pretty accessible, but I'd recommend playing it on at least Normal because of the nature of the game. The writing isn't good enough to carry the entire experience,(Although this is debatable with The New Order) and while the setpieces are beautiful and can sometimes cause you to stop for a moment and appreciate just how wonderful some of the details are, the core of the game is in the struggle and the creativity and perserverance that come along with it.
It's not a long game, but it's a very interesting one and I'd recommend it for sure to anyone who wants to have a blast and likes killin' nazis.

The grand campaign is the meat of Empire: Total War, and it's there where you're likely to spend the most amount of time. The game stretches across the 18th century and lets you choose from a number of world powers, from Great Britain and Russia to fallen domains such as the Maratha Confederacy and the Ottoman Empire. Once you choose an empire, you can select from a few different campaign types that determine victory conditions and campaign length. Whichever you decide, be prepared: Even a short, 50-year campaign can take a good amount of time to complete, given that each turn requires strategic thinking on multiple fronts. Battles usually determine how regions are won and lost, but diplomatic relations, economic strangleholds, assassinations, and many other subtleties must be tweaked and considered at each turn, and they have noticeable impact as the years progress. If this sounds overwhelming, or if you're an American history buff, you'll want to check out the Road to Independence campaign before jumping into the grand one. This is essentially a long American tutorial that slowly introduces you to the basics and culminates in a grand campaign of its own.
The factors you must consider run the gamut, starting with an important new feature: the technology tree. Three areas of research and multiple subtrees let you improve your military, industry, and philosophy; in turn, your choices may benefit your economy or your success in battle. The benefits may seem minor at first, but as the campaign wears on, their effects are more noticeable, and your choices within these trees must be informed by the strengths and weaknesses of your particular empire. Do you concentrate on industry and use sheer numbers of troops to overwhelm your enemies, or do you focus on naval improvements and reap the ensuing benefits of successful trade-route blockades? As your campaign wears on, your needs may shift, whether because enemy blockades require a stronger navy, because you are spreading quickly across land, or because your economy is unable to sustain your growing army. Technology is also a limited diplomatic option, given that it's a commodity that you can not only trade during negotiations but also steal from foes. Additionally, it's not easy to convince a friendly nation to offer technology. Even when offered multiple technologies or monetary compensation, your closest allies rarely accept a request to share even a single technology, which makes it a limited political tool. In Empire: Total War, knowledge is more easily stolen than shared.
In fact, your more successful political dealings are the underhanded ones. Your agents may differ between nations (for example, gentlemen and rakes for the British, scholars and hashishin for the Ottomans), but the tasks are similar: covertly disrupt the affairs of your enemies and potential enemies. Religious agents such as missionaries will slowly but surely convert the populace, staving off potential rebellion in newly captured regions. On the other hand, the impact of religion is not as deep or impactful as in the Europa Universalis series, in which social and diplomatic events are more fully explored. Regardless, it's great fun to cripple whole economies, especially when your strategies work in tandem with each other. Sending in a naval fleet to seize enemy trade supplies, sending another directly into an enemy's port (and therefore obstructing incoming goods), and dispatching an agent to sabotage commercial ports can have profound effects. In cases like these, an angry, resource-deprived public and cash-strapped armies then ease the way for a quick triumph.

While I do recommend this game, it is still massively frustrating and repetitive.
I wouldn't even write the review, except I want to give feedback.
Pros:
1. The art style is really, really nice.
2. Just, the art style man. Take two points.
3. It is rather fun the first few minutes of the game when you think you've got the hang of it.
4. It does feel satisfying to level things up.
5. Oh, that catapult. Oh, that catapult! It is awesome!
6. When you get the catapult, and start taking out hordes in less than a minute, it feels pretty awesome.
7. The new mounts look pretty cool, I guess...? (I honestly don't know because I've never gotten them.)
8. For some reason, I really like the inventory system with the coins.
9. The new worlds sound intriguing, I guess. (Still don't know. Never gotten there.)
10. There are some nice tense moments at night.
And unfortunately, that's the most I can really say for the pros. While it's a fun time killer, there's a certain point of the game where it takes a turn for the worse, and the fun quickly turns to mad frustration, and from there, it's basically a point of no return. I'll get to that more in a minute.
1. The villagers/cilivians are kinda stupid. You have a wooden wall on day 35 a long way away from camp, they'll sit there instead of the obviously much more protected center. Or how there's only one or two guards on one side, and ten on the other side (the side without any monsters), and they still don't do anything. Also, I might mention that although there was a catapult there, two capable builders there to man it, and a horde on the other side of the wall, my group of soldiers (about ten), decided to not do anything to take care of the horde. The horde then procceded to break down my defenses, kill everyone, and basically (progressively), ruined my reign and won.
Thanks, guys.
2. Now that we've talked about their awful mistake and my ruined reign, perhaps we should go more into that, huh? I was doing pretty well, gotten to stone age, started work on the boat, had about 20+ soldiers, multiple walls (upgraded stone), a catapult, and all four armies/commanders or whatever started. It was pretty fun at the time, I was sure that I could do it. I could get to a new land, and try to maybe get some mounts. This was like, my third or fourth time playing the game (second, if you only count the update), so I was pretty happy. But everything went downhill when they decided they weren't going to use the catapult. There was no reason not to! It had ammo in it, all they needed to do was throw it! But they couldn't even do that. Because they broke through, and had the number advantage, they killed all my men, destroyed the catapult, (and since there was no other men anywhere else along the walls), they destroyed practically all of my left side.
This would be OK, if it wasn't around day 27, when monsters attacked every night, days were only two minutes long, and you barely get enough gold to recruit two archers a day. Much less get all my builders back, build back all the walls, get my army back, and get the capapult built again. So every night, the monsters would attack again, and bring it all back down to the basics- not even the basics, now that I think about it. And the worst part, was that I had a whole other side to the army on the right side. And yet they didn't do a thing! It was incredibly frustrating to have able soldiers not do anything even when the entire left side needed help.
As it became increasingly clear that the entire kingdom would get wiped out, and everyone would die, I decided I should just hurry and finish the boat. Try and get the heck out of there. But unfortunately, they kept breaking through whatever I put up. Killed whatever guards I hired. It wasn't because I was a bad player, it was because I simply could do basically nothing.
When I had one guard, 1 farmer, no walls, no people, no builders, no money, and no boat, was when I finally accepted defeat and let the monsters take the crown. Day 36 was when that happened. I knew there was no hope, but I kept going on anyway. Even though I knew I was just delaying the inevitable. And that was pretty frustrating and stressful. So yeah, point of this whole story is: it becomes increasingly stressful and frustrating, and that's really not how playing a game should feel. Playing a game shouldn't be a chore.
Worst part, is when I lost, I didn't feel motivated or determined to go back and try again. I was frustrated and tired of the game. And I don't feel like this game deserves that, and I also don't feel like it's a good way to make players come back.
3. The whole guards thing. Like I mentioned before, there were no guards anywhere. It would be so much better if they evened themselves out between the two sides, or even better, you could tell them which side you want more on. Though that might be hard to do, so just having them even out the sides would suffice (or even just going to the side that's being attacked more).
4. Like I said before, once you screw up (even if it's not your fault), the game's over. You lost.
This would be fixed, if it was even just the tiniest bit more forgiving.
5. Like others have said, it gets repetitive. You do the same things over and over again, which is mostly wait.
6. The days are very short. I head out in the morning to go recruit people, and by the time I get back, it's night.
7. You mostly wait through a lot of moments.
TL;DR
It's got some good pros, and a lot of potential, but it is very, VERY frustrating, stressful, and repetitive. I hope there's some good feedback in here.

A "sequel/cross-quel" to the original Kingdom game, New Lands delivers a stunning amount of new content, while carrying over the essence of the original game. Would I say buy both? Of course, it's not like playing on easy and hard mode, it's like playing Solitaire and Free Cell, same-same, but different.
I am a huge fan of New Lands, having recieved it for free after playing the original Kingdom from early on, and I was initially surprised to see a new game in my library, then I was stunned by the amount of new content, and how fantastic it was.
One of the best parts of this game is how much the developers take player feedback and suggestions into account. If you'd like to see something in the game, put it up on the discussion boards, the developers ACTUALLY LISTEN TO PLAYERS - it's like finding a unicorn (which you can actually do in this game btw.).
Like its predecessor, Kingdom: New Lands doesn't hold your hand. It gives you little tips along the way, but largely, you're left to figure out what to do on your own, and what strategy works best for you. There is a fantastic guide in the community page which is essentially like the Kingdom Bible -
Highly recommend giving this a read if you're stumped, heck just give it a read even if you think you have it down pat! Definitely recommend for old Kingdom players who are trying to figure out all the new things!
Overall, Kingdom: New Lands is a fantastic successor to the original game (which you should also still play and buy btw), I've already racked up a ton of hours on this, and the new features are fantastic (all hail the Hermit of Baking omg.). I cannot thank the humble developers enough for all their hard work, and for actually communicating with the community and letting the players suggest new features and whatnot.

(or Epic Manager for short) mixes elements from management games like Football Manager with RPG elements from games like Adventurer Manager and from board games such as Dungeons and Dragons. -
The story takes place after the end of a great war which unified various, once divided, kingdoms under the Realm of Astraeus. Despite bringing relative peace to the land, the end of the war meant that a lot of soldiers were left without a job. Unable to provide for their families many of them got together and formed guilds of adventurers that would roam the realm looking for quests but, due to bad management, a lot of them were led to ruin and some, even their deaths. In order to provide a relative safe space for adventurers to work a league is created for adventuring agencies to compete. The winner of said league will then be chosen as the ultimate Epic Manager. This is where you come in.
You play the role of the manager of an adventuring agency and you get to create your own by giving it a name and creating a coat of arms. Since you’re
the manager of the agency, you’re not an adventurer yourself, so you have to hire adventurers to go on quests for you. This means you’ll have to pay them weekly wages, how much that will be depends on the contract you’re able to negotiate with them before you hire them. Still, if you can’t afford to pay the cost of a week’s work, that will be covered for you at the expense of some of your fame.
The way the
works is as follows. On the game map you move/act in turns, which are split into 2 phases, first you give orders and then you see those actions unfold. Each turn corresponds to a week in game time and in each week you have a certain amount of scouts you can use to look for quests, sabotage other agencies, buy access to portals, which you can use to travel between towns, among other things. At the end of every trimester the 2 agencies with less fame will be eliminated from the league and at the end of each year the top 3 agencies will be promoted to the next league. Your fame is determined by things like taking contracts, completing quests and discovering new locations, where you can activate portals. As you play you’ll eventually gain points and increase your agency level, allowing you to upgrade your agency granting you various different perks and abilities.
The Adventuring Agency League is definitely the most captivating and unique feature of
for me, but the game does also have some other neat little mechanics that combined together make for a very appealing whole. For example, everyone in Astraeus worships a certain god and every now and then one god will be stronger than the other, granting bonuses to it’s worshippers (your adventurers). I also like the fact that you can take quests with different nobles that aspire the throne of Astraeus and, in doing so you’ll be opening new job opportunities in the future. However, dealing with one noble might create some friction with another one and the same goes for other agencies. Rival agencies can try to steal your funds, spread rumours about you - decreasing your fame - but they can also try to appease you with gifts.
Travelling throughout the map can be done by either moving your parties through the different territories or by using portals to instantly go from from city to city. Resorting to traditional travelling means or setting up camp can trigger random encounters which can be something as a fight, drinking challenges or some mysterious stranger proposing you something. This part of the game handles like your typical Dungeons and Dragons run by resorting to dice and percentage chances.
As far as combat goes, it works pretty much like in most turn-based party games with the objective being to eliminate all hostile forces while trying to keep the losses to a minimum. In each round your party members will have a turn in which they can act and use their action points (AP) to attack, use an item or skill - unused AP carries over to the next turn and each turn your characters will gain more AP. The combat is varied thanks to different types of damage (e.g. ice, fire and physical), different buffs and debuffs as well as thanks to the huge variety of classes ranging from warrior, spellsword, witch doctor, cleric, monk, thief, archer, etc. Each character has 4 base stats that will determine their role, combat which determines their physical damage; agility which determines their chance to land a critical hit, dodge an attack and how early they act in a turn; arcana which determines the effectiveness of your spells; and charisma which determines how much AP does a character have and how much they regenerate at the end of each round. While fighting your characters can also get wounded and because of that they’ll have their overall HP reduced. Also, like the way it works in Darkest Dungeon, once one of your characters loses it’s HP, it will enter a “near death state” in which the next hit will kill him permanently (still, you’ll be able to recover their gear).
Considering it’s still in Early Access, I’d say it’s already a pretty good and fun game, but that does not mean there isn’t room for improvement. For instance, I’d like to see actual animations of the various characters attacking their enemies, instead of just swinging their weapon in front of them. Also, as I took various different quests I came to notice a lot of repeated quest dialogues and I guess it makes sense, since they come from recycled random encounters and quests but I’m hoping that more work is put into adding more variety and more different and interesting lines.
So far I’ve only noticed a rather annoying issue and it appears to happen randomly. Sometimes when loading a saved game, or starting a new game, the game will just stop responding on the loading screen and I have to close it by force. This however doesn’t mean that it won’t happen again, for I’ve had this happen like various times in a row. It is a minor nuisance and the developer is already checking the issue but I figured it should be pointed out nonetheless.
Epic Manager can be described as a tycoon RPG game influenced by board games in which you manage your own agency of adventurers as you compete for the number one spot in the League in order to become the Epic Manager of the Realm of Astraeus.
Currently the major systems are all in place, now it’s only a matter of time of balancing, refining and adding more content. As of right now the game is already fun and already has that “1 more turn” feel to it, it features lovely visuals, a solid combat system akin to any other turn-based party combat game out there and an intricate system of relations between warring factions.

AirMech is a wonderful blend of a futuristic cybernetic real time strategy and an overhead dual stick shooter. For me I like dual stick shooters and real time strategies, so this game felt like a joy to play. Then you throw in, single player, cooperative play and player vs player, there's a lot here for everyone to enjoy. It controls like a dual stick shooter, left stick to move, right stick to shoot. There are mouse controls for those without a 360 controller. Since you are an air mech, you can transform from a jet or helicopter by pressing the left trigger to a giant towering robot. On the ground you're much slower, but you can fight the ground troops with ease. Then if you need to get across the map or fight enemy aircraft, simply transform and fly there. You can buy upgrades during a match, but you'll need to pick them up from one of your bases. Different mechs have different weapons and abilities like a sword or bombs, but without powering up abilities they feel pretty useless compared to guns.
The object of each game is to take the opposing player's (or bot's) home base. Its just that simple. Like a MOBA (multiplayer online battle arena). Your home base generates computer controlled fodder troops. These troops will automatically seek out other bases and take them over. So if there is an abandon base on a map, they're sure to find it, but if there's a tank guarding the base, they're sure to die trying to take it.
Each base requires four troops to capture it. These four troops then guard it from turrets on the top. If the enemy's fodder troops come, they'll just be mowed down. They just walk into their doom. Everything gives your mech experience to level up during the match.
When you get low on health or low on fuel, just fly back to one of your bases. Each base is somewhat different and has a different amount of healers and refueling devices. The more devices, the faster you'll be healed and refueled. If you run out of fuel, you'll fly slower. Using your shield and extra abilities will drain fuel, but I can't say that I used it that often. You can even pick up a unit, hover over a base and refill the unit's health. If you can't make it back to a base, change to your robot form to slowly refuel. Its a nice system. If you die, you're out of the game for X amount of seconds before you respawn at your home base. You can speed up the time by one second for 2,000 or so credits. Credits are your in match currency.
Since this is a real time strategy, you'll also be building and leading units to victory. You can pick them up, move them around, select them to command where they go. These units along with your upgrades require time to build them. Once they've been built, you pick them up at a local base, and put them on the ground, one at a time. It doesn't matter what base you pick up your units, just that its one of your bases. The units don't heal themselves like you can. Instead you'll have to rely on specific healing units that will recharge health of nearby allies. Each unit requires credits to manufacture them and their upkeep. So if you don't have enough credits to support a large army, you will need to drop a unit into a base to recycle it before you'll be allowed to make a new unit.
Before you begin, you can chose from your inventory of units to assign them into a nine unit menu. So if you've got two-hundred units to chose from, you can only use nine types per match. These units are soldiers, vehicles, mechs, turret guns, cash generators, mines and so on. Everything that you'd expect from a real time strategy. You can also select your pilot, air mech and equipment for your mech.
The different pilots each have different pros and cons. The default pilot Hawk has 10% credits, 5% credits earned, 5% unit build speed at the cost of 3% unit damage resistance and 7% air mech attack power. Each pilot has beautiful art work and there's something that fits your play style. You'll even find Youtubers as pilots done in the same beautiful artwork. I guess its a way to thank them for their publicity.
The game does a great job of introducing you to the game without punching you in the face that there are micro transactions in the way of diamonds. It lets you get completely through the fifteen challenge tutorial. Each challenge is a quick tutorial you'll blow through in no time. There are even star rankings, so you can return for better ratings, but its so simple there's no need to other than experience and gold called kudos.
Leveling up unlocks new parts, pilots, mechs and units that you still need to buy with gold (kudos). Its an easy system like every other gold (kudos) and experience system. To keep things interesting the achievements (quests) in game will also give you a bonus of gold for accomplishing them. Things like destroying ten tanks in a single match. You can even spend diamonds to get gold and experience boosters for those that don't like the grind, but really the grind is the game of chess that AirMech is. Every match feels enjoyable, not just that but every match feels fast paced, unlike other MOBAs that can last usually an hour. I'm no fan of MOBAs, I often get bored long before the match ends. They feel like true grinds, while AirMech is enjoyable because its not truly a MOBA.
There are different air mechs to buy, either with default gold or if you want something unique you can purchase premium versions.  It doesn't look like there is any difference in statistics between the gold bought air mechs and their premium diamond counter-parts. The only difference is visual. You will look cool when flying your neon gothic helix helicopter or your BlackOps helix helicopter instead of your standard gold bought helix helicopter. Cosmetics are good way of doing micro transactions. However, I can still diamond buy an premium osprey helicopter without being a level 8 to unlock the default osprey helicopter.
You can gold buy enhancements for your air mech and equip them in the hanger before you go into battle. Each piece of equipment that you put on takes up part points. To keep things balanced each mech only has so many part points. So do you want a fantastic shield or do you want several good upgrades instead? The choice is yours and you can have fun buying and tweaking your mech to your hearts desire.
There are several play options, solo where you play by yourself in either skirmishes of 1 vs 1, 1 vs 2, 1 vs 3, 2 vs 2, 2 vs 3, 3 vs 3 or a survival facing waves of enemies defending your home base. Survival turns into a tower defense game. The three survival maps are built in spirals allowing for multiple access points into the map. You'll need to cover them all if you're going to survive all the way through. You can also redo the challenges and tutorial in solo play.
In player vs player you and an ally compete in 2 vs 2 matches and this is where it becomes a grind. It is a drastic departure from the fun and joy of playing against even a difficult computer opponent. Humans know what wins a match and how to keep from losing. This results in some matches that took me around two hours, before someone gave up. I'm ready to throw in the towel at twenty minutes during each match. I'm not willing to go back and play again, due to how dull and monotonous it is. Its not a knock against this game, so much as its a knock against all MOBAs. I just can't invest the time in one sitting for something that begins to feel like work.
Since this is a competitive game, there's an area where you can just watch players play live. Its got an elegant filter that you can quickly find the type of match you're looking for. It lets you learn tactics without having to look up guides or watch videos, not to mention scout future opponents. Its a nice touch that keeps everything in game.I watched several matches to see things play out to understand what works and what doesn't.
I ended up having a lot of fun without spending anything.

This game is got its pros and cons. Also, this review may contain spoilers.
Let me start by saying that this game, Mafia II, is possibly one of the biggest staples to my childhood. I have played this game for a very long time. The reason I have played it nearly 800 hours is because I was one of those kids that I was not allowed to play Grand Theft Auto. I know, its corny to say, but I was one of those kids. But I do now have nearly every single GTA game. Even V.
Lore:
The lore of Mafia II is really good, to be honest. I like the backrounds of each protaginist and antagonist. I think they are some of the best developed characters in a video game inspired by GTA. The lore follows a man by the name of Vito Scalleta, whom is a immagrant from Sicily. He moved to a city named Empire Bay, where he met his childhood friend, Joe, a local bully who likes to rob stores and the such.
At the age of 18, Vito and Joe one night decided to rob a jewely store, and they got caught by a nearby patrolling officer. Whom caught the two. After Joe escapping with all of the jewarly, Vito was caught and sent to jail.
Vito was then shipped to Sicily, where he fought the fasists and nazis, where he was wounded in combat.
As the story goes on, Vito and Joe join the mafia, right after being illegaly discharged and sentenced to jail, after stealing gas and ration stamps.
That is a brief of the beggining that is the awsome lore of Mafia II.
Pros:
Good Lore
Good Char
Decent Graphics
Good Levels
A option of using clothes.
Cons (Prepare):
Buses and Taxis that you cant use (unless you count the beggining, which you pay .92 cents to go to your moms house.)
The Clothing stores, besides the one in uptown, are simply the same store over and over, besides certain times there are diffrent shades of colors of shirts.
Boring weapons.
90 percent driving.
"Step on it, Vito!"
Strip Club you cant use (Sorry, just had to mention it.)
No jobs or side missons.
Pretty stupid DLC.
Gets mundane after a few hours of gameplay.
No CO-OP or Multiplayer mode.
Most buildings are fake (Aka, you cant go in them, and the ones you can go in, are many miles radius apart)
Unrelistic cops and gang members
Steals lots of things from the movie "The Godfather" (I swear to god, just watch the godfather and you will see.)
Overall:
If you really want to buy this game, like, for real, go on amazon and purchase it for 8 dollars. Its a WAY better deal. Just, play any GTA (Yes, even london.) and you will see its way better.
Why is this review positive?:
The game has brought me alot of fun. Its gotten me through alot, especially when I was not allowed to play gta. Childhood staple, as I said. But if you really want to play a mafia game, get II, because its way better than III...eugh....

The game is very polished and has all the signs of being an enjoyable game.  However, as of .25 it is horribly overtuned by which I mean way too difficult.  And stressful.  Even with the most aggressive save-scumming (saving games, reloading upon non-ideal results), the second league is unwinnable.  I have every confidence that the game will be fun once they make it easier.
There is one critical issue in the concept of the game.  The RPG elements cause you to get attached to your adventurers.  But the Tycoon part of the game punishes that attachment since your developed characters will get prohibitively expensive.  Dealing with this dynamic might be the core conflict of the game and the reason why it is challenging.  However, it is difficult to appreciate that mechanic in its current state.

I have a video covering this game if you'd prefer to check that out instead. It's long but I try to cover as many aspects of the game as possible.
I very much enjoyed my time so far with Epic Manager. The combination of turn-based RPG, complete with leveling and gearing up components, with the management aspect has been a lot of fun so far. Given the variation in the NPCs you can hire and the wide variety of classes/skills, I feel that replayability is fairly high.
PROS:
+ The turn-based combat is enjoyable. While I'm sure there are a few mega-builds, there seems to be viable flexibility with classes, skills, and strategies.
+ Random encounters spice things up and gives it a pen-and-paper feel
+ Lots of upgrades for your Agency to pick from
+ Multiclassing opens up lots of options for upgrading heroes
+ Lots of classes to check out
+ Gear, potions, consumables, Adventurer contracts and agency level-ups gives gold a lot of uses.
CONS:
- Random encounters are often more difficult than quest battles, making quests seem less significant than maybe they should be.
- Party members can get really good or really bad traits during random encounters based purely on RNG.

Mafia 2 really suprised me. I've been thinking about playing this game for a while now and i regret waiting so long.
Mafia 2 puts you in the life of Vito Scaletta, living in the city of Empire Bay. All of the different missions and cutscenes are done so well. It feels like you really are living his life. It feels realistic, with great sound design, good graphics at times and the cutscenes are great. The story is interesting and really well done. Often when a game is done i feel like it's been a nice story and that's it. Chapter closed. But in Mafia 2, i felt like there was so much more to expierence, I didn't want the story to end. Because it really is a story, not just a bunch of missions with a few cutscenes inbetween. Mafia 2 also makes you do unnecessary things, like long drives back to your house just to go sleep, putting on your clothes every morning etc. But at the same times these are also the things that make it feel like you really are living the life of Vito Scaletta.
Let's talk about the amosphere and the world of Mafia 2. The city breathes atmosphere and looks amazing. You do have the ability to free roam but there's just not much to do in the city of Empire Bay, except for some small activities and some collectables like finding wanted posters and collecting all of the different playboys. However the city does feel alive, especially for an older game. The cars look good and drive okay and the music throughout the game and on the radio stations is amazing. The game runs smooth and all of the characters are really wel done.
I highly, highly recommend Mafia 2 to every singleplayer lover. The game has a great atmosphere, enough action while staying realistic at the same time, and everything just feels right. Definitely one of the better singleplayer games out there.

Before I say anything else, let me clear the air - I'm a red-blooded two-fisted American straight white male who found Duke Nukem's cigar-chomping sexist mass-killing schtick hilarious. BUT... what do you say about a game you progress through by murdering mobs of faceless mooks? That game mechanic goes beyond "it's been done" to the point of "why are we still doing this?"
Among the Sleep is different. Its protagonist is non-gendered skillfully enough that I could easily assume it was a he... but a female player could just as easily assume it was a she, and neither of us would find anything "weird" about that.  And I didn't beat up, much less kill, a single other character in the entire game... even though it was a horror game, and a legitimately scary one.  And even though in the reveal at the end of the game I was presented with more than sufficient reason to harbor ill-will toward the antagonist... the natural progression of the game didn't force me to, but allowed me to /discover/ a touching, compassionate gesture instead.  That, again, felt perfectly natural when it happened.
Make no mistake, this is a horror game, it is a creepy one, and it has some truly scary moments in it. It is captivating, it is not a light casual romp. And yet... it breaks completely free of the "kill mooks to progress" mold without feeling in any way forced. Do yourself a favor: set three to four hours aside and Play. This. Game.

While I recommend this game, I do have some setbacks the devs might want to consider.
1. The system of voting for a mayor needs some fine tuning. The founder of a city can be demoted as mayor if enough people vote for somebody else. In some cases, a city will have no mayor because of a tie in votes. This is flawed -- I believe the founder should be the mayor in the event of a tie, assuming the founder is still one of the candidates for mayor.
2. The TOS for this game says no multiple accounts. This is another flaw in my opinion. I believe this rule should be amended so that you may have multiple accounts, so long as you are not using them to manipulate the market or using them to advance/cheating. E.G. RuneScape explicitly allows multiple accounts in their TOS but indicates they must only be used in a legitimate fashion, and not for gold farming. Also, a lot of new players are unaware of this unless they've read the TOS, so maybe some kind of alert in the tutorial could help dissuade people from doing this, although I do believe an adjustment to this rule is really the better option.. just based on how other games do things.
3. The achievements are straight up whack. You can get 1k gold as a reward for an achievement at a stage in the game where 20 million gold means nothing to you. It's like.. "Thanks. Uh. Why did you make this an achievement?" The rewards should be better balanced, which brings me to my next point.
4. The wheel, more often than not, awards a dinky amount of gold. This is another case of adjusting reward ratios based on the player's progress in the game.
5. You can only buy/sell chest keys on the trading house if you've unlocked X amount of those chests. There is no tracking system in place to tell you how many you have unlocked nor is there a tracker to tell you how many more you must unlock before you can trade them to other players.

6. The game does not tell you that you can click on the right to collect resources. Most new players go through the mundane task of clicking on each bin individually, when clicking the icons on the right of the screen only takes about a second.
7. I've tried to incorporate myself into the community, but the higher level players seem to be mostly elitist and believe their opinions are fact, and because you're a new player you cannot possibly understand anything. I will no longer attempt to incorporate myself into the community, as I get enough toxicity and elitist attitudes on League of Legends.
With these setbacks (and probably a lot more), I would still highly recommend this game.
There are weekly city raids from Thursday night to Sunday (in my timezone which is Pacific time) and you can unlock a decent amount of rewards by doing the raids religiously. They also, at least since I have been playing, do events every single weekend and it's honestly the highlight of my week. (Yeah, I'm a nerd, but to be fair I'm writing this review and your'e reading it so you're a nerd too :P)

It might not sound too bad but if you do the math as I have it will take you forever. Here it is:
There are 25 non-package heroes in the game each with 7 inventory slots.
If it takes you ONE WEEK (which means you're playing the game pretty hardcore) to craft a lvl40+ Mythical it will take you 7 weeks for one hero.
Multiply that by 25 heroes and you have 175 weeks. That's 3 and a half years if everthing goes perfect and you're ONLY crafting these items. No money maker items, no ocarinas, no other crafts, nothing inbetween.
I had fun and I tried to stick around hoping CloudCade would listen to the community but there's this massive smokescreen on the forums where only one CC employee shares info and makes promises that never gets fulfilled.
Don't lose yourself in this, you'll regret it.

This game makes you act as the shop owner, who commands that one specific item be crafted per craft slot purchased. You then have to wait for it to be crafted, then you can sell it to a customer or suggest the customer purchase a different item that their character class could also use. You will also have to go to the Inn to initially hire each hero once, then slave them away on missions for more resources. Along the way their equipment will break and you will have to replace it.
There is a lot of game play in this game. But medium level stuff is going to kill your want and ability to play this game for longer than ten minutes once you get to level 14 or more. I have started setting my 5 slots to crafting stage 5 equipment for 20 minutes... then closing the game and coming back when I feel like it. Although your crafting workers will gain skill and these items crafting time will lower as you demand they craft more items in that area of expertise.
How to spend your real life money? Every step of the way the game asks you to purchase gems to spend on in-game perks.
For instance:
*Your equipment breaks: want to fix it with x2 gems?
Solution: Instead of fixing any equipment at all, just discard it and craft a new item.
*You want to upgrade the size of your shop one stage: Want to spend earned gold or 250 gems?
*You want to purchase the right to hire a new worker: Want to spend earned gold or 1,000 gems?
*Run out of wood/iron/leather/leafs/resources: Want to refill them instantly with gems?
Solution: Upgrade city buildings to produce more specific resources. Purchase more resource bins with gold. Upgrade Resource bins.
*You earned a free spin on the wheel of prizes! After spinning: Want to spin again for 15 gems? No...
I even won a single free spin on the wheel... smh. Winning a free spin should have been 2+ free spins, not "You just wasted time spinning the wheel for no reason, want to waste more time spinning again?"
Etc.
They give you a tiny amount of gems through gameplay (I earned 130 gems by level 14, more than 20 hours active game time) that barely add up to enough to purchase some of the cheapest furniture (ranging from 50 gems to 1500 gems) which absolutely give you bonuses to gameplay, however minor they may initially seem. Furniture can be upgraded with gold. Which means the hearts each gem furniture gives you will be upgraded also. Also, on mobile, you can watch ads for a whopping 2 gems each 30+ second ad.
If they took away all the ways to blow massive amounts of gems, and made them just boost furniture or character design I would be happy. Just shoving it in your face left and right is really sickening to me.

I've seen several other reviewers compare this game to Binding of Isaac and kidney punch it with these comparisons as much as humanly possible. I'll be the first person to admit, I love Binding of Isaac. It is a great game, between vanilla and Rebirth I've got over seven-hundred hours of Binding of Isaac and I will also be the first person to tell you that I think it unfair to compare the two.
Yes, this is a rogue dungeon crawling game about suffering, where you time your projectiles other creatures who also exist in a perpetual state of suffering, but it offers some subtleties that compliment the gaming experience in a completely different way. Between each level your are offered your choice of a few new randomly generated levels to choose from, each with its own unique attributes that are usually focused around making you feel sore in the bathing suit area.
The art and music is charming with gothic overtones and playful undertones. My feelings toward the game are quite different though there are some distinct similarities between it and Binding of Isaac. If you want another Binding of Isaac game though, pick up Rebirth, it's amazing, but there is no need for another developer to create a clone of a game that exists. This product stands alone in its own light (or darkness rather).
Gameplay wise this game reminds me of Gradius more than anything. It's more about dodging than getting more powerful to kill bigger uglier baddies. In Gradius a player found themselves weaving in tight spaces to avoid getting hit and dying. This game is a ton of that, squeeze in the little space that isn't on fire, covered in caltrops, or saturated in electricity, then shooting your pew pews hoping they'll kill the guy who is trying to derp you in the bathing suit area.
It may not be a game for everyone, but I wish it was.

HunieCam Studio is designed as a time and resource management sim where you assign jobs to girls to rake in the money, allowing you to recruit more girls, purchase bonuses that can further increase cash flow and boost fan numbers for even more. The base end goal is to amass as many fans as possible in an ingame 21 days. Mechanically there's a good number of clever mechanics, like the aforementioned relationship between fans and money (specifically that fans pay up depending on what kink you deliver) or the ability to equip accessories to the girls that can do things like boost speed of tasks or give them new kinks to deliver to fans.
However, I found that I just wasn't all that motivated to keep playing at it. Once the game has gone through its various options (which takes little time at all) the game starts settling into repetition. There's a certain degree of entertainment in trying to work out the optimal way to attract fans, but the motions themselves aren't particularly interesting and requiring players to actively click or hold click to collect feels like unnecessary slowing down.
The main goal is meant to be attracting as many fans as possible within 21 days, with wardrobe coins rewarded that unlock new hairstyles and outfits (that you only see when viewing a girl's status screen). Past that there's an endless mode if you want, but I struggle to understand the reason you would want to. Or restart and repeat to earn more coins. It just kinds feels like more effort than what I get out of it. It's not a terrible game by any means, but not one I'd say offers more than many of the other titles on Steam.

There is also no gallery where you can view the CG's after you get them, which I feel is a big feature of VN's and it's not good that it isn't there. Personally I was expecting something a bit more in depth.
