Pros:
-The Wolf in the campaign story does not underestimate you as much as he did in the first stronghold. This makes for a greater danger being played in the pieces of story before the missions, between the missions and afterwards. I am not going to spoil the ending but I wonder how much of the Wolfs army he has left and if, story wise, Hunting down the Wolf can come in at a later stronghold game.
-The Jackal is a worthy henchman and one I want to see in more strongholds from now on.
-The many types animals a trebuchet can launch is second only to stronghold crusader 2 and it I like their plague clouds more in 3. The Military campaigns mission 11 is fitting to try with this. Reload speed and all. Not that the timer allows you to be slow in this regard.
-The kind lord entertainment and cruel lord punishment system is twice the size of unit hitpoints, twice the size for happiness, twice the size for productivity and twice as many degrees to your kindness and cruelty, I have two screenshots that may show it better. The Stronghold wiki doesn't have the information at the time of posting this review.
-Housing space for happiness makes your economy more customizable, even around the lower populations.
-The ranger is a cool unit.
Semi- Pros:
-The night is as dark and terrifying as it is supposed to be. The burning hay bales are a good enough answer too. I wonder how well it would work in a stronghold skirmish battle. The problem here is that Stronghold 3 has no skirmish mode. Dat potential though.
-The feasting honor you can gain is incredible. It may go overboard in the amount.
-The system you place buildings with does not find it disturbing if your peasants or military units including your lord is there. Not so many annoying "Can't place that there milord" timings, if any. The downside is that this placement system being 3D can lead to a lot of imperfect placements and military buildings are plagued by this most of all. Especially the towers. Making this stronghold simultaniously the one with the most cautious and least cautious placement.
Semi- Cons:
-I don't have much of a problem with how the water looks but I don't like it either. I have screenshots on this too, just not of a level with an animal of the sea in it. Players that want to see those should try free build.
Cons:
-Bugs include military units (no peasants so far) to get stuck in spiky wooden barricades, In or on the Barracks and once for my lord on a wooden bridge towards an estate I was capturing early.
-Once played multiplayer an though the way your lords look can be awesome, I also had a bug as in Iron mines and their tethers not doing anything for the whole game. I'm not saying it would happen every time but that was my first and only multiplayer time in this game.

(This review is based on the content in the original Kingdom)
Day 21 dawns and I have built myself a nice little settlement, with a few farms and some trebuchets. Plenty of archers, lots of workmen. All seems well.
I become cocky and decide to expand even further. I call for the building of barricades far from the centre of my settlement. My loyal workmen run to obey, with my battle-seasoned archers in tow.
The night is too much. My subjects are now stretched too thin to defend against the onslaught of creeps. In the morning, I examine the remains of my little kingdom. Barricades are down; my trebuchets are in ruins. My loyal workmen and archers wander, stunned, palms outstretched for whatever coins I might throw to them. They have forgotten who they are. Their tools are in pieces.
Desperate and with only a handful of coins, I provide a few with hammers to repair what they can. They perform admirably, but with my farmers gone, I do not have the coin to support them and not all of the projects are completed.
The red moon rises. My remaining archers fight through the crimson night, taking down hordes of creeps, but the lack of trebuchets is sharply felt and a group of creeps breaks through my final feeble barriers.
I flee.
Somehow, the sun rises. Day 23 has dawned. We have made it through the night. I turn back with the intent to pay my respects to the fallen and try to rebuild one last time.
A horde of creeps descends upon me. The sunlight has not driven them away, no! Fuelled by their midnight victory, they charge forth.
My crown flies from my head.
I recover it as I flee, but within a few steps my horse is exhausted. There is no escaping them now.
The creeps advance as my crown is once again knocked from my head. This time, I know it is for good.
10/10 would die watching my kingdom fall into ruin again.

Our Darker Purpose has had the unfortunate luck of existing in a world that has already experienced The Binding of Isaac and will be forcibly labeled as a pretender and compared to that game until the end of time. Let it be known that looks are quite deceiving, and Our Darker Purpose's resemblance to Edmund McMillan's indie blockbuster begins and ends with the top-down, twin-stick shooter appearance that both share.
Where The Binding of Isaac is a fast-paced, almost bullet-hell game, Our Darker Purpose is much less about quick reflexes and more about patience and planning. You will never achieve Isaac levels of speed and destructiveness in this game, because that isn't the point or the core of its challenge. This game is about endurance and taking in the world around you. There are times I've felt more engaged by Our Darker Purpose's gameplay than Isaac's simply because it is a more demanding game. If Isaac is about reflexes and becoming mighty, then Our Darker Purpose is about staying two steps ahead of the game, because once you perform any action, you are committed to it.
The game features a wonderful art direction and soundtrack that blends together into a beautifully gothic piece of design that I fell in love with from the first trailer I watched. There is a detailed lore and story woven throughout this game that is surprisingly esoteric and adds a flavor of mystery to this pleasantly Dark little journey. Similar to the original Dark Souls, the different elements of this game support each other in such a way that were any one of them removed or altered, the entire game would lose its unique atmosphere.
Long story short: Don't go into this game expecting anything similar to The Binding of Isaac. It isn't a copycat just because it bears some surface level similarities. If you allow yourself to approach this game on its own terms, you will find a unique game whose world is enchanting and challenging in its own right.

One sentence review:  All the difficulty, metagame, and child abuse of Binding of Isaac but with more maturity and polish.
Our Darker Purpose is an action roguelike very similar to Binding of Isaac - your shots can be angled with movement, there's a significant metagame, it's Nintendo Hard and each playthrough makes you stronger both in terms of your experience and unlocked potential.
If some of the more immature elements of the Binding of Isaac turned you off though, then this may be more suited to you.  The artwork is elegent, the music just as good, and while the controls could be better failure in Our Darker Purpose feels very much one's own fault over simply being dealt a poor hand which is more a factor in Binding of Isaac.  I'm not sure of the fun, game-breaking elements of BoI are present in Our Darker Purpose -- I've only beaten one chapter -- but this is a game designed to be played through repeatedly.
If you like hard games, if you like a different experience each time, if you enjoyed Risk of Rain, Binding of Isaac and other games where you've just one shot to complete it but don't want to be screwed over with simple bad luck then this could be the game for you.  If you enjoy Tim Burton, "A Series of Unfortunate Events", and top-down bullet-hells then this is also the game for you.

First off, BLR for at least the past two years has not been pay-to-win. I don't know why recent reviews are saying this. The only thing real money gets in you in game is cosmetics and faster access to gear. You can obtain anything non-cosmetic by playing and never paying a cent. I have never spent money on this game and my account has everything I need. Overall this game has one of the most forgiving F2P models of any game I've played. If you want an example of a P2W FPS look at Warface.
I have played this game for a long time and have played FPS going back to Doom 2. The skill ceiling and floor in this game is very low compared to FPS that attract world class competition (Quake, CSGO, Overwatch, TF2). In the absence of any kind of ranked matchmaking system anyone who is fairly good at FPS will look like a god among children in most lobbies. The bads get stomped, naturally they get upset and start throwing hackusations. Which would be funny if the community couldn't get people banned on bad evidence, but they have. If you are actually good at FPS games it is worth looking at for it's novel mechanics (temporary wallhacks), fast pace (compared to other non-arena FPS) and generous F2P model. But do not expect to be treated fairly by the community if you do well.
As for the game mechanics themselves, the balance of the standard game is kind of lulzy because of gear and depot items (items you buy for points earned during a match). The new mech can run as fast or faster than a player, still has tons of armor and kills instantly. You can buy a railgun that 1 shots and has perfect hip accuracy. Of course there's a katana too. Pretty standard ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t for games nowadays I guess. Fortunately the primary weapons are all fairly balanced in that they are all more or less laser accurate with very little recoil. If you are a decent FPS player you should do fine with all the starting gear. Inf fact, you should be able to dominate most lobbies with the standard AR.
The time between updates is several months now and Hardsuit Labs doesn't plan to make many radical changes to the game or completely new content (aside from the occasional seasonal items that no one wants). The game is pretty old and reaching the end of it's life on PC. It's a pretty novel FPS that is worth playing but don't expect to be deeply involved.

Look, for a browser like game, I've never seen a game like this, at least in term of
business managament and comerce.
This game allows you to open your own store, hire your own workers and make
items and equipments to sell to the adventurers that shows up, alongside that,
you unlock new recipes of weapons of either the same type, or different type,
or even reducing the crafting material count of the item, aswell as increase the
chances of crafting a higher grade item.
The better the item, the higher the price, but you also have social skills to use in
the trade, at the cost of some hearts, you can offer a discount to gain hearts,
at the cost of a less pricy item, overcharge the the item to gain more lucre
at the cost of hearts, or even give a chat to the buyer to have the chance of gaining
or losing hearts.
There is also a second fact, if the equipment you sell to the adventurer is better than
the one the adventurer is wearing, the adventurer will equip it, but nothing stops you
from crafting the item yourself and giving to the adventurers, so they have some gear.
Later in the game, you may even end up receiving adventurers at your shop offering you
goods they found in some undisclosed location, you can bargain for lower prices before
buying, or refusing to buy the item.
The game also features a Mission system, which in the inn,  you can send your costumers to raid a
(timed) dungeon, which after the timer runs out, you can check the result of the dungeon raid,
I just don't recommend you to send your costumers to their private quests, I did those 3 times and
those quests ended up failing, making the costumers unable to do missions for around 4 hours,
which is a complete .
Beside the most impressive fact in this game is how the Town system works, if you create or join
a town, you and the other citizens can invest on the structures to unlock new characters, new
workers, or even to increase the number of resource gathering per hour.
The only con about the town system, is that if a citizen leaves the town, all the gold it have invested
on the town structures will be gone, so you may end up even losing a character that were unlocked
in the town due to that.
And to finish the good part of the game, sometimes a npc surges at your shop, requesting a large number
of items, when you complete that npc requests, you gain a good reward. I even had to use the market in
the game to buy some of the necessary items from other players, and the good part is that they did
a good price for me, so I were able to complete the npc requests.
Yes, this game have a market system, you can sell the things you do for a nice price, and then later check out
for lucre, or you can look on the market for a item you are looking for and then buy it for the best price as possible.
Now, the annoying part of the game, is that having the npcs entering and leaving your town several times can end
up being boring, since it's a chore to craft and sell the items to the npc, but you can try to offer them some more expensive items disponible in the shop instead, if you have the hearts for that, and try to overprice for a nice lucre.
There is a limit for almost everything in the game, like furnitures placed, workers hired, how many items you can craft
at the same time, and even workers you can have.
You can buy the expansion for the coins you make selling items for npcs and players, or by using gems that are the game cash item, but if you don't meet the level requirement for the upgrade, the price will be insane (like, you make around 5k coins with some sales, the price of the upgrade is 300k because you have not the level for it), and sometimes you will feel like needing the upgrade, but will be unable to buy it because of the insane price, that unless you spend for it.
The arena is the worst part of the game, you first join the arena to be shamefully beaten, you may end up finding a enemy player with characters of ten times more might than your characters, which is very absurd and primitive,
the game should try to find challenge based on around the player might, so the battle have some chance of winning,
and the tutorial arena fight you can't even refuse, so you are forced to lose miserably.
Almost customization items in the game are only by gems, while a few coin customization and upgrades are unlocked by levels, generally, only 1 furniture or customization is unlocked per level.
So, there is my review, the game is not really that bad, but at the first day, you may end up addicted so...

This is a criminally overlooked and underrated gem.  The game is essentially a modern update of the Sega Genesis game Herzog Zwei.  But if you've played any of the following games, then you'll be familiar with the kind of gameplay in store: Future Cop LAPD (PS1), Freedom Fighters (PS2),  Glory Days (Nintendo DS), and Toy Soldiers (XBLA).
You take direct control of one "hero" unit whilst requisitioning NPC units at will.  The units adhere to basic commands like "attack" and "stop" but cannot be individually micromanaged as in a traditional RTS.
All the while, "creep" minions pour from your and the enemy base.  Your minions (infantry) take over outposts after taking up garrison within them.
AirMech is an immense amount of fun.  Highly recommended if you enjoy tactical multiplayer action.

This is a well balanced and thought provoking tactical game. I'm not quite as fond of it as I am of the flagship Arcen games AI Wars or The Last Federation, but it has many of the same elements - high replayability, a lot of soul and charm, simple but pleasant graphics, and a bit of a steep learning curve. It's more accessible than AIW or TLF but there will still be times when you might feel the chill grasp of analysis paralysis.
For the price I would absolutely recommend this to anyone with even a passing interest in tactical RPGs and rogue-lites. You really do have to be interested in tactics though - this isn't an action game and it isn't a plot heavy RPG, nor is it a compulsive loot'em'up. In many ways it's a tactical puzzle game more than anything, though there's still plenty of robot blasting and mech flavour.

It is an interesting  game, especially when on sale, there's a lot of playtime for your money. But you have to enjoy tactics and tinkering with abilities. If you are looking for high polish and story-driven adventures, this is not for you.
That being said, the higher difficuilties are just frustrating and the achievements like winning with a single bot will only please a glutton for punishment. Totally ridiculous. In addition, the developers tried to be funny smarta$$es with their quips. Maybe focus on better balancing and a little more depth next time. This game could have been really good instead of "good enough when on sale".

I learned about Our Darker Purpose from reading a Game Informer review (They gave it an 8.75) and  based on the cool looking stillshots they had of the game, I felt the need to try it out. The first thing I noticed about the game was the Atmosphere: The dark, gothic visuals juxtaposed with the  brooding, orchestral soudtrack and the cynical humor parceled throughout the game made for a wonderfully melancholy environment that I just loved. The soundtrack particularly stood out to me as I am an audio engineer and I really appreciate how the music absolutely nails the mood of the game. The second thing I noticed about Our Darker Purpose was how ungodly difficult it is. The gameplay is deceptively simple but tense and addictive. you mainly enter a room, run around throwing fire at enemies while dodging ememy attacks untill you clear the room, level up, pick up items, etc. The difficulty lies in the various enemies and their increasingly powerful attacks, the general scarcity of health, and the fact that when you die, the game is over. I know several people who started playing this game but gave up after a few hours because the game was too hard for them. I, on the other hand, just found this game too good to quit. The rooms, items, and abilities when you level up are all randomized which means that the game is different every time you play. After playing and dying more than a few times, you'll start to understand that good reflexes, pattern recognition, a considerable amount of luck, and sheer tenacity are needed to beat this game. Overall, I think Our Darker Purpose is amazing and I would recommend it to any gamer who can appreciate the gothic atmosphere, dark humor, and is not willing to back down from a real challenge.

This game is getting a lot of crap for being too close to Binding of Isaac. To be fair, it does resemble Binding of Isaac a lot, a keyboard, top-down shooter with accumulation of items and perks. The mechanics differ enough to give this game an entirely differnet backbone, though, and let it be said that Avidly Wild games did not rip off Edmund Macmillan in any way, shape, or form.
That being said, though this gives some pretty good Binding of Isaac type gameplay, whether it helps the addicts who are weaning themselves off that famous game remains to be seen. Our Darker Purpose's art style is, in my humble opinion, far more beautiful and intriguing than Isaac's quirky and humorous one, and the music in this game is subtle yet stellar, offering a nice, edgy background to the game's ominous atmosphere.
The lore in Our Darker Purpose is uniquely amazing. Binding of Isaac came with tons of items and an allegory within a story, but it's story is hardly as good, interesting, or compelling as that found in Our Darker Purpose. Many words went into the lore of this game and for that, Avidly Wild, I applaud you. Cordy is a character one can sympathize for, have fun with, and imagine a backstory for in the dark orphanage she lives in. The fragments about bosses, items, and Edgewood are equally fun to read, and all offer a dark humor that is quite well done.
Our Darker Purpose adds more choice than Isaac as well. Isaac's customization had two options: yes or no. You took the item, or you didn't. In this game, the perks and items are a bit more varied and a bit more easier to alter. Arguably, Our Darker Purpose is more user-friendly and easier in that sense. The wiggle room allowed by its choice of perks upon level up and its item stores allow one to build up Cordy in a more specific and designed manner than Binding of Isaac.
Now that I've said everything it has over Binding of Isaac, let me warn you about what NOT to expect from this game. Many people fell in love with the sobbing little boy sitting on poop because of the game's learning curve and skill requirements. You had to be fast on your fingers, or else the unforgiving monsters of the basement would get you. In Our Darker Purpose, however, speed and reaction time is less important. Cordy, though she moves smoothly as of the most recent update, will never hit the speed of Isaac with speed-ups, Wooden Spoon, and the Belt. Though this might seem like it makes the game easier, the enemies in this game are far more advanced, difficult, and tankier than those in Binding of Isaac. This game prioritizes thought over reaction time, and you'll find yourself frustrated not because you didn't tap down fast enough, but because you didn't think to roll at the right time.
TL;DR: Our Darker Purpose has the same surface mechanics as Binding of Isaac, but a deeper story, fresh graphics, and an entirely new item customization system. While it will never replace the mad speed dashing and the crazy bullet and fly frenzies in Binding of Isaac, it offers a new dimension of thought and planning while in the midst of combat. It is definitely worth looking at and getting if the abovementioned bonuses are attractive.

Long before Binding of Isaac (BoI), there was a diverse cornucopia of rogue-likes. This is not one of them. Instead, it borrows whole-heartedly from the formula that made BoI so successful. The similarities make it impossible to review in its own universe.
First, the difficulty is increased relative to BoI. This isn't neccessarily a bad thing, but I would recommend you play that game first if you are unfamiliar with the top-down rogue-like.
The artistic direction is superb. It still certainly draws on themes from BoI, but still manages to differentiate itself through its story-telling which was by-and-large non-existent in BoI. The story is generally told in the form of text with accompanying images, through small chunks of "lore" found after accomplishments, or by overhearing the conversations of sacks of potatoes. The small details like chattering furniture paint a more complete picture of the Edgeworth School for Lost Children.
The quantity and variety of items is somewhat lackluster. Most items act solely to adjust the unseen variables of the system (e.g. +10% movement speed. +10% range.) The items which alter gameplay stand out, but are relatively rare and thus, the stat-altering items feel monotonous by comparison. Sure, it is easier to design several items around the "attack speed" variable, but grabbing those items is not as impactful as picking up one that changes the trajectory of projectiles.
However, ODP play the rogue-like balance well. As opposed to a more hardcore rogue, it has a system of persistent upgrades known as "classes" which grant the player new traits. The classes add depth by removing some of the randomness over multiple playthroughs while not detracting from the difficulty. Additionally, it incorporates a "leveling" system within each individual session that allows the player to augment the strength of the character to suit his styles.
Overall, if you like BoI, you will like Our Darker Purpose. You are getting the same dish cooked and served by a new chef.
If you haven't played BoI, you can still enjoy Our Darker Purpose, albeit with a slightly steeper difficulty curve.
In either case, if you are looking for a challenging game saturated in gallows humor, I would recommend Our Darker Purpose.

Aesthetically excellent but outrageously tedious otherwise. I appreciate the attempt to make a game like this with very light one-button mechanics but the ultimate execution is pretty terrible.
This is a game of waiting, and long, mindless trips back and forth for hours with little to no reward for the 'effort' put in, and so many of the design decisions that led to this situation feel pointless, or things that were added purely to pad the game out. This is a game of a few, very small decisions at the start of each level (which are almost always the same each time), followed by often an hour or more of little more than waiting for coin generation, and endless marching back and forth across the map to collect those coins and make tiny, unfullfilling upgrades to unexciting pieces of equipment.
It's a grand shame that this new version does so little to address these substantially unrewarding mechanics and instead focuses on adding considerable late game content - content that can only be accessed by force-feeding oneself through this game's awful grind.
And this is with quite a heavy reliance on uncontrollable AI. It's been improved markedly since the previous version, but this is still a game where your success can hinge terribly on whether your archers feel like hunting deer that day, or which fortifications they may decide to defend. And that's before we even find out whether they'll actually hit any targets today.
My play time for this title is quite inflated because a game where you make no decisions and often have nothing to do is good platform for catching up on audiobooks. But then there are so many other, better games that fill that 'undemanding and pleasant' niche without being so throughly unrewarding in the process.

SPOILER FREE REVIEW
For my reviews I tend to look at 4 main categories; the story, gameplay + design, performance and extras. For each category I will give a score then the overall score is simply the average of these. This helps to identify the good and bad parts of the game.
The overall score I give Wolfenstein: The New Blood is 8/10. But please look at all the scores.
If you do not wish to read the whole review then a summary is provided at the end.
1.THE STORY
The New blood is a prequel to The New Order.
(With that said I recommend reading my review for The New Order as I will be making a lot of comparisons with it.)
It is set in 1946 were Nazi Germany is winning WW2. The allies are desperate to try and take down the advanced technology factories which are fueling the German war machine. Hence you agent Blazkowicz is to be sent behind enemy lines and do this mainly by taking out the brains behind it all, General Deathshead. This is pretty much the whole aim of the game and apart from this there is not very much else. This was rather disappointing as The New Order had decent character backgrounds which added to the whole feel of the story. Furthermore, the use of newspapers, letters etc was once again heavily present giving an insight to the lore of this universe. What sets The New Blood apart from The New Order is the more supernatural element to the game in terms of specific enemies/bosses you will come across. I did not like this as I prefer a technological advanced Nazi Germany to a supernatural one. In other words keeping it more realistic.
In terms of the length of the game it was without a doubt very short, even suprisingly short. I thought with The New Order being somewhat short at around 20hrs they would make this longer but no, completing the main game and extras takes on average 9hrs. For a completionist it takes around 17hrs. This is very disappointing, this is somethig you expect from a minor DLC.
The story gets a rating of 6/10.
2. THE GAMEPLAY
Like The New Order this game is an action shooter. The New Blood improved on many of the drawbacks from the previous game, such as the options of sneak/guns blazing and the engagement. As mentioned on my review for The New Order the major anoyance of having an option of sneaking when it was boring and pointless is now improved upon. Now there are areas were sneak is the only option otherwise you die. This is much better, there is more suspence, more enjoyment and makes sense for an action game. Since guns blazing is more fun when the option presents itself, right? The engagement was much more compelling in this game. Like the areas of sneaking there were areas of full on mayhem with some horde like objectives. Very enjoyable.
The same weapons are present from the previous game with only a couple of new weapons. I would have liked there to be more but this time I felt satisfied to the end of the game with the weapons I did have. Though this is probably due to the very short story. :/
The design of the game was top notch, from the beginning you only see a typical 1940's style environment but later in the game you see the increasing use of technology. Also as the game became more supernatural you came across tombs and a stone type architecture for which wolfenstein is known for.
The gameplay gets a rating of 8.5/10
3. PERFORMANCE
This game unlike its predecessor performs well. After the optimising failure of The New Order they made certain it ran smoothly. I had no issues on my laptop or pc. When the settings are put to the max the environment looks very nice. Good lighting and shading effects are obvious and the physical features/rendering share similar results. What I do not understand is why the memory space required is so large for such a small game. 37gbs for a game which is only around 10 hrs long is mind boggling.
The audio is very good both in terms of the voice acting and the soundtrack/effects. I find the wolfenstein games are always performing well in this. The mix of enemy troops shooting commands amongst explosions and shooting is very engaging.
The performance gets a rating of 8.5/10
4. EXTRAS
Wolfenstein games are packed with secrets/extras. There are collectables to be found throughout the story and like I said for The New Order finding the secret rooms themselves are more enjoyable than the actual collectable. Once again in certain points you are able to play missions from the original wolfenstein game. I found these missions to be almost as a break from the fast paced action of the game. Sometimes forgetting what I was doing in the story. Other extras included bethesda brand logos such as nuka cola and skyrim helmets making their way into the game.
The extras get a rating of 9/10.
SUMMARY
Story; Somewhat lacking, poor character developement, good lore, interesting universe, strange supernatural elements, very very short story. 6/10
Gameplay + design; Very engaging, good sneak and action segments, Would have liked more weapons, satisfied to the end, great design from beginning to end. 8.5/10
Performance; Game worked smoothly, No apparent issues on both laptop and pc, huge memory required from such a small game, graphics are good at max settings. 8.5/10
Extras; Collectables throughout game, option to play original wolfenstein missions during certain points in the story, use of other bethesda games logos and items found hidden in story.9/10.
Overall Wolfenstein; The New Blood gets a rating of 8/10.

This game was really a surprise.  I buy a lot of bundles and I've been going through and playing some random games from them.  Most of them are pretty bad and just worth playing til the cards dropped.  So I loaded Boo Bunny Plague randomly without knowing anything about it at all.
Right away I noticed that the game is super creative, with great visuals, style, music, and songs!  I'm a big fan of parody music, like Weird Al, South Park movie, Family Guy songs, even Anime Music Videos.  So this game really clicked with me.
As I played through it, there were some frustrating things that hurt my enjoyment.  Honestly, a game with a good story and funny songs should be pretty easy, so almost every player can see the story and hear the songs.  Then "hard" and "impossible" mode can be as hard as you want to make it.  I'm probably not great at this kind of game, but I found some of the battles really hard.  This was greatly compounded by the fact that if you quit and reload, you go back to a much earlier checkpoint (I think there's only like 6 of these checkpoints in the game).  Luckily, if you die, the respawn points are much more frequent, so as long as you never actually quit you're ok.  But there's especially one section with 4 bosses in a row, and if you save and quit at any point, you have to replay all 4 bosses every time.  If you could quit and reload at the respawn points the game would be a lot more pleasant.
Despite all this I was able to beat the game.  I came a bit close to quiting on the final boss, and if I did I'm not sure I would recommend the game, but ultimately I had a fun time and I'm glad I beat it.  So it ends up being a recommend from me.  The devs are extremely creative and I hope they can come up with more interesting and funny material!

I wish there was a neutral rating. Because this game has a lot of things wrong with it, but not enough to say "never play this game!" For the price, it's about right. You're paying for about what you get.
The main character is obnoxious, the jokes try too hard and all the story is kind of very in-your-face and crammed into small amounts of time. They give you so much at once and yet?? Not enough. I never REALLY know what's going on. The controls are okay, the voice acting is pretty decent (the jokes are not, mind you) and the only real fault I can point out is that a lot of the game is obnoxious. The characters and songs are obnoxious. Mostly Bunny. Bunny feels like if Deadpool was written by a 12 year old who was going through his "lawl random" phase and his "Edgy OC" phase at the same time. The mechanics of the game, bare bones, work fine. Not fantastic, but fine. I have a hard time with the story and the characters because they're either obnoxious or I don't understand what's happening. If I can't enjoy the decent-at-best game controls and mechanics because of the kind of bad world that you opted to put around said mechanics, then it's hard to enjoy anything about the game, aside from in an ironic sense.
However, all in all, it's not completely awful. It's not a BAD game. It's decent. This is a case of "You get what you pay for." If this game were to cost more than like $5, then I would judge it a lot more harshly. It's decent. If it was possible, I would give it a neutral rating.

This is my least favorite total war game, I just could not really get into it like the other total war games.
It showed me that a ranged combat focused total war game is a bad total war game. Land battle is just boring imho, and you have to micromanage all the time to avoid friendly fire. There are tons of unit in this game, but pretty much all of them are men with muskets in different colors. Unit movement is glitchy (horses sometimes slide on the ground without moving their bodies lol), AI is glitchy (like in most total war games, but happens more often, like AI melee infantry just stand and let you get free shots at them).
I really dont like how they nerfed cavalry in this game, they will drop like flies if getting in the range of line infantry, they are even not good at chasing down routing enemy now because they would get stuck in a 10 seconds long dueling animation with a roundting militia like WTF. Now most battle pretty much plays like getting your line infantry forming up formation, and then just watch them shot at enemy until rout, or maybe charge enemy if you got number advantage / enemy better at range / have more cannons etc. This kind of battle certainly does not appeal to me who like the melee combat in the other total war games.
Anyway, I will sum up my opinion:
>Land battle is god awful, repetitive slow and boring
>The newly introduced Sea battle is good but require a lot of micro-management
>New campaign features like technology are welcomed addition.
>Major nerfed generals and cavalry. Generals do not give speech anymore, they are so generic. Melee Cavalry are so underwhelming, because their small number, they can be killed easily by pretty much everyone including artillery and infantry with bayonet and box formation. Dragoons/ ranged cavalry are pretty good though.
>AI is very predictable, but you can say the same for the other total war games too.
>Hands down the Worst soundtrack in total war games ever, seriously it is so bad almost make my ears bleed. especially the "Native American" soundtrack (and they even recycled the old M2TW Native American soundtrack in empire, so lazy), along with their jaw-dropping OP land armies makes the Native American my worst nightmare in empire total war. Even though by the same composer, the sound track is much improved in rome 2, although still miles away from the legendary Jeff Van Dyck's work.
After investing more than 100 hours in Empire, I still think I liked Rome 2 better than this game. As I recall Empire also had a really glitchy launch, and it is the start of the DLC policy in total war series, I really dont understand how a lot more people hate rome 2 than empire.
I would not recommend this game unless you really like the time period, there are much better total war games out there, and my current Top 1 is still Medieval 2 Total War

Cobi Treasure Deluxe is a 'Match 3' puzzle game developed by Cobra Mobile.
Plot
There is no plot in the game. Basically Sally the seahorse needs your help to solve puzzles, but its just an excuse to make you solve the puzzles.
Gameplay
The basiss of the game is to match the same coloured shapes in a row of three. There are three game modes:Classic, Ship Shape and Sally's Shape.
Classic is your standard puzzle game mode where have aim to score as many points as possible by completing as many matches as you can. Similar to 'Tetris' you start with some shapes on the screen and you have to clear them with the shapes dropping from above. If the stack is too high the game ends and your score is recorded.
Ship Shape is similar to classic except that you have a timer that resets once you reach a certain number of matches.
Sally's Shapes is basically a puzzle mode where you have to clear all the shapes on the screen within a short amount of time.
Graphics
Visuals are quite basic. It doesn't look great with lack of detail in textures and such, but it serves it's purpose
Audio
The music is decent, giving an aquatic vibe while your playing. Sound effects are left to be desired. There is no voice acting in the game.
Overall, there isn't much to go on here. It's a basic 'match 3 game' which doen't have anything unique to hook players and keep them going.

Kingdom: New Lands is genuinely one of my favourite games of 2016. It combines city building, exploration and management elements of other games but instead of repeating the same tired formula that has been used for these games before, they changed it up a bit, in that it is a side scrolling game that does not require a bird’s eye view or a free camera to make it a city builder. If you were here to get a quick opinion on the game, all that you need to know is that the game is certainly worth the price and is not only a fantastic game but a fantastic experience as that’s really what this game is, an experience.
Gameplay
Let’s begin with Gameplay. The gameplay revolves around you as the king collecting coins to build up your great kingdom. For the most part I found the gameplay to be relatively solid, the only real problems that I found with the system were that later on in the game you tend to run out of coins quite regularly, even with farms and traders. Other than that I enjoyed the gameplay (what little the game actually contained) quite a bit.
Visuals and Sound
Graphics and Music are next and both of them are splendid. The graphics in Kingdom: New Lands are visually impressive as they have taken a pixelated art style and theme, then they have really amped it up by giving little things like the water and fire movement. It makes the art style feel much more impressive then it would without these little animations. As for the music it suited the game very well, there were enough songs there to keep me interested and entertained. My favourite part about the music, is the fact that when the weather changes the song changes. It shows that the developers put that extra amount of effort in to make sure that their game was as good as it could be and I commend them for doing so.
Performance
ARGHH! Another review that makes the performance section Obscelete, obviously from the pictures, the game is not CPU or GPU intensive at all. I mean if you're running integrated graphics from your older sisters uni laptop, then you might see some issues. But if you have anything other than integratted graphics you should be fine.....yes even you running the extremely outdated Nvidia GT 710.....yes even you can expirience this game in 1080p YES 1080p! What a splendid day for you isnt it?
Negatives
Now it’s time to discuss my gripes with the game. Firstly, let me say that the world you’re in isn’t very big, it took me around 3-5 minutes to find the end of it. Now granted there are evil portals which normally cover up the end of the map but it would have been nice if the worlds were just a little bit bigger to really immerse me into exploring and adventuring.
The next problem that I have with the game involves your horse that you ride around on. That horse tends to run out of stamina fairly quickly which led me to believe that you would be given the option to upgrade said horse later on in the game, but so far I am yet to find anything that allows you to do so. This is a real pain as your horse is really slow and immobile, if they were to add in a stables earlier on in the game which you could use to upgrade your horse, this wouldn’t be a problem.
My final negative for today lies with the monsters in the game, each monster is the exact same as the last monster that you encountered, the only difference is that some will have masks on to protect them. I would have liked to see a larger enemy variety in this game as it is in dire need of it.

Overview
Overall Kingdom: New Lands is a phenomenal game and a true follow up to its predecessor! It has fun (yet limited) gameplay, beautiful sound tracks and stellar visuals, it is only really let down by a few issues like enemy variety and the size of the world that you travel in.
-Joshua Upham

There are definitely things to like in Our Darker Purpose. It has great atmosphere backed up by a great art style and music. Everything is functional, but the more I played, the more one thought kept coming back: "The Binding of Isaac did this better."
Our Darker Purpose plays very similarly to Binding of Isaac, but just about everything it does, Isaac does better. Isaac has more variety of powerups and enemies. Isaac has a deeper and more interesting resource management system. Our Darker Purpose is much more focussed on the moment-to-moment combat then big picture balancing of resources. There are no keys, and your "bombs" are used exclusively for fighting. Most upgrades offer only numerical stat increases. The actual gameplay, however, has different ideas. Hit detection is awkward, enemies and hazards are more annoying or frustrating than interesting, and for all the focus on numerical upgrades, you never really feel more powerful than when you start. Isaac had it's share of numerical upgrades, but on any given run, you were bound to find at least one item that fundamentally changed how you approached the rest of the game. Each run felt different and unique. Each run of Our Darker Purpose just feels the same, but with the numbers shuffled around a bit.
At the end of the day, if you spend all your time with a game thinking about a different, better game, then that's not a very good sign for the game you're playing. If you've completed everything in The Binding of Isaac and really need something similar to hold you over until the remake, you'll get some enjoyment out of Our Darker Purpose. To everyone else, I cannot recommend this game as long as The Binding of Isaac exists.

Our Darker Purpose is a top-down action roguelike with light RPG elements and a deliciously dark, gothic set of sensibilities. The game has bits of “The Binding of Isaac” and “Don’t Starve” in its family tree. The humor and art owe a bit to Tim Burton and a great deal to Edward Gory.
Movement and combat is in the classic twin-stick style. You comb a floor of randomly laid out rooms for useful items and the chamber of the boss guarding the way forward. Each time you enter a room you’re locked in until you’ve cleared all enemies or overcome some other hazard, so you can’t just rush through.
ODP is set in a towering, Victorian, half boarding school, half orphanage called Edgewood. The school is a nightmare Hogwarts, teaming with darkly comic fates for poorly behaved or unwary students and ruled by an unseen but amusingly malevolent administrator. The bits of lore and narrative slowly unlocked through play are gothic black-humor at their finest.
You play as Cordy, an adorably pale waif with a permanent expression of bemused worry. When the faculty and staff of Edgewood abruptly vanish Cordy barely survives the purge of the small, weak, awkward, and unpopular children that immediately follows. With nothing to lose and nowhere to go but up she sets out for the top floor of the building, searching for answers and a way out. Provided she can survive the savage gangs of fellow children that have formed in the absence of adult supervision and the stranger things scuttling in the shadows and crawling across the chalkboards of the darkened school.
Fortunately Cordy has inexplicably developed the ability to hurl small darts of flame to defend herself. While Cordy can only hurl flame in the four cardinal directions she can move and shoot independently. An extremely limited number of chalk-bombs and an evasive roll (crucial to avoiding damage) round out her modest set of starting abilities.
Early attempts to ascend Edgewood invariably end in failure and death, a fact the game itself is quick to tell you to expect. Indeed it’s not mechanically possible to clear ODP on your first playthrough. Overcoming a major boss for the first time advances the narrative and adds a new set of variables to the game, but also ends that particular run. Like all true roguelikes ODP is intended to be played many, many times before completion.
Edgewood is a stark, relentlessly hostile environment. Healing juice-boxes, money, and other useful items are in short supply and invariably guarded. Attrition as much as anything else usually ends a run. Learning the attack patterns of the various inhabitants and hazards is critical to long term progress. Finishing a floor without taking damage is an accomplishment to be lauded.
ODP is highly challenging and carless play will end a run in short order. Each attempt does help you slowly unlock new items to be found and build up a modest set of permanent bonuses. This helps create a sense of progression and that your efforts are being rewarded, even as you die time and time again.
While primarily an action game ODP does manage to offer meaningful character development choices and interesting items. Each level-up offers two randomly selected but sizable stat upgrades. Some options include penalties still worth considering, like a permanently slower move speed in exchange for a large chunk of cash.
Many of the items that can be scavenged from Edgewood’s chambers change Cordy in fundamental ways, like giving a massive boost to attack rate while making her formerly accurate shots spray out in a random arc. Some of the most powerful bits of gear break after you absorb a certain amount of damage (as if you needed another reason to dodge), while others require completing difficult challenges to unlock their power.
Of course there’s no guarantee you’ll be offered useful items or upgrades, and everything is lost when you die anyway. This is normal for Roguelikes, but it can still be frustrating when bad luck dooms an otherwise promising run. The game’s other chief sin (significantly harder to forgive) is that creature hit-boxes don’t always match up with their models. While the game is two dimensional the “camera” is implied to be at a slight angle, meaning shots often pass behind an enemy’s head.
Reasons to play: Deliciously dark, gothic humor and art. Challenging twin-stick style gameplay. Meaningful progression from run to run.
Reasons to pass: Very high difficulty level. Slightly miss-leading hit-boxes.

This game is quite a neat gem of a strategy game.  I picked this up due to me liking one of their other games, AI War- Fleet Command.... that one was cool as it was an asymmetrical warfare 4x-kind-of game... but it was a bit of a beast to figure out all the do's and don't and whatnot.  Bionic Dues is certainly easier to pick-up-and-go.... basically you are the resistance fighting the evil robot empire in a megatropolis-type place.  You pick 4 Mechs out of a decent selection of different types, each with different buffs, weapons, etc.  You then pick a pilot which gives you a set of various advantages.... then you fight your way through the city in grid/tile turn-based strategy combat goodness.  You pick what areas of the city to attack when and based on where you attack there are different results for winning.  Attacking a shield-manufacturing plant would likely yield better shields.... an engine-factory: engines.  Etc.  Or you can attack the enemy's mech-building capabilities or any other number of options.  There is even an option to attack special facilities that give MASSIVE upgrades to your mechs, essentially turning them into an entirely different, and better class.
Loot and equipment plays a major part of the game..... through spending earned cash or finding via mission rewards you have the ability to DRASTICALLY alter each of your mechs.  A non-combat type mech could potentially be given certain upgrades to make one of it's weapons shoot at such long range that they wouldn't receive enemy fire.... or a rocket launcher's blast radius could be expanded to where you could wipe out entire rooms.  There is LOTS of room for customization and it's really one of the super-neat parts of the game.  The different starting mechs are wildly different and each one can be VERY useful when used the right way.  This certainly qualifies as a "Thinking" game.... it's not testing your fast-twitch muscles or how fast you can click- you pick 4 tools and then continue modifying them as needed until you feel strong enough to bring on the final battle or you run out of time and are FORCED into the final battle.  The intro song is pretty neat, too.

I backed the Kickstarter years ago, and for a long time considered that to be a mistake.  The developers released the game way too early, in my opinion.  It was more of a tech demo for a long time.  Recent updates, however, have made it into an interesting actual game.
You have to mine multiple resources and build a castle.  There are multiple combat roles (knight, halberdier, archer, arbolist, alchemist/bomber, and wizardy healer thing), so there can actually be a bit of depth to unit placement and such.  There are also pylons that you need to use to heal your units, light the map at night, and capture additional "crystals" that are used to generate units, both friendly and not.  Like many other games, there are occasional enemies during the day, and lots at night.
There are multiple modes:
Creative - a peaceful building mode (you still have to mine resources and manage your Bricktrons, so it's not the same as the Minecraft mode)
Invasion - a wave-based horde-like mode
Conquest - spread across the map by capturing crystals.
There are still definitely places to improve.  Some of the pathfinding and AI for your Bricktrons can be a bit wonky or slow.  Multiple Bricktrons occasionally try to do the same thing, and after it's done, the other units just kind of stand there for a bit while they try to figure out what to do.  Sometimes the rules can be a bit unclear when it comes to what building blocks can be placed where (especially with the wooden platforms).  The developers seem to be quite active and communicate clearly, though, so I'm fairly optimistic.
I would recommend watching some recent gameplay to make sure you know what you're getting into, but it's definitely a game on the up-and-up.

I really want to be able to recommend this game. The idea behind it is phenomenal; it combines all of my favorite factors of RTS and creative construction games. Unfortunately, the major flaws of this game can be summed up in a simple statement:
It's still an early access game.
Aside from the less-important flaws (such as many scattered typos, incomplete tutorial, and complete lack of any semblance of a "story"/campaign), the major problem with this game that upsets me is that it is often just plain unplayable.
The game has huge load times, and is very resource-heavy. And I do not have a low-end computer; this game should not be a problem for it.
But beyond that, quite frequently, the game will completely freeze for a second or two. And this period of being frozen often leads to other issues, such as glitching comands given (placing blocks in the wrong place, telling units to go somewhere I wasn't trying to click, etc.). Thus, the entire gameplay consists of trying to get a couple actions in, waiting for the game to unfreeze, fixing the errors that occured during freeze, then repeat.
An entirely different point of interest is the abysmal AI. This isn't something I can really go into too much depth about, because words do not describe how horrible the AI is. Trying to get archers to attack units from walls without running down off the walls and in front of the castle to attack is a huge pain. Also, workers will extremely frequently get into little groups of 2-5 passing around resources (such as a stone block or something) and just standing in place until they are manually told to do something else. There are many other issues with the AI, but as I said, it's just too much to get into.
I would like to note that the most recent update that claimed to improve AI actually made certain aspects of it significantly worse.
I really hope the devs can figure these problems out, because I want to see this game become playable. But frankly, it was a pretty big insult to take it out of early access.
I will continue to play this game, as I love the idea so much, and I will modify this review as applicable.

A perfect prequel to the New Order. It mixes the innovation of The New Order with the tradition of Return of Castle Wolfenstein ( nightmare levels).

Fun, simple and well rounded shooter.  This isn't a masterpiece by any stretch of the imagination but it will give you a fix for wolfenstein for sure.  It's only a short romp through Draculas castle of abominations but each area and act feels unique and well designed.  The music is well composed but sometimes doesn't quite match or fit with what is happening on screen, it tries too hard to control the players emotions and fails in that aspect, a more eerie ambient soundtrack would have been more fitting I feel.
The stealth mechanics are nice and easy to get a hold of, hide behind objects and eliminate key targets to prevent support from arriving. The cartoonish, OTT nazi enemies provide a dangerous obstacle with releatively good but fair accuracy and  a damage level which implores players to explore for extra armour, ammo and goodies.
The difficulty of the game has a wobbly curve, I beat the game on Uber in 8.2 hours completely blind, the challenge started to ramp up before petering out when the 2nd half of the game kicked in, without spoiling; the enemies became significantly less threatening and much easier to eliminate.  The finalé offered pickings of a challenge with me requiring a few retries, but with little variation or tasks to complete while fighting, the boss becomes a simple trial and error affair, a short one at that.
Sometimes I feel by beating this game using the stealth mechanic I did cheat myself out of some excellent battle and shoot em up sequences, there are arena type zones in each act where enemies patrol, you can choose of course, to go all guns in, but beating it with stealth seemed like the challenging and perfectionists option.   Overall, this game is a snack, a delicious snack that I'd happily have another one of.  You won't have a problem enjoying it, and its flaws are so short lived while it pushes you into the next hole of doom, you'll have forgotten about them while you splatter the brains of the SS across fine runic pillars.  If you're a member of Antifa, this game may infact give you an erection.

Wolfenstein: The Old Blood is definitely not a bad game at all. However, it's also not a
game. The Old Blood is a prequel to "The New Order" which I enjoyed quite a bit more than this one. Whilst it's really nice to have this game so we can play through more of the lore in the Wolfenstein series I do think that the developers cut quite a few corners and some of the decisions they made bothered me; like with no ability to have more than 1 save and the A.I. feelnig very clumsy. Whilst playing I also found the 'perks' system quite annoying just like I did in 'The New Order'. Having to repetitively kill enemies and reload checkpoints just to unlock a few perks is somewhat boring and tedious. I think more thought could have gone into the perks system.
The Old Blood is also not at all devoid of bugs. There are still quite a lot of bugs in the game. Although I didn't come across any gamebreaking ones I did encounter some very annoying bugs. One in particular was that on the 2nd level when you are supposed to get the scope for the rifle, I reloaded my save after getting the scope as I missed a gold collectible. Reloading my last checkpoint caused the scope to disappear from both my rifle and in-game. So I had to restart the whole level again (the scope is right at the end so this was annoying playing on Über difficulty. Even after a full level reload the scope STILL was gone. So I played through the WHOLE game without the scope, thinking I'd hopefully get another chance to get one, but I didn't. This made certain levels like the Cable Car quite frustrating... Finally, the whole 'cover system' is just a pain. You can't enter cover manually, as it counts as
only under very specific circumstances and leaning whilst in cover is just terribly done.
I have really mixed feelings about recommending Wolfenstein: The Old Blood but I am still going to. Given the quality of the graphics and gunplay put together with the good voice acting (especially in German) and array of collectibles and classic RtCW easter eggs, I'd say it's worth €20 in its current state. However, if it was even €5 cheaper I would find that a perfect price point given that you won't get more than 15 hours out of the game even on the hardest setting and it has basically zero replay value after you have gotten all the collectibles and finished the map challenges. Maybe buy it at €19, but definitely get it whilst on any sale.

Soooo... It's review time again... Guess which thumb it's going to be... Well, not very difficult, you saw it before you even got in here, didn't you, you little exhibitionist.
But let's not dwell on that, let's go in and go through why this game irks the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of me as a great fan of the original and Crusader.
1. Massive inconsistencies.
- My peasents can tear down a stone wall with their spiked sticks, but my battering ram can't? Is my engineers working with styrofoam?
- Can my units enter my wall via the stair? Yes... Sometimes. Can they enter the enemy wall via the stair? ♥♥♥♥ no, just tear it down, why would your archers want to position themselves on higher ground to deal with that counter attack?
- Ok, I get that deer was considered the property of the crown and hunting them was illegal, but shouldn't I be able to choose if I want to hand my peasents some venison if they are starving?
- Map size. Maps in the campaign looks big, but are mostly useless because either they are too small to get a good castle running, or the travel time will be way too long, so production will be cut in half by a random enemy archer positioned behind a tree and invisible on the minimap.
- Placing a stone wall can work. Want a gate? Well ♥♥♥♥ you with an extra wide mace, that thing will take up five times the space wall unit, and what you think of that is of no damn interest to us.
2. Glaring balance issues.
- You remember how you had to either outbuild, sally forth or build Ballistas to deal with the enemy catapults tearing massive holes in your wall? Well you don't have to worry about that, because the styrfoam edict also include your basic range siege engine, so the catapult has to roll up into convienient archery range before they can attempt to get the wall down, in stark contrast to the defencive Mangonells who can now fire three times that range. Which brings me to the second point.
-Archer target priority. Whatever happens to be closest is by far the most dangerous thing in the world, be it a wooden box, a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ peasant or a bumbling pikeman with no hope of reaching you. Screw those other archers in the back massacering your troops, you has a wooden frame to fill with arrows. It's like they all used to work as cashiers and now has to take the que one at a time and damn everything else.
-Micromanaging the economy. Listen here, I'm here to kill things, build a castle and optionally burn it to the ground when I get bored. I don't want to have to care about how many pints of ale the local drunks get, I don't give a single♥♥♥♥♥♥about how many candels my priest thinks he need to tell people they are going to hell for fornicating with the sheep och I really REALLY don't care how many pieces of spare clothes there are in the castle, enemy soldiers are coming to kill all of you, perspective people!
-Hitpoints/movement speed vs attack. This is my biggest gripe so far. Archers are so stupidly OP that mace men or even pikemen are barely worth noticing. Just spam archers and no one can touch you castle. You don't even have to wall it off, just build a labyrith of walls and set the archers on top. The enemy will just walk slowly towards your lord and die as  misassembled IKEA porcupines.
-Burning logs dropped from the wall will roll further than a catapult can fire... And they are instant kills.
3. Massive bugs and useless fetures.
- Soldiers stuck next to walls.
- Useless terrain. Can't see what's a hill and what's a slope.
- Useless walls and towers. Half the time the units will stand around wondering what's so great with the base of this structures.
- Achers won't register that they are being shot at and will rather die than take one additional step to get those enemies in range.
- Terrain will for no apparent reason refuse to support your buildings.
- The minimap will show the area you're currently looking at with no good overview. Also, it's tilted a bit.
- Thanks to the lack of houses, your castles production of soldiers can be locked by a single enemy killing off workers in a remote part of your domain and good luck finding where he is.

Bunny is a robotic children's toy who was given artificial life by a computer virus. After meeting his BFF, a military prototype robot named Gunny, he quickly discovers that being a toy means he's not quite as tough as his deranged mind has lead him to believe, and he certainly doesn't have a military grade auto-repair like Gunny does. For all intents and purposes, this is a decent game - especially considering I paid 0.29$AU for it. I would only recommend it at this price though.
The gameplay is reminicent of any Puyo Pop style game and plays well enough. There is 3 modes: Classic (Arcade/High-score), Ship Shape (Survival) and Sally's Shapes (Puzzle/Speedrun?).
The graphics are decent: fun and cartoony, obviously aimed at pre-teens. They seem to be a little low-res but not overly so, as if this game were about 5-10 years old.
My main gripes are as follows:
1) When you clear gems, the other powerups don't activate. This is especially annoying once the Oil and Slime are introduced and/or you've lined up a good lot of powerups. This is unlike any similar game I've played and means difficult gameplay atop of lack of combo-making opportunities.
2) While keyboard controls are available (and much preferred), there's no shortcuts to activate prompts. This leaves you quickly fumbling for the mouse and potentially causing a game over. Also - again, unlike any similar games - you can't rotate the other direction. This is needed once the game speeds up and rotating 270 degrees instead of 90 can cause problems.
3) The background in the Ship mode is way too distracting.
In summary, it's a game that brings nothing new but added frustration but worth the sales pricing.

Decent game, good time waster.  Premium currency can be obtained free, albeit slowly, so I would tend to ignore the whiners that it is a P2W game.  What winning?  It isn't even competitive except in the completely avoidable and unnecessary PvP, which in itself is fairly new.   Does cash make the game go faster? It sure can!  Does it allow access to a more extensive blueprint line?  Of course.  More character customizations?  Well duh.  When does it not in any free to play game?  Are you really that new to this whole online gaming thing?  But none of those are necessary to play or advance in Shop Heroes.  If you have patience, dislike action based games, and like a bit of a random loot roll now and then, I recommend giving this a shot.  I find it relaxing since I can cross-stitch or read while waiting for those double barrel shotguns to finish crafting.  Might finish that book yet.
What I like:
-Easy to learn.  Yep, no needing to haunt Google or decipher a poorly managed wiki to comprehend the gameplay.  It is simple and straightforward, though I am not sure why a pendant requires enough leather to supply the NFL with footballs for a year, in addition to enough iron and steel to attract bulk buyers for General Motors.  But I digress.
-No active time based stuff.  You don't have to finish what you start.  I don't mean be lazy; I mean if you are playing and there is a knock at the door, you aren't going to die, lose loot, miss an opportunity, etc. if you go answer it.  Your game progress will still be there when you shuffle back to it with that newly purchased/opened/eaten box of Girl Scout cookies.  Nothing lost.  Now go wash the Thin Mints off your hands.  You pig.
-Trading.  The trade house is active and vibrant and offers a 'play it your way' dynamic to the game.  Some players go for crafting mastery, one thing at a time, some for unlocking new items as soon as they can, others play the trade house like a gem-driven stock market.  Don't let people in world chat tell you there is only one right way to play.  In fact, ignore  world chat all together.  They only want your Thin Mints anyway.  Those pigs.
Now, things I find not so rosy.
-Math.  The math seems incredibly broken.  I can send a hero out with 2 sadly underleveled pieces of gear, both with a 10-12% break chance, and it won't break for like 6 missions, if at all.  But, I can buy or craft a flawless piece of gear at the heroes level with a 0.9% chance of breaking and it will, at most, last 2 missions.  Not once in a while either.  Perpetually.  Seems the luck is programmed to try to force you to shell out gems to re-equip your heroes and send them back into the fray.  Good thing I am patient.  And like crafting.  Re-equipping after every mission is nigh unavoidable.
-Fusion Pot.  Expensive and slow to upgrade in levels, very expensive to unlock a 2nd slot.  Also, you can't use the fusion pot while it is upgrading, which is contrary to anything else you upgrade, such as workstations, resource bins, and storage items, which stay in use while upgrading.  That becomes an issue when upgrades get to the 16+ hour mark.
-The last and admittedly minor one, is a trading house bug.  It is constantly yelling telling me I can't exceed a maximum price, before I have even set one.  It also glitches upon entering a price.  I can type in 100,000, hit enter, and it will randomly change itself to something else.  That hurts when I don't realize it reset my 100,000 to 10,000 and I submit the listing.  Especially since you are punished with a 3 day cool down when cancelling.
Long and short of it, it is a quick download, a pretty smooth port of a mobile game, and free.  I like free.

At first, this game was very frustrating, since you are a box...I do love unique and new game mechanics, so this game quickly grew on me :)
I adjusted the camera sensitivity down, which ended up making thing much better.  I also used a controller, which is probably ideal.
It is a unique and cute concept, basic 3D adventure, but as a bouncing box.  This puts an excellently unique and most times frustrating spin on the adventure/action classic.  You move unevenly and often bouncing in undesirable direction, which means you have to change your way of thinking about motion.
All in all, there is lots of game play here (This game is HUGE), great level design and a good amount of open world scavanging for hidden/scattered collectibles.
Humorous and playful, with beautiful graphic design...Definitely worth a play through!
ACHIEVEMENTS:  Mostly story based with a few collectibles, so not too difficult.  There are a few time trials, which I am not a fan of :(
My only wish is that this game was longer! Very fun!

FTL is an indie spacecraft game where you control the actions of your ship and crew.
Disclaimer: You will die and fail horribly the first time you try. Probably the second, third, and
times you attempt to complete the mission.
However, despite that, it's an amazing and fun game, with a great soundtrack, and I absolutely recommend it to anyone who enjoys either space, rogue-likes, or both.

Overall I have a love/hate relationship with this game and is a game I go back and play every once in a while. This is one of the games where your choices matter more than other games. Every credit invest in either on your systems or in weapons, every crew member you rescue or purchase, and every system you choose to explore feels important as you set up to the end. Also since you can only recover health by visiting the randomly generated stores, unlikely random encounters, or in the rare case you find a specific type of drone every hit you take to your hull hurts more and more as you play the game longer.
Now this game is a rogue like and the only change you unlock between each run is the ship and type of the ship you start the run with. Once you get a few runs under you getting to the end is not too difficult but it is a rogue like and on some runs you will just be screwed. Particularly when you are squaring off against the end boss. The end boss does not change but what you employ against will.
Some notes and advice on the end boss. As this is kinda spoilerie in what your fighting I will make it blacked out but I wanted to add it as the boss is the most frustrating part of this game and may affect your purhase.

Among the sleep brings a real great atmosphere of dreams and nightmares, Alice in Wonderlands type, showing a coherent view of a house at night from a 2 years old child who just want her mother back. Everything seems higher, noise louder, cracking sounds like growling. That's a great job indeed, the gameplay fitting perfectly to this 2 year old.
Graphics and animation are quite decent, sometimes really good, the voice acting is great, and the story simple but effective.
There's two bad point to the game : it's too short, which lead to the second bad points, it's a bit expensive for what it offers.
But I'm not hiding my pleasure, I'm glad I bought it. If you feel like supporting the team, buy it, otherwise, you might want to wait for a steam reduction. But this is a game you need if you like scary and dark style.

I'm not good at writing reviews so bear with me here, alright?
First off, I'll say that I've grown up playing the EBF series and the Ge.Ne.Sis. series. Both game series mean a hell of a lot to me so I'm kiiiinda biased....No I don't have two asses... Stop playing the impossible quiz for a second and listen.
First off I'm going to talk about the music and then...eh screw it. I'll talk about a subject when I think about it.
Ok, so the music in this game, like the other 2 games before it and the 4th after it...ABSOLUTELY ROCKS! It's so awesome to listen to! The music suits the exact situation it is in, from towns to forests, battles to game over screens...It's just so amazingly awesome! I love the arranges as well but I still like how there was a bit of minimalist charm to them~
Onto the characters.... For Matt, we have your usual brain of mush, button mashing, lovable idiot. He's so cool. Since the first EBF, he was always the embodiment of DPS...a big stupid jock with a sword bigger than him. I LOVE how we were able to swap his swords out for certain fights for that elemental edge! He was always pretty damned strong but as with all DPS...you spent ages healing the guy. In this one, He's a little more...Well he is certainly a bit smarter and much more "I NEED this" in terms of his personality, which is great! I love his character growth from DPS buffoon to DPS smart-a$$. His comments on things and his in battle text are always funny~
For Natz.... As everybody who is a fan of the series will say.... BOOBS!!!....Ahem...anyway.... Natz was your standard mage without any story or character and it only felt like she was just there so Mat doesn't die stupidly...but in EBF3...her character came to life and became the Natz we know...the chick who doesn't take crap...but gets it anyway. Before she used to always be in the back, making it like she was your average mage but in this and in EBF 4, she sits in the front lines with Matt showing that she has guts...and probably some balls as well...Good thing we can't poke those.... Usually the more level-headed member...."usually"
For Lance... From badguy ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ to friend of awesomeness, this guy makes his debut in EBF2 but comes around in EBF 3 and 4. Your standard military gunner who is tactical, level headed and precise...usually. Yes I use that word a lot, get used to it... I love that he not only is a "Synergist" but also a backup healer! (For those who don't know, Synergist means he does status stuff) The effects on his weapons were always super helpful in battles and especially his gear...
His character development in EBF 3 really helped people look at him differently than that one guy that was ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t to beat in the previous title.
For the skill system... The skill system in this...TRUCKING GENIUS!!! Most games give each character a set of skills and that's that. No whining, no complaining..."That's what it is so deal with it plebs" but in this game... Not only did the characters have set skills which are obvious to their equipment...there were skills that all of them could learn and you had to decide WHO got them! In my opinion, this was a GREAT move! That means you can have one of the characters be able to do something they normally cannot, like Matt using magic for example. Sure...it doesn't hurt that much but still.... Giving him the
lets him heal the party and do damage! You can give it to Lance if you want but...yea... Anyway... You could hand debilitating skills to Natz to make sense or give them to Lance to keep the DPS rolling with Natz! It is such a good system and I just wish other games had it too when giving you multiple characters in an rpg.
The locations were pretty cool. I love the 3D graphics on a 2D plane with 3D uhh... implications? I don't wanna say it is 2.5D because it doesn't seem like that but then again...I'm no techie so it might be...who knows? It's like mystery meat, nobody knows what it is...cept the maker..s-shut up...
The items...nothing really to say here.
The weapons and clothing... Now...this was a fun idea! Getting random in battle events to happen when you upgraded them to a set level? So awesome! The different combos you could make were baffling! Well...not really but you know what I mean... You could go with a mainstream, failsafe outfit for all 3 that ups their stats and covers weaknesses...or you could mix it up focusing on the battle events to turn the battle in your favour despite being weak to them, you could overpower them with sheer skills. Though all of us have to admit... That Air Strike between rounds is the best thing in the game. Can't deny that one.
The bosses were all pretty difficult in their own right as you went through the game. There were no real super jumps in difficul-- oh yea... The Cosmic Monolith...Um yea... ♥♥♥♥ that guy... anyway... Other than the final boss, which can take anywhere between 10-45 minutes, the bosses and enemies in the game were perfectly staggered with the player levels and stats making it a wonderful transition that never left you feeling overpowered...unless you grinded...
That's all my brain is going to let me review so yea...hope you all liked it. Please be nice to me... I'm tired as I write this late review. I just found out today this puppy was on steam.

Despite its being great fun, and the fact that there's really no reason not to try it since it is completely free, EBF3 really only serves as an introduction to 4. This is not to say you shouldn't play it but it is shorter and more simplified than its sequel. In fact it is the ideal place to look first if you are thinking of grabbing EBF4. It has the same lighthearted sense of humour and the same mechanics, albeit in a lesser way, and is certainly worth a few hours of your time if you are looking for something bright and breezy. Sure it has its origins in flash games but that doesn't stop it from being a good game - unlike a lot of the mobile-port trash that you actually have to pay for currently doing the rounds.
If you enjoy this game then support the dev and buy at least one of his other two games. He deserves it.
