TLDR edition: Overall, it's a fun, cheap, colourful and interesting modern take on the classic platformer genre, and even though I've barely started it, I've had well worth the sale price from it, and have many more hours of enjoyment to go!
Pros:
- Cute, clean and colourful graphics
- Real throwback to the 90s
- Large worlds to explore
- Lots of collectables
- Varied content between puzzles, exploration, platforming and challenges/mini-games
- Fairly easy and casual experience
Cons:
- Rolling and jumping mechanics can be clumsy and hard to direct
- No real story or purpose to what you're doing (goes with the genre though)
Full Length Review:
After having an itch for a 90s platformer rear its head in recent months, and after being put off Yooka-Laylee because of its price and length, I saw Unbox on a bundle site sale at what worked out to be about £2. So I took a gamble.
My initial impression was of the voice acting. Garbled talk just as in YL and Banjo Kazooie in the old days. I had to chuckle given this was my YL replacement. I did the quick tutorial and then worked on the first world.
The game has 3 distinct worlds plus a central hub world. Each world have various collectables to gather in order to progress to the next one, and eventually 100% the game if you wish. I am currently at the end of the first world and have found most of the hub world's collectables after about 5 hours of playing. Each world has a varied aesthetic and is pretty large - far bigger than I'd have expected.
The mechanics do grate on me after a while, with it being difficult to direct the rolling and jumping aspects. I like that you can double jump, up to a maximum of 6 times before having to refill health (basically a charge mechanic). Health boxes are plentiful and checkpoints are everywhere, which also fill health to max. Basically the 6 charge is your limit to attempt a particular jump or to land somewhere.
In terms of content; you have your exploration with 'golden tape' to collect. 200 in each world. Then you have mystery diary entries to find; about 5 in each world from what I can tell. Finally, you have 'Stamps' which are awarded by solving puzzles or completing challenges - little "race" types where you have to deliver a letter across the island in 5 minutes or fight 20 enemy boxes in 2 minutes etc. Unlock enough of these Stamps and you can fight the world's boss and progress to the next world.

Pretty original open-world cartoonish game with cute landscapes. It takes a while to get used to the character's odd responsiveness and the multiple jumps (with a stock of jumps that also act like life points), but then it's all good.
Just 2 big weak point:
- vehicles physics is really painful (for instance, if you barely scratch a wall, the car will stop as if it hit a 100 tons block of concrete), racing with those is horrible, with the ridiculously short timers making it even more painful. Thankfully, you don't have to use them much so it's not too bad
- mouse sensitivity is too low, even when set to the max, so the camera is a bit of a PITA
And 2 slightly weak points:
- the "plot" is ridiculous, with some dialog being only partially skippable
- you can't save whenever you want (but there are many save points scattered around the world, so that's not really an issue)
Very good game.

Potential spoilers and plenty of opinions following the first paragraph.
An incredible concept that just did not pan out. The visuals are decent, the sounds are genuinely incredible but the gameplay and story just aren't there. Gameplay is very typical for a first person horror-adventure game, in line with the recent first person horror-adventure games Amnesia and Outlast. You walk, you run, you crouch (excuse me, crawl), you hide and you pick up objects as needed. The hiding mechanic isn't necessary for a majority of the game. Nothing new except in this scenario you're an infant. I do not recommend this game at $19.99 at all. I paid much less and still would not recommend the game just generally unless you're really convinced you'll like it.
The game is never really scary and most of the time I felt as if the antagonist was actually helping by conveniently guiding me through opening doors, creating footsteps, etc. The fact that you are an infant did not change anything for me unfortunately. This could be due to the fact that the game is in first person and I didn't feel immersed. I don't think first person works well for this type of game... you're playing a predefined character that is not developed in any way. In Halo, you get Master Chief, a very memorable character built through dialogue and cutscenes. In Skyrim, you're roleplaying a character that is not predefined by the story but by the player. This idea doesn't hold up for every game but doesn't help with this one.
Another problem I had was that I often missed what was going on during visual moments. I had no idea things went flying in the kitchen, I feel like I missed things when the lightning flashed in the house. I would just hear these sound cues and look around and not see anything. I guess I was playing wrong during these moments.
The story begins holding your hand in the first few minutes and continues to pull you closer like a protective parent. Just to make sure you completely understand the story, we're going to treat you like a child and keep you completely aware of what you're doing and what is going on at all times. There's no thrill or mystery and if you understand what's going on very early in the game it's hard to be fearful of anything to come.
I did not enjoy this game.

A solid RPG that's free and fun, can't really beat that deal.  The story & characters aren't meant to be deep but the game does have its humorous moments.  The combat and item systems are well done.  Music is pretty good as well.
The game is fairly simple in design.  You start in the only town with 3 characters to use.  You'll venture through 7 different environments battling enemies, leveling up, killing bosses, opening chests, & getting quests.  Each environment has a quick travel point right before the boss that allows you to instantly teleport back to the town.  The town has a couple shops where you can buy wearable equipment, forgeable items, and health/mp/status related items.  Each of your three characters has their own unique set of skills (fairly sizable) that you can upgrade as you choose throughout the game.  You'll have limited points to upgrade your skills at the start/mid points, so your choices will matter, but you will be able to unlock everything before you reach the end.  You'll also find a plethora of permanent stat upgrade items throughout the game that allow you to customize your characters further, you could keep your characters well balanced or buff certain characters to excel in certain stats.  Each character can equip a weapon, armor, and a hat.  The game has an autosave feature, but you can manually save the game at any time outside of battle.
Combat is the game's main focus point and is where it really shines.  All enemies & bosses are viewable as you walk around, so you choose who you would like to fight.  Each environment has enemies on its “main path” that you will have to fight in order to reach the boss; once you kill them they will never respawn.  Enemies off the “main path” will respawn if you go back to town or to a different environment, so you can grind for extra XP or skill points should you need to (I played on the hard difficulty and never had to grind at all).  Enemies off the main path are often guarding chests or paths that lead to chests, so you're given incentive to fight them but don't have to if you don't want to. Combat is usually quick and simple.  Battle animations only last around 2 seconds or less for all attacks/spells (the exception being characters' limit breaks), so no sitting around for 10 seconds watching a character cast a damn spell.  Enemies start off simple but get stronger later on.  Enemies can be permanently scanned to see what elements and status effects they are weak/strong against.  Unlike a lot of RPGs, status effect spells and buff/debuff spells can be very useful in combat and are often essential against advanced enemies and bosses.  The mid and late game bosses are both difficult and rewarding to defeat.
The game has a unique equipment system that I don't recall seeing before.  All equipment starts off at level 1 and can be forged up to level 5.  All of a character's base stats are multiplied by 1.00 (So 30 base attack X 1.00 = 30 attack power).  When a character puts on a piece of equipment, instead of giving an increase to a stat (such as +30 attack), equipment gives an increase to a character's multiplier in various stats (such as + .15% to attack and + .10 to magic defense, so that 30 base attack is now multiplied by 1.15 = 35 attack power).  Instead of getting better and better equipment, you'll receive equipment that buffs/debuffs the multiplier for different stats, give different elemental/status resistances, and occasionally have a unique bonus that will unlock upon being upgraded to level 4 or 5 (such as automatically casting regen on your party or having a mammoth attack your enemies).  Even your starting equipment is viable at the end of the game, as no equipment is necessarily better or worse than any other equipment.  What equipment you want to equip will usually be based on what element enemies are currently weak to, what elements you should increase your resistance against, what stats you want buffed, or simply because you like the special bonus it provides.  Forging equipment is as simple as acquiring the necessary items, either by finding them in chests, receiving them from combat, or buying them at the shop.
Some NPCs give quests, all of which are fetch quests.  You'll eventually find the items in chests or through battle.  The quest log lets you see what quests you have completed/outstanding and shows whether you have the necessary items to complete them.  Some of the rewards are pieces of equipment or permanent stat boosts, so running through and completing side quests once you get to the end of a zone can be helpful.  Completing quests are the only real backtracking you'll do in the game, but all NPCs are reachable once the main pathway is cleared, so you never have to fight enemies to get back to an NPC.
Not much more to say.  Combat is solid, skill/equipment systems are diverse and interesting, occasionally funny (especially a couple of the achievements).  Would've enjoyed the game just as much if I'd paid a couple bucks for it.  Looking forward to EBF4.

I'd like to retract my prior harsh statements on ODP. What also made a huge difference for me was the updates in the hit detection. Which also shows that the dev's are listening, updating and I commend them for that. Surprisingly, the updates also balanced the games difficulty more and the shots seem a little less cheap. You still get stuck on just everything but is what makes this more challenging. What ODP does have in common with Binding of Isaac is how it is played. In BoI, the game cannot be beaten in one run, which is where ODP shares a commonality. The only other 2 things in common between them is the game play and large selection of random powerups. I am still a little disappointed in the mini bosses. A little more effort in the character design would go a long way and makes a huge difference both in first impressions and the replayability but I'll look past that. ODP overall is a good game, sorry not $14.99, but on-sale good. I can now recommend this to any twin stick shooter fan. Beware, this game should display a large "early access" sign, because it is rather unfinished.
...at least that is how it feels to me at the moment.
You basically run along a maze of rooms tht are mapped automatically while you enter them.
In those rooms, you either face monsters (some of which are creative while some are not) or end up with a vending machine.
Because most rooms will be filled with monsters, I'll simply skip the vending machine.
Fighting those monsters is where the game shows its lack of polish:
- walking around is slower than most monsters can walk, so they'll catch up easily and (without displaying a special animation) will take a bite off of your health
- in order to "outrun" those monsters, you'll find yourself rolling around the rooms aimlessly (while always having to push the space bar again for each roll)
- you actually have to fight monsters, or rather shoot them with small fire balls - which would not be too bad, were it not for a terrible aiming system (you can walk diagonally, but for some obscure reason are only able to shoot vertically or horizontally)
- there is no visual feedback for a hit besides the white number floating up (the enemy does not stop in place, there's no blood, no bursting flame, no ...) which kind of ruins the whole fight monsters in almost every singe room-principle
- boss monsters (I've only faced a dragon so far) will follow a set path and ignore the player (they would probably follow that path even if there was no player), with only a few flames appearing on the ground from thin air stalking the player and trying to catch up with him (again: those flames are as fast as the player if not faster, so you need to roll around - again)
- the animations are rather stiff and resemble games of the Play Station-era (which would be fine, if this game was a homage to those times - but seeing that there is no further resemblance, I am not willing to follow that thought)
Overall, I can't help but wonder whether this game might have been enjoyable if it had seen a lot more polish.
...or had been honest about its unfinished state beforehand.

Kingdom: New Lands is an amazing updated version of the original Kingdom; Kingdom: NL is amazing. This small, almost quaint indie game really is fun for the fair price of £10.99. the game is massive compared to the original content in Kingdom, I'm going to give you a short run down of how great this game is.(tl;dr at the bottom)
The game is fairly simple in almost all gameplay aspects, you make money, you spend the money and progress to the next island. I won't lie, when I got Kingdom I didn't like the look of the graphics that much, I got the game regardless, though they may look not look like the best, they fit with the game and it fits well with the theme of the game, which is survival and progression. The jist of the game is that you fight enemies called "Greed" which will attack you at night, you build up during the day by making money and recruiting new people into your Kingdom, assigning them jobs such as archer and builder, surviving and then leaving the island to expand your kingdom into the next island. You might be thinking "Does the game just rinse and repeat? What do I do when I get to these other islands?" Every time you leave the island, or lose the game on that island you'll unlock a new thing to explore and figure out what it does. There are a lot of guides that will help you if you get Kingdom: NL so if you ever get stuck on something, check the guides.
The mechanics in this game are simple, and after a solid 30 minutes to an hour you'll get a good idea as to what to do, I don't want to bore you as to what to do, put simply, you gain money, you spend the money to gain money, you survive and explore. I want you guys to figure it out and enjoy the game as it's meant to be, explore the game and enjoy it! I didn't want to spoil the game for you guys so I have to make this review seem very "basic", sorry.

Kingdom: New Lands is what I would consider an incredibly replayable game along with the original game, Kingdom (now named Kingdom: Classic). I would definitely recommend this game for people who enjoy a bit of simplicity but also a challenge.
The art that has been made in both the foreground and background of the game are very beautiful pieces. While understandly not superbly realistic, it does give off a very appealing view while playing the game. Personally, my favourite is the usage of the flowing water directly in the foreground, in which you can see all the reflections and such mimic your and your npc's actions, along with being affected by weather (the water ripples when it is hit by rain droplets, pretty obviously but even then, they did that superbly well). The colouring and objects in the middleground and background are very suttle, which I enjoy quite deeply, there are no overly flourescent colours nor any particularly dull colours and it blends in quite well while you're playing.
The gameplay in Kingdom is also a very appealing aspect, yet again in my personal opinion, while they do implement repetition within the gameplay, that does not cause the game to become dull (I did not find that the repition caused me to bore, I did not even find it particularly noticable while playing). The added features from Kingdom: New Lands that were not in the original are also a big bolster to the enjoyment of the game. I found that being able to slaughter all the animals I found with my bear allowed me to save a considerable amount of time when I desperately needed those one or two coins to build a new wall or hire new hunters. The variety of statues, horses (along with bears as well), town centre and other small add-ons to the game bring a lot more possible paths to take during your gameplay. While there certainly are things I wanted to be improved on, such as improving the overall performance of the NPCs (since some of the time they do random, stupid things which typically end up in them being attacked by the monsters).
Overall, the newest release of the Kingdom games is a game that I have found to be a relaxing yet challenging game that you normally do not stress not get frustrated on, I definitely reccomend it if you're a casual gamer and enjoy more lax games such as this one.

In Among the Sleep, by Krillbite Studio, you will take on the role of a 2 year old child who just had his birthday. You are eating cake in the arms of your mom when there is a knock at the door. This is followed by an argument, and then your mom coming back in with a present. You then fast forward to around bedtime/nap time, I'm not really sure which. It is then that the game takes on a nightmarish overlay.
The visual look of this game felt like it fit with the character being a 2 year old. I'm not saying that it was rainbows and puppies, but there were those softer colors, even when everything was dark. The levels of this game were beyond creepy, especially for me because I have an almost 2 year old, so I could see myself in his shoes. There is a slight terror to knowing that something bad could happen right out of the corner of your eye. The levels span from a deserted play ground, a library in a forest, small sections of your house, and more. There are villains that creep around as well. All I have to say is you are going to need to hide from them, or you will suffer a restart of the section you are in. I also really enjoyed the companion, the teddy bear that helped me along. All I had to do was hug it and he would produce a little bit of light that would help me see through the darkness.
The sounds in this game are extremely creepy. Once again it was doubley so because I have a young son, and hearing those noises creep around in a dark area would scare the pants off me at that age. I also think the voice acting in this game was spot on. I could see the roles of the mother and the teddy bear in the voices given.
The controls of the game are your usual configuration with WASD, shift to run, ctrl to crawl or get up, space to climb, and the mouse to control the camera and interact with objects.
Though this game wasn't as long as I would have hoped, it definitely had enough there to keep me on my toes, and hoping that nothing was going to get me around the next corner. There is just something about this game that awakened long gone fears of my childhood, and the fear of what is in the dark. In this respect the developers did a great job. To be honest I can't really think of anything I found clunky or missing from this game. I will tell you this, the twist is a hell of one, and I'm not going to tell you what it is because you need to play this game to find out, but when the game ends everything kind of makes better sense.
There were definitely puzzle aspects to this game, most of the time it was moving objects so that you could get to a different location, but there were a couple of times where the developers threw in a mechanism just for a small section of the game that changed things up a little. A couple examples of this would be throwing objects to knock something off a shelf, or collecting a specific type of object so that you could weigh down the end of something so you could get to the other side. I'm not saying that this was a bad thing, but I would have liked to see a little bit more of these mechanics, to do them once and then seeming to throw them away made me feel like they were afterthoughts in the game creation process.
So lets get down to the part that most of you want to know, and that is should you play this game. The answer is yes, you should play this game, and you should play it in the dark, at night, and pray that no one sneaks up behind you while you are playing. This game gets an 8.9 out of 10.

Before actually rating the game, I suppose I should give a little overwiew to the series for the newcomers, to better understand what's going on:
Epic Battle Fantasy (EBF) series started as simple (if not simplistic) flash games that parody old-school classic games (mostly Final Fantasy, but you can find other references to well known old games, like Legend of Zelda or Kirby, or even some cartoons and anime), created by Matt Roszak (AKA matt-like-swords, kupo707, KupoGames and hell knows what else). Before the EBF series, he mosty used to create amateur animations that date back to as early as 2004. Considering he's around 26 now, I think you can imagine they were created and uploaded for fun, as a hobby.
Anyway, back to the game.
The first game came out in 2009 and consisted exclusively of constant enemy waves and a boss fight every now and then until the very end. No savepoints too. The only "break" you had was a single potion shop. The fights themselves weren't very special too. Most of the time, it went like that:
You have two characters: damage dealer and a healer - equip the the damage dealer with the right weapon - spam one skill - the healer spams multiheal ability for 99% of the game.
Of course it changed a bit on highest difficulty, but still the premise was the same.
It was Matt's first try at this kind of game and it kinda worked.
The second game added a few RPG elements, and by "a few" I mean that after every few waves of enemies (or a boss) you could upgrade one of your stats and pick a skill. It wasn't a deep system, but it was surprisingly fun to think of new strategies that it introduced, but othet than that, it was pretty much the same as the first game, with constant waves of enemies and bosses (this time you had two checkpoints however, each allowed you to save a game and also featured a mini-game where you kill undead cats as NoLegs -also a cat-the series' mascot)
EBF3 is basically Matt's first semi-serious game. What do I mean by semi-serious? I mean that it's still very simple, rather short and not very deep, and it's also a browser game (the Steam version, which is free of course, only added stuff like higher Resolutions, fullscreen, turbo mode etc.).
But it's a start. It features an actual overworld which you can explore, search for treasures, secrets and quests.
There's also a normal levelling system and a whole lot of skills that can be upgraded separately. Combine that with more than 80 unique pieces of equipment and you get a fun jRPG-esque game which offers plenty of customisation and different tactics to defeat an enemy. Combat is still the main focus of the game and its core hasn't changed: you have a party, this time consisting of 3 party members, each with own strengths and weaknesses, battling waves of trash enemies and bosses until they die, not much to say.
The quests featured in the game are nothing more than simple fetch quests (or rather, getting some random crap from chests and enemy drops and giving them to an NPC), but hey - they're there.
The game isn't very long either, I finished the Steam release in under 8 hours while getting all the achievements, but those were fun 8 hours.
Overall, if I were to compare EBF3 to budget games and AAA titles, that would be obviously unfair. The fourth game might be closer to that.
But as a simple browser game brought to Steam, I believe EBF3 deserves a solid 9/10.

The best "rogue-like" game on Steam for the price. Has incredible replay value with the different ship options and difficulty levels.

Note: I've beaten the game with every ship on the hardest difficulty.
THE GOOD:
You'll get un-winnable scenarios 50-15% of the time (varies depending on your ship) but the rest of the time you feel like your choices are in charge of your fate. From what you buy, or don't, to standing your ground or running, virtually every choice not only matters but is crucial (at least on the hardest difficulty). Never quite knowing what you'll get while still actually allowing the player control over their fate is a balance too rare in rogue-likes.
Excellent soundtrack.
Good variety of weapons, ships and upgrades (only some are far better than others).
Super cheap nowadays.
THE BAD:
There is unfortunately a "best" way to play. While the game can certainly be beaten using other methods boarding ships to kill crews and stacking scrap collector augments always gives the most scrap, points and eventually the most powerful ship. This negates half the ship upgrade choices in the game. Sure you can win other ways but there isn't any reason to do so other than achievements.
Enemy crew AI is also too simplistic, mainly in how it prioritizes the shields over anything else. This pushes you towards some exploit game play.
Rebel fleet ships can be farmed for points negating any replay value for scores.
BOTTOM LINE:
Excellent game. Buy it if you enjoy randomized game play, tactical resource management, and a challenge, in a pixelly space setting.

Best Thing About It:
Strategic game, equipment management, and missions all work very well together.  The choices you make in the strategic layer have a big impact on the way the game plays out.  Bionic Dues is a game that succeeeds on the sum of its parts.
Worst Thing About It:
The art direction.  It is an unattractive game.  The "dungeon runs" are hideous, and the remote controlled robots theme  doesn't do much for me.  I would have much rather seen this game themed as a Star Wars style, rebel strike team or even a G.I. Joe style special ops theme.
************************************************************************************
I recommend this game.  You should play in iron man mode and learn to roll with the tough decisions and consequences you face in the strategic portion of the game.  Every turn the enemy is growing stronger, but you have a lot of different ways to attack and weaken the enemy, and ways to strengthen your own forces.  The strategic part of the game is great because every choice and every event has a real and visible effect.
The "rogue like" missions are also fun, because each game the enemy builds and deploys various robots that behave in very specific ways.  FIguring out how to exploit these robots' weaknesses while avoiding a variety of attacks is fun, and each play you face different mixes of robots--so its like a proceedurally generated combat and stealth puzzle.
Each game counts down to a final confrentation, and what the enemy throws at you depends very much on what occured throughout the strategic layer of the campaign.  Enemy forces composition and "bosses" are randomly determined each game, so there is a lot of variety.
My only complaint is appearance and theme.  I'm really not into the remote controlled mechs or the pilots or the "grid look" of the dungeon crawls.  Its a great game though, and I recommend you learn to live with the passable art direction and enjoy this very well designed game.  I give it a big yes.

Bionic Dues is one of Arcen's many cross-genere forays into the gaming market, this time coming up with a rather compelling turn based roguelike hybrid. Bionic Dues is what you'd get if you crossed a traditional Roguelike with FTL and then baked in the theme of Mechwarrior. What comes out is a mixture of RPG-like progression and turnbased tactics layered ontop of a strategy meta-game that provides a high level of replayability between campaigns.
In Bionic Dues you command a 'team' of four Exos (mechs), each with their own weaponry systems and specializations that can be further customized by acquiring loot from winning missions or finding/hacking chests. The caveat to this 'team' is that you can only pilot one of your Exos at a time, but can switch between them at any time during the missions.
Before the game starts you choose up to 4 Exos from a pool of 6 types, and then pick your commander who will provide a unique tactical advantage which will drastically change how you play the game. All of this is wrapped up into an FTL style mission selector which will give you some choice as to how your path through the game progresses, and ultimately help you stave off defeat. Losing a mission or a unit does not necessarily mean the end of the game either as traditional roguelike permadeath is optional, which is what really allows the campaign metagame to shine.
Each mission you embark on has its own objectives and unique attributes, your goals range from kill all the enemies to destroy certain targets, to simply just evade and escape in time. In one mission type, all of the cover is rigged to explode when destroyed, knowing this and using it to your advantage to take down enemies you couldnt easily kill otherwise is just one useful strategy to employ against an overwhelming force. There are roughly 20+ different mission varieties as well, and choosing which ones to embark on between re-fitting your Exos is critical to your success.
If you try going head to head with the enemy in this game without realizing their weaknesses, or your own strengths, you're almost certain to be in for a rough time. Understanding the quirks of each of the 45+ different enemies, how they move, shoot, and affect other enemy units; all of that is necessary for survival. Once you understand a few of the game's less well-explained quirks, you begin to realize just how much depth there is to the combat. The sheer amount of unique enemies can be a little daunting at first and some combinations can lead to complicated and outright unfair or impossible situations.
One example of this is that early on in the game there are enemy bots which will one-shot you with their explosive missile weapons. After a few missions into the game they will probably begin to out-range you too and can kill you in a single shot. Ontop of that they have shields that would deplete a sizeable chunk of your ammo supply to destroy, if you could survive that many turns to kill them. Thankfully they have very little ammunition (unless an ammo bot is nearby) but are not always the best shot. This type of enemy can be dealt with in multiple ways: a long range Exo, a stealth unit thats immune to splash damage (but not direct hits such as the Ninja), one capable of shooting around corners with splash damage, even detonating obstacles or certain enemy bots nearby. Thats not to mention mines, sentries, or simply just stealthing past it.
Pros:
- Procedurally generated map and mission layouts.
- Huge variety of enemies (Changes with each new game)
- Wide variety tactics to use, if you're creative enough.
- 6 different Exos, 6 commanders, and 6 difficulty levels.
- Loot system allows you to customize aspects of your units.
- Large number of mission types with different rewards.
Cons:
- Too many enemies can make missions drag on a little sometimes.
- Inconsistent difficulty based on starting choice and random factors.
- Randomized enemy deployment can lead to unfair combinations.
- Can easily spend too much time on the Exo customization screen.
- Level design and aesthetic feels a bit bland and samey after awhile.
Conclusion:
Arcen has done a good job with Bionic Dues, but its not without a few pitfalls; the sheer variety of enemies, interactions, and range of difficulty levels can lead to inconsistent experiences between games. New players have a lot to learn and will need to pay attention to enemy sensor and weapon ranges as well as learn to use the environment, mission types, and ground-targeting to their advantage. Using sensors to provoke enemies and lure them to you in the right order, and employing the Science Exo's EMP pistol (which does not use up a turn) to disable enemy movement and block hallways can be the difference between success and failure.

It's hard to make a decisive yes or no recommendation for Empire: Total War.
On one hand, it's one of the glitchiest games in a series infamous for it's bugs. At it's worst, units refuse to move, stop to reform into positions you didn't tell them to, or sometimes even refuse to fire altogether. Thankfully, glitches of this magnitude are rare, but can sometimes be bad enough to cause you to lose battles because your units simply don't follow orders.
On the other hand, it's the largest Total War game. You can create colonies in, and be actively engaging in wars, across three different continents- Europe, Asia (both Asia Minor and India), and America. There's less faction variety between groups of the same continent (for example, European armies are very similar), but the variety comes in when an army of one continent engages the forces of another. Europeans, Ottomans, Indians, and Native Americans all fight differently.
As well, Empire takes place in a hugely underrepresented time period. Very few games take place in the 1700's, and Empire does a great job of representing musket warfare. Combat is slower-paced than games like Rome or Shogun 2, and tactics are focused on gaining artillery advantage.
I end by recommending the game, since I enjoyed it, but your enjoyment depends strongly on your interest in the time period, and your tolerance to bugs.

I give a very conditional recommend for this game. It feels that every game in the Total War series would be great games even if they only live up to half of what they aspire to be. In Empire: Total War's case, half is about right. The game is incredibly ambitious, and while it does get some things right it also leaves many fundamentals broken (though arguably these are present in every Total War game). When things are good though, the game is a thing of beauty, and there are no games quite like it.
The good:
- The scope of the game is immense - covering all five continents in one of the most interesting and volatile period of human history
- The battle simulation actually feels like a simulation - cannonballs bounce as they hit the ground, spilling dirt and crushing infantry. Soldiers stationed on top of fortifications fall to their deaths when the walls they stand on lose integrity and collapse. Weapons can jam, and you can hear the distinct clicks of misfired guns
- Sound design and animations are fantastic. The game allows you to lower the camera down to shoulder level with the solders, and you can hear the whistle of cannonballs flying overhead, the marching steps of the infantry, and see the meticulously animated reloading sequence
- The game is very, very pretty. The characters, ships and buildings are extremely detailed, and you can put the game into slow motion to see beautifully rendered explosions of the ship's powder mags, the splinters coming off ships as cannonballs strike them, and line of infantry taking turns to shoot at each other in battle
The bad:
- The AI, in both campaign map and battle, is extremely dumb. On the campaign map the AI likes to move units around singly, instead of combining them so that they stand a better chance of survival in case of an ambush. The AI also marches armies directly into interception range of armies more than twice its size for them to get crushed, and attacked a besieged city twice with two half stacks instead of combining both to overwhelm the player
- In battle, the AI flounders badly, sending units up against the the player's line singly instead of moving the entire line, allowing the player to concentrate firepower and wipe them out individually in otherwise well matched battles. In addition, the AI appears incapable of using buildings and fortifications at all - when defending a settlement, instead of installing units in buildings, the AI will simply march them towards the player to have them slaughtered
- Other curious incidents include the AI leaving his units as sitting ducks for 45 minutes while I wipe out half his force with a squad of howitzer due to my artillery advantage, charging at infantry using light cavalry, who got wiped when said infantry formed up into box formation, and placing infantry within melee distance of artillery, shooting at my infantry unit while ignoring the canister shots decimating his unit
- The pathfinding is horrible. This is especially apparent with units on fortification. Tasked with fighting an enemy on fortification, a unit would split itself in two, with half climbing the wall while the other half attempting to walk through the gates, even though the gates are not captured. Ordering a unit on fortification to attack the enemy with the fortification cannon is a hit and miss affair, since there are no 'man cannon' order, you have to rely on the game guessing your intention, otherwise the infantry would march out of the gates to confront the enemy on the ground
- Ordering a unit to attack an enemy is a hit and miss affair. Sometimes, when ordered to fire on an enemy that is already within range, a unit will wheel around leisurely and ready itself to fire, instead of SHOOTING THOSE ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥S ALREADY. Similarly, ordering a unit of 120 men to engage a unit of 60 enemies in melee will sometimes result in 60 of the 120 men breaking formation to engage the enemy one-on-one while their compatriot stand in formation like idiots instead of ganging up on the enemy
- Artillery can be ordered to attack ground outside their range - they will try, but their shots will fall short and miss - but not to attack units outside their range. If you do, the attack fails silently, and they would revert to firing at will at units within range. Artillery also do not prioritize units properly, sometimes firing at fleeing enemies over nearby enemies that are still shooting and thus present a bigger threat
- Artillery units cannot target to avoid friendly fire. I'm not just talking about friendly fire when your infantry is standing in front of them, but they'll hit themselves (!) when they fire at an angle.
- Diplomacy is a joke. While the AI makes an effort at realpolitiks and recognize when the situation is hopeless, they usually does so far too late. In addition, the AI often makes completely ridiculous, such as Austria offering India a piece of Europe in exchange for a trade treaty.
- The game is buggy. Enemy units will walk through gates which have been captured by the player, even though those games are suppose to be locked visually. A single horse would get stuck around a rock when entering the battlefield as reinforcement, making the entire unit untargetable, and thus forcing me to bring artillery to shoot at them point blank to end a battle where every other unit has already fled

If you didn't like the first Kingdom, you might like this one.  Previous owners of the classic Kingdom game got this one for free, if that isn't evidence of how great these developers are I don't know what is, your money will be well invested in these games!
Kingdom: New Lands takes the survival kingdom building of the original, and add's the much required depth to prevent the gameplay from quickly becoming stale.
Instead of having a single kingdom that you either win or lose depending on whether you were lucky and really fast, your goal is now to construct a boat in order to reach the next island.  This change of win condition's completely overhauls the initial problem the previous game had.
For one, you don't feel like you have an artificial time limit anymore before your game becomes impossible to win.  Instead, your goal is to construct the boat before your kingdom gets overwhelmed, and instead of an artificial time limit you have a literal one.  The enemies will eventually become far too great for you to handle, season's will change and winter will cause your farms to stop providing bounty.  Eventually your only choice will be to complete the boat and flee or perish.
However, this changes the games overarching difficulty in a good way.  Instead of starting in the max difficulty and figuring things out through long and drawn out trial and error, you now start on a very easy to beat island to allow you to get your bearings as well as create a surplus army to bring onto the next island making reconstruction faster and easier.  This isn't just recommended, it's practically required at times.  Each time you complete an island, the next one is harder, until you finish the final island and win, or fail and lose and be forced to start back at the first island with your previous ruler's spirit guiding the new one.
But losing is far less painful in this game.  As you advance to new islands you can locate sign's which if you purchase their paper for a measly 2 coins, then regardless of whether you succeed or fail on that island you will gain a new feature at the end of the level.  This feature applies to the map (Most don't apply to the first island, but that islands easy anyway) that your new ruler spawns on, and allows you to alternate your strategy accordingly.  Maybe the new feature will provide the edge you needed to overcome that previous run which seemed nearly impossible.  But adding a new feature everytime you succeed or fail an island allows you to continue coming back to see what new feature you've unlocked, and if you can finally win in the end.
The new features provide exciting new things such as new mounts with individual stats and special abilities, new statue's which provide buff's to your entire kingdom as long as you throw money into them, and best of all you get little helpers that can sit on your horse to allow you to upgrade your towers beyond the final level into special structures that provide either utility or superior defense against the overwhelming odds.  You can view the discussion boards if you want to spoil the details.
If you were an owner of the previous kingdom game, then congratulations you already have Kingdom: New Lands and can play it immediately!  What are you waiting for give it a try.
However if you were ever skeptical on purchasing the original kingdom because of what you saw on youtube of other's playing it, maybe this is the kind of game you were looking for instead.  Because I know for certain I am glad that this was created, it fixed all the problems I had with the previous game which I tried to like so much.  And now that this exists I can finally enjoy the music, visuals, and gameplay all together.

NOTE: This is a rather lengthy review. Be warned.
I have very mixed feelings about this game. On the one hand, there is something about this game that keeps having me come back for more. On the other hand, this game is so belittered with bugs and has such a small amount of content that I would not consider this game a full release. Coupled with the asking price of 23€, I’m having a very hard time recommending this game to anyone at all in its current state.  This is my current experience with the game as of version 1.0.3a, having played mostly conquest co-op and some invasion, dabbled with the world editor, and so on:
The game itself is poorly optimized – just pressing Alt to show all tooltips of stockpiles and workshops sends the FPS down below 10. If you have a very long game and you end up with 40ish bricktrons, the FPS starts stuttering quite badly as well. There is also a rather bad memory leak in not only the game itself, but also in the Steam overlay for the game, should you enable it. After playing online with my friend for about an hour, the steam overlay had accumulated over 800MB of RAM usage, with the game itself taking up about 3.5GB. If you do end up buying the game, I’d greatly recommend turning the Steam overlay off for the time being, as that way you can play the game for a longer time before having to restart. Luckily, the loading times are rather quick, considering I’m using an HDD.
There is also a fairly large amount of bugs in the game. One of the most frequent ones is the resources being placed inside terrain and the like, resulting In it being thrown far up into the sky. There’s also a certain amount of pathing errors where bricktrons will randomly walk in the completely wrong direction when they intend to return resources to the stockpile. A major multiplayer bug that I found as well is that sometimes when quitting a multiplayer session, the local save of the game gets corrupted, so that if you attempt to continue it, you need to have the joining players delete their save of the world, else they get stuck in the void upon entering. There are many more bugs that have occurred to me while playing the game, however I struggle to remember them all and I may come back to edit this should I encounter them again.
As for content, there are certain areas that are well fleshed out and some that are desperately lacking. Currently there are about 6 combat classes – Halberdiers, knights, artificers (Which are two-in-one mages and clerics), rangers, grenadiers & arbalests. The classes themselves feel different enough to warrant their existence and I tend to use 4 out of these 6, mainly due to the grenadier's collateral damage not harmonizing well with knights being in the fray and due to halberdiers' need to be up-close where they'll take damage not warranting the small amount of damage they deal. With that said, I’d personally like to see another melee class such as an axeman/berserker to round it out, but otherwise the combat classes are in good supply. There are four enemy types, or perhaps rather “levels”, however outside of invasion mode you rarely encounter anything other than the most basic corruptron, at least on normal difficulty, which makes Conquest mode quite monotonous if you do Co-op (EDIT: I redact this as I noticed that after playing a game for some hours, they do appear, and it's fun and pretty darn challenging if you haven't built up your defense). There is a good amount of variety in building blocks’ shape,but being limited to only building with stone and wood makes the building palette very slim. I wonder why there is no such thing as building with glass, as that is a resource that can be created in the game. I also would appreciate a way of editing the terrain paint, since if you place something that you later destroy, there is no way to turn it back into grass. Normally for RTS-games this is not an issue, but since they incorporated a building aspect into the game, it is very rudimentary at times.
The building system itself is also very finicky, as you soon will learn, because bricktrons will not be able to build very tall unless you build extra stairs for them to reach for the taller blocks, which begs the question why there is no such thing as a scaffold block that allows for directly upwards travel, but can only be built against other blocks. Currently you are forced to build extra stairs next to your builds and monitor them in order to make sure the bricktrons don’t get stuck. There are also some other interesting inconsistencies, such as when building wooden pillars you can stretch beams up to 4 blocks out, but with log pillars you can only stretch them 2 blocks out. Other problems I find is that there is a way to raise terrain and one to lower it, however the raising of terrain does not go very high, about 1-2 blocks, which makes the feature quite pointless. This is also the only way to build with dirt (Should you want to), as far as I know.
The maps are great and can actually be edited to suit your own preferences in terms of the number of crystals and player spawns you want, or if you want to alter the terrain entirely you can do so. The map editor itself is rather clunky, however, and desperately lacks an undo-button in my opinion, as one misclick can ruin all the progress you’ve made so far. The fact that there is a map editor at all, however, is great, and while it does take some time getting used to, once you do there is little to stop you from creating a great map. I did notice, however, that the map overview in the editor shows no crystal spawn locations. Having that available in the map overview would’ve been great. It also would’ve been good if the map overview would be available at all times and not force you to stop what you’re currently doing in order to look at it.
Other annoyances in the game is things such as the lack of a message that tells you that your bricktrons are under attack, the bricktrons get very confused at times when they attempt to build something but then realize they cannot get to where they are supposed to build, among other things that I again struggle to remember at the time of writing this.
That said, the game has a fair amount of good stuff and aside from stability issues, the idea is very sound and could potentially be a great game worth the money. The music is great, the sound effects are really good (Although I tend to confuse mining umphs with hurt noises) and the game is very well stylized. I also must give props to the names they give the bricktrons as they're just lovely. If they fix the optimization issues and add a little bit more content and building blocks, I could recommend this game. As it is right now, however, I simply cannot. It surely can grant a couple of hours of fun and I struggle to find a game that is exactly like this, but for the price tag there is no way this is acceptable as of 1.0.3a.
As a side note, this game’s been prototyped since 2011. I don’t know anything about the development process or the studio as I only got this game recently, but I feel it’s been through a lot of rewrite or been developed very slowly if this is all that’s come out of about 6 years of development time.

This is afun and silly f2p turn based JRPG without horrible microtransactions.
You can play the game as much as you want without having to pay anything unlike most other f2p games which are either very lacking in content or you have to pay for every little thing.
It does improve on things that I found annoying in other JRPG's such as there are no annoying random encounters.
And you can save whenever you want, so you don't have to end up playing for another half an hour just to be able to save your game, especially if it's late and you're tired and just want to sleep and not have to keep playing.
But unfortunately it's lacking in a good story and is just a flash game.
I like the little touches such as whatever armour or weapon you equip changes the appearance on your character as well.
I didn't like how there is a lot of backtracking, you do have to grind sometimes to upgrade skills and equipment and when you fight a boss and realise you haven't invested in a certain needed skill and have to reload and grind to get what you need. It's a bit annoying, but a mechanic all JRPG's seem to have.
It's alright for a free game, I got bored by the time I reached the desert and didn't feel like playing anymore, there's not enough depth, nor does the game have a story that compels me to keep playing.
I can't really reccomend if I get bored of a game before completing it.

Hey you, Yeah you!
Do you like mobas?
How about RTS games?
Giant Transforming Robots?
If you said yes to any of the above, then you should try out Airmech. If you didn't, it is still a free game and you have nothing to lose.
Now you may be asking: "What is Airmech?" Airmech is moba style Games with some Real Time Strategy elements mixed in for a fresh spin on the classic moba gamestyle.
Players control Airmechs, giant mechs that are able to transform into various planes and helicopters at the will of the pilot. There are currently nine different airmechs(as of me typing this) that players can choose from, and more designs are planned to be added in the future! Each of the nine different airmechs play differently, each are equiped with different kinds of guns, missiles, and melee weapons along with 8 preset upgrades that will be unlocked as the mech levels up each match.
Each mech also has 8 slots for the many buildable tanks, soldiers, turrets, and other things that the player uses to help the team advance or defend an area. These eight units are picked by the player before the start of any match. In addition to the player built units, each teams fortress automatically spawns basic soldiers to help capture outposts and attack the enemy.
In the base gamemode, two teams of atmost 3 Mech pilots(Players) fight each other to gain control of the outposts around the map while trying to advance to the enemy team's fortress and destroy it. The Outposts around the map work as unit builders, where players can pick up the various units they want to spawn during the match. Not a big PvP(Player versus Player) enthusiast? Don't worry! this gamemode is available in co-op mode(One team of players vs one team of AI controled Airmechs) and solo mode(one player and two AI vs an AI team).
The other big gamemode is called Survival. This gamemode pits four players against an endless onslaught of enemy units, whose soul purpose is to destroy the team's fotress.
Now you might be thinking: "This all sounds really fun, but how pay to win is this game? Whats the catch?" And thats just it, there is no catch. Anything that can alter competitive gameplay in any way is bought with "Kudos", the currency in this game that is earned at the end of every match. This stuff piles up quickly and is only earnable through playing the game, but don't worry, once you start playing you will never run out of kudos!
So what costs actual money in this game? There is also another form of currency called diamonds. This currency is the "premium currency" of airmech. This premium currency is used to buy cosmetic items and Ultimate items, aswell as being the currency of the player market.
Cosmetic items are things that make your Airmech look cool. these range from Airmech skins, unit skins, different laser and exhaust colors, helmets for your airmechs, and pets that fly around you. None of these have any effect on gameplay.
Ultimate items are... well, Ultimate! These items are stronger versions of the buildable units and Airmechs that are normally usable.
"But you said that paid items won't alter gameplay!"
I said competitive gameplay. Ultimates are only usable in cooperative gamemodes, so if anyone is using them, they will always be on your team. Ultimate units are really just used when you want to dominate the AI team without as much effort.
Lastly there is the player market, where players can sell various cosmetics and items that are no longer sold in the shop for diamonds.
Is it worth putting some money into this game? I certainly believe so. But whether or not you want to is up to you. I strongly suggest playing airmech for a couple of days before deciding to throw all of your money at the screen. If you don't want to put any money into the game, don't worry, we won't judge!
Thank you for reading this review, I know it was a long one.
I hope you give this game a try, and enjoy it as much as I do!

Hmm... where to begin.
First up, this is an Arcen Games title. The guys who took a dump on KB/M users with AVWW 2, and insulted them after they finally gave in and provided "real" mouse support for it.
Now that that PSA is out of the way:
The game is a little bit like AI War in a single city. Interesting for a while, but it gets repetitive and grindy in all the wrong ways. You'll spend far more time hunting for the "right" upgrades and managing your inventory than engaging in missions.
Short ranged units are at a horrendous disadvantage, given that many rooms are loaded to the brim with enemies with medium to high range weaponry, and the investment needed to make their weapons viable is extreme. A Sniper unit will outperform an Assassin unit 100% of the time. And the game likes to set an Assassin in the default party loadout, and the fact that it also sets two heavy AOE units in the default loadout should be a key warning sign.
Of course, the RNG Gods play a key role in this game, and like the RNG Gods everywhere, they are fickle, arbitrary and hate you.
The lack of real campaign customization is another drawback, but that is a common issue for Arcen games. Sometimes, it's good to have a real short burst game, and other times, a longer campaign would be more interesting. Sometimes you want to give yourself a moderate challenge in ways that the few selectable "challenges" do not provide.
Let's move on to other parts:
The audio tracks are taken from AVWW 1. This does not surprise me for some reason, although I must say I'm disappointed, especially since the audio doesn't add to the experience.
Graphics: It's a tiled game. No surprises, no real expectations, although background (or environmental) images would be nice.
All around, I'm just not able to recommend this game. It's just missing far too many little things, and Arcen has done better in the past.

I hate to say it but if the development team had put as much effort into refining Boo Bunny Plague’s gameplay as they did the soundtrack, this could have been a very enjoyable game. Poor controls, bland level design, and last-gen graphics just make the experience so disappointing.

Boo Bunny Plague is action adventure game, that suffers from not-so-good level design and weak combat, but despite that it's worth playing. And here is way.
You play a bunny-robot named Bunny, that accedently receive consciousness, but he is not very bright. Another robot saves you from the factory you are in and from here starts your adventure for auto repair for Bunny. But nothing is what it's seems and soon everything goes wrong. The insane (in a good way) story and the boss battle are the things that kept me going. I wanted to see the next boss, the next crazy cutscene. In almost every cutscene there is a songs perform by the characters and the dialogue between them are well written. All this makes me smile and in some points even laugh and this mean the game is doing somtething right.
The graphics are decent for indie game. The textures are not good looking, but the world and characters are all cell shaded, like in comic book and you may not notice it. Sometimes, when you hit enemy letter coming out from him, just like in a comic book. Now that I think about it, from this game may come really good comic book.
The level desing is simple. The places you visit are different enough, but layout is not very creative. I can't point a single level, that is stuck in my mind. They are not good, not awful, just okay.
Like i wrote in the beginning, the gameplay it's not that good. You have regular 3-4 combo attack, jump and hit, and the right mouse button is your sheeld. That it's, not very deep. The weapons for Bunny are little unusual – guitars. They are eight and you can find them in the world or some NPC will give it to you. Some are on fire, ice, lightning and they do additional damage.
Enemies you face are all the same. Barbarians shooting with crossbow, other attack you with sword or axe. There is also giant blue monster. But they are all filler. The real battles are with the bosses. Here is where the game shines. They are different from each other and may give you hard time. It' boss battle, after boss battle, after boss battle, after boss battle. It's madness. One advice – choose highest the difficulty.
Voice acting is good, every actor fits really well with their character. On the other hand the sound design is questionable. Some sound effects are just week. But the soundtrack is amazing. Even when i'm wrighting this review i'm listining it. In addition to the song performed by the characters there are really good punk, hard rock and metal tracks. I couldn't find name of the performers, so I assume they are some undergound bands, although one song sounds like AC/DC. But in some places i notice i can't hear the music, despite it's increased to maximum.
The controls are fine with mouse and keyboard. You can play with controller, but i did't try it. The game is not long, between 2:30-3 h, but it's not very expensive. I think the length and the value are perfect.
While I played Boo Bunny Plague I felt like I was in a cartoon or comic book. The game is charming, sweet and I had fun. Nice humor, crazy story and characters, amazing music, great boss battles. All this make me recommend it, but keep in mind the simple level design and combat.

Is Boo Bunny Plague a good game? No, not at all. Still, if you enjoy stupid comedy and goofy songs you could do far worse for the price.  Despite the repetitive gameplay featuring one lonely attack and a lame regenerating shield, I enjoyed this game for what it was. Worth $5? Maybe. I picked it up on sale for less than that though and I regret nothing.

I felt the need to clarify my point a bit better and make a better review so I can properly describe why I don't recommend this dumpster fire of a game.
Pros:
+ Its cheap now. Small comfort for me now, but at least it won't dent your wallet if you choose to buy this.
+ Its functional. Didn't really break the game when playing it, which is surprising considering the rest of it.
+ One of the boss fights was pretty interesting and original as far as I know. So its got that.
Neutral:
+/- I guess the soundtrack is pretty okay, even if Boo Bunny sings in some of the songs.
Cons:
- Holy ♥♥♥♥ing hell, Boo Bunny is the worst. He's one of those "intentionally annoying" characters that devs seem to think makes them clever for creating, not realizing that intentional or not, they're still annoying.
- The game's visuals are muddy and really ugly. Textures are so blurry they might as well not have bothered in some cases.
- The characters are so painfully underutilized. They show maybe one part of their character as if we were supposed to know that already so they don't elaborate much and one bit of their personality since they get very little screentime, and they expect that to be enough for us, leading to the characters all seeming rather undeveloped.
- The humor in this game just falls so PAINFULLY flat. If you don't find Boo Bunny's annoying "lul so crazy" humor funny at all, you'll get nothing from the humor of this game. I've heard it compared to Deadpool's style of humor, but I really don't see the similarities since this game lacks comedic timing.
- Animation is pretty lackluster.
- The combat is so abysmal. Hope you enjoy an uninteresting and unevolving attack system, because its all you have for the entire game. A jump attack and an attack combo with a special depending on your weapon is all you get. Repeat until everything stops moving. You just wail on them until they die. That's the entire game. Oh, and did I mention that Boo Bunny also says one of maybe 3-4 quips EVERY SINGLE TIME YOU HIT SOMETHING?! Because if you didn't find him annoying before, the game wants to make really damn sure you do through gameplay at least.
- All the bosses are cliche save for one. If you've fought any sort of boss in a beat-em-up, you've pretty much fought the bosses here. One is literally just a straight copy of the Ganondorf fight from Ocarina of Time even.
-The game is really short. Considering the pain the game gives you, I consider it a virtue, but others might not think so.
-This game ends with sequel bait of all ♥♥♥♥ing things. SEQUEL BAIT!
2/10. While some find enjoyment out of this game, I don't see a single redeeming quality in it. Maybe the humor isn't for me, maybe I missed some nuance in the combat, or maybe I just don't get it, but regardless, this game is just horrible. Avoid this game at all costs. Its painful to play and I can't think of a single reason to buy it other than as a horrible prank on your friends.

Having owned and enjoyed the original Kingdom for hours, this new iteration, which is free for owners of the orginal, adds more depth, variation, challenge, and other subtle gameplay changes that vastly improves upon the original formula.
Notable additions/changes are:
NPC characters can RUN now. It makes a huge difference in pace and balance when you need something done fast.
There is now a finite amount of land on both sides of your kingdom; one side has a massive demon portal that cannot be permanently destroyed, the other side has a port where you can build a boat and escape the island. Which brings me to.....
Islands. There are now 5 islands you can conquer, so there is a resolution to the game instead of battling endless waves of enemies.
You can also ride a bear. Why wouldn't you pay $15 to ride a ♥♥♥♥ing bear into battle?
Also unicorns. But really, bears are where it's at.
If tower defense games or strategy games in general are your thing, buy the original so you can get this expansion for free.
Minimalistic, but complex. Simple, but challenging.

This expansion adds a lot of new things to the game, that you will have to unlock.
The objective of the game is to survive until you can escape the island.
There are five islands that get larger and larger with more portals along the way.
You are a King/Queen whose only power is to redistribute money.
You build a base, you hire people to protect it and farm the land.
(Put 7 coins into the wooden rocket to unlock the better walls)
Eventually you will have enough money to build a bout and escape.
Your enemy comes only at night and every about five days a stronger wave will arrive at your walls.
You can and sometimes will have to destroy the portals in order to progress, but that will also trigger a strong wave.
The more you wait the harder it will get, so I went for the clear everything between me and the dock strategy as fast as I could.
You unlock new items by paying two coins to a directional post, which is located usually in the direction opposite to the dock and on the 5th island it is next to the coastal portal at the opposite edge to the dock, but if you explore in the first 2-3 days you can bribe the enemy. Once you unlock a item it will have a chance to spawn, starting with the next island.
There are new mounts, some with abilities.
New statues and the old ones, the knight statue is a bit risky.
And finally special builders for interesting and necessary buildings for latter stages.
Because you can't control the units directly, you are at the mercy of the AI, archers and farmers are redistributed at the worst times, builders stay outside the walls after they cut trees.

The Full Review: My Castle Story
After years of hardwork from the developers, it's everything I expected it would be and more! The resource gathering, the building mechanics, the soldiers, corruptrons and crystal capturing it's all there! The multiplayer seems to function more than well enough, especially in Competitive play, I only had one hiccup with a Co-op session where my friend couldn't use his Bricktrons and crashed out of the game, my best guess would be there were too many orders running around as we were quite late in or internet issues. But other than that it's exactly what it says on the tin! However! It must be said that there are a few things that could possibly be improved! Below I'll list some of the issues I've encountered, how I've worked around the issue, and how I feel it could be fixed or improved if possible.
Learning How To Play
The Issue - It can be quite tricky learning how to play, especially if you jump straight into an Multiplayer game because from my experience I didn't get any Tool Tips on how to get started.
The Way Around - If you start a Single Player game at first, you're given Tool Tips that guide you on how to kick start your Bricktrons and get them working!
Possible Improvements - Perhaps some Video Tutorials accesible via the Main Menu? And or to have some more Tool Tips that explain how to use more advanced crafting benches or blocks. (Along with the option to have the Tool Tips display during a Multiplayer match, as they did not for me atleast)
Crafting & Resources
The Issue - Over my past few games, I've found my workers not working on certain equipment that I needed pronto! I assigned them to the bench, tried forcing them to work it, breaking the bench and starting fresh but all to no avail! Turned out they simply didn't have one of the resources available even though I had asked them to produce it, problem was they had no where to store it as they'd made too much of a different resource that used the same material instead!
Possible Improvements - It would be nice if it was clearer what materials you need in order to finish certain equipment, as well as to know exactly how much of each resource you have in your stockpiles, that way I could find out what it needed and make sure I have at least one of each resource available.
The game isn't without its issues, but the game does work 90% of the time, the other 10% you might hit a roadblock and have to really think for a second about what the issue is, then solve the issue, but every issue I've had so far is resolvable and it's mostly down to a lack of communication from the game to the player, would be nice to have an info bubble above things when "This can't be crafted because: You're out of Iron!" or to just have more information readily available about every item and how they're used etc etc.
Like I said, personally I enjoy it! But I can see and understand where some people may have issues with it, I've just managed to find a way around these issues and or simply gotten used to how the game functions! If you're interested in the game, or already have the game but can't figure certain things out, drop me a message and I'll be happy to teach you how to play and maybe have a match or two with ya!

Pardon any innaccuracies in my Invasion review section I did not play this mode as much. Invasion mode starts sending powerful enemies too soon with the "tank" enemies coming before wave 10 and an hour into a map. These enemies require a lot of resources as they are best handled by knights and ranged in combination.  Knights take about two and a half minutes of furnace time to get the 5 Iron ingots required, but before that you have to mine the iron which is not abundant enough and then assemble the knight kit. With waves coming every eight minutes which includes the time since the previous wave, this mode is too difficult.
On large maps sometimes bricktrons take illogical large paths to do project that has the same priority as a closer project. They will also do this when collecting resources to build.  This means you can want to build a wall or castle to defend but even if you build a quarry and stockpile next to the project, bricktrons will go for a two-minute walk to old resources for either no reason or because you couldnt collect resources  near the project fast enough. Also if you ever make a mistake bricktrons take forever to respawn and it seems to be based off of enemy kills and resources collected.  Try respawning ten bricktrons with ten bricktrons left alive.  It takes as many resources as it does to spawn them originally. Good luck now that time has passed and enemies spawn stronger and in larger numbers.  There is no coming back. There is also no autosave.
I mostly played Conquest on Arrecibo.  I tried multiple strategies to beat this but ultimately either got bored (6 hours+), defeated, or realized my strategy wouldn't work anymore so I had to reset. All three following strategies seemed to work on smaller maps like troubled Heaps but this game is not balanced well for larger more satisfying maps.
Strategy A:
Build a defensible point with sentinel wards, walls, and ranged units.  Send worker1 out to draw enemies back to the point. Send worker2 to cap the point (hope no random roaming enemies see him).  Run worker1 around while ranged units pick off enemies.  Cycle through enemy bases until victory.  Fail because warlocks start spawning by the time you can build a good defensive point and their ranged attacks are accurate enough to eventually take the workers down.  Also enemies respawn too quickly to allow you to capture more than a few nodes this way.
Strategy B:
Build castles around each node.  Fail because even with a good amount of sentinel wards per base you eventually get too powerful enemies and your bricktrons are too spread out to get weapons and get to the base in time.
Strategy C:
This seems to be the one that works but took so long I got bored and is written with Arrecibo in mind. Note that arrecibo is arranged like a flower with petals - the outside areas can all be accessed from the center but bridges and tunnels are needed to go between "petals".  This strategy only makes sense if you spawn on the outside so restart if you spawn in the center. Build defensive walls with sentinel wards and if you have workers to spare ranged units.  Use this to cut off enemy access to multiple bases at the same time.  Clear the center if you'd like but every time you clear a node you risk a wave of vengeful enemies, the plus side is you have more room to work.  Build a significant sized army with mostly ranged units. Use bridges and tunnels to move around and capture nodes on the edge of the map.  Pay attention to the map and which areas are easy to block off or have a large amount of enemy "nodes" on the petals.  Eventually get bored because of the resource collection problem I wrote above making later projects take too long to build.
I also had a few things that feel like technical errors or quality of life issues.  After 40+ hours on recored I have no idea how to make the camera move correctly.  Sometimes it swings wildly when you want short movements and sometimes the opposite.  Sometimes it adjusts to the height the "pivot" rests sometimes it doesnt.  I could only find one way to adjust the height of the "pivot" with ctrl+shift+scroll but it was painfully slow. You can neither command units to move if youve zoomed out too far nor click on the minimap directly to make them move.  Good luck with hasty retreats.  Also X-ray mode is worthless for its intended purpose and i prefered to leave it off when I needed to look in tunnels.

Gonna give this one a tentative recommendation. If you grew up on Rareware games and similar 3D platformers like I did and are looking to relive some of that sweet sweet nostalgia, no need to keep reading, this game will absolutely scratch that itch. If you're still skeptical however, read on, because there are a few quirks to Unbox that may make or break your overall enjoyment of the game.
The first thing that I would like to point out, is that, despite the fact that Unbox successfully capitalizes on N64 and early Playstation platformer nostalgia better than any game since... Well probably Psychonauts... It still feels like a new-generation game. The game environments have more in common with the likes of Far Cry and Uncharted than they do with Banjo Kazooie for example, and although the level design is still highly detailed and very good overall, there is an element of realism to the game enviroments that is not shared by the games that Unbox has been frequently compared to. There are pros and cons to this increased world size and realism, one major pro being that the game is a satisfying length and feels full of content even though the story only takes you to three different locations. The drawbacks are most notably that the stamps needed to progress through the story can be hard to find, environments aren't varied enough and ultimately will end up being boring after spending some time in each, and platforming is a little quirky even beyond the obvious caveat that you play as a box and, as such, control like a box.
That said, one of the biggest strengths of the game for me was the actual controlling of the box. A lot of people have pointed this out as a con, but to me it actually adds a nice challenge to the experience. None of the platforming is particularly difficult, and when it is harder than normal checkpoints are placed very generously, so the bulk of the challenge comes from how the rolling box actually handles. I found the controlling of the box to be satisfying and realistic even though some players might find it clunky. The movement is held back a little bit by an unorthodox control system (at least with an Xbox controller which I personally used for the whole game), but given that there is only about 4 different functions, the control scheme will very quickly become familiar to you, even if it isn't perfect.
This brings me to, in my opinion, the biggest shortcoming of Unbox, the "minigames". I call them that because I don't know what else to compare it to in other similar games. Basically the story is progressed by collecting stamps, anybody who played Mario 64 or Banjo Kazooie will be familiar with this as they are functionally the same as Stars or Jiggys in those games (respectively). However, despite them serving the same function in progressing the story as more are collected, the way these are actually collected is different. In each of the three worlds, recurring characters will give you "missions" which are essentially just minigames. These can be fun at first but the real downfall of these minigames is that they are effectively exactly the same on all of the three worlds you travel to. You eventually come to expect exactly what each character will ask of you. There are some outliers but for the most part these become quite the grind. They are also not particularly difficult in and of themselves and the difficulty instead is creating by imposing an arbitrary time limit on almost all of these excursions. One of the worst offenders is a racing minigame in which the player is tasked with just getting from point A to point B in a certain time frame, sometimes these races include cars as well which just seems like a clunky and unnecessary addition to the game, and the game would've been significantly better without the inclusion of this mechanic. Some stamps can still be collected by just stumbling upon them or solving puzzles like you would in Mario 64 or most Rare games, and these are definitely the highlights of this stamp collecting aspect of the game, but that said, these stamps tend to be last resorts as there is no way to find them in the giant worldspaces other than stumbling upon them, whereas instead you can be directed to the minigame options with a giant arrow.
Overall, despite these flaws, my opinion of Unbox is that it is definitely worth it if you're looking for a potent dose of nostalgia with some modern flair and mechanics. This blend of new and old works more often than it doesn't, and the game succeeds through vibrant worldspaces, unique platforming and movement, and entertaining characters, even if it is brought down a little bit by it's core stamp collection mechanic. I got this game for $10 in the Humble Bundle and definitely think that is a fair price, so keep a lookout for it on sale.
