Among the Sleep is a first-person, atmospheric horror adventure game for the perspective of a 2-year old child. Everything is huge. Crawling and staggered walking are integral to how you move around. Your childlike imagination is incredibly active. Norwegian developer, Krillbite Studio, have done an amazing job at placing you in the onesie of a toddler and then subsequently placing you in a night where everything is going bump.
Among the Sleep uses a whole arsenal of horror techniques to keep you sweating and on the edge of your seat. As I mentioned, it is an atmospheric horror game. A dark house on a stormy night full of creaks, with the faint noise of a plate breaking or muffled voices can be terrifying. Especially at first when you’re wandering through the house as doors creak open behind you, the sound of heavy footsteps echo throughout the house, and there are shadows framing what I assumed at the time were burly, axe-wielding convicts. I would advise playing the game slightly brighter than recommended setting. Not because I’m a coward, but more because the recommended gamma setting was too dark and I couldn’t actually see what I was doing. Though the game does provides a solution to this. There is a “Hug Teddy” button which causes Teddy to light up, softly illuminating the darkness around you.
While I’m generally not a huge fan of horror games due to being a bit flighty and preferring games that empower. But I still enjoyed the horror in Among the Sleep academically. Having you play a toddler was an interesting game elements that I’ve never seen it before and thoroughly enjoyed. The game might seem steep in price for a 5-6 hour game, but you pay more for a 2 hour movie, and a lot more for games that that far less unique and well-thought out.

How to fully describe this thing...
Purely as a game, Boo Bunny Plague would be mediocre and you should know this if you plan on playing. At its core, it is a 3D brawler, though the controls are a bit clunky, the hit detection sometimes off (hello projectile reflection mechanics!) and it doesn't look too good. I'm sure you could tell from the screenshots.
Fighting most enemies is just an excercise in mashing the left mouse button (or jump attacks if you like being efficient), but the boss fights are all quite well designed, really. Spotty projectile reflection aside, the bosses can all pose a challenge and I'd say are the meat of the game. Perhaps in a potential sequel, the devs could cut down on the standard enemies and just shower you in bosses.
And god, is it charming. Every moment, every impromptu musical number (And there are many!), every line of humorous dialogue just makes me feel like the devs really loved making it, from the writing to the voice recording, etc. You can just tell this was a labour of love, not just some generic shovelware made to fit release date.
All things considered, it is a rather short experience, really only worth one playthrough. There are a few collectibles, but otherwise, yeah...
Pick this thing up in a bundle or on a sale and prepare for a few hours of entertainment, as long as you can come to terms with its other flaws.

Then there's the shield meter, which honestly is a pointless gimmick because it doesn't really stop people from attacking until your shield energy is gone, leaving you with two choices.  Hit and run, or hit and get hit by everything else.
How the story is executed is kind of irritating as well.  The jokes aren't placed well at times, voice acting goes from Dynasty Warriors bad to pretty okay.  Bunny, even though I like the character, got on my nerves quite often, and there felt like there were a fair bit of things that weren't explained in the game.
Don't get me wrong, I would love to see a sequel, or even a remake of this game.  But only if they fix the awful combat they had in it.

Let me tell you about this pretty game called Boo Bunny Plague.
I picked it up using some of the rare Steam funds that I only seem to get once in a blue moon while it was on sale, and honestly I do not regret a penny. This game proudly holds the title of "the first game that made me buy it instantly after watching the trailer."
So what is this game about?
It's a game about a metal toy bunny who just wants to make the money required for an auto-repair, and along the way he goes across an intergalactic journey with his three pals trying to earn that money. I can only describe it as a linear action/adventure game, similar to games in the PS2 era. I loved my PS2, so to see a game that was so new yet classic-feeling at the same time was really something.
But where this game truly shined was in its creativity. There's no exaggeration when I say that this game is really freaking funny. There are hilarious moments with every cutscene, and even during the gameplay itself, which are either original jokes or references. In the first half of the game, the subtitles definitely made me crack up a few times.
On that note, the voice acting is brilliant. Each voice actor truly gave their characters life and personality, and a lovely singing voice I might add. Yes, there are numerous songs in this game, and for some reason, I love it. I've never seen another game do anything like it, and it worked beautifully. I am actually listening to the soundtrack while I am writing this, which I got with the game.
Oh yeah. It's not just the singing I like, but the music too. It's so memorable I catch myself singing random songs throughout the day.
How is the actual gameplay like? For me, it's smooth. I used the highest graphics settings and the game looked beautiful. This may be different for other computers though. The graphics themselves may not look as "detailed" as modern games, but personally I enjoyed the cartoony feeling this game gave me.
The controls are simple to understand, and I used a gamepad for it. The levels themselves aren't too difficult, and there's an amount of different guitars to collect, some of which are optional and hard to find. Bosses occur very often in this game, and while some of them are easy to defeat, others are tricky and cause you to think before you just rush in and attack. There usually isn't a large penalty for dying, you'll just respawn instantly at the beginning of the room, or somewhere a few seconds from the point you died at.
When completing the game and finishing the credits sequence, you unlock Impossible Mode, which, as you would guess, unlocks a much harder version of the original game. There's not much else going for it besides an achievement for beating it, but that was enough for me. By the way, I should mention that the game itself is rather short; it would take an average playthrough about two to three hours or so to beat it. But that doesn't make the game bad; I've played countless games that are short, but have loads of charm and memorability to me, and this is among my favorite. I've actually played through the game three times at the time I write this, once on Impossible Mode. It's a heavily enjoyable experience and I've actually found a few funny bits that I missed on my first playthrough.
The combat system is very simple. For the most part you have to mash a single button to beat enemies down, and hold down another to activate a temporary shield. Some of your guitar-weapons, however, have special effects to aid in combat.
Another enjoyable aspect about this game is that it makes no darn sense. As the plot unfolds you're asking yourself just what the heck you're playing, and it kept me entertained the whole way through, what with Bunny's singing episodes and Gunny's overuse of the word "Yes," which I have begun to take up when I type to people.
Many of the levels are linear without a whole lot of exploring, but I can guarantee you'll get a laugh out of the game at least.
Also, the developers are very involved with this game, and they will be very responsive to almost any question or concern you may have. In my very recently developed passion for roguelike games, I stumbled upon Our Darker Purpose on the Steam frontpage. Initially I was going to discard it as another indie game that sold entirely on the premise of its pretty art, but seeing as it was a roguelike, I decided to try out my new payment method by buying it.
Well, those ten dollars could have been better spent.
True to its roguelike nature, the game thrusts you upon the ruins of a school that changes every time you play the game. The thing is, you'll find yourself doing that way more than it'd be fun to.
Don't assume I'm giving this game a bad review because of the difficulty.
No, it's because of the unfairness. There is practically nothing for your character (a distressed, half-goth-half-moeblob shy little girl named lovingly named Cordy) to do once an enemy has set their sights on you. What I imagine must have initially been designed as an evasive roll is instead little more than a glorified burst of speed where you can still be hit by the enemy. The rest of your abilities are terribly uneffective attacks -or at least, I assume they're attacks, by what little information I managed to absorb from a "tutorial" consisting of a few scribbles on the first room of each new game. It's nigh-impossible to dodge enemy attacks, and skill has naught to do with it.
The entire game's design either lacks foresight or is simply lazy. The majority of characters have a terrible lack of animations; Cordy herself only has an animation for her roll, and an animation for her walk. Getting hit by an enemy elicits little more than a "blink" from your sprite, reminscent of those from a past-decade arcade beat 'em up. Even the menus are strange, allowing you the use of your mouse in one menu, and taking it away from you in the next one. Like I said, the game offers you little-to-none information on just what the ♥♥♥♥ you're supposed to do, and it wasn't until my third death that I took it upon myself to navigate the jumbled menus to see if there was anything as my reward for future progress. True enough, there was a "Counselor" in one of the menus to whom I could pay the "favors" I earnt at the end of each level in exchange for tips.
Like I said, the game didn't tell me any of this. I could have potentially gone an entire playthrough without even realizing there was a friendly NPC in the main menu. There may even be more helpful stuff out there for me to find. Perhaps if I type in the Konami code I'll get a lightsaber? If I don't experiment I'll never know.
Those are the two main downfalls of this game. The lack of information, and the tediousness of the design. Oh, and the unfairness; did I mention you're screwed for the whole game?
Now, the game has just come out, so it may be unfair for me to write a review this early. But you're supposed to release a game when it's at least completed enough to be /fun/, not as a half-baked cake with an IOU.
If you're looking for a game with similar art, get Don't Starve. If you're looking for a roguelike, get Rogue Legacy or Spelunky. At least at the moment I am writing this review, this game is not worth touching.

An excellent challenge, difficult in all the right ways.
Anyone looking for a change of pace from Binding of Isaac or whatever your latest roguelike is should absolutely check this game out. Thoughtful, well-balanced controls combined with well designed encounters leaves you with a game that rewards you for your increasing skill at surviving, while setting the bar higher notch by notch across four robust chapters.
When they say brutal difficulty, they are not joking. Straight into the first chapter or even the first floor you will find yourself barely scraping by your first few runs, but though it may be unforgiving, it is also fair. The difficulty curve is smooth, and every monster has a clearly obvious attack pattern, every bullet is easy to track. Nothing you come up against will surprise you, but that doesn't lessen the challenge. If anything, it adds to the enjoyment. It's very satisfying to come out the other side of a difficult boss battle unscathed knowing that it was purely your skill and experience that got you through it.
Character customization is fairly robust in the form of 'lessons,' powers you unlock over time and can then mix and match at the start of the game. Through this system you could, say, shoot while rolling. Or, alternatively, shoot further while standing still. It's a nice way to complement your individual playstyles. In addition, you can level up through your run and choose from a pair of random perks to further enhance or alter your play.
Combine that with 80 items and you've got plenty of variety run to run to enjoy. Certain items even offer challenges of their own to activate, and the most powerful can break after you take damage, further incentivizing smarter and better play.
It's not without it's certain annoyances, however, and the worst offender is probably the room terrain. Objects can be 'sticky' or in fact be angular when they do not appear to be so. Seems minor until you realize your dodge was halted by an unseen prong sticking out from a desk, or a bouncing projectile suddenly taking a hard 60 degree turn off the door frame. You can learn to adjust to this, but it's counterintuitive and could have been better executed.
Those small issues aren't be nearly enough to throw me off what is a great game. One of the few roguelikes I constantly walk away from with a sense of satisfaction, as I and the game both know I did better this time than the last.
Highly recommended.

This was my first game by Matt Roszak and I enjoyed it very much, though it starts to become more clear what this represents with a brief history.
Matt started off making animations, with his first one being called simply "no-name", and it had the first appearance of an EBF character, Matt, based off the creator. Eventually, in Attack of the Black Mages 5, we saw an early form of Natalie in the form of the White Mage. Around this time Matt started making games, with his first being mecha dress-up, which has been used to make several bosses, as well a quick-draw game called Brawl Royale
Eventually, Matt made his first turn-based RPG, simply called Epic Battle Fantasy. In it you played as Matt, the series offensive, and Natalie, the series healer. It didn't have much and isn't too interesting, only really play it if you want to understand a bit more history to the series. Then EBF 2 came out with a more coherent story tying in with the last game. It had more mechanics and was quite enjoyable, still worth playing. It introduced the first new party member, Lance, as the final boss.
That brings us to this, EBF 3, Matt's first big game. It has a good overworld, plenty of hidden treasure, amusing dialouge, an OK story, and anime boobs. Solid combat with a variety of skills (though not in all elements) and numerous enemies with different weaknesses, as well as many equips with varying effects, making customization strategically useful. It stars amazing music by Phyrnna (then called HalcyonicFalconX) and the final boss is great, with changing elements requiring you to go with an element-neutral strategy or to switch things up throughout the battle. Dialogue FROM Akron was interesting, making him less than flat at minimum. Completing it 100% does require a bit of luck alongside strategy and grinding, but you are rewarded with a bit of unique dialogue from the room behind Death. Overall an enjoyable game and quite good considering the developer's humble begginnings. Most (but not all) of the negative reviews I found were crude and not fair, but this game isn't flawless. Either way, check Matt's games and old animations.

Though certainly not up to the level of Matt Roszak's recent work (Epic Battle Fantasy 4), Epic Battle Fantasy 3 nevertheless presents a fun diversion. The fact that lessons were learned from game development and applied to an older work retroactively is great and EBF3 gains a lot by the numerous small improvements (e.g. being able to see a unit's Scan during battle), which is especially impressive considering that the game is still free.
The music is amazing, though sometimes there's some slight dissonance in the world and its music (for example: a sad song during a decidedly not sad snowy town). It should be mentioned, however, that the music direction is better than EBF2 and continues to improve in EBF4.
The battle system is simple, but never dull. A variety of skills help to set a unique strategy, though here too the trend for greater customizeability continues to EBF4.
The story is nothing spectacular, which should be mentioned, even if it doesn't try to be. However, the character interactions, while mostly humourous, do give some actual character development. The main characters may not grow out of character archetypes, but their dialogue is enough to keep one interested. Here we have one of the biggest improvements EBF3 has over EBF2.
On the whole, EBF3 is the middle game in a series of steady improvement. While not extraordinary on its own, it does serve as a reminder of how far the developer has come and is an acceptable entry point to the series.
PS: I spent way too much time in the character creator.

After spending over 500 hours on this, i think the game is a fairly decent way to pass some of your free time.
I mainly play PC games and don't own a mobile device, so I'm glad to see these types of games offered here on Steam.
The microtransactions don't have to be that painful, unless you are the type of completionist who cares about earning every gold star. You can gain a decent amount of free gems by playing the game co-operatively. After you reach level 15 in the game, (probably less than 24hrs of gameplay required), you can earn gems from other players using the global Trade House. The best use for early gems, is to get gold, any amount of gold that you gain can speed up your progress tremendously.
If you feel you can manage to reward the devs at Cloudcade a little for thier work, the Fountain of Gems offers 100 gems per day for 30 days, which seems the best deal at $9.99USD for 30 days.
As I mentioned you can earn a Gold Star, if you manage to hire all 20 available workers. Sadly gaining that star will cost you close to $100USD for the two premium workers.
It's beneficial to be in a city by yourself for the first 20 levels or so, and then joining a mid-level city will give more advantages. Every city buiding gives some type of passive bonus, and an instant bonus when you invest in the building. The investment costs for a solo player are going to be much lower, which makes it much easier to take advantage of those bonuses.

HunieCam Studio is a cute management simulator with lewd humor. But is it a good game?
The game is short and somewhat simple. A character named Kyu (known from HuniePop) hires you to take care of a cam girl business. You have 21 days to get as many fans as possible. After skipping the tutorial, each round will take about 1 1/2 hours to complete. There's no real story to the game, just you running a business.
You can hire up to 18 different girls, 8 of them returning from HuniePop. You can only use 8 girls at a time. You improve their skills so they can get more fans, more fans bring them more money and with money you can buy ads for new fans. The game goes a little more indepth with stress levels, addictions, private sessions, STDs and specials items, but it's all kept very simple and straightforward so there's no difficulty in understanding the game.
To collect your skill points, money, fans and items, you have to click each building. Clicking a building will also make the action go quicker. But don't worry, this is neither a clicker game nor a wannabe mobile game. Holding down your mouse button over a building has the same effect as clicking it constantly, so your hand will be spared from pain.
At the end of your 21 days, Kyu comes back to judge how well you did. Based on your fan count, you'll get a phallic trophy and some tokens to unlock hairstyles and clothes for your girls inside the menu. Getting the diamond trophy is difficult, the time and money management is key to your success. One mistake can slow your process down and miss the deadline.
Compared to HuniePop, the game lacks further challenges inside the game (aside from a "rock-hard mode" after getting diamond) and most of the achievements can be earned in very few playthroughs if you have the right strategy.
Overall this game is a competent yet simple and fun management game that's good for beginners of the genre but probably too uneventful for the casual HuniePop fan.

Almost a 3D Platformer throwback masterpiece. It's got the graphics, the level design, the game structure, the writing, the atmosphere. The game is well balenced with a good difficulty and a decent amount of content.
But the game has you controlling a box. Rolling a box around is the least satisfying movement mechanic I think I've ever experienced in a 3D game. The camera bobs constantly as the corners of the box flip, and the physics are fully fleshed out in that concept. This all gives me a huge headache - the camera bouncing looks terrible, and the boxes are very difficult to control. The "jumping" is more of a "throwing yourself into things" in the vein of joke 3D platformers like Goat Simulator, and it wasn't satisfying to control there and it's not fun here.
If the developers ever make a mode where the boxes have legs and it controls closer to your usual 3D game, I'd happily recommend the game again.

Unbox is the kind of game you play when everything stressful is going on in your life. The cute visuals and music help get across what kind of game this is going to be. From talking to the diffrent boxes, finding collectibles, to exploring the diffrent worlds, this games is one I can play and immideatly have a nice day. But is it fully worth it?
PROS
- The worlds are massive. I found myself exploring each world for hours in hopes of finding new secrets. The detail in them is incredible, and they immideatly get the theme across.
-The music, while simplistic, is nice. It reminds me a lot of the 3d Mario games. Each song is fitting for each of the worlds. Altough for some it can be a little repititve.
- Each character has a unique personality that let you know rightoff the bat what kind of box they are. Wheter they are a jolly happy box, a worker box, or a possible homicidal bunny box, each of them has something that makes you like them
- All of the challenges ar simple and fun. None of them felt unfair, and I looked foorward to seeing what the next would bring to the table. From time trails, to exploring the maps for collectibles, each challenge requires you change playstyle in some way shape or form.
CONS
- The physics in this game, while functional, have a tendency of being a little messy. I found myself getting stuck a few times, and even had to restart a challenge or two due to some weird physics glitch.
- While I was not expecting Metal Gear levels of storytelling in a game like this, the game could have been even better with more bits of story. This become evident towards the end where everythig just becomes rushed because they needed a reason for boss battles.
- While I love collect-athon games, this is one of the weaker ones. Outside of a few cosmetic unlocakables, there is no real reason I found for collecting all of the tape and stamps outside of getting 100%.
- The combat in this games is just very clunky. It ranges from being simplistic to frutrating. You will go from slamming enemies, to doggin missles that range from being slightly annoying, to instant kills. This is especially proven in the final boss fight, where I found myself getting 1 hit KO like 20 times.
-Lastly, the game almost feels too short. With only three worlds and a hub world, the game almost feels incomplete in some way. I feel that the game would have benfited from having an addotional two worlds to make the journey feel satisfying.
While these cons may seem frustrating, I still had fun with the game, and look forward to whatever the developers have next in store. If a sequel were to be made and fix some if the issues this first one had, I feel we will have a good tribute to the old N64 collector games. While $16 may seem like a lot and I would personally wait for it to go on sale, if you have the money and are looking for a relaxing fun time, get Unbox!

Turn-based strategy game. The robots will attack you and you have 50 days to prepare. You can do a variety of missions to collect gear or weaken the enemy. 1 mission equals 1 day. 1 full playthrough of 50 days took me about 10 hours.
Pros:
-There's a lot of costumization: 6 different exos to choose from each of them with their own strengths and weaknesses and lots of gear to choose from.
-Large enemy variety, every sort of enemy needs to be dealt with in a different way.
-Some strategic choice in choosing missions.
-1 mission for each of your 4 exos that upgrades it with extra weapons.
-Missions themselves have a lot of tactical depth thanks to having 4 different exos available each with 2-6 mostly different weapons.
-Lots of replayability if you like the combat system: each mission feels different thanks to procedurally-generated levels.
-Missions are short (15 mins) so you can play when you don't have a lot of time.
-I personally really like the soundtrack.
Cons:
-Lots of different types of missions with different win conditions, but most of them feel the same because they all require you to kill most of the enemies in a level.
-Can get repetitive if you're not a fan of the combat system: you'll be doing basically the same thing with the same 4 exos 50 times until the end of the game.
-The way achievements work is a bit silly: same achievement for every difficulty level.

I feel I can now recommend this game. Whilst it's a little clunky and can be beaten in just a couple of hours, it more than makes up for that by sheer force of concept.

The level design is very well crafted and you rarely find yourself wandering round in circles looking for something to do. It's a little linear in places, but you feel more like you're being guided in the right direction rather than simply being on rails.
However, it's taken six months since release for me to be able to actually play the game as it's been absolutely infested with bugs. One showstopping glitch made it impossible for me to even complete the first chapter, hence the negative review I originally posted here. I still have minor bugs including achievements not working, but at least the game is now completable for me. If it works for you, it's a fascinating original game. On first impressions when I started playing this game, I wasn't too impressed. The difficulty seemed all over the place, there were a lot of numbers and stats everywhere, and things were confusing. But, if you stay on and keep playing, you eventually start to get a hang of it. There is a bit of a learning curve here, but the game has a very nice tactical depth to it and can be loads of fun.
Upon starting a new game, you get to select your preferred pilot and 4 mechs/exosuits. Each pilot has a bonus perk of some sort, and each mech has its own strengths and weaknesses, some being more offensively based, others more to do with support stuff, like hacking and stealth. So it's up to you to pick your preferred team.
The campaign itself has a simple concept - a robot army is going to attack your HQ in 50 days. Do whatever you can to prepare yourself for this attack. Each mission you do in the city counts as a day. You can go for missions where you find shiny new gear for your mechs to make them stronger, or you can go for missions which weaken the enemy and slow their expansion. The best thing is, you can see on a side of a screen the details of what units currently comprise the enemy army, so you can see how it is affected after every mission you do.
The missions themselves take a form of a randomly-generated dungeon with tile-based movement. You can swap between your mechs at will, but doing so counts as a turn, so you have to be very careful in your advance. It is very easy to make a wrong move and to have several enemies on you at once. Both, your units and enemy units, might feel like glass cannons. You could kill an enemy in 1-2 shots, but so can they! So you have to utilise tactics to outsmart them - use range or perhaps area of effect weapons, or even just pull back and surprise them around the corner. You can even deploy sentry turrets to help you in firefights if you've got any available.
And in between missions you can customize your mechs with the loot found. The customization is very rich and detailed. Each mech has several slots where gear can fit in, ranging from weapons, to shields, to propulsion systems. It can feel overwhelming at first because there are a lot of things on the screen, but you do get used to it, and everything in the game has a description if you're unsure what something is.
Speaking of descriptions, they're fantastic. Everything has an edge of humour in it. When you hover over an enemy, an object, or anything else in-game, you see a bit of funny flavour text about it.
The music is also amazing. I first got interested in the game when I've heard its main theme, which is very beautiful with great vocals, but even the tracks that play during missions are also great.
I've been enjoying the game so far and started a new campaign already. I would highly suggest to play the first game on an Easy or Casual difficulty level to get familiar with the game. After that, the higher difficulty levels don't seem as bad anymore.

Boo Bunny Plague is a....... . . ... .. .. ?!?!?!?!!?!?!?
Wait. What the crap did I just play?
BBP is a musical action-adventure where you play as an idiot robo-rabbit. He's the non-sequitor type so sometimes you have to leave the review in the microwave for a couple minutes so it can cool. He has a few friends but they're as useless as PEAS AND CARROTS. Seriously though I'm going to break it down. This is a short game (I consider this a plus) and you'll spend most of it fighting bosses and questioning reality.
I'll give points for getting the humor right. For the most part it's good-natured, and I even got a few laughs out of it. Even when the jokes miss I'm usually in a state of shock thinking "What? Did they do that? Are they really doing this? whAT?" so I just sorta gloss over them. BBP also has a really good soundtrack, which I suppose is expected considering that this game classifies itself as a musical.
And then there's the game-play...hmm. As I said, this game is mostly boss-fights, and they aren't too bad. I wouldn't put them at the level of Platinum (the developer), I probably wouldn't even put them at the level of U.S. Gold (remember those guys?) The boss-fights are sloppy, suffer from weak mechanics, and yet they aren't too bad. They're certainly functional, and this game deserves kudos for putting forth the effort to make every boss different. Some bosses even require different strategies, which is not something you see everyday. Also there's an incentive to finding every guitar, as bosses tend to be weak to their special effects. The rest of the game is spent killing vikings, there is a platforming section, and don't forget the part where you dodge rocks while crossing a rainbow.
Did I mention this game is short? Short games are underrated these days. I probably could have beaten this game in under 2 hours if I didn't want to kill so many vikings (hate those nerds). You can play through this game, get 90% of the achievements in a single run, and even if all you remember about it is: "Things happened and then I saw some credits", it's still probably better than grinding out another experience level in some J-RPG or eliminating all of those crazy Russians that have infiltrated your base for the 1,356,742th time.
All that said, don't drop whatever you're playing just to shoot through this game. Objectively* speaking, Boo Bunny Plague is not a good game. It has heart & spunk though, and sometimes you just gotta have a little of both. If you ever find yourself undecided on what to play next. If you're wondering whether you should play Shadow of Mordor, or Bayonetta 2, or Civilization: Beyond Earth. This is the perfect time to play Boo Bunny Plague. Don't try to make sense of this decision, just roll with it.
*Yes I totally just used the O word in a review. OH WELL.

Overall there are some good laughs and decent boss fights to be found in Boo Bunny Plague. The boring levels are for the most part forgivable, as the player knows they are working towards the next interesting boss fight or funny musical interlude. My main criticism is that the combat lacked depth and level enemies didn't vary enough. For the price Boo Bunny Plague is definitely worth a play through and has earned 6 out of 10 from me.
STORY
I actually really enjoyed the crazy storyline of Boo Bunny, and loved the ridiculous face-offs against some pretty famous gods of Viking mythology. I have to reinforce though, this game is a musical as well as an action adventure, and for the most part the songs littered throughout the game are very creative and funny, but occasionally out stay their welcome.
GAMEPLAY & COMBAT
Gameplay and combat in Boo Bunny, is simple, with the player being able to slip straight into this game and get the hang of it quickly. This straight forward control systems seems like a blessing initially, but soon becomes the weak point of the game. With a one button combo system, a difficult to use block mechanic, clunky movement controls and a touchy camera, things get stale quickly but this is alleviated slightly through some fun boss fights.
Fighting against gods like Thor and Tyr are exciting, and the challenge in this combat is in trying to analyse the patterns and work out their weakness. I am torn about the control system in Boo Bunny Plague, on the one hand it is boring when implemented in each level, but when considered in the realm of boss fights it is still clunky but far more entertaining. I won't go into any more detail about the boss fights as they are the core of the game, but I will say there is one boss in particular that has a very clever design.
VISUALS
Graphically, Boo Bunny looks like an early cell shaded game from the PS2/Xbox era, though I am not sure whether this was done to make the game more feasible to create or as an art style choice. At any rate I think this dated-vintage look works for the game and apart from the odd clipping and collision detection issues I enjoyed the visuals on the whole.
MUSIC
Boo Bunny's music is a central point of the game, and I found myself having a good chuckle through many of the songs. There is the option to purchase the deluxe edition, including the soundtrack and a couple of other goodies, but the songs in my opinion are a listen once affair, and are more entertaining when heard in context.

For an actual review:
The combat in this game is incredible and satisfying. It feels legitimately skill based, even though there are levels and gear. A skilled, ungeared low level player can still totally dominate an unskilled person with everything unlocked and geared out. It feels like it would be pretty pointless to try to get min/max-y with this game as no matter what small advantages you give yourself with gear, proper allocation of attribute points, and an "optimized" combat deck, someone who really feels the flow of their moveset, and just has better instinct/skill is going to win, almost every time.
The story is pretty meh, feels like its setting up for more (hopefully). I dont really know what more to say about it honestly, there isnt much there.
Really if this game had more content for the PvE mode, it would be one of my favorite games in a while. Im not even entirely sure what it needs, maybe like dungeons of sorts, instanced zones with several mini bosses and a main boss at the end? An actual tower to climb where enemies get more powerful and in higher numbers the further you go up? Im not sure, but it definitely needs something.
tl;dr Amazing concept, wonderful execution, super satisfying combat brought down by server issues and a general lack of things to do.

Story/Characters -
There is next to no story in this game. The only story to speak of is that you are employed by who I assume to be Kyu to manage her camgirl operation. That is it and as for characters well..they all have little bios you can read about them and they all have appealing designs but aside from the occasional lines they speak when you interact with them there is little to no characterization which I was honestly fine with when it came to the original Huniepop girls because I already got to know them before but I could honestly care less about most of the new girls. At the end of the day though this isn't the kind of game you play for character or story, I mean did anyone play Diner Dash for the story?
Visuals/Sound -
Okay I know I am in the minority here but I actually don't mind and even enjoy the art direction. True I would have preferred the visuals of Huniepop but considering this is a spin-off and not a sequel I am okay with them experimenting when it comes to the art and honestly I think it looks pretty good. Its more cartoony and less anime looking sure (though the anime-esque qualities are there) but its bright, colorful, and fun to look at. It's not quite as "sexy" as the last game either but that wasn't the main reason I liked Huniepop anyway, not to mention the developer clearly states that the erotic qualities of this game were meant purely for comedy purposes and not for fap material (unlike the last game which was kind of a combination of the two).
As for the music it is a bit repetitive but it still has the same fun and poppy sound as the last game, it serves its purpose. The sound effects are all really appealing and aid in making the game more fun. The voice acting much like the first game isn't AAA quality but the cast all clearly has talent and do a pretty good job.
Gameplay -
This game is essentially like those old sim management games (again like Diner Dash) mixed with those clicker style games you find on mobile all the time. Yeah it isn't very deep and the replay value is limited to unlock-able outfits and high-scores but that is honestly what I was expecting out of this games and you know what? I had fun, yeah it won't be something I will be playing months from now but it is fun to pick up and play here and there and can honestly be pretty addictive. As far as these kinds of games though I think this deserves to stand among the best of them (for one NOTHING is locked behind a wait or pay model like a ton of newer games of this type).
Verdict -
The biggest difference between this game and the first one for me is that the first game was a "don't judge a book by its cover" scenario. On the surface it just looks like another ecchi visual novel game with candy crush thrown into the mix and in its basics yeah thats what it was but the visual novel aspect stood out with its fun characters and humorous approach to its erotic aspects not to mention one of the most addictive and surprisingly deep bejeweled style puzzle mechanics out there. This game however is something that I honestly feel like you'll know immediately whether or not you'll enjoy it. If you like this style of game and don't mind the art change then you'll probably like this game, if not then you likely won't. This game aside from some similarities with the humor and some returning characters is NOTHING like the first game so don't assume that because you liked the first game that you will like this one they are two different beasts and deserved to be critiqued as such and not constantly compared.

I just finished up playing this game today. I backed Among The Sleep (Krillbite Studio﻿) on Kickstarter﻿ last year, and while my recommendation is "with reservations" (particularly at the game's $20 price point, for an approximately 2-hour experience), this was certainly a game I felt was worth playing, and I'm glad that I helped crowdfund it so that it could exist.
A "first person horror adventure", you play as a 2-year-old child who can crawl, toddle slowly, and do some limited climbing. After being put to bed, you go on an adventure through the sinister environment (your home at nighttime), first to rescue your teddy bear from the drier (your mother stole him from your crib to wash while you were sleeping), and then find your mother (progressing from your home to increasingly surreal environments).
The game has some light puzzle elements, but nothing challenging. At certain points (particularly if you knock something over and make noise), you'll have to hide from various "monsters" (a walking tree in the woods, or an animated coat from the closet, for example), but I had never actually SEEN any of these monsters until midway through the game when I turned up the brightness after repeatedly falling into bottomless pits that I was unable to see at the game's intended gamma setting (I had still known when I needed to hide due to audio cues).
While I can't say that the game does anything particularly remarkable with either the setting, story, or mechanical elements of the game aside from your avatar's status as a crawling, toddling two-year-old child, that alone was a novel enough experience for me to consider it worth playing.

This game, man, where to start?
I'll start with what I liked I guess. The art style, story, voice acting, sounds, level design, virtual reality compatability, and concept as a whole are all generally great. Its a very nice game to look at, even though I didn't play it at it max settings, it still looked great, I mean, there are plenty of games that look a hell of a lot better, but coupled with its art style it does look very good indeed. The sounds are also very well done, they add a real eery atmosphere to the already weird yet interesting environment, one that would suggest you and your Teddy Bear companion are never alone. The story is also fantastic, with a seemingly paranormal setting, the ending outcome of the story is obvious when you take into consideration the fact that you play as an infant child yet provides an answer to the puzzling chapters of the game. The voice acting, although there isn't much of it, is very well done. The voice acting of your Teddy Bear is perfect, as it conveys a nice friendly tone with a dash of authority and protection, similar to that of a brother and companion. The voice acting of your Mother brilliantly shows the things a mother experiences with their young children, and how a child may percieve her. I don't own an Oculus Rift myself, or anything that does a similar job, but, using one with this game would have been such a cool experience. Finally, the idea of taking the place of a child is indeed, clever, as its puts a complete twist on your perception of the world, as you see the events infront of you, and all you can think is that its some sort of paranormal ghost, or demon, yet come the end you mearly had to look at the world through a scared toddlers eyes.
Now, the parts that I personally did not like. The length of the game, the optimization, and some of the balancing for the monsters. Honestly, when I finished I was a bit disappointed at the length of the playable story, from what I remember there was only 6 chapters, according to Steam, I've only played 2 hours of it, and I was afk for a decent amount of that, so I'd say it was an hour to an hour and 45 minutes or so depending on how well you solver puzzles, get past monsters etc. I also felt that the optimization of the game wasn't great, as I've played games with a lot more going on in them at a lot better framerate, not that my PC is in fact the knees of the bee, but this may be as simple as it being more suited to NVidia graphics rather than AMD (which I use). Finally, on one chapter, I felt like it was a little hard to escape past the monster, this may be my fault, but it did seem a little unbalanced due to the limited speed and defense the player has. Most of the things I have a problem with though, could be fixed with patches and DLC.
Overall, I would heartily recommend this game to anyone who enjoys puzzle-horror games, as this one has a good blend of the two, as well as a well written story, terrifying set of monsters, eery setting and a very good sense of immersion. I'd give it a 7.9/10 and am very happy with the amount of I money paid for the game.

First of all I would like to say, if you ever see this game on sale, pick it up, no question.
Among the sleep is one of those games, comparable to journey, where the actual gameplay tends to step aside for the atmosphere and the meaning of the game. Though this game is a "horror" game, it dosen't feel too much like one, mostly puzzles and an errie enviroment to boot. On top of that the game is quite easy, you could probably go through it without dying once (which I could say on your first playthrough would be quite hard to do, as juding what places you are and aren't allowed to drop to are a bit odd).
Mostly what you'll be doing in this is solving several easy puzzles and once in a while hiding from a monster that only appears in a few parts of the game, which I would have to say is my biggest complaint. Many people talk about the length of the game, but to me, the game felt as long as it needed to be (besides the kinda abrupt ending that felt like it was a tad lazy). One thing I will say though, is keeping in mind that the game is easy, you should explore the levels, look at the drawings. The levels have all these extra areas to explore, not to artificially add to the length, but to discover and add to the game.
Overall the game is great, if you see it on a sale, pick it up no question. If you are looking for a game that is going to hit your feels and stick with you for a while after, and don't mind the $20 USD price tag, this might be what you're looking for.

I've been a fan of the Stronghold series ever since buying Stronghold 1 at its original release. I loved the combat, economy, strategy, and building aspects of the original, and each successive Stronghold release was an improvement over its predecessor.
I missed the initial release of Stronhold 3 due to raising two daughters that prefered playing "Smash" and "Kart" console games with their dad instead of my "old people" games on PC. And although I had not played 3, I had read the reviews and heard the reactions, and was very aware of the negativity surrounding it, but it just didnt seem possible. A Stronghold game that was not only dissapointing to the series, but possibly the worst game to be released that year. It was unthinkable to me, and I would not believe it until I played it myself.
That day came not long after creating my Steam account. After finding the Stronghold 3 store page, I was instantly taken aback at the bright red thumbs down sitting in its info box and the feeling of "any hope that 3 wasnt that bad" slowly left me. It only took a few minutes into the first mission that I finally accepted the truth, Stronghold 3 is a terrible game.
I cant recommend Stronghold 3 to my fellow gamers. If you find it on sale for $3.00 or less, then maybe, but only if you are a fan of the series. If you've never played any games in the series, then I suggest starting with any of the prior Stronghold games, as each is an excellent example of what is great about PC gaming and well deserving of all the praise they have received.
I personally feel Legends is the pinnacle of the series at this point, but Im holding out hope that someday we will see "Stronghold 4 coming soon" in our news feed and that it will make us forget about the travesty known as Stronghold 3.

This is an enjoyable RTS game, as far as it goes. It includes some relatively unique mechanics and can be a lot of fun. Unfortunately, there are some major drawbacks, which, hopefully, the developers will remedy soon:
1. Overwhelming micromanagement. At present, you cannot do anything but look around the map while in pause mode. This means that if you have more than a handful of "bricktrons," they can be impossible to control in a timely manner, much like herding cats, especially consdering #2.
2. Lag. As the number of units and structures in the game increase the lag gets extremely frustrating as it can take several seconds (up to about 15-20) for your units to respond to a direct order. The developers seem to have based this game on the brictrons having a modicum of intelligence in that they can determine, on their own, the priority of the next task on the todo list (subject to any priorities you assign in the UI). The cost of this is that it takes time for the bricktrons to deduce this priority and, depending on the map and mode (Sandbox, Invasion, or Conquest), can literally make or break your game.  BTW, Invasion mode is, unwinnable, like any castle defense game. The best you can hope for is surviving multiple waves of bad guys ("Corruptrons").
3. Need for Optimization: Some might say the lag problem is the fault of old or less powerful equipment. While this may have some truth to it, the game needs to be tweaked and optimized. It's a bit of a stretch to expect people to go out and drop a couple of $K to be able to play a $25 game. (I say this as strictly a PC player. I do not own nor do I play consoles, so I have no idea what problems or costs might be related to those game systems.)
Having said all of this, I still would recommend this game. It's fun (to a point) and is reasonably priced in today's market.  I have only played the game for 5 hours or so, at the time of this review but so far the entertainment value has been about $5/hour, or about equal to seeing a movie. But the longer I play the game, the cost of entertainment decreases, unlike seeing a movie multiple times.
What remains to be seen is where the devs will take this promising game as it matures.  IMHO.
UPDATED 9/24/2017: After several more hours of game time, I want to add a few more items to my list of fixes needed.
4. Pathfinding: As the game progresses and you have about a dozen bricktrons, you'll find that they easily get lost and sometimes wander off into enemy territory. One thing to watch for is if their path is blocked by fallen bricks, etc., but beyond that pathfinding degrades quickly at about 12 bricktrons.  Coupled with lag as your structures increase, late game activities involve a lot of work if you are to survive.
5. AI: The AI seems to either go to sleep or is unable to handle complex situations. For example, say you build a wall that's 2 rows deep. If the outer layer gets damaged to the point where you need to replace bricks (not covered by a repair task), the AI doesn't seem to understand that you are patching a hole and the hole in the outer layer persists.
Still giving this a thumbs up in hopes the devs will fix these problems.

An inspired Cel-Shaded adventure (with it's share of bugs) I'd have a hard time not reccomending this game.
First off, It's built in unity. You know what that means for the most part but for those of you that don't basically put it has next to no options graphically wise. Not that it's needed. The game's style outweighs the look. Boo Bunny aims for a comic book style with it's Cel shaded graphics (see Windwaker, Cel Damage, Sly Cooper) even so far as to include comic book style BAMFs and POWs.
The Audio has to be the strangest and best part of the game though. Aside from the general audio strangeness (It's quiet at some points and louder in others) the soundtrack is one of the most amusing and head scratching bouts of confusion in the game. I found myself just staring at what was going on and laughing. The VO work could leave something to be desired but again it awkwardly fits the whole game.
Gameplay wise, it's a little less. Bunny moves very awkwardly at least by modern standards. I found the KB + M controls more comfortable than the X360 controls but I guess that comes to preference. It's very much inspired by old school hack n slash games though, so the awkward movement and janky animations are almost endearing at the same time but that's probably the old nostalgia goggles making me think that.
There are a few bugs that I've encountered, Bosses shooting through walls, enemies bounce around sometimes and (although not a bug) the hitboxes seem really weird. Heck, I'm writing this review right now because the game crashes after I Alt+Tabbed out.
Difficulty is also a little strange. At the start, the regular enemies will kick your buns while the bosses go down without so much as a whimper. The first five bosses fell for the most part without even landing one hit on me.
The game lacks some explination too but it's almost part of the fun to try to figure out the bosses weaknesses.
I feel like with a little bit more polish, BBP could be a beyond great game but for me right now it's just sitting at really good. It's a fun game, give it a shot.
SIDENOTE: The crash I just mentioned wiped all my data. It looks like BBP only saves your game when you actually select quit from the menu. Disheartening but it wasn't overly hard to get to where I was.

Short description: Altered The Binding of Isaac.
The shop description uses pretty words and says you keep the "lessons" learned between playthroughs, considering the theme you might believe you keep abilities or passives for subsequent playthroughs; you don't, the system is actually a point reward every floor, the harder floors giving more points, which after your death you can spend in the main menu for passives, which not only minor, are limited in acquisition, they are in no way game-changing, for example, improved 15% crit chance while in short range of your target. If in Isaac your success depended on farming exploits or rolling useful items at the start, here it is even more randomized. Although there is a leveling system in the game, when you level you can choose between two abilities, some with partially detrimental effects, but worse, even these options are random abd you can easily get a nearly worthless roll every time. Frankly, that's not difficulty, that's merely luck-based gameplay, akin to playing dice, as your natural projectile and such can be nearly useless in most situations.
Additionally the rooms are cluttered with big junk that not only stays in your way, but actually have uneven, rough hit detection and often hold you in place if you walk near enough, making you that more vulnerable.
Yet again, if you liked Isaac, you might like this more randomized version (you could finish Isaac without a single item if you were good, here you'll be struggling with movement and projectile issues.), if you haven't played a roguelike before, try Isaac before coming around this.

This has to be about the worst computer chess game I've ever seen. The whole layout is cumbersome and unintuitive. The AI presets are wildly imbalanced (IF you manage to find them in the first place). You will NEVER get a satisfying win from the Fritz engine because it resigns every time it gets into a position where you can force mate in several moves whether you saw it or not. The 3D engine is poor and hit or miss whether it works at all. It's not just a case of "you can do anything with this engine but it's not for beginners" it's more like "the engine is quality at its highest settings (other than the fact that full depth analysis seems to take forever) and it has a highly extensive openings system (that you will never work out how to learn from)". Even chess enthusiasts who are perhaps swayed by Fritz's background as a 'serious' program should steer clear. About the only novel addittion here are the funny voiceovers and even they become just annoying after a short while. Do yourself a favour and go pick up one of the old Chessmaster games instead.

Fritz 13 is the last 'Fritz' by the original authors - version 14 used the Pandix engine by Gyula Horváth, and the forthcoming version 15 is apparently going to use one by Vasik Rajlich, who had his Rybka engine's world titles stripped for plagiarism. They are doubtless "better" engines in terms of being able to beat Fritz 13, but even on the weedy hardware (an AMD A4 cpu) I run Windows on and even though it is limited to using only one CPU, Fritz 13 is looking at many millions of positions a second, and has checked every one within 20 moves within very few seconds. This means that unless you are a grandmaster, on its best settings it will destroy you every single time.
So why get it?
Well, you don't have to play it on its best settings - it can adapt its level of play to yours - and, more usefully, you can use it to learn how to beat other humans by showing where you're going wrong.
Don't forget to read the help files: there's a lot of impressive things this can do.

I even found some user designed 2d pieces you can install in you're fonts directory.
On the downside deleting games in the database and uninstalling/reinstalling didn't work as expected. I prefer a program to remove everything (files, registry entries etc.) when you uninstall. Because it didn't I deleted some files manually and when I reinstalled they didn't get installed so I ended up using a system restore.
Overall it's best chess software I've used so far with a good interface, lots of features and flexibility.

(Very minor spoilers)
This game is set before The New Order, but in whichever order you play it in, it will still make sense and be fun.
In short, it's an insanely fun 'old-school' shooter that is worth the money and the time you would spend into it. It's rather short, but on a sale I can't help but recommend it. Admittedly, while the game doesn't start off very nicely (it does, but during the first chapter there is a super linear forced-stealth section which really feels at odds against the rest of the game), it continues wonderfully and really takes you into some great spectacular breath-taking locations, such as Castle Wolfenstein and Wulfburg (Wulfburg is a village and one of the main areas in the game, where you get to meet probably the most characters in).
There isn't as much character development as in The New Order, which isn't necessarily a bad thing but it fails to compare story wise. Gameplay wise, it remains identical to The New Order with a few really badass weapon additions such as the Grenade Pistol. As you progress, and towards the end of the game, you get to meet the Nazi Zombies that we may or may not love. If zombies is what is bringing you into this experience, you won't get too much of it and it's only valid from Chapters 6 to 8. The graphics are actually very nice especially in Wulfburg, but the game definitely looks old. Wolfenstein 2: The New Colossus is running on the id Tech 6 engine, which is the same as DOOM (2016) and that is DEFINITELY a fantastic thing to look forward to!
Also something that quite bugged me was having to press E every time you wanted more ammo, armor or health. This could really take you away from the action especially when it gets tense. In DOOM 2016 you do not have to press E to get anything, so I think they should follow the same system in Wolfenstein 2 (coming 2017 can't wait!).
The game's music, voice acting and overall atmosphere surround it are all great. I especially love William 'B.J.' Blazkowicz' voice. This game also has Swastikas, which are very appealing to look at. Already better than Call of Duty "WW2" (Lenny)
Anyway, to conclude, it's definitely a worthwhile standalone expansion (pretty similar to Red Dead Redemption Undead Nightmare, the GTA IV episodes and Far Cry 3 Blood Dragon). I give this expansion an 8/10. Truly fun.

In Among the Sleep you take control of a two-year old child. The game starts with an opening scene where you celebrate your second birthday. Your mum feeds you some cake before taking you upstairs with a birthday present delivered by someone who your mother does not invite in (maybe the father). The gift turns out to be a teddy bear, which comes to life and acts as your guide throughout the game. Shortly after you are off to bed, you wake up in the middle of the night to your cot being dragged across the room before tumbling over. After some wondering you realize that your Mummy is not in her bed and you set off on an adventure of sorts to find her again. It is clear that you are in a dream world but the further you go into the game, the darker it becomes.
The control system is good. You have two main modes of getting around, walking and crawling. Crawling is faster, but you ca not carry anything or hug your teddy (he gives you light when you do so). While walking you are slower but from the standing position you can climb up onto furniture and boxes. In fact all the animations throughout the game are good. A cool little feature is when you pause the game, the child brings his hands up to cover his eyes.
The graphics are good so far, could be a few more details but nothing big to complain.
Sound plays a huge part in the game. Teddy will talk to you sometimes to help guide you through the story but usually you are listening to the sound of your mum humming a lullaby with you trying to head towards the source. Also you can hear some eerie music, creaky doors or floorboards or other objects moving or falling.
The game itself is too short. I finished it within 109 minutes.
Among the Sleep is not scary at all but it has a great atmosphere. The ending of the game is pretty shocking. I will not tell you anything, you have to play and see it by yourself.
I can recommend Among the Sleep but you should wait for a discount, 19,99€ is a bit too much for only around 110 minutes of gaming.

Among The Sleep is an atmospheric, puzzling game that plays like a horror game but is technically an atmosphere test in disguise. Finally a studio that creates horror that decided to take a frickin' break from all the blood, gore and overexcessive monster designs. Now we have a monster that is completely black, hides in shadows, and each form of it rumored to be the child's parents. I'd favor to talk about each aspect of the game and what it does well.
THE STORY: 60% 6/10
To be honest I didn't like the story, because it didn't make any sense. Also it was too abbrieviated and ended way too fast. It would be nice to have a couple more levels according to the little video at the end of the ATS demo. Those in my opinion looked way nicer and refined. Also if you were to add the missing levels as DLC I would screech, that would be nice. So basically the story is you are a two year old child who goes to sleep one night only to be awoken by some noises and a supposed paranormal being. It is only until you  find out your mother is missing  and see the first monster you know things are wrong. You take your teddy bear and venture through three stages *Five technically throughout the entire game*. It's... a nice concept but as I said. It doesn't make sense and it's too brief. At least explain in the game how this happened!
THE LEVEL DESIGN: 100% (Solid 10/10)
The level design is ABSOLUTELY GORGEOUS! I seriously love every single part of it and it's entirety. It kept my one, colorful eye on the screen and it's like a replacement for the story. The story is low brow but the graphics are the highlight of this game. Every single level is amazing and beautiful. It's odd how something so spooky can be such eye candy at the same time. The level design even reminded me of myself since when I was younger I had odd, strange dreams from time to time that resembled this game, and after I saw Among The Sleep's level design I flipped my♥♥♥♥♥♥and went totally crazy over this game. I'm even working on a game similiar to this that will be created on Unity, *Fun fact, Among The Sleep was also made on Unity*
THE CHARACTERS 90% (9/10)
Now there aren't many characters in Among The Sleep. *If you don't count the monsters, I'm not counting them since they've got no personalities and just want to capture you*, pretty much we have the child themself, the child's mother, Teddy, and the supposed father of the child which we can get traces of in the introduction of the mother in the first chapter. I'll talk about the mother first. The mother is the supposed main antagonist (due to her connection with the odd tree monster in the fourth act) By the end she seems to be a redeemed villain and still loves the main protagonist. Now we should talk about Teddy. He is one of the main protagonist alongside the child and he helps them manuever through the nightmarish parts of his dreams. The ending which involved Teddy is very creative and I love his character.
CONCLUSION:
Among The Sleep is a great horror game to play at night due to the buildup and spook the game brings. I recommend this game, it gets a 9/10!

Among the Sleep. Holy Russel Crowe. I cannot stop the praise shooting from my mouth. I Let's Played this for my channel, and you can find the footage in it's entirety here.
The premise of Among the Sleep is you are a two year old toddler, trying to find your mommy in what has become a living, breathing nightmare. While the game never stops reminding you of that one simple goal, it doesn't wave it around in your face like others do; it is the main objective of the smaller storyline but you are not constantly bombarded with it enough to make you feel uncomfortable.
The cast of characters is small, featuring only three main characters (You the Toddler, Teddy, and your Mom). The voice acting, however, is marvelously done. For the small cast and the small script, the voicework imbeds you in the game. For that matter, the entire game's soundscape is gorgeous from the lullaby-like background music to the sometimes spine-vibrating sound effects. Everything makes you feel as if you truly exist in this world, alone.
The level design is beautiful, taking items one would see laying around a household and twisting them into mighty structures; a park becomes a shadow-cast forest, a set of drawers is an insurmountable mountain, closets are deep caverns where the darkness goes to cling... While there are only four main level segments in the game, they are sprawling, each taking thirty minutes to traverse through in their entirety and every corner beautifully defined and articulated.
The gameplay itself is simple, you control a toddler. You can crawl, pickup objects, walk, run, and hug your teddy. While very simple, you'll be using all of this to ford a nightmarish take on reality, collecting and interacting with objects, engaging in some platforming, and navigating very dark areas. Occasionally you'll come face to face with a monster, which will scare you, making it difficult to see and navigate, as well as filling your ears with the game's version of the traditional, 'jump scare noise.' In darker segements, you can hug your friend, Teddy, to generate some light for you to navigate. While this makes things easier to do, in many cases you won't ever need to hug teddy as you can navigate in the dim lighting.
The game is as short as it really needs to be, only clocking in at about two hours. The storyline isn't overtly complex, so instead of forcing more unessecary content out of it, the devs made this game short and (not so) sweet when it came to the story itself. While many people may not realize it until the end, this game is based around one very pevelent social issue we face today, and it will shock you to your core when you reach the game's finale.
Overall, Among the Sleep is a great game. It's short, but sweet, and while it does have little replay value, I'd love to play it again with a loved one. Every production point of the game is absolutely beautiful, but sadly it is pitifully short. If you're not convinced, wait for the price to drop by a few dollars in a sale, then pick it up. You will not regret it.

A baby's first horror adventure; A rather intriguing idea which unfortunately is not explored in a wholly satisfying manner. You play as a baby whisked into a dark slumberland with your mother ominously gone missing. Dreaming up a way to find and save her only by walking, crawling and grabbing objects is the idea here. A bit of adventuring is required, then.
I don't generally have a problem with games featuring very little actual gameplay if the story, environments or the general atmosphere are interesting enough. None of these elements are that compelling in Among the Sleep. The sound design is a strong point and manages to create a few heebie-jeebies, but for the most part it's just you toddling along in pitch-black corridors, bumping into furniture and other things in the night. There's not really that much to do, and the levels, while metaphorically rich, are a bit too abstract for their own good.
Also I must have played a few too many horror games, since for me the most frightening figure of the whole game was the supremely unnerving walking and talking teddybear, who is actually supposed to be your friend and mentor. I think the way the game introduces him is done completely wrong, unless they were specifically aiming to present him/it as a suspicious character. Never trust the teddy.
Anyhow, after a couple of hours of wandering in the dark doing the same things over and over again, the game ends. The story does not end up being a complete waste, but overall, I was hoping for a somewhat stronger finale. After all, the gameplay stuff in between start and finish wasn't that brilliant either. I really wanted to like this game, but it's just too flawed. Both the single player and multiplayer modes left me frustrated. The AI that manages your workers has a lot of problems. The pacing is REALLY SLOW. The combat, tunneling, and crafting mechanics are difficult to manage and the AI tends to trip over itself, forcing you to go in and micro your units for basic tasks. Honestly, this game should be in Beta so that the developers can get the feedback that they clearly need.
A few examples of things that really annoyed me:
1. I had plenty of planks, rope, and fabric stockpiled next to a workbench. I tried multiple times to make archer kits. Nothing happened. Then, I tried directly assigning a Bricktron to the task. The worker wandered around aimlessly for several seconds before giving up and moving to another task. Mind you, I was desperately trying to fend off an attack while this was happening.
2. Many times, you go to build a wall, and the AI isn't smart enough to build it in the right order to avoid creating impassable obstructions or walling out your workers.
3. You just don't have very many workers, and they tend to do stupid things, making their tasks go slow. Supposedly, you are supposed to expand your base and get more workers using capture wards. I never got that far, since it takes a while to make wards, they are very vulnerable to attacks, and you constantly have to babysit the AI. Don't forget, you can't just tell them to build a ward (even though it's a "structure"), you have to "craft" it, THEN have a worker place it as part of a "construction task."
4. Iron is challenging to obtain, especially since you have no idea if a particular tunnel or quarry might produce some. This is a problem given how important the resource is to crafting.
This game can't decide if it's a castle building simulator, a tower/castle defense game, a crafting game, an RTS game, etc. It tries to do too much and ends up doing it poorly. If a "version 2" of this game comes out, I might be interested in taking another look, but not until then.

The release of Empire was an utter travesty on the Total War series, and while many of the original game-breaking problems were fixed, there remain remenants of a rushed production and bad decision making, worst of which is a weak AI that does not even begin to border on logical. You will be lambasted by offers to trade your major provinces for tiny island colonies almost every turn. In battle the AI will ignore your regiments of infantry and rush through them in an attempt to attack your artillery. You will have to take almost every province of a nation before they'll decide to give you peace, so you can deal with the other four nations that declared war on your last turn.
There are many bugs still in this game that at times greatly removes any sense of pleasure in playing it. Cavalry clipping into buildings and being stuck, some armies completely ignoring your intercepting armies and rushing around them to do nothing more than raid your farm, and artillery aims for the extreme left of a formation at all times. Simply opening the government tab sometimes greets you with a giant, orange square as a graphical glitch one would think CA would have taken the time to fix.
It is a shame because the scope of this game is great, and no one else had done a project like Empire, but that is solely what makes it playable. Had CA any competition, Empire would have failed. I would not suggest getting this game at full price, not even $20 to be frank, and warn you against purchasing this rushed shell of a game of what could have been.

This game tries very hard to be Binding of Isaac. In some ways, it succeeds, but in others, it fails.
Our Darker Purpose features a fairly dark storyline involving rogue children in a boarding school of sorts, with a faculty akin to The Addams Family. Gameplay is very reminiscent of Binding of Isaac, as are the controls. Instead of bombs, you have chalk, which you can use to create puffs of chalk dust that damage and stun enemies caught within. Items are gained from killing minibosses or found in rooms similar to Binding of Isaac, though the game is much less accomodating and even the item rooms are generally full of traps and environmental hazards waiting to kill you. You have a dodge roll available (on a 2ish second cooldown) that can be used to move quicker or get out of tight spots, and works well with. You get health potions in the form of juice boxes that can be stored and used when needed, and rather than crying to damage enemies, you use some sort of magic to throw fireballs (this isn't really explained, at least in the first two chapters, which is what I've seen of the game as of the time of this writing). Completing levels and achievements earns you a currency which can be spent on unlocking permanent bonuses (extra juice box slots, for instance), and there's a number of passive bonuses that can be toggled on or off (you have a limited number of slots to fill with these, so choosing a set that works for your playstyle is key). This allows for a feeling of progression even when you aren't actually winning. This is good.
The game has more RPG and less arcade feel than Binding did - you have a character sheet of sorts with actual stats like crit chance, dodge chance, damage resistance and hit points, all visible to you at any time you care to look. Items increase or decrease these stats, and damage you deal or take is shown via floating numbers so there's much less guesswork than in Binding. Similarly, items tell you exactly what they do when you pick them up (or review them on your character sheet) so there's no need to try and figure out what that thing you just picked up does.
The game offers some interesting flavor / lore text attached to items, and bosses all come with a few paragraphs of lore (which becomes viewable when they're defeated), and occasionally after clearing a room the furnature (!) will have little conversations with each other that you can get tidbits of story hints from; I can't comment on the quality of the storyline conclusion (nor would I in a review such as this, but that's beside the point) as, as mentioned earlier, I haven't finished the game as of yet, but it's got enough mysterious elements to keep me interested.
The game isn't without flaws, though - the biggest of which, in my opinion, is the hitboxes. They're very illogical in some cases, and it becomes a matter of trying to memorize what each enemy's hitbox looks like so you can hit them reliably. It's difficult to explain this without illustrations, but some enemies have a hitbox covering their entire body, while some, the hitbox only covers their lower half, some have hitboxes that are wider or skinnier than the actual sprite, and the furnature / obstructions in the rooms have even stranger hitboxes - from some angles, shots will go through them, and from others, shots will 'hit' them without actually touching them. This is by and large the most frustrating thing about the game, to me. It also doesn't help that the characters are very tall and thin, for the most part, so it's significantly more difficult to dodge something from the left or right than it is from the top or bottom, as your hitbox is significantly larger on those sides.
Some of the room layouts can seem pretty unfair, especially considering the hitbox problems noted above. A particular enemy may normally be no problem at all, but in certain rooms, because of the number of unkillable traps and obstruction placement, may result in losing 30+ hit points (out of the base 100) before being able to kill it. While this is, naturally, part of the game, the room layouts in Binding of Isaac never felt anywhere near this big of a factor.
The art style is very similar to Don't Starve (this may be a good thing or a bad thing, depending on your personal preference), and this art direction certainly doesn't detract from the experience. The animations feel a little lacking, though - characters have a 'walk left' and 'walk right' animation, and an 'attack' animation, but not much else. Granted most games of this style use a similar system, but it feels much more noticeable here than in others due to the detail of the sprites.
Overall, the game is quite fun. It doesn't feel as polished as Binding of Isaac did, but if you enjoyed Binding's gameplay, you'll likely enjoy this, too.
The Good:
- Flavor / Lore is well done and interesting
- Dodge roll mechanic leaves you feeling more in control
- Items are interesting and varied
- Gameplay is fairly addictive
- Has a definite 'Just One More Try' effect
- Bosses are varied and interesting (and numerous)
The Bad:
- Hit boxes are a little funky.
- Some room layouts feel unfair, even very early in the game
- Animations feel too lackluster considering the detail of the sprites
Overall Verdict:
Good game, worth the $15.

Now, my main concern for New Lands; I feel like it's great for new players, and that it's much of an upgrade from Classic, but did it really have enough content for an entirely new game? However, the addition of islands, new mounts, and these tweaks (as far as I can tell, I've only played to the third island, so take my review with a grain of salt) feels like it could have been added in a few separate updates. Nevertheless, I would reccomend this game over Classic, as it does have the fixes and gameplay additions that fans have been begging for since the game came out.
