I have played Boo Bunny plague for 2 hours. I thought it was alright, good for it’s price.
- Some of the dialogue is amusing and the music is cool
- Generally the actual combat isn’t very interesting and mainly consists of swinging an assortment of guitars at run of the mill enemies, but some of the later bosses were interesting
So your abilities in combat are limited to swing your equipped guitar and a manually activated protective shield that has a limited charge. There are no special moves aside from a third consecutive guitar swing which will do extra damage and have an area of effect. The charge of your shield will regenerate but health and shields can be replenished by picking up shield or carrot powerups which will respawn.
-----You can hit snowballs back towards ice men by swinging your guitar at them. But this wasn’t really very effective or particularly fun. So I usually just swung my guitar at most enemies without bothering to activate my shield because you can’t move or attack while shielded. When you are low on health you can just kite enemies around while you look for health pick-ups.
-----Other than that you can run. But there’s no dashing, sprinting or rolling. But I think that kind of feature would have been nice. One of the bosses will moves exactly as fast as you run and once you are in his range it is can be very difficult to avoid his attacks. That is until you learn to stand on top of vehicles which will explode causing him to be stunned. You can toggle run mode and move even slower by walking. But I’m not sure why you would want to do this.
-----Sometimes your robot friend will accompany you in battle and if you hit him he will fire his guns killing all enemies instantly within a short radius. He will despawn and reappear after sometime before you can activate this ability again.
-----At one instance I noticed that he had trouble finding a path out an area and got stuck. I had to go in and coax him out. I also noticed that you and some AI controlled characters will clip through some of the walls.
-----While you don’t really have any special attack you can equip different guitars which have different effects and deal more or sometimes less damage. New guitars are hidden around the different environments. I found my first new guitar by belting up a hippy. It was an acoustic and made love hearts appear when used. I’m not sure what was special about it aside from the comedic value. Some of other guitars I found were imbued with fire and lighting and did extra damage over time.
-----The first few bosses were pretty straightforward and not really challenging. Most of their attacks could easily be avoided just by side stepping or running away. There is almost always plenty of respawning health pickups you can use to replenish your life whenever it gets low.
-----It didn’t really start to get interesting or hard until I encountered the bosses War and then Famine. You couldn’t just simply beat the latter into submission, there is actually a special way to defeat her. Finding out what that was puzzled me for a fair while. After her the next boss Death was also challenging.
-----The games graphics definitely aren’t fantastic. But a fair bit of effort went towards populating the world with some colourful characters and some obvious parodies of the Thor featured in films over the last fer year and the band Slayer with a song and very a very Slayer like emblem.
-----The game is really more about the music. After all it is a musical. The fact that characters in the game frequently burst into song during cutscenes or even during the action was kind of cool. Real music is a nice touch.
-----In regard to dialogue and lyrics, not all of it was amazing. But some of it was amusing such as that of the Vikings who occasionally call out ‘Kill the rabbit’ like Elma Fudd.
-----The enemies that I encountered so far other than bosses were all vikings. Unless you count the robot bunny ‘competition’ and assembly line machines you encounter at the very beginning. I thought there would be more variety to the hostile entities you come across.
-----But their was a fair bit of variety to bosses you encountered. There was a giant toy robotic T-Rex, Thor God of Thunder posing as a ‘Village (person)’ construction worker and so on. The most interesting were the four horsemen of the apocalypse. Each was a variant of the Robot Bunny protagonist or one of his friends, the succubus, the elephant man and the military robot. A moment during the introductory cut-scene of the latter felt very reminiscent of Borderlands.
I enjoyed playing this game. For it’s price the game is pretty good. I think it’s worth taking a look at.

For the uninitiated, Epic Battle Fantasy 3 can be a really hard sell. It is my personal favorite RPG of all time, but most people will disagree with me. There is almost no story whatsoever, the overworld is small and very linear, and the hand-drawn art style, while I think it looks perfectly fine, will be a turn-off for some people.
However, this game has, in my opinion, the best battle system in any RPG I have ever played. It is simple to learn, yet has lots of depth. The abilities are very interesting to use, and the status effect system is very powerful, yet well-balanced.
Positives:
+Astoundingly-balanced battle system
+FREE
+Shorter RPG experience (for those who have little free time to play a 60+ hour RPG)
+Decent soundtrack
Negatives:
-Almost non-existent story
-Uninteresting overworld
Overall, while it is my all-time favorite RPG, I can't really justify giving it a 10/10, given the flaws it has. So, my personal score is 8/10. Give it an hour or two sometime, you might just fall in love like I did.

As someone who thought that this was going to be an easy 100% achievements, this is NOT TRUE! If you are just someone that is looking for a free, fun little retro inspired JRPG, and many jokes that refer to classic titles, then play this game, on Normal or Easy difficulty.
Why?
This game is HORRIBLY unbalanced!
As I tried to do a completionist run, I attempted the game on the hardest difficulty from the very start, Epic. From the very start I started to regret it. From the very beginning, you will be fighting 3+ monsters at a time. On top of that, while you only have attacks that ONLY hit one target once, monsters will have attacks that either attack you more than once, attack all your characters, have a chance to add a poison/stun per attack, or ALL OF THE ABOVE! From the very start of the game this is unfair, when you can basically be killed in 1 turn. You don't even learn spells/attacks that can attack more than once till you are almost at the first boss. So the game turns into a nightmare of a grind fest, killing all the enemies that you can up to a point, going back to town, then going from the start again to try and level up to fight the monsters that are killing you, get to the next screen where the monsters are harder, repeat to make very small progress.
Then when you managed to make it to the boss, bosses as you would expect, have tons of health. On top of that though, they will spawn endless amounts of enemies, and either have a healing spell, or the enemies they spawn have healing spells. These healing spells usually heal for more than the amount of damage you can deal. Because of this, the bosses can take almost an hour!
Another issue that started to arise was starting at chapter 3, enemies started having 1 HIT KO moves (very rarely,) and they spammed them! After reaching chapter 4, this was the main reason why I could not progress. If I was not able to kill all the monsters before they got to attack, they would use their 1HKO moves, and they more than likely hit me (probably because the game hated me.) Even using gear to increase my dodge chance to 80%+ didn't even help ever.
Having sunk 10 hours into 1 playthrough and only making to the 4th chapter, I had to give up. I could not deal with the painful grind that I had to do to level up my characters/gear. Being at lvl 26 and not even half way through the 4th chapter, and STILL struggle with the enemies with their bullsh*t 1HKO moves, multiple hit attacks with poisons/stuns, and just being damage sponges, it's not fun. This game is technically only 4 hours long, and this should not be that bad. I know that grinding is meant to be a part of these kinds of games, I'm not new to these games, and I've grinded FAR worse games than this, but this grind is only made painful on the very small progress you make, and how unbalanced it is. And the main overall story/plot isn't very interesting. I honestly didn't give a damn about anything or anyone.
Now, this is to all the people that are gonna say "You are just playing the game wrong." I've leveled up my gear, I'm maxed out my spells, I've done all the things that people have told other people, and none of that matters. I experimented and tried the game on Normal just to see if there was a huge difference. In 20 min I beat the 1st chapter...
PROS:
- Fun little retro inspired JRPG.
- Funny dialog. (But I didn't really care for it.)
- Runs great, never crashed.
- Good selection of different enemy types.
- Good amount of gear.
- Good amount of spells you can choose from.
- Short, can be beat in 4 hours (on Easy/Normal.)
- Very bright and colorful.
- Music is OK. (I ended up turning it off when I was grinding and listening to my own music.)
- Achievements. (You get an achievement for clicking on bewbs.
CONS:
- It's HORRIBLY unbalanced on harder difficulties.
- Enemies have cheap moves far too quickly into the game.
- Common Enemies have 1 Hit KO attacks and use them often.
- Side Quests are nothing but fetch quests and are quite dull.
- Playing on harder difficulties requires a nightmarish amount of grinding.
- Some may not like the art style.
- Some dialog is cringey.
If you are not a completionist, then play through this game on Easy/Normal, as it's an OK game (and it's free!) But this game is hell and unbalanced, and I simply can't recommend it for those reasons.

Wolfenstein: The Old Blood
"The alternative history, the violence, the horror of war and it never gets old"
Genre: First Person Shooter
Developer: MachineGames
Engine: id Tech 5
---------------------------------------------------------
The Old Blood (2015) is standalone prequel of The New Order (2014). You play as William B.J. Blazkowicz, the main protagonist of Wolfenstein, working with his partner “Wesley” to infiltrate Castle Wolfenstein and obtain a secret folder to locate General Deathshead Compound (main antagonist of The New Order) and stop their losing war.
The world represents an alternative history 1946 and set under the rule of German Technology become far more superior than anyone could expect as the game doesn’t hesitate to deliver minor details and strong background. It’s surprised that the game could deliver personality and perspective of each character in very short moments. They are memorable and well-written with strong background and great voice acting. You feel strong connection between The New Order and The Old Blood through cutscene and dialogues.
---------------------------------------------------------
The gameplay is mixed formula but well implemented between old school shooter and some modern mechanics. Fully arsenal, half-regenerated health system, smart cover, and dual wielding. The gunplay itself is very solid and gives satisfied feedback. Bullet impact, weapon recoil, sound, gore, and destruction are things you definitely expect from every fight. Enemies in The Old Blood are aggressive. They could flank you from side or behind, constantly toss grenade to flush you out of cover, or rush when you are in tight spot. Moreover, you’re free to play stealthy or gun blazing because of well level design that supports both routes.
Collectables and secrets are fun to hunt with interesting documentary. This include all classic levels from Wolfenstein 3D (1992). Challenge mode encourages player for smarter move to achieve best score.
---------------------------------------------------------
In the other hand, I feel like small RPG element is unnecessary to play in specific way and disconnect the game flows. The first level after prologue introduces player for stealth mechanics, but somehow it becomes too repetitive and tedious section. Pre apocalyptic Wulfburg has great open environment, but it’s very short and overwhelmed by undead force which is less threatening than Nazi enemies.
Excessive amount of health and armor in every corner could ruin an experience even on hardest difficulty. I also prefer optional pick up system as found myself running around area smashing pick up button during intense gunfight.
Engine id Tech 5 introduces great visual from distance and detailed character models. However, some environment textures look muddy in closed range and the engine still issues texture popping.
---------------------------------------------------------
Wolfenstein is more than shooting Nazis and emphasize single player experience at its best. People who are not familiar with this series can enjoy gameplay and understand the story as well. I highly expect improvement and innovation design on The New Colossus this year, third coming titles of this fantastic reboot franchise.

Fritz for Fun 13 is the best chess program I have played. Prior to this I played fritz 5.32 as white and Windows chess as black. In friend mode the program is quite sharp without being impossible. I've only played 3 games so far and each of them was very instructive. Fritz pushes the margin and makes you think. It doesn't play mechanically where you have to survive 20 moves then it makes an obvious blunder. It plays a full game and not a gauntlet you have to survive through. The 3d chess pieces and manual board orientation offers the perfect viewing angle as if you yourself were leaning over a chess board pondering.
It offers a lot of tools for practice and such but I play chess for fun and am not too critical. The evaluation profile window and the main engine window with the control board are staples of fritz for reviewing your games to see how you did. For positions where you don't understand why the computer uses the line it does in the main engine window you can use the analysis options to analyse a given position and it will show the branches saying why this and that doesn't work.
The only downside to Fritz for Fun 13 is it only supports one core. The only real downside to that is you can't use the 8 core Houdini engine to evaluate an opening in great depth and see what works and what doesn't(This is assuming you know the basic openings e.g. kings gambit declined, pirc, english, dutch ect.). You can get around that however by downloading the Arena GUI and running 8 core houdini from that.
Conclusion: Perfect game if you like playing chess for fun; this is to say you play to match your wits against the computer and not to memorize chess databases and pantomime.
After playing 13 games against the engine I found the friend mode to be too soft compared with fritz 5.32. You can blunder your way through a game and still win. With 5.32 I've played about 500 games and win on average 1 in 5. With fritz 13 I've played 13 games and have won 4 and lost 1. The longest time spent on one move might be 5 minutes. Longest game might be 20 minutes. I've played 50 minute games against 5.32 because it creates more difficult positions and if you make a single mistake you lose unless you are better than the base engine which I am not. Also it seems the fritz 13 engine has disappeared entirely. I only have the option to use the fritz 6 engine. The only way I have been able to get it back is to do a second install with the setup file which spreads files across multiple hard-drives.
I played another game against fritz and lost my queen at the beginning of the game and was down -6 and still managed to end up with a draw. I think I was even +3 eventually. I played another game where I had hanging pieces(trying out a new chess set) and the computer didn't capture them. Brutally obvious captures on the control board the computer ignores.
Aside from the generosity of fritz there is one particular position that I have difficulty playing against computers and that is roaming queen positions. e.g. Rook, minor piece, 2 pawns vs a queen with other pawns on the board. It's difficult simply because of the number of moves a queen can make on an open board and the computer calculates them all instantly. e.g. move 1 it can make five viable moves. Move two it can make 5 viable moves from each of its previous 5 viable moves. Continuing with induction by move 4 there is 625 move combinations(identifying the permutations is labor intensive). I have played many games over the course of my life. Good games, bad games, and everything in between. I thought that it was unlikely that I would ever come across a game that was not only barely functional, but also thoroughly uninteresting. Imagine my surprise when I finally stumbled across the opportunity to play Stronghold 3.
Things started with the tutorial. Everything went by fine. That was the last time things would be that way. Between the bizarre physics, frustrating collision detection, terrible AI, along with a long list of terrible design choices and a cynical approach to post-release support.
The very first real unit is able to access, the Spearman, is not the same Spearman from the original title. While the unit has the ability to throw a javelin, the usefulness of this tactic is negated by serval circumstances. Firstly, the unit is slow. Beyond slow. Think Swordsman from the original title, minus the extremely high defense, leaving them extremely vulnerable to archer fire. If the javelin was meant to counter this, it fails miserably. The pause between throwing, the limited range, and the way in which the AI selects targets renders the ability into a burden. Oddly, the Spearmen are more than adequate at destroying walls, much more so than catapults. The bad design extends to castle construction. No longer are you able to build elaborate, interconnecting wall systems. Any attempt to connect a section of wall to another section leads to a dead-end. You are also unable to control the thickness of the walls or add crenelations on your own. This is done for you, to the game's detriment.
Further defects are exhibited in the AI's inability to navigate around structures. In some cases, the AI simply stops moving before its destination is reached. This phenomenon extends to attacking. More than once, I have witnessed my units freeze in the middle of a fight. Ordering a new action does not have the intended effect, as units tend to freeze for a brief moment before carrying out the order. Any type of fine-tuned maneuvering is next to impossible. This proved to be a problem when I was forced to fight against the game's unpredictable physics engine.
Much like in the previous games, the player has the option to lay traps. Among these traps are flaming logs which a player may deploy against incoming infantry to devestating effect. However, the way the logs travel and the way the game calculates damage turn this feature into yet another pain. I have seen logs travel half-way across the map on a flat field, wiping out everything in their path. They need not be rolling, as merely touching the logs will instantly kill anything. Because the AI is terrible and has no sense of self-preservation, it will happily walk into a stationary burning log without hesitation. Oddly, flaming hay bales launched with considerably force do not damage the enemy in any way.
I would be more patient with these flaws if the game was not boring. The cut-scenes are concept pen-sketches narrarated over with decent voice acting, but are colorless and lack detail. None of the other characters speak. Compared to the characters in the orginal game, they are totally lifeless. There are no unique personalities, quirks or anything to distinguish one character from another beyond their name. The challenges, such as they are, can often be brute-forced. Instead of providing new tools, the game often snatches them away in favor of showing off gimmicks. Using the hay bale mission as an example, the player is presented with a night-assault. Beyond spawning archers and flinging flaming hay bales, there is little input on the player's part. The player is not allowed to build or produce or do anything other than address objective in as strict a way possible.
My main objective in playing this game was to decide whether Stronghold Crusader 2 was worth buying. Thankfully, playing this game has convinced me not to do this as the game has not been well maintained since its release more than half a decade ago. The game is still badly designed and little has been done to address this. I obtained this game in a bundle, along with the original games. I am glad that I did not pay for it directly.
Even on sale this game is not worth it.

ETW is one of my favourite ever TW games. Yes, it is bugged and some of its mechanics these days seem a bit cumbersome (in particular the many problems involving fortress siege battles).
However.
This is the game that first introduced ship battles into TW and it did so in a most splendid way. Once you have mastered sailing a few of those first rates in a line and actually firing when you want them to, the ship battles are a great joy to behold.
This is the game that also first did some satisfying gunpowder battles on a high level. The UI is nice and manageable and the battle landscapes show the first deviation from the rough landscapes of former games.
Also the scope is impressive. As the game was separated into three continents, you really had a sense that you were sending your army far, far away into unknown lands. They were realistically cut-off from your help. They had to establish themselves in a new territory or perish. I never again had this sense of unknown or adventure in any TW game.
So, yes, the game makes me more melancholic as the years go by, because like me it seems more and more of a relic, but in its day it was great fun. And yes, it still is fun, if you add that extra bit of patience for a bit of software that was programmed ten years ago.

This game shows a great deal of promise and has some interesting mechanics that could potentially provide a nice change of pace compared to other games in the genre.
The problem, at least in its current state (review written at launch) is that it really doesn't stand up well in comparison to obvious influences like Binding of Isaac. I will list some of the issues I have with the game at launch, some may sound minor but have a very real impact on the way the game is played.
-- movement speed --
The starting character (there may be others to unlock) is woefully sluggish. This slow movement combined with much-quicker-than-you enemy projectiles and othewrwise acceptable mechanics like your momentum affecting your own projectiles can lead to frustrating and needlessly tiresome encounters.
There are a number of perks available at level up that profess to increase movement speed, these are either completely incorrect in their supposed effect or the gains are far too minimal as even after taking more than one such perk there is never any noticable increase in your movement speed.
The interesting thing is the roll mechanic which acts as a little boost to evade enemies, the inclusion of which would have been unnecessary if the overall movement wasn't so awful. What I'm curious about is whether the roll was added to compensate for the overly slow base movement speed or whether the base movement speed was deliberately made that slow so as to make the planned roll mechanic relevant and useful.
-- hitboxes / collision detection --
The hitboxes on both the player character and some enemies is, in my opinion, a little off. I suppose the issue here is that the hitbox on the player character is a little too big, a hit is registered even though your character sprite wasn't contacted by the projectile, environmental effect, etc etc. It's true that with continued play you would probably adapt to this slightly too big hit box and learn to compensate but you shouldn't have to, a game like this needs a reliable, accurate and finely tuned hit detection system.
In contrast, enemy hit boxes seem, at times, bafflingly arbitrary and with zero reference to their character sprites. More than once I've seen a projectile pass straight though an enemy without registering a hit, only for the next projectile on the same trajectory to instead register a successful hit. Again, this type of game thrives on tight, accurate hit detection, which at present, just isnt here.
A lesser issue is with collision detection on environmental objects. This could well be tied to the above issue of your slightly oversized hit box but occasionally you do get stuck on environmental objects, even though it looks as though there is room enough to get by.
-- pacing --
This is more of a personal one but I really feel the pacing of the game needs to be addressed, both in terms of character progression and item acquisition. In short, leveling up seems to take a little too long. Combined with the...underwhelming, shall we say, perks that you get on level up, this makes the whole level system seem honestly quite redundant. I never once found myself pleased, excited or glad to have levelled up, it just doesn't feel like much of a reward.
Item acquisition is probably a bigger issue, more specifically WHEN you get items. This game lists Binding of Isaac as one influencing game and it really shows. In Isaac however, there is a reliable and reasonable pacing to item acquisition. By and large each floor has one item room and an item from the boss room. There's no guarantee either one will be any good but at least there are reliably (keys allowing), AT LEAST two items per floor.
This game does not have item rooms on each floor nor does it provide items as rewards after boss fights. In fact your most reliable source of items are the occasional mini-boss enemies (like elites from Diablo). These enemies are fairly few and far between however, you MIGHT find one per floor and some floors don't have any by design. This means you end up with very few items and the majority of itemsa you do find are unremarkable. I'm being quite generous when I say unremarkable by the way.
I should note you can get items from vending machines but most are limited use and almost all are more than you can afford given the relative scarcity of money.
All in all, despite how critical you may feel I've been, I really do think this game has potential and there are some things to enjoy here but there are more things that I feel need to be addressed by the developer before this game can really be recommended.
In short, if you want to play an enjoyable but challanging twin stick shooter with tight controls and good pacing, play Binding of Isaac. It's pretty much all this game aspires to be and is considerably cheaper to boot.

Our Darker Purpose is a gorgeous game in many ways. The way the story and setting is drip-fed to you via talking desks or boss descriptions allows you to engage with it or get on with the gameplay itself, and the writing manages to be funny without being cringe-worthy. The music is also truly amazing, perhaps the best I've heard in any indie game.
I find the gameplay particularly engaging as well. On the surface it does hug closely to Binding of Isaac gameplay, with randomised rooms, unlockable items and locations, starting over when you die etc. But it does go beyond that. The emphasis on choice over randomness is far more evident in ODP: Each time you level up you choose between two perks that may boost your attack or survivabilty in some way (life leech, attack speed, or some more exotic perks), and you unlock lessons that you can equip before a play-through that can have a dramatic effect on your gameplay. You can also choose which floor to enter after a boss battle, and each floor may have different enemies or modifiers to them (enemies will drop more juice boxes, won't have champion enemies, you and the enemy will take more damage etc.)
These elements allow for less of a feeling that the RNG was against you, and more that if you die you messed up in some way. It also means that even if you are having trouble, you may unlock lessons that will help you in the future, so there is always a small sense of progression without making the early levels feel trivial.
One downside to the game is that earlier areas can feel repetitive, as there is a smaller set of potential enemies and items that you will encounter. Earlier levels can also look a little too grey for my liking. It also isn't clear how to unlock each of the lessons - something I find frustrating but other people may enjoy discovering the unknown.
Over all its a good game to play for several hours in a row or just half an hour, and its easy to sink at least 30 hours into the game (for those who care about replayability). And the music is to die for - that cannot be said enough!

Bad:

Scaling:
The game has a terrible sense of scale. Your basic weapons take several hits to destroy an enemy unless you're using your best weapon. Meanwhile enemies frequently destroy your exo in 2 hits easily. This pairs with the problems of impact I listed above.
♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ AI:
The AI literally has defects in this game. Which makes each enemy type follow a specific behavior. This is a fine idea on itself because it gives the player something to exploit, however it's so terribly implemented by having the robots constantly shout things about "Where'd you go?" "No no no, not that way". When they do kill you (And they will) you feel like your death is at the hand of ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. Also making an enemy that can shoot at any direction in it's large range with OHKO missles and no indication of where it may target is♥♥♥♥♥♥game design.
So yeah long story short is the only way I've found to get through this game is by taking AoE and Snipers and just out ranging everything in this game. It's not fun, it's not challenging, it's tedious.
The game has some interesting idead but they're put together so haphazardly and the game suffers from good feedback and poor balance.

This game is good, it has low system requirements, interesting gameplay and it sounds wierd ('cause MOBA became from RTS), but it is something like MOBA+RTS+Shooter (not an FPS, but the shooter). It has all the best things from all the genres, but the worst things from F2P games. But let start my review from positive sides of this game, and there are a lot of it.
You know, it is something medium between MOBA and RTS: you control only one unit and you can't control others (like in MOBA), but you can buy units and tell 'em what do they need to do (like in RTS). But the part from shooting is the best - now you don't need to target the unit, you just need to shoot in them! The gameplay is not just about destroying towers & base, I mean you need to destroy the base, but you don't need to destroy towers (here they are actually other little bases), but you need to capture them. From the beginning, you theese bases are holden by neutral units, that are actually hard to destroy. There are a lot of maps to play so you will never be bored. And the best part of this game is main units you controll. They are actually transformers: flying like planes and walking robots. They have different skills and they're really balanced. Also, there are no roles and no artefacts so it is not so good part of this game but it still fun. There are not so much of mechs, you unlock it by leveling up and buying, but they're really cheap, so basicly leveling up is enough. You get a lot of kudos (in-game money in this games) and exp for even a match with bots, there are also VIP to get a double kudos n' exp, but it is useless. There are units to buy (also by leveling up and a little of kudos), characters (unlocking them is exactly the same) and some other features. But there are also one more way than VIP to get more kudos with exp and it's free: just build some structures in non-match base in game menu and you will get some % of extra currency or a wheat field where you can sell wheat for kudos (so you don't need to be nerd to unlock something in this game). Match continues 20-40 minutes, but I think it isn't the limit or minimum. But now let's talk about one con, but the big one.
The game has got some kinda imbalance between novice, nerd and donater. There are diamond currency and it is real money currency, but you can get something from missions. Good thing is that mechs you can purchase by theese diamonds are only the skins which aren't better than free (the only thing you can purchase 'em with any level). But there are "ultimate" units and characters that haven't got level limit and they are powerfuller than free ones, but good thing is that they are excluded from PvP. Next is upgrades and they're free, but it's like arts, but not buyable in the match, you buy 'em in game, so that means that nerds will win novices 'cause first ones have better mechs. But even after this, balance in this game isn't as ♥♥♥♥ed up as in ♥♥♥♥♥♥ MOBAs like Prime World or Panzar.
I reccomend this game, one of the best MOBAs in the MOBA market, and yes, I think it's MOBA, not the RTS 'cause you control one unit, you can't build buildings, etc. It's MOBA with parts of RTS and Shooter. Enjoy it!

Pros:
*Favorite combat system in a game to date. A make-your-own-moveset fighting game is a dream game, and I'm so happy that it's a thing now.
*Beautiful scenery. This game looks gorgeous, though the environmental textures can look a bit off.
*Perfect price for this game.
*Co-op and PvE is pretty fun. I enjoy being able to kick prospect♥♥♥♥♥with a partner or two.
*Great bosses. Though lacking in variety in some areas, the bosses are tense fights that pit you against difficult odds.
*Good learning curve. This is a game to dedicate time to learning the ropes and mastering them. Make use of your time to master your moveset.
*Every fight is challenging, but not too brutal. Even the weakest enemies are a decent threat. I enjoy a game that refuses to hold my hand.
Cons:
*3-5 hours long. No joke, the story and map will take you 3-5 hours to fully explore. I guess this is a base foundation for future content to come, but as a full release, it's quite a bit short.
*Server instability in numerous regions. There should've been an open beta before release to stress test the servers, though fortunately, the devs are dedicated to solving this problem.
*Several bugs including AI running into each other, crashes, and controls rarely locking up. The latter only happened once, and the rest either break immersion,♥♥♥♥♥♥me off, or look rather awkward.
*Story is mediocre. though to be fair, that's nowhere near top priority. That being said, I wish the beginning setup had more weight to it later on.
*PvP is an unbalanced, broken, and terrible experience. I can't go one match without fighting someone who either heals mid-fight, shockwaves you out of bounds, or spams light attacks so you can't do anything without using absorb. Here's a recommendation for the devs: ban healing from PvP and fully heal the person who wins, so that they won't have a reason to heal. Also, there's one particular map that's poorly designed so that shockwaves can knock you off just about anywhere with a large hole in the middle. Stay away from PvP until it's more balanced in the future.
VERDICT: Overall, I'd highly recommend this game for people who like Soulslike games, people who like fighting games, and people who like martial arts, but steer clear of the PvP unless you're a cheap ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. For its price, it's worth every penny, but could use an increase in length, variety such as new locations and weapons, and tweaking the PvP to make it more balanced for those with slower movesets.

I've been playing this game on another platform in case anyone is wondering why I only have so few hours played.
This is just my opinion on the game, the devs, and the situation based on my perspective as a player:
After months of unsatisfaction and hope that things would get better, I have to warn people that this game is pretty much a scam.
The game hasn't received a proper update in over a year. Important bugs and UI issues still haven't been fixed, problems that make the game tedious, frustrating and boring haven't been addressed, no new features were added to make things interesting...
Meanwhile the devs did two things:
1) They promised content, fixes, updates, etc.
2) Every month, they released 3 packages at $15 a piece that were way overpriced for what they did (even $5 would be expensive, IMO).
People have been buying these time-limited packs because they thought improvements were coming soon. Instead, the devs just made empty promises. They made polls on the forums to pretend that they wanted feedback, they published lists of stuff they were supposedly working on, they made excuses every week for unexplained delays, they blamed most of the situation on the Community Manager and replaced her by someone who just apologized more for delays... In other words, they did everything they could to save their reputation despite not actually doing anyting good for the game.
A few weeks ago they also started to lock critical topics on the forum and they deleted old topics where they promised more content. It's kind of funny, I thought this would happen so I kept screenshots of these things... I guess I have enough experience with dishonest developers and their money-grabbing tactics to see these things coming.
The worst they did is that they even banned one of their loudest critics and top players from
for "racism", for jokingly referring to the Chinese company owners as "our Chinese overlords". As if it wasn't bad enough, from what I've been able to understand that comment was made in a
Discord channel. The forums mysteriously became much less critical after that, everyone obviously started to worry about their game account getting banned for made-up reasons. Long-time contributors to the community, who had special status on the forum acknowledging their efforts, also mysteriously lost that status after criticizing the game and became less vocal about their complaints.
Well, recently the devs anounced that they hadn't been working on any of the things they promised. Instead, they had spent all their time making the game available in China. They said the promised fixes, improvements and additional content would come later, and they released 3 more packs at $15 a piece anyway.
The thing is, I don't think any fixes, improvements or content are coming. They pretty much lied for months about working on this when it's now clear they weren't, so I think they don't plan to work on it at all, they're probably just trying to sell as many packs as possible until the game stops making enough money.
So my advice: don't spend any money on this game. It's overpriced, the devs are lying about working on content, they censor criticism, and they try to hide the old promises they made. The content you can buy is overpriced, it will take you a very long time to use it due to broken game mechanics, and it's very unlikely that things will ever get better.
It's one thing when devs make plans for new content, but then unexepected stuff happens and they can't finish the work. It happens. But in the case of Shop Heroes, it seems they never had any serious plans to begin with, despite saying otherwise. And that's not acceptable at all.
You've been warned.

To make it short and sweet, yes I do recommend this game based on its merits alone in standing up as a short but sweet experience with an experience more compelling than you'd expect from literal cardboard boxes.
Now with that, here are some pros and cons:
Pros:
-Quirky 'box' characters
-Heavily inspired by late 90's platformers with regards to gameplay and worlds
-Plenty of collectibles and costumes in game to try on
-Active Publisher/Developer that still constantly reachable online and releasing free updates
-Charming humour (may make you groan or cringe but guaranteed to make you react)
-Variety in quests, boss battles, and world design
-Hidden Eastern eggs and nods to other games/pop culture moments
-Sound effects and music that keep the atmosphere alive with energy
-Multiplayer included!
Cons:
-No built-in steam shop support (not even for custom costumes)
-Game under 10 hours of gameplay unless going for 100% completion (currently at $17.99 steam at time of writing)
-Controls are frustrating (as to be expected by controlling a box, not a sphere)
-Camera-work equally frustrating, especially when giving you 'hints' from Bounce
-Load times inbetween game start-up and world loading screens strangely long
-Lack of actual game walkthroughs/tips online to help if trying for true 100% collection goals
-Tutorials/Help Tips can seem never-ending at times, as what at first will feel helpful and guiding through confusing parts (especially the initial tutorial) can devolve into repetitive information, especially when asking for locations of certain items or challenges
Overall it may seem like a game that can leave mixed impressions and I won't deny that it certainly will try your patience at certain times. However the game is built that way because it motivates you to go 100% collecting all the way if that's your cup of tea. Otherwise it doesn't mind if you focus instead on just the main story and that by itself is worth the game. Also much of the gripes I listed in cons you either get used to or are acceptable when viewed overall at a game that does a lot of things right and if you like a challenge with regards to modern platforming, is right up your alley than.

This is one game whose metascore I very much disagree with. Polished like the biggest jewel on the crown of a king, this quirky platformer generates a feeling I haven't felt for a long, long time. This is the kind of game of which I would have strong, fond memories, had it come out when I was a child.
I think those critics just don't get it, and are applying an inappropriate set of standards. You wouldn't evaluate the animation of a Disney movie with the same standards with which you would evaluate a painting from the Renaissance era, would you? No, you wouldn't. That would be stupid.
Ignore the metascore. This game is one to experience -- it's cute, ridiculous, satisfying, and surprisingly large.

Firstly, this review is from a player who has already played the first version and so most points rasied are from that point of view and probably more relevant to existing players.  However, new players might be interested in some opinions of the difference between each version. So, feedback:
The previous Kingdom base game was great, and the mechanics of the game, after some patching & tweaking, worked well.  The 'new lands' version however has disrupted the balance that the game previous achieved with the addition of a lengthened game spread over several islands.  Issues include:
- Starting a new kingdom on each island from scratch.  It is now quite repetative and tedioius, especially since the first 2 islands lack any diversity, such as;
- Lack of additional mounts on the first 2-3 islands means your horse never changes to a better one (getting sick of eating grass) and makes the first point about camps even worse by dragging out how long it takes.
- Lack of portals on the first 1-2 islands (though they are slightly smaller worlds I think).
- The save system (or forced contol of not being able to actually save at will) was fine when there weren't 'levels' as it was more of a challenge based game (improving your survival count).  However, now that there are levels, and considering how much repetative effort you have to go through to get through the first few islands/levels, the save system could do with more user control (ctrl+alt+delete when your crown is taken and returning to the game does not work as a work around).  Being able to resume from the same island for example.
- When you died, and before it was a matter of management, you aimed to improve your day count.  But I find there is no motivation to imrpove your day count of the first 1-2 islands, making them undesirable to be repeated.
- the advertising would have you believe that there are new features, such as new mounts (bears and elks and such) and new characters.  The characters however do nothing but wander around you camp, and I never saw any of the new mounts (it even lacked the black horse).
Above is what I feel are non-personal points I feel need to be improved before I can give this game a better rating.
Personal feeback: I died on the third island from one tiny mistake in managing the freaking horses stamina (damn grass, and lack of better steed) whilst getting another camp going 'yet again'.  After restarting the game back on island/level one I am not motivated to play this again (unlike the previous version).  Again, this is due to the lack diversity and interest in the first 2 islands/levels.  It's as if the levels have been gutted in order to save the diversity for the last levels.  The only new thing on island/level 3 was more portals (though there was 1-2 on level 2).
Overall I still rate the first Kingdom version highly, just not this 'new lands' version yet.

This game is incredible. I wish I could recommend it to everyone, but I do think it's more of a niche hit than anything.
If you're dead set on trying it, I suggest not reading too many reviews and getting to know the game for yourself. This is a game where a great deal of the fun is in learning and discovering the world on your own - I cannot stress enough that it absolutely does not benefit from any sort of spoiling. I personally don't usually mind spoilers before I play most of my purchases, but I'm glad I didn't stumble across any for Kingdoms, because I have no doubt that it would've changed my experience drastically.
If you're having doubts, I do think you should give it a shot anyway; the first couple of hours are a good feel for how the rest of the game will go, so if you don't like it by then you can refund it.
Last thing before pros and cons - I think the developers are wonderful! Kingdoms: New Lands is the standalone expansion to Kingdoms: Classic, and anyone who owned Classic before its release got it for free. Considering the amount of content that they added to the game, this was
Free stuff! Yay! I chose not to mark my product as free because technically I did pay for the base game knowing that I was getting the expansion, so I'm not biased in a way that someone would be if they found New Lands in their library without knowing why. Anyway, onwards with the review.
+
is great and changes to set the mood very well
+
If you played Kingdom Classic, there's way more here, and it's a lot of fun to unlock and use all the new stuff.
+
One resource, one goal.
+/-
It's well done (and I adore it), but it's not the best that I've seen, and I know plenty of people are put off by pixel graphics.
+/-
Some might like the idea of simplified controls, some might definitely find it frustrating and obtuse.
- I feel like my 'up' button feels sorely neglected and will never forgive me.
-
If you're the sort who's very attracted to the hot-handed punishment of the roguelike or procedural death labyrinth, this may not satisfy your particular brand of masochism.
-
It's a design choice they had to make, admittedly, but I feel like they could have squeezed just a tiny bit more depth out of their game. I would elaborate, but I'm afraid that doing so would give away a little bit too much of how the game works. As I stressed earlier, it's a big deal, here.
Kingdoms: New Lands is, in spite of its flaws, an objectively good game. I'm not saying you're objectively wrong if you don't like it,
because not everybody enjoys everything in the same way. I don't enjoy plenty of very good movies, does that make me wrong?
Don't answer that. In any case: I like it! You might too. Or you mightn't. Who knows?

Now, since that's out of the way;
with 6.4 hours invested in the game over the course of about 2-ish days, these are my thoughts, opinions and overall views of the game as it is now. (Aug 30, 2017)
Since it is the main selling point of this game, I'll start with the online functionality.
It's iffy right now. The dev team has made it clear that they are working on fixing it, but currently the server issues can cause: Lag, world loading glitches, enemy loading issues (being in a completely clear area then suddenly being surrounded by 5 enemies) respawn issues (respawning with a black screen or not being able to hold F to respawn) and an overall jittery feel to the gameplay, however, about 3 of the hours I spent playing were spent online and I really only had issues when the servers started to crash. again, something they're working on. When the servers are stable, the PVP is fluid, fun and functional, allowing you to befriend strangers and practice or learn new moves. You can also add someone you've met in-game on steam through one of the many altars scattered throughout the world. I recommend doing this if you meet someone who's company you enjoy, as
other than the limited selection of emotes.
Many of the reviews I've seen say the fighting in this game is just button mashing and hoping something hits.
It's not? at all?
while the AI is rather stupid and is generally easy to beat (especially any sort of non-boss AI) the bosses each have a unique fighting style that requires you to adapt by changing things up a bit. YOU WILL DIE multiple times while fighting certain bosses, it's just the game telling you to take a different approach.
being able to have fast attacks ready after a dodge is important and certain abilities can turn the tide in your favor in both PVE and PVP.
Weapons also spice things up a bit, providing a boost in damage as well as a different set of attacks. drawing a weapon in the middle of a fight can make your approach less predictable, as you can also withdraw your weapon mid-combo, finishing the combo with a different chain of attacks.

A short but sweet singleplayer that teaches you the mechanics quite nicely
Lots of secrets and gear for you to discover, rewarding you for going and fighting those guards instead of avoiding them.
a very nice soundtrack with fitting music for each fight and new area.
Lovely graphics that suit the somewhat cartoony style
Fun PVP.
Screwy camera angles when backed into a corner or fighting inside of a few areas.
Currently unstable online gameplay
a few oddly sloped areas that result in awkward deaths...
a somewhat grindy method of learning new moves that punishes you for fleeing from a fight

Add optional AI to the Meditation-bot that allows it to fight back in a specific way, maybe by being able to set it to the AI of bosses you've beaten?
allow larger rewards for winning a fight when it comes to learning new moves; waiting and blocking the same attack for a while to learn it just feels lame if you start doing it late. (Like I did, don't make the same mistakes)
More emotes! we could use a Wave, Sit and Point emote and maybe a few dance ones as well?
A way to warp between Altars would be nice as well, but I understand why this wouldn't be added.
More weapons (though, they've already said they will be adding more in the future)

Nice game. I haven't played Epic Battle Fantasy 1 & 2, but this game has a solid RPG core.
[+]:
The humor is very welcome and goes very well with the game and characters. Turn-based battle style is always pleasing and enemies can sometimes come in waves. Abilities can be learnt on the go as long as one has enough AP through fights. Some monsters have to be cleared to access blocked areas. Status effects disappear right after a fight. Nice soundtrack.  Scanning enemies with a scouting device by someone who knows how to analyse monsters(the guy with the gun) to get valuable information on the enemy and update your bestiary(something that makes sense). Characters comment relevantly when stuff happen, and it does look like special attention was given to this: like when you just learnt an ability and use it to inflict damage on a specific enemy that is weak against it or if there's a secret nearby. Changing equipment changes appearance of the protagonist everywhere, everywhere!
[-]:
Teleporting between teleport points can be confusing as the portals in the warp zone are a bit confusing and unnamed, but are OK once gotten used to. Equiping equipment is a bit confusing, but enhancing them is very very easy and intuitive. Completing side quests is a bit confusing, as items can be dropped randomly or bought for very different prices, and acquisition of these are not very clear, plus the quest tracker doesn't give any location whatsoever of the quest-giver.
The GUI could have been more polished, and I'm guessing it is...in Epic Battle Fantasy 4(which I haven't played at the time of writing this), but that's how all the game developers do nowadays anyway. Plus at this moment, this is free and I guess more of a promotion for Epic Battle Fantasy 4, which is not free.
[Performance]:
The graphics card DOES matter (personally), I have an integrated graphics (Intel HD Bay Trail) and gameplay is a bit choppy on MAX, have to put it on LOW resolution and frameskip ON in order to even have the game be playable, especially during screen transitions(very tolerable) and battle(most annoying, very laggy at higher settings).
- Intel Atom Z3735F (with Intel HD Bay Trail)
- LOW = unplayable ~20fps , frameskip makes it barely playable.
[Note]:
There is no cloud save, and save files are not in My Documents, so beware ... Learnt this the hard way.

After having just beaten the game on the hardest mode, I think this is probably one of the most fun RPG's I've played in a while. It offers a very cutesy art style, and can fool you into thinking that this game's battle's are just as childish. Well I can confirm,
That i've never been happier to be proven wrong.
After beating the game on Epic difficulty, I was genuinely ecstatic, and I truly felt like I earned my victories. The Battle system is deceptively complex, with no two monsters created with the same strengths and weaknesses. Although this applies especially to the bosses, it can be said for normal enemies as well that if you mess up a turn, (on harder difficulties), You will be surprised at how many ways enemies can 100-0 you in 2 seconds flat.
This game never felt grindy, which is something all Rpg maker's should strive for, as it is the golden style they should all strive for. A lot of battles are optional, and I rarely had to "grind" at all, even on the higher difficulties.
I beleive this is because the reason i lost battles was because of MY inputs in the fight. I never once thought
"Oh, this monster is way too strong for me to kill, it must be like twice my level!", because the truth is, level does not really matter too much in this game. What matters in this game is YOU making smart decisions in battle. Because even after grinding my *ss off, there was no difference to how fast a boss KO'd me. This is a very unique element in this game that i beleive makes it the classic that it is.
Oh and one last thing.
Some of the Music in this game is AMAZING. Be sure to turn it up and give it a listen! It really makes repeating a boss fight for hours on end that much more tolerable.
A really fun, challenging and well-paced RPG.

Unbox feels like a kid who's starstruck by their own parents. It thinks so highly of what they do and tries so hard to emulate them, and it's cute but ends up falling short because of a fundamental lack of understanding.
Right out of the gate the game holds you on a leash through a forced tutorial for just long enough to be aggravating, while dangling pickups here and there in your face but saying "oh no, little Billy, you can't get those just yet!" if you attempt to stray so much as 2 feet off the trodden path. Then, by the end of the tutorial, you are familiarized with your titular Unbox ability which allows you to take as many as 7 consecutive jumps at the cost of your health meter. It is how you will mobilize yourself through the rest of the game, scrounging for the obligatory collectibles and completing (re)quests in the form of instanced minigames. You can also stomp with B to hit buttons or defend yourself.
This never changes. This is the entire game.
It controls awkwardly, because of a semi-accurately simulated "rolling box" physics model for your movement, and jumping, unboxing, and pounding are mapped to RB, LB, and B respectively. The cast of characters is flat and insipid, with probably 90% of the population being literal clones of the oblivious, happy-go-lucky, incompetent, bad-pun-spewing stooge by name of Zippie and the remaining 10% being pretty much the same one-note caricature besides. Both the hub world and the first main level you go to have very similar, very repetitive caribbean-themed music with two-chord backing tracks and I never want to hear another steel drum in my life. The graphics are nice! I like how everything looks. But even all this aside, the game's primary stumbling block is that there's a blatantly straightforward and yet completely squandered opportunity for a good sense of progression.
Stamps are foisted as the most important pickup because they apparently unlock new worlds, so they got that much right (although I seem to have access to at least 3 worlds from the start anyway). There are occasionally special fragments tucked away in really well-hidden places that are kind of fun to dig for. But simultaneously the most prominent and pointless pickup is golden tape; it is the bananas / musical notes of Unbox, with a whopping
to collect on every single level, and yet it serves
. Perhaps it unlocks an extra cosmetic or something, but if the developers were riding on cosmetics as a main driving force of the gameplay then I'm not sure who they were making this for.
You start the first world with all of your abilities. You don't unlock extra jumps. You don't unlock rounded edges to make movement easier. The only things you unlock in this game are cosmetics and doors. There
a much more intriguing system in place here, perhaps requiring you to gradually unlock progressive extra jumps per level, meaning you'd have to make do with the lower areas at first or come up with cheesy ways of exploiting physics to sequence break. Maybe your progress in the separate worlds would dictate how much of the hub world you could access. But when everything's set in stone from the start, the entire point of the collectathon genre has swooped by overhead. It's like if you started Saints Row 4 with all your upgrades and superpowers at their full cap; yeah, you
go around and collect hundreds of glowy pickups, but why would you want to?

I'm pretty sure if the movement was clean, I probably would have had a little more patience for the game.   Maybe a marble madness theme?  XD

I don't know what to say about this game. I can't reccomend this highly, but I won't say I won't reccomend it.
To simplify what it is, it's a rougelike turn based mech game. Permadeath is optional.
And...I honestly expected more than that. The biggest highlight of the game is the main theme. It's
good.
Take a listen while you read this, if you want.
If you do/are listening to it, let it sink in for a moment.
It's pretty cool, isn't it? It has a pretty serious tone while just being a generally badass way to open up the main menu to the game.
I actually got overhyped when listening to this. Now, granted, I did get a free key from one of PC Gamer's key giveaways, but..I'll still judge the game as if I bought it.
But...I think it's because my expectations sky rocketed, that I didn't find the game as AMAZING as I did find the theme.
It's pretty fun, though. You have (Up to four) mecha suits that you start off with, and use their diverse abilities to destory robots. The robots are taking over the earth, and they've reached your part of the city. When you start the game, you'll be told you have 50 days until your hometown is NUKED.
Yikes. Time to kick some♥♥♥♥♥
You're able to pick four mech suits out of six available, and I only found one being...pretty damn useless. Every other mech suit is rather fun and has a decent difference from the others. One thing to note, is that when you find parts to upgrade yourself with, you'll find that the suits don't ever get to change weapons. The weapons are pretty much bolted and weld into the suit. You'll find modifications that'll allow you to make them stronger.
Science: This suit isn't reliable for combat. It has 50% bonuses to ALL Computer stats. Perfect for hacking and inflicting viruses on foes. This one is the one that'll be in any group of four you will make, because of how damn useful the Hacks are.
Brawler: This suit's a weird one. I thought it would consist of short range weaponry that'd pratically all one hit kill. But, no, it's armed with a X cross bomb, a shotgun, and a pistol. The pistol's a waste (3 turn cooldown, but it doesn't count against your turn. It's..unbeliveably weak. You actually need to focus on building it up to...one shotting the lowest leveled foes. It's pointless unless you JUST need to shave off a few remaining points of health, so you don't waste your other weapon's ammo.) It's still a blast to use, though. You can make some pretty neat trickshots with this one.
Sniper: Style. Obliteration. A flippin' life saver. It holds one of the most powerful sniper weapons in the game FROM THE VERY START. Whenever this special sniper rifle's ammo count is an even number when you fire it, it's a free turn for you. Holy.♥♥♥♥♥♥ It's got the 2nd lowest ammo out of the Non Epic weapons, but it's just so damn satisfying to use. It also has an ungoddly amount of range. Safe to say, this suit is just so awesome. It's fragile as hell, but you would probably know how to use a sniper, don't you?
Ninja: I'll be honest. This is the suit I have a problem with. But, to be honest, it's not BAD. It's got a bonus to all Propulsion stats (Which, by the way, includes the ability to dodge traps and your stealth turn counter) and it's stealth doesn't break when you fire your weapons. Pretty neat, but...Unless you have the Epic Ninja (I'll explain in a moment.) don't expect to do very much unless you focus on giving the Ninja as much stealth as possible. Stealth, in this game, is pretty nice. Every single suit has stealth, and can upgrade the amount it has. The Ninja's just perfect for this stat. If you activate Stealth, each turn you spend moving around will cause the counter to go down by one. The stealth break if you fire a weapon, drop a sentry, use mines..but not actions like hacking a door.
Assault: A good all around suit. Even has 60% bonus to health. It comes with a grenade launcher, a machine gun, and a laser. Nothing else really special about this suit, except that it doesn't have the weak as ♥♥♥♥ pistol.
Seige: Rocket. Launcher. Enuff said. But, alright. Seriously, THIS ROCKET LAUNCHER. It has the least amount of ammo for non Epic weapons, but, holy crap. This thing can wipe out an entire room and IT'S HUGE AOE. I can't stress enough that this thing is by far the STRONGEST ROCKET LAUNCHER in a game I've ever seen.
On top of having six different Suits to use, with four to pick at any start of a new game, you also have six different suit commanders to pick from. Now, these people are VERY unique in having different "powers" (one of them quite litterally) and the one you pick can have a heavy impact on the game.
Axis: The "Scout" of the commanders you can choose from. Here's a picture for the example of someone without Axis's ability.
Now, here's Axis's ability.
This is Axis's power. Allowing you to not only see farther on the map, but you can BYPASS a mission to get to another that's connected to it. If you're picky on missions, or want to open up the map without wasting your days, Axis can be worth it.
Emma: Emma's power is all about the store. Not only will you get much more money for selling items to it, the store's contents are usually better than if you played someone else.
This is someone's inventory, that isn't Emma.
Now this is the inventory of Emma, with the price power she has.
So, in a nutshell, a extreme shopper.
Meg: All item you pick up are basically better than they should be. The game explains this pretty well. A "mark four" item would have the stats of a "mark six" item, and so on.
Rey: Oh, boy. This guy's outta control. He has the power over time, but only in the way of being able to restore a suit's health all the way back to 100% twice each mission. Tuck: Eh. He's able to see loot everywhere on the map. Not really the best ability.
Genji: Can I just say how badass this commander is? He's so ♥♥♥♥ing badass, that he starts off the game with ALL HIS SUITS BEING OF "EPIC" VERSIONS.


Epic suits have more guns than Duke Nukem up their robotic asses and have more spaces for modding capability. Holy ♥♥♥♥.

If your looking for a review on this game you've come to the wrong place, but if your looking for an outstanding pie recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients:
1. 6 tablespoons unsalted butter
2. 1/2 cup white sugar
3. 1/2 cup brown sugar
4. 1/4 cup water
5. 1/4 teaspoon cinnamon
6. 1 pinch salt
7. 5 apples - peeled, cored and sliced
8. 1 pastry for double-crust pie
Directions:
1. Preheat oven to 425 degrees F (220 degrees C).
2. Combine butter, white sugar, brown sugar, water, cinnamon, and salt in a saucepan over medium heat. Bring to a boil, remove from heat and set aside.
3. Roll out half the pastry to fit a 9-inch pie plate. Place bottom crust in pie plate; pour in apple slices.
4. Roll out top crust into a 10-inch circle. Cut into 8 (1-inch) wide strips with a sharp paring knife or pastry wheel. Weave the pastry strips, one at a time, into a lattice pattern. Fold the ends of the lattice strips under the edge of the bottom crust and crimp to seal.
5. Pour butter-sugar mixture over top of pie, coating the lattice, and allowing any remaining sauce to drizzle through the crust.
6. Bake in the preheated oven for 15 minutes. Reduce heat to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C), and bake until the crust is golden brown, the caramel on the top crust is set, and the apple filling is bubbling, 35 to 40 more minutes. Allow to cool completely before slicing.

Backed this game 5 years ago on Kickstarter. I can say the years leading up to release were buggy as hell. But now in 1.0+ the game is stable and very VERY enjoyable. I am extremely happy with the final product and highly recommend it to anyone.
After a few years of forgetting and remembering the development of this game, I decided to reinstall and give it another shot after 1.0 was released and I was shocked at how the game changed for the better. It felt like a polished, well built game and is addictive and extremely fun!
The addition of new enemies like the Mini Corruptrons, Biftrons, and Warlocks; new Bricktron classes like Artificer, Halberdier, Alchemist, and Arbalist; Wards; and Conquest mode all make this game feel like true strategy game.
Multiplayer is a must try! PvP adds a whole new aspect to the game, and Co-op Conquest and Invasion is an engaging challenge.
Overall, I give this game an 8.5/10;
Cons:
The learning curve is fairly steep and the controls/UI navigation feels a bit wonky and takes some getting used to.
If you find yourself unprepared for a Corruptron attack you can wind up getting stuck in a loop of your Bricktrons dying and respawning and dying again to the same few Corruptrons that can't capture your crystal because of your respawning Bricktrons. If you find yourself in this situation you should count it as a loss and restart.
The game can be very challenging in single player, even on the easiest difficulty. Luckily the game encourages you to edit the JSON files and make your own difficulty preset.

Extremely intersting fighting game with beautiful art and sound.

This game takes it a step further and gives you almost 100 moves to learn (you start out with more than enough) during the story and after. You can set up your own 'decks' of attacks, each attack starts and ends in a different quadrant, allowing you to chain combos and switch to different atacks mod-combo. It's similar to For Honor in this regard, however with the player-made combos, you will never fight the same enemy twice. Each player will have their own way of playing in their 'school.'

I would heavily recommend this game to anyone. The $30 price tag is steep for such a short single-player experience, but the multiplayer makes it worth every cent.

TL:DR
Pros:
-Very Good Balance
-LOTS AND LOTS AND LOTS (AND LOTS) of customization possible
Neutral
-Lack of actual story made up for with atmosphere (think Dark Souls with a worse ending).
-Grindy progression
Cons:
-Servers are potato right now (temporary launch issue)
-Region locked (temporary)
-Stats are locked. Once spent, thats it.
-Game is hard until you manage to unlock more moves
Pros:
- EXTREME amounts of customization. Armor gives stats and there are nine armor slots. Trade out damage for defense and vice versa. But the real king of customization is your combat deck. Learn moves, use them however you want, and make your own sweet martial arts combos. Want to use all punches? Go for it. Want to use a bunch of fancy flying kicks? Nothings stopping you. There is a ton of customization in this game. If you're someone who likes to try out every single combination in order to find the best one...good luck.
-Balance is pretty good despite when you first start the game and think Windfall is op. Forbidden and Windfall seemed balance. Khalt may need a slight buff.
Neutral things
-Story/Atmosphere The game is basically Dark Souls in this regard. You're in a strange land, given a task with very little about the why, and there are crazy people everywhere. Unlike Dark Souls the ending is...well its not really good. Kinda cool but also not. I'm putting this under neutral because some people will like this and some will not.
-Grinding moves. To learn moves for the combat deck, you have to guard against them. Some NPC's you don't even need to block and can take down quite quickly which doesn't help with learning anything for your deck. Some people like the grind, others don't so it's under neutral.
Cons
-The online play is awful right now. Like terrible. Servers have, in my case, barely been up at all. When they are up they've been fine but that require thems to be up. Should be temporary
-Building your deck is painful at the beginning. Once it gets started you notice how much better you are but being limited in your moveset sets you back pretty signicantly.
-Stats are locked. Moves scale like dark souls, corresponding to different stats like strength and dexterity. This means if you start spending stats and mess up, you're done. Need to have a build in mind when starting. That said, it is possible to beat the game without investing heavily into your stats. Still an issue.

Epic Battle Fantasy 3, at its core, is a standard JRPG.  You wander around the world, looting chests laying around the place, speaking to NPCs for quests, and battling foes in turn-based combat.  You gain equipment and skills as the game progresses, and certain enemies are weak against certain elemental spells and weapons.  Finally, you can buff your attacks and debuff your enemies in the ultimate quest to make your percentage points bigger than their percentage points.  However, this isn't simply a game of numbers.  Laid over the mechanics are a beautiful aesthetic design (both musical and artistic) and a light sense of humor.
A common complaint about experience-based games is the grind often associated with them, but this game is designed well enough that you shouldn't have to grind for levels; though, it can sometimes give you the upper hand, especially on the higher difficulties, to go back and fight some of the more difficult battles once or twice to gain an extra level, some skills, and cash and items with which to upgrade equipment.
Overall, I quite enjoyed this game; if I had to pick out one downside, it would be that Epic Battle Fantasy 4 improves upon this game in every conceivable way.  However, seeing as this game is absolutely FREE, I can't

It seems to me there are two good ways to handle real money transactions in a "free to play" timer game like Shop Heroes and other timer-based games (Fallout Shelter, Realm Grinder, Adventure Capitalist, etc.):  1) allow players to use real money to purchase costumes, pets, and other flair that does not affect the gameplay; and/or 2) allow players to use real world currency to speed up timers, and allow players to progress more quickly.   Shop Heroes does both of these things.
Unfortunately, Shop Heroes also handles real money transactions in a third way: it prevents players from accessing certain key workers (and the achievements associated with these workers) unless they pony up real money.  It is worth noting that these key workers are extremely expensive ($40 or $50 each), and that there is no way to unlock them with either of the in-game currencies.
Had I known that before I started, I would never have downloaded or installed the game.  But I just discovered it, and I immediately uninstalled the game (despite 1300+ hours of investment).
If you are looking for a few hours of clicking, Shop heroes is fine.  But, if you're going to take the game seriously, please take note that you won't be able to access the whole game unless you pony up almost a hundred bucks.

What is Unbox?
Unbox is a throwback to 90s platformers with obvious inspiration being taken from games such as Glover, Conker and Banjo and Kazooie on the Nintendo 64.
You play as Newbie, a box. I take it you understand the title of the game now.
Newbie was created by the Global Postal Service, GPS for short, with the sole aim of saving the floundering company. Newbie was created not only is a sentient  box, but also a self-delivering box, which would not only save the company money, but save it from bankruptcy.
Controls:
Well, you're a box, you move how a box would, turning is delicate, the controls can be quite jagged and can be at times, tough to control. I found that when I was moving faster I was definitely struggling more, but if you pace your movement and try to aim your jumps and movement it becomes more fluid.
There are a number of moves which Newbie has in his arsenal including slam, unbox, and jump.
While movement is tough at the start, it gets easier the more you play it, don't let the initial frustration throw you and spoil the experience for you.
Soundtrack:
The game sounds like Banjo and Kazooie, the NPCs all respond with similar meeps and merps, as well as having similar interactions with the player. These small details help the player to embrace the world and the retro vision the developers had. Either that or they were too cheap to pay for voice actors, or they weren't sure what a box would sound like.
The soundtrack is alright, a bit repetitive at times, but it fits each world well. If you're a collection enthusiast it could definitely grate on you, and considering the game is somewhat of a collectathon I could definitely see that happening to some players.
In Conclusion:
Unbox is a very fun game which is suitable for a lot of people, of many ages, it has an expansive and colorful environment and quality gameplay to boot, while being not too difficult, it's also not too easy and definitely has replay value. Would I recommend it? Definitely.

Unbox is a very charming N64-style collect-a-thon platformer.
In Unbox you control a box(duh), that can move, jump and unbox(essentially a extra jump). You have to collect a certain ammount of items in the levels to proceed to the boss fight and then to the next level.
Which levels is quite big and detailed world, being almost a open-world-lite per level. You have several quests and activities, like rescuing other boxes,  races, challenges, and even combat against the "bad boxes" It offers good variety if you just want to progress, although it might get a bit too saturated if you aim for 100% every level (but then again that's true for most of the games in the genre)
Made in Unreal Engine 4, it does look pretty good, even more so coupled with the charming artstyle. The worlds are full of detail and are consistent throughout. It's very pleasing to the eye. The worlds are also pretty different from one another which keeps the experience fresh (a oil rig, a tropical island, snow mountains and a jungle with ancient ruins).
Soundwise, it's quite good. There's lot of sound effects and details that help the world come alive, and the banter from NPCs is reminiscent of stuff like Banjo and others. The soundtrack is alright and it fits each world well, but it is a bit flawed in there's little variety in it and each theme can be repetitive in itself, so while well composed those themes might be grating while trying to 100% a level.
As for controls: it handles exactly how you'd think a box would handle. As it is a box and it has corners, you will get the expected behaviour from it which will make it a bit erratic compared to what you would expect from other games with characters that have a more "smooth" appearance and gameplay. It takes a little bit to adjust(20-30 minutes), but when it does, it becomes natural and it handles quite well. The unbox mechanics, which consists in essentially adding a extra jump(up to 6 max). It makes it a game very fun to speedrun, coupled with the momentum physics that can make you go roll at very high speeds. I was worried it would trivialize the game too much, but after playing it for a quite a bit I don't think it does. Making big skips and jumps still requires skill and for you to have proper control of the character.
The boss sections aren't bad, but they might be too simple for their own good. It doesn't feel like you take full of advantage of what you learned from the levels and that's a shame. It would be really good if they added more platforming on those sections.
All in all, it is one of my favorite platformer games in 2016, with a few flaws, but I heartily recommend it at the current price(it's also 12$ on the new Humble Bundle). I'd love to see a bigger sequel in the future, this could become really special with the right budget.
