First off, I'd like to say that I saw this announced a while back and have been pretty stoked about it since. However, I was kind of disappointed when I finally got my hands on it a couple days ago. Furthermore, I only have two hours on record so there may be some later content that I did not access and therefore cannot know that it might relate to the things that I am going to write about below. Also, I guess I'll add a TL;DR at the bottom.
____________________________________________________________
For the first half-hour or so, I found myself lost in the game's charm. It was fun rolling around as a little mustachio'd box with all my other sentient box friends but it grew kind of dull after a while.
After the tutorial was over, I went on to just start collecting things because that's what you do in this kind of game. Just to explain this a little further there are three different kinds of collectibles: Gold Tape (the plentiful, 'coin-style' one), Trapped Zippies (the bonus 'free your friends!' one), and Stamps (the main 'star-type' one). Those three things are what you'll find around the world of 'Unbox.' Now, here is what I think could be improved on:
I feel like there should be maybe one or two more types of collectibles. Having two hundred rolls of Gold Tape strewn about each world comes off as a little lazy, especially considering these are the types of items that tend to be collected while on the way from one objective to another. While there are plenty on the roads and paths, a lot of them are also quite hidden so the player must search high and low for them all which, normally, wouldn't be so bad but there are just way too many. I think changing the amount from two hundred to one hundred and then adding a new collectible would be a better option.
Next, I'd like to talk about the difficulty and other things related. The game feels far too easy and I understand it's supposed to be a casual collect-a-thon (and that's okay, I love games like that) but 'Unbox' lacks something that keeps me engaged. I breezed through whatever challenges were in my way and the only difficulties I had were from the wonkiness of trying to roll around as a cube-shaped object. While I understand that is the point of the game, I'd like to say that it's too much here. A game can be wonky and still feel right to the player (think Katamari here or even Starwhal if you've ever played it) but this game does not do that for me. Instead, I would find myself frustrated that I failed missions or missed an item due to a messed up jump because my box was laying at an awkward angle or something like that. I think the gameplay would greatly benefit from something that could add a level of fluidity or smoothness such as slightly rounded collisions or much less rough terrain. In short, the only challenging part of this game is its handling and not in a fun way.
Continuing on, I'd like to mention the less important aspects of the game such as writing and whatnot. I say, "less important" because I know that these things weren't the developers' primary focus here, but since this is a review, they're worth mentioning.
To put it bluntly, the story is not good (spoilers ahead). It's like this: GPS (Global Postal Service) is going out of business because they can't stop losing people's stuff. As a last ditch effort, they started manufacturing sentient, self-delivering boxes. However, this didn't entirely work and they were still in trouble. So, as a last-last ditch effort, they designed a totally new and improved box that was supposed to be much better than all the others (that box is the player). Then everyone keeps saying that you're the only one who can save GPS and that's pretty much it. ...or is it?
Almost immediately, a good 'ol 'mystery character with an ambiguous moral alignment' arc is thrown in. There is no build-up, there is no point, there is only 'Mystery Box.' He also very quickly reveals that the G in GPS doesn't stand for 'Global,' but in fact 'Galactic' so this also has something to do with aliens and/or space or something. It just feels like the developers didn't really know what they wanted to do with their own game. Also, they do this thing when you continue your game or travel to a different world that automatically tries to replay the most recent story-related cutscene and I don't like or understand that at all.
That being said, I do really like the world that 'Unbox' is set in. The idea of sentient delivery boxes that just want to bring things to people is cute and fun. There's also 'Mop,' a box that used to deliver mops until marketing research decided that wasn't really selling. He's sad and that makes me sad because all he wants to do is deliver mops. But anyway, the game is beautiful, the environments are great, and I really love the concept. I just really don't love the writing. In addition to that, the villains, otherwise known as the 'Wild Cards,' are super annoying. I don't mean they're annoying as characters, they're annoying in-game. The player will occassionally come across these guys whilst in the middle of going somewhere or doing something and they don't add anything to the gameplay at all. They just knock you around and they're a nuisance. But I guess that belongs in the gameplay section? I'm too lazy to move it and it's a kind of acceptable segue into the fact that I also hate Bounce. This character is also incredibly annoying because he/she/it never stops giving me useless hints from the tutorial. Please add a 'Turn off Bounce' option for everyone else to enjoy.
Finally, I'd like to address bugs. At the time of this review, 'Unbox' is at v1.02 and still contains a number of bugs. This is pretty okay due to the game being brand new, but it's a necessary thing to mention in a review.
To conclude, 'Unbox' is a fun game in its own right. However, it falls short of what one might consider to be a polished game and its only saving grace is the creativity of the concept and world. There are just too many smaller issues to ignore, which is why I cannot recommend this to others.

What do I think about the game. Let's start with the graphics; if you are looking for decent graphics, sound effects, cool background music,fast game progress and fast paced gameplay you're at the wrong place. Darkwind is nothing from above, it does have explosions, it is hardcore as hell,  I like to call it a "risk it 4 a biscuit" kind of game. Why? Here's the reason.
If you really want to progress faster in this game you will defenitely want to make friends, which is pretty easy since the community is flawless.
You start off with nothing but a few gangers each with a skill and dang there's loads of skills to mix and level up on each of em. For example a driver which uses the machinegun OR heavy machinegun skill - more aim while driving.
So you just finished the tutorial and you got showed the basics but that's not enough, do a few race, deathrace or arena events to learn how to handle the cars better, time shooting at the right time...
Next... When you enter the wastelands, you want to do it with what we call "veterans", players that have played since the game came out, basicaly. They will help you out with commands and some basic tactics of where to position your vehicle/s. (You can rent a vehicle for $5000 in your garage.)
In the wastelands you can die pretty quick, so can the enemy, (kinda, depends) you can get shot in the head with a car rifle a side of the vehicle armour is destroyed, or earns a hole in your hearth... hmm what's next... Oh right! You can combine various weapons, engines, armour types, tyres on your ride and well you can lose it aswell. If you drive a small vehicle with a big gun the recoil from a Heavy Machinegun + a simple Machinegun is "simply" suicide. Once all the scouts pilots are demoralised, you lose all of the vehicles and end up on foot in the wasteland full of mutated creatures and your only hope to survive is a gun, yes you can have handguns if you don't feel like dying >.<. Shotgun, pew pew, Machinegun, Rife, and a crossbow.
So yeah it's high risk low profit in your first 50 hours I'd say?
Is it worth playing? Yes, yes it is if you are patient and willing to surpass that massive learning curve.
Almost forgot, the game has around 50 people most of the time active, they are all kind to fresh meat. =)
salutes to; captain, clocky, HeadWa and many many more people - Rekahs. (oh and ty to I forgot his name for the Buzzer, I'll come back soon)

For Honor was said to be the next best melee fighting game. However, with horrible balancing issues and being Ubisoft in general, it fell WAY short from what people were hoping.
Absolver drives For Honor into the dirt and into the grave it should be in.
Main points:
* Stunning visuals and graphics
* Performance is accecptable, would like the default 60 fps cap to be removed
* Next-Level combat
* Okay story
Absolver's main strength is in the combat, and god is it good. With 100+ moves that can all be chained together without interruption makes the fights fast paced and flow. The AI do become fairly predictable, usually spamming the same moveset from one stance. The PvP is absolutly fantastic. With a dedicated 1v1 system, duels are very fun and are a good way to prove who is superior.
However, with numerous server issues, playing online with other people is hit or miss. I state the obvious that having no online sucks, but I know that Sloclap is doing their best to keep servers running.
Overall, Absolver is a easy to learn, hard to master fighting game.

Don't be fooled. This game is incomplete. Plenty of bugs and unfair situations. For example, enemies capable of shooting you through walls, 'cover', and completely random drops. As well, the game does a sort of lazy attempt to explain things to you, or fails to tell you additional helpful things. For example, when completing an armory mission, you MIGHT find loot boxes on the map which will give you mission specific parts. The tutorial neglects to tell you at the end of those types of missions any exo that survived will reward you an editional part.
As well, despite pictures and the such that shows having more than one party member (I use the term loosely), you can only have one of those 'mechs' out at a time. You can freely switch from one to another (something I don't think is ever explained at all), but it uses a turn.
How things play out when switching isn't exactly clear. What if you are cloaked, turn orders, being within range of an enemy when switching, etc.. it's all a bit unclear, and there is no help function in the game either. At least none that I found.
In regards to enemies shooting through walls, I encountered an enemy, a boss enemy to be more specific, that states that it doesn't attack, but will shoot at whoever fires within it's range. Apparently, this goes for players who are undected, several rooms over, cloaked, etc.
A modest pool of health, long range, decent attack power, and the ability to shoot you whenever you are within its range, regardless of position.. leads you to being caught in an unfair, uphill battle.
Then there are some bugs that I found. Your mouse cursor and buttons sometimes don't line up, glitches that turn all your stats to zero, the ability to use in game saves to your advantage (getting a better item from a loot chest).
All in all, the game has potential, but numerous issues leave me quitting the game in frustration or disappointment more than anything else.
I would recommend buying this game for no more than $2 if you're still interested.
The issues I have had with this game can be fixed with some updating, I'm sure. But right now, I wouldn't recommend it.

Empire: Total War is a rather fun combination of real-time tactics and turn-based strategy. Overall the Fifth game of the Total War series, this was the first Total War game I have played, and I enjoyed it a great deal. I started off with the tutorial, which covers both ground unit real-time tactics, and naval warfare. Following this fast-paced, easy to use tutorial, I began playing from the Settlement of Jamestown. The learning curve was very easy with this game, and it was surprisingly fun for a turn-based game. Normally, I don't find these types of games enjoyable, but there was something about Empire: Total War that had me wanting to keep playing.
Historical challenges are available, including several notable historic battles, The Battle of Brandywine Creek, Fontenoy, and so on. Conquest is the ultimate objective of the game and this can be done using not only military units, but Exploration, Trade, Politics, and founding other colonies. You have the option of playing almost a dozen different main factions. Campaigns allow you to play through American colonisation such as Establishing the colony of Jamestown, to the French and Indian conflict, and even the War for American Independence.
I really enjoyed the historical aspect of this game, and also how it is part turn-based and part real-time strategy. I think Empire: Total War does a good job of weaving the two separate game styles together into a seamless whole. I think based off my enjoyment of this game, I may enjoy some of the other Total War titles as well.

I cannot recommend this game. There are around 425 recipes you can unlock only by crafting, additional 150 are locked through their store, and up to 6 can be bought in each of the packages. To obtain the locked recipes, you must (1) risk opening a random tiered chest or (2) use daily-earned fragments.
This seems fair at first until you realize how horrible the statistics are. I opened roughly 40 chests and never got 1 blueprint. Others speculate the chances of finding a blueprint is around 5%. I quickly learned that higher-tiered keys cost about the same amount as an unbreakable item. I could decide to use fragments and buy the recipes, but you must buy every recipe underneath it level-wise. Also, their fragment amount scales upward per item. Buying one recipe can take a whole month's worth of daily fragments and not even benefit your own heroes. These recipes are the only ones that add special effects to the items and are unbreakable for your heroes at certain levels.
Another problem I saw was the statistical chance of items breaking on your heroes. The majority of the items have roughly 3% chance of breaking, but one seems to break everytime. I recall a 0.5% item breaking right after sending the hero out. They don't seem to accurately represent what I encountered in the game.
The only reason I enjoyed part of the game is because it is an idle game, pure and simple. I just had to remember to never buy any chests and equip my heroes with unbreakables or the cheapest item that's around 3% break chance.
I can't get enough of this game.  Super addictive.

This is the first horror game that I have played, and despite the fact horror games usually don’t seem that appealing to me, Among the Sleep was the first to actually get me to buy and try.
Of course the main appeal to this game, at least in my opinion, is the quite dramatic perception change compared to usual games. You play as a 2 year old boy, who can barely walk and whose perspective on life is a lot different to us adults. It’s actually pretty cool being so small and everything around you that in normal situations wouldn’t be a problem, suddenly becomes a challenge. 
This game is also quite surreal. You aren’t quite sure what is going on at times and it is never really spelt out for you, so on a certain level, this game is open to interpretation. It has a strong message to it, but the way that it was done and the details about the game make you wonder slightly. 
The level design was fairly creative, the general mechanics are all the same for how the baby gets around, but each level had a different thing going on. It wasn’t too repetitive and of course that works in its favour. 
Horror wise, someone with anxiety like myself would definitely get a little worked up playing this in the dark on their own. The ambient sounds and noises are definitely enough to rustle you and it definitely caught me out a few times. But like I mentioned before, I don’t exactly play many horror games so I wouldn’t know what those Horror veterans strive for. Compared to other games I imagine that this isn’t the scariest of games.
I think the only thing about this game people might not be so happy about would be its length. I personally don’t mind short games, I think as long as the game has core strengths to it, I’m happy with it being short and sweet. But other people might not agree. It took me 3 hours to finish the game (and start a new one to go back for 1 achievement) but it definitely felt shorter.
TL;DR : All in all, this game has an interesting story, great atmosphere and the tiny-man’s perception is new and refreshing for any game let alone horrors. Only fault being it was pretty short (for most people, I would assume).

An update to the above review,
The developers, for whatever reason, added in additional (somewhat pointless) achievements for gathering collectable drawings throughout the levels.
Having already 100%ed this game, I may have just been a little salty that I had to go back and re-complete for collectables that added nothing to the game, but honestly I don’t see why it was necessary.
It would have been nicer if the drawings you collected were something you could actually look at and throughout the game help piece together more interesting little bits of information about the family or something. I had already played the game, so me and my boyfriend played it through the second time around together.
As I imagine it is for many horror games, there isn’t much replay value for this game. The second time was a lot less interesting to me and I don’t think my boyfriend enjoyed it all that much either. I’ve found recently that I definitely get scared from horror games easier when alone, so maybe this is purely an “alone, playing at night with headphones” type of game.
There seemed to be a few immersion-breaking bugs and glitches this time around that killed any ambience in the game (I.E. The monster glitching out and laying horizontally on the floor walking in a circle like a spooky Catherine wheel).
Going back to do another run and get all the added achievements took me up to a 9 hour total play time. Which seems to mean that it took us 6 hours this time around. A lot of time was wasted looking around the nooks and crannies for collectables. Which I honestly think kind of distracted from the game. But I know that slightly OCD people like me and my boyfriend may not be able to help themselves.
All in all I think the game was better without the collectables, and it seems to very much be a “play once” kind of experience, but as much as I have moaned here, I still like it. Give it a go.
TL;DR : Decent story and an interesting perspective from a toddler’s point of view. It’s pretty short and they have added in a batch of fairly tedious new achievements for gathering collectables that in my opinion distract from the game. It’s a “play once” kind of game but I would still definitely recommend it.

Good day fellow gamers.
Today I will be recommending a game created by Cloudcade, Inc. called “Shop Heroes” This game is a free to play, cross platform game with optional micro transactions.  This game is available for IOS, Android and PC, so there is a pretty good chance that everyone can play it. This game was green lit on Steam in August, 2016 and has been a massive hit with the steam community with more that 3 million people already playing worldwide, although for those of you who haven’t experienced this gaming sensation then I will convince you to give it a try.
Firstly I should explain what this game is about, Shop Heroes is a tale about managing your very own fantasy shop and becoming a young entrepreneur, but it’s more than just that… Shop Heroes also allows you to unlock adventurers who will quest for you and gather rare resources from across the land. You can use these to create stronger items for your fearless adventurers or you could sell them to make a quick buck, the choice is yours! Multiplayer is also available so don’t hesitate to get some friends to play and help you out with your growing business chain.
Shop Heroes has many features including:
> Individual abilities for each adventurer.
> 29 Quest Resources (Shiny gems, Elven dew, etc.)
> 10 Shop resources (wood, iron, leather, etc.)
> 20 workers which are sorted in tiers from 1 to 5
Even though Shop Heroes has only been in beta for a little over a year, it has already become a game of this magnitude, which is absolutely amazing, in my opinion of course.  One of my favourite features, not about the game itself but installing it is the download size. Personally my internet is quite bad so I don’t tend to download games that take a significant amount of data, although Shop Heroes is different, it only takes 234 megabytes of data which is about a quarter of a gigabyte, this is extremely good for those who are not able to play a big game but would like to experience one that is fun and fulfilling. Another of my favourite features is the marketplace, this is a place where buyers and sellers some together to make trades to give adventurers or fulfil daily requests. And one more feature for those who don’t like to spend a great deal of money or none at all, the game gives you the premium currency “Gems” every time you level up or when you complete a daily quest. You can also sell items on the marketplace for gems as well.
Shop heroes also has a competitive arena system, where your heroes can fight someone else’s heroes, rewards vary from gold to gems or even rare resources, it depends how far you go to climb to the very top of the ladder.
This game has 7 different tiers of items these include Normal, Good, Great, Flawless, Epic, Legendary and Mythical the price changes depending on the item quality, and after you produce a certain item a number of times then you will produce it at a particular quality every time. You can also obtain higher quality items by using a piece of apparatus known as the fusion cauldron. This will fuse 3-5 items to create 1 exceptional item. This is also a good tool to clear some useless stock into a sellable item.
And finally a new but interesting concept is that of city raids, every so often a city raid event will initiate and because of that the whole city that you are a part of can participate to receive gold, gems, chest keys and even exclusive raid items (Play to find out!).
So in conclusion I highly recommend this game for the novice, the veteran, the toaster internet, the competitive gamer, basically just about anyone, Thanks for taking the time to read this mediocre review about a sublime game.

Unbox, a game that is an open world platformer, it's like Super Mario Sunshine and Mario N64 but in 2016 which brings back the nice nostalgia feel.
The game is very kid friendly which sometimes brings out the cringe but overall it doesn't change much of the experience.
The story seemed weird from the Steam page, it made me think "Do I seriously want to buy this? The story seems pretty bad tbh..." For some reason it wasn't as bad, it was very original at the same time.
This game is VERY open world, I've found no invisible walls nor death barriers (The only thing close to it was glitching up high into the air, hitting something on the way down)
There's 4 worlds you can play around in, they are:"Other Base" AKA the main hub world, it has all the collectibles aswell as alot of secrets and areas to explore. "Paradise Isles" which is the first proper world you're sent into, it's multiple small isles with one in the middle with a huge tower connecting them all together , you move around with fans that push you up high into the sky/ boost you in a direction, or just hop onto a plane. "Parcel Peaks" is a icy mountainous area, it has a similar layout like Paradise Isles, there's alot of mountains joined up by some bridges, it has fans that let you move around quickly, it's probably the most fun area aswell as the icy parts make you go flying around (So you can basically ski) There's also a rally track."Isla Con(smth)" Is a tropical island, it features a rally track, a dead volcano, ancient ruins and secret areas inside the mountain, it isn't like the past 2 areas, themed off of small islands joined up together but instead a huge island. It's got multiple villages. Shrek Swamps and overall it's covered in some water.
The world is very detailed and seems like alot of care was put into it.
This game has alot of cutscenes, I can imagine the developers struggling with them as it's a game about boxes, can't do much animations on them as they're cubes.
The cutscenes themselves weren't bad, except the boxes flying in, they just seemed so unnatural to the game's physics, it's not a huge problem but it was annoying.
The game offers alot of collectibles, 200 Golden Tapes which aren't rare but there's alot of them scattered around the map, 18 Stamps which are rarer and harder to find, 9 of them are found from doing levels for the main story. 10 Captured Zippies which are a little difficult to find but not as difficult as Stamps.
When you're close to a collectible you'll hear a sound or Bounce (one of the main GPS guys) will tell you a hint.
You can also go to Bounce if you're ever struggling to find an item, it'll give a general area screenshot to help.
You unlock alot of things for your box, hats, mustaches/face wear, skins , clothing.
You get them from collecting specific items, finishing missions, finding some characters to talk with...
in 8.1 hours I've finished all of the main story, with getting 100% on The Hub world (collected all the Trapped Zippies (1) and 200 golden tapes) , around 20%-25% on the other worlds.
I tried speedrunning the story though, you could probably get 10 hours of doing the main story if you would take your time, to get 100% on everything I'm guessing around 10-20hours if you're quick enough.
You can have up to 4 save games, so you can speedrun one save, take your time on other one, speedrun , 100% speedrun.
The game was made on Unreal Engine 4, that's pure pleasure to read if you're a lover of graphics.
If you've never heard of Unreal Engine 4 it basically is one of the most detailed game engines out there.
If you want a rough idea of the game on max settings 1080p check out my screenshots.
For a small dev team who made the game in under 12 months, the graphics/world is very detailed, nothing is un textured or out of place.
The only texture problems are when you select a new box, it'll not render proparly inside a shop but when you walk outside of the shop the box will render in proparly.
pure gold.

The game feels like alot of care and love was put into it, it's a genuine platformer game with so much open worlds that came with the game that nowadays would be considered DLC. (I wouldn't mind DLC, this game already has huge worlds to explore with alot of content)

While I wouldn't call it a bad game, I wouldn't be able to reccommend it to anyone unless you can get it on sale very cheaply. The good points are the graphics, the game mechanics (except the driving, although that was by design) and the story. But these are completely overwhelmed by the big three problems I have with this game:
1. Padding. There is a ludicrous amount of padding in this game. I honestly think that two-thirds of the time I spent playing consisted of going from point A to point B in between cut scenes. If there was something to do or see on the way then it would be one thing, but there isn't. The game even has you waste time cleaning floors and toilets on several occasions in quicktime events. One of the best examples though is when you go to or leave an apartment building (your's or Joe's) you have to enter the building from the street, which is a new area the game loads, but then the game makes you walk up three or four flights of stairs to the actual apartment and there's absolutely nothing to do or see in between. Why not just bring you straight to the apartment and the ensuing cut scene when you enter from the street?
2. Length. This is especially bad considering all of the padding, but even with that the game is absurdly short. I took my time and still completed everything in eighteen hours and change.
3. Empty world. The world of the game is pretty decent sized, and aesthetically it's very good, but it's so empty that there's absolutely no incentive to do anything other than the story missions (there are no side missions to speak of). There are maybe a dozen or so stores, but probably only a combined five different variations therein. You can rob the stores, of course, but there's virtually no incentive to make a lot of money and it gets old fast.
Also, two relatively minor problems: the decision to make the cars' steering realistic for cars of the period (which is to say, awful by modern standards) was a bad idea since it makes driving (which as I said there is A LOT of) a chore intead of fun in any way. This is especially true because of the second probelm, which is that they decided to have the cops come after you for hitting other cars and speeding. So since every car handles like a boat, you just have top cops constantly trying to pull you over. This can be a major nuisance when you're just trying to get to the next mission objective.

As an open world game it doesn't really work; there's no encouraged exploration and not a whole lot to do outside the missions. I don't think there'll be a whole lot of replayability either. But seeing Mafia II for the story and the fun, then yeah, I recommend it. It was a fun ride and the story gave me a few good laughs and nice surprises here and there. At times, that 50's atmosphere really shone through and grabbed me in all its glory too. I couldn't keep away from it until finishing the story, so overall Mafia II was a nice, enjoyable, polished experience.

Mafia 2
Some of you might compare this to the GTA-series but Mafia 2 is a lot more fun and realistic. In this 'short' review, you're going to read why you should buy this instead of GTA.
I'm going to structure this review like that:
First of all, I'm going to talk about the plot.
2nd of all, I'm going to be talking about the technical information, especially graphics.
My 3rd point is going to be about the atmosphere this game makes you feel like, including music, details, characters and collectibles/extras.
My last point's going to be my conclusion and my final statement.
I hope I can help some of you guys to make your decision whether buying this game or not.
Plot:
You play as Vito Scaletta, son of Sicilian immigrants. Because of a jewelry store robbery at the age of 18, you get arrested. Instead of going to prison, Vito decides to serve as a paratrooper in the U.S. Army, Operation Husky. About one and a half years later, a battlefield injury causes your homecoming. Joe, a friend of yours, manages to get you counterfeit discharge papers so you don't have to go to the Army again. At this point, the thing gets rollin'. Joe helps you getting in touch to various mafia members. Soon after, there are plenty of jobs waiting for you...
Technical information:
Mafia 2's graphics are a feast for the eyes and  very "eye-candy-like" in many ways. The game was released in 2011, there's no other game out there this old running that good with that kinda graphics. All in all it's a beautiful game with many graphical details which make this game look even more beautiful.
Atmosphere/Feeling:
Mafia 2's charming and all good vibes. It's bedecked with gorgeous 1930's-60's music, from Mr. Sandman to Lucille, there's something to suit all tastes.
Details are a big deal in the world of Mafia 2. Besides the 50 collectible Playboy magazines, which are pretty, pretty awesome too.., there are plenty of things to collect but also things that make the game a lot more realistic. For example, if there's a police car next to you while you're driving like a freakin' maniac, the cops are not gonna let you go. Whether you try to escape or gently pay your speeding ticket, is your own decision. The cops are a lot smarter​ than the ones in GTA anyway. They do not forget your looks or your license plate number, unless you get dressed in something else or take a visit at the body shop. Another awesome feature is the radio, wanna know why? Everytime you make a little mess, like a gunfight or something, it's broadcasted on the radio. In my opinion, that's pretty cool and realistic.
Conclusion/Statement:
The feeling Mafia 2 spreads is unique. Everytime I play it, I feel like I really was in the 1950's. It's a truly masterpiece and my favorite game of all time and I think it can't ever be beaten. If you're into 3rd person shooters, buy it. If you're into adventure games based on a great story, buy it. If you're into any kind of atmospheric games, buy it. If you're annoyed by online games and just want to relax while playing an awesome game, buy it. It doesn't matter, anybody who thinks he has already played a perfect game, try Mafia 2.
If you actually read this completely, I'd like to thank you, it took a damn amount of time to write this but it was fun, though. Just because I could re-experience this game with all of its nice parts and features.
Also thanks to 2KCzech for making this game, I hope there will be another Mafia game developed by them in the future.

So while there is a lot to love about this game, a lot of aspects of it kept nagging me and eventually left me frustrated. So in the end I am going to focus on the negatives of this game, because overall I don't think I can recommend it. While the story, characters, and setting are all amazing, there are also a lot of basic game elements which continually cause problems.
First of all, the money is POINTLESS in this game. I was so excited to build up my wealth, maybe move up in the world of the mafia, use my money to upgrade some things. NOPE. The money basically moves the plot along, and they REGULARLY decide to just take all of your money and possessions away. So glad I bought all those guns, because ten minutes later I lost them all. Great. So glad I stole all those cars so I wouldn't have to worry about money. Oh what's that, you are taking my money again? Screw you. There's no point in focusing on money, until the one mission where you are forced to and you have to start from scratch again.
Another thing, the mission locations are terrible, in that you will find yourself driving from one point of the map to the very opposite point of the map, sometimes only to realize the person you were looking for wasn't there and you have to drive all the way BACK to where you started. Or you have to drive all the way there to drop someone off, and THEN go back to your place which is again on the other side of the map. It gets extremely annoying.
I really love the idea of being wanted in this game because the police can identify you in three ways: via a wanted vehicle, via your appearance because you are wanted, or just from being in the immediate area of you doing a crime. I thought it would be really cool to balance all of these and having to find different ways of escaping the police. NOPE. I could be doing nothing, waiting for the light to turn red, but three police cars will smash into me blaring their sirens for some reason. I guess I just looked guilty.
But the thing that pushes this over the edge for me from a good game with a few annoyances into a game I didn't like would be the saving. The only way you can save is for the game to auto save during missions. However it does these SO far apart that it can be frustrating. Multiple missions start when you leave the house, so sometimes you have to drive all the way over to the other side of the map to start the next mission, only to open the door and someone throws a grenade at you. So where do you start? When this next part of the mission started? When you opened the door? Nope, way back at your apartment. Drive back over again, and again, and again.
This game was amazing in a lot of ways, and I probably would have been more forgiving if I had played it when it came out. But as it is I was glad to see it end, even if that ending was absolutely terrible.

When an indie game gets five years in development, you expect the final product to exceed what was initially laid out in the kickstarter pitch that started it.  Yet, after putting in some time with the initial  full release of the Castle Story, it's clear that a good game does not always come from a good idea, even when it's given plenty of time and money for the process.
Back when Kickstarter first started taking off, Castle Story hit the ground running like many of those early adopters of the platform and generated nearly seven times its funding goal.  Like many people, I got caught up in the fanfare of being on the ground floor of cool game ideas and backed this game along with plenty of others.  Some games I backed turned out well, but Castle Story seems to have had some real problems given that it was in development for so many years and delivered something that feels so clunky and lacks any real depth.  Looking at the KS trailer compared to the finished product, it's strange to see how little it has changed in all of that time and how the initial concepts of the interface seem to be even better than end result.  Whatever went down between August of 2012 and August of 2017 to give us the game that we got a few days ago must be an epic story that I'd love to hear.
Like any game, the first things I do after tweaking settings and checking out the main menus is look for a tutorial.  Some games have it separate while others integrate it into the new game setup.  Castle Story just simply doesn't have one.  At least not anywhere in the game.  The tutorial that does exists is on youtube and it's not even linked in game.  This is something than can be forgiven in a lot of circumstances, especially if the game is intuitive or extremely simple, but Castle Story is neither of those.  The menu system, crafting, building, and virtually any aspect of the game features so little basic instruction that it's easy to spend your first ten minutes not progressing in any way.  I had the advantage of streaming these bits and having a helpful person guide me along in chat, but it was still overwhelmingly frustrating and straight away gave me a bad omen for what was to come.  When a game has such unappealing initial steps, it rarely redeems itself going forward.  Castle Story as not an exception.
The most egregious offense in this game is the gameplay UI.  It's hard to explain just how clunky it is, but it seems like when most developers try to limit the amount of clicks and submenus, Castle Story's developers seemingly do the opposite.  Actions will often have several paths to get to them, not even considering keyboard shortcuts.  Performing actions will have you going in to menus, doing long clicks and awkward combinations of right and left clicks, and resizing selection areas clicking arrows and dragging it around.  Even after many hours of using this, I still found myself making mistakes and not remembering what all I needed to do to get something crafted or built.  Yet, as I moved forward in the game, it was easy to see that cumbersome UI is a product of  poorly designed gameplay.
Nearly every aspect of the game involves a convoluted process to achieve.  It shares so much with other detailed 'city' building games like Settlers and Banished, it seems odd that more of those games' logical designs weren't implemented.  The real issue starts where most everything in the game starts the stockpile.  Rather than having a single building that workers will store resources in for retrieval, you're required to build a sea of these individual square stockpiles that eventually take up the vast majority of the space you're working in.  Each will hold an arbitrary amount of a single substance, however the problematic AI will often block in stockpiles so that empty ones can't be filled, and then if you're not micromanaging a task, they'll fill all of you stockpiles with a resource, preventing other resources from being stored.  If you want to use these resources to craft something, you may end up missing a component.  Yet rather than telling you this, or what things are missing in the UI, you have to click on the area something is being made and hover over it to find out what is missing, then fumble your way around trying to find out why it doesn't exists, or hasn't been harvested, or wasn't being stored, or wasn't being accessed from it's storage area.  Something that is normally handled in games like this with a simple menu system featuring clear concise information turns into a hassle that bogs the game down even more.
I had originally believed this game would feature a linear mission progression system that would have you going from map to map trying to succeed in taking it over and building an effective castle and community.  However, you're relegated to three choices, a conflict-free sandbox mode, an Invasion mode that has timed waves of enemies (called Corruptrons) that you must keep from destroying your home-base crystal, and Conquest where you also have random waves of enemies coming for your crystal, but your objective is to capture other crystals around the map.  These are all free form, so there's no real progression or anything.  A progressive mission design would help in allowing the player to at least learn how to play in lieu of a tutorial by slowly ramping up the requirements of each map.
When it all comes down to it, even if you stick with it long enough to get the hang of the game, playing Castle Story just feels like you're pulling a dozen anchors with glue on your knees and a stomach full of greasy fast food.  When you're not fighting the interface or the mechanics, you're trying to accomplish something that just takes too long.  I slogged through two and a half hours of a Conquest map trying to get the hang of the systems and inching forward.  By the time I searched the internet a couple dozen times and got my pitiful army wiped out a third time from the ever-spawning menace, I just didn't want to play anymore.  Building anything more than the bare minimum castle for protection was just a waste of time, and even doing that felt too slow.  Now, I think I should make it clear that I don't have problems with slow games.  I play games like this all the time and enjoy them.  The older I get, the more I find value and pleasure in games that are fun without making me test my reflexes at every turn.  Yet with Castle Story, no matter what I accomplish, it still feels like I'm trying to run through waist deep water in the process.
I wouldn't recommend Castle Story to probably 99% of the PC gamers out there.  There are many design flaws throughout and even if you manage to figure it out, it doesn't get much more appealing.  That 1% out there that would like it are people that really enjoy the aesthetic (which is nice) and want a game that takes some effort to learn.  But even then they're going to have to learn to appreciate the fairly shallow game that it actually is.  If you think you're the 1% here, give it a shot, but I can only say to do it when it's really really cheap.

Wolfenstein the Old Blood is an okay FPS in general, one that tries to merge the old with the new: fast and frenetic, strafing combat and unrelenting difficulty of the old FPS games with the focused level design, gritty storytelling and design and COD-like combat we have been oversaturated in these last couple of years. The results for me are mostly a mixed bag.
The good bits: Weapon design, usage and feeling are just right, with a beefy sound design and decent recoil that is homage of the good old days of Quake, Blood and Painkiller. Game looks gorgeous and filled with details and rich textures. Artistically the Old Blood looks authorative and cold, as well as stunning and melancholic. Sound design and music are also impressive, with a great and punchy soundtrack filled with heavy bass and distorted droning guitars, and the same goes for the overall sound design. Dialogue is great, clever and brisk and all the actors give their all to add another level of immersion to the game, with German soldiers stealing the show with genuine kraut banter. Game has an unrelenting pace with swift, quiet stealth segments followed by chaotic, dangerous frontal assaults that loop constantly. Every level has a few set pieces that open up enough to provide the player with a couple of options in how they’ll subdue enemies: they can flank them stealthily, throw a couple of grenades to break out the enemy groups and then pick them off individually, you can make them follow you as you set up a trap in the small room where you have all of the control and riddle them with bullets, etc. Enemy AI is decent enough to provide a constant challenge, as they try to flank you and attack you when your guard is down or you’re reloading weapons.
The bad bits: Story starts interesting but runs out of steam half way through. The two main adversaries are underdeveloped and leave weak impressions. Levels do open up from time to time to provide more tactical maneuvers, but most of the time they are a bunch of tight corridors that only have one way to progress, making them boring at times. Old Blood sometimes tries too hard to reach that “shock” factor which makes the entire experience quite silly and childish, but those moments are fortunately rare. Most of all, the biggest minus goes to the hit-scanning enemies that can frontal-lobe you from ludicrous distances and have super-fast reaction times: if you sneak and peep your head for just a second and the enemy sees you from 30 meters away, he goes full agro on you until you are absolutely dead, and all further attempts to go stealthy again are impossible. They are so inhumanly twitchy it can really drive you crazy on higher levels of difficulty, and make the game tedious at times.
But as an expansion for Wolfenstein the New Order, developers really did try their best with giving you a lengthy, high octane story you’ll enjoy most of the time. At times Old Blood feels like a sweet nightmare fuel of the 90’s and 2000’s FPS games as you have a blast while you shoot and crunch enemies on your way, and in these moments Wolfenstein the Old Blood absolutely shines. At other times it all still feels too much like COD-copy, with too many limitations in level design and high-time-to-kill philosophy that is just not fun. Fortunately these sour moments are rare, and I eagerly wait to try the main story of the New Order and the incoming New Colossus.

Old Blood wants to do it all & for the most part, it succeeds.  It starts off like a spy story, turns into sci fi action, then takes an AWESOME creepy zombie apocalypse vibe at the end.  It's all quite atmospheric and well done, and again, the horror turn is so good that it makes The Old Blood a must play.   You'll be surprised at how serious a story with a hero named BJ can be.  The gameplay is equally varied.  You can play it guns blazing and get one of the best shooting experiences in the biz.  Or you can play it stealth and still feel like a ninja bad♥♥♥♥♥throughout.
If I had a criticism, it's that people playing stealth may find the forced action sequences -- usually boss fights -- to be extremely difficult.   If you make stealth such a big part of your game, you should make sure people can do that all the way through, otherwise they won't be ready for the action turns.
Overall though, Old Blood is a top notch FPS that does both action and stealth well along with delivering AAA story & production value.  Recommended!

Bionic Dues is another game by Arcen Games, and it features many similar elements as their most popular series- AI War Fleet Command- AI Rebellion, weakened humanity, difficult/punishing gameplay, sharp difficulty curve, slow paced thoughtful gameplay, occasional oversights in the tutorials due to game mechanics.
However, where AI War was a strategy game involving often absurd numbers of ships, in extreme cases numbering in the tens of thousands, Bionic Dues is a much smaller game. The city map is randomly generated, as are the actual maps from what I can tell. The abilities and variation between the various "Exos" the player can pilot are both interesting and well definied, with each having a 'niche' that is generally obvious (brawling, assault, sniper, hacking, etc), but with smaller 'modules' that allow you to customize each "Exo" to fit your own playstyle. The difficulty ramps up rather well, but I've found on lower difficulties its easy to become slightly overpowered. Individual variation between mission types helps keep the game from getting repetitive, as do various "Pilots" you can select from the beginning that give you a bonus that will significantly effect the nature of your play. (One gets bonuses for the shopkeepers, one starts out with epic units, one has the ability to pursue missions futher away, etc.)
The game is not without flaws. It has the Mass Effect problem where every mission gives you loot for surviving units, and most missions have hackable doors and lootable cans, making keeping track of modules, especially late game, a bit of a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥ It also occasionally becomes
open, with a lack of really clearly defined goals besides "upgrade your equipment and survive the invasion in 40 days".
The soundtrack is mostly rehashed from AI War, with a few new introductions. It fits the game well, but players looking for a new album by Pablo Vega may be disappointed.
I feel a need to point out that the turn based element is one I particularly like. Preforming any action costs a turn (moving, shooting most weapons, hacking, etc.), and then the robots will each move. However, Bionic Dues has no request prompts, so if you simply want to run across the map you can do so in realtime, but you can simply step away from the keyboard at any point if you wish and the game will wait for you. It allows you to pick your own pacing- Will you run in blasting anything that moves as the robots charge you down? Maybe you'll sit back and analyze each robot and pick the most efficient attack pattern, or maybe throw down an ambush using automated defenses, mines, or an enemy you hacked into being on your side.
If you don't like replaying games trying to work different mechanics, Bionic Dues may not be for you. Those looking for a well developed story will find very little of that here (lots of setting, but the plot is something you make yourself).
In any case, I happily recommend Bionic Dues.

On its own, this is a well done time-killer.  After thirty hours or so, it still seems polished, the artwork is well done, there's a lot to do and balance upgrades around.  But where this thing really shines is as a background game you run when you're doing something else.  Like what?
- Waiting in dungeon queues for any MMO ever, or ranked queues for high-level moba games (or waiting on a rez)
- Playing old school city builders like Pharaoh, where your city is running perfectly but you're waiting until they finish building that $*^#ing pyramid/obelisk/etc.
- Watching television series that everyone tells you are great, but you just can't seem to get into
--  True story: This game helped me get through the first few episodes of The Wire
- Talking to your mom on the phone...
Seriously, I don't just mean this in a humorous way, it just makes the "boring" parts of my regular gaming habits a lot more bearable.
There's nothing really deep here.  You manage the shop (buy, sell, manufacture), the city (unlock heroes, unlock professions, boost rate of materials), and heroes (run quests for rare mats, manage their equipment).  You never actively control the heroes in the dungeons like recettear, which is a bit of a shame because then this would make it appealing to a broader "gamer" audience I think.
It is free to play, and there are microtransactions.  I don't feel like you have to purchase anything, particularly if you're strapped for gold to upgrade things.  You can auction the treasure chests you find out on quests for a fairly hefty sum that helps you a lonnnnnnnng way early on.  (If you really want a ton of money early on, but the starter pack for like $5 and sell the leather key that comes with it for 2.5 million gold.  You'll be golden for a long time.)
The only area where I felt I really wanted to purchase something early was in unlocking the additional active worker slots -- without these, I had to swap workers in and out to craft some regular items I wanted to equip to my heroes.  But I tend to treat the free to play games like a demo for which I'm deciding if want to spend $0, $5, $10, or $20.  I could rail against the fact that it's microtransactions at all, or I could just hand them $20 after fifteen hours and enjoy myself thoroughly.  I chose the latter.

Would be a great game if not for the horrendously inaccurate item breakage percentages, which make you think you can send heroes on at least half a dozen quests without their gear breaking but in actuality their gear breaks with regular monotony, which means you are constantly fighting a losing battle between making $ and keeping your heroes equipped.  Also this has a knockon effect to upgrasding the city, especially if you seem to be the only one investing in buildings it becomes very expensive very quickly, which then has a rweverse knockon effect to keeping heroes equipped.
If you dont mind this time of "hurry up and wait" game, it is definitely a nice RPG esque version, but it just becomes a pay to pregress cow too quickly to be fun for long.

I had to purchase this game on launch and give it a shot. I have to say, I think this game is excellent. I'll start out with describing play style, then talk about the positives and negatives.
Obviously, this is a platformer game bringing back the days of Banjo Kazooie, Spyro and Crash Bandicoot. In regards to world and feel, it seems that Unbox hits it right on the head. I felt like I jumped right into a platformer world which made me happy. If was to compare the movement to the likes of 2D Nintendo games, I feel like it would compare more to a faster Mario play style than say a slower Donkey Kong Country style. You do have a lot of control over the boxes movement and it feels pretty easy to get used to.
On the positive side, well, this game is just really positive. The world is bright and fun, the interactions are light hearted, and the game sucked me in almost immediately. I was compeelled to start obsessing about finding gold tape because that's how I typically play these things. The box was fun to control, and yet surprisingly challenging. I thought the number of jumps you get would make it a bit easy but quickly found out how difficult it can get, but not in a super frustrating way. The game is definitely fun and I can't wait to try out some local co-op on the PC with friends!
My negatives are minor at best but I'll point them out. First, there are some reports of bugs but I only ran into one. I tried max view distance (depth?) which lets you see more of the world on your screen. Max is bugged for my setup and all I had was a strange fuzzy tunnel on the screen. Anything less than max worked fine though and I quickly settled back to the 90 default so I could see up close better. Second, someone already mentioned this but I felt like reiterating it. You can tell that this game was made on Unity. The boxes look great, but some of the world objects look a bit rigid for the rest of the world. I'm sure it's because Unbox doesn't have the art budget other titles have, but it isn't something that bothers me while playing.
Overall, this is a great game to sit back, relax, and enjoy the afternoon with. These are the games I love to play when I just need to de-stress! I'm really looking forward to Yooka-Laylee when it comes out, but we have a little ways to go before it releases. With the current 20% off promo, I feel like this game is a steal and you should definitely get it before the 12th! Support the platformers!!!

This isn't a game you play on a laptop while hanging out with friends.  This isn't a game you play while listening to your iTunes playlist in the middle of the afternoon.  This game can only be played late at night, in the dark, with the only sound coming from your computer speakers.  When you do, you will lose yourself in the mind of our main character, a two-year-old, as he tries to make sense of the intimidating world around him.
What makes this a "Horror" game does not come from gratuitous amounts of gore, or the living dead popping up out of nowhere.  It comes simply from crawling around, taking in the sights and sounds as you try to determine if what you are experiencing is real, a nightmare, or something that adults take for granted that is unsettling/horrifying to a toddler.
The game doesn't last long; it only lasts a couple of hours (free DLC on the way)!  But it isn't meant to be a game that occupies your bored mind for hours and hours of replay on end.  It's meant to be an experience, and it was.  I hope you decide to try this experience as well!

If you're a fan of the classic Rare/N64 3d platformers then I think you will have a blast with this game. They nailed the tone/feeling/gameplay of the era but in their own colourful inventive world of sentient self delivering boxes.
The gameplay mainly consists of free roming around the different worlds doing challenges for a cast of different Box characters scattered around the worlds. If successful you will receive a stamp form them. There is 20 stamps to collect in each world and 200 gold tapes scattered everywhere. The gold tapes are everywhere from just around on the floor to in some really hard to reach places (eg. On top of a really tall tower). There is also 10 caged box NPC's that need freeing in each map aswell as a Boss to beat. You can't face the boss until you have collected enough stamps to do so.
That's where the games one main mechanic comes into play, to move around the wolrds you can do a normal jump but you can "Unbox" while in the air to perform a double jump if you will. The great thing is that you can do it up to 6 times to get some serious air, you'll be flying thru the sky trying to land in some very hard to reach places coz you can see that shining golden tape just waiting to be collected.
You can only "Unbox" once for each Health box you have (up to 6). These Health boxes are in abundant supply tho so you rarely find you can't use the ability. There is also checkpoints scattered  around that when used will fill your health boxes up aswell as count as your next spawn point incase you die.
That brings me to explain that there is no real dying in this game. You will see tho that you can't hit the water more than once without "dying" which sends you back to the last checkpoint you visited with no consequences. You migh find that some collectables are so far out that you won't have enough Health boxes to get back to land, you can hold down a button/key and it will respawn back at the last checkpoint. You might get crushed by stompers and other hazards around the worlds but again all it will do is respawn you at last checkpoint.
So as i'm sure you can tell this game isn't supposed to be anything more than it is. A casual kid friendly collectathon game which has been a joy to play. You definetly see the Banjo-Kazooie influence all over this game down to the text boxes, the noises the NPC's make when talking and just the general gameplay similarities. I'd say this game is a lot easier than Banjo-Kazooie but I have only just unlocked the 2nd of 3 worlds from what I can tell (correct me if i'm wrong), so I don't know if the difficulty ramps up but I can't imagine it.
You have a main Hub world which also has stuff to collect in and which gives you access to the Worlds thru doors in different areas of the Hub. The worlds look huge and is really fleshed out into what theme it is supposed to be. The first one being a tropical island them and the only other world I have seen yet is a snow themed one complete with slippery snow. Can't wait to see what the next theme will be.
I found myself amazed at just how well it all works maybe being used to so many broken releases nowadays, it was such a nice suprise to play this and it just oozes Nintendo like quality control. I haven't encounterd a single bug/glitch while playing with a solid 60fps. Seriously if you like these type of games you will have a blast.
There is even local 4 player races and battles which I haven't tried yet so won't comment on it.
Higly recommended if you like the games which it is inspired by. However if you like your games challenging, you probably won't find satisfaction here so probably give it a miss. The only real time you might notice a difficulty spike is when you are doing challenges for stamps as some of these are on time limits, which means you might fail a couple of times but they're still easy enough to get thru.
If you do wanna just sit back and and enjoy a well made original nod to the golden era of the N64 then pick this up you won't regret it.

The chronic oversaturation of the mafia in our international media has taught us much. Mafia II is an attempt to chronicle these teachings in game form. Fact number one: mafia men do lots of killing. Fact number two: they like suits. Fact number three: mafiosa don't call each other mafiosa; they use the term 'wiseguys'.
I've cross-referenced facts one and two with Mafia II, and they're definitely right – a lot of killing and a lot of suits. Fact number three isn't. 'Wiseguys', with its implied streetsmarts and cunning, doesn't fit Mafia II's mobsters. It certainly doesn't fit the mid-level gangster the game asked me to tail early in its middle act, who didn't have the presence of mind to check his rearview mirror as he drove away from a literal hatchet job. Had that guy done so, he'd have seen Sicilian-born WWII veteran and new-boy mobster Vito Scaletta about 20 feet behind, dressed in a red and white cod- Hawaiian shirt, driving a hot pink corvette with 'BUMS12' proudly displayed on the numberplate. That guy was not very wise.
The other guy was me, and I was trying to be too wise. As Mafia II's protagonist, my first attempt to trail the escaping mobster ended in failure after my original car choice – an inconspicuous '50s saloon – was outpaced with ease on the motorways. I only chose that car, snatched unattended with a bit of pavement minigame lockpicking, to satisfy the mission briefing, which said my mark would notice anything too obvious. Dutifully I wrested against the vehicle's slightly clunky era-specific handling to try and keep pace. But after my AI target had pranged his own vehicle six times against anything and everything in his path, I realised that such forwardthinking wiseguyishness wasn't entirely necessary on my part.
That Mafia II so effectively harpoons its illusion of real life, showing its characters to be machines acting out prescribed paths, is to its detriment. But the fact that I bought into it in the first place is the game's greatest strength.
It's not that Vito is a sympathetic character. Returning from a war he held no moral stake in – after a botched robbery, it was that or prison – he joins the local mafia, even though his mum told him not to. Naughty. From there on, he relies upon menace through the typical mafioso triple-threat: punching, shooting, and scary staring. Best buddy Joe occasionally dips a toe into 'comic relief' territory, but then ducks back into 'just a bit nasty' land, gets his pistol and shoots everyone in comic relief territory. Those poor clowns.
The player's supporting cast eschews any chance to get really creative, instead furnishing the game with another layer of dark-suited, dark-haired professionals, hitmen and higher-ups that blur into one mass. Driven by his need for money and respect, Vito is encased in a series of ever-widening shells, each step up the mafia ladder (a ladder made of guns) giving a new set of faces to watch in cutscenes: but they're all congealed clichés, culled from a hundred Bronx Tales and Godfathers. The dialogue is wellwritten and excellently acted, but it feels mechanical, the spoutings of a supercomputer sat in a shady office with its dials set to 'lightly-accented macho threat.'
It was the city that drew me in. An amalgamation of New York's streets and Hollywood's hills, Empire Bay is as interactively sterile as all other 'open-world' game-cities, but it's been coated in a veneer of dreamy credibility. Each street and hallway has a feature – a man shouting at an open window; a woman pressing her ear to a door; the sound of an argument. It's easy to see these details written down in a design document, but it gives Empire Bay a genuine rhythm, a pulse that Liberty City lacks. Plus, it helps that it is – on hefty machines – stunning. Turn up in the city in winter, and the streets are caked in snow, with layered bands of crystalline white on the untrodden paths contrasting with slush on the roads. And the lights! Even as the game transitions out of the 1940s and into the '50s, Mafia II's waxy lighting remains consistently arresting, casting pools of gold and yellow on windscreens.
But there's no point to any of it. The city breathes and grows, changing as the missions span the years, but it never moves or cries out. The game is presented in chapters, and each chapter has you wake up in your home. Vito, I can inform you, is a man who sleeps in the same vest and pants for nine years. Before the poor, smelly bugger can even get dressed, he's hit with news and a job. The game forces you to drive to a location: once there, Vito either shoots some men, punches some men or drives to another location.
As their cheery local mafia man, I'd pop in to see my contacts. Need any guys whacking today? Anything nicked? Want me to punch a lady? I was good at all these things. But, always, no. To deviate from the missions just wastes time: you can rob shops, but won't procure much loot; you can pester civilians, but will only get police pressure. For a city dripping with incidental detail, the game slapped on top of it has none. Not that this is a mechanical problem – 2K Czech have never made any bones about Mafia II being a linear experience – but when the city itself looks so inviting, it's a shame you can't do more.
Unless you make your own fun, that is. I enjoyed people-watching in a city where every pedestrian and car driver has the situational awareness of a frightened rabbit. Drive near one of the AI humans on foot and their preset reactions kick in, launching them in a seemingly random direction. Sometimes, this would be toward safety; more regularly, they'd hurl themselves into speeding traffic.
Having a woman – a few moments earlier happily strolling down a sunny street – chuck herself in front of a nearby van is certainly a surprise. Having that van then swerve to try to avoid her and plough through another three pedestrians is brilliant. Having that van then be spotted by a police car, having those police open fire before getting squished by the panicky, blood-leaking van driver, is better than another cover-shooting 'kill 50 goons' story mission.
And those are too regular. Combat is supported by a pleasing system of gunplay that leads to weighty, inaccurate firefights heavily reliant on ducking behind cover. The enemy AI – so stupid at the wheel - doesn't redeem itself through Mafia II's battles. Bad guys just pop up and down from the same spots of cover like sharply dressed moles: whacking them is simply a matter of waiting. Early in the storyline, Mafia II displays a convincing unwillingness to murder indiscriminately, surmising that the repeated and wholesale murder of swathes of humanity isn't the mafia's major focus. This was the time I built my connections, prepared my lip for wobbling when my contacts became friends and my friends went to sleep with the fishes, as all mafia friends do. But then, three quarters of the way through, it forgets all that, and puts you up against waves of baddies, dehumanised after all that work to build Empire Bay's factions into tangible things.
Mafia II is a mafia movie run once through a game grinder, and that's simultaneously the worst thing about the game and the compliment it was developed for. In telling a story as convincing as most Hollywood depictions of the Cosa Nostra, 2K Czech have accomplished exactly what they intended to: only at the end does the artifice topple slightly, piling one too many game-cliché mass-battles onto the pile. But detach the story from its very familiar housings, and we're not left with much: a bit of walking, a lot of driving and too much shooting. Each is good, but rarely superb.

Let's get straight to the point.
Pros:
-Incredible soundtrack on par with AAA games and even superior
-Game aesthetics is consistent and the transition between various levels feels natural while very clichè
-Lots and lots of references to classic RPGs and games like Pokémon and Metal Slug but also anime like Gurren Lagann
-Gameplay is fun and intuitive for both new players and experienced ones, no huge walls of text to describe every single thing that most RPGs do, rather you can test in-game what is better and learn from it
-Interesting enemy types, even when they're just a different element they don't look like a reskin at all
-Grinding, while present, doesn't feel forced. Most bosses (And even some enemies) are challenging, but if you're having troubles most times all you need to do is level up once
-Skill system is not related to the level you are, rather you unlock new skills by improving your current skills or learning new ones
-Most weapons and armors when fully upgraded have game-changing abilities, giving you plenty of playstyle options
-Earning medals/achievements is actually fun, for once
-Dev actually listened to fans and improved the Steam version of the game by adding things like an in-game slider for the music and other options
-It's FREE
-The jokes and "memes" while being a bit dated still manage to make you giggle and remind you of the earlier internet days
-Effects during combat are beautiful to look at
-NG+ is present and gives multiple options, making it easier to get medals in case you forgot to scan some bosses
-Challenging harder difficulties
-Boobs and boobs accessories
Cons:
-It's a game made with Flash, so slowdowns are present
-Sadly no real way for a 720p or bigger resolution without fiddling with game files (not recommended) and the fullscreen option is just upscaled and blurry, which is sad because the game art is very pretty and would benefit from it
-Frame rate capped at 30, you can get to 60 by using the speed up option but rather than switching between 30 and 60 it just speeds up the game, and even then it slows down a lot while playing, recommended for people having trouble with keeping 30 frames, frameskip is also a valid option
-Some osts don't loop well
-No controller support, it's possible to bind keys to your controller with external programs but mouse is still required to navigate menus and during battles
-Some minigames can be really annoying if you plan on getting all achievements, although none of them are required to progress the game
The game for what it is, is a solid 9.5/10 for me, it's a must have for fans of turn-based RPGs.

Positives:
- Scouting is very fun, especially with other veteran players.
- The game is hardcore and you can lose your vehicle(s) and gang quite easily, especially if you scout solo. It is not an easy or forgiving game, especially with unskilled gangers.
Negatives:
- Huge time investment to skill up gangers, to go scouting, to do pretty much anything.
-The developer of this game, Sam, has moved on to bigger and better things. There will probably be no more content added to the game, there are skills like cycling that your characters have but cycles aren't even in the game and probably never will be put into the game. Do not spend any money on this game if you are hoping for serious improvements or ANY additional content added in the future. It is highly unlikely.
- The game is very time consuming no matter what you do. Scouting takes a very long time usually and if you decide to do events, there are specific times when events in each town start so you may have to wait an hour or more for a specific event to start. Yes, you can start your own events once every 30 minutes, but the rewards are much less than the ones that are on timers.
- There is a bug where the npc vehicles can shoot through the ground/terrain and hit you and when you shoot at them, you shoot the ground. You think you have positioned yourself in a good spot, only to get damaged or even killed due to this bug. VERY VERY ANNOYING OR EVEN GAME BREAKING. Why has this not been fixed? I was excited to try this game out because I love the rogue-like genre. I was not disappointed, and ended up with a very satisfying - but still brutal - experience.
If you enjoy the rogue-like genre, robot theme, turn-based combat, and lots of death and loot, then you will enjoy this game.
The aesthetics are decent - the robot models and animations are nothing too fancy. The music and sounds are good, but I personally found the opening (menu) song annoying after a few repetitions. The random dialogue that the enemy robots shout out is comical - ex: "why was I programmed to feel pain?" Eventually, I just muted all the sounds and played my own music.
The controls are simple and quick to learn. There are pop-up tutorials and the feedback when you hover over things is very helpful. The learning curve is minimal to moderate depending on your experience with the rogue-like genre and grid/turn-based games. The difficulty can be adjusted, and you will most likely not be playing misery for a long time - unless you are a glutton for punishment.
Gameplay is fast-paced and unforgiving - your goal is to prepare for an inevitable final battle against the robot horde (similar to the end-game boss fight in Faster than Light). You are presented with a randomly-generated map layout with branching missions. Doing a mission (regardless of failing/passing) will unlock the rest of the missions that are connected to that particular branch. Depending on the difficulty you are playing on, you will get x loot pieces per surviving robot member (aka Exo) after the mission is completed. You will also get different loot types depending on the mission you select - for example, laboratory missions will give you more computer modules. Whenever you fail, your HQ will lose a hit point, and if you reach 0, you will lose the game. Completing salvage missions will repair some damage to your HQ.
After every mission, more enemy robots are manufactured - you can hinder this by attacking robot command centers, which reduce the number of days before the final battle. You can also hunt down boss robots, making the end-game battle a bit easier. Be warned, these missions are extremely challenging, and should not be attempted until you have acquired mid- to high-tier gear. Your Exos do not level up - instead, you upgrade them with acquired loot. You can select 4 different Exos to make up your party, and you can even select 4 of the same type if you wish (this is not recommended). Examples include a sniper, ninja (stealth-based), and science (hacker/support) Exo. The character you select at the start of the game will give you different bonuses - I strongly suggest you select Tuck for your first few playthroughs because his sensor ability (allows you to see the objective and any loot containers) will increase your situational awareness greatly.
During mission gameplay, you move with the WASD keys and use the mouse to select weapons/skills. You travel as a single entity, so switching Exos will use one turn. This is critical to understand because you will automatically switch to the next Exo if your current one is destroyed - and I would die unnecessarily because I would waste a turn switching my science Exo to a different one, giving the enemy a free shot (and usually a free kill) at the Exo I switched to. You can blow up some doors, but others will have to be hacked in order to get to the loot containers within. Terminals also require hacking points, which is why a science Exo is essential to anyone wanting to maximize loot gained per mission. Many missions just require you to reach an endpoint mission marker, which is usually deep in the far end of the map. Each Exo can stealth past enemies for a short amount of movement spaces, but only the ninja Exo is able to attack while still staying in stealth mode. Some loot containers/terminals may restore your ammo, shields, hack points, or stealth points, however, some terminals may disable a random weapon or deplete all hacking points - such is the way of RNG-based games.
Overall, the game is a lot of fun if you like challenging grid/turn-based combat, and any rogue-like enthusiasts should give Bionic Dues a try.

A very positive surprise. In this game you control robots, "Exos", destroying enemy robots and collecting loot from the battlefields. The turn-by-turn mechanics are familiar from roguelikes such as NetHack, but the scifi setting reminds me of FTL. Cannot go wrong with that recipe!
Between each mission you are returned to the City Screen where you can also go and customize the Exos. This part, too, reminds me of customizing the spaceship in FTL: you need to select the most appropriate weapons and tools to all slots of the Exos and keep in mind the power constraint.
In the game you only control one Exo at a time, so no squad-based combat here. You can always swap the current Exo to another one, but that costs one turn, like everything else. The challenge is, of course, how to kill the enemies without getting killed yourself. Going in with your laser blazing usually ends in you getting killed, so you need to be more clever than that. One strategy is to use Stealth, get close to a powerful enemy, infect it with a virus and watch it kill the other enemies.
Once your Exo gets killed, it's out for the rest of the mission, so when you've got four Exos in total, you in a sense have four lives in each mission. The Exos have different strengths and weaknesses (just like the ships in FTL are different from each other), so, for example, getting your hacker Exo killed might make it impossible to hack impassable doors behind which loot usually lies.
The achievements seem to be something that actually need to be pursued, compared to some games that reward you with five as long as you just complete the tutorial. Finally, I'm also enjoying the game's soundtrack, which also has songs with vocals.
