Randomized top-down turn based "dungeon" crawler (1 turn = 1 move, like one step in cardinal direction or taking a shot, for you and your enemies). Your "party" can consist up to 4 different "members" of various "classes", but you only get to control one of your "party" members at a time, and swapping them in and out is a move on its own.
And there's also Mark XXVII Looted Epic Loot of Looting system thrown in for a good measure.
Except instead of going deeper into a fantasy dungeon, you go deeper into a sci-fi city in order to fight off crapshoot AI menace or your corporation will nuke the city, just to be sure, which means millions of lives lost as evac is, apparently, not an option (due to hand-wa... I mean, overcrowding).
The city exploration facet adds whole new dimension to the game - instead of one direction, down, you get a choice where to go next and the web of accessible missions grows as you go. Do you want to focus on particular type of loot? Make yourself stronger or enemy weaker? Or perhaps the next mission is not too great, but is located strategically and you need it to unlock path to some juicier mission in sight?
In default settings you get 50 missions/days to prepare for the ultimate showdown, each passing day meaning enemy robots grow in strength and number for assault on your base, and you are hoping to keep up, occasionally bringing them down a notch or two.
This is quite a roguelike experience, although permadeath and iron man mode, iron man mode, aren't turned on by default and who knows, maybe you want to keep it that way, at least at first, because the game is rather not easy as it is.
And it is actually a thinking man's game, if you just want to go guns-a-blazing, you're in for a bad time. It's not a top-down twitch shooter; you need to be very deliberate in your actions.

Wonderful unique turn based and creative game, fun and addictive. If you like turn based strategy games you will love this. The game is finish able even on the first try. There are several types of missions, and which one you choose can have a significant impact on how the game progresses. A new game starts on the city map where you choose from a web of different mission types. As you complete or fail missions, more are revealed. You win the game by either surviving the inevitable final bot onslaught, or lose when your headquarters are destroyed. There is a lot of replay ability value as your strategy will need to change depending on the lead character you select and the mech team you select. During the missions, you only control one mech (called "exos" in game) at a time, but you have four in your stable. There is a ton of generated loot you can use to improve your exos with, which you get from completing missions, find in chests, or buy from the shop. You can swap your exo for another at any time, though it will cost you an action. You lose the mission if all four exos are destroyed. There are six different exo classes, with an epic variation of each. There are also six different pilots to choose from, each with a unique ability. A solid game, that gives you a deep tactical experience.

TIPS TO ENJOY THIS GAME
===================
Castle Story is not perfect in its current 1.0 release, but there is a great game in there and perhaps these tips will give you a chance to enjoy the game within the two hour refund period ;)
1 ) There is in game help explaining all the basics, click on the '?' icon in upper right corner (and press 'P' to pause game while you read it).
2) Use the hotkey shortcuts (F1 - F5 keys), just using the 'F1' build key will save you several mouse clicks in the slightly fidely UI. Look in 'Options - Keybindings' for all the shortcuts and keys.
3) First thing you should do is chop down some trees, build one or two chopping blocks and a bunch of stockpiles (always have a few empty stockpiles so your cute yellow guys don't stop working).
4) If a task is not being worked on or completed, check you have the resources required and at least one empty stockpile if needed to store an 'item'. You can check what resources are required by holding RMB on the 'factory' (workbench, altar etc) and hovering mouse over the item to be (or is being unsuccesfully) crafted.
5) Following on from point 4 above, it is possible to set stockpiles to only recieve a specific item by holding RMB on the stockpile. Although over using this does more harm than good in my opinion, I do find it helpfull to do this for certain items on stockpiles placed close to the 'factory'. This helps you easily see if you have the required resources.
6) You can enable mouse edge scrolling in options, when playing fullscreen I had to enable 'allow mouse off sceeen' (or something) first.  Also, use ctrl-click to remove unwanted/misplaced block blueprints and there is a delete (trash bin) icon bottom right to remove selected task (it's easy to miss but super important sometimes).
7) And now the 'biggy' - the game starts to 'lag' (pauses/freezes), which can get quite bad - a few seconds freeze every 30 seconds later in a game!. In version 1.0 I have not been able to stop this completly, but it is possible to reduce it to infrequent short pauses. The issue is caused by the AI pathfinding on an ever changing 3D voxel landscape, so if you reduce the number of things pathfinding it helps. Use more soldiers and don't have too many builders/gatherers or leave some unspawned bricktrons in your home crystal and only spawn them (hold RMB on home crystal) to replace lost bricktrons (or set a bricktron to 'Do Nothing' - select him then HOLD RMB on him). Also, saving and then reloading the game every few hours can help.
So, would I buy this game (I was an early backer). I would probably not buy it at current price or until the 'lag' issue is resolved. However, I am still giving it a thumbs up as despite the issues, am loving playing it ;)
EDIT - If your bricktrons get stuck while mining, you can manualy tell said bricktron (or one of his yellow friends) to dig voxels by selcting bricktron then hold RMB on voxel to be dug and make a way out. If his bag gets full, select bricktron then hold RMB on him and select 'Drop Load'. I dont find this happens too often and the AI does a generaly good job of building stairs etc as they go, but occasionaly the rather simpleton bricktrons will be gazing up at the sky instead of concentrating on what there doing.
Note that the HOLD RMB radial menu options are dependant on the currently selected object (LMB click). So for example, if you have a soldier selected and hold RMB on a factory, you will get options to attack it etc - so you may need to LMB on the factory or empty terrain first if you want to manufacture something. Once you grasp this, the UI does start to make more sense ;)

After how ever many years of development, the team on this  decided they were  ready for 1.0, and I wish I could say I agree.
I've tried to give this a shot, but unfortunately this isn't ready for primetime. Issues I experienced just trying to poke around and learn the game in sandbox mode.
- Building anything other then a plain stone wall is an exercise in frustration. If you want a ramp you need supports, and if you want supports you need pillars of some kind, but guess what - there is no way to build a tall pillar without access to the upper parts, which requires a way to get up there - in the end you need structures to support the structures you need to build your structures. Onerous to a fault.
- Poorly documented - simple mouse-over information doesn't exist, so you can't tell what is needed to build a thing, let alone what it does.
- Incredibly poor player feedback. You create a job and... nobody does it. Why? Who knows! The game won't tell you why people aren't doing a thing. It got dark and everyone stopped working. Ok I said, maybe they won't work in the dark, ill make light pylons. The game will let me place some, but nobody is building them. Apparently I need the right workshop first but I couldn't discover this without first building ALL THE WORKSHOPS and checking the context menu for each to see who had pylons. Issues like this smack of what happens when your only feedback during the dev process was the developers, and diehard fans - i.e. people who know the game already. For everyone else, good luck figuring things out.
- Meanwhile I had no iron, but a rock face next to me with plenty. So I ordered a tunnel. Nobody built the tunnel. I tried deleting that and making a new tunnel. All the bricktrons run off to dig my tunnel... and the first guy dug one voxel worth of tunnel, while the rest complained they couldn't reach the tunnel. And then they stopped trying. This occured with 3 seperate attempts at this ♥♥♥♥ing tunnel, never getting farther then 1 cube dug.
- Fine I said, ♥♥♥♥ the tunnel. Lets dig a quarry, how hard can that be? It's just a hole in the ground. So I ordered a quarry dug. Nobody worked on it. I assigned workers manually. They walked to the spot of the quarry and sat down doing nothing.
Honestly ♥♥♥♥ this game. It's an exercise in frustration, with bugs colliding with an awful UI that doesn't convey enough to the player, so you'll be left wondering if you can't do a thing because you are missing a resource, or you hit a bug, or because you don't understand the mechanics. It isn't going to make it clear which is the case. God help you if you want to try and alt-tab out to research it - you'll need to sift through 4+ years of beta information, always wondering how much if any of what you are reading is still applicable.
Stay away, or at least wait for a few more releases. I would request a refund, but I paid for this 4 years ago when I kickstarted it.
Edit - On reflection, I'm probably a little harsh with my wording above. "F this game" isn't the most insightful commentary. That said, I wrote the above while angry and frustrated as a direct result of the issues I experienced, so there is something to that.

A decent game that can entertain you for some time. I enjoyed it for it's approachability thanks to the Parity patch, but now I am starting to wish that I could play this wonderful game pre-Parity.
Gunplay is for the most part, tight and well-implemented, and map variety in terms of setting is actually quite large. Most of the time, it's in an urbanized setting, but these areas differ widely between each map, from the city slums, to a besieged construction site.
Another little nuance about this game I find incredibly interesting, is that all players from the get go, have the ability to see almost every other player on the map using their V ability. This evens up the playing field somewhat for newer players who learn how to properly use the VISR, and generally prevents camping.
Generally.
Oh, and if you noted the almost from that previous paragraph, I put that there because of the fact that you can purchase a cloaking module that hides you from plain sight and VISR. But only for a short amount of time. So, nothing ridiculous.
A complaint I have of this game though, is it's servers. Most servers I play on nowadays are well under max population, and few servers are populated at all. Most gamemodes are similarly abandoned, as it's almost always TDM or FFA with perhaps one or two lobbies of this game's co-op survival mode online.
Oh, yes. This game does have a co-op survival mode. Pretty neat eh? It's actually quite fun, and is a fantastic time killer for around half an hour. Or would be at least, if the servers were actually populated.
Another issue with the servers, is that ping can sometimes skyrocket absurdly for some godforsaken reason. It might be a result of this being the PS4 version of the PC game (yes, I know. twatthe♥♥♥♥), or maybe for some other reason. Regardless, it's an issue.
Overall, 8/10. It's still a great game- assuming you find some people to play with. Oh, and if said people haven't paid any considerable sum of money to purchase items.

AirMech is a top-down Action real-time strategy game with its main concepts influenced by the old
Before giving a review of the game, I should elaborate on my taste in games as the reviewer. I like new ideas and new game mechanics, I prefer old classic strategy games over modern ones and I'm not very fond of the Free-to-play model in principle. I have been playing strategy games since the original Herzog Zwei in the very early 90s.
Your play and control one of various mechs, where the default one is a jet fighter. What they all have in common is that the unit is directly controlled by you as in an arcade game. Compared to a "normal" RTS game, this unit acts as your mouse cursor.
When you are in the air as a jet/chinook/saucer you can pick up units, fly them off somewhere and place them where you want, as well as giving units different commands such as "hold ground" and "attack enemy base".
When you transform into a mech you walk on the ground, can fire on ground targets and generally support your troops with different mech abilities.
You start with a home base where you can build units. The goal of the main game mode is to destroy the opponents base. In addition to the starting bases, the maps have outposts which can be taken over to earn resources faster, in addition to act as recharge stations when your mech's health gets low or when you run out of energy.
The game matches are played 1vs1, 2vs2 or 3vs3 either in player-vs-player or player-vs-AI. A survival mode similar to tower-defense games lets up to 4 players defend a base against several incoming waves of enemy units.
Since your opponent will be constantly fighting you over additional outposts as well as harassing your main base and your units, the game can become very hectic and fast-paced. The times you win, it feels very rewarding.
The game has tons of customization options. Where Herzog Zwei had around 8 different units, AirMech has over 60 units. However, you have to select a subset of these for your avatar character before starting a match, and only 8 different units can be in your build menu at any time. In addition, your mech can be enhanced by various upgrades.
There are also cosmetic upgrades to make your mech and units stand out from the rest. Which brings us to..
The game is free of charge, which in of itself is amazing. I'm also happy to say that there aren't any balancing issues due to the profit model; the game is not "pay2win" as some people accuse free-to-play games of being. The company earns money on people buying the in-game currencies, which is used to buy units, mechs and upgrades in the game store. If you don't use your hard-earned cash however, you get credits for just playing the game and meeting daylies. If you are familiar with Blizzards Hearthstone, you know basically how it works. Someone who spend money on the game save themselves from maybe 4-6 hours of gameplay, which is the time you would need to get the basic units. Other than that, the things for sale are mostly cosmetics, such as a tank skin with a gothic look.
I love the main game mechanic! In RTS games such as Starcraft, when you get over a certain skill level, the game is won based on who can dish out the most commands to the most units in the least amount of time, all else being equal.
In AirMech the mouse-clicking fest doesn't happen because unit commands are given via your mech, and your mech is limited in how fast it can fly around. It gives people with not-so-great reflexes (hello me!) a fighting chance, but still requires skill. It's just that AirMech requires a different skillset than RTSes like Starcraft and Command & Conquer. It's an RTS, but also an arcade game.
The graphics style in the game is superb, and my modest computer from 2011 plays the game at a decent framerate. I know that a lot of gamers like flashy graphics, and the more realistic games look the better. If you're one of those, you won't find that here. But AirMech doesn't try to look realistic. Rather, the developers went for a more cartoon-like look with very colorful scenes. I prefer game graphics which decides for a certain art style, rather than games that adds all sorts of HDR lighting, blooming and depth-of-field.
The whole game interface is really well made. Menus are sharp and descriptive. After logging in, you'll see a chat window where you can talk to other players, find opponents or people to play coop with. The community seems very friendly towards beginners.
This is mostly nitpicking, however there are some things that goes against my personal preferences.
While the overall artistic style of the game is great, some of the abilities or unit skins you can get are just strangely out of place graphics-wise. The "boomer" unit can be made to look like a Creeper from Minecraft. That doesn't fit the game at all! The overall style of the game is a kind of post-apocalyptic future where mechs control the earth, but here you have creepers in the battlefield, and mech abilities in the form of witches on brooms? If other players like it, that's fine by me, but it would be nice to be able to turn it off or be able to choose default skins/models for all players that are more consistent.
As the game is in the free-to-play category, the developer/publisher needs to make money somehow. And that brings me to annoying attention-grabbing and nagging. Whenever I start the game and enter the main menu / lobby, the game nags me to give referral links to friends (basically free promotion) and get in-game currency in return. In addition, the game highlights the store icon and your current credits sometimes, and hints you to spend your credits and buy more in subtle and not so subtle ways. This is incredibly annoying! I'd like to focus on playing the game, not get nagged on to spend money and treated like a walking wallet. Even if a game is free to play, it should be possible to turn off all the stuff which distracts you from the main game.
Note that the actual game matches are void of this problem. It's only in the main menu/lobby.
Herzog Zwei which this game is influenced by was great because of its game mechanics and its simplicity. But the free-to-play model is incompatible with simplicity. The end result is that the number of units and items in AirMech is inflated quite a bit. It might sounds strange that more choice and customization could be considered a bad thing, but here it is. The game would be vastly better by less choice and complexity, but I suppose the publisher would be making less money that way.
Despite the nitpicking above, AirMech is incredibly fun to play. And it has something for everyone, whether you are a hardcore competitive RTS player or a casual gamer. Play PvP ranked if you enjoy competitive play, or team up with other players against the AI otherwise.
You can use mouse+keyboard or an Xbox 360 joypad, and getting into a match takes seconds. A match lasts for between 10 and 20 minutes, so you have time to play in your lunch break if that's your thing. The strategy and tactics in the game can be incredibly deep depending on the experience of the players, and no two rounds are the same.
The game's presentation suffers a bit from the free-to-play market model and it would be nice to be able to pay once to get rid of the "give me more money!" nagging, but nothing is perfect. And again, the game does *not* give paying players any advantage.
I give AirMech 7.5 out of 10. It's free! At least install it and give it a try.

Since the player’s list of tasks is geographically diverse (units and turrets are produced at command hubs that can be captured, and must be ferried around the map) and incredibly time-sensitive, the player must hurry themselves breathlessly around the map being economist, logistics manager and combatant by turns, and shirking any of these duties is detrimental to their overall game state.
Leave your build queue alone for too long, you’re depriving yourself of the support of the at times vital support of artillery, heavy tanks, or harass vehicles. Leave the front lines alone for too long, you’re leaving your units to be free money and levels for your opponent. Neglect your upgrades (which can only be applied at a structure, away from the frontlines) and you’re depriving yourself of tools to get yourself further ahead in the match.
I would go so far as to say, and I do not say this lightly, that AirMech is one of the most mechanically demanding strategy games I have ever played. It is not quite as frenetic as StarCraft 2 can be, but barring that I cannot think of a game that puts this sort of onus on the player to act and think quickly. Making poor choices in game is immensely punishing in a way I am pressed to describe in a way that’d be meaningful to my audience. Just pumping out whatever units you want is giving away money and experience to the enemy. paying attention to the wrong thing for too long can lose you critical momentum and map control.
And the beauty (in my mind) of this all is that the singular focus of the AirMech unit itself means that this game can be meaningfully played on a console. AirMech Arena for the Xbox One is in early access testing right now, and has been on the Xbox 360 for… I think about a year? Maybe a couple of months. The player is by needs a little less able to multitask, but the game is eminently playable with a controller.
This is NOT a comprehensive overview of the game. I have not touched at all on the game’s monetization model, which sells unit types and AirMech upgrades (and could easily be considered to give advantage to players who are willing to drop money on purchasing these things, which is potentially problematic though I personally don’t mind the model) but… I had to take a moment and share the admirably focused design of the core game experience, which I cannot help but appreciate.

Right now, this game offers an amazing single player experience. Which is great for me since i prefer single player games, but the developers did admittedly advertise the game as an ONLINE fighting game . Sadly, even for me in New York, the online play was very laggy and there we obviously a couple of bugs. My very first 1v1 on release day was lag free and a fun experience. Now, a few days later, any pvp match is a rubber banding mosh pit of stun locking and 5 second late dodges. My real issue with the game is the range that NPCs can detect you. This game does not have stealth, but this ridiculous range means that a 1 v 1 can easily become a 2 v 1 the moment you move a little too much. No matter the level, due to the camera locking mechanic, anytime you damage an enemy, 2 v 1s are pretty damn frustrating. There is no option to adjust the field of view. So when you are in a 2 v 1 and hit an npc, it is extremely easy to lose sight of the other npc and be stun locked from behind by the attacker. I think the fix for it is to offer a toggle so the camera does NOT instantly lock when you damage an enemy and the range be halved for NPC aggro. That way 2 v 1s that are done purpose like some of the boss fights still exist, but I do not get randomly stun locked and full off a ledge because I could not see 2 other NPCs ganging up on me in the middle of my fight with another NPC. I guess like with all games now-a-days, wait a week or two to purchase if you want great online. Buy it now for a great single player and a decent online experience.  Also the game is region locked if you did not notice. Not an issue for me but it has obviously♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off a lot of others.

This game, while not very long, is a hell of a lot of fun. It does a fantastic job of rewarding you for using blocks, parries, and dodges, and punishes you for just trying to button mash. The combat really makes you feel like your hits are powerful and the enemies hits hurt. The Art style is beautiful and the music, and lack of in some cases, really compliments the game.
There are a few issues, though;
-The camera can get buggy sometimes when near a wall or in a confined area, causing you to either stare down at your character or try to see through the wall itself.
-Any more than a 2v1 can get pretty hard to manage as the AI tend to stagger their attacks so its difficult for you to get any hits off.
-The game is pretty grindy which, for me, isnt a big deal. I like being able to fight a lot of enemies just to learn their attacks for myself, but I can understand some people not liking that
-Overall the main "story" is pretty short, it took me just under 5 hours to complete. There is some endgame stuff, however, like creating a school of your own so your friends can join and learn moves from you.
The game is a ton of fun, especially for $30, and the devs have already said theyre going to be releasing more endgame stuff in later updates.

I'm chosing to leave a positive review despite the current state of the game because I really want this game to succeed.  And it can.  There is a small but dedicated and passionate team behind the game.  They mastered the core gameplay loop on this one, it's simple and easy to learn but difficult to master.  Single player works just fine offline (great choice not to require constant online else the game would never succeed with the current issue) and is lots of fun, if you're into that.  You can go in, refine your style, fight the bosses and when server issues are fixed take that stuff online.  Just... be aware of the current issues.  For some of us, this is the closest we could get to our dream game and it must succeed.

I admittedly bashed this game before for being too hard and to some extent, it is.  I would still prefer an easy mode that allows me a bit more freedom to do what I want, as well as an in-game explination as to what certain objects and people do. The "New Lands" version starts you off on an island with only one side to worry about as opposed to the "Classic" version, where you had portals on both sides.  In essence, there's some progression in terms of difficulty, but it's still easy to screw up without knowing it.  For example, you may think to build some walls in between you and the portal to slow down the enemy, only to find out the game's AI automatically moves your archers and catapult up to the farthest wall.  The game doesn't tell you this until it's too late and you watch your men get slaughtered cause your wall wasn't upgraded enough.
The new content and the fact that this version is free to Kingdom owners is a plus.  The first level is still difficult for me and will be for beginners, but from what I read if you die on future islands you have to start all over again on island one.  EDIT: Apparently that's what the map is for...another example of a missed opportunity to inform players as to how the game actually works.  ;)

Okay, so this is my review of the ACTUAL game, not the PC Port. I wanted to make the big "Don't buy this broken trash" thing very apparent. If, through some random act of God you get a working copy for your PC, here is what I think of it:
Some people out there are fans of Street Fighter. Some people are fans of Tekken. Naturally, since both are fighters, and Capcom likes crossing over with everyone they can, it was natural that they'd meet. And they did... in Tekken 7.
That's my biggest complaint about Street Fighter X Tekken. The two systems are not compatable in the slightest. Street Fighter is a Jojo's Bizarre Adventure/Fist of the North Star inspired supernatural martial arts series. Tekken, while crazy, is mostly about real martial arts techniques and simulating them. Even their control schemes are vastly different: Six attack buttons vs a button for each limb.
The end result is that while the Street Fighter characters are just fine, the Tekken characters only barely resemble themselves. Between Jin firing energy dots and Xiaoyu using strange magical... slashy things? Anyway, my point is that these Tekken fighters don't seem to fit in any of the two universes. The designs are there, but the moves are not. For that reason, it seems less like Street Fighter vs. Tekken so much as "Street Fighter + these one-off characters you'll never see again." This is why some fighting franchises better lend themselves to crossovers; Capcom and SNK, for example!
With that said, how does Street Fighter + These Newbies hold up? Well, the game engine is remarkably similar to Street Fighter IV, at least, in most respects. Some new gimmicky features have been added, like a Tag Tournament System (not like MVC but more like Tekken Tag Tournament) that unfortunately cannot be turned off for straight 1v1 matches, a mode that grants you immense power at the expense of basically forcing you to win in five seconds, the ability to charge your super move for no meter and leave yourself wide open and telegraphed... that's what I mean by gimmicky. These features don't do well in actual combat, least of all since you're basically tethered to your partner character.
Wait a sec... isn't there one extra gimmick I missed?
(PLEASE SPEND $5 FOR NEXT PARAGRAPH)
Oh yeah, Gems! THE thing that drove the Capcom haters nuts. Honestly, gems are about the least intrusive thing in this game. They activate when you do things you already do in fight and provide effects that, as far as I know, are incredibly minor. Honestly, you probably won't even need any of them, which is good because this stuff can get expensive!
(PLEASE SPEND $20 FOR NEXT PARAGRAPH)
Speaking of expenses, this game has quite a bit of DLC, and it's not managed well. The game's DLC system isn't quite like SFV's, but I'd best describe it as "Unlockable Content Behind a Paywall". Indeed, 12 characters are locked away and the only key is your hard-earned cash. Aside from the Gems and the Characters, most of the DLC is fairly minor. Some cosplay DLC, and some new outfits for the cast that look good on the Street Fighter guys, but make the Tekken guys look less like themselves, like Bryan Fury as a clown with a blocky toy robot Jack.
(THE NEXT SECTION OF THE ARTICLE CAN ONLY BE READ ON PS3 BROWSER)
And one more for the trifecta of doom: console favoritism. More and more, each console port misses a bit of content from the big package, to the point where only the PS3 and Vita versions are truly complete. Sadly, for those of you who jurry-rigged this game to get it to work, you will find that the PC has the least amount of content. 1 alternate costume for each character, the cosplay outfits for the DLC characters, and some other cosmetics are gone, but the big loss is that the PC version is not only missing Cole and Sony's two mascots, but Mega Man and Mokujin Pac-Man are also missing. Well, missing in the sense that they cannot be accessed in-game; their files are buried in the code, but cannot be activated. It baffles me how they can do excellent ports like Ultra Street Fighter IV, then completely fail with this. You know, aside from the game not working without applying power tools to it.
Should you carve through the game's code and rip out the missing characters, you will find them... not what you expected. Both Mega Man and Pac-Man are not the Capcom and Namco mascots you remember, but jokey versions of them with a humorous twinge. Mega Man takes the form of the man of the infamous American cover of the first NES game, a joke that got a laugh out of Mega Man's creator Keiji Inafune. Similarly, Pac-Man pilots a massive mech based off the quintisessential joke character of Tekken, Mokujin. Both are very weird, very silly, and contribute to a feeling that this game doesn't take itself too seriously. Given one player character is a literal bear, that's not too surprising.
What IS surprising is the modeof the game I spend the most time in: color edit. Indeed, you can create whole new palettes for each character in the game and their costumes. Each color is free, thankfully, so you can create some interesting looks. Or you can sin against nature and create something hideous with glowing purple skin and clashing colors on all angles. Or you can be incredibly uncreative and recreate your favorite color scheme from an older game. Or you can be just plain rude and not edit them, meaning you can potentially fight a mirror match with two guys who look exactly the same. Good luck!

WOW, this game really took me by surprise.  No, seriously, I had never heard of this before it released on Steam, but I decided to take a gamble and buy it, and I'm blown away.
If you miss the 3D platformer/collectathon genre, and maybe you've been disappointed by some other indie attempts to mimic that genre, I think maybe you should try Unbox.  It does have similar gameplay to those N64-era favorites, but it's kinda doing its own thing at the same time.  Unbox isn't a straight-up clone of Mario 64 or Banjo Kazooie.. it sets out to provide a similar type of game, while bringing its own unique flavor.
The controls are solid (at least on a controller, I haven't really tried Mouse/keyboard yet), the gameplay and world seem polished, and the game gives you some really big, detailed worlds to explore, collect things, and complete challenges in.  It even has boss fights!
At the time of writing this review, I've played about 2 hours, and I've only just reached the second world (not counting the rather large hub area), and I'm having a great time. I've been collecting any collectibles that I've come across, and I plan on going back for the rest later, because I'm actually having enough fun to maybe 100% this.
If I had one thing to complain about, it'd be the music.  It's not bad or anything, you just hear it looping over and over and over and over again, and it gets kinda old after a while.. or at least the first world's music does.
Anyway, this is exactly the kind of thing I was looking for, and I was glad to stumble upon it.  It gets my full recommendation.

A decent game, if you enjoy market and economy, which is all this game really is. The goal and premise in the game is that you run a shop. What you sell is up to you, and depends on what kind of workers you hire to produce items. This means diversity in the market which makes for an active economy. Focusing what you craft means you can use your profits to buy things you're not able to make, or spread out more and be independant at the cost of slower progression.
A large part of the game is that you'll take residence in a city, either of your own creation or by joining one in the community. The purpose is to work together with your fellow players to invest in the cities structures which provide buffs and upgrades including resources, heroes and more features.
Questing is done with your heroes, who are also your patrons. They'll bring back loot which functions as resources for crafting, ontop of other things like gold, rare gear, item chests and even in-game currency. There's also weekly weekend raids that your city can participate in for special rewards. When you find a nice city of people you get a good sense of community and helping eachother.
The free to play system seems fine, from what I've seen of it. Paying for Gems (in-game currency) just means you'll save time, but this game is meant to be a time waster. You can get Gems from plenty of sources in the game, like quests, daily logins, special item orders, achievements and just selling randomy stuff you craft to other players. It can be used for plenty of things, but once again, just saves time. You can also sync your pc and mobile accounts. Great for casual or serious players.
If you really want you can just play pretend Star Trek.

text:
Short Version: Equip right or die on your quest to kill the demon.
Long Version: So this is all and all a very solid game. The place it really shines is combat and progression. As someone who's played a long line of turn based RPG's, I can easily say the EBF series has some of the best working combat systems in the genre, which has been something that's always had me coming back to it. And while it doesn't really change up the game in any insane ways from other games in the genre, everything here is extremely polished and that alone makes it a great journey.
Combat: You have HP. The enemies have HP. You have a magic knight, mage, a gunner, and a legless cat as support. You attack, use skills, magic, and items until the enemy is dead. It's the tale as old as time, but EBF3 just refined the mechanics very, very well so that the whole game feels pretty smooth. Although EBF3 does include a wave system, so that some battles are actually linked together without a break in between. It's rather neat, and makes you think ahead before you finish off all the current enemies.
Progression: EBF3 does this cool thing where it shows you all the skills you can learn off the bat. You just have to gather the AP to learn them (Something you obtain from all battles). You can learn the skills in almost any order (Some do have prerequistes) and upgrade them as you go through the game. You will feel a definite shift in power as your characters go from what feels like new adventurers to powerful heroes that could take on anything.
Equipment: You know how it kind of bites in most JRPGs where when you equip the next armor level, it doesn't actually change the character's looks? Well, EBF3 is the game where every single armor, weapon, and headgear changes how a character looks. And a lot of the armor sets are pretty fantastic (The Officer's Uniform is a personal favorite). But a big part of the game is how equipment is very important to how battles play out. Resistances will make or break a battle, as well as weaknesses. But the game gives a very, very generous option to change your equipment in the middle of combat in case you made a mistake, or your enemies change and you need to switch to a different weapon. Another very, very cool thing the game does is it's upgrade system. You can upgrade your equipment which provides the standard increased stats as any normal game, but the higher upgrade levels straightup give new abilities to the equipment your using. Example, some weapons gain the ability to counter when hit when you upgrade them higher. One last cool thing it does it how the weapons stats are all balanced with each other, meaning you don't actually obtain better gear as you go through the game, just different gear. No gear is better then the rest, but it depends on the current situation which gear is the best. (That being said, Heaven's Gate is the best sword)
Difficulty: The game is extremely fair with it's difficulty. Because the game increases the amount of experience you get by area, it is very difficult to become extremely overpowered and just slaughter everything early. Not only that, because of how it works, Grinding is something I almost never needed to do throughout the game, save for one period near the end of the game, and even that was only for around 20 minutes. And I played the game on it's highest difficulty, Epic, where the enemies all did 60% more damage automatically. The Bosses are also appropriately balanced, and often require more then a little thinking to defeat. That being said, the game's secret room, unlocked only when have all 60 achievements/medals is entirely unfair and completely evil.
Story: There's a demon which sucks up the powers of the the three protagonists because they needed to be weaker so we could have a game. Story isn't the intent of the Epic Battle Fantasy series, and it's mainly used as an excuse for the game's fantastic combat and several jokes. This does mean this isn't the place to look for a deep story or long running narrative, but this also means you don't need to play any of the other games in the series to be really prepared to play this one.
Closing Statement: This game is pretty fantastic because it achieves what it sets out to do. If you're looking for complex storytelling, look away from here. But if you're looking for a pretty fun time on a game that has a fantastic battle system, a great equipment system, some good comedy, and don't feel like spending any money at the moment, this is the place to go.

Short, blunt and honest, so stick with me here.
Gameplay is top notch.  Refining your personal style, executing it and exploring the world is a simple yet satisfying formula.  Don't need to be an expert at fighting games to enjoy it, just hop in and have fun.
However, it is pretty buggy at the moment.  If you're looking to hop right into the multiplayer, don't bother.  It's either too laggy or you won't connect.  When it does work, it's great.  Other flaws will be ironed out over time, but they do exist.
I'm chosing to leave a positive review despite the current state of the game because I really want this game to succeed.  And it can.  There is a small but dedicated and passionate team behind the game.  They mastered the core gameplay loop on this one, it's simple and easy to learn but difficult to master.  Single player works just fine offline (great choice not to require constant online else the game would never succeed with the current issue) and is lots of fun, if you're into that.  You can go in, refine your style, fight the bosses and when server issues are fixed take that stuff online.  Just... be aware of the current issues.  For some of us, this is the closest we could get to our dream game and it must succeed.

This game is a sexy blend of DOTA style combat and RTS that can be played 1 v 1, 2 v 2 or 3 v 3. Survival mode makes the game play like a tower defence game.
You control an Airmech which is basically a transformer. When in your air form you move fast and can carry units, issue commands to groups of units and more. When grounded you take the form of a combat robot to dispatch enemies and boost allies depending on the Airmech you chose.
All Airmechs provide different gameplay experience. Your load out from mech, pilot, item, optional parts and the units you will be able to build in game is your choice. There is also many cosmetic items from alternate skins to little critters that follow you around.
Game is true F2P with only player market and cosmetics blocked for non-cashers. The game can be purchased for a 1 time fee called Airmech Prime which unlocks most units, all mechs many parts and much more.
Airmech is a blend of genres that does enough to become a new genre in its own right. Best RTS game in years imo, very smart game from a small dedicated dev team.

If you want to be taken by the hand while learning the ins and outs of a game, this is not for you.
If you need great high-def graphics to enjoy a game, this is not for you.
If you want a forgiving game, this is most definitely not for you.
However:
If you like unique games, don't mind scanning through the forums and wiki  for answers, enjoy games set in a wasteland like Fallout or Mad Max, and want a challenging, unforgiving game in a persistent world where most learning will be done by comitting fatal errors, look no further! Once you experienced nearly your entire crew getting killed and lost all your vehicles on what you thought would be a routine run, you will show your true face. Can you fight your way back (through many setbacks along the way) or will you tuck your tail between your legs and run?
I haven't regretted a single minute in this game, including - or maybe especially - these setbacks. Your special prodigee, who you spent so much time on in order to make him a worthwhile gang leader, may be (and most likely WILL be) dead in the blink of an eye if you slightly misjudge a situation. You will find yourself getting very attached to your gang members, but also to some of your vehicles. In fact, some cars will be more important to you than some gangers, and you'd rather risk someone losing a limb (yes, it happens) or his life than having your car captured.
That's Dark Wind for you.

A free-to-play game that can actually be played for free – there are a ton of ways to earn premium currency that don’t require you to spend a cent (I haven't, and don't plan to.)
You run a shop which sells weapons/armor/items to heroes.  Many of those require rare items to craft, which can only be acquired from dungeons. So you kit out your heroes and send them to gather the materials you need. As your heroes become higher level, they’ll request better and better gear, which requires higher-level rare materials, which means running higher level dungeons, which means…
All the while, you’re constantly upgrading your shop – starting off with a tiny little space and a single crafter, you’ll eventually have an enormous facility buzzing with activity.
Every week, cities that are high enough level to have a castle host a raid dungeon, where everyone in the city pools their resources to unlock gold, gems, keys, rare crafting materials, and (if you’ve got a lot of dedicated, preferably high-level players) exclusive blueprints.
If I had to name some negatives:
PvP is almost exclusively the domain of ancient players who have fully equipped their heroes with legendary weapons and armor. It’s not impossible to beat them, but it’s an uphill battle that requires strategy and a little luck. Complete hero quests to unlock their abilities to have a fighting chance.
Shopkeeper level-ups really, really slow down in the mid-20s and 30s.  The only suggestion I can give to new players is to level up your heroes – the higher level they are, the higher level the items they’ll request, and the more XP those items will be worth.
Anyway, I’m having a lot of fun slowly unlocking more and more of the high level blueprints.

I thought I'd put up a review for this really underappreciated little game.
Developer Arcen Games makes wildly creative, deep, and eccentric genre-benders, the most celebrated of which is their asymmetrical space RTS/4x/tower defense, "AI Wars." AI Wars is clearly a great game, but somehow it's this one that I keep coming back to.
Bionic Dues is Arcen's take on a "roguelike," but of course in proper Arcen style it is totally unique.
Basically, it has a lot in common with a proper roguelike: you guide your characters through a series of procedurally generated dungeons. But there are a *lot* of interesting twists:
- You have 4 characters, (which are actually some sort of mecha exoskeleton?) in any combination of "classes," but can only use one at a time, and it takes a turn to swap them out.
- Loot and inventory customizaton is of primary importance. Each bot has *tons* of inventory slots, in several categories, and each class is different. Carefully poring over the hundreds of components you find, and optimizing their arrangement on each robot chassis, balancing your overall strategy, is the part of the game that I find utterly addictive. (It feels a lot like ship design in Gratuitous Space Battles, another of my favorites.)
- There is a sort of top-level strategy layer linking the dungeons. In between runs, you re-arrange robot parts, and choose your next raid target based on likely risk/rewards and your overall position in the map, with a global counter ticking down to a final level full of particularly nasty enemies.
- Understanding enemy AI and abilties is really important. There are a lot of enemy bot types, with simply-defined behaviors that are nevertheless complex in their interactions, and they appear in randomized combinations that can really change the way you approch a given dungeon.
- The game can be played with a number of different difficulty options, and core gameplay modifiers like the addition of permadeath, ironman mode, and time-limits on turns. This really allows you to tweak the game to your liking; you can choose to allow save-scumming, seeking the perfect run, or you can make it a much more tense and chaotic affair.
One thing that needs mentioning: a lot of the art assets are just awful-looking, especially on the strategy and inventory-management screens. To enjoy the game, you will have to be able to get over this, and see the item illustrations as purely functional conveyors of data. This works fine for me, but I'm sure it turns a lot of people off. Thankfully, I think the dungeon art is pretty nice-looking.
Frankly, I also found the music and voices to be awful (though a lot of the sound design itself is pretty nice,) and I tend just turn it off and listen to my own music.
Despite all the ugly warts, I keep coming back to this one. If you like procedural turn-based dungeon crawling, and find yourself spending a lot of enjoyable time comparing stuff on inventory screens, this might be a good one for you.
I also like that it lends itself well to short play sessions; you can pop in for a quick dungeon or a bit of stat-crunching without feeling too committed. It's also a good game to have running in the background while you're doing something else, taking a turn now and then.
All in all, this is a deep little game that's well worth its price tag - at the time of this writing, it's available at the ridiculous sale price of $1.99, and no roguelike fan should miss it.

Ok, while this was a rocky road to start, don't be fooled.  When I first picked this game up, it was confusing, and rather intimidating.  The tutorial, while helpful, was not as informative as it probably could have been.  Adjusting the difficulty of the game, you will find a wash of text information that not only doesn't make any sense, but really won't make sense till you actually get into the game, so I just recommend starting on normal so you can experience some challenge, and some life lessons that the easier difficulties will probably not provide.  Unfortunately, alot of the mechanics of the game are hidden, much the same as many Rogue-likes in the genre.
Bionic Dues places humanity (in a city) on the brink of extinction.  You are the last suriving folks in a quarentined city.  You are also made fully aware in the first minute of the game, that the government is going to glass the city (bomb it to crap) to kill the out of control infected robot invasion menace (you included).  You are placed in an overworld map, and a variety of missions will spawn around you.  This layout changes with every game, so don't expect to plan your routes.
You will find when you first start the game, that there are alot of mysteries as to why the game is so damn difficult.  But after you start to figure out the mechanics of the game you will make more and more progress.  The issue is, that with every mission you take on, fail or succeed, the monsters of the game level up and grow in number.  This can be frustrating, but stick with it, it gets ALOT better.
Every monster in the game has a unique personality, that when properly exploited, will spell the only real way to succeed in the harder difficulties.  A mission can still be finished with lack luster gear, if the proper enemies are present, and properly manipulated.  Granted, equipment, the proper enemy spawns, and level layout, are random, so no gaurantee that the moons will align.  Be sure to save often, it is a total lifeline.
Unfortunately for my gameplay experience, when I figured out how the game worked, the normal difficulty was a simple steam rolling session of success after success after success, minus a few situations that totally screwed me. The early portion of the game is most certainly difficult.  The slightest mistake can end with one if not two of your Exo's being destroyed instantly.  But later on, your Exo's can take so much damage, that it they are comparable to some of the boss monsters in the game.  Don't get me wrong, even when you get that powerful, things can still happen that can shaft you, at least that remains consistent.
Bottom line though, this game will easily give you hours of entertainment.  The game is incredibly fun, surprisingly deep, and should give quite the lengthy playtime if you like challenging yourself with the levels of diffiuclty (misery being the real way to play the game)  I do recommend this.  Its got a little strategy, its got alot of random chance, and given the mechanics, it can either be easy, or challenging based on your preferences.  Definitely worth the investment of time and money.

From the moment you start this game you can tell where it gets its inspiration and thats the games of Rare in the 90s. From the cute nonsense babbling characters to the light sense of humour, this is a love letter (no pun intended) to the likes of Banjo and so far I love it. The first world is brimming with charm; from the boxes that follow you around and welcome you to the little cars you can drive. I always think that you can tell the quality of a 3D platformer by how much you want to just forget about the point of it and explore, and this one had me doing it from the start (which is frustrating that it starts with a locked in tutorial).
Amount of content -
1x Hub World
3x Quest Worlds
Each world will take you around 2hrs minimum. I think most people will play it for between 8-10hrs and it took me 16hrs to 100% it. There is enough content to warrent the asking price, especially when you consider that the quest worlds are considerably bigger than a level in a game like Banjo.
Gameplay -
On the surface this is a collectathon like Mario64, Banjo etc, but it is not just copying them and I love the fact that it is also trying to bring something new to the table, which comes in the form of the unbox mechanic. This allows you to jump up to 6 times without landing, enabling crazy big jumps. The game suggests your health is connected to the unbox mechanic, however there are very few things that actually make you lose health which for me does diminish the excitement of it by the end.
Another way in which it builds on the platformers it takes inspiration from is the amount of character interactions. Not only are their quests to find, but people to talk to about the world you are exploring adding further flavour to the world you are tumbling through.
The difficulty of the game is similar to the likes of Banjo with a mixture of stupidly easy to more fiddly tasks. However the tone of the game gives you the feeling of relaxed fun even when trying to judge the gap between two distant boats you want to jump to.
Finally there is the customisation of your plain brown box. Completing the tasks and parts of the story lead to customisation unlocks which means you can turn your boring packaging into a weird bounding wonder. So if definining the protagonist your way is important to you then it is there and it is easy to do (you just need to find the tailor, which took me about 10mins after the first island unlocks).
Graphics and Technical Stuff.
The graphics are a mixed bunch with a combination of some great water textures and rock textures combined with some very plain ones mixed in, which works for the most part but at times can seem a little strange (watch the video above and you will see what i mean). However I found its short comings did not hinder the gameplay, which based on the first world I love.
It has an uncapped framerate and on my 970 rig will all settings maxed I was getting around 100fps at 1080p and there were no noticable major dips or stuttering. You can adjust things like FOV if you want and I know this is an important issue for some.
I would like to note that the game did crash for me while I was messing with the settings, but I suspect this was my firewall, because when I logged back in I had to allow the game access to areas my firewall didn't auto allow. After this initial crash I had no other bugs or crashes playing the game, however there was a little screen tearing which was largely removed by uncapping the framerate (others have suggested turning on vsync in your GPU control panel).
Controls -
How the character controls is important in a platformer as much as any other and I found the controls to be good; although controlling an object with sharp corners meant I needed a few moments to get to grips with how the box handles (because it does handle like a box and not like a ball). The vehicle controls do feel a bit looser and I am not sure how much that is me or the game.
The developers recommend a controller and because it is a 3D platformer I would agree, however I found it perfectly playable with WASAD and a mouse (mouse controls the camera and unbox mechanic while keyboard is used to move jump and interact). I could not get my DS4 to work with it natively, if that is how you like to game. However it worked great with my Xbox Elite and its paddles.
One issue I forgot to mention when I reviewed this initially was the fact that the controls are not customisable. So if that is a major issue for you, then you will need to take that into consideration.
Multiplayer -
This is local only and while it looks fun from YouTube videos I never had a chance to play it.
For Parents -
There is nothing in this game that would not be suitable for children of any age. The fact that enemies do not damage you, (only push you flying into the air and into the water grrr) and the fact that all enemies are boxes make it very kid friendly. Humour and tone has some more mature ideas but there is nothing sexual or particularly violent underpinning this game.
Overall-
All in all, I think this is a great game and I love my time within it. It is the 3D platformer I have been waiting for and wet my appetite for Yooka next year.
Hope this review helps anyone trying to decide whether to buy it. My advice is watch the video above on the shop page, it really does give a very good idea of what you are buying.

Absolver is a uniquely-crafted and intricate fighting game with a lot of depth and an enjoyable world to explore. While the main campaign, which clearly takes some cues from Dark Souls in the layout and presentation of the world, is fun, the clear meat-and-potatoes of the game is the PVP combat, which is also where the game truly shines. There's no other fighting game quite like it, and the Combat Deck system allows for tons of variation on movesets. Dodging, weaving, and putting in the perfect flurry of attacks on your foe feels fantastic. This game absolutely makes you feel like a martial artist badass, and that's all I really wanted.
There are some unfortunate server issues that plague most online games, but these should hopefully be ironed out soon enough. When these fixes roll through, I would highly recommend Absolver to anyone looking for a unique take on fighting games.

The game is a set in mad-max like setting, gazzeline is expensive, cars have guns and armor and all that, you shoot others to loot their cars. The game is also turn based, so it's expected to be slow - idiots that have a problem with it shouldn't really review a game that they don't like just because it's turn based. The game is rather simple to get in, you get a vehicle, you mount guns on it, you assign crew to it. One drives, other shoots. Or even the driver can shoot if you like. Unfortunately a few mechanics of the game aren't explained, the only way to get to know the unexplained mechanics are through community interaction, like demoralising - how does it work, you just have to ask. But the basics aka the driving/shooting is explained in a short tutorial. The game doesn't have any bugs as far as I seen, you shoot at others - they recieve damage depending on from which side you shot. You take damage if you get shot at, you damage tyres if you do too sharp turns, you damage your armor if you ram into a wall.
Another thing is permakill feature in this game, which isn't that much of a feature used in newer games. If your crew dies - you have to hire a new one. If your car is destroyed, it's destroyed. No fixing it. I myself like permakill feature in games, makes it more tedious when you're playing against a player (You mostly play against bots in this game however.) and you have to be more careful with your turns.
So yes, the game works, it's good, but it doesn't look good because it's a game from year 2007. Other than that, you can get rich and good without investing a buck into it - just "roll" a scout with other players, get new cars. Sell them or keep them. Your crew gets experience and get better the more encounters they survive.
However, once you get rich and can take on any encounter, the game begins to be rather boring - there isn't anymore to do other than maybe fight other rich players for their cars. But it is fun till then, and that can be more than 100 hours.
Most that review this game negatively are just casuals who can't handle losing their first car, really. The community is friendly as hell, and they will even give you a car if you ask nicely enough.

For an early access game this was surprisingly good, I mean few issues, relative stability, workable controls, it was all there.    However I was only there for the mechs, and the game did have a few mechs for you to play with.  Basically there's 4 default mechs that fall into the light to heavy catergories, then you have the option to build your own mech.  Now I know at this point you're probably drooling, but the options are limited.  Basically you pick a chasis, and you;ll be using the same chasis as one of the defualts, so there isn't a lot of variety there.  4 chasis, which you can customize the paint, camo, stickers, and logos on, then you get to add some weapons to your mech's hardpoints.  Each chasis has its own base armor rating as well as speed, and point level.  So everything you add onto your mech costs points, and adding extra armor will take points and reduce your overall speed.
Weapon types are very vanilla, gatling guns, lasers, rockets, flamethrowers, nothing out of the ordinary or jaw dropping for that matter.  However you can still customize quite a bit, trying to create that perfect battle mech.  I go with low overload weapons, usually gatling guns, gatling lazers, and maybe a rocket pod so I can spam my opponet.  Most players I saw were using the railguns and after a few shots would overload their weapons then stand around like an idiot while they waited for their weapons to cool down.
Your mech has several hit locations on them, each with its own raiting.  So your opponent, or you, can prioritize certain parts.  For me and my mech Tiny Savage, I circle my opponet and target the legs, once the legs go you'll have a hard time being able to turn effectively, then I just keep running circles and blast away.  Or you could knock out a certain weapon system, or just shoot at whatever part of the mech you feel like.  Just note that once your cockpits health gets low, you'll start to seem some distortion going on, and you'll have a hard time seeing things.  If this happens, or your mech has taken a beating, just find your nearest repair center which will have combat ready in no time.
I will say that the AI is dumb, like dumb as a bag of rocks.  Often times they will just run to a location and stand there the entire game.  Other times they'll take a certain amount of damage and immediately stop fighting and run back to their base to try and repair themselves.  Matches can take a while to complete, especially attrition, because somehow those ticket counters never seem to go down fast enough.
Overall I would suggest that you check this game out, especially if you're a fan of mechanized combat, but I'd wait and see if this thing goes on sale, because the $19.99/$14.99 I spent was a bit much for an early access game that doesn't have a whole lot of content in it. All things considered though, its a good game, and its fun, I put 76 minutes into without even realizing it. So 7/10 mostly for the lack of mech types available, and the terrible AI, however I expect all of that to be fixed once this game launches fully.

This game is very rough.  No tutorial that I could find, and although there is a bot option in Instant Action, other players do join pretty quick.  I guess just check the key bindings and figure it out.  It's not too bad of a learning curve.
The game plays pretty good.  The lightmechs are real fast, the heavy mechs slow, though with 3rd person view only (for now - develepers stated working on cockpit view) and crazy jump jets it sometimes feels like you're piloting a figurine on a tabletop not a multi ton mech.  It has some large, wide open levels and I've had some pretty intense battles.
There is a decent selection of pre made Mechs, some you'll even reckognize form Battletech or Mechwarrior.  They all have different capabilities and the developrs have done a good job making some feel and handle very different, some refinement is needed.
The graphics are right now fairly rough but I expect texture updates eventually.
All in all, if you're looking for arcade type combat in mechs try it out, I  imagine after some updates the controls might turn a bit more.....realisitic?  Is that possible in a fictional game?  Anyway, hopefully you get what I'm trying to say.
If you love giant mech games and know what buying early aceess can mean and the risks involved (such as games never being finished or taking radical turns and not being the same game you bought) then I recommend it, as it's on sale (or was) and 5$ is decent to support the developrs.
If not a huge fun but a moderate fan, or missed the sale, it might be worth waiting to see the game in a more polished state before decding to support it or not, and you might get another sale in the meantime.

Ok, I get the roaring debate about the place for this type of game on Steam. I would have agreed with you in my early 20s but... I LIKE CASUAL GAMES in my older age. So I guess having them show up on Steam is kinda useful, if there is a market then I guess it belongs.
The game is a wonderful and first ever balanced game for a "pay to win" game. First of all, you aren't really competing so.. "pay to .... accomplish some goals faster.."?
I feel like every step of the way there is something to do! From mastering items to building up my town/city, to upgrading my workshop and using the marketplace.
You can buy gems and advance quicker, but to what end? You are competing against progress, take your time. It is obviously grindy, but common you knew that going in didn't you?
Although it is a grind it seems quite varied and rewarding. I'm often looking forward to something happening soon. If there is little happening I play with the marketplace and try to make something happen.
There is actually a method to this game, the very early game is a resource struggle, so you fix that.
Then it's advancing your inventory of items, so you build to unlock more. Then you need special items to make some things. You send out your adventurers, but soon they need powering up, that becomes your focus. I find the game often shifts it's aim and it keeps from getting boring.
Finally the best part is you can sell items for gems! Therefore with enough effort you can actually get to a point where you don't need to pay anyway. IF you do wish to pay to advance progress then you will get to that point sooner therefore it's kind of a win win. Such a good balance for a pay for progress game. I never feel I am forced into spending money.
Top marks for what is essentially a free game. I will be investing a little money in time, not because I have to because I don't. But because I feel the developer has done a great job and deserves some encouragement to produce more stuff like this.

If you have played kamidori alchemy meister, this game is the online multiplayer version of it (not including the steamy scenes, turn battles, love interest questlines, etc). It has great pieces of character designs from its chibi to anatomically correct close-up portrayals of the NPC Heroes, almost as if at first glance this will be a great shopkeeper simulator game. This is a time-consuming progression game, so expect in-game purchases to spruce up your gameplay.
Be warned though, it is highly addictive if you are new to this game spending hours and hours managing and improving your travian-like city and your store. It's exciting collaborating with your neighbours and doing event raids as you discover and create new things. Then comes the part where this game is not very recommended for you.
1. World chat is a mess. No private messaging. No mute button. No tooltips, rules and relugations displayed in the chat.
2. Outrageous pricing of in-game purchases. It is not worth it. People may argue from the game that it is worth spare cash, but those players are from other platforms. I would rather spend my spare cash on DLCs of other games.
3. Gets boring midgame (lvl 25+) where you have to grind and stare at the monitor for days. This separates them from games like Adventure Capitalists and Clicker heroes because it gains gold when inactive, unlike this game.
4. It screams "Give us money" with a guise of free to play. From character cosmetics, down to the shopkeep cosmetics, up to the chests.
5. A waste of time

1) There are a lot of negative reviews that say things like: "Stop putting mobile "games" on Steam." Disregard them. It'd be the same as saying something like: "Stop putting F2P Korean MMOs on Steam."
2) The game has a mobile/FB, F2P format. It's no where near as restrictive as typical of the format, though you may find yourself still waiting periodically for things to finish.
3) The veterans in the world chat are usually very helpful, up to and including assisting with the crafting of higher-tiered items. There are, of course, jerks across the board, but they aren't so common.
4) There is a premium currency. It can be acquired easily enough through play. The majority of the developer income seems to come from limited-time special item packs. Everything base is completely accessable otherwise.
tl;dr - Jerks are screwing up the review system by not reviewing the game itself. It's free, it's a fair diversion, and it's not P2W. If being a shop NPC is your kind of thing, you'll probably like this.

I've played a ton on a diffrent steam account but because i went inactive on that account it delted itself :(. Anyways, Empire Total War :D what can i say it's awesome. It feels real, not by the game itself but by what the game does, you actually feel like your in the late 1700s ruling a government. The Ships, Troops, City managment, map layout and everything is downright perfect. My only complaint is diplomacy, i kinda always wanted it to have an animated leader like in Civilization V, otherwise no complaints its also perfect.
What does this game stand out in?
-Combat is realistic. This game has put in so much detail in the littlest things, its just perfect. I feel like im on the battelfeild during the 1700s.

During the summer there is no snow, during the fall snow starts to come down in the north, and in winter all the normal places that get snow during the winter have it. -Nations. This game has all the most important nations, major, minor, you name it of the entire 1700s in their realistic spots on the map and with their territories already put out. That had to take a LONG time to do like seriously, it's great to see all these natons.

Nations- With the Darthmod Empire mod you get to do allot more and i believe the game should have allowed these options from the start. Nations like the newly born United States of America should have been in the normal version of the game for you to play as during normal gameplay. I do have to complain about that.
Otherwise the game still is great on its own. I HIGHLY recommend that you buy the entire game for $17 or better yet just pay $5 for the game when it's on sale cause it's a very good stragedy game.

The Epic Battle Fantasy series (or EBF for short) is a fantastic series, with an interesting origin story. It began as a simple wave by wave RPG, without much reason as to why you fight. It featured many cameos from famous franchises. In this installment and on, this was where the series began to adopt its own identity, saving cameos for mere references (some more obvious than others). I am a huge fan of the series, and I'm excited to see it reach beyond its "flash" game status. It may look, sound and play like one, but Matt (aka KupoGames) Rozsak knows to stretch its limits to create a wonderful game.
The customization is wonderful in this game. There are three characters, two of them male and one female. This dictates what equipment they can use. All three have their own unique weapon, and those weapons including their clothes, can be forged to become better. You may find certain equipment just plain better than others, if they essentially give the same resistants. The characters' clothes appear in the pictures of the dialogue boxes, and while wandering on the overworld, and of course in battle. I love when games do this.
The music, by the amazing Phyrnna (the game explains this in one of the menus viewable from the main menu) is phenomenal. Easy to get stuck in your head.
This is where I shift to comparing this one to EBF4. Obviously, you may think that this one's better because it's free on Steam compared to that, right? Well, I suppose, but...
I'd argue the fourth game is much better. Menu management was slightly more difficult in this one compared to the fourth, even playing this one before. In EBF4, gone is most of the text walls, and statistics and elements are made into easy identifiable pictures. When seeing enemy weaknesses, instead of percentages (like in EBF4), it is just text in this game. I personally don't find it a problem since it typically wouldn't want to use a resisted element on an enemy, but for those who have a hard time remembering which enemies actually absorb or resist elements it can make it quite a hassle.
You can always scan enemies to see their weaknesses and resistances. However, in this game, you can only scan one enemy at a time, and only Lance, can do it. You can always flee from the fight and restart to get free scans, but this may be tedious. In the fourth game, the scan becomes a scanbot, and a Summon that anyone can use, as well as being able to scan every new enemy in battle. Obviously I can't be too hard on it, since this one did come out first.
The game's humor, you could say, comes partly from Internet memes. Obviously not everyone is going to care all that much for it, but the humor doesn't neccessarily stop there. I'm not going too much into detail because well... its a side thing. Humor isn't that important here. There are a few grammatical errors, but that's alright. It shouldn't ruin your fun of the game. Many of them are also probably intentional anyhow, for the "illiterate" NPCs. I'm sure I've made a few in this review anyhow.
At its core, this is an RPG series where the main idea is just having fun destroying foes with sheer numbers, and obliterating them as their waves come. It definitely takes its inspiration from other RPG series, but it's all in good fun, and it revels in its craziness.
TL;DR
If you just like having a fun time, and a fairly difficult albeit short game (hey we can't be that ambitious for a previously Flash game) this is the one for you. If you're deciding on this game or EBF4, I would say start with this one, even though I've mentioned the other one is better. This is free, and in case you linger for more than two hours on the sequel only to find its not your style, you should let this one dictate how much you enjoy the battles. Yes, the menus are a bit more difficult to manage in this one, but the battles are what count mostly. Base your opinion on that.

Don't mind the hours; I've played this since 2010 in-browser
Long ago, in the days before I had Steam, I spent my time playing free games online, and I still remember a handful of true gems that I would gladly pay money to play today (meanwhile there are some expensive piles of garbage still being made to this day). Epic Battle Fantasy is one such gem.
It is said that, to be successful, you just have to be a little bit better than everyone else, and in every way, EBF3 delivered. It was visually and auditorily appealing, full to the brim with hilarious dialogue and vivacious characters; the kind you'd want to be friends with in real life (as opposed to boring, only-tells-you-what-to-do, tutorial-bots I'd seen in so many others).
I was thrown into an entire world, a series of games created by an excellent developer, and I have fallen in love with every aspect of it (and I eagerly await the release of EBF5).
But enough about my experience. You want to know why you should give this game the time of day.
I'll tell you why:
Because it will make you laugh incessantly and nostalgically.
Because you will meet new people and want to get to know them better.
Because you will feel the rush of hearing the sound of an enemy's skull crushing, or the elegant creak of a chest opening, revealing loot you've never heard of before.
Because you will find hilarious and mysterious surprises around every corner, and wonder what else lies in wait for you to discover.
Because you will learn everything you need to know to get the most out of EBF4, which takes all the great aspects of this game and guilds them in a polish of pure, unadulterated, fun.
Because this is a game series that you find only a few times a generation, and it'll be something for you to share with those to come.
This is a series created by someone who truly loves what they do, and it's alarming how infrequent that can be in the free-to-play genre. This game is not pay2win. This game is not swarming with ads. This game is not a shoddily-made, RPGMaker practice-project. It is a good game. It is a great game. It is a game you should download right now and I DARE you to prove me wrong.
*DISCLAIMER*
Extreme nostalgia may affect the perspective of title portrayed in review.
(but seriously, there's not much need for reviews on free games. Review it yourself lazy bones.)

As a long time Steam user and a user of phone games i for one am glad to see this game reach steam. No it's not a heavy action game or a fast paced game in any sense. Its a relaxation game. If it's not your cup of tea fine move on.
However if you love strategy games, market games or even building games where you can build your own shop and town then this is the game to try. It can be slow to start but there are many good techniques to get going quickly. And the community is very friendly and helpfull. Ask arround in game people will tell you how to get things rolling fast and even help you do so. My advice is build up your net worth (invest in town and upgrade shop) then start buying wood keys with the free gems you get. they are worth about 250k gold if im not mistaken and cost 4-7gems. You then sell them for gold to build up your shop some more until you can do leather keys. After that you should have a decently upgraded shop and can start working towards earning gems and gold on the AH simultaneously. There are better techniques out there but this one is simple enough for any new player.
