Shop Heroes is a Free-to-Play [Facebook, mobile] brought to Steam. I played it orignally on Facebook and was over the moon to see it brought to Steam as another free-to-play.
The game consists of you being a shop keeper and adventures come in, requesting gear/weapons/jewelry. You start with beginner recipes and move or "upgrade" into recipes the more you master the one before it. The recipe items increase in gold earned when they increase in rarity. As recipes get higher and more complex in items needed, the time to craft also increases. You have access to different "stations" to craft in, workers and resources. Upgrading the stations and resources also takes increasing time as they go up in levels. They are both still useable, of course but it can become annoying waiting as you can only queue on at a time.
As you start out, you can create your own city and evenutally join another if that's your interest, or recruit players for yours. As you level the individual buildings they can unlock other buildings at higher levels that do different things. Some buildings reward a new adventurer, increases their level cap or experience gain. Other buildings reward access to different workers and their individual levels and experience boosts. Iron Mine, Saw Mill and other buildings related to the resources can increase the hourly rate your resource boxes "refill". It will get very expensive over time, it's best to be in a city with other people if you want fast gains. Now, if you leave a city and go to another [I believe, will edit if wrong] there is a 1 day cooldown in joining after leaving and you can take some, if not all of your initial investments from the last city to your new one. Invested into the Town Hall 20 mil gold? It can follow you to the next city, increasing theirs by 20 mil gold, when you join.
The Inn ins where your adventures you get/purchase hang out. Sometimes they can have quests for you they need done or you can send them out on adventures as you level your INN in your city. The quests you send them on for crafting components also take time. Some are short, 5 minutes or so, others start to increase in 20 minutes, 1 hour, ect. Your adventures do need to be geared too! I believe you can equip them with gear you've crafted, gems [the pay with cash currency] or gold you've earned yourself.] It does have a "break %" on it, so try and not get things too expensive unless you're willing to have it break a few missions in.
The entire game is a gather your resources, set queue, wait for the crafting time or upgrade timer. It's somewhat an idle game, there is no need to sit and stare as the timer works down or itself out.
I recommend the game based on I find it enjoyable and relaxing. I have gotten a bit addicted and tied into it because I can leave it up while I take care of other things, as it needs minimal interaction. Yes, you can use real life money to get WAYYYYY ahead. Is it needed? No, NOT at all. Just have some patience, there are enough "adventure quests, make me this many of that quests and even in the free rolls you get can have a chance to give the currency. I have yet to meet a pay wall in "Pay real money to get further" and I'm level 23, have almost 100 hours invested on the steam version.
I can not speak on the PVP aspect that is a bit hidden away [to me] in the game, I think that may be where the "pay to play" aspect people feel it comes in. I don't mess around in it much, so I can't comment any on it.

The story mode is barebones and can be completed in less then 3 hours. The multiplayer hardly works, and when it does, it is full of people who build their movesets to spammable and ultimatly will destroy you over and over. Out of the 3 initial fighting styles, only one is feasible and used because it allows for quicker spamming and stun-locking. The levels are sometimes confusing to the point where the final boss is hidden in a spot that seems to take an average of 3-4 hours to find (look at the discussions, that boss is the second most brought up question). Karate moves look and feel great, but again, if they arent spammable, you wont use them. The AI are good, but the targeting is bad, if more then 1 npc attacks you, it is extremly difficult to fight them and the camera gets stuck in floors and walls while trying to follow them. The biggest downside however, is the fact that the servers that were promised are almost nonexistent, and multiplayer (when it works for the first time in its release) is very laggy, npc and players alike will often dissapear or lag out from the game entirely, unleashing a flurry of attacks from an invisible location as their body stands 30 feet away
The single player was the most fun part; for the most part everything looks and feels great, but the shortcomings listed above make this game feel like a concept demo. I personally grew tired of the game very quickly nd requested a refund. If the game improves or gets updated and fleshed out I would be more then happy to buy it again, but for the moment, this game isnt worth it unless you have money to burn

While this game is relatively short, the combat system alone is worth the price. Too few games try anything new with their mechanics, while Absolver jumps straight into the deep end of the "new ideas" pool and completely re-invents the 3D fighter in all the best ways. I've never before been given the freedom to make my own style of fighting and have it feel like it was my own. Sure, some games give you a degree of choice in your combo execution but Absolver takes it to an entirely new level.
The game is very "Soulsy" in the sense that very little of the lore or mechanics are explained to you. Much like Dark Souls you're given a vague sense of the buttons and lore that for a lot of people may be frustrating. That said, if you've already sunk many hours into the Souls series then it really won't be a big deal (and you may even appreciate!) how little the game tells you.
I honestly have few, if any, gripes with this game. I wish PvE were a bit longer, but not necessarily because I think the game is too short; in fact it's because it left me wanting more!

Now that the servers are working more consistently than before. I can say that I definitely recommend this game ONLY if you're big into PvP. That's the main focus of the game. The PvE is there and is still fun and challenging though.

This game plays somewhat like a roguelike dungeon crawler. You spend a turn to either move or take an action, then all the enemies do the same.
Each mission takes place in an enviroment of connected corridors and rooms where you get aggro from nearby robots and use your abilities to either avoid them or kill them. The goal of each mission is to achieve objectives, leave the map, and get diablo style prefix-item-postfix style loot, complete with color coding for rarity.
You have a team of 4 different characters (exos, human sized robots) but they all occupy the same map tile, and you can only have one active at a time. That's the twist in the particular dungeon crawling game. It takes a turn to switch between your exos, which you'll want to do because the different exos have different abilities and limited resources like ammo and hitpoints.
After each mission you can customize your exos with all that neat loot you've been finding. The various parts you find tend to be multipurpose, so there are always choices to make, both about what exo gets what part, and where on the exo to put the part.
I found the exo equiping part of the game very satisfying and had several super tricked out exos specializing in incredible shield tanking, firepower, stealth/virus attacks, and stealth/virus attacks near the end of my first game with the default character and exo setup.
Overall, I'd say this made the medium difficulty campaign fairly easy. The final mission(s) were mostly a chore to hunt down all of the bots. I've yet to replay the game, but replayability seems high since you can pick different character bonuses and exo team composisions each game. Not to mention all the random stuff.
Having played AI War, The Last Federation and Skyward Collapse, I would say Bionic Dues is my favorite Arcen game.

This looked like a fairly old school style of  2D turn based mech combat game in a simple table top arcade style, but with some decent refinements.  I got this in a bundle deal, so yeah, it cost me about nothing.  I wasn't especially interested in this title, but gave it a try, and hey it has cards ;)
The first time or two that I tried it out I didn't find it very engaging.  The menus could be better, and the learning curve is rough at first.  The graphics are not expected to be fancy in this sort of game and they aren't, but they aren't bad and in an arcade time killer like this it's the gameplay that counts, and it has excellent depth, challenge and  balance once you begin to get attuned to it.  The music isn't bad, and the theme is pretty catchy in a Japanese arcade kind of way.
You choose missions from a map, and prep for each mission by choosing a pilot and 4 (out of 6) of your exo-suits, which you customize before each mission.  In missions you can switch between suits at any time at the cost of one turn, and the mission fails if you manage to wreck all of your suits.  Customizing the exo's is fun as you find loot and upgrades along the way, and can spend loot at the upgrade store which also gets in new items of course.
You definitely can't just plow your way through this one.  There are plenty of firefights, but it's more like a chess game at times.  You might find health or ammo during a mission, but it's rare, so you're forced to choose which of your suits could best use it to get the particular mission done.
Not gonna be anyone's main game, but like I said;  pretty fun, challenging, cheap, time killer, trading cards and shades of Jpop.

This game is like a chubby girl in your parallel class. You often see her going by, she's never dressed nicely, she never hangs out with fancy people. She's so nerdy with her big round glasses and her fashion sense is terrible. But. She has a pleasent smile. And her voice is so soothing. And she likes the same space games as you do! And even makes you think that "Hey, maybe Star Trek TNG is kinda cool too". And you realize that, even if she looks like a microsoft excel graphic got filtered inmario paint, you enjoy her company! And you want to spend hours and hours discussing different topics and going to different places with her! And you kinda start feeling attracted to her, and start bringing this chubby gal everywhere you go, on your ipad, on your laptop, and you never find yourself thinking about her lame framed glasses,  and instead you focus on her amazingly designed game mechanics and music and strategic gameplay. And sure, sometimes she would bring up very unfair RNG topics, and make you feel cheap about having to deal with missile ships in your first system, but hey, nobody said that a perfect relationship is easy.
Then, after spending hours and hours of quality time together, and you feel like you've seen it all, and had great runs with her, and she gave you the most amazing and awarding feelings of accomplishments in your life, because you've managed to beat the big capital boss ship using the sneaky teleport-and-capture-the-personnel tactic, - she brings out the mods, and the fun never stops.
tl;dr - Ignore the bad graphics, enjoy amazing game. Chubby girls need love too.

Mech games in general are very niche these days. There are a ton of dev sponsored events but they usually have quite a few players and the one i was able to make it to was extremely fun. Expecting ea games that are niche to have large playerbases is a false perception that is probably influenced by ea titles like dayz or rust that have very large playerbases skewing the fact most ea games just dont draw that many people no matter how good they are. these are mostly indie devs without large marketing budgets.
This game has the framework to be great. There are, in my opinion, certain mechanics missing that would make the game more dynamic and fun, i.e. rocketjumping on the ground, so like ac3 being able to boost for a short time to gain some speed and be a dodging mechanic all in one. The sniper rifles and long range weapons are a great start to make this game go in the direction the devs seem to want (from my experience so far) as a more militaristic, average pased mech game relying on positioning, aim, and teamwork.
Not to mention, the devs on this game, unlike many many ea titles, actually listen to and respond to the playerbase. I mean the real intention of ea is to help developers develop and finish the game youre purchasing....right? Ive mentioned a few ideas to the devs so far, and i wont say I had anything to do with them adding it in, but for example the long range weapons i suggested a few months ago, well guess what? They put it in the game! And its a really great addition. In my opinion this factor alone makes this game well worth a measly fifteen dollars.
This game will grow over time, with the cockpit views, more and more weapons and mech types, more customization of the mechs themselves, better ai, better graphics (already looking really sharp with the shader changes), and of course, the soon to be redmund favorite of faction wars. I havent been this excited for the future of an ea title in a long time.
Sure there arent many people in servers very often, but I mean Im not sure what youd expect from an ea game like this. Plus the devs come from a background of writing backends for netcode of games with other studios (i might be wrong on the terminology) gives me great confidence that MP play will be stable and lag/choke free in the future, especially when your faction might lose their last territory from a missle lagging and winning someone a match.
10/10 must buy for mech lovers.

edit: updated a review to give more info a bit
This is one of the most 'solid' EA release I have ever played. If you are looking for a solid Mechwarrior-like combat, this game can give you that. There are things that need polishing. However, the downside is that you can hardly find people to play with due to the soft launch. Devs are fixing things and will do a proper launch soon.
To top it off, it is a Team vs Team, heavy mech combat. You cannot skate around super fast and do crazy manuever like Armored Cored's mech. Your mech is basically a tank with legs, so no fancy movements.
You build your mech from several chasis(will be adding in the future updates), put on the weapons and equipments. To balance the fight smaller chasis is faster, but less armor, and carry lighter equipments. Bigger chasis is slower, but tougher, more armomr, heavier weapons, however, loadout comes down to the battle points, you cannot just put anything in there, it is limited by battle points for each mech, and different mech will have different points.
The combat itself is fun, especially with another player. There is AI support for both single and multiplayer match, but it is not that smart, however, they do there jobs well, especially when they are with players. Combat will be tactical to certain points that you need to manage your weapons, you can fire all weapons at once or as a selective group, which can be set in the hangar. Weapons have its effective range, some can easily overload your system, and some weapons' projectile do travel the distance, so they can be dodged.
There may be claims that it takes too long to take down a mech, which is not true if you know what you are doing. Your mech (as of the current build) has 3 parts, torso, and 2 legs, and around 7-8 additional parts depending on your loadout. These parts have their own HP, so if you just shoot at every part, not just particular part. It will take a while to take down a mech. Mechs can be take-down by destroying their bodies, or both of their legs.

Kupo has always made games that shine, and this is one of them. A lot of love and work has been put into EB3, as evidenced by the strong gameplay, engaging dialogue and genuinely entertaining difficulty. While EBF4 is a step-up in every way, EB3 is free and it'll tell you if you would like EB4 (Which isn't very expensive, either!)
The game is a decently deep turn-based RPG, focusing on the three party members; Matt, who likes swords, Natalie the mage and Lance the colonel. They each come with a variety of custom skills and abilties to unlock and level up, providing multiple different play-styles. There is also three slots of Gear for each character, for head, body and weapon. While the standard style would be Matt as a tank, Lance as DPS and Natalie as support, you can switch it around however you want. Matt can be a proficient Mage DPS, Lance can be support and Natalie can...Well, she can be a mage, but the choice to bonk things with her is there.

Among The Sleep is a huge disapointment. Not only delivering 2 mere hours of entertainment after so much hype and tease is Ubisoft-level ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥gery, but the game itself doesn't make it up for it.

This was... kind of disappointing. Now, that's not to say I didn't have fun with the game. There is a lot of good stuff to it. However, Among the Sleep is painfully short at only two hours long, and is really more of a 'roadtrip' game, where you look at stuff and experience stuff on a very linear path that, once experienced, really doesn't have anything else to offer. Furthermore, the biggest issue I came across was the monster(s). They were too easy to hide from, and I'll be honest, they really aren't all that threatening when you can just dive into a closet or under a table and know they won't try to look for you. One last big complaint I have is this: stop with the static-y screen when looking at monsters developers! Seriously, whenever you look at a monster the screen erupts into a static filled mess, and rather than scare me, it just irritated me and distracted me from the game. The thing that should be scary about an unknown creature is the very presence of an unknown creature. If the static eruption didn't happen, I probably would feel more of a threat, because the actual creatures and their designs, while simplistic, do in fact have a bigger than life feel when seen through the eyes of the toddler you play as. So Krillbite, in your next game, stop with the static thing. If you want to do something like that again however, try to be slightly more subtle about it, rather than have the screen scream 'YOU ARE FRIGHTENED NOW! OOOOHHH SO SPOOKY!' Stop it. No, I'm not scared, I'm annoyed.
Now, despite ripping into some of the more major problems, I still recommend this game. Why? Because it is absolutely gorgeous. The aesthetic of the game is incredible, being colorful, but still very dark and creepy, and while the actual graphics of the game aren't the best, they still lend to alter the perceptions you ight have of the world. At the beginning, I found my own mind playing tricks on me, making me think there were thing in places where there was nothing, much like a child would. I absolutely loved that the enviornment of the game could do that on its own, even more so than any of the monsters. The mechanics also lend themselves well to the ideas of the game. You have on your journey a teddy bear that you can hug for comfort, and teddy then acts as a light source to help you see the path you need to go down. When pausing, the toddler covers his face with his hands to hide from the scary things, again bringing in the feeling that this is a young child in a big threatening world that he doesn't understand. To open doors, you need to get chairs to reach the knob, and you move faster crawling that you do walking.
So, overall, I think that this game does have some good things to offer, and as Krillbite's first game, I think they did a decent job. However, I don't recommend dropping twenty dollars on this game. Wait for the price to drop, and/or wait for a sale.

I have absolutely no clue what is causing this, as a game of this style doesn't seem like the kind to put heavy strain on a gaming computer, but I have some serious problems with this game. In Kingdom: Classic I would have significant periodic lag slowing the game down and making it choppy and unresponsive for periods. I have seen some people complaining about lag in the late game when you may have hundreds of archers, but I never had any problem with that - my lag spikes come seemingly at random.
In New Lands it's much much worse. Instead of getting choppy every once in a while, which I could deal with, New Lands will completely freeze for up to 10 seconds, then return to be playable but extremely choppy and with no sound until you hit ESC and load the menu. This will happen with only a few minutes between freezes. It's so bad I had to stop before the first day just to write this review, because I have not been able to find any helpful information online and I hope the devs will notice this, because I *REALLY* want to play this game.
PS. Apparently Steam won't let you write a review until you've had the game running for more than five minutes, which also tells me I have a whopping 1 minute on record when I started writing this review. It's that debilitating.
EDIT: After some troubleshooting and a lot of emails exchanged with the devs, the freezing bug turned out to be a sound device issue. I managed to work around it by disabling every sound device but my headphones. The game still stutters a bit, but it's playable. I'm changing this to Recommended.

This game is a pretty good attempt at a side-scrolling stunter. The controls are a bit oversensitive and the bike has to rely too much on boosting to get up hills and things (the tires need more grip!) but the gameplay is solid and fairly challenging. I have to note that the game seemingly has no function to change resolution which can make it display improperly occasionally, and there is no support for triple-screen, though such a feature is very welcome in these types of games. There is no function to change controls either. I highly encourage the developer to add these features to their next title.
At its very core it may be a poor mimic of some mobile games, but this one doesn't pester you with ads or keep features behind a paywall. Having to put up with the seizure-inducing visuals, Voodoo-era graphics, and crazy "music" is part of the challenge, and one should not write this game off simply because it offends your senses. These individually terrible elements come together to make a rather skillful game, and one can be proud for merely having finished a single stage.
In short, this is a top tier kusoge that you should play at least once in your life.
Is it art? Perhaps. It is definitely the kind of game a sensationalist reporter would blame for the collapse of society, and for that reason I must recommend it.

Kingdom: New Lands is the expansion to the original game Kingdom. The original game kept me busy in it's beautiful forests and country sides while being intranced in the calming music. This expansion has changed so much that it's hard to know where to begin, but I'll break it down into four catagories:
This game in Kingdom: New Lands consists of defending your kingdom against waves of enemies, doing this by building up defences with the money you earn when your archers kill animals or farmers finish their crop. These enemies vary from small and easy to kill to large and near unstoppable. The gameplay is kept fresh between games due to the random map generation. Also this is all accomplished with three buttons.
The graphics in Kingdom and Kingdom: New Lands amaze me they are incredibly beautiful yet simplistic. To put it lightly they are stunning, and now with the addition of seasons they are near perfect.
The music in this game is composed by ToyTree and let me just say the music is great to listen to, in game or out. I highly recomend getting the Royal Edition so as to get the soundtrack with the game.
Alot changes in each game of Kingdom: New Lands, this is due in part to the rando map gen and the rouge like elements, but also to the large amount of options available to you in game. This game does not lose it's steam after many playthroughs nor does it detract anything from the expierience.
Overall Kingdom: New Lands sitcks with the best parts of the original Kingdom while bringing an incredibal amount of content to the table. Buy it now, show support for devs who add this much content to a game! (Also most of my time in this game was without steam so I have near 9-10 hours overall through betas and such.)

I honestly like this game, it kills time and it fills in that "management" type feel that I crave for.  I'll also be honest, there are some things I simply don't like about it either.
Pros:
1. It's fun being able to accumulate resources and spend them making weapons/armor/trinkets and other various pieces of equipment and then your skill upgrading in said equipment to either have them cost less resources to make, or improve in quality.
2. There's a ton of upgrades to get outside of making equipment, whether it's your workstations or your storage containers.  If it's one thing I enjoy doing in a management game like this, it's upgrading stuff.
3. I can't say I was too fond of the "waiting for resources" bit at first, but once you've constructed 3 bins (be it iron, wood, leather, etc.), you'll find you won't have to wait very long before you can continue producing stuff.
4. The idea of being able to fuse lesser quality items into higher quality items for your Heroes to wear was pretty neat, can also use it to make room if you're a little short on storage space.  Got too many Broad Swords?  Make higher quality Broad Swords by fusing 2 or more together.
5. While you CAN be online and open your town for other people to join to help your upgrade your Forge, Mine, etc., you can also set it to Private and try to do it on your own.  While this slows your progress, it also fills in the need of wanting to do things yourself.
Cons:
1. The waiting.  The waiting can wear on you, especially when it's on resources (before you buy extra bins, earlier on in the game), ontop of that, crafting higher tier equipment will require you to wait several minutes before it's produced.  You'll kinda find yourself twiddling your thumbs a lot, so I'd suggest minimizing the game and playing/watching something else while your resources come together.
2. Your "customers" are the same people who are your Heroes, who you make equipment for.  Oddly enough, they come around, really often I might add, to buy the stuff that you produce.  HOWEVER.  I'm not sure whether it's a bug or not, but there are times when I'll have several of these Heroes coming into my shop, asking for the same low-tier item repeatedly, even after Refusing it the first 30 times.  And making the item they want, or suggesting another, doesn't fix it.  So you're forced to either shoo them away constantly for another Hero in hopes they'll buy something you actually have of value, or expend any Energy you have with a suggestion.
3. Some of the upgrades, mainly Worker total, are VERY expensive.  I realize this is where they get you to spend money, but hot damn, you'd think they'd have made it at least a little easier.  I don't mind the idea of buying these blue Gems to speed things along, but in terms of Gold amount, some of the stuff is a little outrageous.
All in all, I like it.  It's probably not the best time-killer out there, but it'll definitely do the job for you.  If you enjoy progress, then by all means I suggest it, if you're impatient, well, you should probably look elsewhere.
TL;DR - Lots of upgrades, build your resource bins first, fuse cruddy items into higher quality ones, I hope you're patient, and I hope you're ready to make a million Pocket Knives.

For someone like me, who loved the first Mafia, the announcement of Mafia 2 was like a dream come true : I spent many hours pretending to be a real Gangster and crying at the tragic ending of the story. After Mafia 2 came out, I read many reviews and my expectations of another Masterpiece in the gaming history quickly disappeared. The game was described as an honest and solid 3rd person action, but nothing so special that could make it memorable : I decided  not to buy it and wait for price drop.
So, after many years after its release, I finally decided to give it a try and discover by myself how the Mafia story would go on (from another perspective). Man, I was so wrong : despite negative comments which sorrounded this title at launch, I really enjoyed it!
The story is fast paced and well constructed, main character Vito Scaletta is lacking a bit of personality, but it is greatly compensated by Joe Barbaro's charisma! Overall, I found it a solid movie plot, my only complaint is the similarity of some mission with the ones I played in the first Game (which highlights missing inspiration during the script writing phase). Technically, it is a good game, much more smooth and playable compared to the past, with good textures and stable frame rate , even with a low end configurations. Gameplay feels enhanced and fluid, cover system works quite well and it's a welcome feature which was needed for this kind of game.
Car physics were improved, and trying to perfectly control the drifting has become even harder (if you choose the  realistic driving mode). Unfortunately, it is not possible to shoot while driving anymore. In the end, despite some minor downsides, I consider Mafia 2 a good sequel, better than I expected. Sure, it is not as good as its predecessor, but I think this is one of the titles anyone should enjoy, if you call yourself a gamer.

Just played this for the first time, out of excitement for Wolfenstein 2 coming out.  While I really enjoyed Wolfenstein TNO a ton, I can't recommend Old Blood one bit.
This game is a short series of bland levels, most of which feel (and, plot wise, are) totally pointless (you go to the castle to find where Helga's gone, and within 15 minutes you know she's in Wulfsburg, but you spend hours and hours afterward going thru castle levels anyway).  Some action segments and the second "omg nazi zombies lul" half of the campaign is OK, mostly from being thankfully short and sweet, but the first half is just a lengthy mess of hallways with no story or character development to speak of.
There are a few brilliant moments of hilarity (the early pair of Nazis berating each other about grammar was my favorite), but most of the game is flavorless stealth and/or guns blazing grunt slaughtering.
Collectibles are an absolutely pointless chore as well.  The Wolfenstein 3D bonus levels are an especially horrible slog, with literally only 2 weapon types and 2 enemy types, and tons of very long, very empty hallways and side-rooms.
This standalone expansion is just generally not fun or interesting, and of course has zero replayability.  It's 37GB and $20 for 6-8 hours of gameplay (mine shows 11 because I AFK often while gaming to take care of stuff).

I backed this game on Kickstarter and it pains to currently write this this Not Recommended review.
The problem with Castle Story may be my own expectations, but I don't think they're too far off base with what the original KS claimed the game would be. When I see this game and hear the pitch, I think it's going to be a (light) colony management game with emphasis on defensive structures. Something like Stronghold, which is one of my all time favorite games.
What it actually is, as of 1.0, is a fairly clunky game that mostly hinges on your desire to free-build various wall shapes with the bare minimum of city/colony building. Goals each game are very basic, and only 2-3 items in the whole game require  a 2+ stage production after refinement. (Iron to Ingots, Ingots to cogs, cogs to a arbelists or catapaults) Everything else is simply gather -> refine -> Craft item. The most complicate it gets is sometimes deciding whether to have your refiner make item A or B, or to build 2 copies to constantly make both. There's not much to it.
I do greatly enjoy the game for maybe 20 mins when loading in a new map, but it plateus extremely quickly and you can even make the strongest melee unit maybe 5 mins into the game if you know what your doing. Ranged takes longer, but I find little reason to worry about particularly strong units since this leads to another problem...
The castle building can look really, really cool. Check out the trailor for some examples. But gameplay-wise, there's no real difference between a simple 3-brick tall fence and an elaborately build citadel... except one takes longer to build and repair. At most, building a 2nd ring of brick fence is about as complicated as you need to get to reach maximum effectivness of a castle in this game. It is not like Stronghold, where a well designed and planned out castle can easily mean the difference between victory and defeat in a scenario.  And for most of the games, your only significant choice is how many of your bricklings to make a dedicated warrior and how many to keep as workers. It's fine and fun for awhile, but I wouldn't pay more than $10 max for that experience. Rimworld will give you hundreds of hours of enjoyment with it's deep systems that Castle Story can't compare to.
Plus, the UI is terrible. It was actually worse pre-1.0, but it took me 20 mins of trying to figure out what I was missing to realize I can right-click-hold on cutting stations to make lumber. Why don't they do that by default? The "job" system for the UI is also extremely clunky and ends up cluttering your bottom bar with jobs you made an hour ago and finished, but the bar never cleared itself. It doesn't work great. There's also no readout (that I can find?) of resources in your stockpiles, making it hard to figure out why certain refineries have stopped at times.
Overall, cool idea, if not unique, pulled off with a good style and cute graphics. It had (and may still have) potential to be great, but it's definitly not there currently. When considering your other options on steam, I cannot recommend this over almost any other game. (Except maybe Towns...)
I'll be more than happy to keep up with development if they contiune past 1.0 and amend this if I see great change, but it's not worth it for now unless you get it cheap on sale or in a bundle.

Now that the game has released, I think is fair to say this is a good game and I reccomend it to people.
Big attraction: Freeform castle building. You build up your structures brick by brick and this gives it a fun, freeform, creative and sandboxy (I know that's not a word!) feel to it, even when under pressure by attacking enemies. The game is a real creative sandbox. The rest of the game (crafting system, combat etc) do well enough to support the game although they are not genre-leading, but it is all tied together and made great by the building.
The sandbox mode offers hours of creative fun by building up castles, defensive networks, buildings etc and if you feel like it, throwing enemies at your creations.
Invasion is where I think the game really shines, building against the clock in the face of waves of attacking 'corruptrons' which forces you to prioritise what to build, how to defend a set location, and struggle as the attackers get more and more dangerous and tear down your defences with greater efficiency.
Conquest is an interesting mode for the game, where you expand out across the map against other forces, trying to control 'crystals' (capture points). Although more mobile than you would expect from a castle-building game and thus probably not for me as much as invasion mode, it is another interesting way to play which combines your building up your forces in a defended location, expanding out and attacking the defences of others, and creating quick, temporary fortifications of your own to defend out in the field.
Also to note: Good music that sets the mood, a good variety of maps and a map-maker + workshop providing limitless options, some not-mentioned interesting mechanics (lights out mode for example, where anything not near a light source is pitch black and you cannot see a thing, meaning putting up torches etc becomes crucial to even being able to play - very atmospheric and a new challenge). A few bugs as of writing this but nothing game-breaking, just a bit more polish needed in a few areas.
TLDR: a solid game where a creative castle building really shines, the rest of the mechanics support it well enough with some interesting twists, lots of maps and a map editor. Buy it if you want to build up castles brick-by-brick and defend them, that is the selling point here.

Before I go into the review I will first say that I am a long time fighting game player and have played in multiple tournaments for different games and have stuck my nose into basically every fighting game that comes to the market. I have been very eager about this game because it felt like For Honor done right. So from here, the review.
This game is unquie as games can get. It has influences from For Honor, Dark Souls, and beat'm ups. The online play is done so flawlessly in the sense of people entering your world and giving you the opportunity to team with them, or fight them to the death. Very much in the vein of Dark Souls.
The combat is done beautifully and flawlessly, it feels like the first well done martial arts in years. If you are coming from For Honor, the combat has similar feeling to this style of fighting although it has what is known as custom combat decks where you can pick the moves in your combos. These moves start in a specific position and will end in a specific position so you can set your deck up to always end in a certain way or cycle through your combos. The ability to nitpick your moves and set up a fighting style that is unquie to you is what gives this game such a mindblowingly limitless sense of progression and content when it comes to PvP. Never will you encounter people who are running 100% the same deck and it will force you to learn not just moves, but the moves your opponent is using together. This makes the fighting in this game not just a battle of skill, but also a battle of witts. The ability to hide certain combat strings to set up better finishers or to have a deck that is pure fast abilities to try and rush down the opponent, it is what makes this game so amazing.
Next is my favorite aspect of the game which is schools, schools can be ran by NPCs and players. You can become the mentor of a school and teach people combat styles and moves, you can be the leader of a group of students. If there is a style you want to master and become better at, this game gives you so many tools to seek out that mastery. I can't even describe how excited I was to unlock schools and finally spar with others in a learning environment and not a PvP environment.
All and all I wholeheartedly reccommend this game for the fighting game fans and for people looking for something different, if you love fighting games, but are not extremely keen on playing against other players. This game offers such a deep system in the online and offline play that there are things for everybody to enjoy no matter your skill level or play style.
Pros:
Extremely fluid combat that feels impactful and rewarding.
Massive list of abilities to have large possibilities of movesets of fighting styles.
An interactive online mode with open world PvE and PvP amongst players and NPCs.
A deep leveling system with progress that matters.
Online play that rewards teamwork and creating communities.
Cons:
Currently the servers are struggling, week 1 of release, but this is an issue that will most definantly be resolved.
Camera sometimes feels awful if you are pinned against a wall with multiple enemies blocking you.
The lock on system feels good, but switching targets does not if you are fighting more than 3 opponents.
Gear generally doesn't feel rewarding due to how stats are given from it, I would rather gear be cosmetic only.

While the basic formula for a rougelike strategy game is here, Bionic Dues ultimately falls short due to balancing issues, bad information management, and generally poor presentation.
Walls of text and disorganized information are repeated issues in Bionic Dues — a problem that begins as soon as you begin your campaign. With no introduction, you're shown a screen with the portraits of four exos (your remote-controlled mechs) and a pilot, and are asked to select your team for the rest of the game. You can only take four of six exos with you; and can only select one pilot of, again, six. Each exo is armed differently, though you're only given a small description of their capabilities on a hovering text box. The same goes for the pilots: each their own brief backstory, and a special ability that affects the performance of the team. "+50% to all propulsion stats—" "A Mark-4 part will have stats like a Mark-6—" "He was able to sneak into the Bahamut Device installations—" But you've been given no story and have no idea what the gameplay is like yet. What's a Mark-6? What does the propulsion stat do? What's a Bahamut Device? None of this has any context, so you're just guessing at what might make an effective team and hoping for the best. If you later don't like your choices — well, tough; you're stuck with it.
Upon selecting your team, you're dumped into a map screen and given a one-page briefing of the situation and your mission. It's then explained that the city is under attack by a robot rebellion, and as the sole remaining pilot, it's up to you to prevent annihilation. That's the extent of your story. No characters are introduced, your pilot is never addressed by name, and the voiceover guy doesn't even explain who he is. As no real world-building is done, and your choice of pilot has no effect on the extremely-minimal story, it makes the whole process of choosing a pilot superfluous. Who cares what their names are, what they look like, or what very brief backstory they each have when it doesn't change anything in the campaign and is never addressed again? "Choose your pilot" could have easily been "choose your buff," then addressed the player, themselves, as the pilot of the exos.
Pressing OK clears the introductory text, and then several more bulletpoints of information are thrown on screen at once, explaining several basic gameplay mechanics before they're necessary. You can go straight to a mission, but the screen is flanked by icons of your exos and enemy bots, with a big green arrow reading "Customize" pointing to your team. Clicking on that gives you another text box of info, and behind it, way more info as you're shown the stats of each exo and every item in your inventory. This was the biggest and most repeated problem encountered: just way too much disorganized information at once, often without context. Each exo has 14 base stats to keep track of, and then as many as five weapons with up to 23 more stats, determined by equipping items to a potential 30 inventory slots.
Get used to the customization screen; with up to 50 missions in the campaign, you'll be spending a lot of time here between fights. This does allow you to specialize each exo with careful delegation of items and theory-crafting, but eventually I got tired of sinking so much time into figuring out exactly which item would be best-equipped where and on which exo, with so many possibilities and little nuances, that I skipped it unless I picked up something that was an obviously big upgrade. This may have been easier with better information management, but everything in this game comes as a wall of text in the same typeface. There's very little colour differentiation, and absolutely no graphics or icons used for quick identification. I started skipping the customization, because it wasn't fun; it felt like homework. However, you can only neglect dedicating yourself to this process so much, as the enemy forces get stronger with every mission. Do it, or eventually you will be outclassed.
See how much information is written here so far? We haven't even gotten to the first mission yet. Each mission is represented on the map by a different icon branching outwards from your headquarters. You have to complete them in succession to explore the city, until the final battle on the fiftieth day. Bionic Dues outright tells you that the final battle is on day 50, which is unsuspenseful. Your basic objective is to grind through the missions, upgrading your exos with loot and potentially weakening the enemy forces in preparation for one final and massive battle of attrition. If you mess up enough along the way, you can reach that final day, fail the battle, and lose the whole campaign.
The battles are turn-based. Your team has to explore a randomly-generated, grid-based battlefield, eliminating enemy robots and potentially destroying certain objectives along the way. All four exos move together on the same grid point, like an old RPG party. Only one of them is active at a time, and that will be the one who can fight and take damage. Moving, firing, using a special ability, or switching between exos takes one turn. Most of the enemies will remain inactive until you aggro them, and then they'll each take their turn after you make your move. They're not particularly challenging; most bots can be dispatched easily by being outranged or lead into traps. However, if you're not tactical, there are times where you can find yourself flanked, cornered, and overwhelmed. You can lose one of your exos in an instant with a poor choice of moves. So what happens then? Can you repair the exo, or is there some sort of penalty? Do you need to replace it, or go through the rest of the campaign with only three on your team? The game never explains, beyond that you'll receive one less piece of loot at the end of the mission.
The way each battle plays out varies depending on the type of mission, represented by the icon on the map screen. For example, some turn all destructable objects into powerful explosives, some have hostages that must be protected, and some power up every exo and bot to perform one-hit kills. This adds a little gameplay variety. However, the battlefields, themselves, are visually very bland and repetitive. They all take place indoors, and the scenery doesn't change from one part of the city to the other. Their dark grey floor colouring offers low contrast from the black, unnavigable negative space, sometimes making it hard to distinguish where you can and can't move your exos.
Once you complete your objective, you have to navigate to the exit of the level. While this does give a chance to explore and pick up any missed loot, this is often dull, as the main objective and the exit aren't necessarily going to be placed nearby each other. Often you'll find yourself navigating empty corridors as you search for the way out, which may not be easy to find. The exit isn't an actual physical exit from the battlespace, but a circle on one of the tiles, which may be hard to spot at times when it's in the fog-of-war shadow. Poor contrast plays an issue here again. Making it to the exit, in itself, is anticlimactic. You'll be immediately dumped back to the map screen, with no victory fanfare or continuation of a story.
Once you've done that, go spend a while calculating how to best upgrade your exos, then repeat the process 48 more times to make it to the final battle. There's no build-up to this moment — it's treated the same as every other mission. The final battle is an endurance run, pitting your four exos against the remanants of the enemy bot army, or as many as can fit in the map at once. It's not harder, just longer. And once you win, your reward? A "congratulations" text box. Then you just sit on the map screen. That's it.
While the basics are here, Bionic Dues falls short, still having massive room for improvement in its gameplay and presentation. Not recommended.

If you take out all of the human precision and care that goes into crafting a well-balanced tactical game and replace it all with procedurally generated hocus-pocus, you have Bionic Dues, a shining example of how NOT to do a game like this.
For the sake of this review, I'm going to pretend that there aren't people on Steam who will try to act tough and say that beating a game that generates everything completely at random is based on some sort of "skill" or "good judgment". There's the power of decision making, and then there's just plain ol' being outmatched by a robot that leveled up several times more than your randomly-generated loot chest equipment can possibly hope to combat.
No, there's good decision making, and then there's numbers. Tactical games have always been about numbers. They have always been about well-crafted maps with careful enemy placement as much as they have been about intelligent team setup supported by guaranteed available items in shops (because the game knows you will need them). Bionic Dues does none of this. Bionic Dues generates all of the maps and the enemies that are placed into them with a computer algorithm. It generates which combinations of enemies will be in a map with a computer algorithm. It generates
with a computer algorithm. Need to outfit your team in order to survive? Too bad. Bionic Dues also generates the items available
with a computer algorithm. Basically, EVERYTHING is generated almost entirely at random. And as much as I'd like to believe that the computer procedures used in the generation of everything in this game are as intelligent and discerning as a human being... they're not.
If you like to sit at a table and roll dice over and over again until you get a certain number, this game might be for you. Yeah, sure, delude yourself into thinking that there is some kind of decision you can make that will mystically cause your severely under-equipped robot to beat a hulking level 7 DoomBot - it seems to be what "roguelike" fans tend to do so they can convince themselves that
they accomplished in a playthrough was totally the product of their
. Is this game possible? Sure. I'm just so not afraid to say it straight: this game is absurdly random. It is a total crapshoot what items I will get, meaning it's a total crapshoot how powerful I will be, and it's a total crapshoot how the enemies will level up, meaning it's a total crapshoot whether or not I will beat them. The game is a total crapshoot. But like I said, some people like sitting at a table rolling dice over and over again until they get a certain number. Some people like crap(s).
P.S. Please, really don't try to say that this review is because I can't handle the game. I've beaten the game 3 times on Expert and destroyed 100 enemies in a single shot. That is so not the issue. Only somebody extremely near-sighted bases their opinions on whether or not they can beat a game. This game is not good. It is an awful representation of tactical games. The tactical game genre should be ashamed of this game, it's giving the genre a bad name.

Bionic Dues is a phenomenal game worth whatever price you can get it for.
Essentially, all of humanity except for you and your group of survivors have been killed by a robot army. In about a month, they will attack your home base and destroy you all. You are the last remaining pilot for the Exosuit, which is the only thing that can stand between you and the robot army, and your job is to run missions to find upgrades for your suit and to sabotage the robots themselves.
The gameplay takes place on a grid and is semi-turn based. Every time you move, attack, etcetera, your turn is used up and the enemy may do something. But it runs so fluidly it almost feels real time. Your objective is different depending on what mission you choose, and that's the fun part.
There is no possible way to do all missions presented in a single game, not to mention the fact that what is available is randomly generated when you start. The fun comes in choosing what missions to do; do you take on the assasination mission and kill one of the bosses early? Do you go to a weapons factory to get shiny new weapon parts for your suits? Maybe you lost a mission and your HQ is low on health, so you need to do a mission to repair it? You only have so much time so you have to choose wisely.
On top of all this, there are several difficulty levels and several pilots who completely change the way the game played. With the pilot I used, it's sort of cheating because you start off with the enhanced suits (whereas normally you need to find them yourself). The other pilots have other passives that make sure no two playthroughs are similar. And of course, you have several different suits as well, but you can only choose four at the start of the game; I used the Science, Ninja, Assault, and Siege (I believe those are the names) but again, it's up to you. Actually there are achievements for completing the game with four of a single suit type, so you could try that. Honestly it's real endless the ways you could play the game.
I only played through once, but it took me 10 hours. I can't wait until I have the time to go through it again. If you like how it sounds, then buy it without hesitation.

Didn't like it as much as I thought I would. It's a turnbased strategy game with mechs where you have 50 days to prepare against unevitable doom by completeling randomly generated missions. The concept is awesome which is to be expected from Arcen Games.
The main problem I had was that the missions felt kindof like a slog and a bit samey. The combat was also pretty cutthroat. You'll usually kill the enemy in one hit and they can do the same thing to you which sounds interesting but I didn't happen to like it afterwards. In most cases you'll blow through the levels killing everything in your path and if you make one misstep, you can die. This is probably done to make the levels seem challenging but it didn't really end up that way.
I'm not sure how I'd change it to make the game more enjoyable for me. I was thinking about making the combat less binary by buffing the health of you and your enemies. Maybe instead of having one mech on the field that you can switch out, you could have a group of mechs on the field. Maybe I would've like a more "classic" strategy RPG leveling up system where you unlock skills by leveling up. It's a bit strange really. Arcen Games removed the slow grindy bits of an S-RPG but in hindsight I actually liked those slow grindy bits.

Airmech Strike is a good PvP focused action RTS game that is a hybrid between games such as Starcraft with League of Legends. It runs smoothly (even on potatos) and has a very tight-nit community which keeps me coming back. It's much easier to get into compared to traditional RTS games and provides a wide range of different units and airmechs (classes/heros) to cater for your playstyle.
In terms of gameplay, you pilot a mech (it's like a transformer) in which acts as your hero. You can shoot enemies with it or pick up your own to move them around. You can build various units from outposts (buildings) such as infantry, artillery and tanks which are used to battle your opponent's army. This outposts can be captured from your enimies but your ultimate goal is to destroy your opponent's base using your mech and army for a sweet victory!
Fights can be intense micro wars or fast rushes which will test the skills of all players. However, battles can become stale at times sort of like trench-warefare which both teams unable to break a deadlock of tank+artillery gameplay. But with the wide range of units with different abilities avaliable you will be able to deploy different strategies which may surpise your opponent and give you an advantage.
The game is free with optional microtransactions but it is not pay-2-win. Perimum currency will only get you cosmetics for your units and mechs which will not alter-gameplay. Everything in game can be earnd in time and the basic units that you are provided with in the beginning are quite solid. The business model seems very fair, heck, very generous and I feel as if you get lots of value for your money if you purchase special bundles.
I live in Australia. I've played this game for 2-3 years with and without using the steam client. In that time I've only met 2 other Australian players. Everytime I played match-making PvP I have always queued up against those two same people. This game is fun when you meet the regulars and start custom lobbies but if you live in the oceanic region and don't like to talk to people, I do not recommend this game.
Overall, I would recommend this game if you're looking for a casual strategy game. It's easy to get into if you've played MOBAs and RTS games. The game play is addicting but what I love most about this game is the community. I've never expereinced such a helpful community before. When I first started playing this game, many experienced players helped me transition to Airmech and have taught me almost everything I know about it! Airmech is a great game and you should give it a try :)

Kingdom: New Lands is an expanded version of Kingdom (renamed to Kingdom: Classic) developed by Noio and Licorice. New Lands is free for owners of the original game (so if you owned Kingdom you might want to check your library!). In New Lands you play as a Monarch attempting to build a glorious kingdom from the ground up. However, this time there are five different islands for you to explore and conquer. It's not going to be plain sailing though; the islands are home to mysterious portals, spewing out things that go bump in the night. It'll be up to you to ensure your kingdom is capable of defending itself against them.

The main difference between New Lands and the base game is of course the introduction of five different islands which you can travel to (in order, they get progressively more difficult). However, there are some other new additions. I don't want to spoil anything so I'll stick to just what's mentioned on the store page, there are some new mounts for you to acquire as well as some new merchants. Personally, I don’t think the additions by themselves would warrant a new game, however the fact that its given free to those who already owned the base game makes this point moot, it'd definitely be pointless to buy the Classic version once New Lands is available.

The most enjoyable part of New Lands, as was the case with Classic, is discovering new things. New Lands throws you in at the deep end of the pool with a weight tied to your foot. You're given no guidance as to what things do what so learning the game is a real case of trial and error, more error than trial. If you're familiar with Kingdom: Classic then there might not be quite as much for you to discover (apart from the new stuff) unless you've forgotten everything but it'll be exciting for new players nonetheless!

New Lands features a day and night cycle. For the most part, you're safe during the day to work on expanding/improving your kingdom while the night is when the things trying to kill you come out. Generally if you're doing work during the day you want to get it started around noon so your workers have plenty of time to get the job done before nightfall. Workers, along with guards and farmers, are hired by buying spare tools, any vagrants you've hired who don't have a tool will go to the nearest available tool they can find and grab it.

It's quite difficult to talk about New Lands without spoiling those discoveries I mentioned earlier, but the game's actual mechanics are very simple. You, as King or Queen, walk around the map on horseback gathering gold coins which you then spend on various things such as hiring vagrants, buying tools for said vagrants, building defenses etc. You do start out with a few coins found on the map but you'll need to quickly establish a way of making more money, I'll leave you to figure that out for yourself. You have no actual control over the people who work for your kingdom, you're basically just someone shouting directions at people. For the most part, there's no issue with having no direct influence over your population, but I have had a couple of situations where the lack of any basic commands is very frustrating.

For example, I had reached the second island and had successfully taken out the portal on one side of the island so I only needed to defend the right side from monsters. Some of my archers got killed during the attack on the portal and I had six archers left back at my castle. Five of the archers decided to defend the left side of my castle, where no enemies were coming from, leaving one archer to defend the right side. Suffice to say I lost the game that night. It'd be nice to see a way to avoid situations like this.

My main gripe with New Lands is the way the whole five island thing has been implemented. Say you reach island three but due to a mistake you end up losing the game, you'll have to start over from the first island again. Now, you might not think that's so bad, it depends what you're looking for with this game I suppose but I found it to be quite irritating to have to restart every time. It's made worse by the fact a lot of the cool new stuff isn't found on the first or even the second island. I understand why it's implemented this way but I'd love to perhaps see a slightly different game mode where you can save your progress at the beginning of each new island so you don't have to replay it all.

The visuals haven't changed from the Classic version but that's certainly not a bad thing. Both Kingdom games have some of the best pixel art I've seen in games, the water effects are particularly impressive. The audio is also great, again unchanged from the previous game. The ambient music is very relaxing and the sound effects are all very good. My only other complaint about the game is that there's no way to re-bind keys. It's not completely necessary, there's nothing wrong with the default bindings per se, it would just be nice to have the option.


New Lands improves upon Kingdom's formula, offering the same great visuals with improved gameplay. It's not without a couple of problems but as a free upgrade for previous owners it's definitely worth playing. As for those who are looking to buy New Lands, it's a worthy expansion to what was a great game.

Seeing the mixed reviews i ought to clear up some misunderstandings of this game.
This game is very similar to the game on kongregate called Swords & Potions 2, both in shop managing and city management. Premium currency IS in the game, however it is not necessary for the progress, nor are you hindered by not paying.
Crafting slots, places for crafters and other things are locked behind paywall OR in-game progress (in simpler terms: level). It's a nice game that you can check back for 1 or 2 minutes every hour or so and freely progress, or just sit at the computer and rush through as much as you can.
For multiplayer elements there is the city upgrading, which is a co-op effort, it would cost too much gold(in-game currency) to build by yourself, so seek out a medium-sized city with citizens around your level. There is also PVP, but the matchmaking needs coding, in the early game it is nearly impossible to get placed in a fair match and it costs a bit of money to "reroll" your opponent.
In the end, please don't trust those rushed 0.9 hrs on record playtime reviews, because honestly, they are just haters, who want a normal game for free or just simply hate mobile games. They tend to forget not everyone can afford or obtain a phone necessary for these kinds of games.
Best of lucks to everyone~

Cons:
1. I understand and can appreciate the cash shop. You guys have to make money too :) That being said - the limit of items you can customize your player with is very lacking. Literally everything costs gems - which are obtained slowly through game play or through cash. I dont expect all clothes/hair/etc to be free.. but a couple free options would be sweet.
2. I hear the servers are same across the board - which is awesome as we can sync our mobile/steam games (or so I was told via Twitter) - but the Steam version is new and we're essentially playing catch up with those that have been playing for the length of the game being released on any platform. ----
That uhh.. that's about it. I've had a few interactions on Twitter with the company - they have been fantastic, and explained things quickly. They even offered to come hang out in a stream when I stream the game to answer any questions! That's so cool.

I didn't expect much out of this game, but I was very wrong. The depth of strategy in this game is astounding!
In combat, every single action you take can mean the difference between failure or victory.
In between every mission, you can select gear for your Exos. The customizaion in this portion of the game reminds me of classic Armored Core (the vast number of parts and effects, while balancing your capacitor load!), and table top RPGs. The variation to parts you can use is countless, and can very easily change the entire play style for each Exo (which are already unique in their own ways).
Finally there is a lot of macro strategy as well. Every mission will affect the final outcome of the game. Every single mission, is to prep you for the final battle. Whether you decide to complete missions that increase your part stock, hinder enemy progress, or even the final battle closer in time, each and every choice will make a difference.
This game might not be a triple A title, but it is certainly worth the price.

Where to begin? I wanted to like this game, I love the theme, the apparent table top inspired gameplay, the apparent depth... but there's just nothing here.
First and foremost the UI is absolutly atrocious and painful to navigate. Menus hidden within menus, and none of it is very intuitive. This alone is unlikely to deter most potential players and if it was the only issue then it would be forgivable, however it merely sets the stage.
The fundamental flaw of this game is the gameplay itself. It is a lie. There is no depth here.
The gameplay is divided between events like racing and arena combat and then patroling which is where you will salvage vehicles and supplies.
In a patrol evry combat encounter will play out exactly the same regardless of what vehicle you have. You will spawn into the map, the enemy will spawn behind you or facing you directly. If they spawn behind you, then you run, spin, form a firing line with the other players and then shoot as the enemy comes into range. If they spawn in front of you, you form a firing line and shoot as they come in range.
Regardless of whether your car is a fast muscle car or an armor-plated SUV the tactics are the same. The physics in this game are pretty good, and if they actually gave the vehicles some decent speed and acceleration, and if the maps themselves and the enemy spawns where different then you could make use of the physics and actually take a tactical approach to the situation, but it is here that the game sabatoges itself. The encounters are lazy line battles and it gets lame quick.
The races  have more to do with luck than the skill of the "driver" because there will inevitably be a giant crash and the winner is whoever manages to avoid it with the least loss of control.
The death races are equally lame because they present little in the way of strategy. Once again it is mostly luck. Pulling ahead means you got shot in the rear by everyone behind you, hanging back means you run out of ammo after dispatching one racer. The best choice is to hang neck and neck with the drivers in the middle pack and hope those behind you target the adjacent races, meanwhile exploiting the firepower of those next to you in order to take out those in the lead. If you are very lucky then those behind you engaged other targets and those next to you are now too low on ammo to destroy you as you try to pull ahead.
If the races were not all stock then perhaps some skill and much needed variety could be injected, as it is now though in an attempt to make things "fair" everyone is given the same vehicle and loadout and so we are left with a complete and utter mess.
Apparently this game has a deep player driven economy and a few other features I missed because they are divided betweem the browser side of the game and/or hidden somewhere in the UI.
This game has been out for a long while now, it still looks like crap, plays like crap, and shows no intention of fixing the core issues.
The community is atually quite pleasant, though some of the more well known players and GMs are passive aggressive ♥♥♥♥♥.

So a friend of mine told me about the "awesome" total war series.

Kingdom: New Lands is the expanded version of last year's Kingdom. It's a minimalistic 2D strategy/town builder with procedurally generated maps.
You are the ruler of your kingdom, and you interact with it by running around and spending coins. Give a coin to a vagrant and they will join your Kingdom. Spend coins on bows, hammers, and scythes and idle peasants will pick them up and become archers, workers, or farmers. Spend coins on dirt mounds and rocks to build walls and watch towers that help you defend against the demon hordes which attack at night. Make sure to keep an eye on your economy though, as you can only carry what fits in your pouch.
Kingdom was an amazing game, and New Lands makes it even better in every respect. It's a very unique and well designed, plus it looks amazing and it has an incredible soundtrack.
If you want to see some gameplay, feel free to check out my video:

Kingdom: New Lands is an expanded version of Kingdom (renamed to Kingdom: Classic) developed by Noio and Licorice. New Lands is free for owners of the original game (so if you owned Kingdom you might want to check your library!). In New Lands you play as a Monarch attempting to build a glorious kingdom from the ground up. However, this time there are five different islands for you to explore and conquer. It's not going to be plain sailing though; the islands are home to mysterious portals, spewing out things that go bump in the night. It'll be up to you to ensure your kingdom is capable of defending itself against them.

The main difference between New Lands and the base game is of course the introduction of five different islands which you can travel to (in order, they get progressively more difficult). However, there are some other new additions. I don't want to spoil anything so I'll stick to just what's mentioned on the store page, there are some new mounts for you to acquire as well as some new merchants. Personally, I don’t think the additions by themselves would warrant a new game, however the fact that its given free to those who already owned the base game makes this point moot, it'd definitely be pointless to buy the Classic version once New Lands is available.

The most enjoyable part of New Lands, as was the case with Classic, is discovering new things. New Lands throws you in at the deep end of the pool with a weight tied to your foot. You're given no guidance as to what things do what so learning the game is a real case of trial and error, more error than trial. If you're familiar with Kingdom: Classic then there might not be quite as much for you to discover (apart from the new stuff) unless you've forgotten everything but it'll be exciting for new players nonetheless!

New Lands features a day and night cycle. For the most part, you're safe during the day to work on expanding/improving your kingdom while the night is when the things trying to kill you come out. Generally if you're doing work during the day you want to get it started around noon so your workers have plenty of time to get the job done before nightfall. Workers, along with guards and farmers, are hired by buying spare tools, any vagrants you've hired who don't have a tool will go to the nearest available tool they can find and grab it.

It's quite difficult to talk about New Lands without spoiling those discoveries I mentioned earlier, but the game's actual mechanics are very simple. You, as King or Queen, walk around the map on horseback gathering gold coins which you then spend on various things such as hiring vagrants, buying tools for said vagrants, building defenses etc. You do start out with a few coins found on the map but you'll need to quickly establish a way of making more money, I'll leave you to figure that out for yourself. You have no actual control over the people who work for your kingdom, you're basically just someone shouting directions at people. For the most part, there's no issue with having no direct influence over your population, but I have had a couple of situations where the lack of any basic commands is very frustrating.

For example, I had reached the second island and had successfully taken out the portal on one side of the island so I only needed to defend the right side from monsters. Some of my archers got killed during the attack on the portal and I had six archers left back at my castle. Five of the archers decided to defend the left side of my castle, where no enemies were coming from, leaving one archer to defend the right side. Suffice to say I lost the game that night. It'd be nice to see a way to avoid situations like this.

My main gripe with New Lands is the way the whole five island thing has been implemented. Say you reach island three but due to a mistake you end up losing the game, you'll have to start over from the first island again. Now, you might not think that's so bad, it depends what you're looking for with this game I suppose but I found it to be quite irritating to have to restart every time. It's made worse by the fact a lot of the cool new stuff isn't found on the first or even the second island. I understand why it's implemented this way but I'd love to perhaps see a slightly different game mode where you can save your progress at the beginning of each new island so you don't have to replay it all.

The visuals haven't changed from the Classic version but that's certainly not a bad thing. Both Kingdom games have some of the best pixel art I've seen in games, the water effects are particularly impressive. The audio is also great, again unchanged from the previous game. The ambient music is very relaxing and the sound effects are all very good. My only other complaint about the game is that there's no way to re-bind keys. It's not completely necessary, there's nothing wrong with the default bindings per se, it would just be nice to have the option.


New Lands improves upon Kingdom's formula, offering the same great visuals with improved gameplay. It's not without a couple of problems but as a free upgrade for previous owners it's definitely worth playing. As for those who are looking to buy New Lands, it's a worthy expansion to what was a great game.

Nowadays when I grab myself a new RPG, I find that most of my time is spent leveling and boosting stats, typically only finding a real challenge if I crank it up to the hardest difficulty, or play a Nuzlocke when it's pokemon. Why is this? Most modern RPGs seem to test the player's patience and ability to continue level grinding and farming drops. This isn't necessarily a bad thing in games such as MMOs, but when I'm enjoying a story-driven single player game, I'd like to feel a little more immersed.
Epic Battle Fantasy, on the other hand, takes the concept of grinding and throws it in the shredder. Most of the leveling you need is obtained just by playing through the story, so the only time you'll find yourself fighting extra enemies on the side is if you want to upgrade some skills with AP, a point system used to unlock new skills and make them stronger. By the end of the game, the player will likely be at max level and have all skills maxed, so being underleveled at any given point isn't really a thing that could happen.
These points aren't even the greatest part of why I recommend the series, though. As I said, in most RPGs you can just grind for some time and then be absolutely golden for the remainder of the game. In Epic Battle Fantasy, however, no matter how overleveled you think you may be, you'll be on-edge and strategizing through every battle, even the normal encounters (Though ESPECIALLY with bosses, obviously). You need to think about what elements to use, and what elements to protect yourself from with equipment, which you can switch mid-battle in case the enemies vary in type.
Without proper preparation, you could start a turn with full HP, and end the turn with a game over. However, this isn't necessarily a bad thing; in fact, I believe it to be an amazing feeling. Plus, if it's too much for you, you can always just hit up easy mode. There's 4 difficulty settings so it's pretty accessible for anybody.
My overall point here is that the EBF games give a nostalgic RPG feel that most modern games can't deliver anymore because they all revolve around grinding for success now. Epic Battle Fantasy brings back the concept of ACTUALLY THINKING through your battles, and I absolutely love it for that.
...oh, and there's boob jiggles :)
