Let me start of by saying this. Dont mention my playtime. I have played this game back in the days on the internet.
I hope I can give you an insight about this masterpiece, that is called EBF3. I will go through every possible aspect of this game and give it a final score.
But what exactly do you do in EBF3?
Its a jRPG, where you go through the game and fight bosses, which become stronger and stronger. You start in a little town after a short cutscene. Afterwards you explore different locations, from a forest, up to a volcano and beyond. Every location has a boss, which you have to defeat, in order to continue your journey. Throughout the game are hidden chests. They often contain really nice items, like weapons and armors. At some places you can talk to NPCs and start a quest. They mostly consist of collect x amount of y. The rewards are really useful though. A lot of the quests will reward you with new skills, which are otherwise unattainable. Overall its a typical jRPG. Kill, grow stronger and kill the final boss.
: 8/10
The story itself isn't really worth mentioning. Your team consists of 3 heroes which loose their powers at the beginning of the game. I wouldn't say that this game has a serious story. It is rather a funny story, which will yet keep you hooked and will entertain you throughout the game. You will read a lot of puns and jokes about Natalies boobs, but they arent really annoying or childish. Matt (the main hero) is your typical swordsmaster, Lance (my personal favourite) is your typical pervert and arms maniac and Natalie is your typical (hot) magician. You will learn to love each of them. Nothing too bad but also nothing too good.
: 10/10
This is where the game REALLY shines. I really enjoyed every second of this game. The combat system of EBF3 is really entertaining and the boss battles are really tough. Beware though that I played this game on the highest difficulty. Even if you level up your heroes, the bosses will still provide a nice challenge. If you approach them the wrong way, you're screwed. Don't get me wrong though. Even though the bosses are challenging even after grinding for xp and materials, they are never unfair. You always know, that you could've done it better and might have saved up your limitbreak for a certain boss attack. As every RPG you level up by killing monsters, after you've reached a certain amount of XP. But other than leveling up, you also got equipment. Equipment in this game is REALLY essential, as it can mean victory of defeat in this game (thats why I said you'll never feel like you have been treated unfair, after loosing a battle). Each equipment part has its own stats. Some have resistances against fire attacks,ice attacks and so on, some apply certain buffs, some weapons deal elemental damage, some equipment parts will increase your resistance to certain debuffs like blind, silence and so on. As you can see, you can prepare yourself for every battle in EBF3. Beware though, there are some enemies who will change their elemental resistance throughout the battle. So you have to change your weapon for example from fire to ice and so on. Every weapon and equipment can be upgraded up to 5 times. Upgrading will cost materials (Materials can also used to complete certain quests). Each upgrade will increase their effectiveness by (most of the time) 10%. Level 4 to 5 will also ocasionally have an extra effect. For example Matts sword Heavens Gate will counter enemy attacks, when it's level 4 and will sometimes cast shine on level 5.
Now to the skills. Every character can learn skills from a skill tree(Each has their own skill tree though). Usually you are free to pick every skill you want in the order you want. But you have to keep in mind that each skill has its own price. From the skill tree you can also learn your limitbreak. Limitbreaks are special attacks, which are avaivable after your characters have taken a certain amount of damage. These are especially strong attacks, which can be devastating.
There are some minigames, which can be REALLY frustrating, if you want 100% in EBF3 and especially if you want to unlock the secret dungeon,which you do once you got every achievement. But if you are patient enough, you will master these minigames too. They also reward you with items and gold.
: 10/10
EBF3 has one of the best soundtrack I've heard. Every location has a song, that will blow your mind and suits the theme of it perfectly. You can easily listen to the soundtrack, while browsing the net or playing another game. I never got annoyed by any song in this game. Best of all? You get every song for free as mp3.
: 10/10
I cant speak for the lower difficulties, since I've only played on the hardest setting. But hell this game is REALLY hard. Some might call me noob, but there were a lot of times, I got so frustrated, that I just needed a break. (Final boss reference ;)  ) As I have mentioned above though, you never want to quit the game forever because of the difficulty. You rather want to try again and again and again, grind a little and then try again, until you've beaten the boss. This game has one of the best rpg combat systems I've seen. Every boss has its own weakness and some certain things you have to watch out for. I really loved fighting every boss in this game. They all were a nice challenge and you had that feeling, that you have accomplished something. The best boss for me was the final boss. I remember back in the days, that I had quit this game, because I thought I'd never beat him. Several months later I tried again and again until I kicked his butt. Best moment of my life. Didn't regret anything. So if you're seeking a challenging game, try EBF3 on epic difficulty.
: 10/10
It is, what it is. It's not 3d but yet the game and its locations look beautiful. Maps are designed with love, they dont look boring or repetetive. Everything is colorful, lively and well thought. I'm judging the graphics based on what it is.
: 10/10 tl;dr
This game is a must have, if you love turn based rpgs. Awsome music, awesome combat system, awesome game and awesome dialogues ;). It's for free and has the soundtrack included. You will have a lot of fun with it. The actual playtime is based on your difficulty you play on. The epic difficulty can really take a lot of time to beat. I'd say from 10-30hours, depending on how good you are.

I put off buying this game for a long time because of the reviews but after some research I decided to pick up the "Complete Pack" during the summer sale.  I had read a few guides and suggestions beforehand so the first thing that I did before playing was to download and install this fan made patch to help with game stability.
I chose the offline version of the patch which removes the requirement for GFWL altogether and adds the console exclusive characters like Pac-Man.  If you want to play online you will need the other version of the patch available on the same link and a GFWL account.  I do have one but I don't play online anyway so I took the trade off for the extra characters.
The other thing I had to set up was my arcade stick.  A 360 controller works perfectly out of the box but unlike Ultra Street Fighter IV although it recognised my stick I couldn't configure the buttons properly and get it to save the changes because it wanted me to assign more buttons than I have.  (For the record I'm using a Dreamcast Arcade Stick and a Trio Linker Plus II adapter so your experience may be different.)
To solve this I downloaded this program:
which you unzip and place the contents in the game folder:
Steam\Steamapps\common\Street Fighter X Tekken
Run the executable and let it create the files it needs to and then it might download some configuration files for your particular controller.  You can then close the program and run the game and you should now be able to set up your button controls in game as normal.
This might sound a lot of steps to take just to play the game but it's really not.  It's just a case of putting things in the right place, running two programs for a couple of seconds and then you should be good to go.
One thing I will note is when I first ran the game it asked to create a new save file and it took a small ice age to do so but be patient, it will finish eventually and that only happens the first time that the game runs.
As for the game itself if you've played USFIV then it will all look and feel very familiar.  Everything feels a bit louder and flashier with the soundtrack and the added effects and some of the backgrounds are a bit distracting at first because there's a lot going on back there but it's a fun twist on what you are used to from USFIV.  The feel of the game is also a little bit more jokey and fun between the characters.
The game plays on a tag team system so you can switch between your two chosen characters on the fly or wait until your health is low on one and switch out to the other to finish the job.  When you do this the benched character will start regaining some of their health bar back at a slow rate so if you are having trouble that may help squeeze a little bit more life out of them.  Once you are knocked out though you are out, the other character will not run in so you have to make sure to switch before that happens.
There are some differences with the moves both in what is available and how they are executed but again you will see a lot of similarities with USFIV.  There also appears to be a way to simplify the motions needed to perform a move but I haven't messed around with that but that may be a useful feature for younger players who are having trouble.  There is also the gem system which can make special moves and cancels easier to perform but again I haven't messed around with this and have just left it on the defaults for now as I'm not really one for tweaking settings and just like to dive in and play but the system is there if you want to mess around with it.
I'm having great fun with it so far and I'm looking forward to messing around with the Tekken characters as I've never played the Tekken series so they should be fun to explore.  I would suggest getting the complete pack when it's on sale because it includes the 12 extra character DLC which includes Blanka who for reasons unknown is not in the base game and the 2 costume packs which even when they are on sale themselves it works out a lot cheaper to buy the whole lot in one go. So if you think you would eventually end up buyng them save a few pounds and buy the complete pack from the start.

Bionic dues is a roguelike, and plays pretty similar to standard rogue games. You take an action, then everything else does, repeat untill enemies are dead or an objective is complete. You get four party members that you can switch between at any point (costs an action) but only one of them can be on the field at a time, so you're really always controlling a single hero, not a squad.
First it should be said that, like most arcen games, Bionic Dues has amazingly good music. Although they are merely adequate as a game developer, they have the amazing Pablo Vega on staff doing all their music. This is especially noticeable in the hauntingly beautiful title track, The Home That We Once Knew.  A song so brilliant i'd recommend buying this game JUST to hear it, despite its other flaws. It really sets the scene and is a truly amazing first impression, sadly it's mostly downhill from there.
This game has an unfortunate problem shared by other Arcen titles, in that the game bombards you with information right from the beginning, telling you in pointlessly explicit detail about the final battle you'll eventually have and how to win it. Aside from being overwhelming and working very poorly as a tutorial, this also instantly takes away any sense of novelty or mystery from the game, and you're never really in doubt about what will eventually happen.  The final battle is hyped and foreshadowed repeatedly, and warnings about it are shoved in your face constantly.
At the beginning you choose four of the six classes, and one of the six available leaders. this is probably intended to encourage replayability, but i didn't really feel any desire to play it again.
After every mission your'e rewarded with a tide of loot with witty descriptions that modify lots of stats, and you can equip your party between missions using these parts. Each squad member has 20-30 equipment slots, so you'll spend a lot of time in there tweaking with equipment loadouts, which is kind of fun at first. However after a while of playing, the system starts to feel shallow, as there's a pretty small range of values that can actually be adjusted, and thusly not much room for "builds" or any real modding strategy. You basicalyl want everyone to be reasonably tanky, and all their weapons to be strong enough to 1-shot enemies, with reasonable amounts of range and ammo. this isn't hard to accomplish.
Eventually you'll stop caring about most of the loot you get, and just briefly scan the inventory for unusually high values, there's too much of it, and once you've seen one +50% damage mod, you've seen them all. There's no unusual combinations or interesting unique equipment, just ever-increasing generic values, the novelty fades quickly.

For modern horror games these days it's not about superstrong enemies but about unarmed and vulnerable players trying to survive in an oppressive and potentialy lethal situation. Among The Sleep takes this approach to a new and original level. You play as two year old child on the night of your birthday in what turns out to be a far more disturbing game than the cute intro scenes suggest.
As a defenseless toddler wondering around a dark house, you have good incentive to stay out of harms way. But that's not the most uncomfortable thing about this. It's the familiarity of the situation. Aliens in spaceships and zombies in castles are scary, sure, but at least they're fictional stories that non of us have had to go through in real life. In this game though we have. We've all been toddlers, and we all know what it's like to be scared of dark rooms and the unfamiliar (which is most stuff at that time). As well as the halucination-like imaginations. It takes you right back to those early memories.
You are accompanied through most of this by a talking Teddy that can light up and even walk around at times. He's no fighter though.
When I first started playing it I thought it was going to be a ghost story along the lines of Poltergeist or Paranormal Activity. Overturned cot, strange sounds, doors opening by themselves, flickering TV and lightning. But the game takes a much stranger turn as the normal but dark house at night gives way to earie and disturbing Tim Burton-ish dreamscapes. The puzzles that need solving are simple enough. You are meant to be a two year old after all. But creeping around these strange yet weirdly familiar places trying to find the pieces is not.
I soon realised it's no ghost story, but a journey through dreams, memories and metaphores. But lurking among this childs imaginative world is somthing real, right now and threatening. It's up to you to find out what it is.
It's a relatively short game, but if you're looking for a game that gives you a fresh and emotionaly intense experience, it's well worth getting.

I usually dislike strategy games. I play games to get away from all the thinking and work I do at school. However, FTL is an exception. This game is really really good, and here are a few reasons why.
1) Graphics- It looks very pleasing to the eye. I personally adore pixelated, non-realistic graphics, and the developers nailed it in this department.
2) Difficulty- The difficulty is perfectly alright. It’s sort of a game where you keep coming back even if you die over and over again. I never found myself raging over the difficulty. Every death is my fault, and the next time I play, I get farther in. It gets this whole rogue-like feel correctly, unlike a lot of other rogue-like games that I’ve played that just make me want to throw my laptop out of the window.
3) Gameplay- As said, this is a strategy game through and through. It’s all about managing resources, making decisions, being quick etc. Making decisions is a huge part of the game. Any decision you make could either reward you immensely or completely screw your run over, and that risk factor is an awesome addition. Each run is different because of these randomly generated decision scenarios and it works far better than I expected at first. The combat is also highly skill dependent. You need to know what to do and when to do it. It’s really fun trying to outsmart the AI.
4) Replayability- This game has a lot of replayability. Each lost run makes you want to do better the next time around, and you keep coming back because of it.
5) Soundtrack- Need I say anything more?
P.S. You will die a lot. And I mean it. It’s not something you can master the first few times you try. Good luck!

I played this game originally on Kongregate, so ignore my brief play time. Epic Battle Fantasy 3 (EBF 3) is funny, quirky and well made and free. Yes. Quality content for free.
Edit: Finished the game. Reviews points remain.
The simple turn-based combat that harkens to a simpler RPG time coupled with hilarious dialogue and references makes for plenty of hours of fun. Plenty of collectibles and medals to satiate the inner-collector, perfectionist and achievement hunter. All of this can be done while listening to the great tunes of Phyrnna, who was responsible for most, if not all, of the music across all the games.
There were several quality of life improvements made that I greatly appreciate from Matt Roszak, the developer (aka Kupo Games). Rather than simply port EBF 3, it was improved upon, and if the minigames were as I remembered, an increase in easiness is VERY APPRECIATED. The link to all the features he added is below
The game graphics are as cute and endearing as ever, though its age did show in the full screen mode due to the resolution. I am however more than happy playing it in its windowed mode and give that and its few missing quality of life features a pass. For a flash game released 6 years ago, the game still holds up well in my eyes.
All in all, a definite recommend to RPG fans. Exactly what it says on the tin, and best of all, there's no need to wait years for its sequel. EBF 4 is already here (free on web only). Just scroll down.
Edit: There is a 2x speed function which I also greatly appreciated since I already played the game before and wanted to speed run it. It definitely helps speed up battles once you're done enjoying all the animations from the skills.

Epic Battle Fantasy 3 was a fantastic game before, and is a fantastic game now. This updated version is a great introduction into the EBF series, as it's free and simpler than EBF4. If you're unsure about whether or not you want to buy EBF4, play this game first - while EBF3 is much simpler, the core concepts are the same.
This game is full of colour and humour, and has a little something for everyone - oversized weapons, adorable enemies, fantastic boss fights, and anime boobs. While on the outside, the game seems cartoony and silly, the actual gameplay is refined and revolves around a lot of strategy, but has difficulty settings for everyone. On Easy mode you can get away with making mistakes, but on Epic mode you've
to know what you're doing and how you're going to do it. Of course, real men play on Epic mode.
Now, my two favourite parts of the game: the boss fights, and the music. The boss fights in this game are actually quite challenging, but not to a frustrating point. They feel fair but tricky, and each boss has a strategy around it that keeps you on your toes. Each boss is different and brute force only gets you so far.
If you've read any reviews for any EBF-related game before, you'll have heard about the quality of the soundtrack - EBF3 is just one of several games with a fantastic soundtrack. The overworld music sets the atmosphere for each area so well, and the battle music is incredible - particularly the boss fights.
Now, unfortunately I have to compare it to EBF4. 3 is like a bite-size version of 4; both have epic music, great gameplay and interesting characters, but 4 is just so much more refined and polished, and introduces so many new mechanics. However, they're both great games. Chances are if you don't like 3, you probably won't like 4...and if you like 3, you'll
4. For a free game, EBF3 still has so much going for it.

NOTE: This review was made for the build 1.1.1.
Epic Battle Fantasy 3 is a parody game and a sequel to the Epic Battle Fantasy series. It's possibly one of the best FREE indie RPG turn-based games out there since it won several indie awards from sites like Armour Games. (Even though it is a little out-datted from Matt's standards)
This version has small improvements such as an added the wave counter, status damage color, and other little changes around the game.
PROS:
+ Incredible Soundtrack (They don't very well though)
+ Unique and fun equipment system (No equipment is leftout)
+ Choose your battles (No random battles)
+ Humorous (Funny text here and there)
+ Several hours of gameplay and much content (15 hours average to completion)
+ Good Replay Value (Many difficulties & New Game+)
+ Several popculture references (From video games to shows)
+ Optional Exploration (Hidden loot)
+ Several Unlockable Extras (NPC Maker and other Art)
+ Optional Sidequests (Not necessary to beat them)
"Meh":
* Visuals (Some are low quality while others are pretty)
* Story (Nothing special, but not bad either)
* Few grammar/spelling errors (Not really noticable)
* Minigames (They were a hit and miss really)
* Puzzles (Nothing special)
CONS:
- Random difficulty spikes (Monoliths...)
- Framerate issues (Won't run on a potato)
VERDICT: Epic Battle Fantasy 3 is overall an amazing game and personally a favorite of mine. The series continues to get better and better as each installment is added. Can't wait till EBF5!
8/10

★ — 9/10 - Nice little adventure with exploration, farming, and crafting aspects.
Other than the death and destruction games I've bought over the holidays, I figured I could also use a cute game to balance them out and after checking out a couple of games, Yonder was my pick and thankfully, it wasn't a disappointment.
The world looks great, the characters and creatures are cute, the main story is pretty easy to follow and to understand, and all in all, it's just a relaxing experience. The farming and crafting aspects of the game are easy to understand but don't expect there to be an in-depth farming system because there isn't one. The crafting system isn't too complex either but has definitely more to it than the farming system. You join guilds for the various jobs and once you've fulfilled some quests for them you get the first tier of recipes from them. After that, you have to fulfill another quest to get the master title which gives you another tier of crafting recipes. Getting to the second tier recipes for each job can take a while but it really depends on how good you are with gathering resources.
Aside from the main quests, there are also plenty of side quests as well as a ton of other things to do, see, and find which requires exploring the entire map. There aren't many restrictions when it comes to exploring the map as you're pretty much free to go wherever you please within the world's boundaries.
Personally, I really enjoyed the game and can't really say anything negative about it. The only thing that bugged me was the character jumping backward whenever they're close to a wall or something which caused me to fall down cliffs numerous times and I had to take a detour to get back to where I actually wanted to go. Thankfully, one can't die from fall damage because there is none.
It took me about 15 hours to finish the game with all but 6 achievements done which I will sooner or later get to and finish eventually. As for replayability, I guess it depends on whether or not the developers add new features to the game. Maybe a more in-depth farming system, other things to work on, or new murk infested areas to explore and cleanse with more side quests. I wouldn't mind if it would become a little more challenging either.
Conclusion: If someone's into cute adventure games with an easy to follow story, crafting, farming, and exploration aspects then I'd definitely recommend this game, just don't expect anything too in-depth.
Suggestion for the developers: I enjoyed the game but personally, I really do think that you should get rid of the troll town. I know it's probably supposed to be a joke and funny but it's really not. It has absolutely nothing to do with the game or the story itself and literally serves no purpose whatsoever so it really shouldn't exist.

So, what to say about Epic Battle Fantasy 3. On the one hand, it's a silly Flash game, it looks like a silly Flash game, it sounds like a silly Flash game, it's written like a silly Flash game and I suppose you could argue that it plays like a silly Flash game, but it's all put together very well. The art and graphics isn't
but the style is very cohesive and the world map isn't so big that it starts to look repetitive. The sound effects and battle animations are cartoony and the characters sometimes exclaim "kek" (sic) or similar in battle, but it works because the entire
has a cartoony aesthetic. The writing . . . well, you're probably not playing this kind of game if you want to experience Tolkien or Rowling, and, say it with me, the silly over-the-top save-the-world plot goes nicely with the silly over-the-top world of menacing giant squid and sentient giant monolith things.
The battles themselves are a turn-based system where you get to attack first every turn, there is no "speed" or "agility" stat, so I guess it doesn't toe the JRPG line
Anyway, there isn't too much to say about the battles except that they can easily fall into the "Fire attack, heal and repeat" pattern and you can probably beat Easy and Normal modes that way, but if you want to strategize a little more there is a bit more you can do with playing with status effects and changing equips mid-battle.
If you want a full list of differences/fixes between this and the web version,
.
There are a couple spelling/English errors here and there throughout the game. It doesn't look terribly professional but they realistically don't have any affect on how the game plays so please don't bother complaining about it. I have no idea if they're going to be patched out by the time the game itself is released or anything like that.
There are a couple places where the music doesn't loop perfectly. But the music's still great so you won't see me complaining that some battle theme is half a measure off at the end or something.
EBF4 boasts a longer story, fancier graphics, more to explore, Battle Mountain and a bunch of other things, but in a lot of strange ways I enjoy this game better. The battle system has fewer moves available and feels less overwhelming to start out with, and there are few enough that you could realistically try out all (most) of them throughout the course of a single playthrough. The game and game world themselves are shorter, and the level cap is 30 (I think the final enemies in the game top out at about level 32 or 33), so the end-game battles feel somewhat less long and dragged out. Lastly, while EBF4 overall probably has better music,
is easily my favorite song in all of Flash games.
Also, the font is in Comic Sans. I personally am in favor of adding DLC to EBF4 and Bullet Heaven 2 that changes all of the fonts in the game to Comic Sans.

I really like this game. It's relaxing and fun - if you're looking for a simple game that doesn't make you work too hard to pass the time, this game is for you. If you're looking for a game where the quests are more complex/difficult, you interact a lot with NPCs and farming/animals, this game is not for you.
Farming is limited to planting seeds/trees, getting animals to follow you back to the farm to adopt by feeding them their favourite item and organising where you want your farm stuff to be placed.  You can then wander around and come back to it to clean up the poop and collect the goods your animals have left you in the chest or feed an npc enough food to get them to be your farmhand so you just collect the goodies and not worry about looking after the farm.
Character creation is very limited and outfits are also very limited. You can dye your hair in game by finding coloured shampoos and can craft outfits/buy outfits but these are very limited.
This game is essentially an open world to run around, collect sprites and unlock sage stones and do simple quests in a beautiful, colourful world with simple animals and npcs who don't actually do that much.  You don't have to worry about any form of combat as far as I'm aware.

From the indie developer Prideful Sloth, based in Australia, comes the farming simulator Yonder: The Cloud Catcher Chronicles.  Yonder appears to be the developer’s first release.  Prideful Sloth states on their site “who take a micro-AAA approach to high quality game development”.  In all respect, Yonder misses the mark for this claim, but makes up enough in other areas enough to get a recommendation from me.
Before moving onto key elements of the game, a shout out to the devs for not gender-locking cloths!  It’s a refresher.
Yonder has a tons of lens flare, and other dramatic and subtle effects that enhance the beauty of the game.  In addition, there are some pretty easily recognizable creatures, like Groffle (kind of like a furry cow) and even has clothing based on this creature.  The game comes with a night and day cycle, a seasons cycle, and weather (though it doesn’t appear to affect much in the game besides aesthetics, and a few missions.  More on that in the next paragraph.)   All the terrain seems to have a purpose too: find a little nook or cranny?  It probably leads to somewhere!
Towns and NPCs leave something to be desired.  Many of the NPCs look like clones of each other.  After playing for 18 hours, I can’t remember many of the NPC’s names or what they looked like, besides perhaps a green-haired chef, and a “wizard.”  While the acoustics of the game are pretty solid, NPCs grunt every time you speak with them, and the gender they may identify with, doesn’t really match their appearance.  Building assets are also very generic looking.  The way to describe it best: is if you went to a theatre, and there was a prop town on stage.
By far, Yonder’s strongest mechanics are farming.  I’ve found that players can maintain up to six farms (though I’ve only found 4 so far), pre-decided in certain locations throughout the island known as Gemea.  Farming is a bit different in Yonder compared to other games.  Instead of hunger, farms have an overall “Animal Care” rating.  Constructible items such as Fodder Throughs (which don’t need to be restocked once built), and the interaction “Care For” seem to improve this stat.  Cleanliness is related to poop that your animals will leave around the farm, which can be cleaned up by picking it up, or having a farmhand take care of it automatically (Farmhands are generic NPCs you can meet in game.  Once these NPCs reach 100% happiness from food items, they can be assigned to a specific farm, where they go into game oblivion aka they just act as a stat to that farm and don’t exist anymore, until a different NPC is assigned to that farm)  Farming is very basic and easy.  Once players can craft the Garden Plots and Tree Plots, players can plant seeds they’ve found from places like barrels, tall grass, and NPCs.  No watering is required, it’s all pretty much automatic.  Simply collect the fruits and vegetables once they’ve grown, and no replanting is required.  Farmhands will automatically bring grown goods into your item chests.
While the farming is strong with this one, tasks and interfaces are not currently on par.  The story is very short and becomes more of  character development, than a story about the island itself.  Many of the tasks also seem very annoying.  For example:
Another quest involves waiting 2 days for
, yet when you
, you skip 3 days automatically.  Players don’t have the option to sleep during the night to skip passage of time, so the best option is to go watch a YouTube episode while you have your client sit there until the time has allotted.  There are some redundancies in the UI too like 7 recipes for “Cooked Fish” which all use different types of fish, but result in the same item.  There is also the issue of not having a mass produce button for crafting, forcing the player to use their clicky finger skills until their desired amount of crafted item.  It’s only possible to track one task at a time on screen, unless you want to open the task menu, or your hand dandy compass, and in addition, when you’re on the farm, your task tracking is on screen.  (Oh also, pushing ESC doesn’t allow players to exit the compass menu, and instead must push R again on the keyboard).
While I may have a lot to say about the UI & tasks, I generally appreciated the game.  There is a lot more positives and negatives I didn’t touch on, but the devs seem to be an active bunch, and while reviewing/playing the game, they introduced a new item called the “traveler’s knot” which is a handy craftable item that allows players to teleport to any of their owned farms.  Make sure to check out Yonder on Steam & PS4

Shop Heroes is an awesome game toward the type of gamers who like to run a shop : crafting and selling items. A game where you as player play the role of non-player character instead of being the hero. Heroes come to your shop to ask for items you craft.
You can send heroes toward dungeons to collect special ingredients you might need to craft certain equipment and weapons.
You can invest gamegold into the town to unlock different structures like temple, garden, hunter's log, school of magic, etc ... and upgrade them.
Further you can decorate your shop, upgrade lot of items in your shop to improve stuff like storage capacity etc...
There is also kind of action house feature : sell toward & buy from other players game items.
Since the game can be played free, I opt for a short review. Better go check the game out yourself:) Don't like it, no money lost.
POSITIVE :
- cute graphics
- total control of your shop : you decide where to place everything as you see fit (chests, carpets, furniture, windows, plants, worchbenches, ...)
- great range of items to be crafted while leveling up (bows, axes, swords, spears, shields, helmets, potions, jewelry, shoes, daggers, hats, guns, music instruments, staves, gloves, boots, etc ...)
- so much stuff to upgrade (= an important motivator as shopkeeper because of knowing you have always a use what to do with the earned game money)
NEGATIVE :
- there is always the temptation present to spend real life cash into the otherwise free game (meaning nothing is realy free in the world, even when it is labelled as free game). When leveling up, the game gets more difficult and real life cash can 'solve' the difficulties encountered. I find Shop Heroes strongly designed with that purpose in mind.
Conclusion : To my humble opinion, the positive aspects outweight the negative aspect(s) and this game provide me so much fun while playing. I think this game is kinda of 'love it' or 'hate it' and that is something every person must decide for him- or herself.

I've been playing Shop Heroes on a smartphone since its early days on Google Play. I've enjoyed being able to play it on FaceBook whenever I was around my PC, to save phone battery and enjoy the bigger PC screen and proper keyboard!
Yes it's a casual game, based on timers. Yet there is no depleting energy bar you have to wait for or refill with buyable currency.
Yes, as most games designed on mobile games' economy model, it has microtransactions embedded.
Yes, as a mobile or Facebook game, it has a double currency system, including one that can be purchased with real money.
I repeat: it's a casual game. You're supposed to wait on those timers and do something else meanwhile. And yes, gems can be used to speed up about everything. SHOULD YOU ? It all depends on you, I have never done such a thing and yet played for several months.
Does that make it a Pay to Win ? Is it mandatory to purchase gems in order to perform ? I don't think so.
the only gems I have "purchased" were through the 'ad watching' system, thus paying them in time rather than money, and more often than not the ad would run while I'd do something else in real life (sorry for the advertisers ;).
Shop Heroes  is mostly a co-operative game, with the ability to create or join a city and make it grow with 24 other fellow players. You invest your (ingame!) money, unlock buildings, bonuses, heroes, etc., and make it a joint effort.
I've never felt there were any competition worth injecting real money anywhere in this game.
Oh yes, there's an *new* Arena where you can compete with other players. So yes, I guess that a PvP element in a game where there also is microtransactions can be seen as a mischievous act. If you see a trap, why fall in it ? Some people may not and sink their money into it ? Wouldn't be the first place...
I've been playing video games for nearly 25 years now, I've been enjoying a wide variety of genres and yes, this game has drawn my interest for some time now. Will I make a purchase ? I kinda feel like I should, in order to support the team.
So I will continue to support Shop Heroes my way, play it the way I want to, and spend whatever resources I want in a responsible manner.
There is an audience for this game and, similarly, it won't suit everybody's taste.
Yet there seems to be a team behind it eager to improve it with (at the time being) monthly updates, so as long as the game's balance doesn't shift, I may keep on playing, enjoy my fellow citizen's "company" on the City Chat and stay in touch with the community on the World Chat here and there.
Sorry for the length of the post, and thank you for reading through it !

When the game finally got out, I was able to see the game presenting me an even far better experience than all I listed a sentence ago. The single player is actually quite good with pretty nice and challenging pacing. The combat system really has depth and even though it might seem complicated at first, you get a hang of creating your own combos and follow hits.
The graphic are just stunning in its own region. The hitting, slashing, kicking and striking sounds are really satisfying. I have to admit, sometimes I unintentionally find my self all tensed up due to how close and intense the combat is.
However, I have to admit, this game is not going to be a competetive fighting game a it is definitely a button masher when it comes to PvP. The reason for this is basic. There are already OP combo decks out on the internet where it is basically an infinite chain. Stack your stat points to stamina and damage then once you start just mashing light attack button, you will destroy either the enemy, or their stamina if they are blocking. The only way to counter this is to have the "absorber" class but if you chose something else, you are dead to that deck which is what the almost entire community is using in PvP.
To obtain this so called OP decks, all you have to do is to go to designated enemies in the game and just grind/farm dodging and/or blocking them. With this tactic, you can acquire the moves to your ultimate deck which universal across all "classes" the game offers you.
Lack of teleport makes the end game roaming a pain. You have to memorise which paths you must take in order to get to your intended place. The game's single player is fun though it is very short. End game events are pretty much not even present. You are bound to doing PvP over and over in order to recall one of the two bosses in the game with a slight increased difficulty.
Overall, the game is good but ONLY in the aspects of single player. The combat feels nice and satisfying but ONLY in PvE. However, considering how short the singleplayer is and how much PvP is required in order to enjoy(?) what the end game section has to offer you, the game falls short. Playing co-op with a buddy is really enjoyable, though it makes the short campaing, even shorter as it is way easier to tackle enemies with an ally by your side. Farming and grinding few hours is the only way to guarantee your ultimate victory in the PvP platform however, you will understand that with this game is nothing more than button masher and will always fall short when compared to For Honor in regards of eSports

Arcen Games makes a variety of games with interesting, niche gameplay, and Bionic Dues is no exception. If you're looking for a little bit of turn-based strategy in your Rogue-like RPG, Bionic Dues will fill that need. Just keep in mind that the game can be very convoluted in the way it presents your goals: your ultimate goal is to upgrade and survive for a pre-determined number of turns before the machines make their final assault on your base. The missions you engage in will determine how strong (or weak) the robot horde is when the final defense occurs. The game can be cleared in a few hours on normal difficulty; the real challenge comes from the harder modes and playing with different loadouts of robotic exos and commander units. The asking price of $10 is more than fair for a game with this level of replayability, so long as you're willing to put in the time to learn the nuance of the rules at play. Even if you aren't, consider buying Bionic Dues on sale if you enjoy more traditional Rogue-like titles.

I usually dislike strategy games. I play games to get away from all the thinking and work I do at school. However, FTL is an exception. This game is really really good, and here are a few reasons why.
1) Graphics- It looks very pleasing to the eye. I personally adore pixelated, non-realistic graphics, and the developers nailed it in this department.
2) Difficulty- The difficulty is perfectly alright. It’s sort of a game where you keep coming back even if you die over and over again. I never found myself raging over the difficulty. Every death is my fault, and the next time I play, I get farther in. It gets this whole rogue-like feel correctly, unlike a lot of other rogue-like games that I’ve played that just make me want to throw my laptop out of the window.
3) Gameplay- As said, this is a strategy game through and through. It’s all about managing resources, making decisions, being quick etc. Making decisions is a huge part of the game. Any decision you make could either reward you immensely or completely screw your run over, and that risk factor is an awesome addition. Each run is different because of these randomly generated decision scenarios and it works far better than I expected at first. The combat is also highly skill dependent. You need to know what to do and when to do it. It’s really fun trying to outsmart the AI.
4) Replayability- This game has a lot of replayability. Each lost run makes you want to do better the next time around, and you keep coming back because of it.
5) Soundtrack- Need I say anything more?
P.S. You will die a lot. And I mean it. It’s not something you can master the first few times you try. Good luck!

First, I would like to mention that Street Fighter X Tekken is a 2v2 Fighting game. Mainly, you fight in pairs of 2, allowing you to switch characters mid-battle. However, if either character in your pair reaches 0 HP, the round ends and the point is scored/tallied.
The game has the usual features with a couple of unique ones implemented.
One feature I really enjoy is the Versus Scramble Mode. This allows 4 players to be on the screen at once instead of the standard 2. In other words, you can have a Simulataneous 2v2 instead of Turn 2v2. This is great, as it allows my relatives to play with me and just hammer the AIs for fun.
However, the only portion I dislike is that you and your partner share HP, instead of having individual bars for each character. Once your bar reaches 0, both players in your pair are KO'd, regardless of who got hit.
I would much prefer individual bars, so that one player can continue, even if the other has been KO'd mid-battle. Who knows, maybe that one player may make a comeback.
Also, This game introduces Gems: boosts that can further aid your battles. These gems have small conditions to complete in game which, if completed, gives you bonuses to your character. These bonuses can include extra power, faster speed, auto Throw Escape, and even slowly regenerate your Special Meter.
Each character can only hold 3 gems, so choose wisely what you'd like to bring into a fight.
Finally, you can see that this game has a lot of DLCs to offer. Personally, I do not recommended getting any unless you really REALLY think it'll add more value to the experience. You can get a decent amount of enjoyment out of it without the DLCs. There are also other Street Fighter/Tekken games that you can buy with that same cash and it would probably be even better than what you're playing. Just look around for alternatives before devoting yourself to its' DLC.

Wolfenstein: The Old Blood is a standalone DLC for Wolfenstein: The New Order, the critically acclaimed revival of the famous nazi-killing series by the same name, Wolfenstein. The game takes place as a prequel to Wolfenstein: TNO and puts you right back in B.J. Blazkowicz, acclaimed Nazi hunter and firearm extraordinaire, and give you naught but a simple objective: Steal a folder containing information vital to the war effort from the Nazis. The key here is that you're stealing from the ancient Castle Wolfenstein, which means that you're going to have to find your way through hordes upon hordes of Nazis, more than likely leaving a mile-long trail of corpses in your wake. Wolfenstein: TOB keeps the gameplay exactly the same as it is in the previous game, which is both practical and convienient for a standalone expansion such as this. The similar gameplay means that no matter who you are it's incredibly easy to pick up and play, even more so if you've played Wolfenstein: TNO. Gameplay-wise this may have the exact same mechanics as TNO, but as a whole game it manages to feel both strikingly similar as well as refreshing and still capable of holding my attention for hours.
As is per usual for a Wolfenstein game, you aren't really here for the extraordinary story and characters so the game ends up suffering in both of those departments. Since the game is focused almost solely on the individual heroism of B.J, most of the other characters have to be killed off, seeing as this isn't exactly the type of game that lends you companions for extended periods of time. Right as I started warming to some of the characters they got murdered in some way that felt preventable to me, like a guy getting killed by a zombie who I couldn't kill because he was given scripted invincibility. This ended up giving me the feeling that none of the characters actually mattered and they were only there to spew a few lines of dialogue and then gruesomely die to further give B.J. reason to continue his massacre. The story was honestly so forgettable that I only remembered the gist of it from the beginning, even though this is a game focused on gameplay it does include a story and that means the developers have an obligation to put work into it, which it doesn't feel like they did.
The story and characters were never really what Wolfenstein excelled at, if you're playing a Wolfenstein game then you're looking for adrenaline filled, Nazi-killing, fast-paced action; and Wolfenstein: The Old Blood delivers on every bit you could possibly have expected. As I mentioned, all the gameplay mechanics and systems from The New Order are kept exactly the same in The Old Blood, meaning you can still dual-wield assault rifles and slaughter your way to achieving different perks, as well as occasionally using stealth to get by. Each and every weapon still feels weighty and as if they all pack a serious punch, as well as having quite nice textures to make every one feel as if it were real. The weapons in The Old Blood are essentially the same as in TNO, with only minor changes or additions at most. The levels are also structured in much the same was as the previous game, being rather linear but with little nooks and cranny's off to the sides in which extra goodies like armor are hidden. Again, the game is still linear but some areas have multiple small paths you can take to flank enemies, not really the level of exploration I would be looking for in a game like this, but it's better than nothing.
Wolfenstein: The Old Blood takes the modernized gameplay of Wolfenstein TNO and smashes it together with the old Castle Wolfenstein feel to make what feels like a modern remake of Return to Castle Wolfenstein.

Wolfenstein The Old Blood is the prequel to the New Order, where Blaskowitz must recover documents from Castle Wolfenstein which lead to the location of General Deathhead's compound, leading to the invasion which starts off the New Order.
The Old Blood returns us to Castle Wolfenstein in all its grandeur and implements similar gameplay and graphics to the New Order whilst offering a new array of weapons, such as a dedicated sniper rifle (my personal favorite), and new enemy types, as well as a new mechanic involving the Ubersoldotten. As this game takes place shortly before the events of the New Order, the enemies and weapons found here are based on the 1946 variants from the New Order.
Overall, the game runs and plays just like the New Order, the graphics are phenomenol, and the story is your typical Nazi killing romp with a twist.
The game is short but is supplemented with the return of the nightmare sequences, this time expanding to most of the maps from OG Wolfenstein, including the boss battle with Hans Grosse (which, for some reason, only took me under 30 seconds, but that's probably because I found the HMG in that level). Despite its length in relation to The New Order, the game doesn't feel rushed but doesn't feel dragged along either. I'd say the length is just right.
Replayability is really just if you want to return to NG+ while playing on highter difficulties. Uber/Death Incarnate isn't really that hard.
I rate it a 9/10, and this definitely pumps me up for Wolfenstein 2.

Have I not reveiwed this stinker yet? Geeze, it was like... two years ago now I played (and beat) it?
Personally, I don't care about the bugs, of which there really arn't THAT many compared to earlier Stronghold titles. The game worked okay for me and I got through the campaign without any real serious issue.
No, where I got upset, where I feel the devs truly betrayed everything that Stronghold stood for, was thinking I was no longer smart enough to build my own castles. That's right, its Stronghold, a castle building sim, in which you don't build castles. On every single player map the castle is already built for you. Oh sure, you can build a wall between two incredibly obvious cliffs to seal off a supposed weak point, but I wanted to build frickin' castles. The first game let you build castles. The first game said "Here's some land. There's a quarry. Choose where to place your stockpile ANYWHERE on the map and, oh, by the way, you're getting attacked in about ten minutes." That's what made Stronghold, Stronghold for me. Sure, they still gave you some castles in Stronghold 1, but they usually destroyed them in the first assault and made you rebuild them, often having to scrap some of the infastructure so you could pull your defenses back to a more practical postion. Stronghold 2 backed off of that, but still allowed for it, and on the missions you were given a castle to start, they were often little more than a ring wall and a single scout tower just to get you through the first attack. Stronghold 3... gives you a full castle on most maps, doesn't want to let you decide where to place defenses (and fights you tooth and nail when you try), and on the rare occasion you don't start with a fully loaded bastion, the places they want you to build are painfully obvious. In short, they've made what once was a good castle building sim into a below average Midieval RTS. For shame.
Throwing salt on the wound is the way they handled the story. The original Stronghold's story was pretty good, and the characters were humorous, colorful, and fun to listen to. Yah, they had dialouge in the first game. Good dialogue. In the first game you were supposed to be afraid of The Wolf. You would panic when he attacked your early castles, and the final two missions against him featured huge battles that saw nearly complete destruction of the castles involved.  Comparitively, the Wolf of Stronghold 3 is a has been that should have stayed gone. Unfortunately this reflects on the protagonist as well who, while a capable military leader in the first game, might as well be a court jester in the third. Even the last few battles, where you go up against the Wolf himself, are so toned down it might as well be a sprawling bar fight. In the end, I was actually happy the game ended the way it did, they both deserved it.
TLDR: If you've never played Stronghold, get the first game. It's infinitely better than this turd, and you actually get to build castles.

Pros:
Fluid and responsive combat system
Lots of depth with the "Combat Deck" system
PvP favors strategy over "better" decks by a large margin. Mixup game and movement is supreme.
Plenty of different equipments to get as drops
Equipment system trades weight and speed for armor, play as you wish
Attribute system caps has high diminishing returns after about 15 points in a stat so players are balanced on skill
Can learn moves from other players while sparring with them
Challenging PvE
Graphics are not so artsy as to the detriment of realism
Journey-like friendships with drop-in squadmates
High replay value
Neutral:
Controller is almost a requirement to play.
High learning curve and a punishing combat system. Some people may enjoy this like I do, but others won't. If you like Monster Hunter, Street Fighter, or similar games you will probably enjoy it.
Playing with a squad is a lot easier than solo
You only see the map when you're at an altar so you have to remember the map as you travel
Friendly Fire is always on even with members of your squad.
You can fall off the map to your death in or out of combat and you can push enemies off too with the right moves. I like this, but it could be a turn off for others.
Cons:
No item trading (and lots of duplicates if you redo areas which you do to learn new moves)
If your whole squad dies you respawn and break party (but you can reform it at the respawn point as long as everybody has the same one)
Playing online can be laggy at times, but this should be fixed later and it's already getting better.
Other Thoughts:
I was initially skeptical about this game because it looked like the combat deck system would be the only part of this game. However, the PvE is quite challenging and the AI has different move-sets, strategies, and plays all the styles. Plus you can learn your enemies' attacks by blocking them. Absolver has so much depth that I am still a novice after 8 hours. I've only just gotten good enough to read opponents decently and sort of wrap my head around deckbuilding. Deckbuilding is interesting because it's not just a stat game, the frame timings and the animations themselves matter a lot when in PvP. An attack that looks very straightforward is easy to block whereas some of the more interesting stance-attack combos are more risky on paper but work out better against other players since they are harder to read. Of course, too many heavy attacks on your deck will also get you in a lot of trouble so there's a lot of balance to be sought after.
I also think this game should eventually include 2v2, 3v3, and some kind of capture the flag or objective style mode.
Some regions are experience server crashes and lag. NA and EU servers are mostly pretty good and restarting the game can alleviate some lag. There are lots of negative reviews from people that are in oceania and the middle east because their servers are really bad. Don't let the servers dissuade you, especially if you are NA or EU. They will sort them out soon and the game itself is very good.
Overall, this game is not forgiving and has a high skill floor and a high skill ceiling. If you do not want to practice and learn the game, then this is not the game for you. If you are a fan of Monster Hunter, Street Fighter, Dark Souls, Tekken, or other difficult fighting game and want a fluid martial arts game then try Absolver.

Among the Sleep is a decent action-adventure title that will appeal to anyone who wants a good scare. Perhaps it is because you are playing as a toddler that the horror adds a depth that most titles like this are missing, but it is genuinely terrifying at times. The ending itself is something that you should not miss as it holds a gravitas that will resonate with you and stay with you for some time. It is rather short, being able to get through the entire game in about two or three hours, but it’s worth the experience to play through at least once.

Vulnerability is a long forgotten element in what made video gaming horror such a powerful thing.  But Among The Sleep has gone to great lengths not to forget this. It casts you into the role of a toddler, turns out the lights, and asks you to explore the shadows.  Vulnerability is effortlessly achieved when the character you control can barely walk on its own. Wobbling along on uncertain feet leads your first person view to bobble from side to side as you advance. Keep it up for too long, and you’ll fall onto your hands and knees where you’ll crawl instead at a much brisker pace. Tilt your view enough to see yourself, and you glance tiny grasping hands, and a body clad in a dark blue onesie with a star and moon print. Pause the game, and the static options menu is brought up only after the infant has covered their eyes with their little hands. It’s occasionally adorable. It’s always, always nerve-racking. There’s something out there in the dark -- how are you supposed to fend it off?

Overall, I had a wonderful experience playing Yonder: The Cloud Catcher Chronicles. I bought it on sale for 15 USD, and I think that would be a fair price for most people to buy it. Personally, I like to think I should be able to get an hour of playtime out of every dollar I spend on a game. AAA $60 titles should give me a minimum of 60 hours of enjoyment. With Yonder, I would be hesitant to pay 25 USD. Right now I have just over 26 hours, and most of that is comitment to complete as many quests as I can, having completed the main story within 10 hours.
While I admire the devs having a vision (that of a game with no combat, built around exploration and crafting), I feel like the game is missing something. There is nothing holding you back from doing whatever you'd like in Yonder - and I don't think thats an entirely good thing. For the quests that require "some number of some item(s)", the typical cycle is this:
1. Walk to where the item is
2. Gather the item by clicking on it
3. Walking back
However, these items are rarely region specific. You're not given a quests to go explore a new location to find a new material, you're usually stucking trying to gather the same 4 basic resources that are found in every location. These quests don't encourage you to explore and see new sights, they just feel like a grind. Tack on a rather clunky crafting system, and all of the build quests become very tedious very quickly.
Furthermore (and this gripe is both minor and personal), I think some sort of progression system would greatly improve the experience. This is /slightly/ acomplished with the Sprites, but enough are just "given out for free" (ie: no puzzle/quest to unlock) that they don't feel very important, and there is rarely anything behind the Murk that is terribly worth getting. If there were items behind the Murk that imporved gameplay or made the player feel more mobile, I think it would feel like a much more rewarding system. I can't imagine how many times I though a hangglider would vastly improve travel, or a multi tool that reduced me trying to select the right tool for each individual gathering spot.
My final gripe would be about player impact on the world. The 5 collectable constellations are very cool, and their coresponding effects on the sky are as well, but that is about is as far as visible impact goes. Besides them and the Cloud Catcher, nothing you do feels like it has an impact. If a region is unhappy, I should feel it. If I've spent hours building bridges outside of towns and planting trees, I should get some sense that my actions are actually effecting the world. The 50% happiness bonus (where more animals are seen) is a great start, but I think this could be pushed a lot further. By the  end of the game, the world felt the same as if I hadnt been there at all. There was no Murck blocking paths, but nobody seemed to care. Abandonded and broken houses were still scattered around the world, lifeless and empty.
I've put 26 hours of my life into this game and I am very happy to have done so. However, I think that with some changes, this game could consume plently more hours from me. As it stands now, I see no reason to play this game again. There is nothing of importance to do in my current save and there is very little vaule in replaying an exploration gme when you've already seen the entire world. If you like walking, cute people, cute animals, walking, clciking on resources, and walking some more, than this is the game for you!
Final aside - do we really need a 1.5 second delay after crafting items? If i need to make ~50 construction kits to construct each bridge, please dont make the crafting so ungodly slow, and please add a sign showing how many you currently have. Crafting is a key element, I dont see why the system is so clunky sometimes.

This is definitely a fun little game. It's very G rated (There's no death or combat) and very much what I'd consider a 'baby's first open world RPG' style game. The graphics are beautiful, the creatures are imaginative, the quests are... challenging... All in all it's a great little game and definitely one I'd suggest to anyone interested in open world RPG style games that isn't quite accustomed to the concept of 'video games'. Definitely a 'gateway' open world RPG.
My only complaints are as follows:
~ The compass is a wonderful idea but the minimap and 'quest tracking' (I'll get to that in a moment) render it completely pointless since they both do the /exact/ same thing.The compass is just... prettier... I guess.
~ "Quest Tracking" is somewhat pointless. The quests are occasionally insanely vague, which can be a lot of fun, but not when you're forced to google for help now and then because they're -too- vague. The quest tracker literally just points you back to the person where you got the quest in the first place. (Ok, sometimes quests like the one where you have to find missing Groffles help you along but most are incredibly challenging to figure out and a little nudge in the right direction is always helpful.) I'm not saying be like WoW and spell it out for people, it'd just be nice to offer a bit more of a hint or just... something that could help along the EXTREMELY vague quests (I'm looking at you, lady who refuses to accept an umbrella in a situation where an umbrella would be entirely reasonable as a quest item but somehow isn't... and yes, I figured it out eventually, but really... I went through two other items before I found the answer).
~"Fishing" is... unique... but it's a bit more geared towards people who use controllers and is somewhat awkward for those of us playing on a keyboard. If you have carpal tunnel or arthiritis it's a genuine pain, speaking from experience, to get any fishing done whatsoever.
~ Crafting is, honestly, a lot of fun but can get insanely tedious and take an outrageously long time. You have to make every little piddly thing EXCEPT some key items such as planks of wood (yet you can cut down trees for wood) and clay pots (Yet you can collect clay...). So not only are you forced to spend ages crafting the same piddly base level item over and over and over and over and over and over and over and over and over again because EVERYTHING uses it for some reason, but you ALSO are forced to drag your backside around the island running from one trader to the next in the hopes of finding someone that's got some planks or clay pots or oil or *insert item here* for sale. It makes no sense when it'd be easy enough to add those to the crafting menus since they're already making you craft a ridiculous amount of junk. I'd rather have to stand in one place for an hour crafting a zillion things than have to do that AND run around trying to either collect enough stuff to trade for the items I need or find a trader with said items readily available (yes they're two different things, no I don't know why).
Those are pretty much my only irritations and suggestions. Beyond that, I absolutely adore this little game. The farming and creative possibilities that come with it are a ton of fun, and the fact that you have the ability to recruit a farmhand is AMAZING (so many farming/resource games overlook this and I'm thrilled the creators thought of it). The questing is frustratingly vague at times but generally a delight. The "Murk" is a fun purpose to everything. And the storyline, as simplistic as it is, is genuinely engaging enough to keep the player wandering forward on the quest line yet not so frantic as to pull them away from simply exploring as they please on the way.
Definitely a great little game!

ONION KNIGHTS: Definitive Edition
PUBLISHER – Insel Games
DEVELOPER – THEM Corporation
GENRE – Tower Defense
THE BASICS:
A very literal take on the “Tower Defense” genre, with more interactivity/direct control. There are no turrets to place atop maze walls, waiting for the inexorable procession of enemies and tanks to blunder through them – Rather, you have direct control over your little knight in a mobile turret (can only go up and down), allowing you to directly upon any area of the screen except the tower itself, which you are defending. Fortunately, you have the aid of three allies: a big hammer-wielding knight who can push foes back, a lady sharpshooter who can lay mines and deal with enemies who sneak past your main cannon, and a tinkerer who fires off homing missiles and the like. You also have access to special consumable “skills” (such as a sneeze that wipes out all foes on the field) and persistent, upgradeable “Hero” units who can help out for a limited amount of time, once per battle.
THE FLOW AND THE STORY:
The Onion Knights have been set the task of defending their nation from the oncoming hordes of the Curry Kingdom! Strap into your cannon, select your special weapon and skill loadouts, cry havoc, and loose the dogs of war! ...And that's about it. Keep the bad guys away from your tower; if they manager to infiltrate and scale it, or your cannoneer runs out of HP, then it's game over, man! Game over!
The game has you setting your cadre of brave warriors against hordes of enemies intent on taking you all down – anything from armored knights and birds to dragons and ninjas to hero-class units that work for the other side! Mow those bad boys down and try to keep your combo counter high, while dodging thrown projectiles and incoming cannon shots.
CONTROLS:
Keyboard only; up/down for the main character (who is always in auto-fire mode) and shortcut keys for your three allied knights, up to three special skills, and up to three special heroes who will pop in for a minute or so to help with the war effort. ESC usually takes you directly to the Quit screen, rather than backing you out of the current menu area.
GRAPHICS:
Pretty darn nice for a mobile port. Cutesy hand-drawn-looking characters and animations.
SOUND:
As this is apparently a mobile port, there's no option to control the volume level aside from just a Mute function, and the game is LOUD at default settings.
OVERALL:
A pleasant little time-waster. FWIW, this is an enhanced port of a mobile game, and it's nice and cheap.
SYSTEM REQUIREMENTS:
Minimal. Win 7 or higher only

Plot/Overview:  Tower Defense, with progression elements.  Defend against the Curry Kingdom.  16 Areas with 160 total stages.  All the other food named kingdoms have fallen, only your's remains..... Defend you Kingdom from a horde of enemies.
Music/Sound:   The music is very well done considering how generic it sounds, and I found myself turning off the sound effects and music after playing only about 30 minutes, it was just too loud and repetitive.  NO SLIDERS, just on or off.
Gameplay:  It's tower defense, with a controllable turret that fires in an arc, and the ability to use hero abilities to fight off the computer controlled minions.  There are roughly 20 heroes you can hire and as you level up you can bring up to 3 into battle with you.  Each of these heroes can level up as well using gold.  There is a premium currency, which are gems, but there are no in-game purchases, you earn gems as you progress through the game, earning puzzle pieces, and completing missions.  These gems are how you buy new heroes.  Hereos are one time use on a level, but you don't lose the hero card from your inventory.
Controls:  The controls are super simple, 3 buttons control your skills(Q, W, E), or you can just click on everything in the interface to summon your heroes, use skills, or use items.  You use the mouse to raise and lower the turret so you can fire upon your enemies.
Recommendation:  Unless you really want a new tower defense game, wait for it to be on sale.

Bionic ♥♥♥♥ing Dues!
To me, this feels like what "Sword of the Stars : The Pit" should've played like. At times, the gameplay will feel a bit off since you're gonna be reacting to the enemies' movement and provoking them, rather than just diving in and killing everything like in most games. Still, that's just a tiny part of the actual playtime, and the music is simply amazing, so it fills up the little downtimes you may have.
Talking about the music, it's so amazing that whenever I stop playing, I always feel like the current track is slightly out of context (especially menu song)... Yet, all of them are so melodious and non-intrusive that it only ends up as a positive experience overall (I've had the menu song loop for ~30 minutes right now...)
So, let's see if you should buy this game or not... What this game offers :
- Squad management : You control 1 character, but can swap between 4 exos. The first thing you do when you create a game is choose your "avatar" (aka 1 special game-changing skill), and 4 exos which have their own specialties.
- Equipment management : Each mecha has a reactor, shield, propulsor, computer and 2-5 weapons. Each of those have 2-4(5?) slots for items. You have to mix multiple stats while managing power usage to create your indestructible monsters.
- Tactical fight : Lay down mines and turrets, go stealthed to "charm" their leader and run away sneakily, Use your shotgun to explode the fuel tank and make everything i nthat room ashes... This game offers it all. I haven't tried the 2 hardest difficulties yet, but the tactical side may even make the game slightly too easy.
- Amazing music : I said it already, saying it again, the OST is  at the very least charming. Not a single time did I thought "Hmm... I should lower the sound!". Screw you roomies, I'm playing Bionic Dues!
- Randomness : Map layout where you pick missions is random, map layout of missions is random, item drops are random... There are a few other aspect that are random-ish, but all in all you have the Rogue-like randomness without it being too punishing.
- Different difficulties : I just completed a game on normal hardcore, it felt easy for someone used to play roguelikes. There are 2 difficulties lower than that, which are aptly named easy and casual, and 2 higher, which should be interesting.
All in all, the choice is easy... If you like Mechas, buy it! If you like roguelikes, buy it! If the game is on sale, buy it! (Honestly, even if you're not a big fan of such games, I'm 100% you'll get more than $5-7 worth of fun out of this game).

A funny mix of ingredients making for a rather good game, overall. You take a group of four "mechs" into various battlegrounds and kill robots. It seems to be trying to create the kinds of "tactical puzzles" which are one of the draws of the difficult moments in roguelike games. The customization is pretty fiddly and unsatisfying, but the combat itself is engaging and provides lots of opportunities to experiment with a wide range of available strategies. The graphics are rather characterless and in some ways the theme feels a bit thin. Also, there's a comic voiceover, which seems like a rather weird fit. Still, if you like roguelikes, turn-based tactical combat, and mechs, this is a good time.

Like Rimworld, at first blush FTL looks both too simplistic and overly complex. The graphics are minimal and the screen is filled with numbers and meters. Your first run will be over quickly and you won't know what you did wrong. But after every play through, you not only get better, but you experience more of what the game has to offer. Like most roguelikes, dying is your instruction manual. You will learn when to stay away from nebula, and when to take advantage of them. You will learn which weapon systems are good in any situation, and which require careful planning and accurately timed shots. And before you know it, you're hoping that you can find a store that will sell you the last peice of a ship you are making. A puzzle that, once complete, will leave all opposition as scrap floating in your wake.
Almost every element of the game is randomized for each run. The order of the levels, the jump-points in each level map, the enemies, the random encounters and the outcomes, the quests, the shop locations and stock... Everything is randomized, which means you can play it over and over and still have a unique, compelling experience. And when the stars align and you get exactly what you need, it's an utter joy.

If you're looking for a game with heavy plot, rich characters, detailed quests, constant rewards, or combat of any kind, this is not your game. If you're tired of all the excitement, expectations and stress you find in other games (or in real life, for that matter), play Yonder.
You'll explore a breathtaking set of biomes, harvest some natural resources at your own pace, and craft things you don't need. In fact, you don't need to do anything at all in this game. There's no agenda, just a loose sense of plot and some quests for when you're feeling productive. To enjoy this game, you need to be comfortable making your own goals; you craft that wedding cake because you want to, and there's no reward beyond that.

I love this game. I've been looking for something like this for ages. I don't always need combat or intense conflict. I don't need jump-scares or constant need for survival. I don't need to be scared of everything and be afraid to turn the corner. Somewhere, out there, someone had a similar vision to mine(and many others) that there just needs to be a peaceful yet beautiful game for those who are sick and tired of constant action. There are other casual games, simulators and visual novels out there but they lack what Yonder: The Cloud Catcher Chronicles does. True peacefulness. Stardew valley,and others, is nice, but why do I have to fight to get ore? Or walk around in near pitch black darkness with no relaxing tune to accompany me? Or even worry about running too fast and ending up at home the next day with a few less of the currency?
Yonder is for those who simply want to explore and enjoy the view. It's not perfect but it's something that I'm happy exists.
Pros:
+Great scenery and wonderful visuals.
+A large open world with things that catch your eye at every turn.
+When night comes, it's actually really peaceful.
+Nice and relaxing music to set the mood.
+The music doesn't constantly repeat and sometimes settles down so as not to annoy the player.
+No intense conflict. No combat. No health or stamina bar. The only way to die is 'drowning', and through this you just respawn on land with nothing taken.
+Quests to keep you busy
+Controls are easy(controller recommended)
+The world isn't empty. There are animals and villages strewn about. You end up discovering a whole town when just following a random animal.
Cons:
-The camera can be a bit wonky, but that can be adjusted in settings.
-It needs a zoom feature as I have to adjust the camera every so often just to see my character.
-The graphics sometimes alter, but it's not often.
-For those who love action and intensity, there isn't much at all. So far the biggest scare for me was traversing a cavern for a quest.
-The NPC's can be a bit dull sometimes. You can't have any relationships with them(not too big of a deal) and they really are there for lore, quests and to fill villages.
-The farming is meh. It doesn't do much for you and seems a bit tacked on. I hope they update and add more to this.
-The way you 'buy' items, trading is fine and all but that should be for rarer items.
This game has its pros and cons, it's honestly up to whoever is reading this to decide if they want it. Remember: No combat. No intense conflict. Tons of exploration,quests and more.
