This game is cute, and relaxing.  I generaly did enjoy playing it even if it is unpolished.  There are problems with crafting and farming, which other negative reviews will tell you all about.  What made me give this game a thumbs down is the story, because there is a crutial element missing from it:  Conflict.
First off, do not read conflict as combat.  This game wasn't made for combat and doesn't need it.  I'm talking about conflict between the pro' and antagonist of the story.  The protagonist (obveously) is the player character.  The antagonist is the murk.  The murk is supposed to be this terible blight that sucks all the life out of the land and those who inhabit it (kind of like the miasma from FF crystal cronicles).  In reality, the murk is an inconvenance.  It don't feel like a threat at all.  Here's a few examples and how they could be fixed, most of which are minor.
1.  If you try to enter a pool of murk, you hit an invisible wall.  That's it.  You can't enter.  This is kind of boring and doesn't make the murk feel dangorous at all.
This could be easily fixed by reusing the drowning machanic from when you fall into deap water.  Just add a sinister partical effect, maybe a debuff (like slower movement speed untill you recover from having the life sucked out of you) and you're done.
2.  No one really seams to be worried about the murk.  There are a few NPCs in the main quest that tell you how bad it is, but no one out side of it.
Certain quests like guild quest should have pre-requisits.  For instance, you talk to the master of the tailers guild and she says:  "I can't take on new members.  The murk killed the cotton harvist...blah, blah, blah...muck level must be below 40% to begine quest."
Try to join the carpander's guild:  "murk killed all the trees...short on lumber...Plant 30 trees to unlock carpinder's guild quest."  something like that
3.  The murk doen't spread.  Once you remove a pool of murk, it goes away permanitly.
Adding a machanic that allows the murk to spread would make it feel like something that needs to be fought rather than something that needs to be cleaned up (like you're a firefighter rather than a janitor).
*side note*  fixing the cloud catcher would stop the spread of murk
4.  (this is the big one)  There's almost no difference between 100% and 0% murk.  Either way, the world is bright and cheary, plants and and animals are abundent.  Murk doesn't really effect your ability to gather material except that you ussualy have to clear a pool of murk to gain access to the   farm in each area.
The concentration of murk should be inversly proportional to the abundance of materials in an area.  At more concentrated levels, anamals should be harder to find or absent all together.  Trees should wither and give less wood.  crops should have a chance to fail and die.  Again, this it to reinforce the idea that the murk is dangerous and needs to be delt with.  Even more so when componded with the murk spreading machanic I suggested in my last point.
There should also be a change in the enviornment deppending on murk concentration.  At higher concentreations, the world should take on a duller more dingy aperiance.  TYonder uses the Unity game engine, which, if nothing else, is amazing with particle effects, so this could easaly be achived by adding fog.  Also, the music could go off key or change to a minor key at higher murk conentrations.  Anything to make it feel as though the murk is sucking the life from the land.

Like most offerings from Arcen games, this one looks and sounds hideous but the gameplay is neat and unique. It's much more accessible than AI War or A Valley Without Wind, but retains similar mechanics and crazy random generation. This one is a turn-based puzzle-roguelike. You manage a team of four powersuits, go into varied dungeon-missions and gather upgrades against an approaching robotic army. You have so many different tactics to employ based on your team and equipment, the levels themselves become like puzzles where there is always a solution if you can figure out the best approach. Kind of like Desktop Dungeons. Do you want to set up a trap with mines and sentryguns and then just make noise to attract the enemies into them? Or should you just employ massive rocket launchers to purify full rooms with fire? Missions are quick and bite-sized and the world map has many of them offered at the same time, making this a game of difficult choices.
There's a doomsday clock here like in most Arcen creations: You have a limited amount of missions to do before the end battle comes, you're supposed to either become more powerful by then or sabotage the enemy forces enough but the enemies grow in power too while you're on missions. If you just grind for upgrades, so does the enemy. You need to pick your desired missions from the map surgically instead of doing everything, just like in AI War.
The graphics and sounds are awful and I mostly ignored the scifi theme and lore, but if you can stomach the ugliness this is quite an interesting twist on roguelikes and a good grab during sales.

What's this?This is Hardcore(well,that depends on difficulty settings)Roguelike about mechs.
Tactical gameplay-not much of a random factor in battles here,so you can see an outcome before it even started.But,of course,it wouldn't be a roguelike if there'd be no occasional surprises from time to time.Mostly,utilizing special abilities like stealth,immunity to splash damage,doing splash-damage shoots around the corners,luring the enemies into traps,using narrow spaces to get baddies in line before an ultra kill-shot and many more-is a key to winning here.
-there's a little intermission part,where you can choose,which mission to take next-depending on a type(around 10 of them)you have different objective and rewards.
-The main objective of the game is to fight off a large robot invasion with only four mechs of yours.You control one at a time,but can transform into any of your squad,using one turn.There are Assault,Siege,Ninja,Scientist,Sniper and Brawler.You can compose your team as you wish,but you can't change your mech types after starting the game.Then you'll have 50 days(50 missions)to power-up your mechs and hinder your enemies' forces(for ex. killing one of the bosses prior to final stage,or decreasing an overall number of enemies in the final battle)
-Customisation-before starting the game you can choose a pilot.Each of them has an unique ability-be it discounts in the shop(between missions),using upgrade modules for your mechs more effectively,having an upgraded sensors and so on.
mechs itself have a few types of weaponry,reactor,computer,and shield.You can install modules into those to upgrade mechs.Depending on the type,they have different starting specs and number of module-slots in each part.
Visuals&sound-simple,but not bad.At least you won't be hurting your eyes looking at the screen.Explosions are quite flashy(and loud!-louder than other sounds,so I advise against turning sound effects too loud especially if you use headphones).Music-well,I liked it,doesn't distract you from the game and blends in well with it.Oh,and the Song playing in the main menu Rocks^^
CONCLUSION
Humble game,yet good at what it does.
If you like mechs,roguelikes and tactical strategies-you'll enjoy this one a lot.For only two dollars(as it is now)-well worth it,especially if content updates will be released in the future(and if to believe the developers-they will).

Anyone comparing this game to Stardew Valley, Harvest Moon, etc. is outright exaggerating. Farming is present but it is so shallow that comparing this aspect to the aforementioned games is nearly an outright lie. You run up to a wild animal with their favorite food. UI pops up "Feed 'x'?">Yes>animal follows you to farm. That is it. No meaningful interaction with them after that. No affection levels. They just poop and passively make a product everyday.
Animals can follow you around as a companion but they get lost, stuck, or outright disappear.
World is huge, empty, and winding. Quests that even take a whole year to complete give you rewards that you already have (scarecrow fashion quest).
No currency, just bartering. Hugely imbalanced farm product sale prices break the game flow even with just one farm.
NPCs are empty. Very empty.
Costumes are not dyable and only come in set colors; very small selection of clothing.
Crafting is fairly pointless. You can buy just about everything you will ever need to get through the game with your insane farm output. Clay is scarce, clay pots are even more scarce. Quite annoying when you need them as a base ingredient for a whole section of crafting.
Sprites are borderline pointless. You collect them to clear miasma but then they are just 'there' after that. They do nothing else and you forget about them entirely.
Fishing mechanic is very weird. Doable, but weird. The arrow is super sporadic and difficult to follow. Huge fish block view of smaller fish. Huge fish are nearly impossible to catch if other fish spawn, as the smaller ones are much faster and give you no time to bait the larger fish.
The feeling of being afraid to post criticism because the devs will mock you in-game via placing your comments into a poop town for 'trolls'. Very mature, a great thing to teach children! I regret putting all of that time into crafting that pointless bridge just to see how petty the resulting area was. 10 Kingdom Coins were not worth all of that time, either.
--------------
TLDR: farming is borderline nonexistant, economy is busted, play this game if you are under 7 years old. I couldn't recommend it to anyone older than that.

Favorite game from Arcen yet. Great indie devs with a positive development philosophy - DRM free, plenty of updates, expansions that don't price-gouge you.
Bionic Dues (mostly on harder levels of difficulty) demands that you make good decisions on all strategic/tactical levels from the lowest level of how you are going to clear a room of bots, to the next level of how you are going to conserve ammo in order to complete the mission, to the next level of mission selection balancing short-term and long-term goals. And finally, deciding on how to outfit your Exos to tie all of the above together. Plenty of decisions to make before you can even start the game - make a party of 4 mechs out of a selection of 6 (including duplicates), choose 1 of 6 pilots with very unique traits, and finally a wide range of difficulty settings make for an absurd amount of replayability value.

Surprisingly fun game despite its very clunky and out-dated animations. The atmosphere is very Thief-like and this is also the only Legacy Of Kain title to feature stealth elements. Oh and you play as a completely evil guy, Kain The Vampire, as opposed to the more heroic zombie(?) Raziel from the Soul Reaver games which gives the game a very dark and cynical feel.
I remember seeing a friend play this on PS2 many many years ago (somewhere around 2004) and as a lil' kid i thought it was brutally scary how there was this game where you played as the bad guy, coldly murdering and sucking the blood out of innocent people. Never played it myself though, but Soul Reaver 1 and 2 i very much did.
The combat is simple, but satisfying and you must suck the blood out of your victims' corpses to become more powerful. The blood effects are nice and you can even perform stealth kills in certain sections, with every weapon having 2 different execution animations. There are even decapitations and you can also grab your enemies and literally have their life on your hands.
The environments differ much from the previous LOK titles much to the fanbase's dislike. I personally have no issues with the more medieval city you spend the majority of the game in. To clarify, in Soul Reaver, you mostly travelled outdoors in the nature of Nosgoth and occasionally crawling in dungeons and tombs while shifting from the real world to the dimension of the dead.
The voice acting, as expected from LOK, is masterfully executed with Kain's old voice actor returning yet again to truly bring his tragic vampire character to life... or unlife. The music is dark, creepy and mystical, highlighting the crapsack world of Nosgoth quite eerily.
The camera is way too far away from Kain for my taste and it can't be changed. As i mentioned, the animations are very clumsy and some seem even unfinished which is strange since the previous Soul Reaver games were animated just fine. Perhaps it has something to do with the fact that Blood Omen 2 was being made by a new another team while the main developers were designing LOK: Defiance at the same time.
8/10

The games two modes need a tutorial. No explanation seems to currently be provided. The two types of building materials seem not to interact as one would expect. This causes needless confusion.
Why can't you build stone on top of wood? why can't you build wood on top of stone? Why don't the archways properly match up to be the size of a proper door frame? a few simple additional building block types would lend to more complex and rich sandbox experience(foundation/flooring, roofing/ceiling). Because so many things aren't built with the intention of having snap points to anything else in your toolkit it makes it very difficult to create using the tools given)
Instead of a complex menu system a basic system for the UI should be implimented unless specific instructions are set. A great example of this is a harvester in any RTS. When you click on that harvester and then right click a resource it will endlessly gather that resource until it is commanded to do something else or the resource is consumed. I do not think the tasks queue that is currenttly in place is bad, but could be slightly improved if a harvester cannot readily path to the resource it should harvest any resource in contact with the selected harvesting task point. That way when you set a task to chop wood a little too far from the edge it would simply harvest through the forest to reach the harvest point instead of "having nothing to do."
Overall I would give the game in its currrent state a B-. It has an interesting premise but needs some tweaking and player guidance. Set up a series of "missions" that walk you through the purpose and functionality you're trying to showcase. Teach your community when and why certain structures are needed in a controlled environment. Leaving this out gives the impression that you are crowd sourcing the answers and hoping someone else will provide the community with a tutorial and probably cuts out a good portion of your prospective clients.

Review for v1.0.0
Note about the current status of "Mixed" reviews: A lot of the reviews are outdated, and have not been updated for 1.0, please read some of the new reviews first.
Castle Story has come an incredibly long way from where it was when I kickstarted it. I have played it off and on, usually with each major release after multiplayer came out. I was given a second key which I gave to a friend to play with. With the release of 0.9, we've been addicted to this game. 1.0 is even better.
I have been an active member of this community for some time now, and my opinion of the developers is only positive. They actively speak to the community and listen to both their compliments and criticisms without issue. They are active both on their own forums, and on their Discord, and are constantly working hard on making this game better day by day.
However, that's a review of the developers, not the game, so here's my thoughts on Castle Story:
Pros:
- Hours of fun in either single sitting or over the course of several days. I could easily put in over 300 hours into this game.
- Learning how to build new defenses for Conquest or Invasion (Coop modes) or even Conquest PvP is a lot of fun.
- Building cool structures, tunnels, etc, is a ton of fun as well, 1.0 has released a ton of new content and the new "Debug Mode" allows you to instantly build blocks and structures!
- Coop multiplayer is addictive. There are issues with it, but they are being diagnosed and fixed, still keep that in mind. Invasion, Conquest PvP, and Conquest Co-op, are all a ton of fun.
Cons:
- The game will start to lag. It is inevitable. AI is a complex and CPU intensive process, and this game is entirely AI. 1.0 adds a lot of new optimizations, and I experience a lot less lag. Check the minimum specs, because if you don't have a 64bit operating system and more than 4GB of RAM, you'll have a harder time playing.
- The AI has issues with it. Sometimes they mess up, but with the release of 1.0, almost all of those issues have vanished. It's only going to get better.
Overall, I really enjoy this game. My friend and I have been addicted to it, if you like these kind of building games with AI instead of controllable characters, you are going to enjoy this game.
Total Score for v1.0.0:
9/10

From your first steps into Absolver's colorfully forlorn world, you'll be sent on a daunting task to rise above the mindless husks of people that were just like you to become a master of hand-to-hand combat called an Absolver.
I'm no expert on fighting games and plenty of other reviews talk about the mechanics, so I'll describe to you some of the sights and sounds you'll be encountering as you make your way through the world, as well as a few other topics and criticisms that I feel are important to note.
Absolver's overall gameplay experience is much like that of Dark Souls and similar games. You, a recruit of sorts called a Prospect, traverse a world made up of different key areas clawing your way through legions of those who have failed the test long, long before you. They remain in the proving grounds where madness and anger compel them to attack any fresh prospects on sight. The enemies themselves range from sad, pitiful drones which can be dispatched in seconds to seemingly innocuous ones who have the capability of dispatching *you* in seconds.
The quiet, solemn atmosphere of Absolver lends itself well to the somewhat grim task at hand. Every broken staircase, tumbling structure, and overgrown path gives way to a subtle story of failure and lost hope for those who came before you. The NPC's you do come by who are there to guide you very much emphasize the "not here to make friends" attitude of the works through laconic dialogue.
Overall, the gameworld is crafted in a pleasing way. I generally like more open areas, but this game won't be unfamiliar to those who have played the Dark Souls games.
As far as concerns, I will say that some of the game's difficulty comes from throwing 4-5 enemies at you at once which ends up feeling a bit cheap and frustrating at times. It encourages frantic hack-and-slash button mashing over the intended fluid combat choreographs.
Also there are no oceanic servers which, while not affecting myself, certainly has put quite a few people in a rough spot with the game. Our poor brothers and sisters down in Australia will have to wait for proper online support for a game that is supposed to encourage cooperative/PvP gameplay.
Very fun and unique game developed by a team who you can really tell cares to make the best PvP experience they possibly can. Looking forward to seeing how this game grows.

Tyran
Early Access
Dragon's Games
Dragon's Games
RTS/RPG hybrid
27th of January, 2017
Singleplayer & Multiplayer
Dragon’s Games is a developer that’s striving to improve themselves and the quality of their games. Mad Nords: Probably an Epic Quest’s a far cry from their now second Steam project, Tyran. From a  fairly generic 2D title built in an RPG Maker lookalike engine, they have now went all in and managed to create a decent 3D competitive game through Unity 5 assets. A success story, if you ask me.
But there’s always a pesky fly in the ointment, right? I know I can be pretentious at times and that I put the singleplayer experience above all else. Frankly speaking, you shouldn’t buy Tyran for its SP even when it shall be polished and ready to be fired up. At its core, this will always be a multiplayer-centric game and I’m perfectly fine with that. This isn’t even a case of partially misleading advertising since the dev team states very clearly, the exact contents of their Early Access stage. The problem stems from the fact that it’s not that much to play for now and it gets boring pretty fast when you can only spar with the AI or with a buddy on just 3 maps. And those aren’t even that big to compensate at least in a vast open space perhaps. At least the Artificial Intelligence can put up a fight well enough. Game may lack in current content but definitely not in scope or challenge.
It shows promise beyond just beautiful effects and graphics. There is lots of potential from a campaign perspective once it gets sprinkled with lore and a convincing cast of characters, which players might relate to. For now though, you’ll have to contend with an almost arena-sized fantasy brawler that draws at least some of its inspiration from Dota 2. Tyran still manages to be a competent role playing game with real time strategy elements sewn into its gameplay. The RPG side is dominant while the strategic aspect comes from the ability to summon and control several auxiliary troops which shall ease the burden off your main avatar. Consider them more like “meat shields” than actually aides in combat, yet you will find them crucial to your victory against seemingly insurmountable odds.
At the very least, those few maps already made available have scenic diversity and the presence of exotic wildlife to farm for XP. The magical and general skill progression is nothing new on the horizon, but it still conveys purpose to your constant in-game grinding. I’m certain that Tyran shall prove even more challenging once you can compete against skilled human players since the AI has its obvious limits. For now you may only play a small portion of what Tyran wished to exibit, but it won’t be a dull playthrough if you decide to pick it up now instead of waiting several more months. You have Cards to it and I can only hope Steam Achievements won’t make us wait much longer for their inclusion.
The reasons for which I’m willing to recommend this game, are related to its creative use of the Unity Engine and the fact that it’s an honest product as far its price tag’s concerned. You get what you pay for and that is a feature seldom found in Early Access titles of the past two years. Dragon’s Games has a lot of work ahead and I expect them to deliver on the many promises which Tyran made to its current playerbase and future customers.

- No SP campaign or lore, present in this Early Access stage.
- Too few maps/arenas to choose from.
- No Steam Achievements.

Unfortunately, after the holiday special, this game went right back to being ridiculously overpriced. However, if you happen to have disposable income or this game finds itself on sale again, I would definitely recommend checking it out.

1989 to 2017, Street Fighter has danced along the top echelons of innovative gaming, riddled with confusing name swaps and a dedicated fan base sprawling in the competitive scene for over 20 years, known as one of the first fighting games to feature a memorable art style and one of the first to push fight sticks from the arcade onto the home market, Street Fighter has a past comparable to few others in its genre.
But with all of this raises the question, where does SFXT stand among the many great titles from Capcom's senior Takashi Nishiyama, and does it deserve to hold the same name? Street Fighter X Tekken is a fun mashup title featuring the same menu and art style as SFIV, and with both the afformentioned and tight controls it would seem as if this game was to be placed near the top but that thought is squandered for two major reasons, support and multiplayer. Online fighting in this game could only be described as a chore, using the archeic Windows Live and riddled with problems after download for many users, including myself. Windows live was trying to be something it wasn't almost 10 years ago and it astonishes me that a game made in 2012 would attempt to use this buggy relic of the past and this is made even worse when trying to join a friend, having to exit out of arcade mode because someone else in your area entered it, only to wait for confirmation of it being your friend(s), or remaining in frustration at someone knocking you out of Arcade mode. This feature nearly cripples the games usability and should've featured lobbies through Steam seeing as said previously, it was created in 2012.
Unless you can get the game for under 10 dollars and are willing to put up with its aggrivating set-up and multiplayer, then do not purchase. Your money would be better spent on SFIV or the 2014 title, SkullGirls, but I'm stubborn and so I'll say that even with all of this, it's still an enjoyable purchase with a solid set of mechanics and a beautiful art style that meshes well between both games cast of great characters.

Yonder is a game remeniscant of the original Fable, without combat and a little more focus on crafting. A silent protagonist washed up the shore of a land plagued from a past accident in need of being restored.
The game featues a beatufil world of different climates with plenty of things to do.
-Collecting hidden items.
-Collecting less than hidden items.
-'healing'certain areas as you progress the game.
-Restoring the habitat.
-Performing fetch quests.
-collecting resources.
-Exploring.
-building farms.
With the economy being barter (no currency) and everything (farms & gadgets) leads on to gathering more raw materials, I found the crafting element to lack depth and purpose. With me only creating things to help me complete specific requirements.
The exploration aspect however, is very good with me often scouring the area after hearing the mews of a little kitten I needed to find!

I really enjoyed this game from the beginning. The art style is cute and the world is beautiful. It's a nice, peaceful game to just play and relax. No battles or deadlines, just take it at your own pace. You can explore a mid-sized open world with lots of animals, biomes, and NPC's to speak with. Collect items as you go to complete quests, make recipes, build, and tend to farms. There's lots to do overall but the main storyline can be completed quite quickly. This does not take away from the game play though.
Pros: Easy to play/learn quickly, relaxing, play at your own pace, lots to do and see, lots of quests
Cons: Your character can't jump very well, swim, or climb, No multiplayer (that I know of), lots of fetch quests (if that's not your thing)
Bonus! The devs added a Halloween event that you can enjoy every in-game Autumn.
I got this game during a Steam Sale but it is worth the full price if you don't catch it on sale.

Brief Karate Fighter is an absurd, nostalgic-like 2D fighting game involving Japanese men in briefs battling against each other in a competition. While it may look like a low budget arcade game, it's actually somewhat deep into fighting mechanics of both the past and present (and maybe the future! Jk idk lol)
When you first start the game, you'll be shown to the menu of course. However, you realise that there isn't any type of tutorial for the game! You also realise that you don't know what the controls are for the game! It's like old times where you had to read the manual to understand the controls. For starters, this may be confusing and/or frustrating as games nowadays include tutorials of some sort. Also you can't bind controls to what keys you wish for, which can also be a pain. The second player controls are even worse (imo), as the binds are in awkward positions. Fortunately, the game can be played with controllers (Xbox's so far, not too sure; dont own a controller) which is presumably (imo) the best experience to play with.
There are 9 characters, each with their own control schemes for their unique attacks. They're pretty balanced (imo), but there are occasions later on in arcade mode where the A.I will just literally kick your a$$. Not to say that's a bad or a necessary thing to add, however there isn't a difficulty setting nor a training mode, which can turn some people off. The game is in English. But before every fight, there's this weird message thing in Spanish(?). Also the narrator(?) and the fighters all speak Japanese. Furthermore, there's no subtitle option in the game, which can leave newcomers with an "eh?" Overall, controls are effy on keyboard (especially for player 2), a minor language barrier despite being in English, and the characters are decent.
Imagine if you had the older Mortal Kombat games and Hong Kong 97 had a child together. This is what it would like. Anyways, the visuals of the game are very reminiscent of the older Mortal Kombat games but at the same time, this looks like it was developed in a low budget (not to say low budget games are terrible tbh). The graphics look arcadey and nostalgic to those who play old arcade fighters. The background stages are just pictures just slapped behind the HUD and characters. It doesn't bother that much but to others, it may or not may be expected for a game that was created from a low budget. Overall, the visuals can be a mixed bag depending on how you look at it.
The music and SFX is very reminiscent of music from arcade fighting games and some consoles (such as SNES, Genesis/Mega Drive, 32X etc; imo). The hits you do are somewhat satisfying to hear. Other than that, there's much really much to say other than the music is nostalgic to those who play arcade music.

Sadly it actually emotionally hurts me to say but this game is disgusting, I have been a collector and enthusiast of stronghold since I was a child. I have racked up at least 5000 hours across the earlier games, and even now when my friends come over to play games stronghold is normally a strong contender in our rts pvp set.
I hardly know where to begin with this game....... it is so bad I just cant imagine where to start as the list is so long.
I guess as I always start with walls that's where to begin, in the older strongholds you would place walls in single squares to allow you to build walls to a custom effect, in this one you build a wall in chunks then hope to god it can connect to something but most likely it cant and will not, allowing troops to poor through a gap you were 100% sure you had closed. Also because of the way these shoddy effects and poor building methods “work” you cant a join new walls to old ones unless they have a specific connection to an end section making junctions for fortifications imposable.

next for me is the fact they have kept the honer system to allow you to train troops, its not enough you need the items, and the peasants and the gold no no now you also need honer a second type of resource that can only be gained through private resources that only your lord can enjoy, as if a simple foot soldier would actually care about what his king or noble was doing so long as the gold was in his pocket.

Firstly I would like to say this is more of a pvp game, rather than a pve story driven game. Think of the pve as a big tutorial building up to pvp.
TL:DR PROS AND CONS:
PROS:
+Engaging combat.
+PVP is fun and balanced.
+Coop avaliable.
+Unique and fun grinding experience.
+Large variety of move and gear customisation.
+Challenging.
+Lots of hidden content.
CONS:
-Shallow story.
-Early access level of PVE.
-Little to no direction throughout the game.
-Large amount of bugs (Still early in release to be fair)
-Can become repetitive.
-Bad camera angles.
-Not much sound (Only punching and repetitive music).
-Unable to re-assign some keybindings.
-Weak weapon play/move sets.
BASIC MECHANICS:
Unlocking moves:
The most important mechanic you will need to know is learning moves, you learn new moves by blocking or using your class specific defensive ability on them, a bar will fill anytime you successfully defend against the attack, any xp you gain towards that move will be stored until you learn the move, however you only get xp if you defeat the opponent, if they beat you and you faint, all the xp you gained in that fight will be lost.
Shards:
Shards are a resource that are used to use abilities in absolver, these include being able to summon weapons, including swords and battle claws, and also use shard abilities such as heal, gravity, shockwave and other such abilities. You gain shards by leveling up.
Gaining new shard abilities:
Shard abilities are unlocked by defeating bosses; mini bosses usually give you Shard abilities such as gravity and earthquake. While the big bosses give you weapons.
Player Versus Environment (PVE):
The pve in this game is very shallow from the start of this game you are told you are chosen to become an absolver, you then have to defeat a number of bosses, around 6-8 if i remember correctly, With 3 being 'big' boss rights. The boss fights aren't really too different from regular enemies they just have more health, and do more damage, have weapons, and have some mobs to gank you mid fight. The ending is unsurprisingly underwhelming, it leaves an open ended epilogue that will lead up to more events in future content updates. As mentioned above pve is where you will want to learn moves from enemies, it will be much easier than fighting against people in pvp and is much more efficient. It has around a 4-6 hour campaign.
Player Versus Player (PVP):
Currently there is only a 1v1 set up pvp mode were you fight other players and gain Combat Trial points which allow you to do things such as fight bosses again but with higher difficulty. You are also able to fight with players in the open world by attacking them a couple of times, this will give you a lot of xp and they have a chance to drop equipment they have picked up (Cannot confirm if this is true or not).
Cooperative (Coop):
You can ask random people to join you and form a party, or you can add people on your steam friend list and invite them to your instance, this will increase the difficulty in the form of more enemies in boss areas and the enemies doing more damage.
Combat styles:
There are 4 combat styles currently in the game, I will give a brief discription of each:
Forsaken: This is a balanced fighting style of dexterity and strength, although slightly favored towards strength, has a parry ability, when you time a mouse direction you will block your opponents attack, and gain frame advantage on your next move (Hits are not guaranteed after a parry).
Windfall: Mainly focuses on dexterity moves, has better dodges that give a lot of frame advantage after you successfully evade an attack (Again not always guaranteed) you also gain stamina on a successful dodge.
Khalt: This focuses on vitality and strength moves, and give the person the ability to completely block attacks, it will also heal them after they block additional attacks.
Stagger:
This is a hidden stance that can be taught by an npc late into the game, or the moves can learned by blocking the attacks of a certain npc. It focuses mainly on offense at the expense of defense, it incorperated moves that evade and attack at the same time.
Overall I would give this game a 7/10.

Shop Heroes is a casual game. A lot of reviewers don't seem to understand this. Resource management, including time, is at the very core.
This game is well polished and has a surprising amount of depth, content and strategy. It's also  actively supported by the devs. (Regular patches, updates etc.) and the customer support is excellent when you do run into issues.
It's not a game you play constantly, everything is based on timers. (Skipping these is pointless, don't bother.) Expect a relaxing game to check into a few times a day, a game you can play for a very long time without having to sink entire days into it.
Shop Heroes is pay to win, most microtransaction options are pretty useless, the various pack offers do give you a major advantage. However, you're not punished for not buying, and the game doesn't grind to a glacial pace if you don't.  Other players being ahead of you has no impact on your own gameplay. Basically, paying is optional and not doing so doesn't ruin the experience.
I recommend giving it a try.

Darkwind is just one of those games that I keep coming back to, even after 5 years of playing.
Let me just start by saying that this game is definitely NOT for everyone. It is based on the tabletop board game Car Wars of old. That means turn based, patient gameplay. You will need to be willing to give this game a significant amount of your time if you want to get the most out of it.
First let me get the bad points out of the way; the UI isn't particularly friendly to new players, the graphics are very dated and you may come across the occasional bug in the game.
That said, the pros vastly outweigh the cons. The community in this game is the best that I have seen from ANY online game. This goes a long way to counteract the hard-to-get-to-grips-with game client. Most people are happy to answer any questions that new players have (and there tends to be a lot of those) and specifically appointed 'marshals' (identified by a username parenthesised by '*'s) are experienced with the game and will take new players out on scouts.
The depth of the gameplay in Darkwind is also second to none, and that is to the credit of the game's lone developer *Sam*. Premium players can have a gang filled with over 50 characters depending on the skill of their leader (mine currently has 57) and each character will be different depending on the skills you train them in. These characters can then be sent out on scouts, travel to different towns or used in town events. The perma-death in this game also makes you actually care about your characters, and mourn them when they're gone - because the aren't coming back.
I've rage quit a few times, stopped playing for months because I've lost characters that were dear to me. But I always come back, because the game is worth it. This is a game that is constantly updated by a developer who cares not only for the game but for the community. Give it a chance and it'll reward you with an emotional rollercoaster and a drain on both your time and your resources. Don't blame me if your wife leaves with the kids because you are spending too long on this game after getting hooked.

After a good 4 years of bad reviews and bad press, I decided to give in to curiosity and see what this game was about.
It's playable, but it's not especially fun.  In the time it took the devs to get this far, it's been vastly surpassed by games like Stonehearth.
(After playing 1.0:)
Same thing.  Playable, but not especially fun.  But I should go into a little more detail.
-The building itself is simplistic in practice but awkward to learn and VERY poorly designed.  Stone buildings that aren't just flat walls have strange rules, and the physics for wooden ones are such a convoluted mess that they just aren't worth the effort.
-Invasions are exceedingly difficult in the sense that building is slow and bricktrons (people) are few and far between.  You simply don't have time to get anything beyond the bare minimum.
-The AI is... workable but exceedingly clunky.  You either give up most direct control of tasks or micromanage like crazy.  Either way, your bricktrons will get in eachothers' way and block eachother.  A LOT.
-Unity engine physics do what Unity engine physics do best.  Which is funny as heck until you realize a glitch just sent some of your building materials flying into the great skybox below.
Underneath is a reasonably ok-ish but finnicky game.  But after a development cycle of almost 6 years, it feels REALLY unpolished.

I love animal crossing, stardew valley, all of that cute, stress-free stuff. And I wanted to like this game, but after about an hour realised this was not what I was looking for.
1. There's no hook.
Seriously. No currency, levels or really anything else that resembles a reward system. I can do boring grindy fetch quests all day very happily but I really need something out of it. Something that reminds me of progression. Otherwise its all just pointless grind.
2. World design
The world is cute and pretty but you quickly realise just how empty it is. Characters consist of a name and a couple lines of dialogue. Animals are cute at first but dont do anything. Towns are all the same apart from appearance. Ditto for everything else, looks nice but very very one dimensional. Its also massive. This makes doing most of what the game wants you to do a TOTAL pain. Walking through an empty world from A to B gets super boring super quickly, to the point where exploration is a chore. And I love exploration! I love collectables!
3. Controls and camera
Havent seen this mentioned but the camera angle is really bizarre, kind of makes the world a fish bowl? Changing the FOV really doesnt do much, but you can make the camera controls mostly to your liking in settings.  The movement controls are really janky as well, and combined these two make the game a bit hard to play for me, at least.
TLDR; Soulless and uninspiring, looks are skin deep, no reward system, bad camera angle. If you want this type of world, BoTW is the place to go, minus farming. Like other people have said, it could have done with a lot more time in development. 5/10.

In a world of possessd mascots killing evil night guards in the name of justice, the story has managed to become...stupid.
One of the biggest things worth mentioning in this game is the fact that there is a legitimate reason to look at all the cameras. You use the cameras to spot the brown bunny and then you use the noise maker button to lure him to an adjacent room further away from you so you can survive the night. However, constant use of the camera, the noise maker, and even the...oxygen gets degraded over time so you must use the computer pad to reboot one or all of the buildings functions. Obviously, while you are meddling with this mechanic the bunny will begin to make a beeline toward your office. The other mascots are dead, or "deader", but they appear as phantoms that attempt to scare you and break one or all of the buildings functions. Despite the jumpscares that occur night after night only one matters, the brown bunny. He is the only one that can kill you but despite the fact that there is only one-ish( I'll get to that in a minute) between flipping back and forth between the control panel, the cameras, and the second set of cameras in the ventilation system, you'll definately have your hands full. The oxygen function is the most important function that needs to be handled immediately because if you remain deprived of oxygen you'll begin to hallucinate. When that happens the number of killers jump from one to two and if any one of them reach you its a game over. If the thought of being killed by a hallucination is bad, you haven't heard anything yet.
Good ending/Bad ending, I'm not going to talk about it right now because it is confusing as heck. I'll go in-depth after I play the fourth game when everything is explained but needless to say I don't understand the hype. Moving along. Sadly, this is the least scary game in the series. The only reason that I'm mentioning this is because this is supposed to be a horror game and neither one of the jumpscares got me. They seemed lackluster and was far more annoying than anything. In true RNG fashion, the fake jumpscares happen when you stumble upon the mascots in the camera and sometimes you will be jumpannoyed up to four times in succession. It will grate on your nerves. Unless I'm missing something you can counter-react to some jumpannoyances but not others. I just don't understand why there is always a sense of clumsy executed concepts. Despite the fact that I happen to like this one the best amongst the three that I've played, it completely sacrafices horror in favor of actually having more control of the game. (Unless I had the blessings of Freddy as I was able to 90% this game in the shortest time by comparison. Screw 20/20/20/20/20/whatever)
Its more of the same with a little bit extra which should be expected from the series by now. If you want jumpy horror than I suggest you play the first two but if you want a slight strategy-esque experience with your Freddy's game that MAY frighten you then I highly recommend this title. The unlockables provided in this game are the best yet but I strongly suggest that you play the games as gimmicky, fun, good time killers. Trying to find more out of this game, story-wise, may leave you praying for that quick jumpscare death.

Blood Omen 2, that game... Yeah, the game from Legacy of Kain which I like to call it the most legit fan fiction to ever be implemented as canon storyline continuation from Soul Reaver 2.
Joke aside, there's many things to love and very few things to hate about BO2. For a sole excuse to patch up the convulsing timeline of LoK, BO2 does exactly that and even more. Not only does it give us a more personal insight on Kain's very personality and growth but it also gives us that very thing which we loved about Blood Omen 1.
At the end of the day, BO2 is very well a 3D version of BO1. In BO1 Kain's inner monologue( thank you Simon Templeman) completed every dull 2D corner of the world with mystical secrecy along with the great character encounters and cutscenes.  BO2 takes you along Meridian and south Nosgoth keeping the very old BO1 feeling of progressing very alive and pleasant, making Blood Omen 2 an adequate name for this game.
While the combat system is a bit more challenging, it is by no means difficult. It can't be denied it can also be unpleasant. Another detail to be added is the wonky animations, which pale easily under the weight of the good voice acting and character interaction in the story.
Overall, I consider Blood Omen 2 to be a proper LoK game and I would EVEN recommend it as a first time playthrough for new LoK fans out there who use Win 7 or Win XP, as it offers a casual overview of the great world of Nosgoth and much more with not very difficult puzzles or fights.
Enjoy!

I've played this on facebook and mobile and now have moved over to steam. One thing that's important to note is that this is not a game for the impatient. Yes, there are a lot of timers. Yes, you can get stuck without much to do if you don't take a couple of seconds to stagger things. However, with some patience and just a bit of strategy you can completely explore all the game has to offer without paying a cent of real money. Does the game prompt you to pay real money for some things? Yes, but it isn't that hard to figure out that you don't have to pay to play. Another bonus is that the higher level players are almost always INCREDIBLY helpful in figuring things out. I've rarely seen a question posted in world chat go unanswered.
This game is also meant to be a semi-social one. Feel like you aren't getting anywhere by yourself? There's a reason for that. Without having other helpful and active players in your city, this game is slow, boring, and seems impossible. Most of the city building is designed to be split up between many players, one loner is not supposed to easily fund an entire city. I recommend finding an active city slightly above your level to allow some growth, but still be able to participate.
Honestly, this game requires a bit of patience to get to the more complex stuff. It scales up in complexity, the higher level you are the more things there are to do. In other words, you won't be getting anywhere near the top of the leaderboards in just a few months. This isn't a skill based game, it's a strategy based sim and it's a pretty fair one at that. Also, I don't think I can stress how helpful and kind the community that plays this game a lot is, especially when compared to other multiplayer game's communities.
Is this game perfect? No. Does this game prompt you to pay when you don't actually need to? Yes, so it's best to ask in world chat if you actually need to pay gems for something. Will there be times where you have to wait to continue playing? Yes, of course, but that's a component of playing any shop sim. Will you need to move cities a lot? Depending on how you play, anywhere from sometimes to yes. Is this game completely done? No, the devs regularly add more features all the time. Things like raids, city requests, and the pvp arena are all features that did not exist when I started playing on facebook. If you think the game is lacking a feature you can suggest it to the devs and it may become apart of the game in the future. There aren't a lot of other games that I've played that are being updated and added to as much as Shop Heroes.

I bought this on recommendations, claiming it was a neat hybrid of something like zelda and minecraft and stardew valley. And while it has a certain charm to it, I could not recommend this game; except maybe as a "family game" that parents could play alongside their younger children (say 6-9). It's a colorful, non-violent world, with a very cutesy aesthetic. Yet, on the other hand behind it's colorful vaneer, there just isn't much to do.
There isn't any kind of drive or direction (outside the main quest); something like stardew valley with a similar gameplay loop has drives, grow bigger crops to sell, to get better farming gear, or expand operations, or craft a bunch of high quality stuff to impress a certain someone, etc, etc.; but nothing like that here. there no gear to upgrade, there are points out in the world the make progress on that are a major resource sink, but there's essentially no reward behind them (so why bother, beside maybe completionism or "to make the world pretty again" (I guess))
The crafting is reasonably deep, but pointless pretty pointless. the fishing is interesting as it evokes actuall fishing pretty well, but also mostly pointless, and shallow theres maybe only a dozen or so different fish. You could farm, but it's ALL automated right of the bat, so there's never any struggle to manage it.
This game had ALOT of good ideas, but squandered them. It's alot of spinning wheels, but it doesn't go anywhere. Again, I think it would be a great family game because it is so light weight and friendly, but all that fluff leaves it feeling pretty empty.

While not being the absolute jewel which Gothic 2 was, Gothic 3 improved a lot of things regarding the game world and added - back then - new industry standards like somewhat contained quest hubs as well as comfort function priorly unknown to the Gothic series. In a way, these changes are mainly what makes it worse than Gothic 2, although Gothic 3 in its entirety still remains a solid contender to Morrowind in my personal opinion. Over these last 11 years I probably spent way more time with the Gothic universe than I did with the Elder Scrolls, because Pyranha Bytes is an infamously awesome developer when it comes to atmosphere, although they are just as infamous for delivering quite buggy and unpolished software. Back when it released (mainly due to the publisher Jowood forcing Piranha Bytes to ship an unfinished product, causing a huge fallout between the two and pretty much burying the franchise) it was a mess. Community Patches have made it perfectly playable without any issues and with a tweaked INI for larger draw distance it actually does look absolutely beautiful in 4k, probably way more than quite a few other games that have released within the last couple of years.
Gothic 3 is basically the German equivalent to Morrowind: An epicly huge island with different weather regions, a massive amount of secrets, caves, quests, NPCs and monsters to kill and hundreds of quests, usually with interesting execution and mostly avoiding stupendous fetch chains. There's a shipload of voice acted dialogue with gritty writing and a world with an atmosphere so great that I would even pick Gothic 3 over Skyrim when it came down to atmosphere alone.
Every RPG enthusiast should at least once in their lifetime have played Gothic 1, 2 and 3. The Gothic franchise to me is for third person RPGs what Planescape: Torment is to isometric RPGs: A gem that way too little people know about and that should be cherished a lot more by RPG gamers.

Gothic 3 stars a nameless hero (you) arriving on a colony only to learn that orcs have taken over the colony and are in the middle of battle! After the battle, you get to choose among 3 factions to help, which are Rebels (against slavery) Orcs (Rulers of the majority of the midland) and Hashishin (artifact collectors)
PRO:
~This game looks extremely impressive for 2006, and by a company thats not very big
~The music is quite delightful, if looping after a long while
~The locations are very unique, with lots of caves as dungeons filled with bandits, monsters, and beasts, to the varied cities and settlements
~The voice acting isnt really good, but its so bland, it makes you laugh either way
CONS
~Fighting in general is the worst thing about this game. Beasts (like wolves) are harder than they should, combo-ing you even while you're on the ground, instantly killing you or taking too much uneeded damage. Humans and Orcs are generally dumb, with them basically watching you kill theit comrades until you kill them, and the ranged enemies almost always hit you, destroying your constant flow of stunning them, having them insta kill you.
~to level up your traits in the game, you have to BUY THEM WITH YOUR GOLD! This wouldnt be a problem if you were able to buy special traits and get basic traits as you level up, but you have to buy ANYTHING you need, whether it be strength, the ability to use large weapons, the ability to lockpick harder locks, and upgrading your swords skill. Yes, you can get your own strengh, hunting, and thievery up, but out of the 10 hours of gameplay, I got, like, 3 strengh that I didnt buy, out of the 100 or so I bought from trainers
~At first, the game doesnt exactly warn you what's a crime and what isnt. For example: After I eliminated the first town of orcs, I looted the entire place filled with slaves without any problems. I go to the local rebel camp, known as Reddock, and just assume I could open a chest, but nope, I was instantly killed, I didnt save, which meant I had to do the first 15 minutes AGAIN!
~this game is EXTREMELY HARD! You'll want to save often after you do a slightly tough battle, because chances are that there's an equally strong monster waiting just around the corner. It was so hard, I had to put the game from Medium to Easy when liberating the 2nd city due to how frusterated I was reloading my last time. I counted TWENTY TWO times I reloaded in the 2nd city during the liberation against orcs!
~Companions are completely useless, theres no weight limit, they can only wait anf go home, and when they fight, they dont attack like you, they barely fight at all!
OVERALL:
6/10

Long time fan of the LoK series, ever since I played the Soul Reaver 1 demo back on the PS1, decided to pick up BO2 together with the rest of the Soul Reaver games just to fill out some gaps in the series timeline.
You play as Kain, the series' namesake, a human noble turned vampire during the events of the first Blood Omen, thought dead after his defeat in a great battle only to rise once again after a 200 year long slumber which has cost him most of his memories, combat prowess and supernatural vampiric powers known as Dark Gifts, he once again has to claw and drain the blood of his enemies on the path back to his former glory and reclaim his position as ruler over the lands of Nosgoth.
Now for the actual review.
Combat feels clunky despite being so simple, you can attack in a 3-hit combo, block, dodge to the side and later on also utilize various Dark Gifts to aid against powerful foes. Various melee weaponry can also be found in the levels or looted from enemies, these weapons can also occasionally be further enhanced by finding hidden shrines which will fully repair the weapon and increase its damage until you replace or break it. Defeating enemies are for the most part optional, although encouraged as draining their blood will restore your health and eventually extend your health bar. Most of the combat revolves around blocking enemy attacks and attacking them during the brief pauses in their assault while also evading special unblockable attacks.
Despite this "rule", certain enemies love to block your attacks even when they're commited to an attack animation. There are also times when your attacks love to pass harmlessly through enemies, while at other times you can hit multiple enemes at once with a single combo. I also had a few moments where I dodged to the side, only to move a few inches despite there being sufficient space to dodge, and then take a beating from my opponent.
A lot of the game's puzzles felt like they were put in just to pad the amount of time you spend playing as they acted as annoying obstacles rather than an intellectual challenge. The Soul Reaver series had tons of great and well designed puzzles by comparison, if Blood Omen is meant to be a more action oriented game, why bother adding such shoddy puzzles while also making combat feel poor? Maybe I'm just spoiled after enjoying the Soul Reaver trilogy.
Progress is saved manually through the pause menu and there are checkpoints scattered through the levels after which you can save the game and later continue from, death will also result in the game resuming from said checkpoints.
I did however encounter several occasions where 2 checkpoints are literarily just around the corner of eachother, while at other times checkpoints were so far apart it made me question if I somehow missed one. There was also at least one instance where a lack of a checkpoint right before or relatively close to the introduction of a new enemy was quite a dickish move. The game also doesn't remember if you had a weapon upon reaching the checkpoint, making deaths painful when you are stripped of your enhanced weapon that can make short work of enemies.
I had problems hearing dialogue during certain cutscenes due to the fact that the music or ambient effects were overshadowing the voices, there's no subtitles or a seperate setting for voice volume either to easily remedy this.
Cutscenes are unskippable, it's not fun to rewatch a cutscene right before a boss fight over and over again because the boss defeated you and sent you back to a checkpoint that's before the fight triggers.
Speaking of boss battles, they were rather dull and repetitive. With varying amounts of repeat X 3 times before doing Y 3 times and slapping them around a bit with your claws. There was also one boss fight in particular that had me completely stumped, as previously there was no moment where a specific Dark Gift was required to be used offensively and was merely used to trigger switches, and suddenly you're thrown into a fight where you're expected to know this ability can be used in such a way. Nothing short of bad game design.
The soundtrack lacks the amount of impact that the Soul Reaver series had, the Eternal Prison level was probably the only stage that actually stirred an emotion in me, I dread to play through that level again.
Thankfully the characters, their development and the game's story are something that I can't complain about.
Finally, a couple of glitches I encountered:
Enemy AI broke down halfway through the Industrial level, it luckily only happened once, it caused enemies to not attack at all, which made killing them an actual challenge since I was unable to counterattack them between their attacks and they just kept blocking.
Had an issue during the Wharfs level where the next area didn't load any textures until I took a leap of faith past the door leading to it, I was very confused why a building had an open doorway that lead into an endless sea.
Several instances of not being able to cross bridges/walkways/doors without jumping over a tiny invisible ledge. This actually got me killed once as a certain drawbridge during the Wharfs level didn't let me land on top of it and instead sent me into the moat next to it.
There was one ladder which was impossible to climb without jumping onto it as attempting to climb it from the bottom would eject me off of it. On that note ladders in general are very finicky about allowing you to grab on to them.
The game crashed on me a total of 4 times as I played through it, it seems to be quite random when it did so as well.
To conclude, in its soon to turn 15 years old life, the game hasn't aged well and was rather painful to play due to poor game design and glitches. As a title in the Legacy of Kain series it is fairly lacking and barely deserves to be part of it. The Soul Reaver trilogy, while none of them were 100% perfect, were not nearly as unsatisfying as this game. The only joy I got out of it was the sadism in slaughtering defenseless civilians for their blood to fuel my assault against the soldiers, thugs and demons armed with selective hitboxes while listening to Kain's arrogant laughter. As much as I'd want to cut the game some slack, both for being part of the LoK series and for being a relic of the past, I can't overlook the amount of things that are wrong with it.

Sometimes I wonder what developers think about when making a game that makes them go… “yeah, I’ll totally sell this game!” even if the price is under $4.
Domestic Dog by Surreal Distractions is one such game. A dog-sim of sorts wanting to masquerade for something with actual substance (as I suppose most “something simulator” games are… ), you will be greeted with absolutely no tutorial and no idea of what the hell you’re supposed to do. Survive, I suppose.
Basically you manage a dog that grows out of some sort of egg – the dog you get is random, and when you die, another one appears (not the same one, so you lose any “progress” made). You have food, water, dog money?, sleep – a few other stats to keep track of, basic stuff. You need to keep those up or you may pass out and/or die in the process. Tip of the day, in case it’s not obvious: You also have to mind cars, since they may run you over.
What to do in the game? Well, be a dog, maybe? Eat, drink, poop, pee (sorry, I mean, ‘fire your weapon’) , bark at other dogs, eat said poo… you have a minuscule map, a shop with pointless things, and pretty much that’s it for the game.
Boring doesn’t even begin to describe it.
There is really nothing to salvage for me in this game: the graphics are terrible, pixelation has never looked so bad, and outdated (sorry, I mean, ‘retro’) bright colors are sure to blind you. Because we all know if we refer to a game as “retro” it automatically must forgive all design flaws. Yup!
The UI feels cluttered and messy, everything seems to be moving, or too bright, or otherwise vying for your attention. The dogs themselves look rather ugly, even for alien dogs.
To crown the beauty, the quite matching but horrifying 8-bit styled music and sounds effects (which are really loud, by the way!) are hideous. There is no semblance of a menu that I could see, thus I could find no way to lower the volume, and quite frankly I didn’t even bother to look beyond the esc key, I just muted everything while I played.
If you enjoyed this then that's great, but it was absolutely NOT the game for me.
So, would I recommend this? Sorry, but no. Steer clear.

I missed the launch day for Steam on 15th and got on the 16th, first time on and spent 4 straight hours. Later that day spent another 2 straight hours and 6 more hours on the 17th. Now the 18th spent 2 more straight hours playing... It's only 6AM, I have so much more time.
The game is simple, a ton of multitasking and nothing to stop you from continuesly playing if you know how to micromanage. Those straight hours of playing I did was that short because I forced myself to stop and take a break.
You play the role of a mayor for a city ( starting out is pretty much a village) and you try to build up everything by making investments with the gold you earn through sending heroes on quests to gather tiny bit of gold and materials, having smiths, leatherworkers, crafters of all sorts making equipment for customers, and finally making sales through the market.
Some say "It's a waiting game". Yeah if you can't micromanage you will get stuck in long waits.
Example...
You have 12 wood and 12 iron. The first customer wants a "Maul" (costs 5 wood[58sec]), second customer wants a "Sledgehammer" (8 wood, 2 shiny gems[1min 46sec]). You don't have the shiny gems nor enough wood to make both weapons.
You can...
A) Craft the "Maul" and wait over your resources to refill and craft the "Sledgehammer" next.
OR
B) Craft 2 "Mauls" saving 2 wood but it takes 1min 56sec.
So you spend 10 more seconds of waiting but have 2 wood left over for say crafting 2 "Clubs" which is 5secs each.
Not every customer will come in all at once but one after another or a min after the first so you can already be crafting one item and another customer steps in so you start that one then 2 more come in and you start theirs then the first is done so you cash in on it. This constant switch can be endless if you know how to MICROMANAGE.
That is just dealing with the customer now you sent some heroes on a few quests that from the first 2 quests take around 5-10mins. If you micromanage this will fly by.
So you keep track of...
- Resources (early on is Wood, Iron, Leather, or if you chose druid as your third worker herbs)
- Stockpile of weapons and armour
- Heroes on Quests
- Current wait time on equipment
- What customer to sell to first or what to sell to them
The customers alone have some features you should keep track of and figure out how you want to deal with on a buisness level. Discount, Surcharge, Compliment, Refuse, Suggest, and From Trade.
Discount : You lower price you request for the item you are selling to them (Gain more energy)
Surcharge : You charge more for the item you are selling to them (Lose more energy)
Compliment : This is seemingly random, you may gain or lose energy with this
Refuse : You turn down their request and lose or gain nothing, Takes longer for them to return.
Suggest : Suggest a different item to the customer (Lose energy)
From Trade : You can buy the requested equipment from the market but can cost more then the sale
With these factors now you run into points such as...
I can't craft what he wants but I can make the next best thing which will lose energy but if I discount it then I make a profit of energy and still make some gold.
You also can buy equipment racks that increase how much energy you get from selling those types of equipment on the rack...
So if the customer wanted a Sledgehammer and you only could make him a Maul but you also have a Mace equipment rack then you can Surcharge the Maul and still make a profit of energy or lose no energy at all with the customer and you make a great profit!
Important bit "Energy" Ah that sounds like a restriction most facebook games have that control how long you get to play so you are forced either to wait hours or pay with real money to continue. NO! It doesn't work that way here.
You have several factors I just covered here that will allow you to always have energy! If you just sell the items the customer wants you lose and gain no energy and crafting COSTS NO ENERGY!

You actually got to investigate with Frank and Joe Hardy, as well as Charleena Purcell from Shadow Ranch, Tino Balducci who is a phone buddy in a later game, and learn about western history, gemstones, dolls, dancing, ghosts...everything interesting in a ND game, this one has.
It is just a perfect balance of a lot of different elements, and is known as one of the best classic Nandy Drew games of all time. I replayed it as an adult and it wasn't very challenging (like Blackmoore Manor, an older and much more difficult game), but it wasn't super easy either (like Kapu Cave). It's perfect and I want to replay it yet again. Definitely worth the price Steam has it for.

This turned out alot longer than what I thought.
All things considered, this particular game in the franchise was a bit of a disappointment, The Curse of Blackmoor Manor and The Secret of Shadow Ranch were far better games than this one in my opinion.  For starters the game is too short with too few locations to explore.  There isn’t even a direct Blue Moon Canyon area of the game either.  It took me only about 4 hours to beat it, (with minor help with a guide on occasional puzzles I admit). For most of the game you are just stuck on a train moving through narrow corridors without really being able to enjoy the highlights of riding a train, such as looking out the windows at the surroundings, being in the main engine room, maybe even driving the train, blowing the whistle, etc.  Not to mention there is always an annoying cut scene when changing cars that can’t be skipped, which for stepping out on the outside of the train and viewing the surroundings you see remarkably nothing!  You never even see the train from the outside!  Unless you count a bad drawing of the town map.  Does the train look the way it does in game as it does on the cover, I don’t know, do you?  Besides the train, there are only two other small locations on a map that you visit, with neither being very big or interesting.
The story is also rather stale with yet another mysterious buried treasure with a random ghost thrown in that you never see or hear about again after seeing ONCE.  You spend most of the game repairing a weird device that just shines a beam at the point of the treasure, and in doing so you use priceless gemstones that end up probably being worth more than the “treasure” at the end (spoiler: huge letdown).  Another let down in game is that there are too many pointless dates and irrelevant names of deceased people thrown at you, providing you with all kinds of confusing information that for the most part you don’t even need.  Also, things in this game just don’t feel at all consistent and are often random regarding events or objective.  Even at the end you still don’t entirely know what happened to the original owner prior to death, his wife, or his engineer as it isn’t really explained.
As for the gameplay, most of the puzzles are challenging, but possible and often rewarding so long as you take time and think things through, (and consult a guide when you can’t).  Most of the art is impressive enough, and the character animations are remarkably better than in the earlier games.  The music is original and has a theme I can only describe as adventurous.  Sounds are good and I didn’t encounter any technical issues throughout the game.  So for the base of the game itself, it was pretty solid.  That is before encountering the biggest problem with the game in my opinion, which is that most of the characters are unintentionally incredibly annoying, with most of them offering little to nothing in the story.  In all of the Nancy Drew games you always do essentially all the work with some help or guidance being offered from the other characters, however, in this game they just drone on and on about pointless, irrelevant information which you are forced to listen to in order to progress through the game.
The only real enjoyable characters were the Hardy Boys, with everyone else being too annoying, rude, pretentious, or just plain out of place.  Frank and Joe Hardy being included in this game was a neat and reasonable cross-over situation, which was certainly nostalgic for those of us that have grown up reading the Hardy Boys, Nancy Drew, and even the Boxcar Children mystery books.  However, I feel that the Hardy Boys were not used nearly as much as they should have been or were used in the right way.  For example, one of the brothers (your choice) gets stuck as a burger cook job for the sole purpose of ease dropping on a conversation about the treasure.  At this part, your just making sandwiches while yet again listening to pointless characters rattle on about useless information.  The Hardy Boys do offer some information and real help unlike the other characters, but that’s about it.  You don’t travel together in a trio or really do anything together except for talking at a table.
In conclusion, I honestly understand what the developers were going for here, and it hurts me so much because this had the makings to be such a good game.  Picture a mystery adventure to find out what caused the mysterious deaths of the company on a train over a century ago as you venture through the Midwest on an exciting 18th century adventure on that same train!  Hop on board a real 18th century locomotive and explore a part of the country foreign to so many on the ride of a life time to search for a lost diamond mine!  Uncover ancient areas of great conflict between Westerners and Native Americans.  Explore ancient settlements and once great gold boom towns gone to ruin.  Gather Clues from non-annoying characters while journeying through hidden mines for the ultimate treasure!
This…is not what you get in this game at all.
So unless you’re a diehard Nancy Drew fan, or mystery fanatic, I wouldn’t recommend this particular game.

Blood Omen 2 is an action-adventure game where you play a vampire named Kain who's awaken a few hundreds years after the event of the first Blood Omen. Vampires are slowly being erased from the world by their ennemies. Kain will then have to join a group of resisting vampire...
The gameplay is simple. You can attack/block/grab. After killing someone, you can drink his blood to restore HP and gain EXP. On "leveling up", your maximum HP goes up which force you to drink the blood of EVERYONE you see. The drinking is nice but after a thousand time, you'll grow tired of its animation. After killing boss, you also gain special abilities to jump huge gaps, hit harder,  etc. Overall, it all get pretty redundant.
The game also has some puzzle to resolve. However, most of them just break the momentum without being very interesting nor difficult.
Despite those flaws, the game is still interesting. If most secondary characters don't stand out much, the main character, Kain is intriguing and charismatic enough to keep your interest.
However, it's not a game you'll revisit once passed since the gameplay gets repetitive. Anyway, it's a game that should keep you occupied for about 18 hours.
I won't talk much about the visuals. They are good enough considering the age of the game (2002). They won't "burn" your eyes.
Personnal Enjoyment : 7.5/10

Absolver is the buggiest piece of mess I ever played. If you were to combat any AI in game while on a slope, they would teleport all over the damn place, go out of bounds, go back to spawn point heal themselves up and fight you again. In this game you can't even heal a significant amount and the tutorial is terrible and doesn't explain any of the combat mechanics.

Multiplatform mid-core crafting game with an elegant design, and a deceptive simplicity that gives way to deeper (and surprising) complexity: items can have mods that affect PVP combat, heroes also have skills that can affect it.
No energy bar to limit how long you play, and the presence of convenience microtransactions is offset by how many free gems you are able to earn by playing. I haven't purchased any gems or packs yet but I estimate having earned about 1500 gems from quests, delivery requests, and City Raid rewards. I have earned maybe another 500 gems from selling freely obtained items on the market; where one is able to buy and sell the items linked to paid-only blueprints, even if you cannot craft it.
I like that this is a game that I can switch to in the background now and then, as much as also be able to zone out and do stuff constantly. Yes, crafting timers are starting to get longer (I am at lvl 31), but one can still have hundreds of inventory to actively sell. It reminds me of a simplified version of EVE Online's trade, minus the schlepping and the pirates blowing you up. Specialize in crafting a few lines of gear, or try to master them all. I think there are over 400 craftable items in-game at the moment.
I do wish there were more customization options for the shop: perhaps walls, or different skins for the structure, or weather and seasonal changes for the surrounding. There could be elements of creative building to design what the shop looks like on the outside as a toggled layer, which would make it more entertaining to visit friends or show off one's own shop. There are at least a fair amount of decorative items purchasable with the free currency, and the size limitation is intentional to make you choose which furniture to place.
Gem-bought decorative items are plenty, but I choose to save up the gems I get freely for convenience features such as upgrading crafting slots to automatically craft pre-requisite items. There could also be some more levels of interactivity with fellow city members, and I would love to see some sort of NPC dungeons or hero-based monster defense game which would encourage different lineups and gear choices. Raid enemies that take hero power into account would also be interesting...
In short, Shop Heroes is a nicely designed shop and crafting sim that has some hidden depth, and relaxing gameplay. It scratches the distraction itch while allowing you to be frequently tabbed or AFK, and has a lot of potential to become even more "mid-core" and compelling. For all of the posts saying that mobile games should not be on Steam... save us the console-war style elitism. Mobile has come a long way, and it's about time there were more cross-platform games that allow you to chill out with a big screen view or quickly make some progress on the go. This game won't be for everyone, but it's worth giving a go if you like games like Recettear and ignore the whining about the presence of a very fair revenue model existing in a free game.

Choices define the way you end the game and the story, so you can beat the game multiple times in different ways. For example, I focused my gameplay in the way of the Rangers, got 100 reputation with them, but since it is a neutral faction, by the end of the game the world did not change much.
Soundtrack is good and sound effects are normal for and RPG game. It suits the sort of Magical Medievel environment and helps you getting in the theme.
Overall, I recommend the game, especially for RPGs fan. It's an 8/10
